The game starts off with you controlling a specific character.  It doesn't take long before you can toggle between characters and head off into the Zed filled abyss.  You do have to earn the trust of any character before you can play as that character.  There's enough story to keep a game like this moving with purpose, yet the game is built to allow you choose not to pursue the storyline.  Randomly generated missions can keep you entertained, while you move your nomadic tribe around to different temporary homes (main base).  Only a limited number of buildings can be converted to be your main base.  Very briefly let me say - this is not a lone wolf style game.  You may go off and handle certain things "on your own", but this game is intended for you play as part of a surviving, nomadic group.
You can upgrade your main base to increase your defensive posture against incoming Zed hordes.  Maybe you want to increase your storage capacity so you can hold more food, medicine, ammo, or construction materials.  Perhaps you want to integrate a workshop to build home made weapon attachments...and even allow for repairs to the limited number of vehicles that exist in game.  There are enough options to warrant multiple playthroughs, and there are enough NPCs with special skills that you can recruit along the way to help you towards whatever goal you have in mind for your base.
You may have limited options when choosing to move your main base, but those options broaden when you start considering which buildings you wish to use for an outpost.  Outposts add a powerful advantage to your surviving group (no...you don't get Daryl).  Outposts allow you to build mines\traps.  You don't actually physically walk around and setup the traps.  Instead you spend some Influence and hit a button.  And...WHAMO!  The next time a horde is tracking through the nearby area.  BOOM.  A very nice feature to have.
Influence is a type of in game currency that is earned through actions that positively benefit your group.  It can degrade over time if left unused.  The Influence system works for the game very well.  It is very fun to break into homes, clear out Zeds, and take all the supplies back to base.  And when you deposit the extra supplies into your base's stash you gain Influence.  The developers did well to make sure earning Influence feels fun!
Fighting Zeds is fun, particularly melee.  Gunplay can be effective, but aim for the head and use a suppressor to reduce the chances of attracting more Zeds due to the noise.  Targeting can be a challenge.  Just because you've lined up the targeting reticule does not mean you are going to hit that exact spot.  Through the building of your character, unlocking special moves & improving gun play accuracy can make encounters very satisfying.  Fighting can quickly drain your stamina.  Without stamina you cannot run and you cannot effectively fight.  You can increase your stamina cap over time.  You can also increase your proficiency with melee combat, which will assist by making your stamina decrease at a slower rate when in combat.  Still...I find it mildly annoying at the small amount of fighting that can generally be handled at any given time.  The developers would tend to agree, as they have worked in a system where you can spend Influence and ask a fellow survivor (who trusts you) to accompany you on missions.  THIS IS VERY USEFUL!

I have not yet played the Breakdown DLC.  I have not completed the game's storyline.  I recommend this game to those who can handle mature dialog, blood, and violence.  Parents, make sure you check out some YouTube footage before letting your child play this game.

Hands down one of my favorite games.
Why, you ask?  The graphics are now dated, some the weapon and character models are lame, and a number of the game systems (looking at you, pawn alignment and NPC approval ratings) are arcane at best and flat-out bad at worst.
So why the love?
Combat:
This game has some of the most nuanced and reactive combat of any PC game out there.  Remember how Skyrim is such a great game for the freedom and exploration it provides, but the combat is a huge letdown?  Well, sacrifice some of that freedom and exploration (there is still a LOT to explore here), and add in some of the combat that makes games like Bayonetta and Dark Souls so enjoyable.
Dragon fights are seriously epic, giant monsters feel gigantic, and the night-time mechanic can make even normal goblin and wolf fights a challenge.  There's a reason medieval peoples were so afraid of the dark.
This game is far more forgiving than Dank Souls, mind you.  There is an optional Hard Mode, but even that can be outleveled for all but the strongest of enemies.  Add in the right Augments and Bitterblack armor, and you can make an Arisen that's nigh-immortal.  But you don't have to.
This game has a decently sized modding community out there on Nexus, and some of my favorite mods are the ones that drastically raise the amount of XP to level.  The intent of those mods is to prevent you from out-leveling content and they allow you to seek out far more varied challenges.  So much of the base game is improved when you haven't out-leveled the fights.
One of my favorite things to do is take a low-level party and try to sweep Southern Gransys of all Hobs and Gobs.  While barely worth mentioning if using normal XP tables, this is not an easy task when you're party is level 6ish.  The fact that this is possible to do (if you play smart), shows how good this game truly is once the focus is shifted to player skill instead of power-leveling.  I would encourage you try an XP mod out for a full new game if you're getting tired of grinding for gear or speed running the end bosses.
Pawns:
Kind of a mixed bag here.  The idea is really neat and contains a rather huge level of customization for your pawn.  It's a lot of fun to dive into a fight with up to three other NPCs (your pawn and two hired pawns).  The problems come from the pawn AI system.  The pawn alignment system is not well-explained, can change mid-fight based on your actions, and can turn a pawn from being combat-effective into a drooling XP leech.
Add in the fact that there are many skills and class mechanics that pawn AI simply cannot use well, and you have to go through a LOT of testing and game forums to figure out a decent pawn build.  This could have been so much simpler and a lot more fun.  Can your pawn be trained and tweaked into one of the deadliest waifus/husbandos in gaming?  Yes.  Can you tear all your hair out trying to GET them to that point?  Yes.  Very much yes.
Story:
Again bit of a mixed bag.  Part of me can't help thinking that certain parts were lost in translation, much in the same way subtitles for Princess Mononoke are far more eloquent and relevant than the English dub.  The story is pretty standard fantasy fair, with a distinctly Japanese twist to it.  I never felt as invested as I did in Mass Effect 2 or The Last Of Us.
The story here is really just a mildly-interesting propulsion to leaving the safety of town.  It's not why you play this game; it's merely the impetus to getting you into some of the best combat in any fantasy game made to date.
The entire affection system which drives much of the story is extremely opaque, leaving you guessing as to where each person lies in how they perceive you.
Are they maxed?  Are they just at basic threshold for minor affection?  The game's method of relaying this info to you is often so subtle as to be indistinguishable, leaving you clueless a lot of the time.  The only way to be certain is to give your target NPC massive amounts of crap they like and simply drown them in items.  This ambiguity of hidden metrics is the game's approach to a number of systems, and remains one of its weakest points.
So while not without its flaws, this game is still a blemished beauty.  What it does wrong can be frustrating, but what it does right it does right better than almost any other game out there.  It's a genuine shame we aren't likely to see a Dragon's Dogma Online over here in the West, as DD:DA has the bone structure of a truly great MMORPG.
TL;DR:  Play other games for story; play Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen to "Git ur haxx 0n" in a large sandbox with some of the best open-world and dungeon combat out there.

Life forge is a charming game with a strong throwback to old rpgs, like runescape, and others that you just can't quite remember the name of. The game has it's bugs, of course, being so new to the steam life, but the fact it's an online game with its own servers built by indie developers who are frequently active, updating, patching, and working towards a better game? Not to mention the surprisingly great community and the fact that it has its own discord which admins are often watching and responding to? It's a feat all its own.
As for the game itself, it is a bit of a grind. Gaining exp for things like crafting and gathering make it worth it, and you can make the grind faster by making better weapons. The game feels simple, and the trio of choices for advancement leave plenty of room for unique builds, especially since you can allocate stats and use any weapon you like, and there's a number of cross-class spells to buy. Having only three base classes in the beginning that split into a total of 9 down the road is a good move, leaving things a little easier to choose from in the beginning.
Obviously the game still needs work. But the admins are always patching, and fixing things. Always active, always listening. It's what a community loves, to feel like they can influence the game in some way with their suggestions, and that the dev's are listening. I fully support and look forward to what it becomes in the future.

Right now, starbound is king of the hill amongst 2d sandbox games.
Without using mods, it offers 18 main biomes to explore, plus several other mini biomes, and planets can contain more than one biome at a time. To progress in the story, you will be exploring most of them.
The building tool can place multiple blocks at a time, and at a distance, the placing distance can be increased by upgrading the building tool, this makes it quite easy to build very big structures: In several other games of the same cathegory, building can give you headaches due to slow placing speed and low placing distance. Plus, this game contains a fully featured colony system wich allows you to choose what kind of colonists will be inhabiting your towns just by choosing the furniture inside rooms. And Plus again, scanning furniture occuring in randomly generated npc villages around the universe allows you to replicate said furniture in your 3d printer, allowing you even more customization in your colonies. I passed days building my main city.
There is nothing that special to combat, you will be shooting into enemies or getting close to get a hit with your sword trying to avoid getting punched yourself. Several weapons to choose from, some of wich can be crafted, but for the most part you'll be using randomly generated weapons found scattered in the worlds you explore. Daggers, swords, longswords, shields, guns, assault rifles, sniper rifles, shotguns, bows and special unique weapons like boomerangs or tentacle launchers are some of the weapons you will find about. Bosses offer a more variegated challenge, with patterns of attacks that need to be memorized, and they are generally far more lethal than the monsters you find normally.
There is a story with some lore into it, but I did not care much about it. It's really just an excuse to have you explore around.
This all can be further improved with the vast selection of mods available for download. Some of these can extend the game quite a lot.
As for the negative side, game suffers from stuttering expecially if you are traveling about at very fast speed. In multiplayers, world sections failing to load are commonplace. This can be made a lot worse if you carelessy install too many mods- but that will be your fault.
Little else to say. It's worth a buy if you like the genre.

However, if you buy this game then you should be aware that you're buying any
and therefore, as of patch #45, there is several bugs in the game on which the developers are actively working. Please don't buy this game YET if you're not comfortable with playing a game under development.
Also see Entrada's "State of the Game 2016" update which will give you an idea of the current state of this game and the development plans for 2017 -
One aspect important to be aware of is that Miscreated aims to be a "hardcore survival game". Please don't expect features such as name tags, friend indicators, mini-map or other HUD items or gadgets on which you couldn't rely in real life. The game presents itself with a very minimalistic HUD, you actually have to find a map and you'll be able to communicate with others or get your GPS coordinates once you found a radio. Storage is also rather limited as is your carrying weight.
Overall MC is a game you actually have to learn in order to survive and that goes from learning which food to carry / stock to which caliber of weapon(s) you want all the way to calculating your loadout weight and available storage for your tasks at hand. Oh yeah, and don't get to attached to your stuff, if you get made then your chances are that you'll get killed as well.
Miscreated is, at this stage, a game for players who love this genre of games, who are looking for a challenge (survival wise, PvP wise or "glitch wise"), who can deal with early-access games and bugs occurring between patches (or being put on the backfire for a while)  and who might perhaps want to contribute to the games future with decent bug reports and feature suggestions rather than rants.
If you're looking for a polished up, glitch free and FPS like game, then MC isn't for you. At least not at this stage and it might never be.
Also check system requirements BEFORE you buy, the game runs on 64-bit systems ONLY which is often overlooked by players.
I will add to my review throughout the next updates. At this point I'm giving the game 8/10.

A solid Total War title, and the one I usually go to when I'm not feeling Shogun 2.
Pros
-Solid campaign map with lots of factions to start from, each with unique objectives. The six (more with DLC) groups of factions feel distinct enough to give variety without necessarily becoming burdomsome for doing so.
-Aethetically great, lots of tight design choices that make the game feel very cohesive in tone and distinct in setting.
-Awesome time period for the main campaign, set between 395-450 AD. History buffs have a lot to look over, as is fitting for a Total War title.
-The in-battle controls and interface are smooth and accessible. New players of the series should find maneuvering formations to be a fairly easy process to learn.
-The Horde mechanic is a fun and interesting addition to the Total War system, giving certain factions (ex. Goths, Huns, etc) a thematically appropriate approach to gameplay.
Cons
-Diplomacy can be...mixed, as is somewhat customary for a Total War title. The AI is all over the place with how/when it will accept certain trades/offers. That said, the system still offers a good deal of depth without becoming burdonsome or killing the pace.
-As touted a feature as the Hordes are, it becomes very difficult to stay in that gamestyle as the game goes on past a certain point. The loss of an army is effectively an entire city of infrastructure, and when multiple stacks of enemy armies become an issue late game it can be almost tedious to deal with. Smart playing can counter this, of course, but I was a little disappointed that I never really felt like the screaming death I should have. Admittedly, this may be more of a personal issue, your own gameplay style may affect this.
-Naval battles are a thing. I personally have never been a fan of Total War naval battles but this is more opinion based than hard fact, so take it as you will.
On the whole, a solid title even without DLC. Total War titles go on sale frequently, and if you have the means, I highly recommend it.

Blacklist is, in essence, an improved Conviction, with a touch of Chaos Theory, and a much simpler version of MGS Peace Walker's Mother Base system thrown in a blender. All of that with the multiplayer Spies Vs Mercs mode that debuted in Pandora Tomorrow. In campaign, you will do all of your prep aboard the Palidin, a large plane that serves as your headquarters and where you access missions and upgrades. You can upgrade weapons, your suit, gadgets, goggles, and even the plane itself with currency you earn by playing the game. Players that hated how conviction focused more on combat than stealth will rejoice that, much like in the early games, you can complete most missions without killing, or even interacting with enemies at all. In fact, the game has a scoring system that values stealth above combat. Also, the night vision goggles are back, with the sonar mode available as an upgrade (I hated using the Sonar in coviction, but I think it works much better here, especially after a few upgrades). Also, the game handles being in shadows (which caused you to play most of Conviction in black and white) in a simple and elegant way. The lights on your suit simply flare up, telling you that you are more hidden. If you liked Coviction, you will like this one too. If you are a hardcore fan of the gameplay in Chaos theory, I would say you should seriously consider blacklist. In my opinion, it is one of the best stealth-action games I've played.

Compared to the original splinter cell, or the later ones like Chaos Theory, I feel that blacklist falls very short... The snazzy black & white night vision goggles that were a staple of the series are replaced with green and work poorly. Actually, the game is so bright that I never needed to even use them, although they didn't actually particularly help when I did since it makes everything look terrible. In the originals, I rarely stopped using my goggles, they were part of what made Sam such a well-equipped badass.
In addition, this is a standard crappy Ubisoft port - no save games, wonky controls, an unforgiving checkpoint system that rarely saves, and of course Ironside is no longer voicing Sam Fisher. Ultimately it doesn't have the charm or appeal of the old splinter cell games. Instead of trying to "ghost" missions by never leaving a trace, the irritating checkpoint system will end up forcing you to memorize quick paths and kill as many as possible so a simple mistake/control issue doesn't send you back to the beginning of the level.

I have loved this game since the day it came out and have gone back to it more times than I can count. It has the perfect amount of difficulty where you can still complete things and get an overwhelming sense of accomplishment for doing so.

's greatest accomplishment is its fluid and responsive combat system. It's incredibly fast paced and highly energetic but the one issue I have is the narrow 'field of view' which can obfuscate larger groups of enemies. The game soon becomes very easy to progress through, especially as more of the overpowering skills are unlocked. The simplistic movement system can be extremely cumbersome, particularly with scaling the environment, as I'd often find myself bumping into walls rather than climbing them, or descending ledges in a tardy fashion while I'm trying to quickly escape a group of enemies.
I found that I would often fail missions due to how the game would behave in a bizarre fashion. One example is where I would accidentally exit the quest area due to how the combat system magnetically locks onto enemies and throws my character's body a few dozen feet towards them, outside the quest radius. It would start to be especially dumb when the game decides to have my character land in front of an enemy, during mandatory stealth missions, rather than onto the wall or ledge near them, causing me to immediately fail the mission. There's also one mission in particular where I'm required to draw out a Warchief by killing 20 enemies in 2 minutes. For some reason, in this strange parallel universe I've suddenly entered, no one wants to confront me so I'm left searching for enemies to slaughter and have failed this mission a number of times now. I feel like I'm going insane. What I initially considered a fun game is now frustratingly tedious and soulless.
In essence,
is pretty on the surface but rotten at its core. It is an unremarkable and miserable experience that does nothing to improve on the modern 'Action RPG' formula that I love to play. It's a shame because it's obvious that the developers put a lot of effort into the lore of this game but
would fade into obscurity if it weren't connected to the familiar
franchise. It is undeserving of a sequel.

I really wish there was a maybe button in Steam right now. The game treads the line between really fun and frustrating. The game is really fun, if you care for the asthetics. There are a lot of problems though.
Maps are littered with little obstacles that halt movement (everything but walls really need to be walkable). This is usually just frustrating, but when you're fighting aggro mobs it will get you killed regularly.
Also, the UI is very very bad. I understand the game is in Alpha, and usually the UI is rudamentary (crafting very much so), so I expect that to change in the future.
Another huge issue is class imbalance. Magi are incredibly underpowered in damage output, wear the lightest armor, and have to stand still to cast. They aren't class cannons, they are just glass. On PvP maps you'll get killed by invisible people in 1 shot. You'd be lucky to even get 1 cast off just to do minor damage before you die and watch them loot you (even if you're higher level). Normally, you'd assume you can just avoid all PvP then, but at a certain point the game soft forces you to level in a PvP zone.
The last issue is there is no controller support. I wouldn't recommend the game at all if you ultimately had to use WASD, Space and Ctrl for everything. I highly suggest using a keyboard remapper to use a gamepad, since the game functions far better with a gamepad. They really need to get on this, as I see plenty of players quit immediately over this issue.
So, basically, it's a very fun game, but very frustrating due to it's early development and some asthetic and balance issues.

Hands down one of my favorite games.
Why, you ask?  The graphics are now dated, some the weapon and character models are lame, and a number of the game systems (looking at you, pawn alignment and NPC approval ratings) are arcane at best and flat-out bad at worst.
So why the love?
Combat:
This game has some of the most nuanced and reactive combat of any PC game out there.  Remember how Skyrim is such a great game for the freedom and exploration it provides, but the combat is a huge letdown?  Well, sacrifice some of that freedom and exploration (there is still a LOT to explore here), and add in some of the combat that makes games like Bayonetta and Dark Souls so enjoyable.
Dragon fights are seriously epic, giant monsters feel gigantic, and the night-time mechanic can make even normal goblin and wolf fights a challenge.  There's a reason medieval peoples were so afraid of the dark.
This game is far more forgiving than Dank Souls, mind you.  There is an optional Hard Mode, but even that can be outleveled for all but the strongest of enemies.  Add in the right Augments and Bitterblack armor, and you can make an Arisen that's nigh-immortal.  But you don't have to.
This game has a decently sized modding community out there on Nexus, and some of my favorite mods are the ones that drastically raise the amount of XP to level.  The intent of those mods is to prevent you from out-leveling content and they allow you to seek out far more varied challenges.  So much of the base game is improved when you haven't out-leveled the fights.
One of my favorite things to do is take a low-level party and try to sweep Southern Gransys of all Hobs and Gobs.  While barely worth mentioning if using normal XP tables, this is not an easy task when you're party is level 6ish.  The fact that this is possible to do (if you play smart), shows how good this game truly is once the focus is shifted to player skill instead of power-leveling.  I would encourage you try an XP mod out for a full new game if you're getting tired of grinding for gear or speed running the end bosses.
Pawns:
Kind of a mixed bag here.  The idea is really neat and contains a rather huge level of customization for your pawn.  It's a lot of fun to dive into a fight with up to three other NPCs (your pawn and two hired pawns).  The problems come from the pawn AI system.  The pawn alignment system is not well-explained, can change mid-fight based on your actions, and can turn a pawn from being combat-effective into a drooling XP leech.
Add in the fact that there are many skills and class mechanics that pawn AI simply cannot use well, and you have to go through a LOT of testing and game forums to figure out a decent pawn build.  This could have been so much simpler and a lot more fun.  Can your pawn be trained and tweaked into one of the deadliest waifus/husbandos in gaming?  Yes.  Can you tear all your hair out trying to GET them to that point?  Yes.  Very much yes.
Story:
Again bit of a mixed bag.  Part of me can't help thinking that certain parts were lost in translation, much in the same way subtitles for Princess Mononoke are far more eloquent and relevant than the English dub.  The story is pretty standard fantasy fair, with a distinctly Japanese twist to it.  I never felt as invested as I did in Mass Effect 2 or The Last Of Us.
The story here is really just a mildly-interesting propulsion to leaving the safety of town.  It's not why you play this game; it's merely the impetus to getting you into some of the best combat in any fantasy game made to date.
The entire affection system which drives much of the story is extremely opaque, leaving you guessing as to where each person lies in how they perceive you.
Are they maxed?  Are they just at basic threshold for minor affection?  The game's method of relaying this info to you is often so subtle as to be indistinguishable, leaving you clueless a lot of the time.  The only way to be certain is to give your target NPC massive amounts of crap they like and simply drown them in items.  This ambiguity of hidden metrics is the game's approach to a number of systems, and remains one of its weakest points.
So while not without its flaws, this game is still a blemished beauty.  What it does wrong can be frustrating, but what it does right it does right better than almost any other game out there.  It's a genuine shame we aren't likely to see a Dragon's Dogma Online over here in the West, as DD:DA has the bone structure of a truly great MMORPG.
TL;DR:  Play other games for story; play Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen to "Git ur haxx 0n" in a large sandbox with some of the best open-world and dungeon combat out there.
I have played for 180+ hours, and have gotten all of the achievements, but none of it felt like grinding. (Except for the BB 3 armor, that stuff is extremely hard to get.)
I accidentally married the court jester.

This is a recommend with reservations.  DDDA has some interesting concepts that I had not experienced in other games, but has its share of annoyances and bores.
The pawn system allows you to create an NPC  companion for your game.  Your pawn can be summoned by other players for help, and you can summon 2 pawns that other players have created.  So its you + 3 pawns in your party.  That made for some interesting parties, and as you level up you'll have to look for higher level pawns, and pawns with just the right skills to complement your party.
The combat is unique and feels much more like an action game than a traditional 3rd person RPG.  Hitting different enemy body parts will cause them to change their combat strategies, or drop a weapon, and its great fun to climb on or grab enemies.  At least for the first few encounters.  Pawns will complement your skills, and at times, combat does feel like a team effort.  Unfortunately it gets repetitive fairly quickly.
As with most RPG's, your level vs. the monster's level is probably the most important statistic.  That means sometimes combat is ridiculously easy, and sometimes you're going to die over and over before deciding to leave that area and come back later.  I'm ok with that, but difficulty spikes without warning are very frustrating.
It claims to be an open world, which is true, but I was very disappointed once I realized that what you see in the first 60 minutes of the game is really all there is.  The landscape does not change much as you progress, and you end up treading the same paths over and over.  Once most of the map was discovered, it turns out the world is not very big at all.  Its just very slow traveling.
Which brings me to one of the biggest nuissances in any game: weight and inventory.  You will need to collect  a lot of materials and items, and you will quickly become overburdened.  This means slow running, and stopping to catch your breath due to lack of stamina.  Want to refill your stamina?  You'll have to open the clunkiest inventory system, mouse over each item until you find something that works, and then exit the menu.  During combat you'll need health pots or perhaps a cure for a debilitation.  Same thing-- hit up your menu, look around for a handful of cures, and continue on.  So you have this fantastic action-style combat system that is constantly interrupted when you have to essentially pause the game to heal yourself.  Of course you can offload all that crap to one of the pawns, but the transfer system is very clunky.  You're going to spend a lot of time in your inventory menus and that's just not a fun way to spend game time.
After 20-30 hours I started getting bored and just wanted to be done.  I couldn't be bothered with the included DLC or even doing the "post game" which just sounds like more items to collect.  If you're a "best in slot" type of person, you might like it.  I'm glad I played, but there are much better games to play or replay.  Its worth playing just to check out some innovative ideas (pawns, combat) but I'd recommend burning through the main quest without getting sidetracked.  If you really like it after that, this game can keep you occupied for many many more  hours.

This is a relatively solid action RPG with deeper-than-average combat. But the writing and the story are so awful that I can't recommend the game.
The dialogue consists of very stilted Olde English language that grated on my nerves within the first hour. As an added bonus, your pawns (NPC allies that follow you everywhere) constantly spout more of this poorly written dialogue as you run around. Perhaps the archaic language fits better in Japanese and this is just a localization problem. Either way, it annoyed me from beginning to end.
And its not like the bad writing brings down an otherwise interesting story. The plot of the game is paper thin and cliche. I plodded through the game's missions solely to check them off a list rather than to learn more about the story or the lore of the world.
If you're willing to completely ignore all the dialogue and story, then you might enjoy Dragon's Dogma. The combat superficially resembles Dark Souls, with enemies having relatively predictable sets of attacks. But at least for my character (fighter --> mystic knight), 99% of the combat boiled down to spamming light attack and a charge ability. There's potential for more depth, but the game doesn't explain its mechanics very well and I didn't have a hard time beating the game without branching out.
Finally, the side quest system is kind of bad. 90% of the side quests are one of the following: 1) fetch quests; 2) kill 10 boars; or 3) escort an NPC with lousy AI and pathfinding. They're just pointless padding.
I'd give the game a 6/10. Not terrible, but not worth playing given the plethora of better made games out there.

If you are saying that this was the high point in all of the Splinter Cell games, you are wrong, sorry to say, the best game(s) of the series to me had to be Chaos Theory, and Double Agent, but I loved Chaos Theory more.
PROS:
Back to stealth (Somewhat): It may not be the best stealth it was years and years ago but it was still nice to see that they actually brought stealth back into the game which surprised me, after annoying Conviction I figured they did what Dead Space, Resident Evil, and FEAR had done to their series.
Multiple ways to do a mission: There are 3 ways to do a mission, assault, panther, or Ghost, obviously me being the total stealth nerd I am I did Ghost, which was really fun through most of the parts.  This means you don't get ghost "Points" for killing, only for Knocking Out the enemy targets, Panther points are for killing stealthy, and Assault is just for gunning down everyone who gets in the way on alert.
Upgrade gear, and the plane: You can buy and upgrade Sam's gear as you go with money you get from missions, which was really cool that you could actually pick the gear you wanted, although most of the gear isn't very useful when it comes to stealth, you'll end up getting a few pieces of clothing for stealth and then you will pretty much have everything you need.  You can also upgrade the plane to give you more things in the field, like health, items show up on the map, etc.
Several missions from old characters: With Sam, Grimmsdottr, and others, even that guy from Conviction that was supposed to kill Sam's daughter you end up capturing him and get missions from him, which is weird but honestly, that guy is pretty cool minus the fact he tried to kill my Daughter.  You get money from the missions they give, which means upgradeable stuff.
Better gear: You get some useful gear, like a crossbow that shoots knock out gas, very useful for Ghost style play I must say, I pretty much used this thing the entire game, I only used the guns for lights and that was it actually, I only killed if it was seriously necessary, and even then I tried to knock out a person.
More points for not killing: If you go through a area without killing/knocking out someone or a group of people you get more points for leaving them alive, which is nice for the ghost side because I honestly try to keep as many people alive as I can, it just seems better that way.
CONS:
Still acts like Conviction: Conviction was one of my most uninteresting games because it went from stealth to basically pure assault with stealth mixed in, and it kind of killed off the series for me, and they still implemented it in the game, why couldn't they have tried to be more like Chaos Theory or Double Agent, you know, when the stealth was actually stealthy.
No sound/Shadow Meter: This was a huge dissapointment to me, I heard they went back to stealth and I was like "Oh they are finally going back to their roots!" Then I played it and that went down the toilet, the only way to tell you are in the dark is the lights on your suit light up, that's it, I can't tell if i'm completely hidden regardless of how dark it is or if i'm just slightly hidden and still obvious, not to mention not having a sound meter f$%ks up most of the game, basically there isn't a way to walk slower or faster when crouched, you just walk and that's it, and you get noticed half the time because of that fact, you basically just have to mash the melee button when you are near a guy because he will end up turning around and seeing you.
Brutes: F*%k these guys, if they notice you and turn to the side you can't knock them out cause you can only do it from behind or above, and when they are in the open you are basically going to have to get behind them or try to go around, but since you can't really tell how much sound you are making you are basically going to end up running past them or "Attempting" to knock them out, and the knock out gas doesn't work cause they have masks on, I ended up hating these guys the entire game.
No killing missions: I'm all for not killing enemies in missions, but that one Cuban camp was just rediculous, I was RIGHT near the end and there was a dog, I figured, I would just kill it cause I ran out of ammo for my crossbows Knock Out gas, I shot it, I lost, because it counted as a "Soldier" are the people at Ubisoft Imbred or something? Dogs are easier to replace than the actual soldiers are for gods sake.
Not much interesting gear: You end up finding the few pieces of gear that do the best in a tactical way (Ghost, Panther, Assault.) and then never try anything else, that's it, you find the things that do well and the other stuff can go f$#k itself because you know that it won't do as well as the stuff you have already.
Never used sticky cameras: I used to use these all the time in other games, I never touched them once, I think it's because once I got the upgraded goggles to see through walls everything involving a camera was useless to me, I never touched the cameras or anything else, which is kind of sad since I used them all the time in the other games.
Characters: Most of the characters I sadly didn't care about, I cared about a few like Briggs and Koban, but the rest I didn't realy care for.  Not even Grimm who's been in the game since the very beginning, that's kind of sad that I end up caring about the guy that tried to kill my daughter and my partner more than the person who's been in the game from the beginning.
WHAT I THINK: After playing through the whole game I didn't think of it like a good stealth game, it was fun and had stealth in it, but I didn't like it as much as I had with the other games, before, probably because I was expecting them to go back to the way they had originally but I was kind of dissapointed with the fact they went with Conviction more. Then again this is Ubisoft we are talking about, they can't do much right honestly, did you SEE Watch_Dogs?  Score? Eh...i'm stuck between a 6-7/10 it was fun, but I didn't get as much feeling as I had with other games, it still acted like Convcition too much than it had with it's predecessors, I say get it on a sale.

A surprisingly decent 3rd person survival game with a professional narrative.  Published by a relatively new independant studio named Undead Labs, I didn't expect much going into it, however found myself pleasantly surprised by how polished the game is.
Some people compare this to DayZ in some respect, and personally I disagree, there is only a single-player mode (though co-op is being looked at), which takes away the entire pvp concept that DayZ focuses on.
With that aside, the gameplay is actually a lot more polished than the current DayZ mod, zombie animations and behaviour are a step up from the survival zombie mod, melee combat mechanics are simple yet complex enough that it takes more than simply mashing the attack button repeatedly, and the overall world is highly detailed albeit a tad small for my taste, it certainly would have been much more interesting with more varied locales to explore.  But I suppose they had been limited by the narrative which takes place behind the scenes (and yes that means there is an actual main storyline.)
Both games have their merits, but if you happen to be looking for an immersive and decent zombie action game without the multiplayer element then this game would be a good fit for you.  If multiplayer or co-op is your bag then DayZ will be your best bet when the game is finally finished.  Either way, you'll have some fun with it regardless.

I was part of the initial Kickstarter to get this game going and have dedicated dozens of hours during the course of its development to a 1.0 release.
Starbound walks the line between a game with objectives put upon the player to encourage exploration and giving room for those who make objectives of their own. For those that look for nothing more in a game but to fritter away hours building up something for the sake of having done it, this game is for you. For those that don't care to follow instructions but want to be guided by a forceful hand to reach the end... you will probably be disappointed.
Story progression occurs through a series of missions and are accessible realatively early on. Being equipped well enough to complete them is another matter and people wanting a very linear experience will have to come to grips with some griding and exploring to see some of the sauce that makes this game just a little bit special.
Starboud is easy to recommend if you want something casual, light-hearted, and slow-paced.

Voxel-based games are nothing new, even if they're "IN SPACE!" However, Starbound is one of high quality. Although it had a rocky time through Early Access, it is one of very few early access titles to get a actual full release, even though some of the features are still lackluster and others are still being updated. The game is playable, even if it's not 100% complete.
What I'm saying is, it's good, really good. And It's not even all here, yet, with more to come. This game gave me the one thing Terraria didn't: Infinite terrain. Not one endless world, but multiple smaller worlds, each with their own biomes and settlements. It's nigh impossible to run out of resources, since if one planet runs dry, you can just go to another. Not to mention colonies and farms and whatnot that you can build on planets, which you can easily go back to later with a flag and teleporter. Oh, and your ship is your hub, a fairly large one, even, once you upgrade it.
And then there's randomly generated weapons and creatures and even crew members, just to add that extra bit of uniqueness to everything you see. It's not Borderlands- or Spore-level randomization, most weapons are pretty similar, and the random creatures don't even have names, but I'll take what I can get at this point.
In short, it's pretty great. A fantastic buy on a good sale, but even at full price, it's worth it.

Graphics have made huge improvement, loot is more plentiful, the overall playerbase has increased, everything now seems to be going in the right direction. Earlier on the games mutants were very scarce and virtually non-threatening because they couldnt catch up to you or they would just bug out and not even register you were there. Now with the new AI and addition of more mutant types the game is a bit more engaging and it feels like their is a bigger threat potentially making players want to group up instead of KOS all the time (which is believe is the intent of the game as a whole). Overall I want to say the game is great right now and I would highly recommend it to any person into this genre.
To the Dev's keep up the good work and hopefully you can turn this game into the primary survival game that people flock too.
Good luck to you all.

Well where to start? At the beginning of course.
The game drops you right into the first mission - the tutorial/Exposé of the story - with no menu before hand. That's fine if you like auto-detected settings and default key binds, but not everyone does and I'd certainly like a real main menu for the game (all interaction is done via the Ingame Worldmap or interaction with characters on board the Paladin Airplane).
But those are minor points.
The introduction into the story feels like the game wants to be a movie but isn't. It is a very hollywood-esque story and as such feels a little bland. While the missions are (so far) quite fun and varied, they are by no means especially creative or challenging. You either get it right or you have to restart and getting it right is more often than not a choice between killing everything in your way or waiting until the next opponent has his back turned.
The enemies or scenarios don't offer much challenge either for the most part. The worst thing that can happen are armoured opponents or dogs (or both) in combination with "Don't get spotted and don't trigger any alarm" objectives.
There is also no lack of gadgets and while having a large selection of stuff is nice (although half the gadgets are essentially the same as the bolts for the crossbow) having too much of everything is not. Even using your gadgets very liberally for takedowns (rather than sneaking around and doing the hand-to-hand stuff) you will rarely be in a situation where you think "Damn I wish I had more XY to take out those guys". You will have enough.
Multiple routes are present in almost every mission/situation so there is no lack of choice there, however some lend themselves more to a certain playstyle than others.
I like the customization the singleplayer offers, though again a bit more creativity would be fun - giving the suits for example extra abilities or special gadgets - rather than having simple liniear upgrades.
Customization in Multiplayer is another matter entirely. If you play this game online PvP rather than COOP, play the Classic mode. The classic mode with its default profiles is fun and challenging and the maps are far more entertaining 2v2. The 4v4 Blacklist modes are a cluster♥♥♥♥ of epic proportions.
It is still very much the best Splinter Cell Game since Chaos Theory as far as I'm concerned.
Update: As the game goes on, it goes out of its way to get you to shoot stuff. For every "Don't get spotted" Objective there is one "Neutralize all the Hostiles" and added to that you get situations forced upon you during which stealth is no longer really an option. The COOP in particular is filled with lethal situations that don't really work in a stealth game.

I enjoy the game. I think it's okay, it's alright. It's not absolutely amazing, but it doesn't have to be. I recognize a lot of the BGM's used because I'm using the engine that they're actually meant to be used on. That said, I want to make it clear that almost none of the BGM's used are author-created. I could link anyone directly to the RPG Maker Restaff packs where these BGM's were pulled.
Still, with that out of the way, I still think the game is fairly quaint. It's not necessarily easy, but it's not necessarily too difficult, either. It has its quirks, such as melee classes not exactly being favorable choices due to how if the enemy moves a single tile you aren't going to be able to connect your hits, while a ranged class does not have this problem.
The big things with the game are definitely accessibility. It's in Early Access, but at the time of this writing, I would recommend to the developer some kind of option to one-time reset your stats if you're under Lv.15 or something. I didn't know there were bows in the game, so I just went STR on a character. As it turns out, as a Hunter, AGI is my primary stat - not STR. I didn't know this, so now I'm running around with 3~4 levels worth of a useless stat.
The movement speed is extremely off-putting. I'm not saying people need to run at 500 feet per second, but the current walking speed is absolutely grueling and works to dampen the fun of the game. It's slow-paced by design, and as a result it's fairly uneventful and predictable. I understand slower movement speed in dark places such as caves and dungeons, but in the open field and especially in towns, you shouldn't be crawling as slow as you are.
The last thing is dialog. Using a keyboard key to interact, but then having to click [Continue] in dialogs makes for a jarring experience. I also can't tell you how many times I dropped my starting equipment on the ground because I thought I was going to equip it. It just makes sense that if you right-click an item, you're going to use it or equip it.
The conclusion is that the game is an acquired taste. If you play it for 15 mins, there's good odds you might hate it, but if you push through, it'll grow on you and you might be like me and go from absolutely hating it to kinda-sorta liking it.

This is where it all started.
I have hundreds of hours logged in this trilogy, both on Steam and on Origin
and I'm still not done with this series, and with its characters. Mass Effect means a lot to me, both as a game and as a story.
The controls can be janky - especially if you're playing as an Infiltrator - and you'll quickly find yourself watching the same npc animations over and over as you progress through the game
but as you immerse yourself in the story it all becomes superficial.
There's so much you can do in this game, including optional quests that have impact on the story in the sequels (nothing too substantial unfortunately, they're more like easter eggs/cameos, but still nice to get nonetheless). I did a completionist run a few months back with my first male Shepard Uriel, and it was well worth the time and energy I put into it - though I wouldn't reccomend it for a first time player.
Mass Effect has its flaws, both in its story and in its gameplay. But there's no denying that it's a classic, and that its beloved by a lot of people, including myself.

For anyone wondering, this is definitely a game worth checking for just $15...and let me tell you why:
1. The graphics are simply breath-taking, from the moonlight shining through the palm trees and reflecting on the wet sand, to looking at the aquatic life through the wavy, crystal-clear water
2. The sounds are as good as the graphics...the waves hitting the island, the crackling of the wood as palm trees fall down, and the realistic, muted noises heard while underwater. I gladly would pay $15 just to look and listen to this game. Maybe just a few adjustments on very few things, but overall excellent
3. Great wildlife. Different patterns of attack and movement from the different aggressive sharks and other animals...humpback whales that slowly come up for air...just, all the cool fish you can find at different biomes and areas of the ocean. And they will most likely only add more later.
4. Infinitely, randomly-generated worlds. No game will be the same. No island. No ocean.
5. It's early access...which is a good thing because it should have plenty of room to grow and get better, so long as the dev's don't let us down.
Now, what I DON'T like that I hopefully would like to see added/changed later on:
1. Buges and issues with physics. Now, though I haven't seen too many bugs, one common one I've seen a few times and read about it sharks (and possibly any wildlife or your own character) will randomly be able to swim through either the sandy island or a sunken ship. Right through the ground/metal walls. In addition to that, I find that a shark tail being able to luanch me 20 feet in the air and push my raft 80 feet away is a bit extreme. I can understand flipping it, and throwing me a few feet innto the water...but not straight into the air. Likewise, although I love how the crafting and real-world items on the ground work, I don't like how I can drag a whole tree while sprinting the same as if holding a small crab. It should be sluggish, and weighted.
2. Lack of item/item variety. Now, there is quite a bit of loot you can find, and a lot of stuff able to be crafted..but it just feels...bland sometimes. There's either the crude tools or high-quality metal ones found in full condition. I feel like, if anything, items can be found in disrepair and lower quality, considering they've been underwater for God-knows how long. Like, a "cracked axe", that maybe has a chance of breaking before the durability is up...or the head of a hammer you have to attach to a stick to make into a usable tool. Idk...just, something. Maybe more plants you can interact with, even if they drop the same materials, just more things needed. Maybe a fishing rod, or an actual gun, bottles of rum or water or whatever...but ya, I'm sure they will add plenty of more to come.
3.Vehilcles and structures. If I'm going to have a tiny raft that a shark can easily flip and shoot into the sky, then I want an option to build a larger, more sturdy boat...maybe more like a modern day wooden boat (ability to make timber as well as sticks?)? I want something that I can eventually build after hours of hard work that will ensure more safety than the same raft you have at the start of the game. Likewise, I would like to see more advanced options for building shelter. Every hut will look the same, out of the same materials, and the same square-by-square design. I'm not talking easy to make, but something different instead of the only option available. Just seems so limited.
4. Inventory. My first big complaint about this: how come I can hold just 4 peices of strings in a slot and also 4 rocks, or 4 large 5-foot "sticks"? I feel like it should either be done by weight, by how large the items is affecting the stack max, or a combo of both. My second complaint? storage containers....although, I like the idea of the difficult-to-survive-so-why-should-I-be-clean-and-organized-when-I'm-starving survival aspect of survival games, I would at least like some form or bin, shelf, or locker out of wood to store items off my person better...maybe something you organize in an inventory-like screen but can quickly pick up like if it were lying on the ground. OR, perhaps the ability to dig trenches or build half-walls on foundations to kind of make a stockpile that won't roll away? I feel at least the main inventory should be more balanced, or perhaps a way to put larger items in the raft without them just flipping off...that way I don't spend 30 minutes going to the nearest island to get wood when there are no trees left on mine.
Although the cons are larger and more detailed than the pros, I definitely like this game think it has great potential. Definitely o nthe right track right now. It just needs more features and perhaps a story or something to keep people's interest for longer. If anything, just enjoy sitting in the sand in the moonlight while listening to the waves. At least sharks can't walk on land.

Voxel-based games are nothing new, even if they're "IN SPACE!" However, Starbound is one of high quality. Although it had a rocky time through Early Access, it is one of very few early access titles to get a actual full release, even though some of the features are still lackluster and others are still being updated. The game is playable, even if it's not 100% complete.
What I'm saying is, it's good, really good. And It's not even all here, yet, with more to come. This game gave me the one thing Terraria didn't: Infinite terrain. Not one endless world, but multiple smaller worlds, each with their own biomes and settlements. It's nigh impossible to run out of resources, since if one planet runs dry, you can just go to another. Not to mention colonies and farms and whatnot that you can build on planets, which you can easily go back to later with a flag and teleporter. Oh, and your ship is your hub, a fairly large one, even, once you upgrade it.
And then there's randomly generated weapons and creatures and even crew members, just to add that extra bit of uniqueness to everything you see. It's not Borderlands- or Spore-level randomization, most weapons are pretty similar, and the random creatures don't even have names, but I'll take what I can get at this point.
In short, it's pretty great. A fantastic buy on a good sale, but even at full price, it's worth it.

At least, in my opinion. It just seems much harder in comparision to titles like Rome 2 or Warhammer and Warhammer 2.
You have to deal not only with constant pressure of barbarian hordes/eastern powers/nomadic invasions/ongoing climate change which decreases your food gain, but also now, next to public order dictating when you'll suffer a rebellion, you also have squalor - which determines how likely your cities are to have disease outbreaks.
But fun doesn't stop here - diseases can spread to other cities by armies! Oh joy.
Graphically, it's beautiful, but it is also a curse - because, compared to Rome 2, it is poorly optimized and despite having a high-end rig, you're somewhat likely to encounter stuttering, THANKFULLY it's usually limited to the campaign map, but your mileage may vary.
Some people dislike starting with an empire already in place, some dislike starting with an empire that is already falling down in place - those people may not enjoy playing Western and Eastern Roman Empires in this game, but that ultimately depends their approach - you can take Western Roman Empire, limit yourself to 2-3 main provinces and engage in a reconquering effort. Rome 2 was about forging your empire, Attila is about either watching it fall or seeing it whitstand the test of time.
Cavalry is a funny issue - many people bemoan it, calling it absurdly strong in this game, and they're not exactly wrong. As if to emphasize the title-character, cavalry units in the game are very strong, sometimes causing regular good spearmen units to lose against a head-on charge of low-tier cavalry. Others love it, praising the game for "finally doing cavalry justice". I suppouse it's more to do with your personal likes and dislikes.
I can fully recommend this game, as I love everything about it as an improvement compared to Rome 2 - maybe aside the actual setting, as I love the ancient times and having to build up your power, rather than fight and retain it.

The reason I'd loved this game turns out to be because I just didn't know there were better alternatives out there. With the releases of new DLC I've noticed more and more how the devs have started to care less and less about said "polish" I mentioned earler.

Insaniquarium! Deluxe is a game I have played in my childhood- as many other reviewers here have. However, even if you are older than 6, I think you may still like this game, I'll explain.
Insaniquarium is an old game, there are 2 things you are required to do: You are tasked with simply buying/feeding fish, occasionally doing certain things to keep bigger or different fish alive (like feeding a bigger fish normal fish, or feeding even bigger fish the already mentioned big fish that feeds on your normal fish, or feeding a certain creature beetles).
The other thing you must do is defend your fish from aliens by shooting them with your laser gun.
You can save up money to bye temporary upgrades that can make your job easier, such as getting the ability to give the fish more than 1 thing of food at a time, getting better food, or getting a better gun (the final upgrade turns your gun into an automatic weapon, making tougher levels super easy).
The main goal of Insaniquarium is to save up enough money to bye all 3 peices of an egg, once this is done, you unlock a companion fish that can help you out in your playthrough. You also move on to the next stage- there are 4 stages and you after you get the last egg, you move on to the fifth and final stage (which is only 1 level).
There are a few modes besides the main story, such as a time trail mode, a normal fish tank mode where you buy and take care of fish without the danger of aliens, and a mode after the main story that allows you to reply the game with all of your companions (and you even get a story of the companions after each level).
Now as to why I recommend this game... it is a fun little game that will keep you occupied if you don't have much money, or you are just looking for something small to play.
Perhaps you are a parent and you're trying to buy a game for your kid- in that case then get this game for them! Trust me, this will be something they cheris throughout their livesand if you get involved and play the game with them, it will be a memorable expirience.
My score for the game is a 6/10 as a normal game, and an 8/10 for nostalgia value.

Bought this game on a summer sale, and if you did the same, you will not be disappointed.
For the Dynasty Warriors veterans out there, this game continues the upward climb back to goodness since the dastardly downfall that was Dynasty Warriors 6.  For new players, this game offers interesting fighting gameplay mixed with you personifying a character in history.
PROS:
The weapon system - Each character has proficiencies with different weapons, ranging from 1 to 4 stars.  You are able to use whatever weapons you want as your primary and secondary weapons, but it would be wise to stick to the ones you are proficient with.  Personally I find this system to not be worth much and stick to the weapon meant for the character (their 'Ex' weapon).  So, for example, Lu Bu, I use two helberds, one for primary and another for secondary.
The levels - I like how they decided to add Hypothetical routes to the story modes.  Granted these maps are largely "aww lets all come together and win yayyyyy" maps, but one could take the historical value in that these battles would happen should the path have been taken in history.
The rest of the gameplay is typical of Warriors games and can be watched on youtube for 5 minutes and understand what its about.
CONS:
Graphics - Why they decided to port the PS3 graphics of the game is beyond me, and whoever decided to do that should be slapped.  Having played this on the PC and then seeing the PS4 graphics, it drove me to buy the PS4 version of the game and replay my progress there.  One caveat that I had not considered was that my game looked much better if I turned the brightness settings all the way up!  Strange...  Graphics comparison videos are available online.
Character design - While I, and many others appreciate a dub to accompany the subs with the option to go back to Japanese voices, some of the English voices are just terrible.  For example; Jiang Wei's voice is bad,  and Sun Quan's is not well done but tolerable.  There are also token words that get very old very fast, such as Jiang Wei/Liu Chan's overuse of the word "Benevolence".  I also dislike how they are morphing many of the characters to look like they are ripped right out of an anime, but I guess we have the otaku kawaii culture that Koei caters to in Japan to thank for that.
All in all: For the new fan a suitable game to try, if you can get it on sale.  For those that have been playing for awhile, give it a shot.

I cannot believe I hadn't played this game. Witcher 3/Skyrim are my standard for RPG's and, although I'm only a few hours in I think by the end of this game I will herald it as inhabiting the same top tier as those two titles.
Primarily I cannot believe I hadn't played this because it has the exact (perhaps better) 'Shadow of the Collossus' climbing/beast slaying mechanic. If there was one thing that could have been improved in The Witcher 3 it is this. In fact, when considering what a delight the combat can be in Dragon's Dogma I may actually prefer it to the Witcher 3. However it does lack the polish and the flair if I were trying to play devil's advocate. Therein lies the power of Dragons Dogma, it doesn't attempt to do things exactly the same as every other RPG. It is not necessarily better or worse combat than Witcher 3, it is more a parrallel experience that is unendingly fun in it's own right. Being able to climb/mount/pick up any enemy you encounter provides a far more immersive experience not only when in combat, but simply in terms of inhabiting a world where that is possible. Where one can spy a dragon in the distance, fire arrows at it to have it swoop in at you and then deftly scale the beast as it lunges, clinging to it's back as it flies vertically to try and escape your death grip. That provides a fierce level of immersion and dynamicism that allows you to be excited by *every* major encounter.
Across the board this seems to be Dragon Dogma's leitmotif; presenting a tradtional RPG experience via gameplay that is brave and adventurous enough to try new things. There are clearly elements that are reminsicient of the Dark Souls games, Skyrim etc. But, much like The Witcher series, Dragons Dogma manages to break out on it's own enough that it provides a unique experience. Fans of in-depth and open world RPG's will not be dissapointed either, very early on in the game I encountered many a 'Skyrim' moment. For example I would be, say, in a cave, for no reason other than I wanted to be, trying to glitch kill ten enemies that are way too strong for me. No idea where I am in relation to anything or what I'd set out to complete. SImply that this seemed like there could be good sh*t, or at the very least XP and I wanted to explore. Everything else fades out and 2 hours pass by real-time where you have ultimate fun doing essentially nothing.
Any problems with this game are likely arise from it's age or it's (slight) JRPG elements. Depending on your rig and what you're used to playing, the graphics for example may be dissapointing for you. When viewed side by side with HITMAN or Witcher 3 it may look downright shoddy. With that being said I often find myself being taken aback by how pretty the games graphcal flourishes can be. Truly the game is immersive enough that if you suspend your disbelief with the graphics for a short time, your brain will begin to fill in the blanks and you won't notice a difference.
AI is also challenged by age, namely your compatriots or 'pawns' as they're called in the game. This can sometimes be frustrating to listen to and is marred further by aged voice acting and dialogue scripting that clearly doesn't understand the 'Olde' English it is trying to ape. However it is by no means a detriment that can't be looked over when considering how enjoyable the game world and gameplay experience is. Someone saying 'MASTERWORKS ALL' 500 f*cking times may get a little grating but you only hear it so much because it's so desirable to keep playing the menu game, upgrading, selling etc. so you can go back out and soak up more of the game world.
Enemy AI is hit and miss, more often than not to the players benefit, this is likely resolved with higher difficulty levels. Enemy behaviour however is second to none. Hind-walking reptiles with spears can no longer walk on their hind legs if their tails are cut off for example. They over balance and try to scurry away on their bellies unable to hold their weapons. Cyclops' will fly into a mad rage when their eye is stabbed. Armor must be cut from enemies. Slicing larger enemies arms will cause them to drop their weaponry etc. I would say more but it's far more enjoyable to figure out in combat.
The story from what I've seen so far will hit enough beats that fans of the 'silent protaganist' flavour RPG will certainly be sated. While people that prefer story over freedom may find less to chew on than Witcher 3 or Dragon Age and may be left slightly dissapointed. As I am progressing I am seeing more epic missions, more story content and I certainly don't think this would be a deal breaker. There are a lot of *very cool* moments that I have not seen in any other RPG that again will offset this difference.
I feel like a fair review score would be 8.5/10
But honestly from my point of view, this is Shadow of the Collossus meets Dark Souls meets Witcher and I'm gonna say 9.5/10

So, the GF and I got this game to play together. So far, it's been pretty great. I love this game already, and I do recommend it, but you should be aware of what everyone is complaining about.
The combat system: you're pretty much limited to 4 directions of attacking, but the enemies are not. To me though, this is not a drawback at all. I don't think any of the complaining players have any experience on older games of say, the SNES or NES era. Ever play The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past on SNES? Combat is very similar, and that is one of my all time fave games. Ah, the combat features a manual shield block, similar to the gameboy Zelda: Link's Awakening, adding some strategy to the fights.
The game is pretty great so far. Ok, the quest line is a little vague at times, but if you really can't figure it out (that's half the fun), there is a wiki online, and some let's play videos. Everything you need to know is available if you look.
The only other real complaint is multiplayer lag; we play on a LAN so that's basically non-existent, but there are some posts in the discussions and a couple of guides that address this issue specifically.
Anyway, the game takes SNES Zelda combat, with Don't Starve's way of harvesting materials/resources, a familiar crafting system that uses specific craft stations (but, recipes are found as drops, that's kinda neat too), variable enemies that require various tactics, a simple levelling system that lets you tailor your character to your playstyle (3 main skill areas: swordsmanship, archery, and magic, combined as you wish), all wrapped up in a nice pixel-graphic art style.
I would also add, the Devs stated a big update is coming, but is some months away. If you're not sure you want to buy yet, wishlist the game and "wait and see". But, I've already got my money's worth.

Voxel-based games are nothing new, even if they're "IN SPACE!" However, Starbound is one of high quality. Although it had a rocky time through Early Access, it is one of very few early access titles to get a actual full release, even though some of the features are still lackluster and others are still being updated. The game is playable, even if it's not 100% complete.
What I'm saying is, it's good, really good. And It's not even all here, yet, with more to come. This game gave me the one thing Terraria didn't: Infinite terrain. Not one endless world, but multiple smaller worlds, each with their own biomes and settlements. It's nigh impossible to run out of resources, since if one planet runs dry, you can just go to another. Not to mention colonies and farms and whatnot that you can build on planets, which you can easily go back to later with a flag and teleporter. Oh, and your ship is your hub, a fairly large one, even, once you upgrade it.
And then there's randomly generated weapons and creatures and even crew members, just to add that extra bit of uniqueness to everything you see. It's not Borderlands- or Spore-level randomization, most weapons are pretty similar, and the random creatures don't even have names, but I'll take what I can get at this point.
In short, it's pretty great. A fantastic buy on a good sale, but even at full price, it's worth it.

Mass Effect was uniquely cinematic for its time, hiding the HUD by default, forcing you to sit through lengthy cutscenes and beginning the game talking about some♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about impending danger and how you're the hero you need, it may as well have been a Hollywood action movie. While this is nice, it would've helped if Mass Effect had spent as much effort trying to be uniquely cinematic, instead of reframing film cliches inside of a video game. The film grain is cute, but it hardly distracts from a painfully simplistic Shepard ("nobody takes my weapon!"/"big, stupid, jellyfish!"), similarly simplistic companions, and more than occasional bad voice acting.
The gameplay itself, while initially fun, quickly becomes monotonouos as enemies rack up more health and your weapons obtain pinpoint precision and perfect steadiness. The biotic mechanic of using a power once every few seconds doesn't exactly make things more exciting, or maybe it does, because playing the soldier class near the end of the game is about as exciting as I-10 in Houston at 7:00 AM. Driving around the Mako in the beginning of the game can be fun, especially when eperiencing the different planet types, but god forbid you're a completionist because you will be spending an inforunate amount of time combing unmanageable terrain in order to get some stupid copper deposit or something for no discernible purpose except to fulfill one of those demonic side quests in your journal. Equipping your companions is a massive chore as you adventure across the galaxy and pick up forty two different copies of mass manufactured equipment across the galaxy and are constantly replacing everyone's stuff for incremental improvements. Parenthetically, grenades are so useless it's a wonder why they were included.
Still, Mass Effect has its upsides. Its cinematic style pairs well with a diverse set of environments, and there are enough side quests to entertain for most of the game. In particular, the final sequence, even if full of tedious combat, is creative in level design and aesthetic. In 2016, it's up to par, but it's a necessary precursor for the full experience of its sequels, and if you can deaden your mind to some of the more repetitive features and monotone characters, it can be fun for a single playthrough.

I absolutely, 100% recommend this game. Be warned, however, this game is NOT for everyone.
A lot of people call this "mindless hack and slash gameplay". They're really not correct in this judgement, and are, in fact, being pretty ignorant towards the series.
First and foremost, let's address the combat. I believe there are 83 characters in this game. Each character can carry two weapons. For the first weapon, you ALWAYS want to have their 'Ex' weapon equipped. This is the weapon they perform the best with, and gives you access to special attacks, called 'musous'. With these weapons, you will have better attack power, better combos, better everything. So with one of these weapons per character, it in turn translates to 83 UNIQUE MOVESETS IN HE GAME. Of course, you can equip any weapon you'd like as your second weapon, so go crazy!
Weapons also come in many different forms. I believe there are 6 different ranks of weapon, measured in stars or dots. This determines both the rarity of the weapon and how powerful they are. 6th tier weapons were added in Xtreme Legends; before this edition you could only go up to 5th level weapons. There are a ton of weapons in this game, so if you like weapons, this game's got it. Additionally, each weapon has 1 of 3 'affinities'; heaven, earth, or man. This is basically a rock, paper, scissors type deal. You want to have a weapon equipped that is strong or equal against the opposing officer's. That's why you have two different weapons; both having a different affinity so you'll NEVER be at a disadvantage.
Like I said before, there are a lot of unique movesets and warriors in the game. This keeps the combat fresh, with all the combos you'll be able to pull of and special attacks to try out. On the harder difficulties, you CANNOT just mash buttons and hope to survive. This is why I absolutely hate when people call this game a "button masher". There is legitimate strategy and skill to this game once you put enough time to access the hgher difficulty tiers.
The actual gameplay revolves around a battlefield each time. Think of it sort of as a third-person real-time combat strategy game. There are different strongholds or forts scattered across the map. If you defeat the officer inside of that fort, you'll capture it, and your soldiers will spawn there. This is how you gain more troops to overcome the opposing army you're fighting. Then, you have more powerful officers of the opposing army you have to take down, and various other objectives to complete. These all happen in real-time, so pay attention to your map in order to know what your current objective is.
There's also a ton of content in this game. There's your basic story mode which has SIX different storylines to play. Each storyline additionally has extra, "What-if" scenario stages that really add to the replayability of the game. That's not all, though! There's free mode, which let's you play as any character in any story. Mostly used for levelling up, still nice.
Then there's ambition mode. This is completely new to Dynasty Warriors and is really quite huge. You're goal is to rebuild this little town. You fight consecutive battles without dying, and the further you get, the more rewards you're given. You colelct materials to level up the town and the various buildings in it, and weapons to level up your warrior and suit him up for battle. It's really unique and I highly recommend giving it a try.
After that, there's challenge mode. You use stock characters to complete various arcade-style challenges. A fun way to test your skill.
So, given all this content, it will honestly last you a couple hundred hours if you plan to 100% it. And no, none of what I said included ANY DLC. That is COMPLETELY OPTIONAL and not needed. I know the base game is still expensive, so I wanted to make sure I addressed this. I still do not have any of the DLC and this game is still wonderful and amazing. I really hope more people give this game a shot and enter the wonderful world of Dynasty Warriors.
