Summary: Terrible as a game, fantastic as an interactive story. Buy this when it's on special; hold your money otherwise. Gameplay Experience: 1/5. Story/Cinematic Experience: 5/5.
The Good: The multimedia in this game is incredible! The graphics, the animations, the music, the cinematics... all of them specially crafted to provide an amazing immersive experience.
The Bad: The gameplay is grossly primitive even by 1980s-1990s standards. 'Strong attacks' aren't 'strong' in the slightest, and yield far damage throughput than spamming regular attacks. The AI is also rather pathetic at all difficulty levels: troops and officers alike merely stand around, look at the enemy, randomly attack, and randomly defend. They didn't even bother pretending to make the combat between enemy groups realistic... instead, you'll often find troops mingling with one another as if they were in bumper cars, and officers are always playing lone wolf running around soloing enemy armies rather than fighting alongside their own troops. At the highest difficulty level, the game degenerates to a button smashing hack-and-slack, providing less of a challenge and more of a time waster towards meeting your objectives and advancing the story.
The Ugly: Prior to this game, the last game in the series I played was Dynasty Warriors 4. There are barely if any changes or innovations from DW4 to DW8...  The gameplay mechanics are largely the same! And no, the three point system doesn't do much except provide a means of spamming switch-attacks for a virtually fool-proof way of beating the enemy. Oh! And let's talk about Ambition Mode for a moment... talk about the dumbest, cheesiest, greatest waste of a feature of any game in this day and age! The randomly generated maps are the pinnacle of generic gameplay. None of the buildings or their ranks do anything of any significance towards enhancing the gameplay experience. Honestly, you waste more time upgrading the buildings than you get back from their virtually non-existance benefits. Bodyguards are also pretty useless; again, their abilities take more time to initiate than you get back from their virtually non-existent benefits. (On that note, I'm disappointed that bodyguards aren't available in the story mode like they were in earlier titles of the series). Weapon upgrading is also a time consuming process that yields little returns: as a game where a two-year old could button smash his way to victory on the highest difficulty level, any weapon will do. Sure, better weapons will make the game go faster, but so would lowering the difficulty level since the challenge is the same, but without as much monotony and time wasting. Something else: this game recycles content like crazy! If you want, for example, to get all of the 5th and 6th weapons, you need to replay missions over and over again... story mode stages from different factions or hypothetical scenarios recycle missions over and over again... ambition mode recycles missions and stages over and over again... Last point: Elephants, the War Elephant in particular... greatest disappointment in the history of time. Enough said.
Bottom Line: If you enjoy button smashing, and believe a challenge (ie. higher difficulty levels) should comprise doing the same thing as before, but taking longer to do it, then this game is for you! Otherwise, the best way to enjoy this title is focus on enjoying the story at the lowest difficulty level: as I've said before, higher difficulties provide less of a challenge and more of a monotonous, time-consuming, un-fun, unrewarding impediment towards beating the stages. In playing the game on easy, obtaining 5th and 6th weapons would be unnecessary, which is good!, as obtaining all of these weapons would otherwise involve repeating stages over and over and over again otherwise... boring!!!

This is like that old school RPG you always wanted to play on your PC two decades ago, but maybe you wanted a spice of Japanese programming in a game like Dragon Age and keep your own party in the Souls games and turn it into Dragon's Dogma, because that's what you'll have.
I've spent more than 90 hours in it and I still feel like I haven't finish it yet, it has enough content to keep you busy experimenting with all the classes, weapons, gear, and skills it has to offer; you can even build your own personal companion to help you out during your quest to destroy the dragon that, somehow, fell from the skies with a bunch of other monstrosities to wreck chaos all over Gransys, your homeland.
I have to be honest, the story is not the strongest point here, nor the characters, even some mechanics and menu navigations are kinda annoying to follow (turning on and off your lantern is a chore), some quests are very repetitive, but the gameplay - the most important aspect - is excellent.
Comboing goblins is never boring, fighting large creatures - although limited in variety - is always fun, moving your character feels great, music is great, that feeling of slashing, piercing and smashing your enemies is great, your pawns that won't shut up ever is not, but you can bear with it, combining hundreds of items to get more potent and rare items to either use or sell is great, there's a lot to do in here; maybe not as many options as, say, Skyrim offers, but it's enough.
This is one of the very rare instances that Capcom made a great game and not many people paid attention because "it's not Skyrim".
Outside of some annoyances, I would recommend it if you find it cheap.

Dark Souls is the rare example of a game that profoundly affected me as I played it. The gameplay and game design are top notch of course, and everyone always discusses the difficulty and challenge, which I enjoy, but by far it just moved me.
The online features are not specifically necessary, but they largely influenced my experience with the game positively. Most games have you save a world on the brink of destruction and then it's happily ever after, Dark Souls begins by telling you that the world is, and has been, dying and there is very little you can do about it. The journey is not about the saving, but in making do with what you have. That even when all seems loss, there can still be hope, and you can still push on. Even when there are monsters and invaders and complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that want nothing other than to harm you, there are also messages on the ground that tell you about a trap, or a sign to summon a Sunbro to help you out. Even just indirectly seeing ghosts of other players walking by reminds you that you are -not- alone, even when it would otherwise feel that you are. That shared experience of going through something difficult together, even when you cannot interact with them directly. The sounds of the bell tower ringing as another player beats the Gargoyles, the views of the vastly and intricately interconnected world. Dark Souls is a masterpiece.

Wasn't allowed to play computer games as a child (which ruled out an nostalgic feelings I may have for this game), but I've still played through many of the old, isometric RPG's that this game clearly harkens to. I'm not done with the game yet, but I frankly feel that there's no competition between PoE and the cRPG's of the 90's.
I read endless stacks of fantasy novels, and my biggest gripe with many games that are "writing heavy" are their highly simplistic and/or hackneyed story lines. Secret powers and coming-of-ages are all well and good, but fantasy has gotten to the point where, I believe, it needs to take itself - and its lore - completely seriously if its going to be self-respecting. I would consider PoE to the "Empire Strikes Back" response to the analagous "A New Hope" of the Baldur's Gate series. Both "A New Hope" and "Baldur's Gate" live in this vacuum free of "sequel interference" (if you'll humor me the phrase), and thus can adhere absolutely to traditional storylines and fulfill the tropes of the monomyth like a well-worn pair of shoes. This isn't a bad thing, but I feel that without taking the lore in a relatively realistic direction you're going to be stuck with a story that's dead in the water. Fantasy RPG's seem to have missed this step, and are frequently nauseatingly boring for related reasons. I think this is why "Empire" was so good: it took the lore seriously, and expanded on it without too much explanation. Perhaps with PoE, we've finally been gifted a game that's willing to take risks with our assumed knowledge of the forms that stories take, and stepping beyond our assumptions. This is a game that excels at making you feel like you're really shaping the world, even though it's probably not changing to fit your decisions anymore than any other RPG. You really create your role, and in a gaming universe where every other venture into Fantasyland is in the shoes of a solitary wanderer with a secret destiny, I found the serious tone of PoE extremely refreshing. This is a game that understands that magic isn't real, its premise is fantasy, and ultimately is just so: a game. But it pulsates with its almost unreadably expansive lore and its dedication to self-maintenance, and I've frankly not experienced that in any other game but Dark Souls, which is a far more streamlined and silent game.

This is going to be a real review arguing both sides of the game. good/bad. This review will tell and show why you should buy this awesome game.
What is state of decay?
State Of Decay is one of the best zombie apocalypse games of 2013 and is based around the choices you make to keep you and your people alive, choosing base locations and gaining resources from around this very varied city.
Good points.
I'm just going to jump straight in with the good points as there are way more good points than bad.
State Of Decay has the best imersion and theme of an actual apocalypse than games costing 3times for and getting very close to dayz levels of imersion. The variety of weapons is suprisongly good, and contains a few awesome ones. But these weapons can break and get damaged overtime and attachments such as silencers will break of and get worn out, creating this real feeling of "Do i use and ubuse it?, or save it?" it is a real nice mechanic especially for a zombie themed open world game. The carfting in this game is also very good, and you can get resources and build new parts for your guns, weapons such as a molatov, or use the materials for upgrading your base which increases your survivabilty.
Bad Points.
Now even though this game is awesome and is worth every penny, there are still some things i must point out for you.
The vehicle mechanics are poor, the vehicles have a very weird driving mechanic and feels as if they lack any weight what so ever, and there are only something like 6 cars in total for you to drive, and there is no vehicle customization, so you cant make a "destroyer of zombies" for yourself. The map is very small when you work it out, tiny infact with only a few main points around and 3 "major" cities. The campain no matter what will always have the same ending, meaning there is no reson for you to care about your actions as they dont affect you much, the story can get slightly boring half way through. And finally. the game isnt sandbox, dont expect a sandbox game unless you get the breakdown dlc, and there is no multiplayer.
Overall this game is great and maintains to be one of the 2013 greats but there are some issues, as this is undead labs first game, this is a great achievment for them and this is a great pc port from the xbox, and im glad to see them put the effort in to gain a great result. Overall i give it a 8/10 and for good reason, yes there are a few issues, but for the first playthrough you will adore it, only on the second/third playthrough will you begin to notice these issues.

I'll write this review for first timers like myself who have always wanted to get into the survival genre and are thinking about it now. I've already done the endless research and read all the comparisons.
tl;dr-Skip DayZ/H1Z1. Get this.
This game, even though it's early access is amazing, so good that I'm taking time out to write a review which I rarely do. The player interactions, never before have I felt such anxiety from a ANY video game, when you see someone, it can go so many ways, firefight, friendship, truce, betrayal, assistance, murder. Never cared for graphics as much as the general population, as long as the game is easy on the eyes I'm good to go but I must make mention of how great this game looks and more importantly how smooth it runs on my PC. This, along with its superb sound design makes for some of the best immersion especially when I play at night with headphones on (recommended!).
It will feel unfair, you will feel lost, confused and you will definitely die....alot. However when you get your first kill it's the most satisfying feeling ever not to mention the view of the dead guy's body and all his loot :) You'll get the hang of things, give it time. There are no gimmicks and crutch mechanics to assist, players have to depend on their brain and logic to survive, think like you would in real life and you'll be fine...mostly. I say mostly because the last thing I want to mention you can't really avoid no matter what, bugs. It's mixed in this department, some complain alot, some dont. I've personally only ever encountered one where I died by stepping off the curb -.- Another is where headshot multipliers don't work all the time. It is Early Access and compared to other EA titles out there barely playable or even selling DLCs before the game is completed, I'd say this game is in a great place right now.
Miscreated is worth its price tag in my opinion and should be in every survivalists library. Remember, trust no one and think like your life depended on it.

I have to say, I'm amazed with Starbound.
I bought it some years ago just out of duty because I started playing on an old version downloaded from somewhere. Let me clarify that the reason for me to do it was because at the time Chucklefish removed the hunger and environmental hazard factor from the game, which are two major points that would drive me towards a game, but I'm a guy of principles who buys the games he downloads and happens to like. The art was great, but the game heavily lacked direction, feeling a lot like a sci-fi terraria, hugely directionless where you just plopped on a planet, built a nice house, and ransacked other species for decor items and maybe some weapons. I was not impressed.
Recently I decided to give it a try if anything because I owned the game and hadn't taken a look at it since two years ago. And honestly, the game is great now. Not only there's a story, but there is a great sense of progression through quests aimed at improving your character, tech to unlock, and a plot that drives you to explore and push onward.
The art is gorgeous, and now that there is a reason to explore the different planets meeting the gajillion of pokémon scattered throughout the game is both exciting and fun. The survival elements are back and although I can see why they took them out of the game, feeling like more of a nuisance than anything involving (there's food everywhere and you'll have no problem staying fed), the element of preparedness and routine gives another dimension to just going down every hole you'll see.
The objectives are distinct, and the exploration is tense since you'll have to double back from whatever hole on the ground you dove into and death means losing a huge swathe of items. A lot of the equipment you'll find is more aesthetic than anything, and weapons are kinda meh, but it's super satisfying when you find that weapon combo that works. Action bars are somewhat small but you can switch between two bars, making the overall hotkey capacity alright. The techs are fun and meaningful, getting a morphball or a double jump that greatly helps with exploration, and weapon abilities are varied and useful most of the time.
The only problems I really have with the game is that the controls could be a bit better for me, like for instance when jumping down a platform you'll keep on going down subsequent ones until you release the "down" button, making it possible to hurt or even kill yourself, or that double tapping in a direction can trigger Dash and send you careening down a hole to your demise. Sometimes you'll also find yourself in some really hard to win combat scenarios, but taking it slowly will help with that so it's not too bad.
Overall though, I think it's a great game and that it has improved leaps and bounds from its SEA phase. The sense of progression is tangible, the settlements are fun, the exploration is intense and the story is nicely told in great pixel art scenes. From an aimless Terraria in space to a proper metroidvania, Starbound has propelled itself to the stars of my library.

This is like that old school RPG you always wanted to play on your PC two decades ago, but maybe you wanted a spice of Japanese programming in a game like Dragon Age and keep your own party in the Souls games and turn it into Dragon's Dogma, because that's what you'll have.
I've spent more than 90 hours in it and I still feel like I haven't finish it yet, it has enough content to keep you busy experimenting with all the classes, weapons, gear, and skills it has to offer; you can even build your own personal companion to help you out during your quest to destroy the dragon that, somehow, fell from the skies with a bunch of other monstrosities to wreck chaos all over Gransys, your homeland.
I have to be honest, the story is not the strongest point here, nor the characters, even some mechanics and menu navigations are kinda annoying to follow (turning on and off your lantern is a chore), some quests are very repetitive, but the gameplay - the most important aspect - is excellent.
Comboing goblins is never boring, fighting large creatures - although limited in variety - is always fun, moving your character feels great, music is great, that feeling of slashing, piercing and smashing your enemies is great, your pawns that won't shut up ever is not, but you can bear with it, combining hundreds of items to get more potent and rare items to either use or sell is great, there's a lot to do in here; maybe not as many options as, say, Skyrim offers, but it's enough.
This is one of the very rare instances that Capcom made a great game and not many people paid attention because "it's not Skyrim".
Outside of some annoyances, I would recommend it if you find it cheap.

First, let me say that the weakest part of this game is the story and characters. Things were happening and I was doing quests for unknown reasons. I had trouble know what exactly I needed to do a few times. And, for an RPG, that's usually a huge turn off for me.
However, what sold this game for me was the character progression and the team based combat. You start the game by creating your main character like any RPG but about 10-20 minutes in, you'll be making your main pawn/sidekick for the rest of the game. At this point, you are pretty much leveling up a partnership of characters. Making two characters that complement each other and then recruiting 2 other pawns from other players is what kept me going through my first play through. The game encourages you to change classes around since the augments you get from each class can carry over to your next class.
The combat, especially against the big monsters were always exciting. If you get the right pawns and they work together well, you can take down these beasts in a very satisfying manner. And boy are there some tough monsters toward the end of the game.
Patrick Klepek said this game was his highest scoring 3/5 he's ever seen. And I think he's right. The story is ok and forgettable. The world isn't that great (I did like how you don't have to fast travel and going out on a quest felt like an adventure every time). And the game doesn't do a great job of explaining the world and concepts to you. But the combat and the classes are the stand out here.
Recommended. It's not a great game, but it's definitely worth playing.

Dark Souls is the rare example of a game that profoundly affected me as I played it. The gameplay and game design are top notch of course, and everyone always discusses the difficulty and challenge, which I enjoy, but by far it just moved me.
The online features are not specifically necessary, but they largely influenced my experience with the game positively. Most games have you save a world on the brink of destruction and then it's happily ever after, Dark Souls begins by telling you that the world is, and has been, dying and there is very little you can do about it. The journey is not about the saving, but in making do with what you have. That even when all seems loss, there can still be hope, and you can still push on. Even when there are monsters and invaders and complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that want nothing other than to harm you, there are also messages on the ground that tell you about a trap, or a sign to summon a Sunbro to help you out. Even just indirectly seeing ghosts of other players walking by reminds you that you are -not- alone, even when it would otherwise feel that you are. That shared experience of going through something difficult together, even when you cannot interact with them directly. The sounds of the bell tower ringing as another player beats the Gargoyles, the views of the vastly and intricately interconnected world. Dark Souls is a masterpiece.

Aside from the "meh" singleplayer, eric johnson trying so hard to be ironside, and the crappy gameplay change from stealth to action that relies heavily on the cover systems and contextual parkour, I have to say the multiplayer is awesome. The control schemes and gameplay are atrocious for singleplayer yet for spies vs mercs it surprisingly fits. Very well actually. Spies vs Mercs is extremely fun, and playing it is almost like playing hide and seek. Mercs seek and kill . Spies hack and hide. The reason being is that Splinter Cell 1-4 have always been slowpaced and stealth, a game that relied on strategy and stealth to complete the mission. So the gameplay change from taking time to learn the enemy AI and patience to a mechanic that heavily relies on parkour and cover system and reflex and what not only made the game easy, but that tactical sense has gone down the drain. These kind of game mechanics pitted against AI makes the game too easy. But spies vs mercs was never slow paced. Even when it first came out in pandora tomorrow, the gameplay is much faster than its singleplayer counterpart. Playing with players does not only take patience and tactical planning. It takes reflex and actual skill. AI is predictable, but humans are not. So the game mechanics are perfect for SvM.

I remember I wasn't sure whether I wanted to buy this game. When I watched Fellowship of the Ring as a kid, I always loved the Moria sequence the most. That feeling of being watched upon entering a dark cave, tiny lightsource revealing sprawling labyrinths of tunnels and hallways, brothers in arms slowly descending deeper and deeper... and then it starts. Armies of goblins pouring from every corner and overrunning the group, a huge troll crushing everything in the way of his mace, and just when you think it couldn't get any worse, you see the dungeon boss. I've always wished to see moments like these recreated in a vigeo game, but I never thought it possible... until Dragon's Dogma.
This game absolutely nails fantasy combat in ways The Elder Scrolls and most others could only dream about. By mixing the climbing mechanics of Shadow of the Collossus, emphasis on team play and active combat skills, it creates a system that's unique and familiar at the same time. Enemies have different strengths and weaknesses and no boss fight is just about slashing at a monster's legs for 10 minutes. You'll be holding onto a griffin's wing 20m above ground, shooting cyclops' eye out and cutting hydra's heads off on daily basis. The variety of approaches, tight mechanics and fantastic animations make each fight seem like an epic adventure which most other games would save for the finale. Here, you'll get one almost every hour.
Each class has its own skills and some shared ones. You can switch between the classes in any town, which is really great for experimenting with your loadouts and playstyles. Balancing your team is vital and while a band of dual-wielders might look cool, they'll be sitting ducks for airborne and ranged enemies, so pick your pawns wisely.
The pawns themselves are both a cool idea and one of the game's biggest weaknesses. On the one hand, they allow for a virtually limitless customization of your own companion and you won't have a hard time re-creating your favorite pop-culture characters or even friends. However, the name "pawn" couldn't be more accurate, as they are lifeless soldiers who basically lack any personality or free will, so don't expect a party of interesting characters with good dialogues and backstories. They mostly just repeat the same stupid tips over and over again. Fortunately, you can turn those off.
Graphically, it might not seem like much for 2016, but remember, this was a console game from 2012, released only a few months after Skyrim and Mass Effect 3, and while the the night skyboxes are pretty weak and some of the textures aren't the sharpest, the game can look truly impressive at times. The animations are simply top notch, with every creature having detailed and believable movement, cloaks fluttering in the wind and even large enemies having little to no problems with getting stuck in the environment or clipping through. It's especially impressive in a game with so much physical interaction with the world, be it holding small enemies, climbing on big ones or throwing and breaking various objects. Lighting in dimly lit dungeons can be very atmospheric and it's refreshing to see really dark nights where you have to use a lantern and often don't know what's 20m ahead.
The second big weakness of Dragon's Dogma is its user-unfriendliness, which can lead to some very frustrating moments. I still don't know how checkpoints work in this game, but I do know that I can't trust them. Sometimes you get 2 saves in 10 minutes, other times you might lose over 2h of playtime because the game didn't consider exploring a huge part of the map and levelling up 3 times a progress worthy of a single save. So be sure to make regular manual saves. It also sucks that there's only 1 save slot, so you can't load an old file and try a different solution for a quest. However, once you get used these drawbacks and keep them in mind while playing, they shouldn't be a significant problem.
While Dragon's Dogma might be rough around the edges in some aspects, it excells in what's important in a game like this, gives you an extremely fun and thrilling experience that you won't find anywhere else and feels fresh even 5 years after its original release.

After putting in over 90hours I can give a pretty solid review now.
Dark Souls is hard. But Dark Souls is also fair. The mechanics are simple, and it's all about timing skill and patience. You can't button mash your way through this. You have to face each enemy as a life or death battle, because even the weakest of enemies can make short work of you if you're not paying attention.
The bright side, is that it awards your skill. Those who can surpass the learning curve will find extreme satisfaction in dealing that final blow to the boss who just wrecked you at least a handful of times.
This game will make you ragequit.
For some of you, it will make you perma-ragequit.
Mistakes are unforgiven and rushing through will surely end in your demise. DaS does not hold your hand, instead it looks at you as you as you approach a boss that's 5 times your size and has the ability to crush you rather swiftly and says "good luck, kid"
The most guidance this game gives are random writings on the floor with typically vague tips. and liars.
Difficulty aside, the story is dreary and soaked in lore, albeit very subtle in it's telling.
Overall, this is probably one of the most frustrating games I've enjoyed, and I would recommend it to those who have lots of patience.

Comely unit cards and building tiles, a challenging threat from the East, visually stunning compared to Rome II overall, last yet not least, moddability. The only thing it truly lacks is a huge campaign following the rise of the Roman Empire, an official campaign ported over from Rome II. Yes, some modders are developing total conversions dealing with that missed bit, it may take years to see such big mod campaigns up and running though. (The only good modded campaign available at the moment is Imperium if you're interested.)
Cons and issues:
- spawning of Hunnic hordes is unimaginably unfunny and imbalanced
- no total conversion moddability and no campaign map editor
- chasing armies around the map is a joke where no agents are present
- standard reinforcement range issues
- sadly, just like most Total War games, not all factions are available to play, and there are no secret unlocks either quite unlike in vintage TW games (yeah, mods make it possible, nonetheless, this is about CA doing it officially)
- just the usual overpriced, downsized DLC rant (DLC/x-packs should be about entirely new content developed exclusively after the game has been finished, not about eternally locking or intentionally cutting out and rationing content already present in the base game, content which remains unplayable after so many years the game has been out for)
- so soon after Rome II came out
- personally, Attila is better than Rome II, however only generally, as Rome II beats Attila thanks to its more ancient setting but is buggier and worse overall in many aspects
Also, Attila multiplayer mode seemed to be much stabler while the multiplayer matches of Rome II crashed on certain turns like clockwork and had to be wound a few turns back, often to meet another CTD several turns later. Yes, Attila was almost entirely crash-free except for standard TW crashes (for instance trying to use the interface when it's processing AI turns, not a biggie, and not something completely unpredictable).

It's basically Homestuck, but in Visual Novel form (but disguised as a point-and-click adventure, because Homestuck). You don't necessarily have to know anything about Homestuck to enjoy it. But if you enjoyed Homestuck you will enjoy this, and if you didn't enjoy homestuck you won't enjoy this.
Every single item you collect can be used with every single examinable- or interactable- object for a unique piece of text, mostly silly jokes or character-revealing snippets. So if you're like me, the plot will progress at a glacial pace and the experience feels exactly like the early acts of Homestuck, only more immersive. And if you're not into that, it'll be over fairly quickly.
On the plus side, it avoids the incredibly long wall of text chatlogs and narration that plagued Homestuck's later acts; whether you're exploring every interaction or not, the pace always feels organic.
Again, if you are a fan of Homestuck you will love this. If you couldn't stand Homestuck's pacing, you may not like this. If you haven't read Homestuck, you should probably do that first, if only because it is free and this game is not.

Speaking of enjoying the world, this leads to my favorite part of the game by far, the soundtrack.  This game is one where you can passively grind on either monsters or various ores to make the gear you need.  Normally this type of thing gets boring fast, but this soundtrack just makes the hours go by like its nothing.  The peaceful scenery of the open environment combined with calm, serene music causes time to pass just like that (imagine I just snapped my fingers).
Don't think that serenity and crafting gear is all to this game however.  Though I have not been able to experience high level dungeons, spending time around veterans and witnessing their struggles has given me insight on a whole new layer to this game I have yet had the privelage to enjoy.  Between incredibly hard multi-man dungeons and caves filled with high-level, deadly monsters expect to rely on all of your skills, as well as planning ahead.  You may need to spend time getting enough arrows or buying potions in order to tackle the dungeons, as well as try out multiple stat builds in order to find one that suits your playstyle.
I could go on and on about this game, but this is a steam review so I doubt many of you have even read this far into it.

An exceptionally crafted RPG true to the nostalgia of its predecessors while creating a whole new experience for the modern gamer. The level of exquisite detail in gameplay, graphics and narrative is exceptional right down to the sound of footsteps on various terrain. The game has a strong Baldur's gate feel based not on the interaction of party NPCs but also how their individual back story plays out in the game. It couples some innovative features in the Stronghold, player classes and abilities. While the essential ingredients of character struggle, the genre of strategic hack and slash along with exploration has not changed, elements of the storyline are novel and the overarching storytelling is superb and enriches the game. As with anything, there are always drawbacks such as levelling caps, bugs and some degree of directionality in the gameplay it does not diminish (at least for me) an enjoyable game. Highly immersive, addictive and recommended for any one who enjoys turn based RPG especially those who reminisce over the golden age of electronic D&D.

While this is by and large a great game for fans of story-driven RPGs, it does contain a number of flaws worth noting I don't feel have been sufficiently covered by the other reviews. Some of the things to be discussed are minor spoilers, so be warned.
One big problem with the game is that the gameworld feels rather static and unresponsive. Time and again, the player gets caught up in major events of the region, which in their passing leave nary a sign of having ever occurred. At one point, fighting erupts on the streets of one of the cities, with wanton killing and destruction all about. However, a few gamedays later there will be no sign of any of this having ever occurred; All buildings previously put to flames have been restored, and one is hard-pressed to find an NPC that will as much as acknowledge the event with a single line of dialogue. This is a recurring trend.
The same shallowness troubles the reputation system. The game tracks both the player's reputation with individual factions, like in Fallout: New Vegas, and their perceived disposition: does the player behave benevolently or cruelly, logically or passionately, and so on. Unlike in New Vegas, however, aside from a few odd questlines the player's faction reputation doesn't ultimately figure into much anything. One can be bitterly hated by a given faction, and they will still treat you just as courteously as ever. Favouring on e faction over another often feels purely a RP choice, as it rarely has any actual consequences. The same is true with the disposition reputation. While NPCs will often note on the player's reputation, this seldom affects the options you have in interacting with them.
Then there is the stronghold. While one would think that being the lord of your own castle who collects taxes and commands their own force would somehow affect the progression of the story, the fact is barely even acknowledged by the inhabitants of the gameworld, and ultimately developing your holding or failing to do so doesn't affect the progression of the story in any way at all. This is fairly disappointing after Obsidian's Neverwinter Nights 2, where the like stronghold played a significant role in the story. The likely reason for this is that the stronghold was a stretchgoal in the Kickstarter, and the devs didn't know for sure if it was going to be in the game until fairly late in the development. The same reason likely contributes to the poor faction dynamics: Too many elements of the gameworld were just tagged on in the course of the development, with no overarching plan for them from the start.
Finally, there is the issue of the player being the Watcher. The idea here clearly draws from Planescape: Torment, in which the player had lived multiple previously lives now largely forgotten. However, whereas in Torment the player continuously ran into the deeds of his former selves, in PoE this never happens outside the fairly narrow critical path. Troublingly, the game treats the player having memories of past lives as a major deal, and them risking to overwhelm the player's sanity is supposed to be a motivation for pursuing the main quest in the first place. As there is a lot of content in the game, the end result is the whole affair feeling increasingly trivial: The player goes about doing thing completely unrelated to their condition, then suddenly the critical path kicks in for a little while again and the player deals with deeply personal issues, which are again promptly forgotten for another 10 hours of gameplay.
Despite these flaws, it's still a very good game, well worth several playthroughs. One can only hope that possible expansions or sequels utilise a tighter creative control, however, so that the end result doesn't end up feeling like just the sum of its parts.

Okay so, this game was just released on Steam but I have been playing the Alpha client for two weeks prior and have sunk a lot of hours (and money) and to it.
DISCLAIMER: This is an alpha stage FREE to play game. There will be bugs, there will be stability issues, there will be a lack of robust content. If you do not go into an alpha game expecting the world, there are a lot of things to like about Life Forge.
Initial impressions upon installing this game were very good, the pixel art is great and not recycled from RPG Maker. The soundtrack and sound effects are excellent, some of which are stock and some comissioned from within the dev community. I reccommend going through the tutorial area before exploring the first area as it will explain the majority of gameplay aspects. You can also level here very quickly through skilling up your professions, which I also reccommend unless you just really hate crafting. The majority of items you use will be crafted, some world items will drop as well, but are not always easily accessible (boss drops) or are rare.
The spells and battling are not overly complex and have yet to be fully fleshed out, but are still fun. Spells and class roles are somewhat undefined outside of a few specializations like the Magi's Cleric role, which was just fixed and given a more healing centric buff which sets them apart from hybrids. The Magi's other two options, Wizard, and Necromancer, don't really have a lot separating them except a few spells so you might want to choose based on what might fit your playstyle in the future. I have not played a Hunter or Page class yet, but from discussions they have a similar set of on-going development and defining within their specializations.
At times leveling will be a bit grindy, whether it is through crafting, or killing monsters, but it is not a horrible grind that drags on. I reached level cap within a week of pretty consistent playing. Level cap has limited things to do at the moment, but they just re-added an end-game "raid" with Steam launch and PvP is always an option. They should have no problem putting out more content regularly.
PvP has its ups and downs. There are definitely some imbalance issues, but what PvP game doesn't have that. They changed it so that the first area is PvP free which was a smart move because it promoted ganking of lowbies, especially if you had not gone to the tutorial and leveled up there to at least 15. You won't run into PvP until the second desert area now. I would say as it stands now there is a good mix of PvP and PvE crowd, but the former can be ruthless at times. In Life Forge when you die you lose XP and a portion of anything you are carrying in your bag. Some people have no qualms ganking you and taking your stuff, so travel lightly and if farming make frequent stops to the town to unload goods. The game offers a good amount of safe zones as well to farm crafting materials without fear of being ganked. PvE death results in the same loss of XP and/or items. Some people will still loot you if they are in the same area, but will return items if called out on it or asked nicely. I made it a habit to prevent dying at all costs by avoiding dangerous areas above your level, and staying out of PvP zones unless no one was around.
Overall I really enjoy this game and it has potential. There is a pretty good community so far in number, and outside of a few dufuses everyone is helpful and not complete jerks. The developers seem to have a good idea what they'd like to do with this game and are very helpful while being engaged in the community. Hopefully they can deliver a solid F2P product and keep the promise of not allowing people to pay for power through the cash shop which right now only delivers novelty items and potions that do various things like reset talents/stats and bless the realm with 2X XP. You can also buy stat/talent resets with in-game gold.

An excellent game with charming characters, catchy music, and lovely, whimsical art.
Be warned, this is likely more enjoyable for people who really love reading and exploring. And clicking on everything.
Otherwise, the game is rather short, but there is more to come in future installments.
Despite it's shortness, there is a lot in it for people who like exploring as I mentioned previously.
You can combine objects in your inventory to get different results, and even comedic narratives if your combo results in nothing else. Not to mention, there is dialogue for nearly EVERY item in the surrounding scenery, so be sure to click on everything and click every object on everything.
There is actually a lot of lore hidden in the narrations of everything you click on. From lore about the world, to the quirks and personality of our main characters, you can learn a lot from the funny flavor text boxes.
The game is fairly easy in terms of puzzles and I only found myself stuck on what to do next once.
It has an easy to follow narrative and easy to understand gameplay that requires little mastery.
As for it's relation to Homestuck, you do not need ANY prior knowledge of Homestuck in order to enjoy this game. Having read Homestuck is just a little bonus, as there are some references to it here and there that gave me a chuckle, being  a longtime Homestuck fan.
Overall, Hiveswap: Act 1 is a fantastic, albeit short, game that I highly recommend getting into now, while it's fresh out of the oven.
Knowing Homestuck, this whole thing is likely to start rolling pretty soon. Both in story and with real life, with it's fans.

Long review:
Alright, let's go through some pros and cons, shall we?
Pros:
- Engaging storyline
- Adorable characters
- High quality pixel graphics
- Excellent multiplayer system (easy LAN setup)
- Reasonable price
- Challenging quests
- Many craftables
- Some biome variety
- Very large map to explore & build in
- Easy to configuire for a Steam controller
- Good battle mechanics
- Singleplayer worlds and multiplayer worlds are interchangable
- Many different creatures
- Good farming system
- Manages to be relaxing while still being challenging
- Good building system

Cons:
- Only two characters
- Very little character customization

As you can clearly see, the pros heavily outweigh the cons. This game is truly a hidden gem, and I highly recommend absolutely everyone to play it, and I can't wait to see what else Owlet has in store for us!

As an Arisen, you are killed only to be brought back to life by your fate, by your curse. You are one of many Arisens in the past and present who also shared the same fate, of having to be the one who saves the world from impending doom wrought by the Great Dragon, Grigori. In your quest you're given the opportunity to do many things.
In short, the game is amazing. Great fantasty setting. Great mechanics. Alright story. Amazing, but fairly small world packed with hours of meaningful, solid content and unique locations to explore. Many different Fantasty enemies that all act realistically (For a fictional fantasy monster/enemy that is) that come in both human and non-human varieties. Great combat system and a beautifullly crafted world full of immersive quests and NPC's. On sale, or full price. This game is worth it. Look past the minor issues that stem mostly from it being difficult to follow Story missions, which means the game does not clearly point you in the right way directly, and the countless unexplained mechanics or moments where story progess will instantly cancel some side quests, if you advance too far. Because this is a slightly flawed but still bright shining gem in the RPG genre that, if left unplayed, will be sorely missed, and that would be for all intents and purposes, a huge mistake.
If you like RPG's, and even certain open world adventure games. Particularly The Dark Souls series and Legend of Zelda series. Then I wholehearedly believe you will enjoy this. Even if you enjoy only one of those or neither of those, but you will find some mechanics more welcoming if you like one of those.
--------------------------------------------------------------------
--------------------------------------------------------------------
When you start the game you are given a few tasks to begin your adventure, a sort of tutorial, prologue experience.
First of which is choosing your class.
The Vocation system in Dragons Dogma is slightly different than other class ssytems of other RPG's. Whilst choosing a class at first might seem like you are locking your decision in for the whole game, this is actually the opposite.
You get three Starter Vocations. Which are available from the beginning of the game
Three more Advanced Vocations based mostly on the weapon choice and skill set of the 3 starter classes with even more skill options and Vocation particular augments and improvements not accessible by the Starter Vocations.
Three more, Hybrid Vocations. That combine two aspects, skill sets and weapon choices of two different Vocations.
The extra 6, of the three Advanced Vocations and the three Hybrid Vocations, are made available later on. But once available, you can change vocation literally any time you want. The more you use a Vocation and experience you accumulate whilst playing as said Vocation, they individually increase in Rank (Rank 1-10). As this happens you gain access to more skills, core skills (Skills not activated by weapons) and Augments. You level each Vocation to Rank 10, and you'll never lose this progress. Upon completion of the game you start New Game Plus, and you will still have your Vocation Rank progress. This makes it so you can accumulate everything the game on one character. No cluttered save system to worry about.
This system allows you create a tailored playstyle at any point in time.
Second of which is is making - Yes, MAKE. - your very own Pawn. A unique follower you handcraft in appearance and class, you determine their skills and provide them with gear. They level up with you. They learn from you, like a child following a parent. If they observe you killing an enemy a certain way they will learn that is that particular enemies' weakness, and will attempt to mimic you as best they can when facing that foe again in the future. All Arisen have their own Pawn.
The Pawn system, and the Pawn Learning system isn't just limited to your Pawn, however. If played online you can gain access to pawns made by everyone else who also plays the game online. With your own Pawn, you can hire an additional two extra pawns made by other players to help you on your journies. They will learn, just like your own pawn will, how to fight certain enemies even if their own Arisen hasn't faced that particular foe yet. But these Pawns do not level with you, so if you stick with the same Pawns for a long time, they will soon become underleveled and unbalanced, too weak to fight the strength of the monsters that are balanced to your level, the Arisen, and your Pawn's level. You can also give Hired pawns gear you find, but because they are not your Pawn, you are effectively gifting that item to the player who created them. You cannot take gear off of them that were given them by their creator. You can not take back gear that you gave to them back once equipped. So do not equip Gear you found, on Hired Pawns. Only yourself or your own Created Pawn. That being said, this is a cool feature because you can essentially gift the best gear you want, to say, a friends Pawn. Who can then use that gear themselves or keep the items you gifted them equipped on their pawn, to utilize gear way beyond their level. Which some may view as cheap, but it's still possible, nonetheless.
From here, you're off. Exploring the world, doing quests, slaying both beast and man in the form of Goblins, Cyclops', Ogre's, Hydras', Wyverns', Cockatrices, Chimeras, Necromancers, Cultists and even common Bandits.
In your quest you will meet NPC's, some of, if helped will actually help you in later quests, or NPC's like a bandit group made up of entirely women who will attack you if you or your pawns are male, (but you can always dress up in womens clothing to hide the fact you or your pawns are male ;) ), and this whilst being minor, is actually quite useful. Speaking to people is an advisement, as you never know what you might learn. If an NPC is quest related they will have an icon over their head, green if they offering a quest, yellow if they have information related to a quest you don't currently have active, red if they have information related to your currently active quest and blue if you can turn in a quest with them for the reward they'll offer. But even when they aren't related to a quest, you can learn things about the world that you might not have known otherwise, such as what types of enemies roam a location, or suggestions as to where you might find a quest.
When you are travelling the world. You're mostly required to do so by foot as there is no direct fast travel system and the map is effectively uncharted, and therefore blank until you actually travel across it and discover the world to reveal the map..But, you can fast travel through the use of Ferry Stones. These items allow you to teleport to the two Main Cities, Gran Soren and Cassardis if not Port Crystals that you manually collect and then replace in your chosen location, throughout the world to act as an additional Ferrystone travel location.
Ferrystones are normally one time use items, but you can actually get an unlimited use, Eternal Ferrystone from your Stash at the Gran Soren Inn. (And Apparently I've hit the character limit..)

The game, while flawed, is still very good.
The 'most helpful' negative review does a good job of listing most of the flaws. There are some weaknesses with the RPG stat system and the level/quest design. It enforces a rather tepid character design, lacking in flexibility.
For example, if you get in a fight in a room, there's no option for retreat. You either kill everything in the room or die. Core stats don't affect stealth or crafting, and the 'might' stat affects *all* damage types AND healing; literally every class is a Might based class. You can't really spec a character for subterfuge and diplomacy as opposed to combat, except in a very superficial manner. Every character ends up playing very similarly.
The accuracy system ensures that 'support' classes are stuck playing support; you can't invest points into accuracy and it's not affected by your base stat choices.  A low-accuracy class such as Priest will end up missing attacks all the time, so you're left with no choice but to use them to buff other characters. Only, you can't buff before fights and the fights are so short, and the number of daily uses so low, you'll barely use them for that either. Some classes just end up overall 'worse' than other classes, instead of being a balanced mix of pros and cons.
Most of the quests are of the "go here, kill/fetch something, come back" sort. I can't think of any that were very memorable.
Still, the rpg mechanics have enough depth to remain fun. Classes like 'fighter' are very flexible; your stat choices decide whether they are defense or offense focused. The best race for paladin tanking is the game's equivalent of 'halfling', which is hilarious. They have very interesting twists on their 'bard' (chanter) and 'monk' equivalents. The world building is quite good. Overall I've enjoyed the 60+ hours I've spent and will probably enjoy another 60+ hours.

I'd heard good things about this, and it surpassed my expectations to become my favourite new game in months. It's very close to what I always imagined the ideal zombie apocalypse survival game to be. And it's not just combat, combat, combat, this game makes you feel hunted and the moments of dramatic tension that arise naturally as you're sneaking around are great.
There's an excellent balance between realism and action, a rich setting packed full of references and amusing little details, and clever use of noise as a gameplay element (loud noises can attract zombies from all over, which is often a risk, but also gives rise to tactics like the use of noise to lure or distract enemies). I also liked the combination of multiple playable characters and permanent death, if you get your character killed, it's final - they're dead and gone, and you'll have to play someone else from their group. It really feels like a loss when a survivor you've been building up into a badass gets torn apart in a raid gone horribly wrong.
Owing to its small budget, it's a bit rough around the edges, but it has a heart of gold and a lot of ambition. At first I thought "another zombie game?" but this was a breath of fresh air to me.

LIFE FORGE is a pixel-art top-down style online RPg as the name states; and it does an amazing job on delivering a fun and well paced adventure in such a setting.   And it is still in alpha so it has a lot of growing that takes place.
I'm not going to give a "Full and Critical" review of LIFE FORGE, as it's relatively new and it is presently in it's early alpha stages, so what I will say before I go onto my list of it's Features and PRO'S/CON'S is that the game plays very well for the stage it is in with bugs that one comes across often times being minor ones or slight adjustments to balance, or a lily pad that you can walk on in a pond that shouldn't be crossable.   More important than that is the staff are actively involved and the developers directly talk with and listen to their community.
The players are a mix of a wonderful majority that enjoy interacting with others and you have a mix of the traditional more cutt throat online gamers; but as with any online experience you 'really' can not judge how this will be for any given person. (But the community is pleasant and isn't toxic.)
GAMEPLAY
Note: I've heard there'll be a system to allow you to set your own key bindings so this portion may become dated.
The gameplay itself plays similar to akin to many older pixel-art with a W,A,S,D format with CNTRL to do a basic attack, left click (or a button) to target and 1 to = for hot key placement, the classes all feel and operate differently and depending on how you build your stats so would your own class.
FEATURES:
- Three Core Classes with Three advanced class options unique to their core class available at level 25.
- A Growing Spell/Ability system where the skill grows in level and ability the more it is used.
- A Skill system for Mining, Blacksmithing, Woodcutting, Carpentry, Fishing, Cooking, Tanning, and Tailoring; there may be more i'm still working on just now nearly reaching the present  level cap on my first character.
- A Talent Tree system that has Offensive, Specialist, and Defensive branches allowing  for great stat customization which there is also a "Level up and stat distribution system" which gives the player control of how their character turns out.
- A exciting and diverse world in terms of play-style, the out-lands are often PvP enabled and perilous in many ways while the close-to-town and village areas are often times safe as are 'safe harvesting zones'; but the greater rewards await in the outlands giving people a interesting slew of options.  (You can't fight someone over a 5 level difference though as to avoid griefers.)
- The games' communication system has Global, Local, and ( !Name Msg) style Whispering presently as well as a strongly functional trading system and a guild system.
- A powerful community where the Developers and staff are actively involved with their work and product, .
- Each class has a interesting unique roll all it's own while often able to accomplish their core role still allowing for interesting party composition versus the usual 'Tank/Healer/Dps/Dps' grind, a skilled player may even solo most foes though some can be tricky given their areas.
- Player driven economy and Crafting; only the crudest and barest of equipment for each 'type' is available with a few exceptions existing at a variety of areas (Often Outland shops with odd currency).
PRO'S:
- Enjoyable style of art that while simplistic stands out and flows throughout it's world very nicely.
- Hilarious shop soundtrack, most memorable i've heard in any MMO.
- An aggressive player will like that they can literally muscle other players out of the 'EXP race' in the outlands if they want or be a shining exemplar of travellers and protect people and ward off red-PKs; this returns the classic and more unforgiving feel older MMOs like Ultima online and Everquest were known for in rough regions, as people who die lose a portion of EXP to the PK and they drop some of their items in their backpack.
- A non-PvP oriented player will find the majority of the community are really awesome so reaching any boss with a group and fighting it is often very safe and a rewarding experience as well as that most of the games' areas lack a "PvP open" tag, including the entire first town and dungeon.
- A harvester feels a real sense of risk/reward on this game, as most won't venture into the outlands to gather materials, while a brave one that does may be at risk they often have zero competition; I found this to be an amazing risk/reward feature.
- Enemies are smart enough of an AI to navigate around most of their environments as well as tend to be problematic enough they're a fun challenge.
- If you love a competative and fluid market, this game has one that is ran by the players, so supply and demand and commitment/reward are a thing here versus everyone buying/selling to the same NPCs.
- Possible to max every trade.
CON'S:
The Game is in alpha so in regards to criticism i'll only give a minor amount, many things are being balanced, improved, altered and as just a player i've watched this game grow even the span of the weeks i've been here.
- Some skills will feel Grindy and areas for harvesting during peak times can prove difficult to manage if theres fierce competition, but a clever person 'can' usually find isolated areas.
- Online experiences with players may not always reflect the fun nature of the game.
- Crafting presently takes back-seat to rare drops, but I suspect this may be adjusted/balanced one day.

My own experience in life forge has been playing a PAGE, in my early days I first found myself in GANDOR the home town of all things new and inexperienced in LF and I quickly set about to looking around the town.   The familiar looking signs of a SWORD, SHIELD, or INN helped me easily enough locate the homes of interest, or lack thereof, so while I might of missed something passing through Gandor I soon discovered a friendly shop keepe who's song I still remember; 'Buy buy buy buy buy buy', at least I think that's the lyrics, but I noticed this store had maybe basic gear sets for each 'type' of core class and only a 1H/2H option for each, and only the crudest of such I was 'certain' so I set about wandering around beating on the turtles I found in the hills while inquiring in chat about the quandary.
It was at this time from the chat I learned about the Player-Economy and then returned to the shop to enjoy the song and purchase a PICK AXE.   Already about a level 12 page from brutalizing the hill creatures I began mining and smithing IRON (Tier 2) tools for myself and even some iron armor; feeling quite confident I inquired about where I might find even more impressive armor or weapons (I am a man that likes cool swords), so I set about my journey through IRON STAR MTN!
I found within the mountain about halfway up I encountered my first hostile foes and within the caverns even came across some level 18 golems; being only 13 at this time I just ran past these until I later felt bold and clobbered one near what later found was a interesting Boss Cavern room that instantly transported me back to those days as a kid where I remembered playing Legend of Zelda and going through the boss' room to press switches and get to the central minotaur boss -- who I noticed was level 20 and there was a passage way to entirely avoid... so I did! Something of a confession to get out of the way before I actually go in and review this game. I was a major Homestuck fan in my youth, and still enjoy the actual material quite a bit. However, I haven't been attached to the fandom for quite a while now. This won't really impact my review, but considering i'm reviewing a Homestuck game... yeah. It's necessary.
It's a game that feels like the Homestuck webseries. That is essentially the best way to explain this game to someone. If they ask, "What's Homestuck?", then they're not in the right demographic for this game. It's not that someone who hasn't been exposed to the comic can't enjoy the game. It's more that they won't be receiving a complete experience, and with an asking price of eight dollars for a game that took me sub two hours to complete, I can't imagine it being worth the price of admission.
As for the actual game, it's a fairly typical point-and-click adventure game with some added bling. Quite a few interactions happen via a communication device to talk with other characters that you can play as. There is a solid main character, but these other sequences with supporting characters do well in breaking things up. The other notable feature is the STRIFE! battles. Now, these aren't true battles. They're more like flashy puzzles. But they're distinct enough from the actual puzzles that I feel like mentioning them. They're fun little diversions with some witty dialogue, but nothing really that special.
Story wise, it's hard to judge considering this is the first chapter of the story. All I can really say is that it's a good setup that manages to leave some good questions to be answered later down the line and establishes the universe to the extent that it's needed for the plot. I like all the characters that have been introduced. They each feel suitably unique, and the dialogue is all excellently written, which is something of a must for a game that's mostly dialogue.
Overall, it's not a revolutionary game. But it doesn't really need to be one. It sets out to make a nice homestuck adventure game, and does that very well. Wether it squanders the potential it has is yet to be seen, but i'm personally looking forward to the next act.

A nice, relaxing game if you like Terraria but are tired of the combat.
This game is a more exploration and curiosity based Terraria, if the reviews haven't said that. The game starts you off as a Guardian of the Galaxy (Not the Marvel version), fleeing from a graduation ceremony cut short. You're then on your newly aquired ship, all beaten up, and sent on a few fetch quests. Anyone coming from Terraria shouldn't have any difficulty with this, as you know the basics of mining. Avoid the spiky rocks, fight enemies as usual (Like a mage with a sword, so to speak), avoid fall damage, and most importantly, avoid the spiky rocks. I have seen many people die from this and whine, it's like they don't know what a TNT Plunger is. Another important thing to note is the hunger meter. Gather seeds and set up a farm as soon as possible, as it will help greatly. Many people die from Hunger, as well. It's like seeds don't exist. Once you get past the tutorial and setting up your first farm, you'll then be far above most others. So, so far above. The Soundtrack is great, and the combat is there, but not overrunning it, but still there and fleshed out, so it's no hinderance, and you could live a peaceful life if you so choose.
I've yet to play with a large server, but playing with friends is fun, even if you have one or two, because it's reminiscent of Terraria, and we've all played it, and had more fun because of it, and no time was spent dawdling on "Aw geeze I'm scared of mining".
I would highly recommend this, and perhaps get a two pack if you have a good friend.

Although somewhat overshadowed these days by its outstanding sequels, Mass Effect remains my favorite game in the franchise.
Mass Effect succeeds with an engaging story, top notch Voice Acting, some of the coolest and most original alien designs I've seen in a Sci Fi game, and complelling, well written characters that stand the test of time.
In 2016 the game is starting to show its age a bit with combat AI that is rough at times, and visuals that will obviously look dated to someone who didn't play the game when it came out. The infamous Mako driving is pretty rough, although not as bad as the console release.
However, the actual RPG elements in this game (as opposed to the Action Shooter direction the sequels were taken in) keep the gameplay more interesting in my opinion. Outfitting your squad before every mission requires strategic decision making and forethought, especially on the harder difficulty levels.
At the end of the day, the strong world building and narrative experience will carry you through any gameplay shortcomings.
If you ever get the urge to delve into the Mass Effect franchise, its absolutely essential that you start from the beginning!

Day 1: I awoke not knowing where i was. I was disoriented (new to game) and mute (mic not working), all I knew is that I was alone. I wasnt too sure where to start, but i was near a road. So I followed it in search of friendly faces, shelter, and weapons.
I ran into a small collection of buildings and managed to find some food and a stow pack. As i left my 3rd house someone called out to me in a friendly manner. I approached cautiously as i dont know what he wanted. But lucky me! He was friendly and had another lost soul with him. He said his name was Brian and his companions name was Neko. I was able to communicate with gestures (F keys) and text (game chat). Neko was mute like me but Brian had lots to say, most of it helpful. Brian handed me a spare pickaxe and said lets stick together.
Brian said we were near a town called Pinecrest, and that we could outfit ourselves with gear and maybe a gun or two if we were careful. So we set out looting the occasional farmhouse on the way. As we neared pinecrest, off in the distance we heard gunshots so we knew we had to be careful. At the next farmhouse we came to, we found freshly killed mutants and knew that the gunshots were in self defense not aggression. This eased our minds a little as the person ahead of us was armed but hopefully not hostile to other humans.
We never caught up to this mysterious stranger, we lost the trail when we split at a fork in the road towards Pinecrest. Nearing dark now and ahead we can see the town. The three of us tired, scared, and seriously lacking in gear set off for for the nearest building.... We never made it.
We were ambushed right outside of town, Neko caught the first shots and down he went. Brian took off into cover, I tried to follow but i blacked out (game crash). And that's all i remember about day 1.
Day 2: I awoke again, alone, right where i crashed, and a little sad because i probably wont ever see my friends again. Yet still had my gear! However meager it was. I decided Pinecrest was a little to large to tackle alone (and at night) so i skirted the town. I followed the road signs to a town called Sultan. It was much smaller and completely deserted. I started at the gas station and grocery store to fill out my pack. It was a goldmine, I found pants and a hoodie (for warmth and more carrying spots) at the Gas, and more food than i could carry at the Grocery.
I headed into town finding no one. I had food clothes and medical supplies but i really needed a gun. i went house to house in the dark, finding nothing but a military canteen. Until at the end of town behind one house in a makeshift shooting range i found a 9mm pistol and 6 rounds in a clip! Again, Sultan is being very good to me.
The last stop before i leave town is the church, outside is a toppled red bicycle, i think nothing of it, in the congregation area and between the pews there is nothing of interest. But in the basement i found what i now know is a rare item. A building guide! in my excitement i almost didn't register the "Click" that i knew to be the sound of a flashlight. I froze, and listened. Nothing. I slowly make my way out of the basement and up the stairs outside. As i reach the top i turn and see a man come out of the church. Before i have a chance to ask friend or foe, the barrel of his shotgun raised and fired. Missed! I raised my own 9mm pistol and pulled the trigger,"click!", i hadn't put the clip in the gun! The in game voip chat explodes with a foreign language, this man has backup and they're on the way.
I took the red bike and pedaled out of town with my loot and my life. Back out on the road i see a sign for Woodhaven and Horseshoe Beach. I figure if they follow me they'll think i went to the town so I headed to the beach as a thunderstorm starts to roll in. Near Horseshoe in an abandoned truck i found another weapon, my own shotgun, and 3 shells.
I reached Horseshoe and took refuge in a house by the water and decided to wait a while to see if the storm would go away (it was ramping up my cpu when on the move 95-99%). I take a deep breath and appreciate all the feels I'm having, today has been a rollercoaster. But its not over yet.
The voices are back, they sound far away but i don't trust it. I passed a larger structure on the way here and i guess its their base. I decide to sneak away under the cover of rain. Out of horseshoe, across the bridge but now there's a large 6 wheeled truck in the trees. Had i not seen it in the rain? Did the men nearby bring it? So i check it for keys and goods. Not only were there no keys, but they had removed the battery, belt, and spark plugs as well.
No good, i guess its still the bike. I don't risk heading by the men and their base, so its left and up the mountain. After a long arduous ride over the mountain i come to a small cabin and decided i was far enough away for a rest. This ends day 2.
Day 3: A new day and im feeling good. A new town was down the road (Woodhaven). Time for me to be the bully or saviour now. I climb down the mountain, (my bike had disappeared in the night) and into town. On my immediate left there's a gas station, in the parking lot are 2 mutants. I walk confidently up to one and blast it with my shotgun, it didn't die. I hit it again and it went down. I turn and switch to my pistol with 6 shots, i miss most of them. I'm not as awesome as i thought. As i turn to run away another mutant shambles into my view and is headed right for me. Only option? Up the ladder on the gas station (most have one) to the roof and wait for help.
Its getting dark and the mutants are still down the ladder, i really trapped myself. I hear some shots ring out and a mutant goes down. Am i saved? No, no I'm not, because the next shot rips into my shoulder. Not a lot of cover up here, and i only have a single shotgun shell left. But i have bandages and food. I could wait the shooter out? Try and run past the last mutant? I never got to decide because the next thing i saw was a black screen with the words "You Are Dead" on it.
9/10 would live to die again.

I won't talk about the game mechanics or anything, instead ill tell you a story.
It was dead at night, I had been shuffling around a house  with my flashlight on looking for stuff, when I heard whistling outside. I cursed my luck and clicked out my flashlight, pulling out my baseball bat. Thats when it got scary. It was pitch black, couldnt see a thing, all I could hear was whistling all around.
"I saw your flashlight." A man said, and I heard footsteps slowly coming up the stairs. I was shaking in my boots now. There was no way out. A light shone up the stairs, but I was in the corner. Up, up up they came, and just when I thought I was screwed.
Bam bam bam! Shots lit up the night, the guys screamed. They were under attack. They started firing left and right, one guy came upstairs hit and I killed him with my bat, the other two were firing out the window. I grabbed the guys gun and his clothes, as well as his gear, and went back down.
"JOHN! HELP US TAKE THESE GUYS OUT!" They shouted spotting me, and I walked towards them. But instead, I shot them both in the head. I called out,
"Im freindly! I helped take these guys out!" Turns out a friendly foreign guy saved me, we traveled together, until he tragically jumped in front of a bullet for me, and then I died by a stray molotov moments later.
10/10. Game will give you great memories.

Suggestions for your first time:
1) Break vases, Boxes.
2) Make a stick, Kill everything that night, lure them into a corner so you're protected. If you cant survive, just close the old mans Door. You're safe there.
3) Learn every Recipe you can on ur first night. Hopefully you get a Sword recipe.
4) Make urself a little house the next morning, it may take a day or two of gathering wood and recipes.
Most of all just try and enjoy the first few nights, stock up, learn recipes. Then continue with the story.

2) Using a hammer on the floor spot where a painting is Placed will cause the painting to remove from the wall.
3) Windows and Doors do not need a previous wall to socket into. They're there own item.

Pillars of Eternity, one more try to make the "sucessor of Baldurs Gate", one of the biggest Kickstarter projects made by rpg veterans Obsidian Entertainment.
So, after nearly 50 hours playtime (i´m around the last third of the game) what can i say to the big promises?
First off, the world of PoE is very detailed for a newly made one, the history, races and classes are partly innovative, partly good old fantasy genre like.
The gameplay itself naturally orientates itself on the old masters, you create your character, who can alter the fate of the world in an epic storyline, while finding allies for his group on the way through the story (which can alternatively be filled with custom made characters.. or you can even try to go through it alone).
Regarding classes there are new ones like the cipher and many known ones from barbarian to priests to the different gods (a nice extra for these is, that the way how they act throughout the game influences how "satisfied" their deity is with them).
Regarding classes and "improvements" here also shows one of the main changes of PoE, there are rather less skills, then usually known in old time rpgs. Also the classes are not limited as how they advance in them. For me, i honestly preferred the old way a bit, when not everyone could learn anything but to each his own. Also it seems to me that especially the rogue class suffers from that choice, as everyone can learn about traps etc. now.. so the only thing really special about them is backstabbing. Stealing isn´t possible anyways.
When advancing in levels the classes differentiate again a bit more through perks, which can be aquired on selected levels (some general, some bound to different requirements).
Graphic and music are top level for this kind of game, only the camera possibilities/movements could be improved, especially during battles or while in towns etc.
Regarding quests, dialogue and story in general there are few things to complain about, the main storyline is branching and quite interesting, the happenings on the way have mostly more then one way to complete them. Furthermore there are different factions you encounter and can ally with them and in general the way you behave throughout the game affects every location/faction. Last but not least you also have the possibility to get your own stronghold, which is to be restored as well as cared about.. and even has an own multiple level dungeon. Personally i would have wished for some more class specific dialogue options (especially the cipher class), but that´s a minor complain.
Your companions are well made and have their own personalities as well as quests, though could use some more banter.
On a further note regarding Obsidian and their reputation for delivering bug plagued games, i think the self management through Kickstarter helped them, as i had few problems in that regard. Also the game keeps getting improved after release.
The downside of the Kickstarter, if you want to call it one, are many KS characters, who stand around throughout towns mostly and some little sh*tstorm made once more by some extremists who were to dumb and fanatic to understand irony.
Conclusio: If you are a fan of (old) isometric, group related rpgs on an epic scale then you can´t do anything wrong with this game.

I was always a fan of the Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape: Torment, Neverwinter Nights games, and I basically grew up on them. When I read about Pillars of Eternity in the latest PC Gamer, I had to have it. Now that I've played it for a while, I remember why I always loved those older D&D games, as I've gotten sucked into this one. It's a very nice homage to those, but feels like it was meant to be played on today's computers by the original audience of those games of the past. The subject matter delves into more adult themes at times, as does the language, but hey, I'm an adult, and cursing in this genre usually makes me giggle.
