As a huge fan of the old Infinite Engine games like Baldur's Gate I had hoped for so much *more* from this game. Whilst it did much to modernise the genre, in many areas it failed to live up to the nostalgia.
Graphics - The game kept true to the art style whilst bringing it forwards into the modern era of gaming, the backdrops were breathtakingly beautiful and it played smoothly without any issues.
Sound/Voice Acting - The sound/voice acting wasn't particularly noteworthy, it wasn't terrible yet it wasnt great either, it didn't really stand out much.
Story-telling/narrative - The story was a bit vague and didn't really have much direction during the first act but it quickly picked up during the second act before slowly tapering off towards the end. There weren't any really exciting revelations or twists that made it wow me. The villain, their motivations and relationship to the protagonist were somewhat interesting but it wasn't anything that stood out. Often at times to convey just how filled out the world and backstory was you're presented with a wall of text which probably wasn't necessary and felt like it detracted from the story at times.
Gameplay Mechanics/Combat - This is probably the most disappointing aspect of the game. The game feels like it's more of a stealth crpg because they limited the experience gained from combat to just the first few initial run ins with each foe type and kept the overall experience gained from combat to a very minimal amount, along with the plethora of items that dropped from enemies being utterly useless, it often felt like the better choice was to sneak/avoid enemy encounters which just slows down the pace of the game. Avoiding combat entirely was also made more desirable by the fact that you were heavily penalised for trying to escape combat or run around or disengage with an enemy during combat which often resulted in the character dying quicker than had you just stayed in place and tried to (but likely fail to do so anyway) tank it.
Spell casting also felt more burdensome and tiring than in the older IE titles because of the resting mechanics of the game whereby you had to carry supplies to rest and were limited to only carry a certain amount of supplies with you, so if you ran out of supplies you were forced to return to a store to purchase more or not rest and not be able to heal, or restore spells for combat.
Itemisation - The difference between a normal, un-enchanted item and a unique item felt lacking. The difference in damage was minimal, I played as a barbarian and would do 80s with normal items and as high as 96 using a unique item of the same type. Another problem with the itemisation is that so many items gave boosts to player stats, but conflicting stat boosts (ie. gloves that give +1 might and boots that give +2 might) would be nullified meant that gearing most slots felt like a waste of time and forced players down the route of jack of all trades, master of none.
Overall I would rate this game as a 6/10, or in terms of similarities to the old IE games it has the combat of Planescape Torment with the story of Icewind Dale, it tries to relive the nostalgia but focuses on the wrong aspects of what made them great games.

Pillars of Eternity is an old school style RPG, similar to classic games like Baldur's Gate and NeverWinter Nights. The player controls a party of up to 6 characters from an overhead perspective, and combat is real time but with the ability to pause and issue commands. I'm a massive fan of RPGs, so I had high hopes for PoE, and it did not disappoint.
What pleased me?
•	Combat system has tactical depth. Some spells/abilities have limited uses, so you need to be careful not to spam them against weak enemies. Even the positioning of your characters is important. Some dungeons have narrow corridors/doorways so you can block a chokepoint with a tank to protect weaker characters. Meanwhile some spells do friendly damage, so you need to be intelligent with use of AOEs.
•	Multiple weapon slots for each character, so you can quickly switch between melee and ranged during combat. Sounds obvious, but some RPGs don't let you do this.
•	Can fully customise each companion's gear and abilities.
•	Most of the traditional D&D style character classes are present, but the nice surprise for me was the "Chanter" class. Its basically a Bard who has access to unlimited summon spells. After suffering through countless video games where bosses have frustrated me with infinite summons, I don't mind saying I exploited the hell out of it and it was glorious.
•	Nice mixture of enemy types - melee, ranged, summoners, teleporters, charmers and more.
•	Story starts off slow, but gradually becomes much more interesting. A secret cult are using ancient machines to steal people's souls, and the player character needs to figure out why they're doing it and how to stop them.
•	Voice acting is pretty good, especially for companions.
•	Lots of side quests, many of which have multiple solutions or ability to support different factions.
•	Character stats can influence your access to dialogue choices or quest options.
•	48 hours to finish the game, with some side quests left over.
•	Very stable, no noticeable bugs.
What disappointed me?
•	The health system is really strange. It would take too long to fully explain here, so I'll just say that healing spells and potions don't actually heal you. As someone who has played a healer since the first Baldur's Gate, I felt like my main character was kinda pointless.
•	Not all the dialogue is voiced, much of it is text only.
•	Weapons can have a wide variety of enchantments, which is normally a good thing, but the lack of an overall indication of DPS means its really hard to compare two weapons and figure out which is best.
•	Your character gains ownership of a stronghold, you can upgrade the defences, hire mercenaries to protect it while you're away ... but ultimately it doesn't really do anything or serve any greater purpose. Feels like an unfinished idea.
Overall recommendation
This is a very high quality game, and apart from a few relatively minor complaints, most of my experience with PoE was very enjoyable. Most fans of the RPG genre should enjoy playing Pillars of Eternity.

As an Arisen, you are killed only to be brought back to life by your fate, by your curse. You are one of many Arisens in the past and present who also shared the same fate, of having to be the one who saves the world from impending doom wrought by the Great Dragon, Grigori. In your quest you're given the opportunity to do many things.
In short, the game is amazing. Great fantasty setting. Great mechanics. Alright story. Amazing, but fairly small world packed with hours of meaningful, solid content and unique locations to explore. Many different Fantasty enemies that all act realistically (For a fictional fantasy monster/enemy that is) that come in both human and non-human varieties. Great combat system and a beautifullly crafted world full of immersive quests and NPC's. On sale, or full price. This game is worth it. Look past the minor issues that stem mostly from it being difficult to follow Story missions, which means the game does not clearly point you in the right way directly, and the countless unexplained mechanics or moments where story progess will instantly cancel some side quests, if you advance too far. Because this is a slightly flawed but still bright shining gem in the RPG genre that, if left unplayed, will be sorely missed, and that would be for all intents and purposes, a huge mistake.
If you like RPG's, and even certain open world adventure games. Particularly The Dark Souls series and Legend of Zelda series. Then I wholehearedly believe you will enjoy this. Even if you enjoy only one of those or neither of those, but you will find some mechanics more welcoming if you like one of those.
--------------------------------------------------------------------
--------------------------------------------------------------------
When you start the game you are given a few tasks to begin your adventure, a sort of tutorial, prologue experience.
First of which is choosing your class.
The Vocation system in Dragons Dogma is slightly different than other class ssytems of other RPG's. Whilst choosing a class at first might seem like you are locking your decision in for the whole game, this is actually the opposite.
You get three Starter Vocations. Which are available from the beginning of the game
Three more Advanced Vocations based mostly on the weapon choice and skill set of the 3 starter classes with even more skill options and Vocation particular augments and improvements not accessible by the Starter Vocations.
Three more, Hybrid Vocations. That combine two aspects, skill sets and weapon choices of two different Vocations.
The extra 6, of the three Advanced Vocations and the three Hybrid Vocations, are made available later on. But once available, you can change vocation literally any time you want. The more you use a Vocation and experience you accumulate whilst playing as said Vocation, they individually increase in Rank (Rank 1-10). As this happens you gain access to more skills, core skills (Skills not activated by weapons) and Augments. You level each Vocation to Rank 10, and you'll never lose this progress. Upon completion of the game you start New Game Plus, and you will still have your Vocation Rank progress. This makes it so you can accumulate everything the game on one character. No cluttered save system to worry about.
This system allows you create a tailored playstyle at any point in time.
Second of which is is making - Yes, MAKE. - your very own Pawn. A unique follower you handcraft in appearance and class, you determine their skills and provide them with gear. They level up with you. They learn from you, like a child following a parent. If they observe you killing an enemy a certain way they will learn that is that particular enemies' weakness, and will attempt to mimic you as best they can when facing that foe again in the future. All Arisen have their own Pawn.
The Pawn system, and the Pawn Learning system isn't just limited to your Pawn, however. If played online you can gain access to pawns made by everyone else who also plays the game online. With your own Pawn, you can hire an additional two extra pawns made by other players to help you on your journies. They will learn, just like your own pawn will, how to fight certain enemies even if their own Arisen hasn't faced that particular foe yet. But these Pawns do not level with you, so if you stick with the same Pawns for a long time, they will soon become underleveled and unbalanced, too weak to fight the strength of the monsters that are balanced to your level, the Arisen, and your Pawn's level. You can also give Hired pawns gear you find, but because they are not your Pawn, you are effectively gifting that item to the player who created them. You cannot take gear off of them that were given them by their creator. You can not take back gear that you gave to them back once equipped. So do not equip Gear you found, on Hired Pawns. Only yourself or your own Created Pawn. That being said, this is a cool feature because you can essentially gift the best gear you want, to say, a friends Pawn. Who can then use that gear themselves or keep the items you gifted them equipped on their pawn, to utilize gear way beyond their level. Which some may view as cheap, but it's still possible, nonetheless.
From here, you're off. Exploring the world, doing quests, slaying both beast and man in the form of Goblins, Cyclops', Ogre's, Hydras', Wyverns', Cockatrices, Chimeras, Necromancers, Cultists and even common Bandits.
In your quest you will meet NPC's, some of, if helped will actually help you in later quests, or NPC's like a bandit group made up of entirely women who will attack you if you or your pawns are male, (but you can always dress up in womens clothing to hide the fact you or your pawns are male ;) ), and this whilst being minor, is actually quite useful. Speaking to people is an advisement, as you never know what you might learn. If an NPC is quest related they will have an icon over their head, green if they offering a quest, yellow if they have information related to a quest you don't currently have active, red if they have information related to your currently active quest and blue if you can turn in a quest with them for the reward they'll offer. But even when they aren't related to a quest, you can learn things about the world that you might not have known otherwise, such as what types of enemies roam a location, or suggestions as to where you might find a quest.
When you are travelling the world. You're mostly required to do so by foot as there is no direct fast travel system and the map is effectively uncharted, and therefore blank until you actually travel across it and discover the world to reveal the map..But, you can fast travel through the use of Ferry Stones. These items allow you to teleport to the two Main Cities, Gran Soren and Cassardis if not Port Crystals that you manually collect and then replace in your chosen location, throughout the world to act as an additional Ferrystone travel location.
Ferrystones are normally one time use items, but you can actually get an unlimited use, Eternal Ferrystone from your Stash at the Gran Soren Inn. (And Apparently I've hit the character limit..)

This game has a number of terrible design choices, an overly simplistic leveling system, and major RPG features that are missing. Namely the lack of a fast travel system and no leveling up, in the traditional sense. Fast travel is basically absent, however you can "teleport" to a mere two different locations, the main towns in the game. Considering the map is a bit large, it leads to long bouts of mind numbingly boring jogs across the country side, worsened still by the abnormally short time you can sprint. Movement in the game is also very slow and sluggish. The default jog speed is a glorified power walk, and sprinting feels about as fast as a non sprint run in almost any other RPG game. You can sprint for about 15 seconds and to make matters worse stamina takes an unnecessarily long time to regen. The combination of these peculiar design choices leads to a heaping amount of time sunk into simply walking from place to place.
Quests are generally shallow and predictable. An abundance of fetch quests, kill quests, and notoriously bad escort quests convolutes the pace and enjoyability of questing. Even main quests are extremely predictable and generic, telegraphing their "twists" and deux ex machina's so far in advance it kills the execution of them. Go investigate a cult meeting thats taking place in a crypt, spoiler; there are skeletons and zombies.  The main antagonists in the game are shallow and cliche. A dragon bent on destruction, the religious fanatic sorcerer, and the plethora of other mustache twirling villains plague the central conflict. The plot is incohesive and an overall mess, and voice acting and writing is sub par. These poor traits make for an uncompelling experience, but there is hope yet...
The combat gameplay is the saving grace of the game. It is very simplistic and streamlined, but in a way that doesnt rob it of fun. Skills for each class are unique and have a variety of different effects and uses. You can grapple large monsters and CLIMB THEM! It is absolutely stellar and a very unique mechanic. You grab onto them, and can freely climb all over their body. Each monster has a different sweet spot, for example a cyclops will have short arms so if you navigate to its back, and cling to its shoulders it will be unable to reach you to throw you off. Climbing onto monsters heads can inflict massive damage, but is a more vulnerable area to be as they will prioritize throwing you off over your allies attacks.
You can have three companions, or AI bots really. I say that because they are not companions in the typical RPG sense, they are one dimensional bots thats only intention is to fight, and not to add flavor or depth. They have no personalities or opinions on anything, there is no playful banter during play, and they only ever talk to incessantly pester you of some obvious battle hint, like when you are 10 feet away from a goblin they will enthusiastically inform you that there is a goblin ahead. Yes thanks for that. The worst moment is basically EVERY time I fight lizards, who have soft spots on their tails which take more damage. The bots constantly exclaim "SEVER THE TAIL!" and the second it is, "THE TAIL IS SEVERED!" There are often dozens of enemies who are all squishy and die fast mind you, so nonstop during every lizard fight its "SEVER THE TAIL THE TAIL IS SEVERED" looped over and over ad naseum.
Another heart breaking blow is the archaic leveling system. Gone are the days of specifying what stats are boosted, or having ANY autonomy or choice in what kind of warrior you want to be. Levels are only ever a passive element, when you level up you are informed, and your number goes up, but that is it. Enemies scale with you so leveling is almost non existent. It takes away the fun of pushing through quests to grow your character. I cannot fathom how or why they chose to do this but it is gut wrenching that they chose to go this route, I hate having no influence over my characters stats. No customization, no nothing. :'(
The item/equipment system is also very old feeling, reminiscent of decades old Final Fantasy games. The UI is terrible and unintuitive. Items are uninteresting and rarely have any stats other than damage. No customization for weapons or armor, and the crafting system is very esoteric, and in many ways isnt worth the time or effort. Skill system is archaic and can only be modified or upgraded at an inn, which makes no sense, but I guess the inn keepers in this game are polymath combat geniuses who have mastered every aspect of battle and only they can teach skills. Also you must ask their permission to change your skills, and cannot do so unless your at an in. Oh they are also bankers of sorts and take care of your item storage. Since there is no leveling up its an extremely peculiar design choice to have players go to the inn keeper for character progression, and very disconnecting.
TLDR:
6.8/10
Overall it is a solid RPG but it feels very shallow and bland compared to most RPGs of the past 5 years. Many bad design choices further rob this game of greatness. The combat is excellent but movement is sluggish, making navigation in the game a chore. No fast travel makes for extreme pace disruption and boredom. Quest structure is also poor, with each quest wildly varying in its location but almost always guaranteed to be far as hell away. This turns questing into a series of  incredibly long pilgrimages to and from their locations, taking upwards of TWENTY MINUTES of time roundtrip for most quests not in your immediate vicinity. The fact that most quests are generic fetch/kill/escort type, makes it difficult to even find the will and motivation to do some quests. Questing is one of the pillars of gameplay loops in RPGs, and because of this games poor design choices with quest structure, it is a crippling blow to its enjoyability. Graphics are a little dated by todays standards, but are still good. Terrain and overall world detail and style is on the bland side, but cities and architectural styles on castles and buildings looks great.
I would recommend this game ONLY for RPG fanatics who are either bored and have nothing to play, or dont mind games which are rough around the edges. For the price of $20-30, it is hard to feel the cost is not justified with this game, despite its many shortcomings. There is a lot to do and some great moments in combat against monsters. This may be flawed and just short of greatness, but it is FAR FROM being a bad game.

내가 스플린터셀을 좋아하는 이유는 두가지가 있어서였는데.
하나는 마이클 아이언사이드의 매력적인 목소리였고,
또 하나는 정확히 내가 생각해온 잠입 액션이었기 때문이다.
아쉽게도 내가 좋아하던  마이클 아이언사이드는 이번 작품에서 성우를 맡지는 않았지만 그래도 괜찮다.
스플린터셀 컨빅션과 블랙리스트는 마치 영화 한편을 방불케하는 속도로 적을 제압하며 그 재미는 충분히 보장할 정도로 잘 만들어졌다.
물론 컨빅션 이전작들을 즐겼던 올드 유저 팬들에게는 아주 미안한 이야기이다.
그 작품을 모두 즐겨본 나로써도 느끼지 않는 바는 아니다.
약간은 느릿한 한걸음 한걸음이 캐릭터와 동화되는 느낌은 아직도 잊을 수 없다.
그렇지만 이 게임을 보라.
완벽하게 만들어진 마크 앤 엑스큐트 시스템과 불빛의 상호작용. 높은 난이도를 자랑하는 AI.
게다가 출전하기 전에 장비까지 스스로 정할 수 있다.
게임은 3가지 스타일로 나뉘며 그 어느것이라도 당신이 정할 수 있다.
적을 기절만 시키거나 사살하거나.
혹은 둘다 하거나!
게이머는 샘피셔라는 캐릭터로 미국을 지키는 잠입, 암살을 계속한다.
그에게 부여된 다섯번째 자유를 행사함으로써 자국과 타국을 지키는 영웅적인 행보를 계속한다.
스토리는 故톰 클랜시의 작품인데 앞으로도 이 스플린터셀 시리즈가 계속해서 나올지 혹은 아닐지는 모르는 일이다. 하지만 이 대단한 작품이 계속해서 나오지 않는다면 필자는 매우 실망할 것이다.

First off, the game is quite a bit more complicated than the previous games, now this may be a good or bad thing depending on how difficult you like your games but needless to say even if you've played the previous games there is a very steep learning curve (that is factoring in the fact that total war games are already a bit harder than normal to get down). Second, Visually the game is very drab out of combat, unlike Shogun where you find yourself enjoying the map and the artistic style of things, I find that Total war Atilla uses quite a bit of brown colors that make looking at the overall map (which is where you will spend a majority of the game) a bit dull, now if we are talking about in battle graphics and everything there are no complaints from me and if anything they are one of the better Total wars obviously. If you're looking to play this game then buckle up, kiddo, you're in for a ride.
Experience the beginning of the epic journey with your custom or default Commander Shepard with a gender of your choice.
Get sucked into a huge universe so full of lore, that three games wasn't enough to fit it all in, no, there's books (three worth mentioning and one worth forgetting) and comics and even a movie. AND there's another game coming next year, how great is that?
Explore a vast galaxy with numerous planets to land on in a huge number of clusters.
Freeze your lovely behind off on Noveria, jump the Mako over pits of Lava on Therum or stomp Geth with them (the Mako rocks, I don't care what anybody says), enjoy the scenery on Virmire (because that's the only thing you'll be enjoying there) and get lost on Ilos (every goddamn time).

Back in about 2004 when I was around 3-4 years old I first found this game on Popcap as the free online version. It had no music, and only one area but I remember playing it for hours. It was simple, but it was the perfect blend of tricky mechanics and pacing that kept me coming back.
Fast-forward to about 2012 to when I was around 12 my father had purchased a Popcap collection that included this along with some other favorites of mine like Heavy Weapon. I remember being glued to it for hours. I'd never had so much fun with it as I had with any other game. At the time I had played stuff like XIII, the Sly Coopers, Ace Combat 5, Call of Duty Finest Hour, Medal of Honor Frontline, and some of the classics such as Deus Ex and Half-Life. Yet the music and the simple structure of Insaniquarium gave me a sense of euphoria that I hadn't felt before at the time. Much of it was childhood nostalgia but I remembered at the time admiring the atomspehere and rising difficulty. For being about 11-12 the amount of fish and money required to finish each level was enough of a challenge to encourage me to keep going. I remembered finding the levels in the 4 area to be outright hell. The concepts were simple to follow, the bosses were varied to create some doubt when entering a new level. The music was very cheerful and inviting, setting a friendly environment for the most part and but even the later levels also created a sense of the rising challenge. There's only about 5 tracks but each sets the mood all on its own without too much duplication, with the exception of the main menu music being reused for level 4. At the time, it was a firm favorite that seemed to encompass everything I found to be fun with elements of management, survival, and even a minor shooting portion thrown in. All within a game about feeding fish. It seemed flawless.
Fast-forward to about 2016 when I opened this account. Having been unable to own a computer powerful enough for Steam for years I was supremely curious to see what was available here. When I discovered that the old gems of Popcap were available I snapped it up instantly (Inspite of it being about $80 at the time). I immediately downloaded the favorites: Heavy Weapon, Chuzzle, Hammer Heads, and of course, Insaniquarium. And so the question presented itself, did the game still hold up 5 years later at the age of 17? Well right off the bat I could say that the difficulty certainly was not what I remembered. When was a kid the game took me quite some time to beat as I said I found the level 4 area to be hell quite often. Well after being dedicated to beating it I swept through the game across a few days with a collective time of about 6 hours. The management boiled down to just setting up a system that got you the money you needed without committing fish genocide and staying within your complusory money-burning budget to get each egg shard to complete the level. The bosses themselves were only a minor disturbance especially because I did not remember what type was what. All except for the Squid monster, screw that one. Being invulnerable and then laying waste to countless fish peoples upon normalizing caused more headaches and vexations than I remembered. The convoluted set-up of guppys to guppy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to beatle ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the level 3 area was both an inviting challenge and a Gordian Knot constructed only with the purpose of slowing down your monopolization of the fish and egg-shard market. Otherwise the levels were still fun. Although shorter on account of me panicking less when fish started turning into skeletons due to Squid and Robot genocide, the fact that they were short kept everything fun and fresh as it meant I didn't have to spend an hour to get through the level. They were long enough for me to enjoy the set-up of the money machine and short enough for me to glide along the levels like the fish I was raising (starving). The music was still as cheery and memorable too. I found myself looking up the tracks afterward and playing them while I was doing other things. The first level especially does a fantastic job and constructing the friendly tone of the game. This game is meant for you to have fun with your fish-slavery and money-grubbing efforts. But holy smokes I need to talk about the Credit music. So when I cut the head off of area 4 I found myself at the big showdown when you need to kill the evil menace sending all the evil monsters to destroy your perfect ecosystems. This battle when even high stakes as your population consisted of your pets, the life-long allies that meant the difference between failure and securing yet another pet. So it was both heart-breaking to see them slaughtered and hectic to keep them alive. When the smoke cleared, I had about 4 survivors. But don't worry, that angel fish you acquired like a level ago purposely stayed out of the fight to keep them alive. So the credits roll as my crew is brought back from the watery grave and in a game with a colorful and bright atmosphere the music is surprisingly somber and sad. It's slow and drags along, filling an empty void with a sense of loss. I really found myself not wanting to leave the game as this music played. For me credits and final boss tracks at their best when I get a sense of loss. If the game is really good and doing its job I should be left wanting more and to never leave in the first place. For how simple it is the credits music really left me in that state. I had to sit through it and absorb it all until the end. It's probably one of the few times I've found myself wanting to sit through a credits screen. For that reason alone I give this game a solid 9/10. For a simple point-and-click management game it does its job really well of giving you a bright atmosphere with a fun challenge filled in. There aren't very many decisions and you won't find yourself regretting your purchases too often but the pacing of the game flows smoothly enough to keep me hooked into capping off every area. With that said my nostalgia did not preserve the difficulty or even the little feeding simulator where you can raise fish for shells and steadily upgrade your community within that tank. That for me took too long to build up any money for anything and if you wanted to get the upgrades for the tank like the Bubblator you needed BIG cash. Cash that you could realisitically only get from doing the other gamemodes. That system would be fine if the virtual tank had more impact on the core gameplay. Otherwise the only motivation for getting said shell currency is for the secret pets which can in itself be the ultimate reward. While I liked killing some time with it it wasn't the Zen Garden from Plants vs Zombies where I could get money at a fairly decent rate for some fantastic new plants and upgrades. All in all the feature is something that you might return to on occassion but I didn't find myself sticking to it long.
So that's it, Insaniquarium. The game about fish-feeding that's so insane, it's kept alive and swimming for over 15 years.

Feel The Snow offers a great mixture of combat, survival, and crafting your homestead with a isometric perspective and a 16-bit feel to it.
Despite the simplicity, FtS became one of my favorites of the genre right off the bat. Albeit, at the time of this review, it could use a little more content (i.e. more uses for stone, maybe another tier of weaponry/crafting?), but that doesn't detract from the winter wonderland feel of the game, while managing to feel like a cozy little adventure.
Combat feels powerful with an attack, a block, and a dodge move, exploration feels fruitful with a host of plans and ingredients needed to craft different things, and inventory management feels tight without being frustrating.
Overall, the only things that really bug me about the game are the hit detection (as blocking is direction-dependent), and the fact that plans and schematics are given out randomly. I was unfortunate enough to find the "Chest" schematic long after I'd dumped wave after wave of items because they couldn't fit in my inventory. Giving the players the Chest schematic earlier in the game would do a world of good.

PoE is a throwback to the older style cRPG's. It uses the Unity Engine to its maximum capability, so load screens might be an issue for younger gamers. I've been around gamming since the beginning, so PoE is like a cleaned up trip down memory lane, everything is brighter and shinier. One of the big problems with the old cRPG’s was that they based the system off of Dungeons and Dragons (2e) and it didn’t translate well to the format, so some of the classes/skills weren’t as useful and were oftentimes avoided. It was also a very real possibility to build an unplayable character that could paint themselves into a corner. PoE has made all the classes and options viable in different ways. They also made farming a possibility if you are feeling underpowered, but you can quickly overpower yourself doing that. The downside to their fixes is that it’s not as difficult as cRPG’s were. This style of cRPG is combat-centric, so if you are looking for something different you should move along. Otherwise this is a great modernization for people that liked the Baldur’s Gate/Icewind Dale style of games.

Not that excellent as everyone claims, but a really solid game with in-depth combat strategies and clever plot. Overall impression of the game is very positive. I give it
.
+ Interesting and clever plot.
+ In-depth and mature world.
+ Likable and well-considered NPCs - both, those you can invite to your party, and those you just meet on your journeys.
+ Excellent graphics. Beautiful, vivid scenery.
+ Good character creation with interesting attribute dependency.
+ Enchanting. Though it needs some polishing, e.g. creating certain point in your stronghold to do enchanting or making it only available at a smithy.
+ Well considered and voiced (english) antagonist (Thaos ix Arkannon).
+ Well written quests. In most cases you need to think twice before completing and majority of them have more than one solution.
+ Challenging combat.
+ Experience gain.  You get XP mostly from quests and only limited amount from slaying enemies. It encourages to search for more solutions to quests than just hacking and slashing through enemies.
+ Feels almost like good old classics (i.e. Icewind Dale or Baldur's Gate series) :)
- Too long loading screens.
- You have to pay for hireling and they cost you a lot. Also they are always 1 level behind. No option to create custom party to play with.
- Maximum character level is 12.
- Lack of more choices to make at times.
- Stronghold is useless. The only good thing about it are additional quests. Apart from that it's pretty much for nothing.*
- Terrible companion quests. They take too much time to progress. You need to keep talking to your team and some dialogues are far too long, tiring and really boring (like Durance or Grieving Mother quest lines). Also some of them seem to be linked to the main plot which disables you from completing them when you want to but forcing you to drag the NPCs with you all the time even if you don't need them. The best idea of companion quests I ever encountered was in Mass Effect 2, where you were simply given a loyalty quest to accomplish and after that the companion received a bonus ability and tightened the relationship with the protagonist. Really, THAT simple.
- Spell uses per rest. I prefered to use ciphers who have unlimited spells pool and their mana is regenerated according to their participation in combat. I would like to see other casters have mana to fuel their spell uses and similar to cipher mana recovery system. OR simply applying cooldowns for certain spells so that you can use them all the time after they are ready to re-cast.
*- No use for the mercenaries you hire. If the stronghold is being sieged they can't protect it. They only make diference if you arrive to defend the stronghold yourself. (Then they fight along your side, but what's the point if you can easily handle any kind of threat yourself)
*- Prison? No point of imprisoning enemies/characters since you have no further use of them anyway.
*- Stronghold buffs. When you rest at your stronghold you get buffs, but they are severely underpowered in comparison to what you get in any kind of inn.

PROS:
Story starts out strong and is engaging.
Most quests give a better option of resolving them than most modern games have where your only options are Good (Lawful Stupid) and Evil (Punting a Kitten)
Combat is entertaining (more so if you're a caster).
The healer class (Cleric) can be more than just a heal bot since it has a nice range of debuffs and some damage spells as well.
Hits all the right spots for nostalgic people of Baldur's Gate/IWD games.
CONS:
Combat gets very easy toward the end of the game once your casters learn their final tier of spells. Mages can paralyze everything, including the hardest monsters in the game which trivializes the fight.
Third act feels a bit more rushed than the previous two.
Ranged weapons are very overpowered. It seems like they want your party to consist of 1 tank and 5 gun using party members.
Main quest line can get lost in the mix of the second act if you are working on all the additional side quests.
Overall:
It felt like an updated (graphically) version of Baldur's Gate, and the isometric playstyle still holds up well today.
It's certainly one of the best crowdfunded games that has been made.
It's a shame there is no option for co-op/multiplayer like the Baldur's Gate series and Divinity: Original Sin
If you do all the side quests, you will spend a lot of time in the game. You'll get your money's worth.
Highly recommended to fans of the RPG genre!

Don't let my 10-hour-playtime on Steam fool you; due to an unknown bug, Steam stopped tracking my stats for Uplay games. I've played
for well over 30 hours, and it's a stealth experience unlike any other.
The Pros:
·
is a perfect combination between Conviction and Pandora Tomorrow.
· Choose your playstyle. Whether you're new to the series or a die hard Splinter Cell fan like myself, you'll definately find your cup of tea here no matter what. There are three different playstyles: Ghost, panther and assault. Ghost will have you completing a level without anyone ever noticing you've even been there. Use your gadgets and avoid getting close to hostiles but take them out in a silent, non-lethal manner when you must. Panther allows you to play a more brutal but still silent approach. Mark three targets, crouch-dash to a nearby fourth hostile, take him out with a stab to the throat and shoot the other three with a silent headshot by simple pressing the button. Assault lets you go in guns blazing, not caring about detection what so ever, as long as it gets you through the level. Unsilenced weapons, grenades, taking hostiles as human shield and bashing their heads against the wall when all the bullets that needed soaking have been soaked. All this can change in the blink of an eye. Situations will rarely feel the same depending on your playstyle. I played hundreds of hours of Conviction, so the Panther style allows me to build upon the experience I've gained through playing Conviction.
· A strong cast of characters. Sam Fisher himself, his daughter Sarah Fisher, Anna Grímsdottír, Andriy Kobin, the new isaac Briggs and Charlie Cole and many others all have a certain chemistry with each other due to events in the previous Splinter Cell titles, which makes the story a lot more dynamic.
· Where Pandora Tomorrow allowed you to choose your loadout at the beginning of a mission,
lets you create your own custom loadouts, complete with primary and secondary weapons and gadgets, but also upgradable goggles, vests, gloves, pants and boots that can be purchased with money you earn for completing missions. This allows you to mold Sam's equipment to your playstyle even further, as your outfit can either be heavily armored or extremely light and stealthy.
· Many cool moves make Sam fast and agile. There are countless animations when you're taking down an enemy which is extended upon by the choice of lethal and non-lethal takedowns, you can swiftly climb along wall, pipes, ropes, ledges and what not, and the "sprint" allows you to move faster and vault over obstacles instantly.
The Cons:
· The shadows often don't look dark enough to be believable. You can, in theory, stand a few meters in front of an enemy and they won't notice the bright lights on your armor. These same lights will indicate when you are visible or not though, so it's generally clear to know when you can be spotted and when you're safe in the shadows.
· If you're not playing with a controller, the controls might sometimes be a bit frustrating. I started playing with a keyboard and mouse and it felt like it didn't offer the precision I needed in terms of movement. If you have an Xbox controller, I recommend using it. Sam's movements feel a lot smoother and the gameplay is overal more controllable when you have a full 360° rotation with a joystick.
The Visuals:
· Superb. Amazing camera positions durning cutscenes, great lighting effects, detailed and varying levels, gorgeous textures. It's everything you'd expect from a Ubisoft game.
Final Verdict:
·
is hard to hate because it offers playstyles for almost anyone, from die-hard Splinter Cell veterans to newcomers to the stealth genre. 9.5/10

The latest edition of Koei's historically accurate action game, set in the tumultuous years following the decline of the Han Dynasty.  If you have played any of the previous titles, this game will probably seem at least somewhat familiar.  Deploy a general, tactician, or otherwise noteworthy character from the Romance of 3 Kingdoms, and rampage across the battlefield, taking out hundreds of grunts, officers, and bosses along the way.  This particular title takes a sort of "best of both worlds" approach to the gameplay, implementing the weapon change and element system of DW7 while also giving every character a unique weapon set like earlier titles--that way, you can either play the characters with their EX weapons, or mix and match for your favorite combination.
Gameplay modes are mostly bog standard for the (x) Warriors series.  All four kingdoms -- Wei, Wu, Shu, and Jin -- have a Musou (story) mode route that mostly follows the progression of the plot of Rot3K, joined by the Lu Bu story mode from Xtreme Legends; and a set of stages for unaffiliated forces such as Dong Zhuo, Yuan Shao, etc.  The XL expansion stages for every kingdom are included, as well.  Within the story mode, you are limited to a set group of characters for each stage; after beating each stage, however, you can play using any character in free mode.  Along with story mode and free play is a Challenge Mode, using set characters to clear one of five different goals.  And each story mode includes extra stages and a special path split, activated by meeting certain goals in each stage.  Usually, this amounts to preventing major characters from dying as they did in the original story.
The last mode is Ambition Mode, in which you build up your own base and army.  Within Ambition Mode, you choose your main officer and engage in a variety of timed battles, where you collect materials for upgrading buildings and forging weapons; as well as battling named officers.  The officers you defeat join your forces, and can be used as bodyguards and as playable characters, if they are one of the many major characters in-game.
Graphically, this game is a mixed bag.  Parts of it closely resemble the Complete Edition released on PS4.  The playable officer models are quite detailed, and have been noticibly touched up compared to the original 360/PS3 editions of this game.  However, level textures and NPC's have not gotten the same treatment; the latter is especially obvious in a few cutscenes, where you can see just how murky and unrefined the skins are on the normal mooks.  Generally, though, it's not going to be extremely obvious due to the pace of gameplay.  Nonetheless, it does seem like they may have skimped a bit on the graphical touch-ups compared to the next-gen console re-release; no real reason why they didn't go full bore.  At the time I'm reviewing this, the game only includes the English voice track, which is missing intermission narration and voice-overs outside of cutscenes; the Japanese track has yet to be released as DLC.  Given how Koei has handled this on console, this will likely be released as a free update or free DLC in the near future.
Other than that, the other major issue with the game is a lack of multiplayer outside of split-screen local MP.  The lack of online co-op is confusing, given that the console versions DO have online play; hopefully this will be changed in a later update.
DW8XL is overall the best game in the series available on PC right now, and among the best Warriors games, period, second maybe to Warriors Orochi 3.  There's a pretty good return on investment in terms of play time.  Five story modes, each with a branching path for the second half; a couple dozen more extra stages from the Xtreme Legends addon; and as a nice time-killer in Ambition Mode, all mean that there's plenty of stuff to keep you busy.

[PC]  Release date: May 28th of 2008. Now, November of 2016 and I can't forget the things I did on my first playthrough of Mass Effect. This game is fun, one of the gems of the late 2000's.
You will be Shepard. Man or woman, you will be immersed in an galatic war. And some of the choices that you will make will influence the stories in later games (such as Mass Effect 2 and 3). That was the promise and developers delivered in a way. Keeping that in mind, and only considering this game, I want to be concise:
+ Atemporal feel: Almost eight years has passed since release and this game can captivate you anyway. Once you enter the game mind set there is no turn back. You forget you're playing an old gem.
+ Over 60 hours of game: I played this game gathering everything and doing all the quests being a Lone Survirvor Soldier Paragon. At least 60 hours of gameplay if you're lucky. Do the numbers if you want to retry changing things, or your class, or your gender.
+ Character customization: Make yourself. Or don't.
+ Skill System: this is fun to play with, because they have and impact in gameplay, not only in combat, but in conversations too. TIP: try to develop Charisma. You will thank me later (if you want control).
+ Weapon customization: this is fun, sort of. See the "sort of cons".
+ Amazing history and pacing: Captivating. The introduction of the set is good. The game hold your hand a lot, but that's not a bad thing if a lot of new names and classes and people and whatever. There is a LOT of backstory and only a minor portion you will have to read. The rest you can hear it or talk your way down history lessons by old characters. Pacing is good, you will not get lost despite the massive amount of information about Mass Cores, races, diplomatic discussions, etc.
+ Elcors: (Funny approach) Elcors are fun. You will understand that later.
+ Multiple choices: this should be explained.

a. Moral System: you can choose two paths in this game being a goodie-I-will.all-do and being and kickass-badass♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(and you will do everything two) . BOTH are entertaining and have their perks. They're quite the opposite though, be aware that sometimes you will say some things that are pretty extreme and there is no neutral-in-between.
b. Questing: There are a lot of quests. Some have major impact in the story, some are kind of unrelated, some give you money. You can go straight in principal missions or do side quests. TIP: do some sidequest to get the feel of the story.
c. Paramour: No. I will not write any further.
d. Galaxy Map: It is a wide galaxy indeed. There is a lot to explore.
- System is detectable: In conversations, you would recognize that when you start. You want to be good? Up. You want to be badass? Down. You want to know more? Left. You unlocked that thingy thing? Up-left; down-left. Kills uncertainty and immersion, but it is ok for some people that want to follow a personality line.
- Unlimited ammo: yes, ammo is unlimited. Some people would be offended about that fact. You will deal with heat and heatsinks. I think this is ok.
- Combat system: In my opinion is fun to play, and your allies are no dumb either. In comparison with ME2 and ME3 (later games of the franchise) is better. But on its own merits the game is fine.
- Stalling: You can stall the story while doing quests. This can be something bad because kills pacing and the sense of dread in the galatic status of things. No kidding. But if you want to stall because you want to do sidequest that can be blocked in later stages of the game.
- Acummulation: a lot of loot. A lot of garbage. Sell all and then...
- Too much money: YES. THIS IS TRUE. Too much money can be a trouble, it kills the difficulty, and the feeling of making strategic decisions on gear. You can buy anything.
- You can't finish the triology on STEAM. Now I cry.
* Some people will say that male Shepard is kind of flat (voice). I think is kind of ok, but I wished a scream once in a while. Otherwise is fine.
No game is perfect.
- Iteration: Some side quests are too repetitive. Go down on the car, explore,
, use, use, go back. REPEAT. This is a mild con, because you see... if you are familiar to RPG and questing, you know you will have to repeat.
- Mako and planet exploration: You will hate it. Because of repetition and unrelated bugs. Getting stuck in a desert planet is no fun.
- Veteran: It is not that hard. Trust me. You will overcome.

Stranded deep is an extremely promising early access game that needs to add more variety and features.
I had been waiting for stranded deep for a LONG time before it's early access release. It was the perfect type of game for me. When it came out I did not enjoy it as much as i thought i would. Don't get me wrong, I REALLY like the game, but I just can't bring myself to love it, and that's because of one thing.
Stranded deep is a very good early access game, it runs exetremely well, rarely crashes. It does have a substantial amount of bugs but most of these are just funny and do not take away from the game, and the bad ones are removed within one patch. The game looks amazing and is such a good idea, and now all the developers need to do is add more things to the game.
As of now, the game is very simple. You go from island to island, explore wrecks, collect loot, build bases, deal with wildlife, deal with weather, collect food & water and survive. This is exactly what the description of the finished game should be (plus escape back home, or any other cool things the developers can think of), it just needs to be fleshed out. There needs to be more types of everyhting. More wrecks (maybe even caves or other natural exploration areas), more loot, better base building, more (and interesting) wildlife, and in my opinion the most important of all: more types of islands, besides the generic, tiny palm tree islands. I would love to see tiny sandbars, or a massive jungled island, or a grassy island, or a large desert island.
Overall, I would reccomend you this game the way i would reccommend any good (emphasise good) early access game. If it looks interesting to and you want to get in on the developement or just join in as the game develops, I would highly reccommend it.

PROS:
Story starts out strong and is engaging.
Most quests give a better option of resolving them than most modern games have where your only options are Good (Lawful Stupid) and Evil (Punting a Kitten)
Combat is entertaining (more so if you're a caster).
The healer class (Cleric) can be more than just a heal bot since it has a nice range of debuffs and some damage spells as well.
Hits all the right spots for nostalgic people of Baldur's Gate/IWD games.
CONS:
Combat gets very easy toward the end of the game once your casters learn their final tier of spells. Mages can paralyze everything, including the hardest monsters in the game which trivializes the fight.
Third act feels a bit more rushed than the previous two.
Ranged weapons are very overpowered. It seems like they want your party to consist of 1 tank and 5 gun using party members.
Main quest line can get lost in the mix of the second act if you are working on all the additional side quests.
Overall:
It felt like an updated (graphically) version of Baldur's Gate, and the isometric playstyle still holds up well today.
It's certainly one of the best crowdfunded games that has been made.
It's a shame there is no option for co-op/multiplayer like the Baldur's Gate series and Divinity: Original Sin
If you do all the side quests, you will spend a lot of time in the game. You'll get your money's worth.
Highly recommended to fans of the RPG genre!

Where can I begin? Pillars of Eternity is Obsidians love letter to the Black Isle Infinity Engine role-playing games of the '90s, gloriously brought up to date with minimal hitches. While the game has gone gold, they're still making balance changes to the familiar(and new) classes.
Anyone that's played any iteration of Dungeons and Dragons will recognize the staples of the Fighter, Wizard, Rogue and Druid for the most part. The games wrinkle on Paladins, Priests, Barbarians and Rangers make them feel unique and their custom classes(the Cipher which is similar to a Psionic and the Chanter, a Bard-like class) stand out quite well.
The combat is point and click with the ability to pause(or slow down) the combat to make on the fly decisions, only really  marred by a slightly finicky "Engagement System"(especially with a multitude of enemies that love to teleport directly to your squishiest party members) and a pathing system that does not want to work at all sometimes.
The story itself is a bit of a standard "thrust into greatness" kind of deal, with your character becoming ill while traveling to another territory and getting caught in what's known as a Biawac, a storm that rips the souls from a persons very being, killing them outright. However, you not only do NOT die but become what is known as a "Watcher", a person that can manipulate souls on a personal level. What starts out as a quest to find a "cure" for your condition or at least find out what happened turns into a race to save the kingdom of Dyrwood from an insidious conspiracy.
Now, what makes the games story good are the interesting NPC party members you get. From the dirty old man of a Priest of Magran, Durance to the jovial giant of a scholar Kanas, the whole cast is voiced and written well.
Onto the writing, it drips with atmospheric detail and is easily the strongest point of the game and quite an enjoyable read.
For a newcomer to the kind of game this represents, it can be daunting with all the numbers and percentages and terms but it offers tutorials and multiple difficulty settings as well. For veterans, this is a glorious callback to the "days of yore" of CRPGs and I heartily recommend it to anyone that's enjoyed an Infinity Engine game in the past.

I'll try to be short cause most people don't read long reviews anyway..
My opinion of the game after having finished it and having 90+ hours of gameplay is :
-- it's basically a remake of Baldur's Gate § Neverwinter Nights with today's graphics and technology.
The story is different, but everything else is either identical or slightly modified.
+ vs -
+ it's polished, I hardly had any bugs at all, it runs smooth, except for the loading screens and save/load games which became longer and longer as I played
+ The monk (which in other games I played was underpowered) was absolutely awesome without being OP. I loved playing that character.
+ The story is ok, actually, it's more than ok, i'ts very detailled and interesting. I even find it well written at times.
+(?) it's got a lot of feature identical to Baldur's Gate, even the "help a man in a fight outside a bar and he joins your party afterwards" (NW2 with the dwarf), to many, this is a positive thing I guess
I can't really think of anything else, it all runs smooth with not to many hiccups.
- It feels like it's not a finished product
- It feels shallow and not coherent, example : big city has riots, you go back there after a short while, almost everything is as before except for one or two NPCs who say a few different things
- though the background story is pretty good I think, the actual conversation scripts and peripheral story writing can be absolutely terrible at times, I was sometimes literally smacking my head
- they did reproduce from the old successfull RPGs, but reproducing from a good game doesn't make a game good.... they didn't build on anything, they didn't push any barriers, they didn't bring any depth to the characters and the story or even the setting, the world and so on.
It felt like a polished but unfinished game. There was no creativity, there was nothing "new" except for details mostly related to modern technology.
Conclusion : It's like playing Baldur's gate I and II and NW 1 and 2 mixed together with today's technology and a different story.
ie, nothing special.
conclusion : I did enjoy playing it for a while though I got bored as well after a while, I only finished it out of principle. And I'm sure many people will enjoying playing it, in fact whoever's reading it, you'll probably have a "nice" time playing it.
But it's certainly not an exceptional game, certainly not as good as all the hype was saying and certainly not worth the price when you compare that to games like The Witcher 3.
10-20 euros, yeah, good buy, but other than that ..

From the makers of Recettear: An Item Shop’s Tale, comes this more traditional action-RPG in the vein of, say, Secret of Mana or even, perhaps, a more primitive form of Final Fantasy XII (the behind the back view definitely lends itself to this). It’s definitely Japanese in origin, as the voice-overs and general aesthetic will attest, but thankfully all the dialog, menus and other text is translated sardonically and wonderfully into English. Add that wondrous old-school aesthetic that plants the look of the game firmly into the PlayStation (One) days, and you’ve got a winner in my book.
The story is a rather unique one; Chante and Elise are sisters, as the subtitle implies. They’re about to get a whole lot closer; being warned not to venture out at night under the ‘red moon,’ (a Blood Moon, perhaps! Good thing they weren’t swarmed by monsters! (A reference to one of my previous reviews, for Terraria!) they do so anyway, somehow being ‘called’ outside. Well, suddenly there’s a big flash of light, and Chante is transformed into a little fairy!
This starts their quest; in order to reverse the transformation spell, Chante and Elise (you control Elise) must travel to various locations, battling enemies along the way, and finding NPCs to talk to and receive new tasks. Chante has received two major boons along with her fairy transformation: the ability to use magic, and a sharp tongue! You may well find yourself in trouble thanks to Chante’s penchant to not keep her tiny mouth shut; it’s like she makes up for her newly small body with a larger-than-life presence.
However, the usefulness of her ability to use the magic crystals that regularly drop from defeated enemies can’t be denied. Lock on to an enemy and hit a button and boom, they disappear in an elemental flash, or your defenses are otherwise buffed up. Combinations of two of the same (at least at first) elemental crystals result in a much more powerful effect.
Leveling is done, much like the aforementioned Terraria, through acquisition of equipment (rings, armor pieces, other trinkets). Before you choose to enter a region in Story Mode, you can choose a Time Trial mode on each area within that region that you’ve unlocked, to try for the best times and best item collection rate.
A charming RPG done in the classic style; it’s awesome to see something like this in these modern times with their obsession with photo-realistic graphics and incredible sound. You who’ve read this space before know my issues with this era’s apparent apathy of its roots; it’s refreshing, then, to see a tribute, as I see it, of those old times; as I said, it wouldn’t be out of place on a PlayStation (One), and I wouldn’t have it any other way. Five out of five, gladly!

I am a die hard Tolkien fan. The first book read to me as a child was the hobbit. I've read through all of Tolkien's work multiple times since I was a kid and I can tell you these stories are sacred to me. I know these games are not cannon, but they feel like they very well could be. From a storyline perspective, they do a really good job of incorporating things we know from tolkien's writing and then filling in the blank sections in history with events that seem highly probable. The twisting of evil in Mordor feels right. The orcs are at the same time brutal and suffering, something that is a requirment for the children of Morgoth. Playing through you come to care about both Talion and Celebrimbor and (as long as you seek out runes and other items of lore) you can see how they fit together as a pair. Although the first DLC is somewhat superficial, the second DLC expands the storyline fully by allowing you to play through the moment when Celebrimbor originally dies and becomes cursed. You see his decent into madness, losing himself and becoming blinded by the need to destroy Sauron. Eventually even Talion comes to this conclusion. Seriously, it just feels so damned good to live the story this way.
Gameplay is of course quite fluid and satisfying. If you go straight for main storyline quests and rush them, you can speed run the game in maybe 5-10 hours. If you take your time and explore the lore and side quests, you'll be able to spend a good 50-60 in the game. It is an open word game so you need to keep that in mind.
I originally played this game years ago and just decided to play through it one more time (this time with the DLC since it didn't exist when I finished my 1st playthrough) and was very happy with the end result. My hope is that the sequel does everything right and we get another really well realized Tolkien game.

One of the best games I've ever played.
It's janky as all hell and you're pretty much expected to go grab the DSFix community-made hack/patch to make it as playable as possible. But past the over-exaggerated difficulty and immense lack of polish, the game's a beautiful diamond.
The pros:
The land of Lordran, is a sprawling and extremely impressively designed fantasy world.
All the lore and backstory for Lordran is so obsfucated and fragmented that it's like a little metagame trying to piece it all together.
The enemies, both the common fodder, the unique encounters and the bosses are big, tough and pretty diverse in their designs and abilities.
There's a wealth of character and equipment mixing, matching, upgrading and infusing to give you any number of unique builds, for pretty much any given scenario.
And the multiplayer, both co-op and PVP, is every bit as fun to be a part of as it is infuriating [unless the other people are hacking, in which case it's only the latter]
The cons:
It's a pretty terrible port. Unless you're a masochist and have made sure to install DSFix and the mouse fix that hooks into it, I wouldn't recommend trying to play it with KB+M, just use a gamepad. I mean if you're dedicated enough, you definitely can learn the keyboard controls, (I know I did) but it's a nightmare without the mouse fix up and running.
The game's getting on in its age. It will always have the fanatics who play it constantly, but plenty of people have stopped or moved on to Dark Souls 2, Dark Souls 3, or the PS3's Bloodborne, all by the same company [From Software] and using the same basic formula. If you're more interested in what a Souls game's multiplayer is like than anything else, DS3 might be your best bet at the time of this review.
As stated earlier, hacking was a pretty bad deal in its hayday. I'm not quite sure where everything stands today, but for dealing with those prudes who are still going hard on the hacks, there's another fan-made hack/patch thing that fixes it to some extent called PVP Watchdog. It will tell you when someone's hacking and give you the chance to kick them out, something you're not able to do normally unless you can kill the other player [which somehacks would obviously prevent you from doing]
The game's difficulty is exaggerated, but it's still tough to get the hang of, and dying over and over to infuriating mistakes can quickly kill one's fun.
Over all, I still think this is a game worth getting. It originally came with Games for Windows Live for its multiplayer, but a few years ago they moved it entirely onto Steamworks; you don't have to deal with having that horrible cancer on your computer any more. Even though it's getting old and people are moving on, there's still a decent playerbase for it, and with all the fan patches and texture mods, the jankiness of the bad port is diminished.

Took 3 times to get into the game, not understanding why somebody would want to play a game that guarantees failure. The third time something clicked and I felt like I was 12 years old again trying to work through old RPGs on the N64 and Sega Genesis. The difficulty doesn't gaurantee failure, it encourages exploration and practice. Having to return to your corpse to recover your souls broke my "run and gun" strat I use in every other game. The emotional tension of trying to recover massive amounts of souls or running low on flasks is like nothing I've felt in gaming for a very, very long time.
No game has given a bigger sense of accomplishment. The shortcomings the game has, mostly in the later parts of the game, are overpowered by the incredible design of the world and combat system. Some say the lore is too vague and difficult to piece together, and though I somewhat agree, I've also probably spent upwards of an hour reading item descriptions. Puzzling even just a fraction of the story out is another sense of accomplishment that you can't get from games that throw it in your face.
If you can get past the initial "Where the ♥♥♥♥ am I supposed to go? What the ♥♥♥♥ am I supposed to do in this game?" phase, the Dark Souls experience starts. Get the basics of combat down, delve into the lore a bit, and start to explore the many extra areas, storylines, NPCs, and loot, and there's enough content here for more than a few playthroughs, each as great as the last.
Play blind for the "True Dark Souls Experience" or if that's too much, follow a guide and check out the ridiculous amount of hidden♥♥♥♥♥♥and crazy ways to play.
I'mma chill though. I can ramble all day about Dark Souls. It's one of those games that you're thinking about during the day and can't wait to get back into when you get home.
I have spent most of 2016 playing this triology.

Story: Mass Effect is a story at its core more than most games, in keeping with its Bioware roots. Games like these are about the closest you can come to a 15 hour interactive book. While it isn't perfect, it's a good story and you do feel like you've read a decent book when you're through. I do have to say though, the obvious ego stroking that is thrown at the player is a little too obvious at times. (8.5/10)
Graphics: For a 2008 game, this is outstanding and still on par with some games just coming out. The "film grain" effect is actually rather nice.  There's something about it that softens the look of the game and makes it look and feel a more abstract, a little like a dream at times. (8.5/10)
Sound: Nice soundtrack, excellent voice acting across the board. Production values are high in general and the sound does an excellent job with ambience and immersion. The only glitch I really noticed was the assualt rifle sound when firing for long periods.
Gameplay: Good. In some ways this is the weakest link in a good overall experience. I've owned this game for 6 years and only today did I finish it. I started it 4-5 times and never got more than 6 hrs in. The first time a computer crash was to blame, the others I just got a little bored at having to play the same 6 hours to get back to where I'd been and stopped playing. This time I stuck with it for a couple weeks and it took me 15 hours from start to finish. The controls are slightly clunky, companion and enemy AI are nothing special. Special powers are not explained. Loot is rather abstract and predictable. Combat itself isn't bad though, the weapons feel meaty and the body count is a fun way to string together a story with some meaningful decisions sprinkled in for good measure. I did notice that all weapons (specifically the assault rifle) overheated much more easily when in the endgame, with between 30 and 70% of normal firing time available if I had to guess. Not cool bro. The Mako is clumsy and not all that fun after a while. So...gameplay isn't bad overall, but they did cut corners here and there. (7.3/10)
Final Thoughts: One of those games that almost makes you wish EA were still in business. In the top 10% of games on Steam and greater than the sum of its parts. (9.0/10)

Honestly I don't know how to feel about this game. At the time being it is good, but it has certain systems in place that really make the game look like a snake that's eating itself. Here's a list of reasons why.
1) People are incredibly unfriendly, and for good reason as killing people for their items is far more lucrative than actually going out into the world and taking 2-4 hours of your life to gather those things yourself.
2) Base building is tedious and far too removed from the base (see what I did here?) experience. In my 44 hours I have only been able to make two bases, because they are so hard to build. Not only do you need the prerequisite items for gathering materials like the hammer and axe, which are pretty scarce, but you also need to find blueprints for specific base items which are even scarcer and dare I say impossible to find. I haven't found one guide on how to build base parts, why make models for items if players are practically going to be cut off from them?
3) Loot is ridiculous. As I said there are essential items that you need that are really hard to find. When you loot an entire town and only find one gun, something is wrong with your looting system.
4) Cars. Cars and basically every single vehicle besides a bike are ridiculous in the way they are aquired. If you are lucky enough to even find a vehicle, which is pretty rare, it will be stripped naked of every single one of it's components, Spark Plugs, Drive Belt, Car Battery, Fuel, oil, and ALL wheels. So guess what now? You have to use the horrible loot system to find these materials, good luck. It's not impossible, but it is extremely difficult.
5) The game never wants you to be safe. Now this could be something that's admirable to some, but honestly it's annoying as all hell. Say you actually by some grace of god are able to build a fully functional base, YOU ONLY GET ONE PUNY LITTLE STORAGE BOX FOR THAT BASE. The game only wants you to have the experience of running around scared for your life, which is fun for a little bit, but get's old when 50 year old texas men tell you to "get down on the ground boy" before killing you and taking everything you have just spent 6 hours of your life getting, it's ridiculous. I get it the game is "hardcore edgy XD" but for the love of god, divy up the game experience a little. There should be moments of peace and quiet, but no you always must live in fear. You may even think you are slick and try to build your base inside a house or cave or radio tower or somewhere the texas hillbilly's can't get you, however the game now totally prevents you from doing this. You may only live in the wide open forest.
For a game that seems to pride itself on being realistic, it seems to take quite a few hits to realism in order to make itself "hardcore". It's not realistic to limit people to one puny storage box, it's not realistic to spend an hour to loot an entire town and only find one gun, it's not realistic to have cars be so scarce and be stripped of literally every single one of their components, it's not realistic to not allow people to build their bases wherever they want, and all just to make the experience "hardcore" for the player. The game wants you to keep the experience of scarcity and running around for your life so much so that it will get in your way and force it to happen. Let people play the way they want.
Despite all of the things I said, I still have fun in the game, even if the experience never really changes from running around scared for your life stuff.

So this is actually a JRPG with some Western paint smeared all over it. It has its ups and downs, but before I go into detail, let me be clear: this game is AWESOME. Below I'll cover some Pros and Cons in regards to important elements in any RPG.
PROS:
- The combat: the biggest pro in this game is the incredibly fun combat. It is fast paced and action heavy, no matter what class (called vocations in this game) you are playing. Most notably a mechanic is in place, that lets you climb any big enemy, which is simply the funniest combat mechanic in the world. Wanna stab a cyclops in the eye? You can. Wanna ride a soaring Griffon? You probably gonna fall off, sicne those things are brutal, but you can. Lots of different enemies have their own strenghts and weaknesses. There really are too many cool small details to even remember them all - it simply must be tried!
- The Difficulty: I like Dragon's Dogma especially because of the way they've handled difficulty. It is very well balanced, sure, but more notably, it almost perfectly mixes the "leveled difficulty" of classic RPG's and the more skill based difficulty of the Souls series.
- Fun class system: classes in this game are called vocations. Each class is levelled seperately and can be switched with the help of specific NPC's at almost any point in the game. Each and every class feels unique and badass for it's own reasons. Magic feels immensely powerful in this game (balanced just fine though). There are so many fun combinations and skills in this game, it's hard to stop playing, simply because you wanna experiement  with them all.
CONS:
- Story: the overall story is good enough, but the way it is presented can often be confusing and un-engaging. You don't play this game for the story and characters though.
- The world design: It's interesting, yeah. But there's a lot of empty traversal and having to loop around stuff. That can be tedious and not fun. That said, the dungeons, mines and so on are actually a lot of fun.
- Wolves: Wolves are a pack of D***s. We hate them.
You can create a cute guy character unlike crappy western RPGs.

Dragon's Dogma has to be in the list of my top RPG's of all time! It is a fun game that I highly recommend you trying!
The combat system of the game is very unique. I have personally never played an RPG where your hero can "cling" or mount a large enemy in an effort to attack weak spots such as the head. In addition, it is a very satisfying feeling to overcome intense and challenging battles against large mobs where the Arisen (your hero) is constantly trying to revive his or her pawns (pawns are like allies in battle).
Character customization offers a large variety of ways to customize your main pawn and Arisen hero. This includes weight, height, hair, eyes, face shapes, makeup, hair color, eye color, and of course fashion and weapon wear. There must be hundreds of different character customization combinations all together.
As of vocations (classes), there are many to choose from. Although you can only start off with warrior, rogue, and mage, as you progress through the story and level up, you can choose other vocations such as assassin, magic knight, etc.
Love climbing or exploring hidden areas? This game let's you have a piece of that. And you know what's better? The fact that you can travel with NPC pawns who help you in battle. Now, 100/10 you will never be lonely again. :)

Great customization options, you could play as a fat, old, black woman or a small 10-year-old, your choice. Size and weight even matter in small ways (small characters fit through a cyclops' legs, heavy characters have a higher carry limit, both cases have workarounds).

Currently the definative Total War and if a player was considering any of the the series to buy, the one I would recommend.
Basically everything that was wrong with the immensely solid Rome 2 is fixed in this game, agents are more useful (although AI does spam their actions big time), campagin is just more solid, AI occasionaly make decisons on the map a cognitive human might, overall the campagin map has just been tightened up.
The reall improvements are on battle game play, finally everything is atually how I would expect it to be. It's little refinements like, how a moving unit is immesurably more vulnerable to arrow fire than a static unit. Battle cohesion and moral play much bigger roles. In rome 2  for instance you could have a quiality unit go full 300 while utterly surrounded and take a good few untis with them just beacuse their base stats are sky high. I'm not sure how the negative bonus is applied in this, but if you are surrounded, you are going down pretty quick.
Overall just the most solid Total War game there is in terms of gameplay (and I include warhammer in that). The only thing I would say it suffers with slightly is the era. As it's a transitional period between Rome and the empires that came after (the dark ages) it's very much play as the vikings before they were viking, play as the Anglo-Saxons before they were English, so a lot of the big name identitys most will know from History just aren't there. The Age of Charlemene DLC moves this along into a better known era, but then this is a far more restrictive campagin (The danes don't even have cav).
But if you want to play multiplayer campagins, or straight up fights, this is my go to TW. 9/10 for game play 8.5/10 overall, so very close to being perfect!

>Going into Hiveswap expecting Homestuck.
No. No. Just stop it there, that's not what you should be focusing on, or looking for. Instead, you should be treating Hiveswap as its' own property, and stop constantly comparing it to Homestuck just because it's made by the guy who made Homestuck. It's not going to be based in Homestuck, will not be focused on Homestuck, and Homestuck characters will likely remain Homestuck - specific characters, as far as we've seen now. So if you're here for something that's like Homestuck or is the "spiritual succesor" of sorts to it, leave. Because you're going to continue to be disappointed.
Well anyway, other than that, I think the game's fun. As a lot of people said, it is kind of frustrating during the first play when you get stuck in certain places (I was using a guide for most of the Alternia gameplay) and if you don't have the patience to click on everything like me, then it's really annoying.
There are a lot of achievements that I believe pretty much capture that "Hussie" comedy, contrary to most who think it's just a forced attempt at humor. I mean, I think a lot of people forget, this is the man who found enjoyment merely in drawing weird human-animal abominations with giant bulging muscles and♥♥♥♥♥♥ Got all on my second playthrough except for the seemingly elusive "Ourous" achievement, which only that one guy who probably used the Steam Achievement program got.
It's a very short ride. For my first playthrough, 2 hours (even constantly checking a guide and suffering through an 'unable to interact with anything' bug) and my second, 1 hour, seeing as I'd basically memorized all the choices and skipped through a huge chunk of dialogue.
All in all, I do think that for what it is, the pricing's pretty accurate. I've seen visual novels with no animation like Hiveswap that go for 20 bucks just because "good art", but we've gotten good art, nice animation, and nice music all for 8 bucks. Pretty good deal, if you ask me.
From my (probably slightly biased) opinion, I can recommend Hiveswap, but I can't confidently say that you will 100% enjoy it.
