A homestuck-themed point-and-click adventure game. As a huge fan of homestuck, I was quite excited for this, but unfortunately I have some gripes with the execution. The game provides very little help when you get stuck, so when a character arbitrarily asks you to fetch her own key before allowing you to proceed and gives absolutely no indication of where she put it no matter how many times you press the literally useless hint button, you can understand if I get a bit annoyed. Most of the homestuck running gags are gone, so no acrobatic pirouettes off the handle will be performed any time soon, which is fine, but they don't seem to want to replace them with anything. The characters are pretty dull, one-note entities with too few chances to meaningfully interact with each other like they would in a webcomic, so despite what some individual scenes or some homestuck style "You are now X" introductions would have you believe, I could sum up all the part 1 characters in about 5 words each. The most interesting characters seem to be the guardians who get zero screen time. I really want to meet this mysterious babysitter, she seems pretty fun, but who knows when/if that will ever happen.
There's also the slight issue that this is incredibly short. I am aware of the drama happening behind the curtains of this particular project, but I'm the kind of guy who enjoys following the main story and only examines random objects in a pretty cursory fashion, so about 2 hours have passed and I've finished the entire thing. I then looked at the achievement list to discover that I missed about everything on it because I didn't decide to feed a stuffed animal with a cracker, but instead spent my time trying to tap dance on a pile of guns and putting a pigeon in a microwave (I'm not weird, shut up). Basically, the achievements just point you to the random comments that the developer thought were the funniest, which would be fine if they weren't all hidden by Steam anyway and required you to rub everything in your inventory against everything in the game world until the friction spontaneously produces Steam achievements (or look up a guide). There was probably a soul-crushing level of effort writing all those possible interactions, but I just didn't want to go look for them. I didn't feel the need to pick every conversation choice in Openbound and I'm not going to waste my time putting batteries in my shoes just in case my character goes on a quick rant about how light-up sneakers are stupid or something.
Ultimately, the game's not horrible, but I feel slightly less impressed with this game's first act than I was at the end of the first act of Homestuck. Yeah, I'm sure the story will pick up from here, and I wouldn't mind spending some time with the sequels when they come out, but as it stands, I can't really recommend this to anyone without it being on a huge sale. Maybe (hopefully) my tune will change like it did with homestuck.

Absolutely hilarious and charming from start to finish, with very likable characters. Puzzles are somewhat straightforward and simple but still require you to do some thinking. I also was quite amused at some of the little things. For example, I love how the human main character uses tapdancing as her main attack. Yes, tapdancing. It's incredibly random and I love it. I also appreciate the fact that troll typing quirks were HEAVILY downplayed, making them easier to read for anyone not familiar with Homestuck.
Another neat thing about this game is the sheer amount of flavor text. Just about any combination of items and/or background objects can give you a different response. Heck, at one point near the beginning, two pieces of flavor text actually reference each other, and I actually laughed out loud when I saw it. Then again, I laughed out loud quite a lot throughout this game.
That's actually pretty much how I'd describe this game: a laugh-out-loud experience. It's bursting at the seams with humor and charm, and I loved it from start to finish. The only complaint I have is that there's no autosave, but to be perfectly honest, that's more of a nitpick than anything else. Either way, though, I still HIGHLY recommend this game to any fan of point-and-click adventure games, particularly old-school, comedy-oriented ones.

So, right off the bat, let me just say that I love this game. It offers a novel experience akin to some of the older PS1-era action rpgs, and is definitely worth ten bucks.
I originally played it quite a few years back, and I got just a little past the mid point before stopping for whatever reason. I recently found myself wanting to revisit a game I'd enjoyed, but never beaten, and let me just say, this did the trick. I clocked in about 7 hours in my playthrough, and beat it in one sitting. It wasn't quite as difficult as I remembered it being, but then again, I guess I've simply gotten better at video games in general since my early teens, which is when I first played it.
That being said, it is quite challenging, yet still fairly so, and the majority of my deaths were during bossfights and especially the final boss. (Minor spoilers ahead, but I promise not to go into a degree of specifications that would ruin it for a first-time player.)
All of the areas in the game are enjoyable to varying degrees. Some are a little tedious, but that doesn't really ruin the overall experience. The bosses are probably the most enjoyable aspect, as each has a decent pool of attacks to choose from, and requires a specific way to be defeated. Dying to a boss your first time facing it is expected, since they do a lot of damage and their attack's damage type isn't always obvious. (Physical damage vs magic damage.) There are also a few mini-bosses with cool attacks that you will encounter every now and then, and despite reusing the same base sprite, add a little extra challenge to the game.
The final boss is really well done, I'd have to say. Some parts were a little confusing at first, and enduced a little more rage than I'm proud to admit, but after you've delivered the final blow and you're watching the credits, you'll realize just how much it took out of you, and that's a good feeling. One of its forms has a crazy amount of attacks, which change slightly after damaging it enough, which definitely keeps you on your feet all throughout.
The game never makes you backtrack unless you really want to, either to farm gold and items or simply to see what all you missed your first time through, as each individual area has its own hidden treasure chest to uncover. Once you reach a point near the end, you can even do a mode that randomly picks areas and bosses to fight, as a sort of arcade-survival mode. See how far you can get and how fast you can advance.
The story isn't anything revolutionary, but does the trick. It doesn't force unskippable cutscenes down the player's throat, and that's a good thing. The characters are interesting enough to care about, even though there aren't too many.
The combat is truly where this game shines. Chantelise features a combination of fast-paced melee combat and an extensive mid-range magic system using gemstones that drop from enemies and some other objects like trees and barrels. As you advance the plot, you gain access to more equipment slots and stronger spells that can be cast using multiples of the same gem type. You even gain the ability to summon familiars to temporarily aid you, and they can really give you the edge in larger fights. The equipment system takes the place of any sort of experience points mechanic. You can equip up to 2 items with the same stat boost. For example, 2 gauntlets to boost your physical damage, or 2 shields to boost physical resistance. It's pretty bare-bones, but not in a bad way. It definitely makes a difference what equipment loadout you roll with in different situations, ESPECIALLY boss fights, where you may end up switching equipment mid-fight several times. (I'm looking at you, crab-boss!)
All in all, what else can I say? The 3D environments are fun to run around in, the sprite-work on the characters and enemies is very pleasing to the eyes, the combat is fast and allows plenty of strategy, and there's even a fishing minigame! Seriously, what adventure isn't complete without that?
I haven't done much of the post-game, since I'm a little burnt out after playing 7 hours straight, but I will definitely be revisiting this game in the future. Once again, it's a great buy for only $10, and it's one of the few indie games I actually like. My thanks goes to the developers for this game's existence.
P.S. - Theres a bug with controllers that makes the camera spin constantly. The way I fixed it was easy and never made controlling the camera too obnoxious. Simply map the camera spin (Left or right, I can't remember which.) to the spacebar and put something heavy enough to depress it on top of it. I did this for my whole play-session, and despite getting used to not being able to turn the camera left or right, and simply have to rely on the camera re-center button, had no real complaints with it.

Savage Lands is an Early Access survival title that has great potential, but it seems that development has been on hiatus for some time now. I have my doubts that it will ever be finished. Even so, what development has already been completed is quite nice; you have a decent survival setting on an island accompanied by a fire-breathing dragon, you have creatures to kill, things to build, and most of the expected staples of survival games. I read one review of the game which compared it to Oblivion in its visuals and general gameplay, and I would have to agree with that assessment. The game is definitely unpolished, and there are loads of frame-rate issues--even on high-end graphics cards--but there is fun to be had.
In its current state, I would not recommend buying Savage Lands. When it is finished in a year or so (if ever), it may be worth picking up, but not now, not in its current state.

This is a tentative recommend.
Pros: The artwork is amazing.
The music is great.
Don’t like the game’s companions...Make your own!

Cons: Limited character development
LOADING SCREEN CITY!!!
Lots of repetitive combat with few “bosses”
Middling points: Story is okay
Combat is pretty strategic...but can be highly random (based on dice rolls)
Graphics are pretty low (good art, low quality)
The game is a crpg...more like D&D than the KoTOR/Skyrim style rpg computer games. This leads to there being higher chance in terms of combat as everything is based off dice rolls of attack/accuracy vs. defenses. But, this also means story choices have a much larger impact on everything that occurs in the world (granted you don’t see many of them till the epilogue).
At the start you have control over your character’s stats, starting abilities, background, origins, etc. There is a wide variety of choices, and they do have in game effects, though mostly due to combat bonus given. The lore attached has less game impact than I would like for how much time went into writing out descriptions. It’s there more for those who are more interested in actually roleplaying their created character than for the casual gamer. The classes are reasonably different, though more or less fall under caster, support, dps categories. The druid and the mage play pretty much the same, cast spells. The druid/chanter/priest/paladin can be supporty. Ranger/Cipher/Barbarian are dpsy. There are overlaps, but the classes are pretty stock.
Once you get into the game, there are three things you should be ready for and (I hope) enjoy: Loading screens, reading, and right clicking all your party on enemies. THERE ARE A TON OF LOADING SCREENS. There are many times you just run from one screen to the next and are required to load. Want to go into a house, loading screen. Forget something, probably loading screen. Delivery quest, loading screen. Turn in a quest, loading screen loading screen etc. For a game that has such low graphic quality, there is a long time between areas, and every area, no matter how big  or small has a loading screen to go through. A lot of game time is spent on them. (I had a book beside my comp. that I read during them).
PoE is a world built to rp in. There is a ton of lore. Books, weapon descriptions, npcs, quests all have an amazing amount of information put into them. The one down (or upside depends on you I guess) is that you have to read about 90% of it. Much of it is skippable for the average gamer (the books for instance) but a lot of the quests require clicking through mountains of text. And the text, well most of it is well written, but as a whole the story is a lot of potential that was just not capitalized on. More on that later.
Combat is tactical, chaning stuns, buffing, debuffing, bursting, healing positioning. Its got it all. But, that isn’t most of the game. Most of the game, the combat is basic trash mobs that your entire party just right clicks on and it dies. The few bosses in the game can be tactical, but some of the tactics are lost to the randomness of the dice roll. I spent 2hours on one boss fight, loading and reloading, to get the perfect set up, mainly so that the boss didn’t 1 hit K.O. half my party in the first few seconds. Strategy won out, but not before lady luck decided she didn’t like the look of my face. So combat was either boring or frustrating with some OMG I JUST DID THAT WOOT moments.
To go along with combat, gear is meh. On my ranger, my upgraded plain bow was better than any bow I found, which was both awesome and awful. I didn’t get the euphoric sense of loot from killing something or from completing quests. I would get items sometimes, but they were generally always side grades. Loot was just not that important in the game, except for getting cash.
Story:	In the beginning the story was confusing, random person has bad things happen and starts on epic journey to become savior of the world type gist. But at first, you have no idea what the heck is going on. The game does not explain very much and much of the time the tasks don’t help you understand much better. Companions join you generally due to doing something for them, but for most of them the reason is flimsy. In the last 3rd of the game I feel the story has a good feel to it, asks questions that don’t really have answers, but makes you choose anyway and in the epilogue you can see how your choices affect the world, which feels good (or bad depending on what the choice did). Past meeting present dictating future, fate and choice permeate the end of the story, but you don’t get that in the beginning or the middle. So much is just clouded in mystery for the sake of being mysterious it just means that the gamer doesn’t care once the story does kick it into high gear.
Overall the game was satisfying to beat, but not something I’m going out to tell all my friends to play, just the ones that might like a more solo D&D feel.

If you are the kind of person who has purchased any of the recent Black Isle remasters from Beamdog, then let me tell you in no uncertain terms that you should go buy PIllars of Eternity right now. It is the nearest thing to Baldur's Gate II since Baldur's Gate II, and if that doesn't already make you champ at the bit, then let me tell you that its a darn good facsimile.
If you aren't the kind of person who has done something like that, then the first thing you'll want to know is that Pillars of Eternity is an isometric party management RPG in the style of the old nineties and noughties games, complete with their beautiful writing, massive single player adventure, and difficulty. While you start off going through the familiar motions of building a character, Pillars of Eternity introduces a few new wrinkles that make it interesting. For starters, while all the familiar archetypes are represented, some truly weird and original character classes exist here, including the chanter who sings harmful and helpful chants, and the cipher, who wields eldritch power to corrupt and destroy the souls of your foes. All the classes feel suitably different, and at time of writing the balance seems to be fairly good across the board. Another thing that Pillars of Eternity does that will probably surprise newcomers to the genre is that every single stat has a direct and significant combat impact. There are no dump stats here and while this means min-maxers will probably be arguing amongst each other for months to come, it is now pretty tricky to gimp your character.
You can also supplement your party of six adventurers by hiring characters you create from scratch at any inn. But this would be a mistake. The game includes 8 NPC companions, and you should do everything in your power to have all of them in your party at some point in the game as their writing and acting is so well done you would be robbing yourself of the experience by building a custom party of adventurers. This quality of writing extends to virtually everything else you'll encounter during the course of the game to boot, and it is consistently excellent from start to finish (with two minor and largely irrelevant exceptions which I mention below). Without spoiling anything, the world of Eora will seem immediately familiar to anyone who has spent any time travelling around Faerun in the Forgotten Realms, but it doesn't just feel different enough to be fresh - it's positively revelatory.
Oh, and did I mention its gorgeous? The area maps are eye poppingly beautiful, and the characters actually animate splendidly, plus there are loads of cool spell and ability effects. In fact, sometimes they can even be a bit overwhelming. There were moments, especially early on when I was finding my bearings, where I couldn't tell what was going on in fights.
The game also features a brand new, proprietary combat system that you'll need to spend a little time getting your head around. And I really do mean that, because this game is hard. Even on Easy or Normal difficulty (which you should probably stick to if you're the kind of person who only plays games once) you will sometimes find yourself badly overwhelmed at strange points as though the game was poorly paced. The learning curve is hardly gentle either, and even if you know your way around this sort of game, there are variations both intentional and unintentional that you wont anticipate in your first few hours with the game. It's a recipe for frustration, and while genre veterans are likely familiar with that feeling, if you're not used to that kind of abuse, expect Pillars of Eternity to test your patience from time to time. Still, the challenge rarely feels unfair (though make no mistake - there are some moments where it feels EXTREMELY unfair in some of the optional endgame content), and it is immensely satisfying to finally triumph over a difficult encounter.
Partly this is because a job well done is its own reward, but partly this is because of the loot! And Pillars Eternity has a heck of a lot of it, and it comes in a pretty smooth progression that reminds me of the best moments of Baldur's Gate II, when you were excited to pick up the burning sword that the most recent boss left behind when he finally keeled over. And best of all, the game smartly does away with the old dumb system of playing inventory tetris, Pillars of Eternity allows you to have an unlimited number of items in your inventory in the form of a stash chest that is accessible at any time with a single mouse click whenever you bring up your inventory screen. For anyone who is used to juggling arrows and quest items, it feels downright civilized.
The game is not perfect, however. Even after a patch designed to address it, the game features a strangely low level cap that you will absolutely hit. "But wait," I hear you say, "Baldur's Gate had a level cap!" This is true, but it was one that you could only hit by importing your heroes and taking them through the game, and subsequent games abandoned them entirely. By contrast, you may make the unpleasant discovery that you are max level just around the time you really feel like you're starting to cruise. It's jarring and unpleasant, and it's best you're aware of it now.
Further, a lot of the kickstarter stretch goal content is terrible. For example, early on in the game you encounter a stronghold which you capture and make your own. While it houses the biggest and best dungeon crawl in the game, it also features a stronghold building metagame that is deceptively terrible. The game is also awash in backer NPCs and memorials - NPCs and gravestones designed by kickstarter backers identifiable by their yellow name bars and tombstone icons. These are uniformly terrible, and you may make the mistake of wasting time reading through them when you first boot up the game. The serious player should regard them as unfortunate concessions to people who wanted to overpay for the game and ignore them completely. It is a real shame to think that these efforts could have been spent on shoring up the game itself.
The only other objection I have with Pillars of Eternity is that it is just a little more segmented than it should be. In each Act you are gated on the world map in some ways that feel pretty silly, and while it still feels pretty modern, it lacks the freeform feel that the very best games in the genre had. Still, this is a minor complaint, and there is lots of great sidequesting and adventuring to be done.
Overall, Pillars of Eternity feels like it has all the things that a throwback to one of the old greats should have, plus a few smart new inventions. It's actually a little short and content light by genre standards, as the game clocks in at around 40 or 50 hours for an leisurely, exhaustive completionist playthrough, and perhaps a little more than 30 for a more main-story-only run. But if we're being honest with ourselves, that's still a whole lot of bang for your buck, and oh boy, what a ride Pillars of Eternity is if you're up for its challenges.

As you read this review, please keep in mind that I have not played other games in this genre (DayZ, H1N1, etc).
When I first got this game about 6 months ago, I first noticed that it was very beautiful (CryEngine) but there wasn't a lot to do yet. The game was just looting and trying not to die. There wasn't a reason to build a base yet, so I never did.
But then the developers started to update it more and more, and the time between updates got shorter. Now there's a variety of vehicles, and with storage added, reasons to build bases as well. The increase in features lead to an increase in players, too, which raised the tension and the stakes, and the fun. There's mutants and animals which add a lot of life to the world. During the day, I'm on edge. But at night, I'm terrified.
I think it goes without saying that when you play a game like this, you should be
of human players than of any creature or monster. This game delivers on that concept. I've never felt more tension or stress in either a singleplayer or multiplayer game before Miscreated.
The vehicles are pretty good but you're likely to encounter a glitch when using them. For example, cars suddenly becoming silent, bicycles getting stuck in a curb or staircase, four-wheeler having a physics glitch (sending it into centripetal hell and killing you in the process). But these issues are rare and don't affect gameplay too often.
Right now, it's pretty easy to get your base broken into; I'm not saying that's an unintended aspect of gameplay, but I wish there was a way to secure my belongings without making a ridiculous floating platform (which the devs are trying to eliminate, anyway). But maybe I'm just too dumb to hide my stuff well.
This is a great game to play
; if you play it by yourself, it's still fun, but you'll become
paranoid, and it's downright terrifying to hear a stranger's footsteps outside when you're looting a house.
In addition to the game's merits and ever-growing features, the devs are highly communicative on Twitter and Reddit, which is really nice, and a refreshing change compared to many Alpha games. I don't think I've had a better experience with an alpha title than I have with Miscreated. This game just keeps getting better all the time.

What do you get when you take Dark Souls, Skyrim, and Shadow of the Colossus and throw them together? You get a very flawed, but endlessly entertaining game called Dragon's Dogma.

Pros:

+There is a lot of content in this game. Oh, you beat the game? It's still not over though. Now you've got post game and everything just got harder. Or maybe you could go to Bitterblack Island and partake in a completely separate quest line with it's own final boss and story.

+The difficulty is challenging in a natural, NES Zelda sort of way. I know most wouldn't agree with what I'm about to say, but I did not care for Dark Souls. The difficulty is forced by surrounding you with cheap enemies that spam you, or gigantic enemies that take up the entire room with attacks that one shot you while you have no space to move. That is such a cheap, artificial way to make a game hard. Dragon's Dogma does not do this. It achieves a natural level of difficulty by giving you a wide array of enemy monsters and bosses that all have their own unique abilities and weaknesses. To fight most effectively, you have to plan out the most efficient party possible and choose your gear wisely.

+You can create your own personal pawn follower and build them however you want them to support you. Your pawn can be recruited by others online, and you can recruit up to two other people's pawns at a time as well.

+This game has A LOT of customization. I spent a good half hour just making my character and pawn. You can even make mutants if you so wish. 9 Different classes and sub-classes, all with their own abilities and weapon proficiencies. Charge into a hoard of goblins with a flaming sword, or levitate across rooftops as a mage. You and your pawn can change class freely at any time.

+One of this game's strongest points is the boss battles. There are a lot of them, and they are very unique. You can climb them and hack off limbs. Certain elements can have an effect too. Cut off a hydra's head with a fire enchanted sword and you will cauterize the wound and slow it's regeneration.

+Pawns learn. They are capable of discovering enemy weaknesses and will point them out to you, and also use those weaknesses themselves. If the undead show up, a mage pawn would know to enchant your weapons with holy magic or fire. They can even learn by your own behavior. For example, casting great cannon creates an orb of magic that shoots homing balls of magic when struck. I've used it so much that my pawn has actually started to run over to me whenever I cast it and spam it with me.

+You have the freedom to be silly. Not only can you make mutants in the character creator, but the game even gives you some fun little derpy things to do. Don't like your mutant pawns face? Pick him up and throw him off a cliff. Cows can be climbed the same way you can climb bosses. You can also climb the hanging corpses at Bitterblack and swing around the room my attacking them while hanging for hilarious results.

Cons:

-Pawn AI can be terrible sometimes. "Oh, you're trying to cast a spell? Let me just run over and stand right next to you and do nothing while a gorecyclops is following me." There are commands you can give pawns, but in my hundred hours of gameplay, I've yet to see them come in handy during combat once. If there is even one goblin on the screen, your party will completely ignore your orders and it can be very infuriating. Some bosses are even best fought without pawns at all, as time that could be spent fighting the boss is instead spent picking up your pawns when they are being stupid.

-The world can feel very empty after a while. Fortunately this game did get an update that added fast travel, which helps this issue a lot, but the main overworld is huge and empty with enemies scattered around. It's good for early levels, but after that you'll find yourself using your ferrystone a lot.

-This game has one of the worst romance systems I've ever seen in a game. Your character gains a beloved, which is something that has effect later in the story. The beloved is chosen based on your affinity for that character. Affinity is gained simply by talking to them or doing quests for them. You could end up with an old man or a child because of this system. You can reach max affinity for a character and still end up with someone you didn't want.

-Only one save. You read that right. You get one save file. Want to start a fresh game with no high end gear so you can try a new class from the start? Well, you're gonna have to delete that precious file you put hours into first. This game does have a new game+ where you can start the game over, but you do keep all of your levels and stuff. While I like being able to hang onto the file I put 100 hours into, the game becomes too easy when you play from the start as a level 100+. Having another separate file would have been nice.



With all of that said and the ups and downs I listed, I would absolutely recommend this game without question.
9/10

Currently the definative Total War and if a player was considering any of the the series to buy, the one I would recommend.
Basically everything that was wrong with the immensely solid Rome 2 is fixed in this game, agents are more useful (although AI does spam their actions big time), campagin is just more solid, AI occasionaly make decisons on the map a cognitive human might, overall the campagin map has just been tightened up.
The reall improvements are on battle game play, finally everything is atually how I would expect it to be. It's little refinements like, how a moving unit is immesurably more vulnerable to arrow fire than a static unit. Battle cohesion and moral play much bigger roles. In rome 2  for instance you could have a quiality unit go full 300 while utterly surrounded and take a good few untis with them just beacuse their base stats are sky high. I'm not sure how the negative bonus is applied in this, but if you are surrounded, you are going down pretty quick.
Overall just the most solid Total War game there is in terms of gameplay (and I include warhammer in that). The only thing I would say it suffers with slightly is the era. As it's a transitional period between Rome and the empires that came after (the dark ages) it's very much play as the vikings before they were viking, play as the Anglo-Saxons before they were English, so a lot of the big name identitys most will know from History just aren't there. The Age of Charlemene DLC moves this along into a better known era, but then this is a far more restrictive campagin (The danes don't even have cav).
But if you want to play multiplayer campagins, or straight up fights, this is my go to TW. 9/10 for game play 8.5/10 overall, so very close to being perfect!

I loved the first three Splinter Cell games. The first Splinter Cell was billed as a Metal Gear Solid killer. As stealth games, both Metal Gear Solid and Splinter Cell both rewarded patient players, although Splinter Cell had a storyline far more grounded in reality.
The fourth Splinter Cell, Double Agent, went for something a little different. The fifth game, Conviction, went for something completely different, and Blacklist followed. I think that Conviction and Blacklist have turned the Splinter Cell games into a far more trigger happy series, and pumped in the action move cliches. Not that there's anything particularly wrong with that, the Syphon Filter games on the PSX paid lip-service to stealth while throwing action movie cliches at you all the time. And I loved those games.
So while I prefer the original games, I enjoyed my quick run through Blacklist, but I'm done with the main story, and probably won't play through any of the side stuff. The only major flaw is that Michael Ironside no longer voices Sam Fisher.
Blacklist is good, but not full price good, so wait for a crazy special or price drop.

But getting the right magic to do decent damage to him can be hard, the slimes are constantly in the way of cleanly dodging him. There are sources of health and magic in the room including a chicken behind the pillar in back.
But that's the thing, all the sources of magic in the fight take way too many hits to open. You can only carry six jewels at any time, and he can jump around enough to be hard to dodge unless you leave the autotarget on him.
You do not get to carry any healing items, I've checked the shop, I've explored everything I could find. This means when you get cheap shot by the first boss there's not really any way to survive.
So yeah, I can't grind to overpower the guy, and I cant buy healing to out equip the guy. That's not really design I can approve of. Worse yet I've seen enough of the game to come that I know how to cast a healing spell, but I can't use it because the game gives you equipment and magic limitations until you beat some bosses. Meaning I'm having undue trouble with the first boss, trying to get an ability from the first boss.
Also every enemy I've encountered with a projectile is annoying to attack, sidestepping them just to get an attack so I can stun lock them. You encounter the bat eyes at the same time as the cloud bugs, each of which uses projectiles in different and very annoying ways, and the latter having no visual distinction from a previous mook.
Wait to get the game on sale, then watch a playthrough on youtube, you'll get about 70% of the value from the game, and none of the drawbacks.  What a shame; this game had such potential.

Camera controls are MANUAL, with a (completely useless and unweildly) 'lock on' mode that requires button taps to toggle in and out of at real time.
Both "modes" are hot garbage with a keyboard.
With the steam controller they are STILL completely terrible as you are forced to manually fix the camera with the top buttons rather than just having a naturally flowing camera as is the case in well designed games (take your pick, there are many examples).
There is no level up system.  Cash is everything and you can't buy stats in an unlimited fashion; what little you can buy is limited by a geometric cost progression (e.g. Max HP +10 item costs 1,000-2,000-4,000-8,000 etc).  Selling is also on a geometric degradation.  If you seel a 5,000 gp item will net you 5000-4500-4050 etc.
Enemy placements and types are 100% deterministic leading to a grindy experience.
Good concept for a game. Bad camera controls. Not a fan of the full clear stage idea.

I could write a book about all the poor design choices in Chantelise.
In short, the game is tedious and clunky with a reward in the form of an extremely rushed, though somewhat interesting, storyline.
Combat operates in 3D with mostly 2D sprite enemies (bosses are the exception as they are 3D models).  This perspective the game has makes it extremely hard to determine distance and you do not want to get hit in Chantelise anymore than you have to since your health and resources to refill said health are pretty low.
Progression is purely item based so no leveling here, but enjoy manually walking over those coins for the first half of the game or so until you unlock the item equip that makes money auto-pickup (but also weakens your character by way of sac'ing stats from other possible equips so you don't really want this equipped since the game is hard).  And since you need to be buying stuff to make your character stronger, money is essentially exp and therefore you can't skip out on it.
Speaking of skipping out on things, Chantelise forces you to fight and kill every enemy in an area before moving on.  This means if you're at the top level of an area and the monster walks off the ledge stupidly you now have to jump down after it to kill it and then WALK ALL THE WAY BACK UP TO WHERE YOU WERE.  And enjoy the flying enemies and the ones that go invulnerable most of the time they fight you.
I mentioned before that the game is hard.  Removing the terrible camera perspective, your combat options are just so limited and weak.  Your attack can get a charged version if you equip an item for it (sac'ing stats in the process of course) but otherwise you just have your 1-2-3 and jump attack.  Otherwise you'll be using magic and dodging.  The magic in this game is actually solid.  I like it.  But what ends up happening is since your dodge is complete♥♥♥♥♥♥and has no invicibility to make up for its ♥♥♥♥♥♥ distance, boss fights end up being you farming adds for gems, maintaining distance, and pelting the boss with magic.  Super tedious.
tl;dr  If you like simple anime storylines just YT this game or find a way to cheat because this game is a waste of your time to actually play.  And the story's like 20 minutes long anyway.

So, Ive wanted to buy this game since a few months but I always hesitated. It finally got on sale for the Halloween and I bought it.
This is my Day #1 experience:
1st spawn
I had just spawned and I started fixing the video settings and trying to figure out the controls. It was night. Like hella dark, couldn't even see my arms. I started strolling around while I somehow managed to drop my only item, the flashlight (accidentally pressed wrong button). Trying to keep moving, I ended up in the middle of a road. Still couldn't see much and all of a sudden another player showed up and made me almost sh*t my pants. "This is it, I'm dead", I thought. But instead, the guy asked me if I needed anything and even gave me a gun with two bullets and a flashlight! I thanked him and he moved away. I kept following the road when I heard some roars. I noticed an infected in a small distance and panicked as I didn't even know how to equip the gun I had, yet. I decided I could slowly go past him and move away but no, that creepy @ss thing started screaming the hell out of its lungs as I got closer. So I started running till I heard wolves. I finally reached a town and in a few words, I accidentally fell from a big height, started bleeding and slowly, died.
Spawn 2
I respawned on a different place and after some time of looting around, I bumbed on a Swedish guy. He was really friendly I couldnt even believe it and we eventually teamed up. He taught me some handful survival tricks and tactics and it was all cool when we heard another guy (a Finnish one) who almost blew our minds with his carbine (he thought we would attack him). He got in the squad too and we all had a good time I believe.
Few things I learned from the Swedish guy:
-NEVER TURN ON YOUR FLASHLIGHT OUTSIDE OF BUILDINGS, you're easy to spot
-stay close to bushes and out of the roads
-always keep an eye on your health stats; everything below 50% means emergency
-try to team up with people (friends playing with you are the best solution) or be careful as they'll probably kill you.
-STOP CARRYING USELESS STUFF. even if you find a backpack (which you totally need in such a game), you want to save space for consumables and weapons. Better thing to do is to focus either on building a base, or a car or just surviving and so keep space for your purposes.
The game is on Alpha version as stated, yet it lacks very few things from its full release. Mechanics are good, physics are awesome, graphics are exceptional. The menu options aren't many and the user interface is kinda good (it could be better but I see the devs have focused on the rest of the game and some fixes). I only found one small bug where an infected had glitched and stuck with an object but after a few seconds it was ok. The day and time cycle vary on each server as I've read however both night time and day time last long. And finally the game is not heavy especially for newer PCs. My old laptop with: i7 4500U, R9 m265x 2gb, 8gb ram, run at 40-60 fps at low settings with native (1366x768) resolution. However I read, systems with older CPUs and GPUs (e.x. gtx 670 or so) can run the game a lot better.
If you like survival games where you can also build a base, create clans or play alone but also like the horror of the infected, this game is totally for you.

After replaying the entire trilogy a few times I am more convinced than ever that Mass Effect 1 is the best game of the series.
Is it the most polished game of the series? No, that's ME2.
Does it have the smoothest combat of the series? No, that's ME3.
Does it have the best-written character/character arc of the series? No, that's Mordin Solus.
But what it does have is the most cohesive design and story, an interesting universe, a great soundtrack and by far the least amount of fan pandering.
It also runs quite well on PC. It does not have a wide array of in-game options or settings but if you are willing to edit some of the .ini files you will be able to really make the game shine.

While it does fall under the genre of 'Open World 3rd Person Stealth/Adventure Game With Climbable Towers That Activate Zones" that descibes so many recent games, it pulls it off really well.
The combat feels fluid and satisfying, the skill tree is reasonable and doesn't take much grinding, the missions can sometimes be a bit samey but always fun and often quite unique.
The Nemisis System is a fun gimmick but has a fundemental problem in that for it to have full effect requires the Uruk to either kill you a lot which is not likely as it's not that hardcore of a game, or to survive your attacks which, unless you specifically let them live, is also not likely as it's fairly uncommon to survive a sword through the face (but to their credit they do sometimes come back and proceed to make you feel bad for giving them brain damage).
The story is a pretty standard revenge/whycan'tIjustdie plot with a side of supernatural-ness that's part of being set in Tolkiens world and while it's perfectly functional on it's own would definitely go down better with someone already a fan of his work who would appreciate the subtleties
What it really does well though is enemy variety, while the basic arrowfodder orcs are the standard big ugly guys with a spikey metal stick, once they attain captain status they get customised to a pretty impressive degree, they're given a unique (plucked from a generator) name and a set of gear that fits the name (IE Kargash Iron Jaw has a metal face mask, Ugog the Butcher has a bag of -probably human- meat, etc) and a little flavour text in form of their motive and a couple of lines they'll say when you cross blades with them or otherwise interact with them, they even reference each other and talk about recent events, it really makes you feel like you're fighting characters rather than nameless bodies, and you'd have to look pretty hard to find two that have much in common.
8/10.

Hands down one of the most mechanicaly invigorating games I've ever played. Loved the combat and fighting interactions... but that's it.
The lore is severely lacking (I have no idea who Lenore is or why the Duke was screaming her name in that one scene. WTF happened with all that crazy tentacle monster under the Everfall? And so, so much more) The game tries to utilize gender roles (Ogres attack women, different clothing sets, etc.) - but playing a female character everyone still says "ser" and the Duchess is inexplicably attracted to you regardless of gender. There's no fleshing out of relationships, I literally have no idea where everyone's motives lie. What drives these characters to do what they do? Who cares, go fight that Griffin that will fly away after losing two health bars because your mage-pawn won't enchant your weapons with fire...
The crafting system is severely disappointing. I love crafting systems but there's next to no tutorial other than "try new things" and if you try new things there's no tracking system. Only way to craft is to have the wiki open and that's just bunk.
Gear. I love the idea of incremental upgrades on equipment, but it's unnecessary once you max out one of the outfits that are included. There's also no lexicon or encyclopedia guiding you towards where you might want to search for the raw materials you're looking for. The system is simply "wander around, slaughter/loot everything you find, dump it all at the inn when your movement is slow as molasses due to weight" (though I admit I like the incremental speed adjustments based on weight. Pack very light to run like the wind, and get bogged down while you loot - it's a good system, but it's a cottage on stilts: no foundation).
If you want to see what this game has to offer, go watch a Let's Play (if there are any out there). And the 100 From A Different Sky tokens are insanely infuriating. No motive, no reward, no point other than "go try to reach these hard to reach places - oh, and sometimes the token will bug out and not be there even after you just dumped all your petrification healing items fighting that cockatrice because your pawns don't know how to dodge, so you'll have to come back and try it all over again"
-----
If the developers implement the same battle mechanics into a game that has a coherent plot line and actual gameplay incentives, I might pick it up if the reviews assuage my fears. Otherwise, I'm looking towards Divinity: Original Sin and the like for my RPG desires. This is one of very few of my "Steam regrets", I hope you don't experience the same.

FIrst off, regardless of whether or not you've read Homestuck, you'll still be able to enjoy this game and all it has to offer. That said, if you HAVE read all of Homestuck, then you're in for a treat!
Since you've (probably) read the "About This Game" section, I'll spare you exposition and instead focus on my experience playing the game.
Pros:
+ the enviornments are gorgeous with a lot of detail
+ very nostalgic (Lisa Frank artwork, Connect Four, Simon Says, cartridge-based game consoles, etc.)
+ the characters are well-developed and enjoyable
+ plenty of Homestuck references to pick through
+ Hussie's and his co-writers' humor shines through the dialog
+ every single item in your sylladex can be used with another item or an object in the enviornment for Joey/Jude/Xefros to mentally comment on (for those with OCD who feel compelled to try every single combination, this may be a con...)
+ combat is interesting and involves a combination of using items in your sylladex with your TECHNICHES (for instance, Joey's ballet shoes let her escape/evade enemies)
Neutrals:
/ the animations (including the cutscenes) are just decent
/ the music isn't anything special and becomes tiresome over time
/ as with point-and-click games, you might get stuck figuring out what to do or how to go about doing it
/ not all the items in your sylladex or objects in the environment seem to get used, which means there MIGHT be extra content you can miss in a single playthrough
Cons:
- [insert requisite "this game is TOO short but good enough that I want MORE" comment]
- you'll use your techniches a handful of times as there are only a smattering of fights; it feels like a wasted opportunity to explore a truly unique game mechanic
Overall, if you enjoy witty humor, endearing characters, and an interesting plot and universe, then you can't go wrong buying this game. I mean, you'd spend more going to a see a 2-hour movie, so what's stopping you? BUY THIS GAME!!

While there is much to like in this game, there are bugs in the game that haven't been fixed since being first reported in 2015, and these will eat away at what enjoyment there is to be had in the game. Parts of the family tree can disappear when characters re-marry, making it impossible to interact politically with them. Agents +/- effects on public order/corruption/etc are as likely as not to have the opposite effect (not an intended feature). Items/The General's abilities/The Army traits/Office bonuses to unit level on recruitment will seemingly randomly subtract rather than add to a units level. I've had a General with +3 to infantry level from gloves, +2 to all recruits from his own abilities, +2 to infantry from Army traits give a +4 bonus in total, and when I put him 'In Office' so that he got another +3 to infantry, the level of the same troops, in the same city, that he could recruit DROPPED 3 levels. Naval recruitment is a crap shot.  Building naval docks might unlock the units it's meant to, but don't bet on it, and chances are you'll be able to recruit naval units that require the naval dock in a provence that doesn't have one. Landing naval units brings it's own nightmares, with limited landing spots that can't be used if the other side has sent ships to them first (which the AI will do in an instant), irrespective of how close your ships are relative to theirs.

I will start off with the cliche review of this game: this game is like dark souls with lolis
You will die in this game. A lot.
The game is structured into different dungeons that must be completed to move on. Each dungeon has 4 or 5 different 'rooms' that must be completed in order. If you die in any of the rooms, including the boss room, you must start the dungeon over again. To complete a room, you must first defeat all the enemies, pretty simple eh? But then they pack up on you and itsnot so simple anymore. There is a mode that lets you play through rooms that you have found already, but it will not progress the story. To say the least, each dungeon will take you multiple tries to complete.
Each room in the dungeon have secret items as well. This is an actual requirement actually: look online for a guide to get you all the secret items. If you miss even one, then you cant get the super secret item in the hidden level of each dungeon, which is vital to get your stats high enough to not get slaughtered in the next dungeon.
Other than the level layout, there are certain mechanics present such as running (yes, you can run), jumping (as in a kangaroo), sprinting (similar to running, but faster and usually away from the enemy), and, oh yes, there is magic. You have six slots for gems that you pick up from defeated enemies. There are different coloured gems for different types of magic. Matching the same type in the order of pickup will allow you to use multiple at once and cast more powerful spells. Casting magic is one of the backbones of this game and you had better get good at it early on or the later levels will get extremely difficult.
And here comes the part about the controls, I don't think I've talked about the controls yet. This is by far the aspect people struggle with the most. It's true that the controls are not at all standard in the West and initially seem very weird and frusturating. This is easily overcome with the use of a controller, but with myself as proof, this control system actually does work well. Fair warning though, it took me about an hour of randomly walking in circles to get to the mastery that I now posses. But now people see my mad skillz and look in awe as my fingers mash the keys in random order trying to kill a goddamn bat.
Overall, I really liked the game. I thought it had a nice story, it was challenging, and ultimately, it was fun to play. I always recomend this game to my friends (to their dismay once they look at the graphics), but they also seem to enjoy it as well.  I also recommend looking into Carpe Fulgar, the localisers of this game, their history is quite interesting. If you are still unsure about the game, try the demo and see if you like it or not, its free.

Great game! Bought all games published by the Carpe Fulgur publisher because I liked recettear, and while I at first considered this sub-par to the two others, over time this grew to be my favorite.
The game has a surprising amount of complexity, and while I found Fortune Summoners to be one of the most complex in terms of fighting mechanics, the simplicity of chantelise moveset is deceptive. Sure, there are only so many ways you can swing your sword. But it more than makes up for it in regards to the magic-system and equipments. Especially the magic! Besides that there are enough end-game content and collectibles to keep you enjoyed for a long time, although you are bound to get sick of fishing eventually ;) (there are other things to do however, such as go for secrets and even extra dungeon for after you won).
The magic system is something I think should be mentioned in particular. If you are playign the game and feel lost with it I highly suggest going to a wikia and read some information and tables. But in short it works like this:
You have a limited stack of magic gems that you picked up. When you cast a magic it uses the one *most recently picked up* (it's a "First-In-Last-Out" stack). You can charge the spell, using more gems when casting it. Gems are of different elements, and what gems are used decides the effect. The first gem used (aka the most recently picked up gem) decides the element, and the number of gems belonging to said element the spell is charged with decides the spell. Any other-element gems used to charge modifies the spell somewhat, such as air cloning it or fire increasing damage. Worth noting is that earth-element might seem useless, but a well-used armor is probably among the most useful spells in the game outside of healing.
A good review also has to mention the negatives:
It might look a bit aged graphically, and the controls are quite clunky on keyboard. I didn't find it discouragingly clunky (quite acceptable tbh, although others seem to disagree from what I read), but still highly reccommend using a gamepad. The game also feels quite difficult the first time you play it, but at worst some grinding to buy max-health would let you overcome things if you feel stuck.
As for why this game grew on me as the best among the three from the same publisher (Recettear, Fortune summoners & Chantelise) would probably be because of its replayability and speedrunning enjoyment. I have to admit to this being the only game I have been speedrunning, but that's largely because of its high replayability value (Especially when compared to recettear and fortune summoners). This increases further by the ability to fast-forward dialogue and the surprising depth of its mechanics.

I have been a fan of Romance Of The Three Kingdoms ever since Dynasty Warriors 2 and it's been a different experience in every release, despite the fact that the franchise is built upon the same Three Kingdoms era in China (around 200 AD).
You play as one of the renowned officers serving your kingdom (faction in some cases), throwing yourself into the battlefield and ready to give thousands of foes some whipping lessons.
Yes, and beyond that as well. Depending on the weapon you choose, you'll get a different moveset to negotiate your way to your enemies' elimination (me and my goddamn rhetorics) and it all gets spectacular in new ways whatever you pick.
Yes and no. Granted, many of the scenarios' outcome are decided upon whose commanding officer gets defeated but there are other kinds of critical objectives taking place, as well. One I can think of is escorting an important officer to safety out of the battlefield, which means you'll have to fight those who stand in the path and putting the mission into jeopardy. (that's the point, after all)
Every scenario also have a set of different events that will decide the flow of battle and it is up to you if you will carry them out for the benefit of your current scenario or the next one. So the strong point being is that it all comes to strategizing your next move. (like, should you carry out that side objective or protect your commanding officer from incoming attacks?)
Outside the gameplay factor, I must say that the developers have allowed to lift up the character's personalities throughout the story, giving them some kind of intrigue value since you can relate with some of them. Cao Cao, for example, has been relatively portraited as some kind of villain at different points but playing the Wei campaign shows that there are different nuances that defines his human values.
By what I've summed up so far, Dynasty Warriors 8 comes up with different gameplay functions and character designs (both in looks and moves) on a familiar preset based on the Chinese history. Having not played anything since DW5, this was a welcoming return when it has made its way to Steam and it's hard to quit when I've gotten into the rampaging and progressing through the battlefields and stories. I haven't tried other game modes such as Ambition mode, but you can find other reviews that touches upon those contents. Ever since Dynasty Warriors Online went down, I (as many other fans) only wished the online multiplayer function would come back again on this release but I can only hope it does someday soon.

Stranded Deep for me is an exciting survival game that puts you against nature in order to survive. It is a fun game that has the feel of really being stranded on a deserted island with dangers around every corner.
Personally I would really recomend this game once they have finished patching it up.

Stranded Deep is an entirely new experience for me, seeing as deep sea survival games are about as rare as they come. But rare isn't always good, and a new experience isn't always the best one. Fortunately, Stranded Deep is far from a horribly rare game, and it's new experience is one that I'll be glad to remember. I'll be covering graphics, gameplay, physics, AI, and overall thoughts in their own seperate paragraphs.
Graphics:
The graphics in this game are breathtaking to say the least. The water's effects and look in this game are probably some of the best I've seen, maybe even the best as far as indie games go. For example, the sun refracts off the ocean rather realistically spreading out across the waves when it's much more set. Not to mention when you're looking into the deep blue, it can easily seem to go on endlessly, raising a few fears in some of the more excitable of gamers. This alone is a pretty impressive feat, in my opinion at least, seeing as water in video games is rarely done well at all, and usually hardly even looks/behaves like water. The actual islands however are a mixed bag. From a glance, the islands look beautiful, usually lush with flora and plentiful with fauna on its beaches; crabs mainly. However, once you take a closer look at the island, that's when you'll start to see some of the cracks on this otherwise gorgerous game. Trees that aren't of the palm variety don't like to seem to spawn correctly half the time. While some trees look fine, perfectly in the ground, others are either partically floating above the ground, and others are too deep, seeing as you're literally able to see where the roots and trunk of the tree simply vanish into the ground. The same can be said for rocks, furns, and even large rocks sometimes. This problem also happens with crates and consoles you find in plane and ship wrecks. Some of the time, the crates or consoles can be partically clipping into its boat or plane.
Gameplay:
The gameplay for Stranded Deep is very immersive. I constantly find myself fearing to leave the island, as to have to face the endless ocean. Even when you have an island set in mind for paddling to, the wild life in the ocean under you can easily startle you. Not to mention sharks will occasionally draw an interest into the large banana colored life raft, almost non-effortlessly rising the tentions. When it comes to just surviving however, it's a rather different experience. When you first arrive on an island, the player can have any number of goals flash into their mind when they just see what in front of them. The player may see coconuts and crab and immediately start prioritising getting food and water. Or they may take more of an interest in the rocks and sticks laying around and may decide that making a shelter is the best way to go. It's always up to the player, and the consequences to the player are always from the players own choices. (Not counting bugs that cause a cheated death.) The crafting in this game was a very fresh experience for me. The system makes for a different feel than with a crafting menu, seeing as instead of making the item in your menu, you're making it right in front of your character. It's an idea I find is executed very well, as you have a very limited number of inventory spaces, and having to fumble around with items in a menu could cause for a very annoying or frusturating experience.
Physics:
The physics in this game are a mixed bag in almost every sense of the word. While some things are realistic, in the case of throwing around items and moving things around, or cutting down trees, others are far from it. A prime example of this is the life raft. Once you put more than a few items in it, it sinks. While this could be made realistic, this is far from so seeing as the raft looks like it's meant for 4+ people. Not to mention that, things like duct tape don't even drop into the life raft, they simply float above it as if there was a piece of ply wood rested over the top. The final problem I have with the physics are how items can react with others. When you drag an item against another item, as you'd imagine, it'd push it along. This is true for Stranded Deep, but it doesn't seem to matter the size, or the weight of the item in question. The most note worthy example I can think of is the glitch that can be preformed with the life raft and almost any object. You jump inside and shove the item against the raft, and the raft will begin to push very quickly in the pushed direction, much faster than the game's raft with a motor.
AI:
The AI in this game is almost astonishing with how in-depth it can be, mainly for the sharks. Each of the three shark types have its own behavior and little quarks about them. For example, if you have yet to aggrevate a Tiger shark, you can sometimes get it to keep its distance just by locking eyes with it. ( Keeping your crosshair over the shark's head. ) While the Blacktip Reef shark is passive, being scared away by coming too close, or even by acting aggressively toward it. The fish's AI are pretty good too, seeing as they rarely swim away from the school and prefer to keep their distance from the player.
Overall, this game was in almost no way a disappointment to me. I feel like I got much more than my money's worth for $15, and would have honestly paid another $5 to $10. The game is still in Early Access however, so bugs and glitches are to be expected. For me at least, any fatel ones have never really happened, and the only bugs and glitches I've ran into are minor at best, and only really break the immersion. If you're a die hard fan for PVE survival games, then you'll definitely want to pick this up. But if not, it may be best to either wait for a few more updates to come out, or even the official release, seeing as there isn't much to do besides survive and explore.

How To Start A Car:
Before you start the car: Locate the gas pedal and the brake pedal.  Get your foot in position with your heel on the floor so you can swivel back and forth between the brake and the gas comfortably.
Make sure that the car is in PARK.  Now start the car.  With your foot on the brake, put the car in ‘Drive’.  Slowly lift your foot off the brake.  Do not give the car any gas.  The car will move forward slowly.
This will be all the speed you need for some maneuvers.  Hover your foot over the brake in case you need to stop suddenly.  Lift it slowly off the brake to start moving again.  You can practice as you learn to drive in an open parking lot.
Repeat the same maneuver in ‘Reverse.’  This slow speed is all the speed you’ll need for backing up in many cases.

Pillars of Eternity: Pillars of Eternity, a Kickstarter (77,000!) CRPG developed by Obsidian Entertainment and published by Paradox Interactive. First a bit of a disclaimer, I have NOT completed the main story of Pillars of Eternity, I am currently in Act 2 and have put almost 30 hours into the game already. Anyways, on with the review!
---->This game takes lovers of RPGs back to some of the roots of some of the most beloved video games ever, titles like Baldur’s Gate, Icewind Dale and my personal favorites Fallout and Planescape: Torment are all great examples of CRPGs and some of the highest rated games of all time. I could go on, but, just know that Pillars of Eternity is a game that will take you back to those great experiences while delivering its own. Like all CRPGs the game takes an isometric point of view, you see everything from the sky, looking down, giving you the ability to appreciate grand landscapes and structures that are beautifully done in the game.Things like large buildings, bridges, forest, swamps, the ocean, all are beautifully crafted and the isometric point of view has always been perfect for show-casing these types of games, it looks beautiful and you don't need a top-of-the-line gaming computer to appreciate it. The music scores in CRPGs are usually on par with its excellent graphics and Pillars of Eternity is no different. Every soundtrack fits the mood perfectly and really compliments the atmosphere and setting, the only music that will get annoying is when combat starts, it’s the exact same every time and gets a bit annoying, but the rest of the tracks are amazing.
---->Gameplay is pretty straight forward, use the mouse and click on the ground to move your character, the mouse is your primary device, you have plenty of keyboard hot keys to use as well to assist with things like selecting characters, formations and dialogue options. The interface is nice and slick, not too barebones, not too cluttered and laid out in a very nice fashion, and easily customizable as well. Speaking of customization the character builder in this game rocks! You have a total of five races to choose from, many of which have sub races, then you have eleven classes to choose from, each one quite unique and different and most importantly, useful, you will definitely find favorites but, from my experience, every class can easily be useful alone and in a group and that is a welcomed addition to any RPG. You'll also get to choose color pallets for your characters, multiple voices, and very beautifully detailed portraits. You could and easily will drop many hours in the character creator and still find new characters to create, the best part is the game allowing this to be used throughout the game, as you get the ability to create new companions in addition to finding story ones early in the game, it’s a nice feature, allowing you to create one of every class and try out a multitude of playstyles and strategies for combat.
---->Combat can be hit or miss, I personally enjoy it, but, I can see it being boring or frustrating to some. First, your characters never do anything on their own, even when getting abused with mace blows or shot at with pistols they will stand there taking it all without ever attempting to retaliate. You HAVE to tell your companions exactly what to do no matter what it is, they will not do anything without an order, and when it’s a party of six, fighting multiple bad guys, that can get a bit slow, this isn't helped by the fact that you'll be pausing combat a lot to tell a character to do something after they've done their previous action. Another annoyance with combat is that characters will often run into each other, and will not attempt to move around each other instead, just running forward till whatever is blocking them is out of the way, this makes unit placement annoying and frustrating, I cannot stress enough how important it is to create custom formations to help alleviate this head ache. I'm harsh on the combat but, overall, I enjoy it a lot, the game lets you be as brute force or strategic as you wish and really rewards you for coming up with clever combos and will definitely challenge you with tough fights that will require every bit of cunning and cleverness you can muster. Magic is a lot of fun, spells are flashy and look amazing and actually feel like they pack a punch, they're exciting to use and I would strongly suggest bringing magic along for any fight.
---->Something else you also get fairly early in the game is the Stronghold, this is a player home that you get to upgrade throughout your adventure, allowing you to add multiple shops, a bounty board, a treasury and more. It’s in a ruined state and will look quite impressive as you get closer and closer to completing all of the upgrades, you'll also be able to hire guards to help defend from interlopers, you'll receive taxes to help fund your adventures, and side missions for your companions to do. It’s an awesome castle they give you early on and access to one of the biggest dungeons in the game, there are some missed opportunities with the Stronghold, one that I will share is you can actually arrest NPCs in the world and put them in your prison...and that’s it. You never get to do anything outside of that and your only option is to release them or they will escape on their own eventually. I'm not sure what the point is and haven't discovered anything you can do with it so it just seems kind of pointless, still the Stronghold is awesome and I devoted almost all of my resources early on to restoring it and exploring the dungeon beneath.
---->So the story, hmm, well I haven't finished it so I can't give you a full debrief on it, however, my impression is that it is not as strong or gripping as it could have been. You find out early in the game that you are what is called a Watcher, someone who can peer into the souls of the living, and see the past lives of that person. Unfortunately this awakened something inside yourself and as told to you by a crazy man, you too will suffer the fate of all of your past lives all living with you at the same time, driving you insane and ultimately to your doom. You set out to find a cure and get swept up into other bigger things going on. The story sounds great, the idea of the Watcher is awesome, it just isn't utilized to its fullest; the world becomes background to your concerns, that is to say that at least from the point I’ve played, the world doesn't seem to care about your success or demise. That is a very fitting setting, but it’s a tough sell to engage the player in, since there isn't a life threatening doom approaching, what was needed was strong personal reasons to motivate the player. Again, this all seems very passive and aside from the occasional staring into space, being a Watcher doesn't seem to really be as bad as the world cracks it up to be.
---->Again this is from my point of view and I admit I have not finished the story, but there are only a few acts and by now I would expect to have a full understanding of all that is going on, if they reveal something later on perhaps my opinion will change, but, it shouldn't take till Act 2 to be invested in any story...

Absolutely fantastic. Very much hits all of the highs that I wanted from an RPG in the vein of Baldur's Gate. The world is big and fairly varied with a number of very different cultures and ideologies populating a new world. The mechanics are tight, many of which are sharper than some of the older cRPG's like baldur's gate, neverwinter nights, or Planescape torment. It just feels great to be able to inhabit such a world again.
There are two things that make this game special for me. The first is that it's a great world to be in, to learn about, and to interact with. There are a number of consistent themes throughout the story that are brought to the fore in a number of different quests and in your relationships with your companion NPC's. I wouldn't call it a "cerebral" game, but it brings up interesting questions and there were many times I had to think about what choice I really wanted to take and how I wanted to interact with the companions. The second is that it's a fun turn-based combat game. While there are a lot of quests and storyline progression that is able to be done through conversation, you fight a lot in this game. And it's a ton of fun (if you like real-time with pause gameplay). There are a number of varied and viable builds for different classes and a lot of different ways to play and do well.

"Overwhelmingly Positive."  Oh, Homestucks.  Never change.
HIVESWAP: Act 1 is good.  It's a well-designed adventure game (a big hurdle to clear, in my book), but it comes across as more of a visual novel than an adventure game because it doesn't present any kind of challenge -- that's not its purpose.  Its purpose is to tell a Homestuck-parallel story in a Homestuck-like way, and it does that very well.
If you're not familiar with Homestuck, you ought to go read that first before investing here... this game's sense of humor won't make any sense to someone who hasn't internalized the jargon and in-jokes.  That might seem like a failing, but there shouldn't be any mystery regarding exactly for whom this game was designed.  It's a Homestuck game for Homestucks.  Are you a Homestuck?  No?
Read the comic.  Be the Homestuck.
Okay, let's mill some build grist.
I finished Act 1 in two and a half hours with about half the achievements.  I consider that a good investment of US$8.00.
The art and animation in this game is great.  It is inspired by Homestuck, but far more consistent and clean.  On occasion I found myself wishing for a momentary dip into hideous crayon blarg just for old times' sake, but it doesn't happen and I think that's probably a good thing.
The writing is solid, although it lacks any of the occasionally mindblowing japery of Homestuck.  There is a lot of text-bubble reading, which is not a surprise and not necessarily a bad thing.  The puns are... well, they needed a lot of puns.  Some of them work, but brace yourself for the ones that don't.
I am suitably intrigued by the characters, the standalone story, and the subtle and not-so-subtle tie-ins to Homestuck that I will be returning for Act 2, but by relying on what has come before the game has robbed itself of an opportunity to create new inexcusable folly.  Again, though, I don't think that was its purpose.
As a final point, I was surprised by how /much/ this game has to do with Homestuck -- I was expecting a parallel but separate story, but it looks from Act 1 like Hiveswap (or perhaps Hauntswitch) will be tied into the characters and events of the original.  This was not unwelcome, and more importantly I trust the author to be able to do this well.
If I have any complaint about the game, it's that it's not Homestuck enough in its mechanical execution -- I was looking forward to wrestling with a Fetch Modus for my Sylladex and interacting with complex systems like the Cruxtruder-Punch Designix-Totem Lathe-Alchemiter sequence of devices from the early days of Homestuck.  Of course, trying to actually code such a thing would have been an unmitigated disaster, so perhaps it is for the best.
In short: this is a great start of a game for fans of Homestuck, and if you're not a fan, you should consider becoming one.  It is time well spent.

Beautiful game, action packed, but even on Rookie mode it's often too hard to enjoy.
Let me start off by saying this is my first Tom Clancy game. Generally I'm an RPG player, but this game looked so beautiful I wanted to try it. From an artistic standpoint, I wasn't disappointed. From the environments, to the character designs it's really quite well done. Lots of eye candy, especially on ultra graphics settings if your GPU can handle it. The fluid movement of the character and the ability to interact with the environment is top notch. There's great body movement in climbing walls, crouching, ducking under cover, and reacting to events around you. There's also great responsiveness from the environs, as walls, vehicles, rocks, and otherwise are impacted by your actions. In terms of the "world" that has been created it's very impressive.
One of the major issues I'm having is being forced into certain play styles. I'm not great at stealth, and many of the missions require it which means I've found myself making one tiny little mistake and having to start over again...and again...and again. After the 8th or 9th attempt it just isn't fun anymore. Even on rookie mode I've found several of the missions impossible to complete and have aborted the mission to try something else. I love the different loadout options for weapons and gadgets, and have tried pretty much every permutation of stealth tactics, but all it takes it one little misstep and the whole mission is done for - even if I've made significant progress. This is especially problematic on those side missions which have no checkpoint - so you have to do it perfectly or it restarts from the top.
I've also become disappointed at being in a mission and going past a door that I can't do anything about unless I play co-op (or a co-op only mission). Well that's all well and good if you have a friend who has the game and you can schedule gaming time with, but since the majority of the mission is single player, why prevent me from experiencing everything in the game just because I can't coordinate time on someone's calendar to help me out? And just to be well-rounded, I HAVE played two co-op games with a friend that could make the time to join me. The co-op is very well done and takes into account teamwork, but with the same limitations as mentioned before - one little screw up and you're both back at the beginning with none of your progress saved.
And then there are the bugs. So many of them. I've been in the middle of a mission and the keyboard just suddenly stops working. The mouse actions work just fine, but I can't get the game to recognize any key I'm pressing on the keyboard. So I just get to sit there and let myself get killed and have to cntrl-alt-delete to kill the game. Over and over this has happened - and it just adds to the frustration of finally making progress on my 10th attempt only to have the game crash. I've seen some posts in the forums that people are having similar lockups every 30 minutes. I haven't timed mine, but it has happened with every single instance of long-term gaming.
Beautiful game and with so much potential - but the forums are full of issues with buggy gameplay (and I should probably mention that awful bug with full screen and windowed mode - don't touch ANY keys when the game is starting if you want to stay in full screen - what the heck is that about). I'll keep trying - but I fear I'm missing out on half the game because it's simply too hard or too buggy to complete a simple mission.
