I bought this title back in the beta days, and I really enjoyed it. It had a short storyline, but I was still quite into it anyways, because of all of the other things you could do, like side quests.
When the official release dropped, I was incredibly excited and Starbound was pretty much all I played for the following week. I loved all the new things it released and just everything about it.
To get into the many things you can do in this game, first of all, the lore and main quests are incredible. It was all so interesting, with the release of so many new characters and cutscenes, etc. I really loved it, and had a great time traveling planet to planet, getting new armor, weapons, and resources, and finishing quests that I needed to do at certain planet types.
The release of Steam Workshop support was also a big hit for me. The community created content in this game is so interesting and diverse, from mechs to simple pet peeve mods. I enjoyed modding the game and adding even more to its great environment.
However, the best thing that I experienced in this game was indefinitely the building system.
The immense amount of blocks, furniture, and the colony system, it all just blew me away, even in the game's beta days. Honestly, I haven't had a hard time building anything in this game. Houses, outposts, even castles... it sets your imagination free. Especially with the mods, there is almost no limits to what you can build in this game. I actually didn't expect that when I first discovered the game. I thought it would all be based on combat and flying your ship, but it actually looks like the developers spent a large portion of their time developing the game's variety in building.
A few months ago, I started slowly drifting away from the game and eventually started mostly playing other games. But, I still like to play the game every now and then, whenever I get an idea for anything that I can't build in other games. I just wanted to warn you that you might have a point, around 2.5 hundred hours, where you slowly get less interested in the game. It still pumped 250 hours into my pure entertainment.
Anyway, thanks for reading this review. I hope that, if you do buy this game, that you have a great time playing it.
tl;dr: If you are pondering whether or not you should buy this game, definitely buy it, especially if it is on sale. If you enjoyed a game like Terraria, or a game similar to it, I highly recommend this game for you.

Here's what I'll say about State of Decay (I played Breakdown, which adds more weapons and stuff): it needs a LOT to make it nice and shiny, but its heart is in the right place.
I started off playing this game because I wanted a Fallout-like game. It seemed like a good buy too, as it was around $15 when I picked it up. I'd read good reviews on Metacritic, and I felt it would suffice as an open-world, RPG-styled game with guns.
I should've realized right away when the game started off (in the middle of nowhere with no tutorial, cutscene, or any kind of explanation) that I was probably not going to like what followed. What followed was me running around and around and around, looking for a "place to call home."
Rage and frustration set in as I jogged around the landscape, killing dozens of zombies with a candlestick, radioing my ♥♥♥♥♥y girlfriend or whatever to come set up a home at this spot only to have her tell me it was indefensible and that I should keep looking. Ugggg...
It wouldn't have been such a problem except that the game was very unforgiving. The mechanics dictate you monitor two gauges: HP and Stamina. Simple enough; I've been doing that since HL2. They would refill after a certain time and little things like aspirin and snacks could bring them up a bit as well.
What I didn't like was that I was being asked to also monitor my sound level, as indicated by a circle on your radar that pops up in accordance with the level of activity you're doing, such as sprinting, searching a cabinet at a faster pace, driving, etc. There are zombies all over the goddamn place, and they all require a good bit of bashing to kill--I'd say 6-10 blows before they die. That's all well and good versus a couple or even three zombies, but any more than that and I was pretty much doomed unless I could make it back home where others would help me.
Too often I would come upon a house and try to search it, only to be beset upon by more than I could handle. My character would go in "Second Chance" mode where I'd have to frantically press "C" over and over until he or she burst from the dog pile like Neo, and then find I had a drastically drained stamina/HP bar and was basically prolonging the inevitable. Apparently, this game expects you to be A-Okay with investing time and effort into developing a character who will be torn to shreds at any given moment. Therfore, realism trumps fun. Fail.
Guns attract too much attention and have far too little ammunition to be useful. Fail. Melee weapons are therefore your standard approach to combat, but they have a breaking point and will shatter in the middle of a fight, leaving you to your fists and feet to deal with the zombies. Fail.
The interface for managing your home base was a gigantic cluster♥♥♥♥. You're supposed to go around establishing outposts, but those require that you have enough Respect points amongst your group. Respect is also the currency used to give yourself weapons, ammo, and powerups (morphine, snacks, etc.), and when you start over at your base camp after your previous character dies, he or she is of course a nobody and therefore gets♥♥♥♥♥♥in terms of Respect, limiting your ability to suit up and go establish outposts and stuff.
Want to take someone along with you to go grab supplies? You need Respect. Want someone to come pick up a supply drop that you don't have space for? You need Respect. Trying to defuse the situation between two warring members of your community? You need Respect. Want a straggler to join your group? You need Trust. It's too much to try and micromanage and quickly becomes an enormous pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Fail.
Of course, there are some good aspects of SOD. For the time that I played it, there were no loading screens aside from the startup menu leading into the actual game. The act of driving was pretty atrocious, as the cars would go from fast to full stop in less than a second, were very weak to damage, and just had terrible physics altogether--nevertheless, they were fun to take and plow through a horde of the undead from time to time.
The world was vast and varied. It's too bad there so many zombies ruining the fun of exploration.
Also, I did like that I had some control over my group; I just wish that it had been better developed. It would have been nice if I could tell members to go out and do tasks, or even if they just did them independently of my command.
This game could have been fantastic, and that's what sucks. Crummy AI (quit fixing the window and just let them come in so we can complete this mission, for ♥♥♥♥'s sake!), bad sound design and graphics, frustrating combat mechanics, and a severe lack of help from the game, in terms of instructions and forgiveness, made the experience extremely unenjoyable and disappointing. Can I get a refund...
TL;DR--This game sucks. Don't buy it unless it drops below $5.00 on a Steam sale.

The main game itself is great, nice concept, good execution overall, and some features that were fun to tinker with overall, so overall, I'd recommend the main game.
What I would not recommend is the DLC.
Minor Spoilers, you've been warned.
It adds pretty much nothing to the game. The "challenges" are a cakewalk, there are no new maps whatsoever (what ever happened to leaving the valley, eh, the entire point of the story campaign?), it has "heroes" which are nothing but units that showed up in the campaign last map as part of the story (that thing that helped make the game good).What's worse, is that some of those said "heroes" died as part of the story, which is completely unforgivable given how recent this game is. The new "weapons" touted by said DLC are at best, bland reskins, especially in the melee area as there are no stats associated with melee aside from how good your person is at that specific type of melee weapon. Finally, the DLC doesn't draw from your previous campaign, which makes any previous playtime essentially little more then practice.
In short, and to recap..
State of Decay, I would recommend, it's a solid game, good concept, fun, and I've seen worse stories.
Breakdown DLC, I would not recommend, at all, to anyone. It adds absolutely nothing relevant, fun, or exciting to the game, ignores the entirety of the storyline the game itself built up in the campaign, and arguably spits on it. There are no new locations, maps, homes, no new zombies to slaughter with a glee that would make Fraud wonder just what kind of person you are, the challenges could be done by anyone, even those who are challenged to start with, and the new "weapons" are nothing to note, and short of a weapons list, you'd be hard pressed to even name any of the new weapons.
The only thing it does do, that could be of some merit to those who thought the game too easy, is increase zombie spawns as you repeat the same missions over, and over, and over again. There are no "choices" that really change anything in this, and it's sad.
Anyway, that's my two cents.

Things I liked:
+ Combat is tactical, visceral, and complex.  Each of the nine vocations (i.e. classes/jobs) has its own way of fighting.  You can climb large enemies in order to attack their weak points in regular gameplay (not just in cutscenes).  There's a hilariously large variety of consumables you can use in combat.  There are enough different techniques and tricks that you will still be discovering new ones after a hundred hours of gameplay.
+ Pawns (i.e. summoned allies created by other players) are an innovative way to add a cooperative multiplayer aspect to a singleplayer game.
+ Many of the boss fights are absolutely thrilling.  One of those is among the best dragon fights in any action RPG.
+ There's a lot of excellent music in the game.
Things I didn't like:
- The math behind combat is poorly thought-out.  For example, because of how defenses work, it's very difficult to make up for even slightly subpar equipment with player skill.
- Not all keyboard & mouse controls can be configured, and the game doesn't make this clear.  For example, by default, F is used for grabbing things and for firing a bow.  You can change the binding for grab, but firing a bow stays on F, no matter what.
- Some parts feel unfinished.  For example, two different characters, at the end of their last side quests, promise to seek aid for you in the final battle.  And those two plot threads go absolutely nowhere.
- For the Dark Arisen rerelease, they didn't bother filling out the aforementioned unfinished parts of the game.  Instead, they added Bitterblack Isle, a festival of power creep and fake difficulty.
My recommendations:
* Ignore Bitterblack Isle as much as you can. It will make you hate the game if you take it seriously. If you've played the DLC stages of
on Hard Mode, you know the kind of grindy, repetitive, power-creepy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you get with BBI.  If you really must get the achievements, just run through once as a level 200 magick archer.
* Don't restart repeatedly, trying to perfect your character's appearance.  Once you've beaten the final battle, you can buy the Secret of Metamorphosis, which lets you customize your character's appearance whenever you want.

I bought this title back in the beta days, and I really enjoyed it. It had a short storyline, but I was still quite into it anyways, because of all of the other things you could do, like side quests.
When the official release dropped, I was incredibly excited and Starbound was pretty much all I played for the following week. I loved all the new things it released and just everything about it.
To get into the many things you can do in this game, first of all, the lore and main quests are incredible. It was all so interesting, with the release of so many new characters and cutscenes, etc. I really loved it, and had a great time traveling planet to planet, getting new armor, weapons, and resources, and finishing quests that I needed to do at certain planet types.
The release of Steam Workshop support was also a big hit for me. The community created content in this game is so interesting and diverse, from mechs to simple pet peeve mods. I enjoyed modding the game and adding even more to its great environment.
However, the best thing that I experienced in this game was indefinitely the building system.
The immense amount of blocks, furniture, and the colony system, it all just blew me away, even in the game's beta days. Honestly, I haven't had a hard time building anything in this game. Houses, outposts, even castles... it sets your imagination free. Especially with the mods, there is almost no limits to what you can build in this game. I actually didn't expect that when I first discovered the game. I thought it would all be based on combat and flying your ship, but it actually looks like the developers spent a large portion of their time developing the game's variety in building.
A few months ago, I started slowly drifting away from the game and eventually started mostly playing other games. But, I still like to play the game every now and then, whenever I get an idea for anything that I can't build in other games. I just wanted to warn you that you might have a point, around 2.5 hundred hours, where you slowly get less interested in the game. It still pumped 250 hours into my pure entertainment.
Anyway, thanks for reading this review. I hope that, if you do buy this game, that you have a great time playing it.
tl;dr: If you are pondering whether or not you should buy this game, definitely buy it, especially if it is on sale. If you enjoyed a game like Terraria, or a game similar to it, I highly recommend this game for you.

By far, the best part of this game is the story. This game has very endearing and hilarious characters,  and extremely well written dialogue. Most modern games with their GPU melting graphics and 9 figure budget are incapable of the basic entertaining story of Chantelise.  The game opens by explaining that Chante has been turned into a fairy against her will, and she needs her sister Elise to help find a way to remove the curse. You're always looking out for the next time the game will allow you to read the next few lines of dialogue.
The problem here is that this is a video game, meaning you actually have to PLAY it. Ugh.
Don't get me wrong - I'm the kind of person who expects an epic story in every game I play. I'm the one in a million who actually ENJOYS cut-scenes. For me, gameplay always takes a backseat to story and characters.
But the gameplay in this title is sickeningly loathsome. It feels like an alpha version of Ocarina of time. It's meant to be an action game, but the controls feel so stiff, and it is very easy to get attacked by an enemy or fall off a ledge because you couldn't see it. Generation 5 camera at its finest. Going through dungeons is a chore - and there are no puzzles, mini-games, or anything else to break the monotony.  To progress to the next room in a dungeon, you must kill ALL the monsters. Miss one? Wander around the over-sized rooms looking for it, only to finally kill it so you can enter the next room AND DO THE SAME THING OVER AGAIN.
As for actually fighting these monsters, you can walk up to them and whack them with your sword. When they die, they often drop money (which can be used in town to buy items) or gems. These gems are used for spells - ex: red for fire. But you'd think you could save up gems and plan to use the right spells on the right monsters. Nope, you cast spells based on which gem you picked up last.  The game is set up in such a way that some spells are VERY useful or useless against the right or wrong monster, but you have no way of saving a spell for the right monster.
Many other reviewers seem to believe this game is hard. No, this game is easy if you pay attention. The problem is the combat is so freaking BORING that there is no way you CAN pay attention. I have played many games where the story is the main draw, and the gameplay is there only to serve as a medium for the plot and characters. But Chantelise is below even that - the battle system is an OBSTACLE, actively preventing you from getting to the next part of the plot (with yet another room filled with generic monsters).
The awful gameplay of this title 'bottlenecks' the fantastic story.
It's a really, really cute game, but it's irritatingly hard and generally unforgiving.

“She’s a goddess, as fickle as they come… and with all the failings you’d expect of an empress and a ♥♥♥♥♥”, Durance says to me in his growly voice. He is a priest talking about his own goddess Magran in whose name he helped kill Waidwen (who claimed to be the living vessel of the god Eothas) during the Saint’s War. Such is the relationship between gods and people in Pillars of Eternity. Gods are not abstract terms used only in blind faith, they are among us every step of the way providing blessing and punishment as they see fit. They are deeply woven within the very fabric of society, with everyone opting for a god to serve and follow. As you start your journey, you learn of Waidwen’s Legacy, a horrible plague beset upon the people of Dyrwood which sees their newborn come into the world soulless. It is definitely true that faith and religion are overarching themes in Pillars of Eternity, but it’s the liberty to create a personal touch provided by Obsidian that makes it so compelling.
You witness a strange ritual at the beginning of the game and something strange happens to you. From there, your motivations are up to you. Nobody designates you as the would-be savior of the world, nobody even tasks you to look into Waidwen’s Legacy. You are simply a person making his way through the world designing your own motivations and choosing your own actions. It was this aspect of the game that I found most liberating and compelling. Too often in games you are simply tasked and/or commanded what to do with clear goals set before you. Pillars of Eternity removes all that which makes the whole journey very organic and natural. It’s devoid of that silly feeling of clearly knowing you have something grand to do, but you simply opt to do a lot of things on the side despite everyone constantly reminding you how the world’s fate rests in your hands. This may be a subtle effect, but I found it extremely refreshing and compelling.
Obsidian was clear on what it set out to do with Pillars of Eternity, it is definitely a throwback to classic Infinity engine games most notably Baldur’s Gate and Icewind Dale. It even looks the part with its rather simplistic 2D graphics that will instantly remind anyone of those glory days of computer RPGs. However, even though Obsidian didn’t really push any big new ideas, Pillars of Eternity is still very much imbued with many modern takes on what we’ve seen and played a long time ago. The visuals aren’t going to blow anyone away, but the 3D character models, some very nice effects and a strong art style go a long way to make it visually appealing, even gorgeous at times.
The combat is real-time with pause, very reminiscent of the first Dragon Age. It is highly tactical with plenty of abilities, spells and traps to choose from. The only problem regarding the combat is the atrociously bad pathfinding. Outside of combat, it works perfectly fine, but during combat, characters will very often get stuck on walls, obstacles and each other requiring you to very closely monitor everything that is going on and manually select each character to get them out of a bind, particularly in confined areas. This can be alleviated to a degree by smart group formation and a bit of micromanagement, but that shouldn’t be necessary. What’s different about the combat is its emphasis on endurance over health. Monitoring health is a long-term affair in each battle, but a far more pressing matter is each character’s endurance level. As they receive damage, their endurance decreases, if it reaches zero, they get knocked out. There are ways to get fallen members back up again and certain classes specialize in such abilities. However, if any character’s health should reach zero, it’s game over for that particular character. So it is possible to lose designed party members for good. However, you can create your own party members at taverns for a fee. There is a large number of character classes and races to choose from, some of which are rather unique such as the cipher class or the godlike race. The downside is the extremely low level cap (12).
The game world is very big, there are quite a lot of different and interesting locations to visit from your map view whereas each location is spacious yet not overwhelming. You will also get your own stronghold ruin at one point which you will be able to build up again and receive various benefits. The best thing about the stronghold is that it hides a massive dungeon consisting of 15 levels and a nasty boss fight at the end. What is overwhelming at times is the lore and dialogue which sometimes goes on for too long. Also, the writing, while generally very good, can get a bit opaque. The main story is interesting, it raises many questions, but leaves the conclusions up to the player. There is a great number of choices to be made throughout the game and a lot of them will be addressed at the very end.
There’s a lot to love about Pillars of Eternity. The way it liberates players by letting them play their own way at their own pace through the story, by letting them decide on both their motivations and actions, the interesting game world and lore, memorable characters and a very tactical combat system. By liberating themselves from existing worlds and publisher demands, Obsidian had complete control to create their best game to date and one of the best RPGs in recent years.

Now boy, if you thinking you're buying a game that had 5 or so years spent in it's making, think again. Keep noted that it's development took a hella of a long time due to an ENTIRE redo of the project (more details somewhere online, no doubt). What you're looking at the store page of is the Hiveswap that was worked on after it got smoothed out. I'm making sure this is clarified, because I'm quite sure there are some here under the mistake that this is a long awaited big content title. But with that nonsense out the way, let me tell you about Hiveswap!
Read Homestuck?:  While many will say otherwise, I say ReAd Homestuck before playing Hiveswap (or watch the awesome dubs). Yes, it's not mandatory, but trust me. You will most certainly miss the importance of countless direct plot points such as
and many many other points only a Homestuck reader will understand. Just do yourself a favor and try reading the story this is adding onto, and if you do play Hiveswap blind, PLEASE keep your theories silent until you read Homestuck. It's improtant to the game's lore in so many ways already. So overall, playable and understandable enough for any, but intended for those that read. Also we know Hussie is a troll, and will use that specific wording "Homestuck hasn't even been made yet!" for a plot twist twistier than the windy thing.
Story: Hiveswap starts out perfectly. We are beautifully gifted with a  taste of the art from the main menu and introduction. You probably already know this part, but Jude n' Joey get attacked by monsters, and flee to their little hideaways to get a grip on the situation. It's a fast introduction that raises enough questions to get the train rolling! Our two main character siblings Joey and Jude make no hesitation to engage in conversation and show off the qualities of their character and writing the moment we are interested to learn. I'll let you learn more about them when you play, but have my word they put no shame on the Homestuck name. Oh, and given the E rating, you will here a lot less cursing in this story, but the humor is dark enough to feel at home. I don't have any harsh feelings towards this development, as it goes with the aesthetic theme pretty well. Oh yeah, and obviously our lovely narration text is detailed and filling our eyes with pixel letters as ever. Every object and interaction have endless possible text to read. What's better is it's mostly all optional to try, letting the player choose just how much detail they get to read. I'll lastly say in regards to the story that is pretty short, even for an Act. But seeing as they also plan the Hauntswitch series, I think there will still be lots to see in the future.
Art: Beautiful! ..But not perfect. Every single background is hand drawn fantasicly, and the classy approach definetly shows. Homestuck's original style feels well left behind aside from the obviously inspired character designs, but the new background approach is very welcomed. My only complaints being that the combat animations don't feel all that inspiring, but being as this is a point and click adventure game, that shouldn't matter (but there is a reason why it's not usually attempted in the genre). The bigger problem being that some room areas feel a little too cramped, and you can't always tell what you're looking at (Might just be me with the weak eyes here, but I don't know). This is difficult when the game doesn't have a scan feature, but I can't say it messed up my game progession. Also a quick seizure warning as there are flashy light moments.
Music: It's Toby Fox hun', what more to say?  Though I don't feel as in love as I did with Undertale's, it's still great and atmospheric. The battle themes have to be where the talent mostly shines, to no surprise. Honestly... I wish I had more to say here. Just try to avoid getting stuck anywhere, as some themes can last a while through the story and get drilled into your head until you progress.
Gameplay Technicalities: It's what you expect of a point and click boy! While I have heard of issues with framrate, none of that really interupted my experience... Honestly it's a very nit picky complaint to make on a game that doesn't require intense movement. And all the glitches I experienced on launch day have since been fixed, you may still find some, as well as some crazy exploits if you search. It also managed to play on my steam link pretty well, which is rare as hell.
Gameplay Features: You have an inventory, stuff goes in, there's endless possible texts. Okay, so what isn't dead obvious or not talked about yet? I guess the progession rate. Hiveswap is one of those games where talking means you did something right. Though the ammount of talking can be quite intense for even the smallest of progress, this is something all us readers are already used to, actually it's far more mild here than in Homestuck standards. It is best to get lost a few times just to explore and see everything, and with everything you are tasked to do between the dialogues, I'd say it all fits well enough. Plenty of easter eggs and optional interactions too, as an essential to any good point and click. The only two lacking points I can think of are the difficulty and the "battles". Hiveswap's description may say it goes for logical and non-dreamy solutions, but it gets a bit too logical... In the sense that any sense of logic can follow the directions it hints at. But I'm not saying it's all the time, as I had a decent ammount of head scratching moments. It just didn't feel as satisfying to solve a majority of the puzzles when the answers were so obvious. So about them battles? Well, while I do appreciate that the battles change the pace of scenes and throw in new ways of thinking for the player to react to, they don't translate to the genre well. Enemies don't really act monstourous, and kinda just stand around until you throw the right random item at them. The game over screen is considered a secret, if that says anything.
Price and recommendation:  A Daedalic title is 30$ off of a sale, and Hiveswap will be 32$ if it continues the 8$ tag ::::) I feel that Hiveswap would be either long as or longer than a Daedalic by then, so can't say the price ain't proper. But I do hope upon finishing it they do a discounted complete bundle by maybe 10% or so if you buy it whole. So is Act 1 worth it now? Yes if you're a big Homestuck fan. If you're a fan but are unsure, I won't argue waiting for more acts to be released. If you aren't a Homestuck fan, wait for a sale because it may be a dissapointing buy, especially if future acts raise the knowledge requirement. And if none of these apply to you but wanna see the story anyway, watch a playthrough!

I bought this title back in the beta days, and I really enjoyed it. It had a short storyline, but I was still quite into it anyways, because of all of the other things you could do, like side quests.
When the official release dropped, I was incredibly excited and Starbound was pretty much all I played for the following week. I loved all the new things it released and just everything about it.
To get into the many things you can do in this game, first of all, the lore and main quests are incredible. It was all so interesting, with the release of so many new characters and cutscenes, etc. I really loved it, and had a great time traveling planet to planet, getting new armor, weapons, and resources, and finishing quests that I needed to do at certain planet types.
The release of Steam Workshop support was also a big hit for me. The community created content in this game is so interesting and diverse, from mechs to simple pet peeve mods. I enjoyed modding the game and adding even more to its great environment.
However, the best thing that I experienced in this game was indefinitely the building system.
The immense amount of blocks, furniture, and the colony system, it all just blew me away, even in the game's beta days. Honestly, I haven't had a hard time building anything in this game. Houses, outposts, even castles... it sets your imagination free. Especially with the mods, there is almost no limits to what you can build in this game. I actually didn't expect that when I first discovered the game. I thought it would all be based on combat and flying your ship, but it actually looks like the developers spent a large portion of their time developing the game's variety in building.
A few months ago, I started slowly drifting away from the game and eventually started mostly playing other games. But, I still like to play the game every now and then, whenever I get an idea for anything that I can't build in other games. I just wanted to warn you that you might have a point, around 2.5 hundred hours, where you slowly get less interested in the game. It still pumped 250 hours into my pure entertainment.
Anyway, thanks for reading this review. I hope that, if you do buy this game, that you have a great time playing it.
tl;dr: If you are pondering whether or not you should buy this game, definitely buy it, especially if it is on sale. If you enjoyed a game like Terraria, or a game similar to it, I highly recommend this game for you.

Feels arcade-y. Tries so hard to be hard to the point it just ends up forced instead of hard, like putting Oblivion on the hardest difficulty. Having weak creatures with a huge life bar doesn't make an action RPG hard, it only makes the player waste more time taking out the same enemies over and over to advance. And from how repetitive this RPG's combat system is, I got bored quickly. Not reminiscent of Dark Souls at all; it feels more like a single player ArcheAge, where instead of pressing numbers to attack, you press your mouse buttons. I thought the combat system against big foes was gonna be fun and innovative, as it's reminiscent of Shadow of the Colossus, however, its execution is poor, probably because most of the foes aren't truly that big. At least it's better than killing giants or dragons in Skyrim.
The intro sucks. There are two tutorials dilligently teaching you how to do the same things, which goes against what some reviewers mentioned about “the game not holding your hand”. Thankfully, you can turn off the second tutorial once you're really into the game. The story is obnoxiously stupid and the characters act in an equally obnoxious fashion. I cringed too hard for too long.
Then there are problems like annoying pawns spamming your ears and screen, which thankfully you're able to turn off in the options as well. If you think Bethesda's companions are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ wait until you meet the pawns. I became stressed even before I got to create my character. The pawn system is fun, but it is not new. It's so simple it pains me to read people calling it creative and/or innovative.
The character creation is below mediocre. I have nothing against the graphics (they're terrible, but I don't care), yet character creation is too limited for a game such as this. Most body features don't feel like they fit, skin textures aren't decent enough, not enough color swatches to choose... the body sliders don't truly slide, they switch amongst an extremely limited couple of positions. For example, if I were to guess, I'd say there are only around ten positions on your character's face you can place their nose, and more than half of such positions look irrealistic or dumb.
EDIT: I've played a bit more. As I've expected, the game has become extremely easy after a while, which reinforces what I've said about it trying forcibly to be a hard game. The enemies are very predictable, the only difference being that they have huge life bars, additional lives, and a bunch of other stuff added to make you hit them more times. Also, in hard mode, they'll do double the damage. That's about it, nothing complex about the battle system besides weaknesses and strengths, which is straight out Pokémon-level of complexity, so you never really have to take a long time strategizing or preparing yourself for a fight.
Some quests don't explain what you're supposed to do clearly, which can be a pain if you're going into this game blind. I've enjoyed that there are a few groups of bandits that don't attack you on sight when you're inside their forts, a thing that makes sense, unlike Skyrim, where every single bandit murders everyone that passes by, which always made me ask myself: “How do they even recruit people anyway?” I've been so badly conditioned that I murdered bandits in DD that were not going to instantly attack, only to be surprised after murdering them that they were initially peaceful towards me.
You gotta be careful where you save, otherwise, you might load up your game and be surrounded by enemies. The game respawns everything when you reload for some reason. I almost died this way when I was playing the game for the second time.
I've had two fights where I felt like I was having fun, both against the same gryffin. First time he flew away, second time I got to murder the thing. It was an easy, quick, anticlimatic ending, but that's the only moment I had fun in the whole game, so...
Also, your stats are dictated by which class you're on while leveling up, a nice system overall. That's what made me decide to try out a new character solely on hard mode to maximize the stats I wanted using the right classes at the right levels. Well, guess what: You can only have one save game. If you make a new game, it deletes the old one. I decided to quit trying.
Sadly, my opinion about the game didn't change. I wish I hadn't bought it, but there's no coming back now.

Dragon's Dogma looks mediocre. Muddy graphics reminiscent of the PS2 era and the voice acting is often Resident Evil levels of ham.
And yet...
It's Japan's interpretation of a Western RPG and it is glorious.
This is a game that genuinely makes you afraid to go out at night. The lighting engine is probably one of the only ones to get the way light works (MGSV is the other that comes to mind, and probably does it slightly better) and there's a strong touch of Dark Souls here. When I say that, most DS veterans will scoff, but there's a sense of real danger here. You don't lose anything when you die....except progress. This game does not autosave very often, and if you die you WILL feel it, especially because the ability to fast travel is VERY limited for a long time. It does come with manual saving, so make it a habit to save every so often, you'll be thankful for it.
Dragon's Dogma is clunky. It's a hodge podge of design that shouldn't work, yet does. It's obtuse, and it doesn't tell you a lot. But in it's own special way, it's charming and beguiling.
I recommend it if you're after a special experience. It will take some time to really "get" but once it does, you'll find yourself coming back over and over again.

With the right mods, and historical appreciation this game is today's most complex historical TW title. This from its onset is in essence Rome2 done right but it's a completely different era. It is the era of the dramatic fall of Rome where unlike other historical TWs , it can be a game with various approaches. Or u can play as Rome and fight for survival from within and your numerous borders. Also u can play as the bringer of the apocalypse as the Huns. This game is a massive step in the right direction compared to previous titles as this game brings better siege attrition mechanics, political system , but also ironically more varied gameplay. I found Rome 2 ironically lack variety of play styles. Rome 2 where every faction u just build up and expand. In Attila there is actual gameplay variety as mentioned above as finally u can play a game of either bracing for the end of days or being the horsemen of the end.                                                                                                   There are of course issues with this game as the performance is well pretty bad however as long as u don't expect to play with max AA or 4K ur fine, there are also annoying or imbalanced mechanics but this can be fixed with mods. Like all TW games or any pic games in general mods are ur best friends use them!

As a generic, cover-based third-person shooter, it's an average game. Think "Uncharted" or "The Last of Us", except all the exploration, environmental puzzle solving, and character development is stripped out, leaving only the combat.
The single-player experience is a series of combat arenas littered with waist-high walls. Each zone punctuated with a resupply cache at every checkpoint. It feels like a compilation of maps meant for the co-op mode of Conviction and it shows. Aside from the story missions, there are several game modes for the missions (no detection, clear the room, and clear the room for X waves).
It's arguable that replayability is built in to the maps due to the score attack mechanism which grades you on your performance in non-lethal (Batman), silent lethal (Solid Snake), and noisy (Michael Bay) playstyles. Why a secret agent -- with a history in covert wetwork -- would be rewarded or even commended for kicking down doors and emptying an auto-shotty into a warehouse full of armored goons is beyond me.
Once again, the concept of darkness is binary, as it was since Double Agent (PC/360). Due to the large number of enemies with night vision goggles and flashlights or the environments which are lit with dozens of light sources per square foot (many of which are ambient or otherwise indestructable), using shadows -- the original hallmark of the Splinter Cell series -- is pretty much useless, anyway.
Stealth is no longer about stalking your prey, waiting for the perfect time to strike from the shadows. Instead, "stealth" has devolved to camping at a corner, dangling from an overhead ledge, or just sprinting up behind an enemy (provided you've specced your equipment for maximum stealth) and mashing the kill button. Speaking of overhead ledges, senior citizen Sam Fisher is more nimble and spry than ever before, able to scale the 10-foot high walls of an office building with the ease of a young assassin Ezio Auditore.
Haven't bothered with the competitive multiplayer mode, so I can't comment on it.
Much like Conviction, this is Splinter Cell in name only. If you must buy, wait for a deep discount. Better yet, just buy an Assassin's Creed title as that's pretty much the direction that this franchise is headed.

“She’s a goddess, as fickle as they come… and with all the failings you’d expect of an empress and a ♥♥♥♥♥”, Durance says to me in his growly voice. He is a priest talking about his own goddess Magran in whose name he helped kill Waidwen (who claimed to be the living vessel of the god Eothas) during the Saint’s War. Such is the relationship between gods and people in Pillars of Eternity. Gods are not abstract terms used only in blind faith, they are among us every step of the way providing blessing and punishment as they see fit. They are deeply woven within the very fabric of society, with everyone opting for a god to serve and follow. As you start your journey, you learn of Waidwen’s Legacy, a horrible plague beset upon the people of Dyrwood which sees their newborn come into the world soulless. It is definitely true that faith and religion are overarching themes in Pillars of Eternity, but it’s the liberty to create a personal touch provided by Obsidian that makes it so compelling.
You witness a strange ritual at the beginning of the game and something strange happens to you. From there, your motivations are up to you. Nobody designates you as the would-be savior of the world, nobody even tasks you to look into Waidwen’s Legacy. You are simply a person making his way through the world designing your own motivations and choosing your own actions. It was this aspect of the game that I found most liberating and compelling. Too often in games you are simply tasked and/or commanded what to do with clear goals set before you. Pillars of Eternity removes all that which makes the whole journey very organic and natural. It’s devoid of that silly feeling of clearly knowing you have something grand to do, but you simply opt to do a lot of things on the side despite everyone constantly reminding you how the world’s fate rests in your hands. This may be a subtle effect, but I found it extremely refreshing and compelling.
Obsidian was clear on what it set out to do with Pillars of Eternity, it is definitely a throwback to classic Infinity engine games most notably Baldur’s Gate and Icewind Dale. It even looks the part with its rather simplistic 2D graphics that will instantly remind anyone of those glory days of computer RPGs. However, even though Obsidian didn’t really push any big new ideas, Pillars of Eternity is still very much imbued with many modern takes on what we’ve seen and played a long time ago. The visuals aren’t going to blow anyone away, but the 3D character models, some very nice effects and a strong art style go a long way to make it visually appealing, even gorgeous at times.
The combat is real-time with pause, very reminiscent of the first Dragon Age. It is highly tactical with plenty of abilities, spells and traps to choose from. The only problem regarding the combat is the atrociously bad pathfinding. Outside of combat, it works perfectly fine, but during combat, characters will very often get stuck on walls, obstacles and each other requiring you to very closely monitor everything that is going on and manually select each character to get them out of a bind, particularly in confined areas. This can be alleviated to a degree by smart group formation and a bit of micromanagement, but that shouldn’t be necessary. What’s different about the combat is its emphasis on endurance over health. Monitoring health is a long-term affair in each battle, but a far more pressing matter is each character’s endurance level. As they receive damage, their endurance decreases, if it reaches zero, they get knocked out. There are ways to get fallen members back up again and certain classes specialize in such abilities. However, if any character’s health should reach zero, it’s game over for that particular character. So it is possible to lose designed party members for good. However, you can create your own party members at taverns for a fee. There is a large number of character classes and races to choose from, some of which are rather unique such as the cipher class or the godlike race. The downside is the extremely low level cap (12).
The game world is very big, there are quite a lot of different and interesting locations to visit from your map view whereas each location is spacious yet not overwhelming. You will also get your own stronghold ruin at one point which you will be able to build up again and receive various benefits. The best thing about the stronghold is that it hides a massive dungeon consisting of 15 levels and a nasty boss fight at the end. What is overwhelming at times is the lore and dialogue which sometimes goes on for too long. Also, the writing, while generally very good, can get a bit opaque. The main story is interesting, it raises many questions, but leaves the conclusions up to the player. There is a great number of choices to be made throughout the game and a lot of them will be addressed at the very end.
There’s a lot to love about Pillars of Eternity. The way it liberates players by letting them play their own way at their own pace through the story, by letting them decide on both their motivations and actions, the interesting game world and lore, memorable characters and a very tactical combat system. By liberating themselves from existing worlds and publisher demands, Obsidian had complete control to create their best game to date and one of the best RPGs in recent years.

This is easily one of the most poorly executed games of its type that has ever been published.
I know, the story is fun.  I know, we waited so long, so we should take what we get.  I know, the devs seem very interactive with the community.
That doesn't diminish the problems with this game.
Minor gripes: Text is at times completely unreadably small.  For whatever reason the game handles long book titles very poorly.  I have several times picked up a book that I cannot read the title off because the characters are so small as to be dots.  Sometimes in stores the text on an item is missing entirely, forcing one to right-click the item and bring up the item's details.  Sometimes NPCs are given 'locations' on the area-level map, spoiling the fact that they are even in existence - and I'm not sure if this is a bug or a dumb game design choice.  And this isn't a case where there's just a location identifier, either - the actual name of the character comes up and does not disappear, regardless of where your cursor is, unlike every other location.
Mid-level shenanigans: Saves don't actually save the state of the game.  I'm not sure what they're doing, but quite often things "change".  I've had inventory items disappear or move.  NPCs change position, sometimes drastically - including hostile NPCs I had carefully positioned against.  Loot crates change inventory - even if I've already looked in them.
Major damned issues:
Combat
So the devs copied the, essentially, the combat form the Infinity Engine games - which is fine by itself, as that's why I Kickstarted the project.  However, in many respects they've dropped the ball and devolved.  One glaring and iritating example is that combat is so messy that it can take a lot of time just determining where each of your party members are standing and who they are attacking.  The line drawing thing is a nice idea, poorly executed - but then, that's probably because the only thing to indicate which character you are selecting is the very faint - often simply not happening due to some bug - glowing of the rather small cursor around each combatant.  That is so frustrating and eats up so much time in some instances that I've actually walked away from the game more than once out of frustration.  The character you select should have a DIFFERENT COLOR.  This is not rocket science!  Holy cow!
Environmental collision is ... random?  Some barrels you can basically stand in, some your cursor around the character cannot even touch.  Very often the 'walls' of a room are visually an entire character or more's space from the drawn wall - which definitely cause you to make critical errors in combat.  NPC's that are not in combat but are on the screen are stone pillars.  They will block you, you cannot push them, and you will eventually have a character drop due to it.
Combat difficulty is also random at times for certain types of enemies.  The most egregious examples are the 'ghost' type enemies.  They teleport and the higher level ghosts can summon lower level ghosts.  What this means is that whether or not you can actually engage with the main ghosts and prevent more from being summoned is entirely random.  It is not possible to predict whether they will summon the lesser ghosts in one place or another, and even if you could, that's not very important since that lower level ghostie will teleport into your back line.  Combining this with the collision and character identification problems makes fighting these enemies torture.  They aren't that hard to kill when you actually get to fight them, tho.  This could be alleviated if Fear effects caused them to flee, but they don't.  Most magic will also effect your allies, so you can't just blast them back from you.  There's seemingly no such thing as an anti-ghost spell, not even for the priests.  That right there is a massive glaring hole in combat.  I thought I was fighting these guys wrong, but every walkthrough or guide I've run across basically says to avoid them.  Just run away.  They aren't strong or dangerous for any reason other than the fact that they are specifically designed to exploit the weaknesses of the game engine, which is cheap beyond belief.
Storyline
So basically most NPCs are cardboard cutouts.  The ones that aren't are fantastic, but most actually are - and they have zero awareness of the world they are in.  Let me go through some examples.  One of the very first sidequest characters, Aufra, is a good one.  So she's pregnant and wants you to get her something to prevent a 'Hollowborn' child. Turns out, can't do it.  So she's nervous because the local Lord kills everyone who bears a Hollowborn.  The problem is that she's still worried about this even after you kill this tyrant.  She's not a character, she's just a cardboard cutout with no purpose other than to give you some XP for opening up a spot on the map.  The dialog options in Lord of the Barren Land often make no sense given what the character knows.  Way too limited.  It's extremely frustrating to be forced into chosing options that are illogical.  The Theorems of Pandgram ... is stupid.  Like, physics-breaking levels of stupid.  This girl wants to use a book from the library, I go to ask the head librarian about getting the book.  My mistake.  The head librarian bans the girl from the library and hides the book - which is not in her posession or even in the room she is in - and that's that.  Then, the girl, will later ambush and try to kill your party because ... something?  OK so this librarian can destroy or hide books with her mind from across a building and the girl, who has studied a specific subject all her life, is ready to suicide (with 4-5 random nameless buddies??) rush hardened adventurers because of the librarian's decision?  That is just plain /stupid/.  But that's tip of the damned iceberg.  More than half of the sidequests are like this and the characters involved are terrible.  My favorite one so far is Blood Legacy.
Blood Legacy involves the dumbest quest design/town design/character design I have ever seen in a game, bar none, and by far.  So there's some Lord in the little town of Dyrford and he's obviously about as shifty as anyone and dumb as a brick - he lets you know up front that he doesn't even know how old his daughter is, but he's sure desperate to find her.  So you go looking.  Everyone is telling you to talk to Tyrgil, and since there's virtually no point to walking around new places without stealthing/searching, you find the key to his back room.  Now there's no point in trying to role play this and waiting for him to go to bed - the characters in this game have no homes for the most part and I don't think a single one has a 'life cycle'.  They all are awake at all hours of the night, never sleeping or eating.  (Which is a massive step back in game design - 15 years ago Arcanum set the standard that NPCs should have lives!)  So you just walk past him like no big deal and unlock the back room.  He and his assistant immediately suicide in a 2v6 fight like 90% of the other throw-away, cardboard villains in the sidequests.  You go down some stairs in the back room and well holy smokes, there is a massive underground lair with Skaen Cultists all over the place.  Well, damn, I get back out of there and run to tell the Lord that I think his daughter is down there and that he should send his ~30 or so well equipped soldiers down there to find her!  WRONG.  You can't even bring up the fact that you are pretty sure his daughter is being held underground by human sacrificing cultists.  That's not important.  Oh, and you can't mention this to anyone in town - or anyone in the game, at all, period.  You just walked into a massive conspiracy involving "kith" sacrifice and there are zero dialog options about this.  None.  The townspeople may very well all be in on the conspiracy, but then isn't that an obvious choice the player should make??

Note that this game is still in a state of development that is along the lines of early beta.  With that in mind, I will probably update this review when it is in a full release mode.
State of Decay is a zombie survival horror game that uses a 3rd-person shooter format to present a story about the survivors.  As the player, you will need to build up a community of survivors with a diverse set of skills to make the most of the apocalypse.  Building comes down to scavenging for materials to build facilities for your safehouse, getting your survivors out there to build up their skills and succesfully stockpiling different kinds of supplies to see them through the night.
In that regard, State of Decay is wonderfully executed.  Fighting feels organic and properly gritty, without silly mechanics that force enemies to wait while you perform John Woo executions in slow-mo.  Fighting is in fact, to be avoided many times, simply because it will make whatever you're actually trying to do more difficult.  That is how it /should/ be in a true zombie apocalypse.  In addition, SoD makes an effort to improve immersion by having the game world continue to develop while you aren't playing it.  This is limited to a 48 hour maximum, which is equivalent to 2 weeks in-game.  This almost always prevents anything truly disastrous from occuring during your downtime, at least if you left your community in a good condition to begin with.
The key to having the least frustration in SoD is understanding when survivor-generated missions are important and when they can be safely ignored.  Not every opportunity should be taken advantage of.  Some of them are valuable for improving your community (or averting a crises), but others merely offer morale increases, which are unnecessary when your morale is already maxed out.
Although there is an extremely wide variety of firearms in SoD, one should learn fairly quickly that, much like the real world, many weapons accomplish the same job in much the same fashion.  The value of weapons comes down to how durable they are for their effectiveness and how easy it will be to find ammo for them.  Melee weapons on the other hand are pretty much two-dimensional.  Find the most durable weapon you can with the weight you prefer.  Heavier weapons are more effective, but leave less capacity available for looting.
Finally, there is actually a story implemented in and amongst the sandbox and you can enjoy it at whatever pace you prefer.  It is linear for the first couple missions, but after that, progression through the story is entirely optional.  That said, you should do them, because they unlock more locations to live and scavenge and the story isn't half-bad.
All-in-all, State of Decay is the game you're looking for if you love long-term success as a result of careful planning and methodical mission strategies.  Session-based gamers - people looking for a quick thrill - should look elsewhere, as the game will quickly become more than you bargained for.  If you'd like a quick description of the gameplay, imagine if you could play The Sims from a third-person point-of-view, with direct control over each family member and hordes of zombies wandering the streets.  Oh, and imagine that the game continues playing with AI in control whenever you shut off your computer.  That's SoD in a nutshell.

This is a game that I enjoy, but can't recommend to someone else. It's not because of the gameplay, that's fun. It's not because of the story, setting, or themes, those are dark and engrossing, an excellent macabre style game. There is one, big problem with this game. R. N. G.
Simply put, it's too random, or rather, the randomness goes to too much extremes. The RNG of this game can literally make or break a Dungeon run, and I mean make it either impossible to win no matter how good you are, or lose even if you're mediocore.
Here's two examples I have experienced in under 3 hours of playing, first the impossible to win:
After beating Mom's Heart, I start a new run. I immediately enter a treasure room to grab the power up, it has a moon like Icon, but I can't tell what it does, so I pick it up to see. It makes it so my shots don't just shoot forward, but circle me in a fixed orbit. That already makes this harder since it is actually less effective than the basic shooting as it's harder to hit enemies and bosses, but what makes it impossible is that in the third level, I enter a room that has three wall spiders, that shoot triple shots, and have a massive gap separating them from me.
Now that shot "upgrade" decreases the range my shots go from me, enough that even when I'm right at the edge of the gap, My shots can't come close to hitting the spiders. So what do I do? I can't kill the enemies as i have no means of hitting them, tear shots or otherwise, and I don't have any bombs to blow my way out as I used the one I had and wasn't given any more yet. I cannot win or escape. All I can do is die or restart. Now that may not sound so bad given I was only in the third level, but imagine that happening in the later levels or the final boss level of a run, just before getting to the boss, being unable to progress because the upgrade you were given makes it impossible to kill the enemies, an upgrade that you can't tell what it does until you use it, or get rid of unless you find something to replace it. That would be a rage quit moment and should not happen.
As for the too easy to win moments, I've had a few of those times where the items i get are just OP as hell. Just recently, I had a run where the first treasure room I get as soon as I spawn gives me Capricron, boosting all of my stats. Then I get an item that gives my invincibility, then I get a few health, speed, range, and damage boosts, some black hearts, an upgrade that makes my shots pierce through enemies, and one after that that makes my shots destroy enemy bullets, in the first two levels. all I have to do is aim and shoot and no one can get near me.
Smaller cases of unfairness are when reward items for beating rooms spawn where you can't get to them, such as on islands or behind unbreakable blocks that even bombs can't destroy. There are also cases where RNG seems to be against the player, such as Red chests and sacrifice room that you have to give health to enter, both of which are supposed to be risk reward cases with a chance to have health and items, but can also be traps. However, 95% of the time, they're traps, making even trying them far more of a burden than an aid.
It's a good game, but very unbalanced. It reminds me of Contra, where some power ups are just objectively far better than others, and where some are worse than having no power up at all. The main thing that should be fixed is balanceing of the RNG. You should also be able to unequip items you don't want and all items and upgrades should be at least better than nothing at all.
Edit: Okay, so can actually drop some items by holding left shift for five seconds. However, it only works with trinkets and consumable items.
Love this game, so much grinding tho. but it is quite fun to laugh at your friends bad runs while you're there getting god combos XD.

Of all the games I have played, and of the few Rogue-like titles I have played, this is one I have looked forward to for a long time.
And now that I have it, I can officially say that this game, while extremely messed up and twisted, is a blast to play, a wonder to behold and a decidedly fun experience for such a dark game. My God, I have fun with this title.
Story:
You play as Isaac as he tries to flee his mother, who believes she is hearing God talk to her, asking her to sacrifice her son. In a desperate move, he finds a basement in his room and escapes into the deep dark underneath, where he discoveres a vast horde of monsters, many former siblings transformed by a darkness within the basement. You are then thrust into his shoes as you try to help him defeat the demons and monsters, along with his mother and other threats lurking within the walls.
Sounds messed up? It is, and delightfully so, as this game explores how religion can negatively affect a child when taken to the extreme, as well as a slew of other symbolic meanings. Even though I myself am Christian, I do agree that when done oh so wrong, it can cause a lot more harm than good when you take to extremes.
Gameplay:
A very simple layout for your keyboard, but it still takes time to master, as there are a slew of items at your disposal that help you fight the dark beings in the basement. Many of them are symbolic, others are curious, and a large few are just  unusual or plain old silly, but all are effective in their own way.
The randomly generated rooms offer a variety of things as you try to find their secrets and get to the end of these rooms, where you face off against a boss to try and go deeper into the basement.
Music:
The music is an eclectic, dark mix of many things that sound electric, metal and choir/orchestral as this game has the music composed by Ridiculon. The major boss themes offer a very intense feeling of dread or power, such as Matricide or Ascension, and the music is just awe-inspiring, in a curious way. I would recommend getting the soundtrack, if at all possible.
Graphics:
Don't let the simple, cartoony look fool you, this game is really good looking, and gets dark really quick with how twisted some of the enemies look.
If that weren't enough, the game runs extremely well on most PCs. Not to mention this looks fun in any way, shape or form.
Rating (1 being the best, 10 being the worst): 1/10 (Gold, Five stars out of Five.)

Honestly if there was one thing to remember about gaming in 2016 it was the rise of survival games. Though some have successfully given players a great survival experience, most have failed, Savage lands is on the edge of this line. The great thing about survival games is that it adds many harsh elements that the player must face; unfortunately, the problem with survival games is that the penalty for death is too severe. Tearing apart all of the players hard work and leaving them on the edge of the beach naked, literally.
Take a look at Dark Souls, one of the most challenging fantasy games out there to this day. Dark Souls and Savage Lands are quite similar in design. Both offer a challenge through PvE that most survival games only offer through the use of PvP. Unlike Dark Souls though, Savage lands feels empty. The world lacks story, world interaction, and NPCs that could make the world feel alive.
To the Devs, I'm not saying remove elements from your game; I'm saying stop adding elements that make this solely a survival game. I wish you would steer away from the survival aspects and steer more towards a Skyrim or Dark Souls type of game.

"Savage Lands" Refers to the protagonist Toby's homeland of West Africa where you must toil for the first half of the game in a harsh, unforgiving wasteland before being rescued by foreigners and brought to the idyllic endgame where you are fed, housed and civilized in exchange for manual labor.
There are better survival games out there.

There's a challenge mode, there's a free-mode to play any mission any way you want and a huge cast of playable characters. For quite a few years I kept hearing how great Mass Effect is. Recently I picked it up on a deep discount and thought I'd give it a shot in large part due to the massive positive reviews and the fact that I am a big sci-fi game fiend. I'm close to 20 hours into the game so far.
One of the recurring themes in overwhelmingly positive reviews for Mass Effect concerns the story and plot. Most of them read something like this "OMG OMG OMG THE STORY!" I'm sure for the junior high school Console Cadet Crew sitting on the living room couch munching fruit roll-ups and guzzling juice boxes while binge playing Mass Effect back in 2008 the story was/is epic. To me, not so much. Mass Effect's story line is really generic and predictable. Insert a generic interstellar alien alliance, a basic ancient alien super race that vanished without a trace (Precursors from Star Control or the Martians in Altered Carbon). Include a generic agent that for reasons only known to him goes rogue, a half dozen or so goofy alien species to interact with, and then mix thoroughly for a generic set of game missions and plot. There's nothing new here folks.
Players start the game learning basic controls at the alien super race mega space station called the Citadel and will spend a majority of the time engaging in character dialogue sessions. The character interaction is limited and predictable as far as the outcome goes. It's a lot like those old 1970's choose your own path novels and that equals boredom. When you do finally get past all the introductory character chatty Kathy sessions and are free to start a combat mission you'll be presented with a lackluster experience. The gameplay is repetative. The ship you command will drop you onto a planet surface in a six-wheeled truck with a sloth of a tank cannon. Exploring each planet surface feels the same- each one is void of any detail and the only thing that will change is the color of the dirt and/or the sky. Roll up to a base, exit the truck and take your three character team into harm's way. You'll know you are about to get shot at inside each base as soon as you see the one room full of crates. It's always those damned crates that gives away the surprise you're about to get jumped by a bunch of bad guys. After rinse and repeating a few planets worth of missions I found I didn't really care what was going on anymore. It's noise.
As far as the combat controls are concerned they are a clunkfest straight out of Sanford and Son's salvage yard- it's pure junk. I think the main problem here is playing Mass Effect with a mouse and keyboard. The game probably was not meant for that kind of precise setup and best suited to a console gamepad. As a result playing it on a PC can be wildly jittery and sloppy when it comes to the combat portions. I'm sure the gamepad funky bunch like it just fine...
To sum up Mass Effect quickly, it is a wildly overrated game that I will finish but I don't need to follow it up with Mass Effect 2 or 3. Mass Effect simply is not that good. It's past it's prime and probably should have stayed on consoles where it could have been remembered fondly by those who loved it. On the PC platform it is a dated game that will rapidly be forgotten. It doesn't work well or at all on Windows 7/8/10 machines so that could be another major reason to skip Mass Effect. It is stable on XP with only minor glitches/bugs.

Dynasty Warriors 8: Xtreme Legends Complete Edition is just outstanding. While it has the minor and typical flaws of a port it's 100% playable and great fun for those who desire a fun hack and slash with an easy to follow and unique story line for each campaign. Let's lay down some pros and cons:
pros:
+Upholds graphical standards of the recent last gen(ps3/xbox 360)
+All the stories of Dynasty Warriors 8 mixed with the the bonus content and modes included in Xtreme Legends!
+Improved gameplay smoothness(many of the older dynasty warriors games had fps drops during the massive waves of enemies getting annihilated even in the console versions)
+Excellent stories for each of the 4 kingdoms(the 3 old originals as well as the more recent Jin dynasty)
and for the first time the ability to play through the story of the "Mighty" Lubu a character known widely throughout the series as the most fearsome of fighters.
+Dian Wei clunking his bald head against Lubu's.
+Dian Wei clunking his bald head against everybody else.(15/10)
+New characters, both beautiful female characters with unique art styles and powerful looking male characters who fall nothing short of badass with all kinds of new movesets and massive combos!
cons:
-Controller mapping is very poor, I recommend using an afterglow a1x controller from PDP, when setting up your button input it feels like you're reading another language and takes about 10 minutes of double checking just to make sure everything is set up right. However, once set up the game runs great just like it would on your xbox or ps3!
-Poorly optimized for live streaming via twitch and hitbox(if you care about it), the game runs flawlessly on my amd phenom 1100t 6core at 3.3ghz and my radeon 6850 at max settings but once I turn my stream on it's all down hill from there!
-Some of the environments have slightly blurry textures, Dynasty Warriors uses a fairly old engine which isn't fully up to par with most modern games, this is easily made up for by the colorful characters and wide array of refreshed battlefields and brand new ones all together.
-This is another personal con, a lot of familiar officer names dating all the way back to Dynasty Warriors 2 are still for some reason important enough to be put into the game but not important enough to have their own unique character.
Final Verdict:
Dynasty Warriors is still going strong, I was blown away by 7 but 8 is the best one yet! While I recognize bits and pieces of the stories from 7, 8 delivers a refreshing and nothing short of adrenaline pumping feel while you slash and crush your way through hordes of opponents. I always say a good game or story has characters that YOU wish YOU could be if it were possible, Dynasty Warriors 8 gives you just that!
Feel free to reply to my review and tell me what you agree or disagree with, always interested in discussing!

Feels arcade-y. Tries so hard to be hard to the point it just ends up forced instead of hard, like putting Oblivion on the hardest difficulty. Having weak creatures with a huge life bar doesn't make an action RPG hard, it only makes the player waste more time taking out the same enemies over and over to advance. And from how repetitive this RPG's combat system is, I got bored quickly. Not reminiscent of Dark Souls at all; it feels more like a single player ArcheAge, where instead of pressing numbers to attack, you press your mouse buttons. I thought the combat system against big foes was gonna be fun and innovative, as it's reminiscent of Shadow of the Colossus, however, its execution is poor, probably because most of the foes aren't truly that big. At least it's better than killing giants or dragons in Skyrim.
The intro sucks. There are two tutorials dilligently teaching you how to do the same things, which goes against what some reviewers mentioned about “the game not holding your hand”. Thankfully, you can turn off the second tutorial once you're really into the game. The story is obnoxiously stupid and the characters act in an equally obnoxious fashion. I cringed too hard for too long.
Then there are problems like annoying pawns spamming your ears and screen, which thankfully you're able to turn off in the options as well. If you think Bethesda's companions are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ wait until you meet the pawns. I became stressed even before I got to create my character. The pawn system is fun, but it is not new. It's so simple it pains me to read people calling it creative and/or innovative.
The character creation is below mediocre. I have nothing against the graphics (they're terrible, but I don't care), yet character creation is too limited for a game such as this. Most body features don't feel like they fit, skin textures aren't decent enough, not enough color swatches to choose... the body sliders don't truly slide, they switch amongst an extremely limited couple of positions. For example, if I were to guess, I'd say there are only around ten positions on your character's face you can place their nose, and more than half of such positions look irrealistic or dumb.
EDIT: I've played a bit more. As I've expected, the game has become extremely easy after a while, which reinforces what I've said about it trying forcibly to be a hard game. The enemies are very predictable, the only difference being that they have huge life bars, additional lives, and a bunch of other stuff added to make you hit them more times. Also, in hard mode, they'll do double the damage. That's about it, nothing complex about the battle system besides weaknesses and strengths, which is straight out Pokémon-level of complexity, so you never really have to take a long time strategizing or preparing yourself for a fight.
Some quests don't explain what you're supposed to do clearly, which can be a pain if you're going into this game blind. I've enjoyed that there are a few groups of bandits that don't attack you on sight when you're inside their forts, a thing that makes sense, unlike Skyrim, where every single bandit murders everyone that passes by, which always made me ask myself: “How do they even recruit people anyway?” I've been so badly conditioned that I murdered bandits in DD that were not going to instantly attack, only to be surprised after murdering them that they were initially peaceful towards me.
You gotta be careful where you save, otherwise, you might load up your game and be surrounded by enemies. The game respawns everything when you reload for some reason. I almost died this way when I was playing the game for the second time.
I've had two fights where I felt like I was having fun, both against the same gryffin. First time he flew away, second time I got to murder the thing. It was an easy, quick, anticlimatic ending, but that's the only moment I had fun in the whole game, so...
Also, your stats are dictated by which class you're on while leveling up, a nice system overall. That's what made me decide to try out a new character solely on hard mode to maximize the stats I wanted using the right classes at the right levels. Well, guess what: You can only have one save game. If you make a new game, it deletes the old one. I decided to quit trying.
Sadly, my opinion about the game didn't change. I wish I hadn't bought it, but there's no coming back now.

Dragon's Dogma looks mediocre. Muddy graphics reminiscent of the PS2 era and the voice acting is often Resident Evil levels of ham.
And yet...
It's Japan's interpretation of a Western RPG and it is glorious.
This is a game that genuinely makes you afraid to go out at night. The lighting engine is probably one of the only ones to get the way light works (MGSV is the other that comes to mind, and probably does it slightly better) and there's a strong touch of Dark Souls here. When I say that, most DS veterans will scoff, but there's a sense of real danger here. You don't lose anything when you die....except progress. This game does not autosave very often, and if you die you WILL feel it, especially because the ability to fast travel is VERY limited for a long time. It does come with manual saving, so make it a habit to save every so often, you'll be thankful for it.
Dragon's Dogma is clunky. It's a hodge podge of design that shouldn't work, yet does. It's obtuse, and it doesn't tell you a lot. But in it's own special way, it's charming and beguiling.
I recommend it if you're after a special experience. It will take some time to really "get" but once it does, you'll find yourself coming back over and over again.
