Splinter Cell: Blacklist is a decent follow up to the much more action focused Conviction, but as usual with games form Ubisoft you have to deal with the horrible UPLAY experience; frequent crashes, stupid connection issues etc and the game suffers from "consolification" (dumbed down, no proper save funtion, flawed Steam integration and crappy controls). Graphics and sound are ok but nothing special.
The single player part of the game is quite nice, ok but not excellent. You have a little more sandbox freedom than in Conviction and the tools at your disposal promotes a stealthy style. Most things are an improvement from Conviction, except for the NV/Sonar Goggles that are completely and utterly USELESS in Blacklist. (yes they can be used to spot mines, but what is the point when I can see the mines without goggles anyway?) In Conviction they were an important and essential gameplay mechanic. The game feels similar to Hitman: Absolution and the stealth mechanics have improved, but still not better than in good old masterpiece Chaos Theory. Sam has acess to a huge number of gadgets and weapons to fiddle with but none of them really feel game changing or more than occasionaly useful in the single player missions as a Ghost. It also feels quite weird to carry a pistol, an assault rifle, a foldable crossbow, plenty of ammo for all weapons, a small drone, grenades, mines, etc and still be an agile wall climbing ninja. It would be much more cool to have a carry weight mechanic that gives me better stealth when sacrificing equipment.
Map design ranges from nice and open enviroments to closed one-way corridors and the difficulty does not scale at all with game progression. Some areas really stand out as great sandbox-stealth playgrounds though, with multiple paths and many ways to achieve your goals.
Enemies AI is no different than in other games but a really nice addition to the game is that some patrols change - one time a guard will block my ninja-stealth path, next time he will be in a different area of the map. Nice! Also the guard dog is a new type of enemy that can be very frustrating for the Sam the Ghost.
Controls work ok but not perfect, it feels like the game was made for console controls and then ported to PC without making use of the huge advantages in a keyboard and mouse interface.
About 80% of the game is quite easy to get through first time even on Perfectionist difficulty and mainly non-violent, that was a major dissapointment to me. Some parts was really tricky in a good way and makes the game shine! But when it comes to the remaining 10% someone on the dev team thought it a good idea to spice things up with forced action movie style scenes that are really corny and completely dispels immersion. Yuck. But then the story to begin with is not exactly original and interesting... Evil terrorists from the middle east and Africa are threatening 'Murica blablablablabla etc. The end of the game was one of the worst in any game that I have ever played - completely void of all logic, pointless and so annoying with stupid frustrating QTEs. Stop that♥♥♥♥♥♥you lazy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s!
Coop missions and Mercs vs Spies are great things and are really cool, with the small problem that you only rarely can connect to your friends so the concept kind of fails... The day Ubisoft learns to write proper networking code is the day we achive world peace and poverty and starvation is no more. Only in dreamland that is. If Ubisoft would start to sell their games without the Uplay-mess and with proper Steam integration instead I would gladly pay 10Euro more/game.
Do I recommend you to buy this game? If you can grab it at a discount price then yes if:
1. you like casual stealth action with a cheesy story
2. don't mind all the Ubisoft crap, a weak story and don't plan to play any coop missions with your friends.
Just don't pay full price and expect a polished AA game. ;) 6,5/10

The world itself is on the small side, with most maps being smaller, more empty and uneventful than what I'd expect from a "Baldur's Gate wannabe". Some classes are interesting and original (Chanter, Wizard...) others could have had more work (Ranger, Rogue...). Downed system is very original even though some times hard to understand what exactly is going on. Itemization could be done better, and the amount of junk one can carry after a dungeon trip is scary.
The Stronghold features are very nice, giving even the chance to use the characters that are not in the party.
Overall this feels like a "Baldur's Gate 1.5". Definitely worth playing, but one still gets more out of Baldur's Gate:EE or Baldur's Gate 2:EE

If you want a modern version of a game like Baldur's gate, this is your answer. This game DELIVERS. EASY but good craft system, loot system is alright, the graphics and spell effects are very good -- there's a LOT to try and to enjoy here. More classes than you can fully expore in a playthrough -- more spells then you can shake a stick at. Multiple caster types, all of which play differently. Fun and simple leveling system that also has it's subtleties in build creation. Story? It's got STORY for DAYS -- literally! Quests everywhere you explore, with multiple factions in each area with a reputation system that effects your dealings with them and has a genuine effect on the endgame. The game keeps a BIOGRAPHY of your character you can read like a story of your adventure -- All sorts of little things like this make this game a splendid example of the genre, but in addition to that there are little improvements here and there that just make it a better game than you're used to playing regarding games of this type. Your character's race/class/religion/etc really factor in to many exchanges and I felt like I got an ending which reflected the decisions I made -- with better detail than any game I can think of previous, and not always in ways I expected! In short, a real fun game, and despite it being a long ride I might actually play it to win it a second time... Not all RPGs can boast that. Combat is fun and strategic. Any cons? Sure -- I wish othere characters than the main character had more participation in dialogues, especially for a game where the dialogues are so strong. Beyond that, the game can be a little text-heavy in places -- long flowery descriptions of places, or dialogues that are longer than we might be accustomed. HOWEVER, I can't really gripe about having MORE content -- just be ready to read if you get into the game as much as I did. THOROUGHLY recommended.

Miscreated is a zombie survival game (actually a mutant survival game, but it's the same concept) that takes place in a large, open world. The graphics are nice, the world is quite detailed, not too small and not too large. At first it's fun to explore, loot houses and meet other players - in most cases, the game is plagued by kos loosers like most other games of the genre, but you can avoid that by playing on PVE servers with active admins.
The real problem with Miscreated however are not the kids who shoot you on sight, it's the lack of actual gameplay. One has to wonder how humanity was overwhelmed by a few dozen mutants who can't even climb over a small fence. There are hardly any mutants in the game world, sometimes you walk around for more than an hour without even seeing a single one. I met a guy who was relatively new to the game, but who had already played for two hours. He asked me whether mutants aren't implemented yet and he was serious about it. All that while we were walking through one of the bigger towns of the game.
On top of that the few mutants that you'll meet are no threat at all. If you see mutants they will often not spot you even at a relatively close distance. And if they finally manage to attack you it's no problem to outrun them since they're slower than you and more or less all of them are outside of buildings. I only met a single mutant inside a building yet, and I guess that was just a coincidence/pathing error since he was directly in the entrance area. Never meet a mutant in one of the upper floors of a building, not even once. In conclusion you only need to fight a mutant if you really want to, and they're not hard to defeat either. You can kill them easily with a basic melee weapon like a baseball bat.
So what else is there? You can craft items, but most of the basic items are either strictly worse than the items you can find by looting buildings or not really necessary.
You can build wooden structures (your 'base'), but I seriously have to wonder why anyone would do that when all of the houses are still intact and would just need to be cleaned up a bit. The base building part of the game doesn't make any sense and it feels like a cheap wannabe Minecraft that was implemented just because 'it's cool to build stuff'.
There is plenty of food and water everyhwere, so dying of thirst or hunger is out of question.
The only reason to explore the gameworld would be to kill other players and play the game like a first person shooter deathmatch. But you have to be very desperate if you need to play this kind of game for such an experience. There are simply far, FAR better games out there if you want to play a shooter. I imagine it's mainly for people who aren't skilled enough to play a real shooter and thus prefer an unbalanced mess like this one to boost their low self-confidence. No one right in his mind would get a sense of achievment by camping somewhere with a sniper rifle and shooting a guy with nothing but a pink beanie and a squeegee on him. But apparently some people do. I can only hope that's not the game's target audience.
So far the developer seems to be more focused on implementing more PvP tools like sniper rifles and more useless base building features instead of working on the actual gameplay. That's quite sad, since the world looks very promising. But unless there are far more and far more dangerous mutants there is no reason to play the game for more than a few hours. It's an alpha version and I hope for the best, but for now I'll give it a negative rating since the game is very far away from what I would call 'enjoyable' and the direction it seems to take (with a focus on a bad PvP deathmatch mode combined with some crappy Minecraft base building) is not what I'm personally hoping for.

Im deciding to write my first review on this game because i feel that it unececarially gets too many bad reviews, and i personally love this game for what it is.
Lets compare this game to dayz because, after all, thats what this game was based off of.
first of all, up to this point, there is very little glitchiness or lagginess no matter how many people are on the server im playing on. this is a huge difference from Dayz standalone where i would be on a server with only 20 peoplle and have a framerate of 20 with people rubber banding all over the place.
second would be the zombies. The zombies in Miscreated compared to Dayz S are much more difficult and interesting, however the combat with melee weapons still needs some work. I find it pretty inaccurate using a weapon like the baseball bat or a fireaxe, its as if there is a very specific place you have to aim to actually land the hit. dayz standalone also has this to an extent, its just different and im not used to it, also, the game is a work in progress after all. The great news though is that zombies cant run through walls! also, there are different types of mutated zombies. one very rare one for example reminds me of a smaller version of a tank from l4d, which is very scary to encounter at night in a heavy storm in the middle of the city. lightning flashes and all you see is a giant silouette in which case me and my buddy promptly dipped out. all in all i like the zombies in this game better than dayz standalone.
some other aspects of this game being already better than dayz are as follows
crafting, structure building, and vehicle parts/assembly all work great (I havent built a structure yet so dont quote me on that)
several guns and several different types of ammunition for guns, all of which work flawlessly
several different vehicles ranging anywhere from a bicycle to a bus, as well as boats, all of which also work flawlessly
almost every room of every building is explorable and loot spawns are realistically placed
hunting works great
The environment is very immersive, in the sense that while there are buildings that are identical to other buildings, the interior is changed so as to add a more immersive experience.
movement such as jumping is very fluid, unlike the vault command on dayz also, when standing on top of tall buildings or structures i dont have to fear glitching through the floor like i do with DZS
With all that being said, Id like to point out some cons as well.
Relatively small map, however they just added an update that adds a whole new, huge city. this leads me to belive they will add more to the map in due time.
Like I pointed out earlier, the melee combat is pretty wonky, Theres not really any way to defend yourself besideds running or fighting back. if you fight back you are guaranteering being hit by the way. Mass Effect is one of Bioware's classics, alongside KOTOR, Jade Empire, and the Original Dragon Age. Nothing that came after those really compares, and in many cases dilutes what make Bioware great (for me: well written characters, rich world building and meaningful choice ahead of light combat).
An ancient evil threatens to return after 50,000 years and eliminate all life in the galaxy, and only you as Male Shephard Femshep can stop it. To be honest, Mass Effect has dated quite badly. the worlds you visit are very small and divided so cleanly that there is practically a sign for 'dialogue section' and 'combat section', divided by 'vehicle section'. Side missions are generic filler on barren worlds, fleshed out by very simple text. Loading is hidden by infamous elevators and long stretches of uneventful jogging, and the world itself feels like a familiar sci-fi soup. You have a wise 'elf-like' race, a warrior race, your ship (the best ship in the galaxy), an ancient evil. With a few name changes, this could very easily be the videogame version of Babylon 5.
Still, the story is engaging, your NPCs are interesting and well-voiced, and the individual worlds you visit, though small, are a welcome change from the sprawling, empty 'open worlds' of 2008-2016. The game also sets up a great trilogy that, while falling short of its potential, remains consistently enjoyable and really the only place you'll find heartfelt and often intelligent sci-fi gaming.
Skip all the side quests, otherwise the game is a little slow. but its an alright game.

Wow.  This is probably the 'game' I liked least this year.
So, why?
There is exactly one puzzle to solve in this game.  The puzzle?  The fact that you have to quit out of the first part of the game, to start the second part of the game.  With the game giving you a warning that you should 'finish part one' first, even though there's nothing to 'finish' -- aside from getting into the endless loop.
The story started off cryptic and interesting.  Honestly, I was expecting something like 9-9-9 / Zero Escape here.  The theme could have been used well.  Instead, it was wasted.
There are literally no choices in the game.  And, realistically, there is no *ending* to the game.  Nothing is resolved, because the entire concept is an endless loop.  That means that the entire game is one big tease.  You're left with questions,
Ultimately, this is not a game.  It's not even like 9-9-9 on the iOS, where you make a few branching path choices...because there's no choice the player ever makes in the game.  *YOU* are not wanted here, aside from as an observer.
I'm glad I got this game as part of a bundle, because I can't condone paying for it.

So, I am new to visual novels, as most of what I've seen out there doesn't appeal to me.  I'm not interested in dating sims / otome, and I'm not interested in hentai or anything explicit.  What I *am* interested in is a good story / good storytelling.  An emotional journey.  Interesting characters.  That kind of stuff.  So it seems like there should be VNs out there that have the great story/characters, without some of the other stuff that gets a lot of attention.  Oh, and I also didn't  want a game where you had to play it a dozen times to get all of the endings (and achievements).
So that brought me to this game, which (after being bundled) seemed like a low-cost entry into the genre and didn't have any of the obvious things I avoid.
Unfortunately, this game at least didn't work for me.
For one thing, as some have pointed out, it doesn't have choices, it's pretty much just click-to-read.  Maybe if I'd realized that in advance, I wouldn't have been surprised / put off by it.  Some of the story was interesting enough.  The premise and subject matter was good.  The most frustrating part was that there are two "parts" of the story, but they are not connected in-game.  It's like you have to know you've done all you can in Part 1, then exit and start Part 2 to continue.  There wasn't a way to connect them in the game itself?  The result was that I was scrambling around for a LONG time (check out my playtime) trying to figure out what to do to continue the story.  The answer, it turned out, was to exit and start Part 2.  Meh.
Anyway, I know this game isn't a crowning achievement of VNs, and maybe not the best introduction to the genre, but I can't really recommend it unless, I don't know, you've played all the VNs out there and noticed that you missed this one.

It's pretty enough, and the first part is compelling.
But from the first episode looping on itself, to the animations, there's a distinct feel of lack of polish.
The "ending" of the second part starts falling apart into vagueness, losing the strong flow of the story before then,
There's no actual ending, and no real resolutions or clarifications of note.
It really feels incomplete, like it was something intended for three parts, then the developer got rushed at the end of the 2nd episode, threw down a few tidbits, and wrapped it up.
Also, the gameplay time is maybe 15 minutes, perhaps longer if you're a slow reader.
Which, honestly, the game might have been worth $3 had it been a polished, 3-part story.
As is, it feels like you're overpaying for a demo- unfortunately.
Now, while I can't *recommend* the game for purchase, the fact that it IS fast and has some compelling elements- both on artwork and plot- means that I can easily recommend it for play, if you got it out of a bundle or something.
Take a few minutes, enjoy the art, and don't go in with any expectations of resolution, and you'll at least get a story snippet that, for the most part, is higher quality than that of most VNs.
If this had been a complete and polished experience, I likely could have given it a review of 4/5.
As is, it's more of a 3/5, and even then only if you view it as a free to play experience.
I can't honestly recommend paying anything for the game, given how incomplete it is, but I can recommend playing it.
Really, if you're the type who likes to support indie developers with good talent but incomplete projects, go ahead and throw in when the game is on sale/in a bundle.
If you're aiming for a complete game, or something that'll leave you with something more than a feeling of 'think what this could have been', you should probably avoid the game.
Kinda confusing at the end, but over all a decent story.

But for a commercial release, I expect better effort when it comes to programming and UI design. The first part of the story ends in a repeating loop, at which point you're supposed to go back to the menu and start Part 2. There's no reason for this. Why not add unlockable choices to find your way to Part 2 from Part 1? Why not leave Part 2 locked until you've read Part 1, and then give some in-game indication that you should go back? Why not do
but leave Part 2 accessible from the beginning with a fourth wall breaking note that you should read Part 1 first? That's not just bad design; it's actively lazy. So is using the default Ren'Py UI.
I want to see more visual novels on Steam, so I hate giving one a negative review. But I really can't recommend
unless the designer gives it some serious polish.

30 minutes of linear visual novel.
You lost your memory, are caught up in a dream, and must escape - and die and be terrified a few times in the process. This two-part "Novel" is a short story at best, the art is simple but effective, and so are the sounds and music, but the storytelling doesn't seem to go beyond common tropes.
This game is 3:4 and scales seamlessly to any resolution, adding black bars if needed.
It would be an ok VN if it was free, but instead for paying what feels like watching someone else play an adventure game, you could pick up an actual adventure and play that for more bang for the buck (Betrayer is on sale this week).

A really good improvement in the series! Combat's a LOT deeper for anyone who stopped on the PS2 games, a lot more depth and flexibility with weapon alignments, elements, and sharing all weapons with affinities; fist weapons on any character is a blast. Even horse control is tighter and more useful, with improved summoning for real mobility with and trampling, with other animal as an option. Bodyguard control is nice too.
The campaigns are a little depressing with some storylines, and the roster has a surprising focus on the children of key characters like Guan Yu now compared to the series roots, but there's the expected branching storylines and hypothetical scenarios, with free mode. I miss the jungle campaign a little, but Ambition mode makes up for it with a small town-building function tied to randomized missions, a real nice collectathon grind that makes time fly. Way better than Create-an-Officer.

Fish tanks provide a beautiful display in your home, with all sorts and sizes of fish, it can be quite addicting watching them interact with eachother, or clean out your tank and even swim in schools of dozens. However, it is a responsibility. Before getting a fish tank, here are some basic rules that you should know;
A great starter fish is a Guppy, they are small, inexpensive and not too hard to care for.
Flakes are a simple and effective diet for fish, and guppies live them! When feeding it to them, they will eventually grow.
When guppies grow, they will begin to♥♥♥♥♥♥out nickels and dimes. When they reach thier maximum size, the dimes will turn into gold coins. This is natural for a fish, and can pay off bills.
Soon, you can try a more advanced fish, a predator Oscar that eats young guppies. Because guppies turn a flake into pure gold, the Oscar manipulates this and turns the guppy itself into a diamond and poops it out. Again, quite natural, it's called reverse bankruptcy.
However, sometimes advanced alien fish overlords will teleport into your tank, and eat every fish you loved. To combat them, you need a gun! I prefer a starter Glock 17, yet later they'll send in heavier alien overlords into your tank, even multiples at a time. Once this happens, you need to buy a sawed off shotgun from your local gun dealer. You have to be careful though, bullets can sometimes break the glass of your fish tank if not used correctly.
You can also use a kitchen knife to kill these 3" aliens and then throw them on the barby to feed your family and friends at a party. It sure will make an impressive entree.
Now, guppies and Oscars aren't the only fish you can get. You can get a minature yellow finned penguin that can get pregnant by the water itself.
Finally, if you want to upgrade your fish, you can feed them FDA (Fish Department Area) approved Asprin Fish Pills that are much better than flakes or pellets. You can also feed them Science Stuff in a jar to make fish♥♥♥♥♥♥out golden stars from Super Mario World.
Thank you for reading, may your fish tank prosper and not be overtaken by alien fish overlords.

This is a good zombie apocalypse survival game. If you like fighting zombies and you like exploring open worlds, then this may very well be a game for you. Minor quibble: once you start accumulating survivors, it can be annoying that the only one able to get anything done is the character you are controlling (even though you can change characters easily so really any of them should be able to deal with various problems), especially when several things are happening at once or you just want to explore and gather supplies rather than dealing with stuff. Another possible annoyance is that the game world continues when you quit the game, which means you need to leave your home base with enough supplies and high morale whenever you quit playing, or you may find everything FUBAR when you launch the game again.
Otherwise, this game is good fun, and exploring open spaces full of zombies is rather intoxicating. I definitely recommend it. :)
[edit to include the Breakdown DLC]
The Good about Breakdown: the progression of difficulty is excellent. It starts off fairly easy, on par with starting the main game, but after a few levels it gets quite tough. Zombies start coming out of the woodwork at the slightest sound, special types become more common, etc. While it's possible to play the regular game and not have a single character die, this is quite difficult, if not nearly impossible in the Breakdown DLC. I like this.
The Bad: It's repetitive. It's the same valley over and over again. Also, it's really not worth the $6.99 price, as this really should be a game mode included with the base game. To charge so much extra for it is terrible.
The Verdict: If you like the main game, then you do want this. However, wait until it's on an extreme sale, because it's not worth the full price.
[edit the 2nd to include the Lifeline DLC]
The good about Lifeline DLC: New environment, new style of playing, new missions, new weapons, and new characters. Actual C in this DLC. Overall it's pretty good, especially since the developers have done a good job keeping up with and squashing bugs.
The Bad: the only bad I can really think of is that it wasn't open enough. You are confined to a ring-road around a city and a few neigborhoods around exits on that road, but you don't get to penetrate into the city as it is walled off (granted it's full of zombies and would definitely be a death-trap, but still it would have been cool to try to sneak in and around the tall buildings and stuff even if it was almost certain death). A very minor disappointment, but there it is.
The Verdict: If you like State of Decay so far, then you'll almost certainly enjoy this. And I'll say its even worth getting at full price. A worthy addition to the game that you won't feel that you shouldn't have had to pay for.

Interesting concept of an open world where you play as a community of survivors in a zombie apocalypse and you have scavenge resources from a small town in order to survive.  Fun melee mechanics, the shooting mechanics feel alittle awkward, in any case, using firearms is limited due to ammo and the noise. Awkward indoor camera angles make it tricky to enter a building.
Main story plot is short and easily played if you are not distracted with exploring the town in your first playthrough. Various playable characters that has some depth and different skillsets. Decent graphics with good lighting, especially with a day/night cycle in game.
DLC tries to introduce a game world without story plot and challenges the player to survive as long as possible. But having only one map kills much of the replayability and the exploration factor of the DLC.

A good move in the right direction of zombie games. Too bad the customisation of the home base is very limited but the upgrades already in the game are good although for customisaton of the players base would have been awesome.

FYI. I got this game from Humble Jumbo Bundle 7;
Most of my issues in this game were probably due to the game being Early Access, but even then, I feel like if a game is in Early Access for two years, and I can't even get past the loading screens... then there's a problem.
---
Don't get me wrong, I love games that are like this, and I'm sure that this game is great. But...
1. The lagg was unbearable for me. Even if I lowered every setting the minimum, with a GTX 970, 8 Gigs of RAM and an i5-4690K processor. I was getting constant spikes. My frames were fine, it was showing me getting 60-80 frames at all times, but just running around with the lagg spikes gave me no pleasure and really made me lose interest. For example, I spawn in next to a zombie and my screen just freezes, just to move around a frame every 8 seconds. Not surprisingly, I died, which leads into my next issue
2. The game almost broke my PC. After getting molested by a zombie, I spent a solid 10 minutes waiting for the respawn button to pop up, and my whole computer froze up during this process. Once I clicked the respawn button, the game stopped working. The game stopped responding, and I could not, I repeat... COULD NOT close the game. At first, task manager refused to close the game, ending the task proved unsuccessful and didn't end up mattering, because my computer crashed shortly after my attempts. Both monitors went dark and my headphones emitted a buzzing sound. When I started up my PC again, I noticed a persistent issue. Even though my computer had just booted up, my cpu was being overloaded, at the same percentages as when the game was running. Task manager wouldn't load anything, all windows processes lagged and I found no help to any of these issues online. My only fix was clicking the uninstall button, which didn't actually work... it crashed my pc again the same way, but seemed to have fixed the problem.
TL:DR;
If you don't want a buggy remake of DayZ Standalone, Arma II DayZ, Arma III Exile or any other zombie survival game out there, then don't buy it.

This is not a visual novel, so don't be surprised there won't be given any choices and different endings to you. It's a short kinetic novel and quite an interesting one. First thing that startled me in the menu was "Begin Game"and "Begin Part Two". When I played the first part, I didn't realize that it was on the loop after a certain scene. So I was skipping it like an imbecile for at last 2 minutes straight. I was confused. Only then I remembered there is a part two. That was unnecessary. The whole idea of it is not new but the characters and the whole situation made it interesting.  I would have never guessed that Eldin is 10 years old. The way he talks and acts (not to talk about his body build). Unique art style and the animations are over the top. I've never seen anything quite like this in a visual novel before. It's a really nice touch. Too bad this beaut didn't last long. It kept me thinking when I was done with it. Since there's no ending and there's no actual beginning, it'll be a real shame to close the case when it's unfinished. All in all it's a good kinetic novel and I'd love to learn more about the characters; about the mad older sibling and the different reality.

While there's amazing animated characters and beautifully contrasted backgrounds with the characters, I found the story too short for the asking price. That is not to say that the author didn't work hard on this and doesn't deserve the asked price for such a great; artistic novel, but to say that the work is entirely too short for something that I re-read and still don't have an hour's worth of gameplay. I've played many visual novels and I think even a dollar less would be an improvement.
As for the story, I had seen the likes of it a few times before as an avid anime fan. However, there were a couple tricks I hadn't seen coming that I greatly appreciated. I loved the tone and as I said before, the artwork is just amazing I couldn't ask for more there. I'm wondering if perhaps there is more to this story yet to be added or if this is all that will be given.
I really hope there will be something added onto this work, as I found myself really getting and loving the story only to be left at the end wanting for more. My only hope is that there will be a continued piece or maybe another story by the author. I'm now a great fan of their works and will definitely buy more-specifically if they had the same horror-undertones as this novel.
Also the sound effects and music just matched perfectly! I'm so happy with my purchase because I got to see all this amazingness but I'm sad it ended too soon. (As I've already said many times in this rambling review.)
GREAT WORK! Recommended if you've got the money to spend for something beautiful. Not if you are running low on funds and are looking for something long. However, it does have some replay value if only because you're left desperate for more!

This is a Visual Novel in which you are told the story from the perspective of one of the main characters - Therese.
Part One opens with death and determination.
Therese awakes in some sort of classical-yet-modern manor, totally clueless as to where, why, how. A young boy named Eldin makes an appearance and - after becoming confused - Therese and he subsequently strive to make sense of their predicament.
There is a confounding mystery to be hashed out, but the majority of the story is of the interactions between two (almost) strangers; of the bonds that can form in no time.
Part Two opens with a promise and a preamble.
Therese awakes in some sort of classical-yet-modern manor, agitated at not knowing where, why, how. A young boy named Eldin makes an appearance and - after becoming disturbed - Therese and he subsequently strive to make their way out of their predicament.
There is a suspicious conspiracy to be hashed out, but the majority of the story is of the interactions between two (almost) strangers; of the love that can seem otherwise.
The art is well-done. There is a stark contrast between some of it; it's obvious that those (background) images that are of lesser quality were made to appear as such for atmosphere. How? "View full-size version in browser" for the first advertised image.
As for the writing, other than a few absent apostrophes and commas, one use of an incorrect homonym, and one misspelling ("breath" for "breathe") - it's perfect English (as I know it at least, fer wutever dats werff). There is a good deal of stuttering ("A-are..." "E-Eldin..." etc.), if that grinds your gears.
The story is great. Will not spoil more'n I already have.
The soundtrack is the worst part of the game. Any collection of sounds confined to seperate "tracks" is owed the title, but I didn't consider the majority of what I heard to be a sampling of a soundtrack; ambience that will either hit you as spot-on or make you wince a bit. To be sure, there is some music and I enjoyed what of it I heard; the music obeys the tone and gestures of the characters (i.e. abrupt or no transitions) and most of the sound will be of the eerie-but-maybe-annoying ambience. And that's just a personal problem, as my ears are sensitive; isn't even the loud noises that bother me, I guess just the pitch of the chanting - crackled in my earholes, yo.
I recommend this game; I think the asking price is fair.
EDIT:
I played Part One twice; Part Two once. Read at my own pace (moderately fast(?)): 57 minutes.
Will probably play through again at least once more.
I would advise saving often, maybe when you hear the music change, just because there are several save slots, and some of the text is skip-worthy after having read twice, but some is worth re- and rereading. And you never know when those bits will come up.

*Edit: the game is much more stable now. It is a very enjoyable game.
I enjoy the game while it is working, but the constant freezing during loading screens makes it near unplayable.

Pros
- Good story:
I'll admit I'm just a casual when it comes to the Lord of the Rings lore and universe but if you collect the side items and what not this game does a fantastic job of developing this universe and telling the story. You don't really need to have watched the movies to understand the premise of the plot or with the development of the world's history, however it does help.
- Great character development:
The main character you play as has a simple plot to him but the situation he is flung into and how he progresses and gets stronger makes it interesting.
- Graphics are gorgeous:
Years later this game still holds beautifully.
Cons
- Lack of unique missions:
Literally the same repeatable quests both main story and side quests, not much variation in any of the missions. The formula is literally rinse and repeat the whole game through and its annoying and tedious, every now and than you will do something new in the main story line quest but only so they introduce a new mechanic of the game.
- Repetitive and unchallenging gameplay/combat:
The gameplay/combat is mediocare at best, given how its damn near impossible for you to die unless you get absolutely swarmed, which happens occasionaly given how the game makes you revisit the same orc compound/forts over and over again with no end in sight to the enemies. You could literally spend hours fighting one long continous battle alone in a fort all the while spamming attack and parry and the battle execute. But than again to be fair its a Batman/Assasin's creed hack and slash style game, so if you like the free form combat systems in games like Dark Souls you will feel pretty bored and disappointed with this lackluster combat.
- Clunky and awkward climbing mechanics:
Climbing up walls can be very clumsy and clunky at times and makes you feel like Ezio Autistictorre. This is due to poor design in some of the walls and occasionally the controls themselves can make things awkard. To be fair though a lot of parkour games suffer from this to some extent. In this game its really a minor annoyance, but in the prime situations this annoyance can ruin a whole sneak job.
- Awkward controls/no target lock:
The reason why I put these both together is that the issue I'm about to describe can be fixed I believe through either avenues. In the middle of a swarm of enemies it can be real damn annoying when you get your combo finisher at the end of a 5 or 8 hit combo and direct it the guy you want to one shot execute but instead you wind up wasting it on another target. This can be a minor nuisance or it could mean your death depending on the situation either way its annoying. Perhaps the worst case where this issue comes into play is when there are dropped runes on the ground and some enemies nearby. When you  try to pick up runes off the ground while there are enemies nearby the game will automatically assume you mean to grab the nearest enemy instead which can be utterly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. (Since grapple and pick up are the same button) Especially if all you want to do is grab the item and book the heck out of dodge.
- Lackluster sneak/assasination mechanics:
All of these orcs must be related to Helen Keller because they are all blind and deaf as a doornail. But than again given how the game constantly spawns in more orcs at random intervals and locations it would be pretty annoying if you had to perform 15 minutes of sneaking to get past one randomly generated mob that you found patroling the travel routes. But this winds up making portions where you actually are being a stealthy assasin that much less satisfying,
- Lack of unique boss fights:
The nemesis system, that controls the spawning of elite orcs in the game, loses its charm really quick especially if you try to farm good quality rune drops from them. The nemesis system is literally just mish mashing a bunch of random buffs or debuffs for the elite orcs that spawn in game. For example you kill an orc elite that is resistant to sneak kills and range attacks, the next elite orc that spawns in could be resistant to sneak kills and resistant to fire damage. Perhaps one of the best examples I can give you of the retardness or epicness of this system, depending on how you view it is this one boss orc that spawned that literally was resistant to everything except fire damage... I literally got a 300ish hit combo on this orc, with my sword just smacking away at him only to do literally 0 damage... The issue I have with this is that this orc wasn't anything special, he was the highest level type of orc but aside from that he wasn't unique. He didn't have unique magic powers or armor or really anything at all that made him unique enough to resist all damage from 300 blade strikes, in fact he looked like any regular orc just with slightly more armor and that was it... This for me deteriorated the games immersion.
Last note: I paid $20 for this game and it was an okay purchase at this price in my opinion, I would not pay more for this game. Nor would I recommend it if you have other games you are interested in or are playing, I would say go through those first and if you literally run out of other games to play than I'd say consider this one.

As you can see from the hours played, I had and have a lot of fun with Attila. So far it's the best Total War (and I have played about all of them and I have played them a lot).
The gameplay differs a lot from culture to culture with each faction facing different challenges and having very different means to meet them, not only when it comes to the obvious things like what kind of army each faction can field, but also when it comes to the "little things" like ... whether you even have settlements or start as a horde. Or public order. Or politics. Or economy. Or religion. All this forces you to adapt your strategy, not only to your own capabilites, but also to what your enemy can and cannot do. (Because of that some of the Culture-DLCs are actually worth it and not just another starting position, especially the sandy one. Celts and Norse are meh tho, just more barbarians).
Every aspect of the game actually impacts how well you're doing - as opposed to Rome II where you could just ignore politics and be fine and public order and culture usually were no big deal (just build a big enough temple, eh?). Attila is actually challenging without feeling outright unfair, like Shogun did, where "challenge" meant the AI cheated and everyone - even your closest allies - just decided to go to war with you for no apparent reason, once you became somewhat powerful.
Also the setting is interesting and they did a lot to make it feel right and that's not just how it looks, but again, how it plays: For example, you get, why abandoning Britain as the Romans is a sensible idea. And you get, why you should migrate your barbarian tribe to the south. Not because it's historically accurate, but because it's a reasonable answer to what the game puts infront of you and how the setting translates into gameplay, starting positions and Huns wanting to burn your babies.
TL;DR:
Saving Rome is hard, but fun. But so is conquering (parts of) it to make your own Frankish Kingdom. And defending that against the Huns. And putting everything to the torch as the Huns. And building up your power and then steamroll everything as the Sassanides. And building up your power to backstab the Sassanides as some jewish desert Kingdom (DLC).
Also it's pretty to watch the world burn.
The only thing that disappointed me is that you do not get to make Rome proper pagan again. Just this Sol Invictus crap. IF I WANTED A SINGLE GOD I COULD HAVE STAYED CHRISTIAN, JUPITER DAMN IT!

I've survived 20 days and so far I'm enjoying the gameplay!  However I have noticed I haven't earned any of the achievements, and technically I have earned well over half of them. Glitch?
What I love:
- Graphics are beautiful.
- Sounds are relaxing and real.
- No crafting window--it's all done "real time". (However, I did have to google how to get started--not sure I'd have figured it out very easily!)
- I do love that I can go about my daily routines generally unbothered.  No random zombies or weird stuff like that ;)  (A few smaller annoyances may make it more realistic, however.)
- Limitless islands to explore!
What can be improved/suggestions:
- True need for sleep. I could play 100% without sleeping with no ill effects.  I know it's natural to be more hungry and thirsty when you wake up, but I find it a pain to have to chug down tons of water and food upon waking because my hunger and thirst get very low.  It's easier to never sleep!
- More diverse interactive plant life for crafting and food.  (Plus ones that aren't good for you!)
- I'd love for there to be a few plants you can make into poultices or healing salves.
- More crafting overall :)
- More diverse animal life on islands.  Insects would be great for eating or for challenges (bites, stings, etc...).  Lizards, birds, snakes, etc...  It's kinda boring that all I have to worry about are sharks and so far I've been avoiding them.
- Islands are almost all the same size with the same or very similar features, including the shipwrecks. So far I've opened the same exact toolboxes, etc...and it's a little boring.  Would be nice to have outstanding features to distinguish one island from the next when exploring.  Plus, there's nothing to get excited about when visiting new islands; that lessens gameplay satisfaction.
- I've found myself accidentally eating things I'm holding in my hand to put on the fire or in my fish trap.  Interacting with something is a long left click and putting in your mouth is a short left click! (Maybe something I could change in my settings, anyway.)
- I've been stranded for 20 days and the moon has been full every night ;)  While the moonlight is great, it is making for monotonous nighttime gameplay. Moon cycles would be awesome!
- I read somewhere you can put out a fire when you're done to save on fuel resources; I haven't been able to figure this out. It would be a nice option to be able to put sand on it or a bucket over it to extinguish it.
- Either my navigational skills are really bad, or the islands aren't on a fixed grid. (Could def be the former...lol.)  I have tried to make a map using my compass but somehow I end up visiting the same islands over and over (I mark them with stick and rocks so I know which ones they are.).  It would be great to have some sort of map generated as you visit new islands (maybe you find one as loot?), and to be able to make basic notes on it (pencil, please? lol.).
- I'd love to find a second backpack!  I've tried to toss a few things in my raft with fair success; but the sharks end up bumping some of it out.  Or maybe if I could use rope to tie some things to my pack or raft?  Just someway to carry more things back to MY island when I've been out exploring/gathering. It's something I'd want to do in real life, not just to make the game easier!
- What about being able to equip clothing?  Found hats, shoes or even gloves would help weather some of the elements when needed. Maybe I haven't played enough yet, but so far I'm not feeling a lot of effect of the rain or temps.  No sunburn, no chills when it rains. When I go in my shelter when it's sunniest or raining, my health doesn't seem to be affected?  This also is making me wonder what the purpose of building my shelter has been for except something to keep me busy?
- The noise for the appearance of tiger sharks sounds like an airplane flying overhead. LOL. Took me a while to figure that out ;)
OH and I've yet to fall from a palm tree ;)  The trick when coming down is to back up (S on the keyboard) and keep your cursor high on the trunk (so you're looking up) as you come down.  Works like a charm :)
That's it so far!  For an early access game, I think it is awesome!  Stranded Deep has tons of potential.
Also, I second one.insipid's review from Feb 27th!! :)

This is the biggest waste of money that I've ever had. My brother and I decided to get this because it was a mix between Minecraft and Castleminer Z. It's as if you took a low budget Castleminer Z, got rid of the good monsters and then threw in  a few good pictures to make it sell. Terrible game, waste of money. If it were a dollar I'd prefer to get Castleminer Z and to save my money.
EDIT: I see that 4 of 5 people downvoted this review. Let me tell you why this game is bad rather than just saying it's terrible. For the price I paid, I would much rather buy another indie game. I felt like the game really didn't play well, and it was buggy. There were numerous bugs when my brother and I were playing that interfered with our experience. The hunger and water mechanics were interesting but I don't want to worry about those when I want to build and kill dragons. I came with the expectation that I'd be able to build, but rather you have to chop trees down and you have a set schematic for the house.
I felt like the ingame experience didn't feel as fluid as it seemed in the trailer/pictures which was another con. I suppose I should have looked at gameplay videos before I bought it, but oh well.
-------------------------------------
Combat
-------------------------------------
Another issue I found annoying was the reach of the weapons. When I wanted to kill a rabid dog or monster that was attacking me, I couldn't kite them and use weapon range to my advantage, which is a downside. In almost every game that I've played that's good you are able to outsmart the enemies and to mess with their pathing or just use range to your advantage rather than just to cross your fingers and hope to out melee them. This was much to my dismay, as it makes for a much less interesting game that is very simplistic in nature.
Having the playability that it does, which is glitchy, and the fact that you can't outsmart enemies is really unfortunate, and it really takes away the satisfaction of killing an AI or exploiting their weakness. Tactics like these make for an interesting game, for example Chivalry: Medieval Warfare. In Chivalry you can stand in a way that your opponent will have to face the sun, and they will be unable to respond to your attacks as quick as they would without light in their eyes.
Another thing in games that I like is when they have a hill advantage, or when your positioning matters in combat. For example when you're on a hill, you can get a hitbox advantage or a bonus to attack. Or maybe being downhill is better because there is more of the opponent's hitbox available to hit as opposed to being up top. Mechanics such as these make for interesting and dynamic combat, and I saw none of these.
-------------------------------------
Building & Crafting
-------------------------------------
When I launched Savage Lands, I came in with the expectation that I would be able to craft and build like a sandbox game. I was excited because it looked like an improved version of the game CastleMiner Z because of the graphics and the fact that it was in development. Only seeing room for improvement, I bought it. The building and crafting system they had implemented was actually the first thing I was upset by.
You start off in a world by a boat, and you have to leave the shore and go find rocks and materials to make tools. Eventually in a little while you'll have enough materials to make a house. When I had materials, I was excited and I had this grand design planned; only to find out that you had to craft a house by using a schematic, rather than to build it by hand.
This was frustrating to me because it removed numerous planes of possibility, and it leaves for a lot less customization which essentially devalues any world that you will ever create.
One of the draws to minecraft for me was the fact that the crafting was so easy, and that each world could be customized to your liking. Once I transferred over to Xbox 360 to play minecraft (I still played on the computer) I immediately despised it. The reason why is because the crafting system was horrible. I mean, it was all right in front of you but you had to sift through categories and categories to actually find what you needed. The crafting found in the PC port of minecraft has a very easy-to-deal-with crafting system that needs some instruction but once you get the hang of it you can effortlessly craft multiple items in less than 5 seconds.
-------------------------------------
Final Note
-------------------------------------
I may not have enough hours on this game, but I don't need as many hours as the next guy to tell you that this game is a waste of your money and a waste of your time. If you found this game fun, that's great! I would not, however, personally recommend this game to any of my friends. The lack of personalization is disturbing, as well as the lack of interesting mechanics. Not having any mechanics to master leaves you with no incentive to keep playing the game. With no skill required, it's just artificial difficulty. Having to run and find food in a randomly generated world isn't a very fun experience when you have limited features to keep the game interesting. 15 years ago this game would have been a hit but let's face it... We're a little beyond that.
All in all I would give this game a 2/10. You saw my reasoning, which led me to write this review. Guys and girls don't waste your money on this indie game. Don't be fooled by their good marketing, this game is not nearly worth anything more than $1. Charging $7 for this game? I would rather recommend someone save up for minecraft (or get mods if you already have it!) or to get Ark: Survival Evolved. I don't have that game because it requires Kernel mode access to your PC but if you're OK with that then that's fine, it's much more quality than this. Even CastleMiner Z is a better game than Savage Lands because it's a fun game to screw around in and there are many new concepts added in the game that make it a fun game. It's a ghetto version of minecraft with neat mobs such as dragons, and they have laser guns etc.
If you try to market an idea, you either have to A. Undercut other producers in the market B.  Add a unique idea that would make buyers more inclined to buy your product C. Have better marketing than your competitors.
Savage Lands, unfortunately, is only using C which is to have good marketing. You're paying for a game that is inferior to others in its genre and I don't even think it's very enjoyable irrespective of the price.

Having finished my first and more or less thorough walkthrough I think I'm ready to write a little something about this game. Short version: this game is beautiful and I enjoyed playing it immensely. And now for details.
I didn't back this game on Kickstarter. I must say I had my doubts, even when the beta was out I wasn't sure I liked what I saw.  Gladly, I was wrong, but nonetheless let me start with negative criticism:
- Bugs. Yes, there are bugs. Back when the game was released there were quite a lot of them, some of them rather nasty. However, bugs are only a temporary issue as long as developers work hard at fixing them and right now Obsidian is doing fine. You can see a lot of communication between gamers and developers going on at the forums, most issues are already reported and will be addressed at some time. Which is why I don't think that bugs are that much of a problem.
- Bad/weird design decisions. Those are much worse than bugs because those are a part of the game. The interface, for one, is far from being perfect. Pathfinding is terrible, especially in battle. Battles themselves are separated from the peaceful exploration which means that pre-buffing or pre-summoning or other things like that are not possible. So there are things like that, but not that many of them. Not enough to spoil the pleasure of playing but for some players probably enough to wince once in a while.
- Backer content. I have deepest respect for Kickstarter backers, but all that backer content is better off somewhere... well, not in the game itself. The tombstones can be ignored, but I would trade all those 'special' NPCs for just one real NPC of Obsidian's design, or, better still, for a little quest.
- Role-playing system. The game utilizes an original role-playing system that was designed to kind of remind you of D&D while not being D&D, which benefited the game and harmed it at the same time. Some things work nicely: combat mechanics work, original classes like Chanters and Ciphers are awesome, ability and skill checks function properly. However, such classes as priests, wizards or druids seem (to me) like they were just copied from D&D without much thought. Also I have a real problem with attributes, skills and abilities. Why don't they influence each other? And why are the skills so odd? Outside of dialogue interaction, each skill has exactly one use. Then there are attributes. For example, in this game Might represents both physical and spiritual power, which means that virtually every class needs Might to be able to do damage. At the same time, Intellect only affects the duration of effects and such, so a Wizard might fare better with high Might and low Intelligence. Interesting, but doesn't make much sense if you compare it to how attributes are treated in dialogue options. In textual interactions Might is just plain physical Strength and Intelligence is, well, how smart you are. This means that attributes fail to describe your character. So do I make a mighty wizard to be effective in battle or do I make an intelligent wizard to actually roleplay in dialogues? Anyway, chances are you won't even pay attention to all this while you're playing. However, in the long run, in case there are sequels, not having a coherent and thought-through role-playing system might do some harm.
- White text on dark background. Had to note that specifically. My eyesight is not perfect, I know, but this bright white  font against dark background is killing meeeee. And there's a lot of reading to be done in this game...
But enough with the negative. The good things! There are actually a lot of them so I'll only mention what comes to mind immediately.
- The game is very rich in content. It isn't some linear sham that gets shorter and plainer the longer you play. The game is very consistent with lots of quests, NPCs, fractions and locations to explore.
- Exploration is pure joy in this game. Actually, I believe that PoE has the best dungeon-crawl gameplay ever. Dungeons are so beautiful, so lovingly crafted, so interesting to explore that I wouldn't probably mind if the whole game was one big mega-dungeon. And I have never been a big fan of dungeon-delving before!
- Options. There are a lot of options in the game. A lot of different ways to finish quests, but also a lot of plain game options. Fast mode, slow mode, bigger fonts, smaller fonts, color-blind mode, auto-pause, languages, subtitles - everything is adjustable and this is awesome.
- Most importantly, this game has that elusive charm that BG2 or IWD had. The feeling that makes you explore map after map until it's morning and your eyes can't read the dialogues anymore. It is immersive, it is thrilling, it is intriguing. Obsidian put their hearts and souls into this game, they genuinely care about it and it really shows. Which is the main reason I have to call this game a major success. Everything that is wrong with this game can be corrected, it isn't such a big deal.
The only thing that you cannot patch is the absense of the soul. This game deals with the problem of human souls and of so called Hollowborn - children born soulless. Today, there are a lot of games that seem to be Hollowborn too, but not this one. I hope Obsidian makes many more games like this and next time I'll try my best to support them early on!
P.S. Something I forgot to mention. Doing a complete playthrough took me 70+ hours, but for some time I had to play offline due to a very odd bug that several other people encountered too. So don't mind the 'hours on record' thing too much.

Excerpt:
I will admit, I was but a wee lad when Baldur’s Gate first came out back in 1998. I watched my father play it and gave it a try myself (as good as a six-year-old could, at least) and I remember being so enraptured by the story and universe. Aside from the lore of Warcraft, it was Baldur’s Gate that helped shape my understanding of high fantasy--not Lord of the Rings, as many people seem surprised by.
Since then, the original developers of Baldur’s Gate have shuffled around the past few years, some of them sticking together, others branching out on their own projects, though it seems to be common to equate Obsidian Entertainment as the most direct successor of the original Black Isle Studios. Obsidian’s known for some pretty high profile stuff in recent years: South Park: The Stick of Truth; Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II; Fallout: New Vegas (and, in a past life, the original two Fallout games), among others.
...
I definitely recommend Pillars of Eternity to any and all gamers, especially those who have been yearning for an RPG like the good ol’ days. Though it was made with a target audience in mind, the fact that this game is easily one of the best games of 2015 thus far, but its achievements and what it represents for Kickstarter projects, crowdfunding, and honoring quality and the passion of game development, as well as the amount of power we gamers have, keeping Obsidian afloat in what seemed to be a last ditch fundraising effort… this is one for the history books.
I’d be so bold as to say that Pillars of Eternity is the cRPG equivalent to Skyrim: it exhibits mastery, charm, and a standard of excellence that ought to make Obsidian proud, and that other developers should strive for.

Daughter of Shadows is a puzzle sidescroller that takes inspiration from various SCPs, from the well-known Wiki.
As a girl who can mind control any men and then use these men as extra health, use them to operate computer terminals, or to kill women who SCP-029 cannot otherwise affect, your goal is to find two keys and unlock the main facility to be able to escape.
The game uses randomly generated rooms so you will not always encounter the same things.
The main draw is the many SCPs included. While there are certainly inaccuracies in how they are depicted and how they act, the game does more right than wrong here. You will need to know about most of them, or have the Wiki open to check, to get the full experience though.
Downsides are obviously the production values. It is a low budget game with not so pretty art and almost no sound. There is no background music and the sound effects all seem very stock.
Recommended for its low price and connections to SCP lore, but if you're not interested in the SCP project then this has llittle to offer that other games can't do better.

A few things I'd like to mention first:
1) I downloaded and installed a patch to improve the graphics (highly recommended)

This is the first review I've written for Steam. I usually pass on writing one but I enjoyed Dark Souls so much, I wanted to throw my two cents in. However, I didn't want to write a review until I beat the game at least once, which I did just an hour ago.
Dark Souls is highly enjoyable. It combines challanging gameplay, exploration and weapon/item experimentation. I tried a few class/play styles until I found the one that fit me best. There is semi-steep learning curve but with a little patience it doesn't pose a major road block. This isn't an action/adventure game. It's a third person RPG. I found that the road to success was patience and learning enemy movement/attacks. While levels and gear help, it's skill that makes the difference in Dark Soals.
The game isn't perfect, I found a few minor collision bugs, sometimes the camera goes haywire or pick's the absolute *worst* angle possible, I also experienced lag during a PvP invasion which almost cost me. There are no game breaking bugs but I'd like to mention that the community had to fix this game (PC). I played through the first half without the graphics update patch. The game wasn't very pretty and it was hard to see certain things (like posion darts headed towards my character). Even with the patch, the graphics are dated  but the game is *a lot* more enjoyable with it. I cannot stress enough how important it is (and it's free).
This game has a lot of replayability and if you purchase it on sale, you really get your money's worth. I've spent at least 100 hours on this title (not sure what it says for hours played). It's worth trying but not without a controler and not if you like to run in with guns blazing.
I plan to replay Dark Souls until the second one is on sale.

Recently purchased this about a week or so ago and sunk many hours into it. Quick synopsis after beating and playing the game.
+'s
Overall good story with many events that happen while you are out on missions and scavenging.
Combat is fluid and easy to get into.
Great map and many places/locations are logically placed and have distinct personalities.
Good voice acting.
Pacing has been done well.  Doesn't rush you along, but if you take too long, events time out.
Resource management is implemented well.
-'s
Combat is a bit wonky.  When you dodge, you lose your target focus and end up swinging into air.
Some of the characters need to be more in-depth.  ie The council man that gives you a car and then vanishes after that. Or the Wilkenson boys.
Would have been nice to convert some resources into useable items.  Like extra stockpile of food or ammo into items so that the character can use.
Camera angle in houses get stuck at times.
Your followers are really not very smart.  They always to get into trouble even if they are the next house over.
Stats between characters are all the same even though they have different perks.  Once you level up stats, perks are not even noticeable.
Conclusion:
Overall this is a wonderful first attempt at a game for the publisher.  It is both easy to pick up and very addicting.  With this they can build up on a much better sequal that's for sure. I very much recommend this game.

I've survived 20 days and so far I'm enjoying the gameplay!  However I have noticed I haven't earned any of the achievements, and technically I have earned well over half of them. Glitch?
What I love:
- Graphics are beautiful.
- Sounds are relaxing and real.
- No crafting window--it's all done "real time". (However, I did have to google how to get started--not sure I'd have figured it out very easily!)
- I do love that I can go about my daily routines generally unbothered.  No random zombies or weird stuff like that ;)  (A few smaller annoyances may make it more realistic, however.)
- Limitless islands to explore!
What can be improved/suggestions:
- True need for sleep. I could play 100% without sleeping with no ill effects.  I know it's natural to be more hungry and thirsty when you wake up, but I find it a pain to have to chug down tons of water and food upon waking because my hunger and thirst get very low.  It's easier to never sleep!
- More diverse interactive plant life for crafting and food.  (Plus ones that aren't good for you!)
- I'd love for there to be a few plants you can make into poultices or healing salves.
- More crafting overall :)
- More diverse animal life on islands.  Insects would be great for eating or for challenges (bites, stings, etc...).  Lizards, birds, snakes, etc...  It's kinda boring that all I have to worry about are sharks and so far I've been avoiding them.
- Islands are almost all the same size with the same or very similar features, including the shipwrecks. So far I've opened the same exact toolboxes, etc...and it's a little boring.  Would be nice to have outstanding features to distinguish one island from the next when exploring.  Plus, there's nothing to get excited about when visiting new islands; that lessens gameplay satisfaction.
- I've found myself accidentally eating things I'm holding in my hand to put on the fire or in my fish trap.  Interacting with something is a long left click and putting in your mouth is a short left click! (Maybe something I could change in my settings, anyway.)
- I've been stranded for 20 days and the moon has been full every night ;)  While the moonlight is great, it is making for monotonous nighttime gameplay. Moon cycles would be awesome!
- I read somewhere you can put out a fire when you're done to save on fuel resources; I haven't been able to figure this out. It would be a nice option to be able to put sand on it or a bucket over it to extinguish it.
- Either my navigational skills are really bad, or the islands aren't on a fixed grid. (Could def be the former...lol.)  I have tried to make a map using my compass but somehow I end up visiting the same islands over and over (I mark them with stick and rocks so I know which ones they are.).  It would be great to have some sort of map generated as you visit new islands (maybe you find one as loot?), and to be able to make basic notes on it (pencil, please? lol.).
- I'd love to find a second backpack!  I've tried to toss a few things in my raft with fair success; but the sharks end up bumping some of it out.  Or maybe if I could use rope to tie some things to my pack or raft?  Just someway to carry more things back to MY island when I've been out exploring/gathering. It's something I'd want to do in real life, not just to make the game easier!
- What about being able to equip clothing?  Found hats, shoes or even gloves would help weather some of the elements when needed. Maybe I haven't played enough yet, but so far I'm not feeling a lot of effect of the rain or temps.  No sunburn, no chills when it rains. When I go in my shelter when it's sunniest or raining, my health doesn't seem to be affected?  This also is making me wonder what the purpose of building my shelter has been for except something to keep me busy?
- The noise for the appearance of tiger sharks sounds like an airplane flying overhead. LOL. Took me a while to figure that out ;)
OH and I've yet to fall from a palm tree ;)  The trick when coming down is to back up (S on the keyboard) and keep your cursor high on the trunk (so you're looking up) as you come down.  Works like a charm :)
That's it so far!  For an early access game, I think it is awesome!  Stranded Deep has tons of potential.
Also, I second one.insipid's review from Feb 27th!! :)

Miscreated is one of my favorite survival games as of late. Available on steam for $19.99 and totally worth it, especially with friends. The game is still an open beta so there are definitely glitches and bugs. Miscreated is, like most if not all survival games, set in a post apocalyptic, open world.
The current AI enemies are mutants and wolves. Mutants are like zombies but they melee attack instead of trying to eat your face off. You rarely run into them outside a military base and the cities. Sometimes there are two or three in the same area, others its just that one. Three to four melee hits and its down. Hopefully they add more types or at least make them more frequent. Wolves are ......wolves XD, I have not seen any up close but I have heard their howls in the forests.
Players start off with nothing but the skin on their backs and a flashlight. Spawns are typically near buildings, seeing you don't pick the wrong direction to run in, and they provide some necessary survival items. IMPORTANT: Always keep at least 1 drink and 1 food on you at all times, its very easy to not pay attention to your status, or go a long time before finding food. As of now, your character is not affected by weather. Therefore you don't need to look for a warm place every few mins.
Yes you have to find most if not all guns and ammo. No, I would not advise shooting any of it at mutants.                                          1. It'll just attract more if they are nearby
2. It'll give away your location
3. It takes several bullets and they aren't easy to come by, depending on the gun you have.
For weapons you have melee blunts, pistols, assault rifles, hunter rifles, sniper rifles, shotguns, bow and crossbow, as well as some throw-able explosives and tactical grenades.
Attachments can also be added to boost firepower. Each gun is specific and you have to figure out what can pair with what.
As far as I know 98% of vehicles are rusted and destroyed (aside from some good looking planes at the airfield that you cant use). If you do manage to find one, you need to repair it. Gas, oil, tires, fan belt, and spark plugs. These are easily found in a auto shop or randomly through out the world.
There are also bikes, just as rare and glitchy. My first one glitched into the pavement, half sticking up and never to be rode again. RIP.
For those who don't know, KoS stands for Kill on Sight and basically separates pvp from pve. Generally you don't trust players but for the most part I've run into little to no griefers, just players that'll help you and show you where some weapon spawns are. Avoid roads and obvious pathways if people aren't your specialty. If I can, I'll avoid a player and definitely steer clear of groups. Hiding in bushes is handy sense they hide you perfectly, especially at night. Mic chatting is based on proximity so your best bet is to hide and type or type fast if the situation looks rough. More importantly DON'T DROP YOUR GUARD.
