There are plenty of things done better compared to the old infinity engine games, although some die-hard fans may see them as downgrades- just because some stuff is done differently. There aren't many NPC companions to recruit to your team, but we are given an option to "recruit" a self-made character by creating them in a tavern, so I believe that makes up for it. Combat is quite enjoyable, but you have to pause a lot to plan your moves. I must admit though that playing on hard difficulty, the game is not a really huge challenge. I found Icewind Dale to be a lot harder, and it didn't even have difficulties to pick from. Overall I can't help but recommend this game. While it has few flaws, I still believe it's truly a masterpiece.

"What do you believe?"
This is the driving question of Pillars of Eternity. In the opening minutes of the game, you potentially find yourself negotiating a hostage situation. Provided that you have the skill set, you can try to deescalate by engaging in a theological debate with a religious fanatic, or you can reaffirm your belief that luck favors the bold by rushing the ringleader. There is a spectrum of options between these two extremes, and this provides but a small taste of what's to come.
"Compelling story-line, deep companions, tons of exploration, moral complexity, and fun, tactical combat"
Pillars of Eternity takes place in a small region on the continent of Eir Glanfath. Tensions are high. A recent religiously-motivated conflict, and subsequent genocide, has opened fresh the unhealed wound of other wars and other persecutions. The population is in moral crisis. Since the end of the previous, the gods have been silent, even with their priests, and no healthy children have been born. After more than a decade of desperation, civilization itself appears to be on the cusp of unraveling.
You begin the story under strange circumstances; a mysterious illness has come over you while travelling. Coincidentally, your caravan's path is blocked by a tree in the shadow of a forbidden ruin. Could the timing and location be happenstance, or could the hands of higher powers be at work here? Either way, life-altering events transpire and you are thrust into the middle of a conflict between nations, gods, cultures, and ideologies.
Throughout the remainder of the game, you encounter many potential companions who bring things you may need to the table. Their help doesn't come for free though. You have skills that they need, as well. Whereas companions in most games come with some elaborate side quest that, frequently, distracts from the main narrative, Obsidian has taken another route. Rather than unlocking some hidden ability or recovering powerful loot, the companions in Pillars of Eternity add value by acting as sounding boards for the main theme. In helping them to resolve their quests, the game asks you, "what do you believe?". If forced to choose, which is more important: your family or your traditions? If no authority figure exists to provide context for knowledge, does it still have value? It is more important to follow orders, or do what you think is right? There are no right or wrong answers; the developers give you a laundry list of nuanced responses to these situations, and the consequences of your actions are almost always guaranteed to surprise you.
In most role-playing games, I find myself coming back to the question, "how would my character respond?". In contrast, "how would *I* respond?" quickly became the norm. Perhaps, by this metric, Pillars is a horrible RPG, but it was nice to be challenged in this way.
And Obsidian has given us a finely crafted setting for asking (and answering) such questions. Eora is a world in the death grip of a culture war. By using allegory to frame "big question" debates that exist in our own culture war, Obsidian manages to ju-jistu us into a "real-world RPG" that makes Alpha Protocol's use of that label a little funny. This is where we get to see the craftsmen of Obsidian at their best and simultaneously show why crowd-funding is so valuable: it takes brass balls make a game about the debate between science and religion. No publisher would touch that in a million years. Kickstarter made it possible and Obsidian owned it.
The last two points I want to touch on before wrapping up the review are exploration and combat. Most of the top tier items in the game can only be found via exploration. This could include completing optional quests, venturing off the beaten path far enough to locate some secluded cove filled with traps, monsters, or high level bandit, or finding hidden content via a skill check. Sometimes the reward for your effort is nothing more than a semi-rare ingredient required for crafting, but hearing that unique chime followed by a party member's "look what I just found" bark always feels a little like finding a forgotten $20 in the back pocket of your jeans.
Regarding combat, Easy is for casual players. Normal difficulty is fairly straight-forward and seems to be geared toward people who want don't want to put too much time into it, but don't want to play with training wheels on either. Hard difficulty may the sweet spot for people who want a challenge, but aren't necessarily gluttons for punishment. I'll leave Path of the Damned for other, braver souls to comment on. Regardless of which difficulty you choose, there will be some encounters that are more difficult than others. Some areas are intended for high-level parties only. This doesn't mean that it's impossible to clear them at lower levels, however that fight would have been a lot easier with the right level 7 ability/talent/spell/etc. While the Bestiary isn't necessary on all difficulties, it is certainly useful and indicative of the amount of thought that went into combat.
Overall, I'm very pleased with the first chapter of this story and I look forward to seeing what Obsidian has in store for the franchise.

An absolute classic of a game. There's so much great stuff in it, but two sequels later I think there are two main aspects where the original has yet to be outdone:
- The level design. Venturing from area to area, unlocking shortcuts between them, seeing places you'll eventually reach far off in the distance; the original Dark Souls has some of the very best level design work ever made, period.
- The bosses. Almost every single boss fight feels unique and is satisfying to figure out how to defeat. Considering there are about 18 required boss fights to beat the game (and a good chunk of completely optional bosses) the sheer variety and quality of these epic encounters is pretty incredible.
This game has become something of a legend in itself. Many developers have sought to pull some ideas from it here and there, but the game's true strength comes from the way everything comes together so perfectly despite a staunch refusal to tell the player how to play and where to go.

I cannot recommend any other game more than I can recommend Dark Souls.  Is it the brutal difficulty that I love?  Is it the breathtaking and engrossing environments in the game?  Is it the awesome bosses?  Is is the fact that the entire game is a metaphor for death and acceptance of death?  No.  The reason I love Dark Souls is the journey that you take as a player.  You die and fail constantly, but along your journey you grow as a player and as a person.  The perseverence you must have when going through difficult games like Dark Souls is something that is personal for each player.  And, though the pvp is pretty fun, this is the reason that I love single-player DS.  The only thing standing between victory and defeat is yourself.  It's something that is at the heart of every difficult game from Ghosts and Goblins to Super Meat Boy, however Dark Souls embraces it as its very essence, as its ethos.
And the best part?  You can get this experience for only 20 bucks.

Definitely one of the best survival games out there. Unfortunately, this genre has been oversaturated with bad, clunky, early-access, pre-alpha "games" that get abandoned or are not updated frequently enough to show the developers interest in the product, or their interest in pleasing the people who are giving them money to fund it's development. /run-on sentence.
Miscreated is not that.
Miscreated is one of the most polished early-access survival games on Steam. It has stunning graphics, great gameplay mechanics, and it simply works. It's not clunky. It's not scary to go down stairs. It's not scary to go down ladders in fear of breaking both your legs. The developers of this game are putting out patches on a weekly basis, and have consistently done so since it's been available to purchase. They prioritize their updates on optimization, versus material things that don't impact the playability of the game. Instead of adding another gun to kill eachother with, they'll do bug fixes. Which is not to say they're not adding more content to the game; which they are. But it's nice to play a game where if a bug develops, you can know for sure that it will be fixed in the next patch.
Miscreated is a perfect example of early-access done right. These developers have their♥♥♥♥♥♥together, and I look forward to seeing how this game grows. If you're looking for a good, rewarding survival game, Miscreated is a great one!

This game is challenge, if you're a fan of the total war series and want to have an experience where you're constantly having to put out fies, this game is for you. For those of you who are new to the toal war series, I would not recommend it.
First off the good. The game is pretty, gritty, but visually impressive. The political tree is there, and if you like playing a political struggle along part of managing an empire that is a factor. What you make your people do affects their traits, and rivals exist, so there is a lot of depth. The whole game has a feeling of winding down, and the world is falling apart, so you do get a feeling of fighting an inevitable decline (which I personally like). Usually with Total War games you bulid up an invincible center empire, expand using divide and conquer, and you are only really threatened at the beginning or by a multifront war, but this is quite different.
The bad. There are a lot of balance issues, cavalry is overpowered, the single player campaign is about as stable as Caligula. The visuals look very "samey" for lack of a better term. The game gets stale once Attila is half way through his lifetime (historically), because the Hunnic faction has razed most of the map and you're left fighting them over the ashes of Europe. The AI will also spam doomstacks, massive armies of top tier units the Huns get for free, and will send against your cities so you can do nothing but sit and defend. This is where it becomes unfun, and that really is a shame.
TL;DR I can't really recommend this one to the average gamer.

bills itself as a mature, psychological thriller with horror elements and for a hidden object adventure game this is a fresh idea. Unfortunately, it loses track of the story halfway through and goes back to tired old tropes, with an unfulfilling ending. While I love when games have a deep story, I accept that hidden object games will often have a very simple, linear story -they’re straightforward, and I’m okay with that. What I’m not ok with, however, is a game getting my hopes up and completely letting me down. Here we have a decent HOAG that bit off more than it could chew in terms of story and that overshadows its positive notes.
We play Alice, an office worker who gets no respect from her boss and is working so much she can’t be with her family as often as she would like. On her way to yet another work-related emergency, she gets in a car accident. After that, I have no idea what happens to her because the game doesn’t say. Sure, it starts off with an opening cinematic that shows Alice alive and well two years after the events of the game but the story in the game itself doesn’t tell us how Alice gets to that point physically. What it does is take us on a surreal journey of Alice fighting her mental demons -I think. There is an evil hooded figure who acts as the antagonist throughout the game but we never learn who it is or anything about them so it’s unclear if it’s an actual supernatural entity or a figment of Alice’s mind. Leaving things ambiguous can work to a story’s favor but that requires good writing.
Alice’s dreamscape is divided into four worlds and the hospital setting where Alice wakes up, perhaps implying she is in a coma after the car accident. Though it’s safer to say there are only three worlds since the fourth is a lazy rehash of the hospital setting. Alice waking up and her journey to the first world are the best parts of the game, they create a very eerie feeling and directly relate to the struggles she faces; with pictures of her family, her birthday on a note and lots of memories of things she’s missed thanks to her job. The first world represents her work life, wanting to be the perfect employee but sacrificing her happiness to do so. These are real life issues many face and deal with, it hits home and had me invest myself into the main character.
But the other worlds lack these qualities. The second world is a mystical looking area where Alice has to help save a tree and any sense of horror or relatability goes out the window and we no longer gain insight into Alice, her personality, or her current situation. The third area is about Alice dealing with an evil witch and as I mentioned, the fourth isn’t even unique. There is also a tree lady in the game who has words of wisdom to share but she serves no purpose at all to the story or gameplay. There are so many directions these areas could have taken to expand upon the main character and her dilemma, especially after the game had such a strong start. We could have explore her past, her family, anything that makes Alice who she is and explain why she is suffering so much now but the writer’s gave up. There is also this theme of Alice having to choose her destiny, at first I assumed that I would have to choose at the end of the game to follow my dreams or continue life as is but no. It’s just over, the end, no resolution or any explanations.
I’ve gone on about the story because it’s the most unique feature this title has going for it, everything else places it in generic HOAG territory. It has lovely graphics though the animations for cutscenes aren’t very smooth. It has scene-setting music as well as full voice acting that is pleasant to the ears. The gameplay is to be expected, a lot of puzzles which were rather easy and some hidden object scenes which I can always use more of but this title had a good amount. There is a fast travel map and a great journal feature, though the the fact that you travel one world at a time leaves little room for backtracking. It’s enjoyable to play though there is no bonus content or extra chapter which is a shame given that the main story ends so abruptly.
Can a bad ending ruin a good game? Sometimes.
offers a fun experience with puzzles and hidden object scenes to keep players busy as well as achievements to collect and Steam trading cards. With Lost Grimoires: Stolen Kingdom and Lost Grimoires 2: Shard of Mystery, World-Loom has become one of my favourite developers in the hidden object game genre, so I had high hopes for Mind Snares: Alice's Journey. Unfortunately the game bit off more than it could chew by presenting a pretentious story, but getting lost in the emptiness it finally delivers. The end result is a pretty bad hidden object game and it's unclear what the creators were trying to achieve, especially with the abrupt ending (ran out of ideas probably).
We play as Alice, a successful bookstore-café (?) chain owner who managed to change her life and became an entrepreneur from a secretary. The problem is, it's nothing more than a delusional journey through surreal worlds that seem to represent this process through some really demented symbolism. So basically the whole game takes place in a bizzare dream world, while Alice presumably lies in coma after having a car accident. (The occasionally appearing evil wraith's true identity is never really clarified.)
The game is broken down into 4 sections (4 worlds) each featuring a trait (balance, wholeness, intuition, strength) Alice needs in order to recover (or to change her life?). Many things have been squeezed into these chapters, with all the things related to our protagonist ranging from notes telling her to stand up to her boss to the extent of dolls lying around all over the place who look like Alice. While some of the content make sense and represent segments of Alice's life, many others do not and seem to be there just to make the game more eventful (sometimes we have to help creatures, other times we have to defeat some for no apparent reason).
The hidden object scenes and puzzles are OK, but there's nothing spectacular about them. Some of the puzzles are more time-consuming than hard. There's relatively plenty of item collection and use, which adds a bit to the game's adventure trait.
The graphics is all right, if you like the surreal environments - I didn't - but even if you like the artwork, it'll still feel messed up, as if the artists didn't exactly know where they were going. It feels like as if someone in the department was under the influence of some kind of a psychoactive drug.
The plot gave plenty of opportunity to place all kinds of environments in the game: doll factories, a mental hospital, swamps and strange forests. None of them feel unique since they could be easily swapped and it would still bring no change to the plot.
Even the large number of cutscenes bring no good since most of them show us traversing through portals and feel they are there just to prolong game time.
Mind Snares: Alice's Journey feels like a mediocre HOG, but that lasts only until we play more and get deeper into the game, right until the abrupt ending (which at least might feel refreshing), where it turns out to be a poor one. It still feels like a quality game if we only take the puzzles and HO scenes (plus maybe the voiceover), but everything else is pretty much a mess. We quickly forget what the developers wanted to accomplish and just want to get over and done with the game as fast as we can. And that's not a good sign in any case.
PROS
+ interesting base concept
+ graphics isn't bad, if you like surreal environments
CONS
- shallow story with an abrupt ending
- unremarkable world and scenery
- many unimportant elements stretch game time
- the implied horror theme is misleading
RATING
3/10

This is a must-have game for Total War fans. The gameplay and music and visuals are great, but what I appreciated most was that it really got me interested in the history of that time period. The only thing it's missing is a Islamic DLC.

The Good
+ Graphics: always a strong point for total war games, the unit models are sharp and the way your decisions change the way the map looks is also nice
+ Real Time Battles: Compared to other Total War games the battle AI is actually rather good
+ Politics: While it is not very polished it is still enjoyable, and a step up from Rome 2
The Bad
- Dimplomacy: Very simplistic, your only real options are to declare war and make alliances, could never seem to get trade deals with the AI
--- Campaign AI: Never before have I had uninstall a Total War game after just 7 hours of playing it, but the campaign AI in Attila makes this game unplayable. I've had armies at the top of the map in scotland sail all the way down to the bottom in africa just to attack my only undefended provinces. I've had factions across the map declare war on me for no apparent reason and then march their forces halfway across the map (even though they were at war with their neighbors). Not to mention that even on normal difficulty the AI cheats like crazy.
Verdict:
The campaign AI makes this game unplayable as anything but a custum battle simulator. Even buying it on sale is not worth it.

Somewhere out there on the internet are a set of composite images featuring the blended, averaged faces of thousands of different humans, male and female. Unsurprisingly, the composite faces are extremely plain and forgettable - placid eyes, neutral semi-smile, medium-brown unblemished skin.
The writers appropriated many stock fantasy tropes in creating the world for this game, but they didn't do it in piecemeal fashion - a daub of Tolkien here, a splash of Forgotten Realms there. Instead, it feels like they grabbed every fantasy setting they could get their mitts on, crammed them into a Blendomatic, and hit Frappe. The result is sort of like those composite photos. Everything's been so averaged and smoothed over that you can't even recognize the specific source material any more. All you can tell is that you're in a fantasy setting. That's it. You can tell because there are tall people and short people, and a lot of them have names you've never heard before, and some of the people have swords and shields and others of them cast sparks out of their fingers sometimes.
There are a lot of words in this game. A lot of lore, a lot of history, a lot of dialogue. Reading is great! I love reading, generally. But reading in this game is like reading the ingredients list on a packet of saltines, or like reading a patent for a new kind of chewing gum wrapper, because the source material is just as bland. I've played for over 20 hours (trying to squeeze my money's worth of fun out of this particular stone) and not once did an element of the world strike me as interesting; not once did I want to explore any more of the dialogue or of the in-game texts than I had to. Compare this to a game like PS:T where I was hooked from the moment I woke up on a cold slab in a transdimensional mortuary and a floating, foulmouthed skull started gabbing at me and I stayed hooked, spellbound, and wanting more until the credits rolled (and then I still wanted more) (and I've played that game again, quite recently, and it's still as compelling as the first time I played it).
It was said in another review that the game feels like it was made by people who hate the genre and hate its fans. I have to concur. They say never to attribute to malice what can be explained by incompetence, but I feel the blandness of this game goes far beyond anything anybody could come up with on accident - it genuinely feels orchestrated, premeditated. A bunch of jerkholes in a board room somewhere drummed their fingers together like Mr. Burns, cackled a dry, rasping, collective cackle and set themselves to the business of creating the biggest "♥♥♥♥ you" of a fantasy setting that the genre has ever seen.
There are negative things to be said about the combat, the music, the voiceovers, the special snowflake kickstarter NPCs, some other miscellaneous gameplay and HUD elements... but why bother? The soul of the game is missing: who cares if the body is flawed as well?
The only positive thing to say about it is that the prerendered backgrounds are very pretty. I think that's about it, and it's actually amusing that most of the positive reviews start out by warning people who want sexy graphics to seek out a different game. In reality, the graphics are the only thing PoE has going for it.

I originally gave this games a thumbs up. Turns out to be a big mistake because I hadn't progressed very far yet. I have to completely change my review after experiencing more of the game.
1. This game is SOOO buggy. They keep releasing patches but the bugs never get fixed, or new ones appear. Some bugs are game ending or corrupt save files. Others are just so annoying you want to tear your hair out. The worst of it is the crashing. This game crashes so often it's silly. Usually on load screens, causing you to lose a ton of progress. Sometimes it happens ON THE MAIN MENU. Obsidian really embarassed themselves with their coding job on this one.
2. The rules system is extremely flawed. It's just complicated and nuanced of a magnitude you can't comprehend. In normal D&D, you have very small, simple equations. You attack an orc with an axe, you roll a d20 and add strength plus proficiency. Simple. But in this game there are percentages and 10 million different stats. The main attributes don't even make sense. It just takes everything you expect from an RPG and flips it upside down. They even took Wizards, which are the most powerful class in D&D, and made them ineffective wimps.
3. The gameplay is extremely flawed as well. The main reason is it's 99% combat. You slog through a dungeon, fighting random monsters room-to-room with no story or other activity to  break it up. Sure, the dialouge is well written and the plot is rather interesting, but the problem is there is so LITTLE of it. And in between the stuff we really want, there is a bunch of bland, repetitive gameplay.  I was expecting this game to be more like Planescape: Torment and stick to Obsidian's roots.
4. Exploration is non-existant. You're confined to small areas in each chapter. You have to progress the main story in order to open up new areas. In addition, maps are VERY small and there aren't many of them.
5. There is EXTREME class imbalance. Certain classes suck and others are rockstars. The way the rule system is set up makes CC, Buffs, and Healing irrelevant. CC and Buffs last less than a minute and can't be cast outside of combat, so you can't pre-buff. Healing doesn't actually restore health, just endurance which replenishes after battles anyway. The only way to play is maximize damage output.
6. Lack of alternatives. The only way to resolve conflict is with fighting, 90% of the time. The game is set up with an awesome skill system. There are 5 skills: athletics, mechanics, lore, survival, and stealth. The problem is that they don't actually use  this system at all. It's completely wasted. Not once did I ever see a situation in which one of my skills permitted me an alternative to fighting. In fact, I've never seen the Survival skill used at all, period. It's such a shame that this excellent skill system doesn't impact the game very much and is totally useless.
7. Boring companions. Your buddies you pick up along the way don't have much going on with them. They just drone on and on about one thing. Ok, we get it, this dude is sad that his brother died, move on already. I finally began skipping through their dialouge and didn't regret it later.
I know I shouldn't be upset over this, but I've been eagerly awaiting this game for over a year. I just expected more from Obsidian. I thought this game was the great revival of old school RPG's, but everything about it is just so...bland.
Pretty much exactly like the old school Baldur's Gate games. Complex, Deep, Strategic, Intense. Would recommend to anyone who appreciates strategic, party-based, sprawling RPGs.

However, I enjoyed Terraria better in every way aside from its music and single-block-at-a-time mining, such as the single planet meaning anything I built, I could re-visit and it had more purpose and felt more like home, whereas in Starbound, if you took the time to build a house, chances are you'll never come back to that planet again, so putting care and interest into building structures and making them nice has little to no draw in Starbound.
Starbound claims it has quests, which is does, but they're just fetch quest garbage that did not entertain me. There is a main quest, but it quickly turns into a "find all 6 (can't recall the #) McGuffins across the galaxy" before you can continue thing. That worked on the NES with The Legend of Zelda, because you literally could not find anything better to play on NES in terms of scope and quality at the time. However, fast forward a couple decades or so, and that same "plot" (gather all the items, period) doesn't work in new games today, without clever twists, so when Starbound had the audacity to demand I do the same thing after I was already hoping to find gameplay elements to hook me longer, I lost what remained of my interest immediately.
Once I passed about a dozen hours of gameplay, nothing interested or excited me, and I simply wasn't having fun. Now a friend wants me to play this with her, so I'm having to bite the bullet and trudge through it all over again, and I'm having even less enjoyment a second time around.

Tl;Dr: While the game isn't inherently bad and I do believe it will improve over time, it's not worth buying in it's current state due to many abhorrent flaws the player is expected to look past.
Let me just start off on a positive note here. This game has a lot of potential, and here's why
- It's an open world game where you can do whatever's in the game's boundaries to survive
- The plot is actually pretty good for a survival game, though I have seen much better
- From what I've seen it takes place in the medieval era, and that gives a very wide variety of weapons and armor to utilize
However, despite all this, the game is flawed beyond belief and this is why I can't recommend it
- Unfortunately, the developer has abandoned the game entirely.
- The hitboxes and combat are god awful.
-- For one, the hitboxes are buggy. You have to be aiming at a specific point on the enemy (if it's not on that one point, the hit won't count) and be within range (The range is never specified).
-- Enemies will glitch all the time by trying to move somewhere, then being teleported back, then moving again and being teleported
-- Enemies also have god awful pathing (They walk directly at you, even if youre above them on a cliff) and never think to go around except on very rare occasions
-- The enemies all seem to randomly hit you, even when it appears as though you're not in their range or sprinting a safe distance past them.
- Two, building up broken down towns or creating your own is tedious as all hell and barely anything comes out of it. From what I can tell, the most you'll ever get from building a town is having more than 1 spot to go and warm up or perhaps having a safe-haven in a PvP server. Other than that, there's only the pride of building something from the ground up, which I suppose is good in its own right, but the game fails to provide this feeling.
- Three, the resource gathering is very tedious and unforgiving (For a person doing a fair-playthrough who didn't look anything up, it took me a good 4 hours of constant gameplay to find 1 vein of iron ore, though to some that might just seem like idiocy). Also, each vein of ore holds 5 ores while stones, which contains clay, whetstone, and stone, give 20 of any of the 3 listed. To me this seems fair, though to others the fact that certain stones/veins are larger or smaller than others and still yield the same amount of minerals is bothersome.
- Four, the models are less than satisfactory, and what I mean by this is that each armor set (except for fur and mithras) are basically just reskins with different stats and colors. To me that's very disappointing, especially when I have a steel spear that looks like junk or a silver sword that's dented and broken in certain areas despite the fact that silver implies it's refined and strong (though in real life it isn't quite good sword material, the issue isn't about realism).
- Five, it's a RAM hog. While I do believe this is a product of poor optimization, and will be fixed eventually, as it stands right now the game tends to use all 8 gigs of my RAM and crash itself after a good 3 hours of playing. This might just be me, I haven't heard of anyone else with this issue yet, it very much ruins the experience if I plan to do a long run.
- My sixth reason as to why I can't recommend it is, as discussed in the comments in a civil manner (Credit to Pyrithe for telling me to add this), is that there hasn't been an update trying to fix all this. I get that certain aspects of the game are hard to program or fix, like AI or optimization, but in my time owning this game I have not once seen an update patching even the most minor of bugs. This is one of the main reasons as to why I can't recommend it, as it would help to not only increase the trust the player has in the developer, but also build the developer's credibility. I know that scheduled updates can also be hard to do and are often only managed by AAA companies; however people need to see that the game they've bought IS being improved in some way or another.
- My seventh, and last, reason as to why I can't recommend it seems very nitpicky and minor, but the chewing sounds. They are obnoxiously loud and annoying. Everything about them is awful, even when eating an apple, in which a simple crunching sound will do, you get to hear the god-awful sound of lip smacking and messy eating of a barbarian who barely understands what happens when you take an axe and slam it into a tree multiple times. As I said, this reason seems very small, but to some people these sounds are so god-awful you have to turn off the game's sound completely, and this can be very detrimental to not only the immersion but also to awareness, as it is often times the sounds of enemies that are the only indication of their presence

I got a lot of hate for one of my previous reviews, so I'm going to write a "real" review and explain why I still don't recommend this game.
For a fair warning, there will be spoilers within the text, so if you haven't seen the game before and would like to figure out all the mechanics yourself, I would advise you to go to a different review.
There are pros and cons to getting rebirth over the original version.
Pros:
60 FPS
Consistent visuals
more items and enemy types
more characters
"consistent" map layouts for a rogue-like
Meh:
item changes and balancing (quad shot isn't op anymore, etc.)
more items means even lower chance to get good items, plus a long grind to unlock everything
gambling isn't overpowered, but is faster
shop upgrades, but requires donation machines
Isaac fight became much more difficult, the blue baby fight became trivial in comparison
Cons:
Everything involving the lost
Everything involving sound design is worse to the original comparibly (subjective, but typically agreed on)
The game isn't "complete" without the incredibly expensive DLC
Only good shop items are candle and stopwatch
hard mode isn't a direct difficulty increase, but indirect through taking away consumables and reducing the chance of
special item generation
And I could go way more in-depth on all of these, and include several, several more, but more importantly than just pros/cons, after the time I've spent playing this game, I realized I was never having real fun with the game. It's frustrating. Winning doesn't even feel fun half the time; you get ridiculously strong item combinations that basically win the game for you. The only moderate enjoyment I got from the game was from being a completionist and getting all of the items, which doesn't warrant playing it as long as I did.
Not only that, but for the launch of afterbirth, the developers of this game thought it would be funny to lock content from the purchasers of the respective DLC. This was in response to the BoI community datamining the way to unlocking the super-secret character the lost, however the amount of content they locked from the community was appalling and frustrated a majority of those who purchased the DLC. After all, as previously mentioned, the DLC is expensive as hell. Afterwards, the release of Rebirth's next DLC, Afterbirth+ was hyped up for having mod support, more items, more challenges, bosses etc. Upon release, however, the mod support that was particularly hyped up to infinity didn't even work. People would have to install mods to get mod support running; ruining the entire point of having mod support in the game. Not only that, but the new bosses added had very few animation frames which were impossible to react to, not to mention how in particular big horn looks like it was hand-drawn in the game by an 8 year old child. The entire DLC felt completely lazily done, and ruined any remaining hope I had for the game's future, as it seems to me that all the devs want to do anymore is milk their game for the most money possible using the least effort possible.
So, to recap: most non-graphical changes or additions made to the game from the original BoI have noticeable downsides, The game is no longer enjoyable to me, even while winning, each DLC is almost as expensive as the game, but the game itself feels bare without all the DLC, all the while the devs are seemingly trying to milk money from the game through lazy development.
Because of all this, I can't recommend getting the game anymore. I had much more fun playing the original Binding of Isaac, and the only thing this version of the game has over the original, in my opinion, is the framerate.

1) allow one extra save slot: there have been multiple times where I unfortunately saved right before dying and no matter how many times I restart, there's impending death within 5 secs, erasing hours of work.

Yes, we all know that the main thing of Dark Souls it's the difficulty, with actually a lot of game mechanics to understand and test. It will make you try a lot and it's actually not that easy for beginners. It can be quite frustrating sometimes if you are not in the right mood, as it can offer some big challenges in certain areas or bosses.
The Dark Souls world is huge and quite open, will take some time to get oriented and follow the story at first. But once you get the hands on it I assure this game will give you a different experience than any other games out there.
On the technical aspects you should install DSFix and use a controller to play this game smoothly, if you don't have a controller then I recommend DSMF(Dark Souls Mouse Fix) to get better and smooth mouse inputs.
Forget about graphics options too, the game lacks of any important one, that's when DSFix come to save us, it offer some internal resolution and graphicals tweaks to optimize the game visually or performance-wise.
I believe they had to rush the PC port due to a lot of people requests to bring it to PC. But please don't throw away this game because of that, it will take a few minutes to install those plugins.
So to conclude, I would say that even if you are not a fan of medieval games like I was and as I mentioned early, this game will give you a different experience from any other game, I would say that it can even change your mind about what you see from videogames nowadays. It will actually make you live the feeling of progressionist and completionism.

My conclusion; Shadow of Mordor, while rather liberal in its creation of entirely new species of beast  (Caragor, Graugs, Ghuls et al) as well as its primary characters (the three bad boys that are the Black Captains being a prime example) manages to stay entertaining, immersive and downright satisfying enough that not only am I willing to readily overlook these newly invented additions to Tolkien's universe, I actually applaud the way in which they were rather seamlessly  - in my opinion anyway - inserted and intermingled with already present Middle-Earth history and lore.
Verdict: 9/10 at the very least, one of my favourite games in my library.  I shall be looking feverishly forward to going blade-to-blade with the Witch-King, his Nazgul chums and that admittedly damn fiiine looking Balrog come Shadow of War's release.

I feel embarassed that this game sat in my steam library for so long without being played. I recently finished this game for the second time, the first time i rushed it, this time i took my time and got the collectibles, why bother? well because i'm a tolkien fan, and every collectible had an interesting story on the background, the main story starts well but then it kinda disapoints.
In the graphics department, go check some screenshots of mine and they speak for themselves, this game is beatifull, expecially the second part of the game (SPOILERS) which is in the Sea of Nurn, the lash green landscapes are gorgeous.
The gameplay, well it's kinda divided in two categories, combat and the nemesis system, the combat is very fluid, similar to the Batman games, you have to dodge, counter, bash, slash, dismember the enemies, it's one glorious, gory mess. The nemesis system it's inovative, i can't count the times that i've killed the toughest Uruks, to then randomly die to a grunt, that goes up in the ranks, as you try to avenge yourself and try to kill him, you find that he remembers you, and makes fun of you for getting your♥♥♥♥♥owned, since the previous fight he got stronger, if he kills you again he will get even stronger, and near impossible to defeat, if you defeat him he still  has a chance to come back, and he remember and bears the scars from the last fight. The branding, you can praticaly control huge amounts of orcs by mind control, and you can betray their bosses, or make them iniciate in trials to other warchiefs, to betray them later and take their actual place, it's really fun, oh that and the movement in this game, that is so fluid, jump, dive, sprint, all very fluid.
I like the attention to detail, and they have it here, they even give you a screenshot camera, with all the filters, rotaitions and all the goodies to take exelent screenshots.
Overall, this is a great game, and a must buy for those who like fantasy tipe videogames or movies like the lord of the rings, don't go in for the main story, the rest of the game it's what makes it so great, i'm anxious to see what they bring in the sequel.

I Should Go...
...Are the words that I occasionally see on the faces of people whom I introduce Mass Effect to. Naturally, it's a given response, since this game is a far cry from what many are used to on both the RPG and Shooting front. I remember almost throwing this game into the recycling bin while I had the PS3 version, since I couldn't figure out how to zoom out on the galaxy map (my fault entirely for forgetting that the circle button exists).
Sure, the game does present a few faults here and there, such as the awkward shooting/cover mechanics, absurdly long cooldown times for powers, optional yet completely barren side missions, limited auto-save points, [some] overpowered enemy biotics as well as a few other caveats that I won't go into detail here, which can completely cripple someone's interest in Mass Effect. A sad thing, since the feeling of carrying over your complete save to Mass Effect 2 is unparalleled on so many levels.
Bioware has always been a dominant forefront for the story driven rpg market, and Mass Effect is no exception. Thus, enjoyment as a whole can be severely limited if the player refrains from making a personal investment in the overall lore, story and characters. And yes, Mass Effect goes above and beyond in providing all three, while also establishing an atmosphere of its own, which makes it stand out heavily among all the other space games on the market. Top-tier Canadian science fiction everybody!
Many of the choices you make in this game will impact you later, especially when carrying over your saves to the next two games. Who you save, what you say, when you choose to do missions, which path you follow, undoubtedly adds a lot of "Mass" to the "Effect" of your decisions, and definitely adds weight to what happens later in the first game alone.
Plus, the PC port is outstanding, enabling you to use most, if not all of your powers during combat in real time, rather than always opening the power wheel on the console versions. Equipment management and gun modding is also much more direct/less in your face due to the redesigned menu system. The new hacking minigames are also a nice touch as well. It's almost as if PC was Bioware's most prioritized platform from the get-go. Definitely better than the delayed PS3 version, which encountered many lip-sync errors, missing textures and frame rate issues. Also didn't help that it always took 12 seconds to save, where the PC port only requires half a second, with the addition of a very handy quick save button.
You'll need to install a few mods and edit the .ini files though if you wish to remove some small hitches, but that can be accomplished easily through the many worthwhile guides for this game (I'd recommend uncapping the game's framerate and installing MEUITM, which allows you to run the game higher than 720p and upscales a lot of old textures). It's not necessary, but the experience is undoubtedly more rewarding with those fixes.
I won't go into detail on any of the main story points and characters, since I wish for anyone reading this review who doesn't own the game yet to find out for themselves. Sure, Mass Effect isn't for everybody, and it might seem underwhelming at first for many Star Wars/Doctor Who enthusiasts out there, but the series as a whole quickly makes a name for itself if you give it time, especially if you make it to the third game, and the eventual fourth if you love the series that much : )

Does online multiplayer matter to you? Does it matter more than cutting down entire armies of soldiers? The game pretty much needs a controller. If you get an xbox controller for windows you should be pretty set.  If online multiplayer is a deal breaker, then the lack of it will no doubt be disappointing. But it is dynasty warriors in its 2000 combo chain goodness.
Dynasty warriors is a game with a fairly simple concept. There's lots of soldiers on the field. You have a name, they don't. Therefore they're more doomed than redshirts on an alien planet made of explosives. You follow the objective, which is usually: "defend point A, kill target B and/or escort person C to point D. There will be about 200 guys between you and the target but as long as they dont' have a name you should probably be able to kill them in two attacks or so."
It takes place during a period of ancient China known as the three kingdoms era. Ca 200 AD. The events of which was made into a novel called "The Romance of the three kingdoms" written around a thousand years later, give or take, based on the memoirs of the people who lived then and fought. It features very hammy dialogue that can put William Shatner to shame and may or may not educate you on Chinese history. It does come with an encyclopeadia of historical information of the era in the game. Though I doubt nobody reads it very much. Needs more sick horse flipz.
I have fun with it. I'm not sure its worth the full €49.99 if you already own DW8 on PS3 or something. But if you can get it for less then yes. If you haven't gotten into dynasty warriors, and would like to, but don't maybe feel like getting a playstation, this is a pretty good game and probably worth the money if you have a controller for it. If you don't then... Its very difficult to play. As it is though it isn't an incompetent port, it is just made with controllers in mind.

First off let me start by saying: this is one fun game.
The game gives you three styles to play: ghost, panther and assault. Ghost means you are invisible, you weren't even there. Panther means you do silent kills, where as assault is run and gun. Of course you get the most points (as in: money) for ghost, but it's perfectly doable using assault. As you mix the styles, you get varying amounts of points for your actions.
Your gear customizations (weapons, ops suit, gadgets) are also aligned along these three concepts. You can use a sticky noisemaker to attact enemies while you sneak by, use a sniper rifle or just pack out your shotgun.
The story is thrilling, there's always a new turn of events and side quests aren't compulsory. While some sneaking problems are tough to master and the checkpointing is rather sparse, little extra tasks like picking up flash drives or capturing high value targets add a little spice into the gameplay.
The final touch is added by plenty of great dialogue and detailed maps with multiple ways through them.
On the downside the controls are sometimes a little awkward, especially the view control, but it doesn't hurt too much.
Overall I would very much recommend the game to anyone who likes sneaking action and doesn't mind trying different approaches at solving a problem, especially at the price point it's sold at.

Pillars of Eternity is a game that many have spoken about already, but it does deserve the attention. If you have ever played the Baldurs Gate and Icewind Dale series of videogames set in the Forgotten Realms setting, or Planescape: Torment in the Planescape Setting then playing Pillars of Eternity is like coming home after a long journey.
To be sure, there are differences such as 3D character models , a different setting and so on. Yet the game has the same timeless quality about it. One of the things the older games lacked was a real impact made by the background/ biography of the character you create, not so here. If you are of a particular faith or hail from a certain region then you can access dialogue and object interaction that can have a variety of effects on the game. And there are other factors as well beyond those two.
Obsidian proved last year that they can make a blockbuster of a game with South Park: The Stick of Truth and Pillars of Eternity is no less spectacular. Unless you abhor games where choices have consequences and loathe a good storyline this is THE GAME to get. There are a few minor issues of course, but those were present in earlier AD&D games as well.
Pro's:
-Deep storyline, with choices effecting real consequences
=Beautiful environments
-Unique and deep characters
-Fitting, lovingly composed music
-The ability to 'recruit' more customly made characters
-Non-violent solutions possible
-Lots of text to read
-Pets
Cons:
-Some quests lack alternative resolutions
-More party members with dialogue would have been nice, essentially now you need to reserve a slot for a utility member or two.
-Custom party members have no dialogue, quests or whatever.
-No miniature giant spacehamster pets
-Nothing to do with backer made npc's but read a really short bit of story.
-Idem dito for the tombstones with backers on them.
-Some content feels cut short
In conclusion, the game is a wonderful experience despite its flaws. One would shudder to think the possibilities if Minsc and Boo had been implemented though. It is my hope that a sequal or game in the same vein will be made.

The plot takes a while to develop, is strong in the mid game, but then falls apart a little in the end game. As it's fairly open to the player to decide their progress, this may have just been because of my specific playthrough or "background" choices.
The biggest detractor were the bugs, most frequently in the combat stats/rolls that resulted in instant deaths of high level party members at the hands of trash monsters. The reputation system was frustrating as well, as some poor choices early in the game could lock you out of different factions and break quests with no option to rebuild rep. Don't play this game without frequent saves!
Most comparable to Baldur's Gate 1/Icewind Dale, I found most of my disappointment in this game was simply because I went into it expecting Baldur's Gate 3, rather than the first in a possible new series of games. The party dialogue and quests are great, but not to the same level of detail as BG2, where party members would interact and conflict with each other, and there were romance options.
My expectation now is that this game is part one of a new franchise. From that perspective, it's a pretty great first game and I recommend it to anyone with 60+ hours to drop into an RPG.

Dragon's Dogma is the result of passionate lovemaking between Monster Hunter and The Lord of the Rings, while Dark Souls watched through the bedroom window nodding in approval.  The game has a lot of rough edges, but it's got solid, well-polished mechanical gameplay and a very rich atmosphere, and those two factors taken together are more than enough to carry the game for me.
Action is definitely the game's forte.  It's a very distinctly Japanese kind of hack-and-slash, in which (depending on your class and weapon choice) you have a series of specific attacks, combos, and utility moves, all of which have consistent timing and hitboxes.  None of that Arkham Asylum malarky that so many Western RPGs seem to ape, which I've always found to be visually impressive but just not much fun to actually participate in.  DD's combat gives you a box of tools, and then lets you apply them as you see fit.
To recount a personal experience of mine (from back in my days of playing this on the X360):  It was pretty early on in the game, during one of my first non-scripted encounters with a Cyclops.  My AI-contolled buddies and I had spent a few minutes whittleing down the Cyclops' health bars and it had flown into a rage in response.  As the Cyclops raised its gigantic spiked club to strike, I rolled between its legs, scrambled up the side of a boulder and leaped onto the Cyclops' back, at which point I delivered a flurry of dagger strikes to the back of its neck and head, struck the killing blow, and triumphantly rode the Cyclops' toppling corpse back down to the ground.  And this had all occurred organically, in gameplay, with me piloting my character through every action in the sequence.  That instance is what really sold me on DD.
Once I got past how enamored I was with the combat and had settled into Dragon's Dogma's setting, I discovered that there was actually quite a lot of depth to the world of Gransys--depth which unfortunately will probably never be fully realized, as DD is pretty obviously a game that had more ambition than it had money in the budget.
Dragon's Dogma is a very ambitious game, and certain late-game boss encounters achieve a truly dizzying scale.  Come for the exhilirating combat, then stay for the rich and absorbing atmosphere.  Just don't expect a too terrifically story-driven experience.  This is the game you pull out when you want to have a fantasy adventure afternoon.
EDIT:  I can't believe that I forgot to mention this.  The character customization is phenominal.  Unlike so very many RPGs, DD allows you to fully customize not only your character's face, but also their height, proportions, physique, posture, etc.  I've made tall, willowy mages and short, whippy rangers with equal ease.

Quite possibly the best game ever created.
The level of strategy required to play this game is nearly incomprehensible; I found myself having to have a piece of paper nearby just to draw out budget plans, and that's not even touching the complex combat system. When combat occurs, there's a sharp balance you have to hold between managing aggression and doing damage; less attacks per second to keep an important character safe, or more to finish him off but maybe propel the alien into your school? It's very difficult to the point that survival horror comes to mind as a genre.
The budgeting system is intense. Allocating funds between fish and weapons borders on art instead of strategy. Don't walk into this game expecting a casual experience. Without spoiling too much, I'll say that the upgrade mechanics are also amazing. While it's usually linear improvement, expect stellar new graphics and sounds along with your stat buffs. There are upgrades for fish, weapons, food, and more that I won't mention.
The soundtrack in this game is absolutely killer. Seriously. It's amazing. You could sleep to the calm tracks, but I can personally vouch that when PopCap wants to build suspense, they build it. They then deliver. Hard. The enemies you'll be fighting in this game are, as previously mentioned, no joke. Those linear upgrades I mentioned are less upgrades and more a scrabble to keep up with the standard of ten steps behind the enemy. Good luck accomplishing even that. And believe me. You'll be pounded with sick beats the whole time.
The cast in this game is great. Deep, dark, thoughtful lines and lovable characters, models, and animations make this game truly beautiful and unforgettable. Every death is truly a tragedy. The end credits are mostly comic relief (literally the first you'll see in the entire game), so they lack a bit in the way of factual information. Through my own research, I've found a few of the character actors:
1. The dolphin's sounds were ripped directly from a Soviet nuclear submarine.
2. One of the "hidden" special characters' grunts are from Sylvester Stallone's first role ever. I'm not sure they attained the proper licensing, but it looks like the beginnings of the lawsuit were swept under the rug.
3. The guppies sound like a plethora of different actors, but is actually just Bill Murray pretending to be hundreds of other actors.
4. The final boss is voiced by Bill Murray acting as himself.
5. The last one I could figure out was the carnivores' bite sounds are the exact same sound as the dog bites in CoD: Ghosts. I'm not sure how that happened, but I promise that if you compare them they're exactly the same.
The last thing I'd like to touch on is the amazing graphical expertise that the art department at PopCap has. Genuinely soothing and peaceful graphics put you into a calm state right along with the soundtrack; that is, until and alien shows up and the advanced gore engine tosses guppy shreds all over your tank. The shading effects are also amazing. Shadows are affected by laser blasts and temporal warp shifts (TWSs as known ingame), and you can almost see the reflection in a guppy's eye as her beloved little sister is strewn halfway across the tank by the razor-sharp teeth of an extraterrestrial. When it needs to build suspense, it acknowledges the hardware shortcomings of the time and leaves a lot to the imagination; however, I promise you that when that suspense finally culminates, you'll wish they'd left a little more to be imagined.
This game definitely isn't for casuals or noobs. I'm not trying to be offensive, but I promise that it'll stomp you into the ground over and over, and its version of a reprieve is stepping back long enough to pull on a pair of steel-toes. The only tip I can give is to avoid indecision because I promise that if you falter for even a second, it'll destroy your guppies so fast that your economy will be irreparably tanked. And if you ever try to turn tail and run, you shouldn't be surprised to find some boot laces dangling from your nose. At least you can take comfort in the fact that the biggest inconvenience you gave the AI was having to dislodge its heel from your colon.

This game is dated, slow, and can't run properly without installing a mod. That being said, this game great. It's a fun ARPG that puts your skills to the ultimate test. Yes, this game is hard. Yes, you will die. Yes, it's kinda the point. Every death you learn about the game. That boss that dunked you with his buttslam attack you didn't know he had? Now you know he has it. That well-hidden boulder trap that rolled down the stairs to crush you? Now you know where to find it, and when to run. The challenge is there, but so is the knowledge and learning to overcome it with your own power.
Any RPG character you want to make, you can probably make it here. Poison Fist Monk? Spell slinging Magic Knight? Zweihander Champion of the Giants? Fire breathing, ninja flipping Dragon-Ninja hybrid? Check, check, check, and after grinding to get Dragon Scales, check!
The visuals in the game are awesome. The enemy, level, and boss design feels unique and original in each area you visit. Blighttown is a toxic swamp of gloom and despair, Anor Londo is as prestigious and clean as it is controller breaking. The lighting bolt spitting snake people in Sen's Fortress. The greataxe wielding Taurus Demons of Lost Izalith. Gravelord Nito is terrifying, Ornstein and Smough are badass and powerful, and Artorias of the Abyss is one of the best bosses I've ever fought in a video game. They're all there to kill you and look cool doing so.
The game rewards exploration as well. There are tons of side paths and secret areas that lead to weapon upgrades, new spells, and extra souls to level yourself with. If a boss is too hard, try another path in the area. Grind up some souls, maybe you'll find a new weapon to bash their brains in with!
If the game really is too hard, try some Jolly Co-operation with a friend! I actually find the game more fun (and less brutal to my blood-pressure) when I tear down a naked-demon-spider-queen together with a friend.
I've finished three playthroughs of the game (two co-op, one solo). My two major complaints are the lack of dual wielding and the game not running at 60fps (Dark Souls HD Remaster Fromsoft please please please). You CAN dual-wield weapons, but it's not very good in this game. Thankfully the sequel fixes that.
TL;DR: Game is hard. Game is fun.

I've played so many HOGs (most not on Steam tbh) and this is one of the better ones if you are someone who is looking for something quick and maybe not too into getting involved in the story. The only reason I say this is because as someone who watches all of the cutscenes, I don't think much would be missed without them. The story itself is following a woman who crashes her car after thinking about how horrible a path she has gone down (her job seems to be the main issue) and is suddenly caught in what I assume is some kind of limbo in order for her to recognize where she has gone wrong and to start taking control of her life to live how she will be happy. You can grasp this concept pretty quickly and the rest of the game just follows through "chapters" until Alice has apparently figured it all out. It isn't a bad story but like I said, I wouldn't say that it makes or breaks the game. The hidden object scenes were decently challenging, I usually got caught up trying to locate one or two objects for a little while. The minigames were more on the easy side but I may be biased since many of the minigames in other HOGs work with the same or similar mechanics/goals. The art and design was very appealing as many HOGs are. Overall I would say it is a solid HOG if you only have a little bit of time and if you care more about the game over the story.

I am eternally grateful to my friend introducing me to Dynasty Warriors 3 back in 10th grade of high school. Since then, I have been a huge fan of Dynasty Warriors (as well as the Three Kingdoms story in general), and have fond memories of he and I playing DW4 latenight during summer vacation - literally every day until 3am (and a morning break in which he would go home, shower and return 4 hours later for more Dynasty Warriors. The joys of a carefree teenager).
I stuck with the series all the way, though burned out on it with DW5 and was disappointed with DW6. I'm still a huge fan though, and I wasn't disappointed with DW7, which renewed my interest in the series. Sadly, shortly after its release, my console bit the dust. Of course, in the end, this was a good thing as it was the driving force to my wife buying me my first ever gaming PC. Alas, no DW7 (outside of jacking a glitchy and entirely foreign JP copy), and I figured my Dynasty Warriors fanaticism would be stuck in the past as memories of the good ol' days.
Thankfully, Koei decided to release DW8 and its XL expansion to Steam as the "Complete Edition," despite actually lacking a number of DLC packs available on the console version (though I've heard DLCs are on the way). And now that its been released, gamers are crying "foul!" at every turn for various reasons. So with all that in mind, and a bit of knowledge as to my background with playing DW games, let's get to it.
Firstly and flatly, do I recommend this game? Absolutely, yes. The game plays like any other Dynasty Warriors game - pick a guy (or gal), insert person into a battlefield and go to town on the enemy. It's repetitive button mashing at its finest. The series has received the alternate title of "Chinese Genocide Simulator," and this game lives up to that moniker. The first story battle, I used my favorite Wu character, Shangxiang, and plowed through 1600+ people before the map was done (on normal difficulty). It was possible to get 1000 kills in DW3 thanks to the never-ending populating gates, which required the death of the gatekeeper before they stopped spawning enemies, but DW4 toned it down and 1000 kills generally required a higher leveled player and a lot of goofing around. As I said, DW5 burned me out - it wasn't very memorable for me, as with 6, so I don't recall how easy it was to hear your character proclaim themselves a true warrior of the three kingdoms. But for me to get 1000+ kills on the very first level with an unleveled-up Shangxiang was a sign of good fortune regarding this game.
Your character can use any weapon in-game, but excels with certain ones, and of course is most proficient with their own personal weapon. You can have multiple musous stored up, and so on and so forth. Basically, the gameplay does add on to what the later renditions gave to the series, so its not like you might as well be playing a graphically improved version of DW2 or 3.
Speaking of graphics, this is another spot where many gamers are angry. The pictures provided in the DW8 store page are apparently screencaps from the PS4 version of this game, but the in-game graphics are PS3 quality, or perhaps a slight step above.  Certainly it appears Koei is guilty of fibbing, but honestly I just can't get angry - graphics don't mean a whole lot to me, and although it would be nice if they looked better, I can still go back and play DW3 right this moment and not have an issue with its block hands and hard-edged polygons. In other words, unless you absolutely NEED the very best you can possibly get, the graphics in this game look fine.
Sound-wise, I haven't heard anything terrible, which is both a good and bad thing. The music in the game offers a variety of songs from previous games, including the more memorable ones from DW3 and 4. This is always a welcomed addition. Unfortunately, I haven't heard any outstandingly bad dubbing. One of the things that makes DW3 such a great experience, then and now, is its terrible voice acting. I won't list them here, but a quick search in YouTube can help you find cutscenes with some of the most hideously read dialogue ever produced. I'm one of those guys who likes it that way, and I've never had an issue with the English dialogue in any of the games. Sadly for me, the voice acting has improved considerably over each rendition of this game, and although some characters in DW8 do not have a well-fitting voice (compared to previous incarnations), it's not bad enough to be memorable like "You flaming idiots" or "Yuan Shu, you have deceived me!"
Another gripe from the community is the controller support, or lack thereof. I've heard everything from the game not recognizing 360 controllers to default inputs totally dismantling typical controller layout. I can only report on what I've experienced, and that is nothing. I plugged my 360 gamepad into my USB port and started the game. It functions perfectly, with every button mapped out as how it would be on a console. The only thing is that, the buttons themselves don't appear in the game, meaning if you want to proceed through a menu, it won't show you the correct gamepad button, or ANY gamepad button for that matter. Coming from someone who plays a lot of low budget free junk or MUGEN, I'm used to this, and I would expect any gamer familiar with gamepad games in general to recognize quickly which buttons proceed and return in the menu screens, and retain that info for future playtimes.
Gamers are also miffed that there isn't an online co-op mode. If this was a feature you desperately need to enjoy this game, it may be a killer for you. For me, I didn't really have much of a fun experience with the online co-op in DW7 (nothing bad on the game's behalf - I just found myself playing with people who had no interest in coordinating with another person), and so I don't really care for online co-op. If they eventually include it, I'm sure I'll play it regardless, but I'm far more interested in whats available in-game presently.
Lastly, there were a lot of issues with freezing, black screens, infinite loads, CTDs, etc.,. Koei has thankfully shown they didn't just dump this out on the PC and walk away - there have been (to the best of my knowledge) two updates now that have patched issues in the game. Although some people are still having problems, I think a vast majority have cleared up and can now play the game.
Having said all this, and if you read all this (congrats), you'll no doubt find me to be a fairly easily pleased gamer when it comes to Dynasty Warriors. And I don't deny that. The game is exactly what I want - big battlefields, lots of kills (or KOs), lots of things to find, level up, etc.,. For others, there are just too many problems to justify purchasing. To each their own. But if you find yourself in agreement with my standpoint on things like graphics and lack of online co-op, I would seriously consider buying this game. It's mindless entertainment, repetitive and the same story and battles that've been told (usually incorrectly) since DW2. But it's my guilty pleasure, and it may very possibly be yours, too.

For the time it took from the ending of the kickstarter and the poorly aged jokes that Hussie made about how much money he earned in total(while absolutely ruining the chance to get any of the stolen money back), Hiveswap is already looking like a worse version of Broken Age, with the beginning starting out decent, then having to buy each "chapter"(aka an actual part of the game that should already exist) with nearly immediate diminished returns. Two things that I can talk positively about the game is that it... looks pretty, and appropriately sets the scenes according to the time period(WOW, REMEMBER POGS AND LITEBRITES? WE'RE SO QUIRKY).
That's it.
Hiveswap is still showing Hussie's absolute mastery of color coordination(which I always deeply appreciated from his Problem Sleuth days), so while what I said was sincere, nearly every single other aspect of the game is severely lacking. Puzzles, if they can even be called that, depend on you having two eyes and a mouse. There is literally nothing challenging in the game itself, even for a point and click: how do you get a key? Don't worry, every single step is described in excrusciating detail, or you have to click on a teddy bear on a whim.
For combat, I'm not even sure how to critique it: The girl won't use guns because it would make combat last one t-sorry, because she doesn't like guns. You can tapdance, you can pirouette, you can flash a light, but it takes you out of having any sort of fun with it when 'options' turn into 'one solution you have infinite time/turns to choose accordingly'.
Characters are absurdly flat, with gems such as "I hate my dad but I'm the main character so I'm also nice" and "I BUILT MY TINFOIL HAT OUT OF CHILDHOOD DREAMS AND FOX NETWORK SATELLITE DISHES", as well as "Tavros, but worse". As having read all of Homestuck, I could not in my wildest dreams expect anything better than what we have now for the characters, but I'd be willing to change my opinion on this as the different chapters come out; looking in from a lets play, as it stands right now.
$8 after two million and waiting months for chapters after years from the kickstarter campaign disguists me, but I'm only holding so much vitriol for this and writing a review longer than I ever would want to read because I KNOW Hussie and the What Pumpkin staff at large can do so much better.

I didn't really enjoy Conviction as it didn't feel like a stealth game. It was basically an action/adventure game with stealth put in. The older Splinter Cell games (such as Chaos Theory) were primarily stealth games and that is what us fans were used to and loved about the series. And it's because of that reason I decided to give Blacklist a chance because it looks like it's gone back to its roots. So what we have here is a combination of elements in past SC games and elements from Conviction, neatly bundled into one fun game where stealth is your best friend. Sure you can take the louder approach and shoot everything (and everyone) in sight but what's the fun in that? Shooting out lights while hanging from a ceiling pipe, and when your prey comes to investigate and passes it off as a faulty bulb, you leap onto him to finish him off with your knife.... Now that's what Splinter Cell is all about!
I haven't completed the SP campaign yet but what I did play so far is good. The graphics are slightly outdated but that's not to say it's poor. Plus, I get a consistent 60fps when playing this so that's defo a plus in my books. Spies vs Mercs online game mode is back where two teams of 4 face off. DISCLAIMER: I loved Baldur's gate played it for over 200 hours.  Played Baldurs Gate 2 for about 150 hours.  So I automatically love this game.  My review of this game is below.
The isometric game and its designs are wonderful.  The story is rich, and the pre-defined script still makes it feel like your choices alter the course of the game.  The NPC's that came from the backers are completely not part of the world and its story, but it does help emerge yourself into the world that you are in.  They are not all happy fun stories.  Some are very dark, some are neutral, and some are very bright.  I got tired of them initially, until I realized that I enjoyed reading their stories because it made me feel like I understood the world that was created for us better.
Some people might complain about the XP system, how you can kill 100 people and not gain any XP until you encounter new creatures or complete quests.  I hated it first as well.  But before I knew it, after exploring everything, i was a much higher level than I thought I was.  I couldn't really anticipate when I leveled but when I did level, it was a gratifying experience.  I couldn't wait to hit NEXT to see if i got a new talent, or what new higher level spells my wizard could cast, or my priest could pray for.
The only problem I had, was that I didn't get to create a full party that I wanted (as I wanted to listen to all of the pre-generated PC's talk.)  Yes, I can create whatever members I wanted, but if I knew what classes I was going to pick up first, I would have chosen a different main character class to start with as some of the other classes just sound awesome.  That just means i'll have to wait for playthrough #2, and maybe #3 to experience the interaction between all npc's and fully experience all of the classes.
Once again, this is a wonderful games.  There have been a few bugs here and there, and they are patched very quickly. Even if it was game breaking or character altering, they have done a great job making sure the patches are retroactive such that you don't lose anything in your current playthroughs.
My one true complaint, is the load times can be really long, especially when loading just a small house.  My PC is quite capable to handle anything this game throws at it, but the loading times can be really long.
5-Stars.

Alright, where to begin with this game...
Let me start by saying, I love this game. I played it when it was released on the PS3 before and after the Dark Arisen expansion, and was genuinely missed when I eventually sold my PS3. So naturally I was ecstatic when I heard it was coming to PC!
Now is it a good port? In my experience, yes. They seem to have actually taken care to treat it like a full on PC release and not a simply a PS3 game that's now on PC. There are many graphics options as you would expect of any modern PC game. While the graphics are not fantastic, (They never really were) they definitely did some improvements over the orignal release particulary with the lighting and over-all quality.
Combat - Honestly, as many have stated, this is where the game shines. It's fluid, fun, and over-all just feels great. Whether you are sniping foolish bandits as a ranger or channeling your inner Merlin with Magic spells that are visceral in their own right it all works well together. Especially a Melee character as you get to climb on a Cyclop's face to stab it's one good eye! (Though any class can climb a large beast, doing so as a mage is...ill advised XD)
Graphics - While it may feel rather dated in several places they are good as a whole and some environments can be downright gorgeous. (Especially with an ENB if you're willing to go the route.)
Sound - I'll admit not my forte, but I have no complaints. The music fits the game fairly well and honestly nothing really sounds weak or off in my opinion. The voice acting is....not that great. Which I find odd because there are quite a few well known voice actors in the roster. Kinda felt like they either phoned it in like Dinkle-Bot or were just given terrible direction.
Pawns - The ever present sidekicks of your adventure. (Unless, like me you tossed them off a very high cliff so you could get some peace and quiet!) It's a pretty fun system that makes an otherwise singleplayer experience more social. If only they would shut the hell up! Creating them is just as detailed as your main character and in fact even deeper when you take into account their inclinations. They learn based on what you do and can mimic you so in a way it's like parenting. They pick up good and bad habits from you, the player which adds an interesting dynamic.
Story - This is where the game tends to fail. While it definitely has some interesting themes in the story especially regarding the "true" ending. The story you encounter through most of the game is rather bland. Through most of the game you are an errand boy for the Duke basically, which in the end has nothing to do with your ultimate fight with the dragon. To say the story is disjointed would be an understatement. Which leads me to a bonus category.
The game world - It feels dead. Now one could potentially argue that this was by design given the grand Mythos at work but I feel that could also be a cop-out and was maybe just a loss of translation from the original japanese game. Having heard the audio in Japanese in the original PS3 release they definitely felt more expressive when they spoke. Which did add some life to the world as a whole but that still doesn't change the sparsity of the world. There are literally only two towns in what is supposed to be a kingdom. And there are still only a few people in those cities. The world just feels lifeless as a whole because of it.
My Consensus - It is by no means a perfect game. But the things it gets right make it an overall fun experience. It is perhaps not for everyone but for me personally it is a game that continues to pull me back even after beating it about 10 times. Which no other game has managed to accomplish. So for that I have to give my recommendation.
