This game built a very solid basement and ground. However whatever built on that ground is terrible.
Well, first lets talk about the character creation. Honestly, not so great. Easy to make a freaky looking man or woman, hard to make a decent looking person. And those voices, I do think they only recorded one man and one woman's voices then simply pitched them. Character creation isn't a big deal for many people and this game is several years old now so I think it's acceptable.
After creating your character and pawn, the journey truely begins. SPOILER ALERT. Story sucks, main story is pretty short and those missions play just like other side quests. You are always fixing other people's problems, your character lack of motivations. Yes, you want your heart back but none of those main quests has anything to do with that. Basically you keep doing other people's jobs and one day the dragon finally shows up then you get a chance to win your heart back by defeating the dragon. Few missions left after you defeat the dragon and finally you learn the lore of this world. Short and unfocused story I consider it is bad. A lot of side quests here or there, none of them are really interesting, not terriblely boring either.
The open world of the main storyline is boring as hell. I don't see why those areas even have names because everywhere looks the same and has those same types of enemies, they are not identical at all. Besides castle and village, the only things left in this world are grass, trees and rocks, and some generic caves as dungeons. Dark Arisen area is a big dungeon. I am not a fan of dungeon but still think it is much better than that empty world in the main game.
The enemy design sucks balls. Not a single enemy is original. All the monsters in this game have been used hundreds of times in other fantasy games. What even worse, the design of these monsters are generic as hell. What even much worse, this game doesn't have a lot of monster types. If you don't count those reskins, recolors or simply differ in size, perhaps around 15 types in total include bosses.
There are a lot of armor sets and weapons in this game which is satisfying. But when you think this game got more armors and weapons than enemies, it is pathetic.
I hope they make a sequel. They built a very solid ground, all they need to do is to provide high quality content.

Before I start this review I have to say this game was my childhood.  I had an actual disc, a DISC.
Don't be fooled by its "casualness",  this game is INTENSE.  Insaniquarium Deluxe is an aquarium simulator.  With a few twists.  Aliens attack your fish, fish can die if they turn green for longer than 10 seconds, and it has riduculous "buddies" that help you through each level.  The goal of the game is to buy fish and feed them so they give you coins.  With these coins you buy more fish, food, potions, and egg parts.  In order to beat the level you must buy 3 egg parts.  At random points during the game aliens will appear and try to kill your fish.  You have to click the aliens to kill them, ALOT.  RIP your mouse.  It also has a quirky and albeit immature sense of humor which when I played it my 10 year old self loved.  There is a buddie named "Preggo".  She is a fish that overtime gets bigger and eventually gives birth to a guppy complete with an absurd fart sound.  I played this game 9 years ago and it was a blast.  I just picked it up on Steam to find out it still is.  So, if you like quirky fast paced games pick it up.
Insaniquarium Deluxe HD,  MAKE IT HAPPEN POPCAP!

Back before PopCap was bought by EA and the company saw the detriments that the very move brings, they made the most awesome "casual" games that somehow intrigued both casual and hardcore gamers alike. PopCap's major successes include Bejeweled, Peggle, and Plants Vs. Zombies, but through playing all of their games for the past twelve years, Insaniquarium is by far my personal favorite, and in my opinion, the most original, creative, and fun.
This game is part simulation, part "management", part tycoon, part action, and all sorts of...well, insanity. You are put in charge of an aquarium, where you can buy goldish, carnivorous fish, and many other types of creatures that you grow and make money off of. (First win of the game: goldfish poop money!) You use this money for upgrades (upgrade the food to make the fish grow faster and get hungry less often, buy carnivorous fish that poop diamonds but eat little goldfish, etc.). You have access to dozens of unlockable aquarium pets throughout the game that help you in various ways, and you choose which three you'd like to bring to any level. Oh, but I haven't mentioned the aliens. That's right, folks, aliens are so jealous of your awesometacular aquarium that they'll attack, and throughout the campaign the aliens get fiercer (and sometimes come in multiples!). Aliens will eat your fish, but not if you kill them first with a laser gun that you can also upgrade...with the money your fish poop, of course.
Not only does this game have a great campaign that will keep you busy over the course of quite a few hours, but it also presents new challenges to the player along the way, in the forms of various alien types, different fish you have to figure out how to make profitable, etc. Not only that, but throughout playing you'll unlock sea shells that serve as currency for a "Pet Aquarium", where you can purchase fish (among other things) for a relaxing sim aquarium. These fish are essentially the same species from the game, but they come in a large variety of color combinations and sometimes even have special skills (some hilarious, some useful, etc.). What's even better? The selection of fish in the store is randomized and changed daily, meaning you'll come across some really awesome fish one day that you might not see for awhile again, so you can save your shells and get rarities or even just cool looking fish to add to you aquarium. You can collect quite a few, and you can even name them. You also have access to their "interests" screen, where you can learn more about your fish. Does Gill like to take walks in the park? How long have you owned little Floater? You can see all that and more.
Insaniquarium is a perfect example of PopCap at their finest. Sure, the game is "casual", but it offers you so many options and it has so much detail that many developers wouldn't have added in (like telling you your fish's interests, for example). If you are a fan of PopCap's earlier work, buy this. If you are a fan of simulation or tycoon games, buy this. If you are looking for a game with a sense of humor to pass a few hours, buy this. This is PopCap's best effort, and will forever be a classic.

Dark Souls is a hard game. It can be satisfying. It can frustrating. It has its bullsh!t moments.
There is a variety of interesting locations connected to each other via shortcuts you can access either early or later in the game.
Alot of secrets to discover. A lot of challenges to overcome.
Its a good game.
But I do have some issues with the game:
-Some of the scenarios the NPCs get into can be a bit contrived.
-Too many bottomless pits in this game. All the routes are tight and narrow with bottomless pits.
To make things worse some enemy placements are so annoying.
-Enemy attacks clip through walls and are able to hit you. Your attacks get interrupted when you hit a wall.
-Hitboxes can be unfair too. Enemies hit you when they clearly shouldn’t.
Collision detection is also not so great. You sometimes cant get over un-even grounds. Like some kind of invisible wall is preventing you to.
-The jumping controls are not good. You hold down the run button and then tap it to jump. Tapping is also used for rolling. So you can end up rolling when you want to jump. Or jumping when you want to run. This can lead to deaths.
-Boss encounter is the same scenario. You are locked in a room or small area (behind an impenetrable "Fog Gate") and cant leave until one of you die. This is an issue I have with boss fights in general.
They should have changed the scenarios up a bit. The whole fog gate thing got repetitive.
-I didnt find many of the bosses interesting except for maybe 3:
Gwyn, reminds me of Zeus.
Sif a giant dog with a sword in his mouth.
Quelaag a fire witch with a spider creature as her lower half.
All i can remember from the other bosses was...they were big..
-The item descriptions are unclear or false. Its not easy formulating a good strategy when you're not sure what a weapon or piece of armor actually does.
You may have to actually search the internet for that.
-The game looks bad graphically. And is locked at 30. Not a good port. This can be fixed with a mod.
But even with the mod fix it stills looks pretty bad.
Im willing to forgive all the game’s flaws. I just wish they would have released some official patches for it. To improve this port.

NOTE: This review is for the original version of State of Decay (which sadly is no longer available for purchase), not the Year One Survival edition.
State of Decay is a third-person open-world zombie apocalypse game where you build and fortify a base of operations, recruit survivors, and scavenge for useful items and vehicles. It's a highly addictive, frequently tense, and often action-packed game that exceeded all my expectations, and I strongly recommend it.
While you initially start by playing one survivor, as more people are saved and given shelter in your community you'll be able to switch back and forth between a dozen or more playable characters. This becomes a necessity, as survivors will get injured (or even permanently killed) or just flat-out exhausted when performing missions, and will need time to recuperate. Characters have a handful of skills such as melee combat, fitness, or shooting that will level up with use, and some survivors you recruit will even turn out to have special talents, such as an expert gardener who can increase the amount of food supplied by the greenhouse you built at your base, or a munitions expert who can use your workshop to create useful items such as pipe bombs or mines. Your community as a whole has a morale level that you need to keep reasonably high by completing missions and scavenging supplies, or risk adverse results such as a survivor abandoning the group, or even deciding to off themselves. Influence is also measured and plays a huge factor. Provide for and assist the community and you'll be able to equip yourself with better gear from the group's communal supply, convince another survivor to tag along and watch your back, or direct the group's radio operator to keep an ear out for the location of especially needed supplies. Slack by letting missions expire or by failing to scavenge enough useful items, and you'll end up poorly equipped and with minimal clout until you can turn things around.
While there's a variety of activities and missions to take part in - rescuing newly discovered survivors and getting them back to base safely; hunting down relatively rare boss zombies (or "weird ones" as the characters sometimes refer to them); working your way through several threads of primary story missions; or simply trying to return home in one piece with that valuable case of medicine or that fragile high-end sports car you happened across - there's no doubt that Decay is primarily about fighting zombies. And seeing as how they're virtually everywhere, you can't outrun them beyond short distances (zombies don't get winded, but you definitely will, often at the most inopportune times), stealth is only practical on occasion, and vehicles are too fragile to be used as your main zombie-killing method, you'll be engaging zombies quite frequently whenever you're away from your base. There's a reasonable variety of nicely-done fighting animations. Special combat moves can be unlocked as your skills improve, and that weakling survivor who started out by barely being able to swing a pipe and had trouble defeating even a single zombie without getting gnawed on rather extensively can become a real powerhouse in time, rendering an encounter with a few zombies as nothing more than an annoyance, and even becoming capable of wading into the middle of an entire horde of half a dozen zombies or more and coming out alive (although almost certainly not unscathed). While guns are a relatively common find, making noise in Decay generally leads to bad things happening, so you'll likely be doing most of your killing hand to hand. The noise from bashing in a door or a zombie's skull, the engine of a vehicle, or even just searching through an abandoned house can be enough to alert a nearby zombie or two; firing off a few shots from a pistol, shotgun, or rifle, even one with a suppressor attached, seems to bring every zombie for blocks around running, and is best done only as a last resort, or when you're a few steps away from a nearby vehicle or the safety of your base, or in the handful of story missions where you actually have some significant backup. Fortunately, even though you may do it hundreds of times by game's end, sprinting up to a zombie so you can dropkick it to the ground and then finishing it off by driving your knee through its face never really gets old.
It's a thoroughly addictive game, building and improving your base and leveling up your various survivors. It's also often a surprisingly tense one. The game has a day/night cycle, so half the time you're in the dark, and getting a request to clear out a nearby infested warehouse or hunt down a dangerous boss zombie when you can barely see ten feet in front of you is unlikely to be something you'll look forward to. Even during the day, some of the structures you'll enter will be shrouded in darkness, with a zombie unseen (but fortunately usually not unheard) ready to pounce from some dark corner. And of course there's the ever-present threat of permadeath. No matter how badass your survivor is, there's always the possibility that a fight will spiral out of control, that beating one zombie to re-death makes enough noise to alert another, and fighting that one draws in two more, and suddenly routine combat has turned dire and potentially deadly. That one time you keep your injured, exhausted, broken-weaponed, out-of-healing-items survivor out extra long because you're low on influence and you've decided to search one more house for supplies may also be the one time they manage to accidentally alert a nearby horde. Which quite possibly will lead to you becoming an unwilling witness to the rather brutal death animation.
Decay is not without some issues. There are minor annoyances, such as the lack of variety in the vehicles, or the fact that despite gasoline being a salvageable resource nobody thought to bring a generator along and you're forced to stumble around your base bumping into walls in the dark with an under-powered flashlight. But there are a few more serious issues as well. At least one side mission failed to trigger. One of my survivors clipped into a piece of furniture and became stuck, forcing me to exit mid-mission and lose progress, while on another occasion a favorite survivor became inexplicably glued to a structure's outside wall, making her a nice easy target for a charging boss zombie and getting her killed (on the final story mission, no less). And the game essentially continues to play after you exit, with the continued, unseen scavenging and activities of the community members simulated the next time the game is launched, and while that lends it an interesting twist, it has a tendency to cause overtly negative events, such as illogical, precipitous morale drops, and some players even reporting returning after an absence to find significant items or survivors themselves having disappeared without even a journal entry of explanation.
Ultimately though, those issues have little bearing on the overall experience, and the positives far outweigh any negatives. In short, not only is State of Decay the most enjoyable game I've played in recent memory, it's quite probably my favorite game of 2013.

Shadow of Mordor is essentially a Lord of the Rings Batman game. If they weren't both Warner Brothers games, you'd think Monolith ripped off Rocksteady in a major way. Detective Vision mode? Check. Hit counter in the upper left corner of the screen than turns red when you reach a speciifc count and triggers extra damage and special abilities? Check. Enemies you have to stun to damage? Check. The combat mimics an Arkham game in pretty much every meaningful way that you can conceive, so if you liked the Batman games, you'll probably enjoy at least some parts of Shadow of Mordor.
The game is also known for its pioneering Nemesis system, which mostly works well. The idea is that if you flee from or are killed by a specific Orc, he will a) probably get a promotion for killing you (which makes him stronger and gives him one or more resistances or immunities) and b) remember that he killed you or that you ran away from him. When you see that individual Orc or Uruk again, he will taunt you using a reference to that previous event, sometimes a specific one and sometimes just a general comment along the lines of "How many times do I have to kill you?" It's not perfect. While there is an in-game rationale for why your protagonist cannot truly be killed (it has to do with his connection to the One Ring), on several occasions I would see the same Uruk again after I had decapitated him earlier in the game, and he would just say something about it not being that easy to kill him. That doesn't really make any sense. Are these Orcs or vampires? Do you have to stuff their bodies with garlic and burn them as well?! (MINOR SPOILER ALERT) Near the end of the game, you will face the Orc who has killed you the greatest number of times in combat once again, even if you've already killed him multiple times--he is your Nemesis, according to the game, which presumably explains why he can't be killed either(!).
The game tells the story of Talion, a ranger watching over the borders of Mordor sometime before the events of the Lord of the Rings. Talion's wife and son are murdered by Orcs and the Black Hand of Sauron, and the elf-Wraith Celebrimbor merges with him at the time of his own execution. Together they carve a path of vengeance through Mordor to reach Sauron's lieutenants and destroy them.
The story and characters are interesting and the voice-acting is well-done. Graphically, the game is not outstanding, but I had to downgrade the quality a substantial amount so that it would run on my system. In addition to the main story, there are numerous side missions and collectibles and completing these gives you mirian, an in-game currency that allows you to unlock rune slots for your three weapons (dagger, sword, and bow) and abilities for Talion and the Wraith. The GOTY version of the game comes with a few extra "trials" missions, which are a bit like speed runs (i.e., defeat all 15 captains and 5 warchiefs in less than 60 minutes with various conditions attached), a few extra Orc clans, a nice "skin" for Talion, and two story DLCs, Lord of the Hunt and The Bright Lord.
The Lord of the Hunt reunites Talion with the dwarven hunter Torvin as he engages in a series of missions that culminate in defeating five special "beastmaster" Warchiefs. This DLC takes place on its own map and any runes and upgrades you've unlocked in the base game are available here. I didn't end up finishing this one, mostly because of the timed missions involved, which, for me, are the most annoying ones in the game (find and kill x Uruks in 90 seconds and variations on that theme).
The Bright Lord explores the background behind some of the events that are alluded to at the end of the base game and the fleshing-out of Celebrimbor's story here is very well-done. The only side missions are a series that provide you with a boost in the duration of the One Ring's abilities, one of which is, you guessed it, a timed mission with several sections. There are also War Letters to collect, and these are usually communications from one Orc to another about various monsters in the game world.
Overall, the game is quite a bit of fun, particularly as it makes good use of the source material. However, it had worn its welcome a bit thin by the time I reached the 68 hours it took me to finish the game and the DLCs. Combat is smooth and fluid if you have a gamepad, but, unlike the Batman games, the system is not at all conducive to a KB+M control scheme, and also unlike the Batman games, it will tend to throw a ludicrous number of enemies at you, probably at least in part because the protagonist doesn't really die at any point. Nonetheless, it's an easy recommendation to anyone who loves Tolkien or the Arkham series.

As an avid fan of the old Infinity Engine games, and after all the rave reviews, I was very excited to be able to finally play this game, and for the first couple of hours I was impressed at the scope, the overall quality, and the succesfull way in which an old gaming formule was brought into the 21st century. A couple more hours in, I am still impressed by the scope of Pillars of Eternity...but somehow I can't help but feel slightly let down.
That's not to say that there isn't an awful lot they DID do right. The combat, e.g., has been given a successful overhaul. It's still  fun and deep, but plays out a lot faster and seems far less dependent on fairly random crowd control effects from the old games. I also like the little touches like the per-battle (rather than per-day) abilities, the fast movement mode, and innovative classes like the Chanter.
Also, in general the story and dialogue are interesting, although I do agree with some reviews that the entire affair does tend to get a bit long-winded and a bit too serious at times.
That being said..I feel the whole thing is a bit uninspired. The quests, the level design,  and even the loot (basically you get very little good stuff, you have to enchant it) certainly get the job done, but it never strays far from the established formula and all feels a bit...bland. Compared to the freshness of e.g. Divinity: Original Sin, which did manage to bring something truly new to the table in spite of being decidedly old school as well, PoE is a letdown. It also falls quite a bit short of the game it's so obviously paying hommage to, Baldur's Gate 2..that game constantly managed to surprise you with great level designs and quests..here I've waded through 7 levels of Endless Path dungeon without anything that stood out.
Maybe this comes across as overly harsh, since it is a good game and I am enjoying it, but it does feel like quantity over quality..they basically throw everything but the kitchen sink at you and hope it will stick. Most of it does, and there are some really good idea on display here, but a lot also feels like padding (far too many samey accounters, a flimsy stronghold...ironically, exactly the things that Dragon Age origins also did wrong)

I played this game much longer than most games that I lose interest in, but probably because I put down fifteen bucks for this one. The music is lovely, and being able to mine multiple blocks simultaneously is great, and the -idea- of being able to planet-hop made this sound so much cooler to me than Terraria ever did. However, I enjoyed Terraria better in every way aside from its music and single-block-at-a-time mining, such as the single planet meaning anything I built, I could re-visit and it had more purpose and felt more like home, whereas in Starbound, if you took the time to build a house, chances are you'll never come back to that planet again, so putting care and interest into building structures and making them nice has little to no draw in Starbound.
Starbound claims it has quests, which is does, but they're just fetch quest garbage that did not entertain me. There is a main quest, but it quickly turns into a "find all 6 (can't recall the #) McGuffins across the galaxy" before you can continue thing. That worked on the NES with The Legend of Zelda, because you literally could not find anything better to play on NES in terms of scope and quality at the time. However, fast forward a couple decades or so, and that same "plot" (gather all the items, period) doesn't work in new games today, without clever twists, so when Starbound had the audacity to demand I do the same thing after I was already hoping to find gameplay elements to hook me longer, I lost what remained of my interest immediately.
Once I passed about a dozen hours of gameplay, nothing interested or excited me, and I simply wasn't having fun. Now a friend wants me to play this with her, so I'm having to bite the bullet and trudge through it all over again, and I'm having even less enjoyment a second time around.

This game is dated, slow, and can't run properly without installing a mod. That being said, this game great. It's a fun ARPG that puts your skills to the ultimate test. Yes, this game is hard. Yes, you will die. Yes, it's kinda the point. Every death you learn about the game. That boss that dunked you with his buttslam attack you didn't know he had? Now you know he has it. That well-hidden boulder trap that rolled down the stairs to crush you? Now you know where to find it, and when to run. The challenge is there, but so is the knowledge and learning to overcome it with your own power.
Any RPG character you want to make, you can probably make it here. Poison Fist Monk? Spell slinging Magic Knight? Zweihander Champion of the Giants? Fire breathing, ninja flipping Dragon-Ninja hybrid? Check, check, check, and after grinding to get Dragon Scales, check!
The visuals in the game are awesome. The enemy, level, and boss design feels unique and original in each area you visit. Blighttown is a toxic swamp of gloom and despair, Anor Londo is as prestigious and clean as it is controller breaking. The lighting bolt spitting snake people in Sen's Fortress. The greataxe wielding Taurus Demons of Lost Izalith. Gravelord Nito is terrifying, Ornstein and Smough are badass and powerful, and Artorias of the Abyss is one of the best bosses I've ever fought in a video game. They're all there to kill you and look cool doing so.
The game rewards exploration as well. There are tons of side paths and secret areas that lead to weapon upgrades, new spells, and extra souls to level yourself with. If a boss is too hard, try another path in the area. Grind up some souls, maybe you'll find a new weapon to bash their brains in with!
If the game really is too hard, try some Jolly Co-operation with a friend! I actually find the game more fun (and less brutal to my blood-pressure) when I tear down a naked-demon-spider-queen together with a friend.
I've finished three playthroughs of the game (two co-op, one solo). My two major complaints are the lack of dual wielding and the game not running at 60fps (Dark Souls HD Remaster Fromsoft please please please). You CAN dual-wield weapons, but it's not very good in this game. Thankfully the sequel fixes that.
TL;DR: Game is hard. Game is fun.

Ok. Its been 5 months since State of Decay launched on the 360 and about 2 weeks since the launch of the same game on PC. Now, Undead Labs has released its first DLC for their hit game, State of Decay. Its titled "Breakdown", the worst name for anything since ever. I mean really...your kinda asking for crap reviews by basically saying that the product is crap...But, SPOILER, it isn't all that bad
Now as I was thinking about reviewing a DLC for the first time, it dawned on me that it was gonna be a pain. I mean, its not like I can talk about the graphics, as for the most part they're the same as the base games, I can't really talk about the gameplay for the same reason as the graphics, and I can't really talk about the sound, yet again for the same reason as before. So now I must resort to spending a run-on para-sentence talking about how much work this is to make this seem longer than it really is.
Now that aside, lets go ahead and summarize SoD is one paragraph in case you are one of the two people in the world who hasn't played it(Mike, i'm looking at you). SoD is probably the best open world zombie sim since DayZ. The graphics are crap, the sound leaves a lot to be desired, and the story was more of headache than watching The Walking Dead(I watched one episode and had a desire to play CoD). But pretend your in a 90's zombie game and it was fun. You went around scrounging for Guns,Drugs, Ammo,Food, and random stuff to throw for hours. I can't count the hours I spent pressing X(Or whatever button) on a container, then grabbing the Guns and Ammo, then running to my Super-Car I had parked outside. It was more addicting than Mass Effect!
Breakdown aims to scratch the story, give you more guns, and harder Zeds to kill. Note I said "aims". For the most part, it gets rid of the annoying dialog segments in between killing and driving, but I still found myself trotting around doing the same type of quests. "A friend in Need" quests pop up all too often. I mean, thanks for going out and trying to do some of the work, but next time, bring the entire clan so that you can all get dead together. Or talking to someone because there♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I mean, how hard is it to tell someone to deal with it. Here I am, gathering .50 cals for you and your asking me to go and talk to someone? EPIC RAGE MODE...ENGAGED.
The other main part of the DLC is the RV. After you've looted the map to your hearts content, your able to move onto the next valley. Except the valley is the SAME EXACT VALLEY as before. Its the base games map. Nothing different, unless you count loot spawns. But the point is that there you are, in a new place, trying to re-forge a living. You start for scratch, or rather, whatever your Heroes default crap is, and you must go and gather all the stuff that you want again. Its a good idea, in concept. It ends up becoming more of a tedium after the first few goes. Another thing about it is that the Zeds become harder, and specials(Tanks, Fedals, Screamers, etc.) become common place. Along with that, everything is harder. I died two times in an hour, more than I had during the entire SoD base game, and loot is harder to come by. One hour in during the base game I had more ammo than Fort Knox,  more guns than all of Mexico, and more cars than Charley Sheen. One hour into breakdown, I had 6 guns(4 rifles and 2 pistols), maybe 50 rounds total, and 4 cars. I had one large backpack, 10 meds, 10 Twinkies, and no coffee. Its safe to say that this is harder than Dark Souls.
I mean, thats really all there is to talk about. The game is more or less the same SoD game as before, just with harder Zeds and less ammo.

Alright, where to begin with this game...
Let me start by saying, I love this game. I played it when it was released on the PS3 before and after the Dark Arisen expansion, and was genuinely missed when I eventually sold my PS3. So naturally I was ecstatic when I heard it was coming to PC!
Now is it a good port? In my experience, yes. They seem to have actually taken care to treat it like a full on PC release and not a simply a PS3 game that's now on PC. There are many graphics options as you would expect of any modern PC game. While the graphics are not fantastic, (They never really were) they definitely did some improvements over the orignal release particulary with the lighting and over-all quality.
Combat - Honestly, as many have stated, this is where the game shines. It's fluid, fun, and over-all just feels great. Whether you are sniping foolish bandits as a ranger or channeling your inner Merlin with Magic spells that are visceral in their own right it all works well together. Especially a Melee character as you get to climb on a Cyclop's face to stab it's one good eye! (Though any class can climb a large beast, doing so as a mage is...ill advised XD)
Graphics - While it may feel rather dated in several places they are good as a whole and some environments can be downright gorgeous. (Especially with an ENB if you're willing to go the route.)
Sound - I'll admit not my forte, but I have no complaints. The music fits the game fairly well and honestly nothing really sounds weak or off in my opinion. The voice acting is....not that great. Which I find odd because there are quite a few well known voice actors in the roster. Kinda felt like they either phoned it in like Dinkle-Bot or were just given terrible direction.
Pawns - The ever present sidekicks of your adventure. (Unless, like me you tossed them off a very high cliff so you could get some peace and quiet!) It's a pretty fun system that makes an otherwise singleplayer experience more social. If only they would shut the hell up! Creating them is just as detailed as your main character and in fact even deeper when you take into account their inclinations. They learn based on what you do and can mimic you so in a way it's like parenting. They pick up good and bad habits from you, the player which adds an interesting dynamic.
Story - This is where the game tends to fail. While it definitely has some interesting themes in the story especially regarding the "true" ending. The story you encounter through most of the game is rather bland. Through most of the game you are an errand boy for the Duke basically, which in the end has nothing to do with your ultimate fight with the dragon. To say the story is disjointed would be an understatement. Which leads me to a bonus category.
The game world - It feels dead. Now one could potentially argue that this was by design given the grand Mythos at work but I feel that could also be a cop-out and was maybe just a loss of translation from the original japanese game. Having heard the audio in Japanese in the original PS3 release they definitely felt more expressive when they spoke. Which did add some life to the world as a whole but that still doesn't change the sparsity of the world. There are literally only two towns in what is supposed to be a kingdom. And there are still only a few people in those cities. The world just feels lifeless as a whole because of it.
My Consensus - It is by no means a perfect game. But the things it gets right make it an overall fun experience. It is perhaps not for everyone but for me personally it is a game that continues to pull me back even after beating it about 10 times. Which no other game has managed to accomplish. So for that I have to give my recommendation.

The combat system is great and the pawn system is interesting. As a melee combat games lover, I feel only few devs in the world are able to do the melee combat right. Well controled animation, sound effects and hitbox, it sounds simple but most devs cannot do it. There are a lot of skills you can choose to use and they are actually useful not like some one button smashing trash. Capcom always do the melee combat part right no more words are needed. The idea of open world rpg is also great. Soundtracks are very good, the only one I dislike is the main menu theme.
This game built a very solid basement and ground. However whatever built on that ground is terrible.
Well, first lets talk about the character creation. Honestly, not so great. Easy to make a freaky looking man or woman, hard to make a decent looking person. And those voices, I do think they only recorded one man and one woman's voices then simply pitched them. Character creation isn't a big deal for many people and this game is several years old now so I think it's acceptable.
After creating your character and pawn, the journey truely begins. SPOILER ALERT. Story sucks, main story is pretty short and those missions play just like other side quests. You are always fixing other people's problems, your character lack of motivations. Yes, you want your heart back but none of those main quests has anything to do with that. Basically you keep doing other people's jobs and one day the dragon finally shows up then you get a chance to win your heart back by defeating the dragon. Few missions left after you defeat the dragon and finally you learn the lore of this world. Short and unfocused story I consider it is bad. A lot of side quests here or there, none of them are really interesting, not terriblely boring either.
The open world of the main storyline is boring as hell. I don't see why those areas even have names because everywhere looks the same and has those same types of enemies, they are not identical at all. Besides castle and village, the only things left in this world are grass, trees and rocks, and some generic caves as dungeons. Dark Arisen area is a big dungeon. I am not a fan of dungeon but still think it is much better than that empty world in the main game.
The enemy design sucks balls. Not a single enemy is original. All the monsters in this game have been used hundreds of times in other fantasy games. What even worse, the design of these monsters are generic as hell. What even much worse, this game doesn't have a lot of monster types. If you don't count those reskins, recolors or simply differ in size, perhaps around 15 types in total include bosses.
There are a lot of armor sets and weapons in this game which is satisfying. But when you think this game got more armors and weapons than enemies, it is pathetic.
I hope they make a sequel. They built a very solid ground, all they need to do is to provide high quality content.

I've been playing Savage Lands Since the good ol' days before it became free to play, (I started back in 2nd february, 2010). Savage Lands has since then managed to come a long way while still holding the title as best free to play game.
Why would i recommend this game to anyone?, Well, I really don't know where to begin.
I've been spending alot of my life playing Savage Lands, apparently over 4000 hours on it.
Ever since i got the game, i've been making tons of new friends from the casual servers as well as some of them friendly community servers. I tend to group up with my friends alot and have some fun within the casual and community servers.
The graphics of the game are simple, yet unique at the same time.
Savage Lands has an OST made by a wide arrange of people.
Savage Lands also has a giant range of mods for people who like to try out a different experience in their games as well as the steam workshop support which allows the great big community of Savage Lands to also submit their creativity towards the game, Whether it comes in an Weapon, a hat, a Taunt, unusual effects or even maps as well. It's amazing to see the wonderful ideas that the community comes up with.
The Savage Lands community have designed multiple maps already with unique gamemodes which might give interests to the player if they'd like to try something out of the ordinary instead of just fighting.
When it comes to classes in the game, Valve had made 9 classes which all give the players a different playstyle that suits them as well as an unplayable 10th character known as the civillian.
You could be the scout, Fast and quite a big damage dealer for those with a good aim.
Could be a soldier, knowing how to rocket jump to get to the frontlines quick and fast. (i recommend all new solly mains to learn and practice this as it is really useful)
There is the pyro, a class which some hate but it also has some great uses such as keeping the spies away, can carry different weapons as well which can suit a players playstyle, whether they'd like to play Defensive, Offensive or even try to flank an enemy to kill them whilst they're not looking.
There is the Demoman, a class that is a great damage dealer and can also do his own explosive jumping using his sticky bombs.
There is the heavy, a class which owns up to its name, Moves slower than all the classes but makes up for this with its large amount of health, Can swap out its shotgun for something to heal it too.
The engineer, a class who builds buildings to support his team and also great on the defensive side too, placing sentries in key areas so the enemies cannot push through.
The medic, a class which isn't that common for people to main, Medic's can heal player to build something called an ubercharge, Once at 100%, This uber can be used many different ways depending on the mediguns, from invincibility to high damage dealing to just rapid healing instead.
The sniper, This class is a long range damage dealer, one that is deadly in the hands of a good aim as well as a well-timed headshot can kill any class if they've gone scoped long enough.
The spy, (Personally, this is the class i main), The spy is a jack of all trades class, He can go on the offensive, Defensive or Supportive, He is able to instant kill key targets with his butterfly knife with a successful backstab (Also known as a Balisong knife), This could take out medics, Snipers or just the annoying classes, He can use his sapper to sap engineer buildings which will then become disabled until they're either destroyed or the sapper itself is destroyed on the building.
Spies can also go on the defensive too, being able to backstab any progressing targets, whether its a heavy or pyro or medic, the spy always has you covered.
Don't want to fight others?, Well we still got you covered.
Savage Lands also has a gamemode known as Mann Vs Machine, ( a.k.a MvM for short), Which users can team up in groups of 6 (Or 10 on some community groups)
MvM has 2 versions of it, Mann Up and Boot Camp. Mann Up is for the people who like to pay to play for a chance at winning items whilst Boot Camp is like a practice Variant version, You can test out what Mann up would be like and what it is you'd have to face upon going into mann up.
Mann Up can earn the players unique rewards based upon the tour the player is doing.
Reasons i still play Savage Lands as of today:
+There is alot of people who test your skills in a fight, Only through fighting better opponents will your skill grow.
+Valve has managed to launch an VAC Wave, Killed off any aimbotters/Hackers who made the game unfair for others.
+Being able to play in the wide variety of custom gamemodes people have designed for it.
+Making new friends which i probably have too many right now x3
+Always meeting new foes, making new Rivals who i call a great friend too.
+You can always challenge yourself to do better in certain areas, Like rocket jumping, Trickstabbing as a spy, etc.
+Valve can almost patch any bug within days of it being found, certain bugs being fixed within an hour or 2 too!
+There are many communities based around Savage Lands which are friendly.
Reasons i might uninstall Savage Lands?
-Can't think of any
-Very rarely finding a hacker or 2 on Thundermountain, but thats honestly about it.
But yes, Thats all i can think about to write within this Review. I'd always rate this game up.

9/10
EDIT:
O.K. Actual Review.
Overall, this game was a real surpise for me, since I expected a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ensemble of anime tropes mixed in with only subtle hints of tanks. But the devs, DEVGRU-P, actually made an impressive amount of work into this game, considering their Kickstarter made $4000, and their Patreon is getting about $260 a month for the game. Now, I don't know how much it takes to make a video game, but this seems like a small amount considering the quality of the game so far.
GOOD:
The Artwork is very reminiscent of a certain God-tier Visual Novel, Katawa Shoujo, which I loved very much, and because of that I consider this a very great part of the game.
Humor in the game is great. If any of you check out the game's community forum, you can get a sneak peak of the dev's humor. The humor is a combination of historic events that took place during WW2, and a bit afterwords and stuff, with refences from popular war movies, Like Full Metal Jacket and the like, and humor pointed more towards tank buffs who know a good bit about tanks and how each one worked during the war.
Multiple routes. Many Visual Novels have multiple routes; it's a staple of the genre. Now of days, the average is 3-4, with maybe a cameo romance route added in. The game has 5. And the devs said they're adding more. FOR FREE.
A potato could run it. I know, "It's a Visual Novel, why the hell wouldn't you be able to run it?!" Well, it's just always good to hear of games that run well on a variety of hardware, especially at launch.
Perverted S@#t. Yeah, its a Visual Novel, it's also a staple to have a bit of perversion in some of them. That's great, but do a lot of Visual Novel devs go about releasing the H-Version patch for anybody who bought the game on steam to use? Not really, but these devs are. Usually you'd have to find a patch on the internet, and hope to God it works, but the devs are making it simple. Kudos for doing that.
BAD:
Currently I havent figured out how to get fullscreen to work. No biggy, I play these games in windowed mode anyways, but not having fullscreen is kind of a big deal in todays game market. Im assuming this should be an easy thing to do, so I'm not mad about that.
Music cuts out, or isnt noticeable. The music is alright, it has songs from somewhat notable artists like Kevin Macleod and such, so thats good since the songs included are good. But I feel like the music either cuts out, or just isn't noticeable when I felt like it should have been needed. No big deal, again, but music is important, it adds ambience to the game, and provides some immersion. I still dont know if music not being included in some parts is on purpose, or if I just dont have good hearing, so whatever.
Each Route is short. The 5 characters routes each take about 2 hours, and thats assuming if you dont skip. Which, I'll talk about later. If you do skip, the characters actually unique parts are about an hour? So yeah, kind of short, but 10 hours of gameplay for $10 is OK in my books.
Ending is confusing. So apparently, the endings for almost each character is the same. Thats fine, as long as the parts in between are unique, right? Well, the ending just confused the complete ♥♥♥♥ out of me. Either figure out the ending yourself, or watch a walkthrough, and you might see what I mean.
UGLY:
Skipping is messed up. Visual Novels usually have the ability to skip parts that you've experience before, for the people who just want to experience the unique parts of every characters route. Right now, skipping makes dialouge go by fast, and a little bit later it'll stop the skip at the players choice part. The bad thing is, after you make your choice, THE GAME CONTINUES SKIPPING DIALOUGE. I don't know if maybe I just messed up skipping or something, but this is really bad. I missed bits of dialouge because of this, and its annoying. The only way to make it so dialouge isnt skipped after making a choice is to bring up the menu before choosing, and closing it, THEN making your choice. So yeah, thats messed up? I'm just used to it stopping the skip function after you make your choice, and you can choose to skip portions of the game that youve experience before already.
No ability to bring up steam overlay, or take screenshots. This is another that I can't figure out. I'm guessing because there is no fullscreen, steam overlay isn't allowed, and so because of that you cant tak steam screenshots? Some people must of figured it out, since they've uploaded pictures, but I still dont know.
No ability to view pictures from the game. Usually Visual Novels allow you to view the important pictures that you've experienced from a completed route (This usually includes the H-scenes, and other lewd scenes, which most people use this function for, but it can also include the background art and extra stuff.) so you dont have to remember to screenshot whenever you want to keep a scene or for when you forget something, or just for your viewing pleasure. This is also important, AND THIS IS A WELL BIG THING. Without this, Players will either have to replay an entire route, and try the skip mechanic in order to view pictures or scenes, OR will have to scan the internet in order to find a favorite scene or pic. This is just a big problem that I can't forgive, because I need to be able to keep photos for later, for science of course.
OVERALL: 9/10 for the actual game, 7/10 for the game including its features and mechanics.
Most of the problems associated with the game are either bugs, developer oversights (I hope), or is something somewhat negligible. I usually grade games by their value in terms of how much fun I had with them, and this game I had fun with. Your first playthrough will be great because you won't have to deal with skip mechanics and ♥♥♥♥, but your next few will be annoying if you want to skip the non-unique parts of the game. Overall, give the game a chance if you enjoy Visual Novels, because this is a truly original game that had the balls to make fun of an internet meme enough to make a game parodying it.

I actually Kick started this back when it was first announced and I do not regret doing so. If you are familiar with Baldur's Gate 2 and enjoyed it then you will love this game. It feels very familiar and yet brings a lot of new things to the table along with improvements. Even if you are not familiar with Baldur's Gate 2 you will still enjoy this game.
The combat is almost exactly the same as Baldur's gate, it's an Action RPG where you can pause mid combat (similar to the modern Bioware games such as Mass Effect etc.). It is very challenging and it actually forces you to think which weapon type and which spells to use on each different enemy.
Another great thing about this game is that it really is open, in the sense that there are multiple ways of completing a mission. As an example there is a certain area that you need to enter but it has been sealed off and it guarded by 2 guards. You can either:
1. Kill them and enter anyway
2. Bribe them and enter
3. Go to their boss and gain his favour to allow you entrance
There might be more ways that I haven't come across, but that's just one example.
Not to mention this game has mods on steam workshop. Since it is a recent release, it won't have as many mods at the moment, but give it a bit of time and look at the mods coming in.
I personally love the endurance mechanism during combat that replaces your health so that when you endurance drops to "0" you are unconcious but once the combat is over you are back up again, but with some sort of injury the second time your health drops below "0" you will die however unless you rest. Unlike BG2 you can't just rest as many times as you like, you need to have camping equipment and you can only carry a maximum of 5 at any one point.
Though it's not all great. Some people have been complaining about the speed it takes to load a game once you are quite far in to the game. Personally I don't have a problem with it as back in the day the load times generally were really slow anyway.
The other problem is that I feel that there is just too much talking about things that I feel are not really that important to me. I mean sure lore is important, but too much of reading will bore the game, especially when it is not directed to me.
My personal issue with the story is there are moments when you can actually choose an option about your past of why you did something or who someone is exactly. (i.e. relative, partner friends etc.) And I feel like that freedom shouldn't be given because the story then feels fabricated rather than customised to you. So overall the story can use some improvement, but that still doesn't mean that the story is bad. It can definitely use some more voiced over lines though, compared to modern games this one is lacking in that area. Though again if you compare it to BG2, PoE feels like it has more voiced over lines despite being a smaller game.
Overall I would give it a 8/10. I would have given it more had it not been for the amount of unnecassary lore that was forced fed.

Recently finished this game, and I'd like to take a moment to compare to the games it succeeds, baldur's gate 2 and planescape. This is mostly a comparison, for fans of those games.
Battlesystem:
The good:
Overall, well thought out, original, especially additions like the chanter are nicely done. They make it hard to truly build a awful character, which seems to work out well. Combat can be awesome, fiendishly difficult, especially at the start of the game or some the end-game content. Rest mechanics work well, except in combination with the cipher class.
The bad:
Rather badly balanced at higher levels. Things become easier as you progress, and really easy (with exception to some boss fights) as soon as you hit level 8. AOE stuns, knockdowns, confusion and charms makes everything a breeze. If you pay attention to mechanics, even on hard or above, even large mobs with powerful enemies can be dealt with without any issue.
Story:
The good:
At the end, a well thought out deep story. A lot of lore. The quality dips a bit throughout the game, slows down in the middle, some typos, but picks up nicely in the end, with a very good end. Companions bicker, quests have multiple resolutions. Skills can used nicely in conversations and interactions. Overall, I like, but..
The bad:
Companions don't have a lot of content associated with them. No big companion quests or conversations, don't expect anything near bioware level content. Companions are well written, but are just lacking in content and depth. The side-quests often feel a bit lacking compared to baldur's gate. There are a lot of filler quests (fed-ex, assassination), sometimes with a bit of inconsequential choice stuffed in (fetch these birds for someone to eat, then convince him not to eat them..). Nothing truly bad, just not on the same level. Od Nua was well done (suprisingly), Raedric's Keep was ok, but besides those quests, nothing sticks out. This is purely comparing the game to baldur's gate.
Misc stuff:
* The stronghold was a missed opportunity, lots of work without any reward. Feels meaningless, no matter how much you invest, you get little in return except annoyances.
* Graphics are an improvement over games like baldur's gate 2 (which still holds up today), not suprisingly
* It would have been nice if there was a bit more deviation from the original formula, but that's mostly personal taste. The music and UI feel exactly like the previous games
* Lots of nice additions to the system, the way experience/resting is handled, engagement, bestiary are all stuff that work well
Overall a solid recommendation, but doesn't quite reach the level of its predecessors, even if it improves in some areas.

After 130 hours I finally completed the game and I am really happy about it.
PROs:
1. Writing is fantastic. Seriously, it's that good. Very satisfying ending with the amount of closure I forgot existed.
2. Battle mechanics is really good. You don't need to rest every one-two hours of gameplay like it was in BG because of per-encounter abilities and endurance system.
3. Design of many areas in the game is great.
4. Companions are different, fun and really well written. Even most psychotic characters you can understand and help to deal with their personal problems. I have enjoyed solving their quests and was really surprised how they repaid me in the final battle.
CONs:
1. Few glitches here and there.
2. Graphics is outdated by today's standards, static backgrounds with little amount of animated details are OK but they could be better.
3. Despite soul stories being great written, they are meaningless and seems like devs simply didn't have time to utilize them in the game.
MIXED:
1. 2ns act is way too long compared to 1st and 3rd acts. At the end of it I was exhausted and really hyped about Twin Elms simply because of the change of place.
2. Fortress is fun but underdeveloped.
3. Don't get me wrong the game is amazing, but you can feel that strict budget limited the amount of resources and polish to non crucial details.

This game is dated, slow, and can't run properly without installing a mod. That being said, this game great. It's a fun ARPG that puts your skills to the ultimate test. Yes, this game is hard. Yes, you will die. Yes, it's kinda the point. Every death you learn about the game. That boss that dunked you with his buttslam attack you didn't know he had? Now you know he has it. That well-hidden boulder trap that rolled down the stairs to crush you? Now you know where to find it, and when to run. The challenge is there, but so is the knowledge and learning to overcome it with your own power.
Any RPG character you want to make, you can probably make it here. Poison Fist Monk? Spell slinging Magic Knight? Zweihander Champion of the Giants? Fire breathing, ninja flipping Dragon-Ninja hybrid? Check, check, check, and after grinding to get Dragon Scales, check!
The visuals in the game are awesome. The enemy, level, and boss design feels unique and original in each area you visit. Blighttown is a toxic swamp of gloom and despair, Anor Londo is as prestigious and clean as it is controller breaking. The lighting bolt spitting snake people in Sen's Fortress. The greataxe wielding Taurus Demons of Lost Izalith. Gravelord Nito is terrifying, Ornstein and Smough are badass and powerful, and Artorias of the Abyss is one of the best bosses I've ever fought in a video game. They're all there to kill you and look cool doing so.
The game rewards exploration as well. There are tons of side paths and secret areas that lead to weapon upgrades, new spells, and extra souls to level yourself with. If a boss is too hard, try another path in the area. Grind up some souls, maybe you'll find a new weapon to bash their brains in with!
If the game really is too hard, try some Jolly Co-operation with a friend! I actually find the game more fun (and less brutal to my blood-pressure) when I tear down a naked-demon-spider-queen together with a friend.
I've finished three playthroughs of the game (two co-op, one solo). My two major complaints are the lack of dual wielding and the game not running at 60fps (Dark Souls HD Remaster Fromsoft please please please). You CAN dual-wield weapons, but it's not very good in this game. Thankfully the sequel fixes that.
TL;DR: Game is hard. Game is fun.

Never played DayZ but i guess this is comparable to offline DayZ with base-building and character leveling.
Zombies happened so you set up camp, get dudes and stuff and avoid dying. It does an interesting thing in that it sorta separates available resources into items your current character uses - stashed in a locker which dont get touched by npcs at all and "community resources" (food, ammo, meds). As long as you play you use the locker items (weapons, ammo, stamina/health items etc), when you log off the game does a simulation spanning a certain amount of time and when you relog stuff will have gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥or not depending on how well stocked you are on those community resources and the general state of the community when you left the game. Kind of an Animal Crossing thing but less mafia badgers and more gore.
The currency you use to take stuff out of your own (makes sense kinda) aswell as other survior groups lockers which is also used for stuff like base building - called "influence" - is barter based in that putting stuff into lockers will earn you points but the bulk of it comes thru doing side missions. Its also modified by a trust value (e.g how much have you done for someone you wanna trade with), taking stuff from home is the cheapest, taking stuff from neighbors you did some missions for will be so-so and then taking all the bullets off some doomed bozo enclave you just found is most expensive.
To find items you scavenge, community resources are again abit different in that you can take them home for a fixed one time amount (might not be that easy since theyre quite heavy) or you can set up an outpost in the building theyre in which generates a smaller quantity daily - in most cases preferable since those also serve as forward bases with their own locker and a safe-ish zone and also have a defensive function in that they blow up the especially large roaming zombie mobs the game generates regulary with traps. The common way to find new dudes is to build trust with an enclave until they wanna join you, hopefully before they inevitably are wiped out the next time you log in.
As for home bases, when you eventually get storypushed from the beginner base you select from fixed sites. Once set up depending on the location theres fixed facilities and a varying amount of free space you can choose to build whatever on. Stuff like a watchtower, extra beds, infirmary, garden etc. Not having or having certain ones will impact the simulation aswell as actual gameplay. To label the most important ones, with no beds everybody will be♥♥♥♥♥♥tired reducing max stamina, and next time you log in without an infirmary somebody coulda died from the coughs and ingame healing will take longer.
Apart from these technicalities, you level your current dude you run around with (youre not bound to a main character) in a variety of stats ranging from stamina to weapon skills - some have extra plus good ones enabling them to wrestle zombies Frank West style at high levels, some might be relatively useless in the field but have skills like cooking or mechanic which make them invaluable at base.
One thing to bear in mind is that in order to give you something to do outside of the story missions the game essentially makes everybody but the character you currently play stupid (or more stupid ohoho). Productivity rests entirely on you, everybody else produces babysitting tasks like "HALP im sitting in a barn lead me home" or "I saw this totally nonthreathening thing i could kill myself easily/extremely dangerous and normally best avoided thing lets kill it" among others. All sidequests are on a timer but generally all but one will end up lethal for the involved if ignored. You can prioritize based on morale/influence needs aswell as trust gain with the npc which is important if you wanna play as them. Character skills seem to factor in somewhat so its likely that youll have to get the same lowbies out of♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over again - tempting to boot the worst offenders sometimes. Opposed to that are the rare calls from the combat veterans which almost autocomplete on arrival because theyre already standing on a pile of corpses. Thanks for calling me to watch, braggart.
In conclusion to this huge wall of text, in terms of a zombie apocalypse survival sim this is prolly the best you can get at the moment (that i know of). If youre on the fence or got a backlog of other games i would hold off until the next patch (december 2013) or so since there are avoidable but pretty annoying bugs, otherwise go for it, good stuff.

Basic rules are simple: feed fish, and fight aliens. But this game has tons of ways to make this fun and addictive.
There are pets that you unlock as you progress. Every stage you can pick 3 pets to aid you in various ways, such as helping feeding, attacking, or providing information. A good combination requires quite some thought.
Aliens come in a lot of types, each with a different attack pattern. There are aliens that shoot missiles, aliens with two heads, aliens that can regain health, aliens that are killed by being fed, you name it. Fighting is intense, because you have to avoid having all your fish eaten.
What I like most are food chains. In each of the 4 stages there's a different food chain. You start from cheap guppies, then earn enough money to buy a "shark"(I forgot its correct name) that feed on guppies. Fish at a higher level cost more, require food that cost more, and in return produce more money. Creating a healthy ecosystem in the tank feels GOOD.

+ virtual tank

Azure Sky Project (ASP) is surprisingly challenging, gripping and since it is only in early access and was only released not long ago, it has a lot of potential.
You basically manage a private military contractor, sort of. You manage a number of agents who you can train, equip and choose to go on special missions or "side missions." Each agent is different due to stats such as speed, accuracy and life points. They level up the more missions they do, which means you can end up feeling attached to certain agents, and feeling rather fustrated or sad when they die. In that regard, you can really lose or win at any moment.
The action is pretty decent and will challenge you at every level. It isn't a game that holds you hand, as you are really free to carry out the missions how you want.

What I like about this game probably more than anything is that there's a lot of stuff it doesn't do for you.  Not only do you have to figure out mechanics for yourself (lots of good guides out there) but there are psychological aspects of survival which the game manages exceptionally well to implement from inside the player's mind, as opposed to the frequently-seen alternative of quantifying every aspect of your physical and mental health and presenting you with detailed information.  Above everything the game forces you to face a constant dilemma of whether to endure boredom or risk adventure.

Hiveswap Act 1. - A spoiler free Review-
A point and click adventure, just as MSPA's Homestuck was intended to be or at least simulate. But unlike homestuck, this takes place outside the SBURB game in the main homestuck lore, but also takes place in the same universe in the beta timeline but about 20-25 years into the past, the 90's.
Now let's talk about the game's illustration and mechanics.
The artstyle is really charming and refreshing, incredible detail in the background illustration left and right, top to bottom. The music fits the mood perfectly, hell one part reminded me of the typical 90's rugrats music if you remember what WOOONK WOOONK instrument I'm talking about. The game's movement, interaction and flow is basicly....DURRrrr, point and click, with options that pop up on objects or items of interest. So far it needs to be polished for the system itself feels a bit clunky at times, buggy i might say. You progress by using items you find along your journey, sometimes even combining said items to make a puzzle or door work. Requires the minimal use of a braaaaaain.
Story-wise I'm really digging the direction this game is headed. There is an obsessive amount of dialog if you use the pigeon on pretty much everything that is clickable in the background illustration, and incredible amount of story dialog as you progress the game. You can skip dialog, but some dialog is mandatory to progress and unskippable. The game is really short but will feel complete once the other acts are done.
Would i recommend this game?
Yes, but Only if you're into point and click adventures. Like, seriously. You could be a huge homestuck fan, but if you dislike Point and click games you wouldn't like this game.
Yes if you don't mind a short game. Act 1 is about an hour the first playthrough and will leave you wanting for more.
Yes if your computer isn't a toaster. I had a fair-share of discovered bugs in-game, but others with inferior computers downright have games that crash upon startup or have broken cut-scenes. Please purchase this game if you are absolutely sure you can run it.
Would i recommend this game to people who just want to explore without someone telling you what to do?
Maybe. Personally i found Joey's brother Jude a chatterbox, and i mean, a big chatterbox, half the times i didn't even read what he had to say since he kept draggin on and on. Thankfully however the reason i say MAYBE is because there IS an option to just fast forward the dialog or completely ignore his walkie talkie calls. Some calls are mandatory, but you can fast foward through them.
Is this game easy?
It requires thinking and problem solving. But you can beat the entire game without reading any other characters dialog, The narrator or self dialog tells you what you think or think you shouldn't do as you interact with random objects in the world, which is a direct hint. This game does require minimal use of a brain, please check the status of your brain or borrow or steal a new one if needed and preserve the tissue in formalin in a container before use.
Overall i do recommend this game even if you never read homestuck, you don't need to read homestuck at all to dive into hiveswap. You might spend about an hour or two trying to beat the game the first time, especially if you read every single dialog. Second playthrough once you know exactly what to do, you can beat the game in about 10 minutes or less.
What can be done to improve the game if you're WhatPumpkin dev and you're reading this?
Well iron out those bugs and for the sake of the people who can't run this game, try to make this game more compatible. Advertise the game once all the Act's are out, some people who are homestuck fans are unaware this game is even out to this day. I'm sorry but this game was poorly advertised, everything including the greenlight was pretty much community spread word2word.
What can i suggest for you, the person who's reading this that might purchase the game, to do to have an ultimate experience with this game?
If you have the patience made out of iron. I would recommend you just wait until all the ACT's are released, that way you can experience a clean flow of uninterupted content, and possible performance bugs fixed. Having a cliff hanger and waiting for months for a new act is a real drag unless you're chill and ok with it. But if you're new to Homestuck in general or a veteran with patience, wait until all the acts are released. And if you're new to Homestuck, you can pass the time waiting for the other ACT's by reading Homestuck : )
Well that's that, review is done.
I'm looking forward to the other ACTs, as well as the rumored but somewhat unofficially confirmed "Hauntswitch" which is an additional game that coincides with Hiveswap. Consider Hauntswitch as "SIDE-B" or Player 2, it takes place in the shoes of the character that swaps in your place on earth.

Dragon's Dogma is a cool game. It has a neat combat system and I love being able to create a travelling companion whose behavior you can fine-tune to your liking. But it's not an open world game. The map may tell you so at first, but the world is really just a pathway from story segment to story segment. there are only about two areas that are not required that you enter in and you only visit the other areas (that aren't cities) only once. Also, the story is very restraining and hardly allows any kind of roleplay or character building at all. Heck, when you get to the end of the story, you literally CAN'T do anything except kill your character and then (Spoilers) everything your character did is, essentially, reset. It sucks to have killed an invincible dragon and ascended to godhood and then being told that everything you just did has happened before and will happen again. Without you. You get the feeling that you just wasted your time saving the world. But the combat system is fun and there's a lot of unique abilities for you to test out on foes. It's not perfect, but it's pretty darn good.  Not the best game I've ever played, but the hireling system is unique.  You can hire "pawns" from other players, so you get pretty unique NPCs to accompany you on your quests.
The combat is action based, but does require some strategy.  You also have three "basic" classes and six more "advanced" classes to chose from.  Fighter/Mage/Rogue if you want to break it down to the basics.  Each class has a hybrid option later on, and each class also has an upgraded version.  What to be an advances spellcaster?  Sure!  Want to mix sorcery and bows?  Go ahead.  Want to be a fighter who doesn't worry about a shield - yep.  Your unique "pawn" is your main NPC and you can customize them just about as much as your own character.  You can then hire up to two more pawns that are either computer generated or come from other players.
You can't just brute force every encounter, either, and some of the enemies are so huge you have to climb on them, or attack soft spots, to win.  Hit a fire based enemy with a fire attack?  Not a good idea, it won't do much.  Hit that same badguy with some ice, and then you'll see a difference.  Smack a skeleton with a sword and see little damage, but wind up and smoke the same skeleton with your shield and watch their health drop fast!
The first 10 levels determine your base stats the most.  If you want to play a variety of classes, switch around at the lower levels.  The class you are when you level up is the class that gets the stat bonuses, but the class you played the most gets your spend-able XP that you use to buy skills.  So, want to improve your warrior skills but level as a mage so you can be a decent caster later on?  Play as a warrior until you're almost at the next level, go switch and level up, then switch back.  There are tonnes of things to alter stats in the game, generally items affect stats a fair bit, and any build can work.  There are no take-backs, though.  Once you level, that's it.  You can't even start a 2nd character without re-starting the game... but it's like that by design.
The game takes some getting used to, and the inventory and crafting are kind of "meh", but it works.  I find inventory management a bit clunky and crafting very tedious, however they did some things well.  You can enhance items.  You don't have to get upgrade 1,  then 2, then 3 if you want to go to the 3rd level upgrade and have both the coin and materilas on hand you can just jump to the best enhancement.  Thank goodness for that.
Also, you can store items in a stash - and it's pretty huge.  You can keep a lot of gear and crafting materisla in storage, and here's the best part.  You can craft while at a storage spot - and craft directly from the stash, or any of your group's inventory without swapping stuff around.  Thank goodness for that, too.  Oh, and another +1... you don't have to lug your junk to the vendor from your stash.  You can sell directly from the stash, this eliminates a lot of busy work carting crap around.
Character size and weight matter.  Too tall?  Can't go into small goblin caves.  Too short?  Can't reach this, or that.  Too light or heavy?  Easy to toss around in combat but hard to hit, or nearly impossble to knock around but easier to hit.
Spells look good, the graphics are okay, the way you learn to use your skills together and make the most of what you can do gives some challenge, and variety.  You can only equip 6 skills at a time, 3 primary, 3 secondary.  You can also have other skills on the go, but these are passive, or linked to other skills you're using.  Most skills have a basic, and advanced, option.  You buy these with points you earn by plaing whatever class the skill falls under.  I might have 9 or 10 skills, but I have to choose which ones to bring along.  Luckily with four party members you can mix and match so you're never at a loss.  My melee character can charge a pretty good distance with a rushing attack, and can hit flying enemies if they're fairly close with a skyward swipe attack, but can't shoot anything at long ranges.  Luckily all three of my backups have long-range abilities in the form of a bow for one character, and two different mages with slightly different spells for the other two.
This game's good, I wish I'd started playing it sooner, because there's so much to the systems under the hood that it takes a while to figure it all out and get used to it.
This is a solid game, a huge RPG by the looks of it, and you can level up for a long, long time.  Luckily the levels start to matter less as you get farther along.  Your skill, gear, class, party makeup, items, consumables, etc. all play a part.  No one thing means you're going to walk over any enemy.  Sure, level helps, but you get diminishihng returns.  As I said, level 1 to 10 increase your stats the most.  11-100 a fair amount less, and even less after level 100.  It works, you still improve, but "level" doesn't mean you can, or can't, do something, once you, and all of your pawns, hit level 30-40 or so.   It also doesn't matter as much if a few of your pawns lag behind by a few levels in the 40+ range.  Sometimes they have skilsl or knowledge that makes up for it.
Worth buying?  Yep, totally.  As much as some parts can be frustrating, I keep coming back for more - so they clearly did something right.

I want to quickly debunk a popular "negative review" that some people have shared, simply because they don't understand the full game, or have done little research.
"- Review: There is NO character progression. It's permadeath. Your character gains nothing even if you play him for 100 hours."
That is entirely incorrect. Yes, there is no skill tree, such as in Infestation: Survivor Stories (I feel sick having to compare the 2 games), yet the progression is still there. When your character is created, you have nothing. Your items are expendable, as they are lost or used over time, but it's not DayZ. You can build bases. The longer you play that character, the more "blueprints" you find throughout the world. I've played for 63 hours and have only found 3 blueprints. There are 11 different blue prints to find, having up to 3 variations of each. Blueprints allow you to build traps, bridges, different walls, powered machinery, etc. Your chacter is able to build a better base over time, which is the only solid way to keep your items long-term. In some ways, your base is your character, and the mesh that is your character is simply a bi-product of how well your base is designed and fortified.
The game has more content than 90% of the survival games I've played, and it's in alpha. They just added radios, with like 6 different bands and 40 different channels, so immersion is wonderful for roleplayers. Among the damn-near weekly updates, the devs have added original mechanics as well, such as a whistle emote that attracts mutants from a distance.
Also, it's 10 bucks right now. Miscreated is well worth 1 Double-Bacon Cheeseburger with fries. Buy it.

Splinter Cell Blacklist is one of the best stealth games I have ever played. It has a great story, good visuals, and realistic sound effects. There are tons of things to do in this game. There is a great campaign, a fun Spies Vs. Mercs mode, tons of challenging co op missions, and you can level up your plane and gear. The stealth mechanics are near flawless, the weapons/ gadgets are well thought out, the voice acting is pretty good, and the AI isn't super dumb like most stealth games. Splinter Cell Blacklist can be challenging at times, but it is very rewarding. I don’t have any major complaints about this game. I have a few small complaints though. One mission made you play the game as a clunky FPS with no stealth mechanics whatsoever. This bugged me a little, but it was just one mission. I think some of the character models are crappy and its difficult to play co op because most people are total idiots. With the few small flaws aside, Splinter Cell Blacklist is a remarkable game and a must have for fans of stealth games. I give SC Blacklist a 9.5/10.
