As you may have already guessed it Mind Snares: Alice's Journey relate the story of Alice set in a modern and surreal as well as psychological thriller genre.
You play as Alice after she had an accident with her car while driving on a bridge. After the car plunges into the river Alice awoke in creepy place: a world made of her own dreams and nightmares. She’ll then need to face her own nightmares in order to be strong and determined to escape from this creepy world.
As every Artifex Mundi game you can move freely in different area (of her minds) and need to solve some puzzles and find all objects in hidden objects scenes. The game has (different difficulties?) and a guest feature: every one of the family can play an independent save and resume the game where they left it. When you first play the game you’ll have a notebook where you have all your objectives as well as all your notes. Adding to that you’ll have a hint button that will help you in many ways but be warned that you may not use it in any puzzle or hidden object scene (HOS)or investigation scene (IS). Hints can be used to know where you need to go, where is the next interaction or to show an object or clue in an HOS or IS or to skip a puzzle. To conclude this part, you’ll also have an inventory to store useful items through your journey.
Puzzles are fine, different and perhaps short. Hidden objects scenes (HOS) have only the classical one (as far as I remember): find objects hidden with the help of their name. Yellow names mean that you need to interact directly with the scene or use an item in the scene.
This game hasn’t any unique feature to differentiate it from the other Artifex games.
(*) :
In addition to no skip or use any hint while playing every puzzles and Hidden objects scenes, there are a few more missable achievements. One requires you to finish 3 puzzles within one minute and another to finish a hidden objects scene in less than one minute. And one hidden objects achievement ask you to find 3 objects within 3 seconds.
Finally if you missed anything while finishing your first playthrough, you’ll need to play the game again. I guess (but I’m not sure) that you need to play on the same profile to get the “COLLECTOR” achievement.

For anyone who likes story driven games, this is one you need to play.  It fits along Baulders gate I/II, Icewindel quite nicely.
Story - I am still playing through my first time, over 50 hours sofar, and I am amazed at how complexe some of the stories are.  It's almost an interactive book at parts, and I have cause myself spending hours reading some of the books in the game because of how indepth they are.  The lore of the world  is intrieging and unique compared to other games i play, and before I am done, I want to create a new charicter and instead make them evil.
Gameplay - I like this play style, so anyone who's played BG I/II or Icewindale already knows the style.  They put far more conditions in interaction then the others though making it so that you can hear a completly atory depending on your choices.  The combat style I already stated that I like, but the only real flaw I see is with autoattack on, the charicters do not alway's listen to my commands and instead, starts attacking agian instead of heading off the monster going after my healer.  This may be a bug that will get resolved, but it's the major flaw.
Graphics/audio - As stated in other reviews, most of story is text, but where the voice acting is, it is top notch.  I am use to fantasy games going over the top when it comes to the actors, but the ones who did this game was far better then most.  Graphics are much better then the older games of this style, but it lacks the eye candy of newer games.  The thing is, while the flashy graphics would not hurt, it's not needed.  This game is compelling all it's own.
World - As mentioned, the world is inticing and unique.  There are the comon dragons, elementals, ect, but there are so many other creatures too.  The only downside is that everything is "soul" this and "soul" that.  It's a flaw of the genra, you choose a subject and everything is based off of that.  There is magic in the world with casters, yet no mention of it in the story.  This is the one flaw in the games concept.  While it's true I am not complete yet, but wouldn't there be groups seeking alternitive cures for the Legecy?

State of decay is one of the best third person survival horror open world game. Graphics is good enough, story is fine. SoD is not a brainless zombie killing game, you are a member of a community stucked in Thumbull county. Player have to manage the community which includes doing favoures for survivors to gain trust to become friends later; scavenging for vital supplies such as food, medicine, building materials. In the game you have a "home base" which can be upgraded with 9 facilities, and also has  space for outpost to build. Outposts extends the safe area and have supply cache to restock your equipment. The game can be played id different ways, someone likes playing stealthy, others prefer brute force to complete missions. Ah, the missions; i found side missions a bit repetitive, but they are okay. Driving cars is useful but makes a lot of noise which attracts zombies. When you are at your base you can change the character you are playing if the other character is your friend. Changing is adviseable to let the used character rest to get their vitality and stamina back to maximum value. SoD is beyond my expectations, i recommended everyone who loves zombie games 9/10.

Shadow of Mordor felt fantastic through the first 10 hours, and then began to drag quite badly. It kept going down hill, and at the point I write this I doubt I'll finish it.
Mordor gets a lot of things right, especially production quality. The graphics are beautiful and run flawlessly, the voice acting is top quality and there are some spectacular 'vision sequence' cutscenes. The game also feels brilliantly bolted together and playtested, I only encountered one notable bug - and that later turned out to be an Nvidia driver problem. Drivers older than 376 don't seem to be effected, so use those.
I also applaud the level design, especially in the second playable area. All areas feel well thought out, but Sea of Rhun stands out because of it's verticality. Most of the areas have multiple layers, allowing you to slip below the Orcs or drop on them from above. It's genuinely fun to play, and it brings out the best the combat system has to offer.
Mordor also has two critical faults, which are almost gamebreaking after a couple of hours. The Nemesis system is a farce, it doesn't work as intended or contribute anything new or interesting. And the combat balance is all over the place.
Combat Balance is Mordor's most crippling weakness. It's terrible. When you're fresh out of the tutorial, you're already strong enough to take on 20-30 Orcs without taking a single hit. After a couple of hours you're maxed out and literally invulnerable against any number of normal Orcs. It doesn't really matter how many they send at you, they're so weak and you can build a combo so quickly that you can simply scythe through them. Shadow Strike Chain, and the Critical Hit system make combat a farce.
Meanwhile, an Archer Captain(who looks exactly the same as any other Archer) can reduce you to 40% health with a single arrow, but will then ignore you/stop firing completely. After that single shot you'll know exactly where they are, and many of them can be killed with a couple of Fire Arrows - an attack you can spam infinitely.
Melee Captains fight exactly like any other Orc. They have exactly the same moveset and many of them look exactly the same. You can bash swords with them if you want, but it's easier to land three hits on one of their minions and then shower them in Fire Arrows.
Warchiefs are some of the weakest enemies I've fought. Most of them appear alone, meaning you can simply stunlock them and keep bashing until they drop. Or pepper them with Fire Arrows(always works!)
This brings me to the Nemesis system. It's a fancy name for RNG, and it doesn't work at all. At one point all four of my Warchiefs looked identical, three of them had the same Weaknesses and two had the same name. The vast majority of Captains you'll see generated are just generic Orcs with more health and damage. The system itself is an interesting idea, but it's badly realised and doesn't work well
I really want to like Shadow of Mordor. It does a lot of things right and only a few things wrong, but those few things absolutely cripple the game later on. Captains feel identical, fights feel identical, and there's no incentive to use Stealth when you can more quickly smash your way through the front door and kill anybody who doesn't like that.
I'd give it a 6/10. That's not enough for me to recommend it, except for hardcore LOTR fans. Find it on sale if you can, but be prepared for a lot of repetition.

Mind Snares: Alice's Journey is a unique hidden object game. Most hidden object games are just hidden objects and simple games, but this one goes beyond.
Graphics: The graphics of the animation are a little outdated. However, I think this is due to making the figures puppet-like, just how Alice feels like a puppet. The scenes are gorgeous and well-detailed without any blur or pixel errors.
Story: You play as Alice, who shares her story about how she decided on making a major decision on her life: opening a business. Her previous job...well...she was pushed too hard by her boss and even did things for her boss that wasn't even work related! Alice misses her time off and a promise was broken. This results in Alice getting in an accident and transported into another world. This story also teaches a good lesson between balancing work and life.
Gameplay: You're probably wondering what makes this game go beyond "hidden object." There are certain scenes with items that you have to make in order for an object to be found. For example, in order to find a written letter, you have to find a knife in the scene and use it to cut an envelope open. Another example is finding a green apple. There are no green apples, but there is a red apple and a green paint bucket. There are also some unique minigames like piecing puzzles, line puzzles, and combination puzzles. These range from easy to challenging.
The only problem I have with the gameplay is with certain hidden object scenes. A few times I clicked on an object that needed to be found...it didn't count. So I tried looking again. I couldn't find that item other than that other one...so I clicked it again and it counted! It didn't count before! Another problem was during one scene: I was suppose to look for a "Sign." Okay so maybe it means like an advertisement or command or an equation. It ended up being a small skull on the wall ... what?
Lastly, another problem, is when you use objects to make objects, you didn't intend to click on it and it's hard to put it back.
Music: I love how the music is unique and it doesn't annoyingly loop on the same track over and over. It changes overtime. Music ranges from suspense, to peacefulness, to horror. A pretty good selection.
Overall: Despite a few annoyances with gameplay, Mind Snares: Alice's Journey remains a unique hidden object game that trumps over the regular ones. With an engaging story, unique and beautiful scenes, and different things to do, this game will get you hooked and you won't stop until you complete it. This game can be a true eye opener that let's you see all the possibilities in life and life is worth fighting for...and an hidden object game that doesn't settle to just be a regular "hidden object game."
Pros:
-Good, engaging story
-Good balance of music
-Unique sets of puzzles
Cons:
-Annoyances with hidden object scenes (click not registering, unable to put object down, one unclear object to find)

Miscreated, a great game full of well-implemented features and a lot of bugs.
I have thoroughly enjoyed this game. I have spent time experimenting with the base-building features and I've got to say, they're really good. Base building allows the player freedom to build however he/she chooses. Every base can be built differently and is unique.
For me, PVP in Miscreated has and will continue to be a big part of the game. This may be due to the lack of PVE content, but it is also a lot of fun. I've spent a lot of time combating both large and small groups. It's a dangerous world, and I really enjoy it. PVE content could be improved by adding more environmental dangers, more variations of mutants and even hordes of mutants.
The survival aspect of this game is spot on. I've had several occasions where my friends and myself have almost died due to starvation. This also forces PVP and confrontation because you need food to survive. It really helps capture the brutality and savagery generally associated with a post-apocalyptic society. However, it is relatively easy to get water through rivers, ponds and much more.
The visuals of Miscreated are incredible. The weather is incredible and I often find myself just admiring how good it is. The developers have done a very good job implementing weather and environmental visuals.
There are many vehicles to choose from in Miscreated. The fact that there are a limited number spawned at once makes getting one feel like an achievement. Unfortunately though, the vehicles have issues. They can randomly cause you to die. This could be by falling through the floor, randomly dying when getting out of it or just flipping for some trivial reason. You can also expect to get disconnected while driving. This often leads to you losing the vehicle to someone else.
There are so many other bugs I can report on. There is falling through the floor and losing everything if you can't swim through the "underworld" quick enough. Of course there is dropping items and having them disappear. I found that quite frustrating. I could go on but the list is long.
Despite the bugs, the game is still amazing and has so much potential. The developers are actively improving and updating the game with new content and bug fixes. It is definitely a game worth purchasing. I highly recommend it.

4: What I've always appreciated about the historical Total War titles, is the accuracy that it has. It may not be dead on but they did an excellent job on making it real.
5: Despite what people say, this game is amazingly optimized. The fact that you can have roughly 8000 Units on the field without extreme choppy framerate is amazing. If you think about it, each soldier has individual animations, and each unit has individual AI targets. The details on the textures and the graphics in general aswell. To manage all this and still get solid fps is amazing in my opinion.
Bad things about this game:
1: Well the first thing you'll see a lot of people get angry about is the DLC plan the company has, if you're going to buy this game - be prepared to get out some money for the blood and gore, and other key factions.
2: One thing to note is the poor way they went around seiges in this game, and its pretty clunky compared to other titles such as Medieval 2. For example many Attila players will say that the towers are OP, and they are definitely. O-P
3: Daft AI, expecially in seiges. I've had many a times when I'm playing singleplayer and the AI cant seem to find its way through the walls, they just run around outside tiring their troops out. So now I, the defender have to go out and attack them which is odd to say the least.
4: This game is a lot like the previous title, Rome 2. Some might even argue they copies a lot of assets from the previous title. I personally have only played Rome 2 on someone elses computer, and I find Attila to have its own unique charm. However just know if you own Rome 2 and put a lot of hours into it - this game might seem copied to that.
Hope this was insightful, if you plan to buy this game - It is a really good game and no one will think its stupid. If you plan not to, no one will blame you as it has more blemishes than some other Total War titles. :D

What kept me playing State of Decay instead of quitting: The bruised versimilitude of it all. Sure, the characters are irritating and behave like idiots, but I love those idiots! NPC characters are interesting and add flavor, and if you get tired of your overpowered murder machine of a survivor, you can switch to a character like Ed, who constantly impresses the zombies with his movie trivia so hard that their heads explode. The way the game lets events and little touches of story fall into place instead of laboriously scripting every goddamn thing is really nice. The game gives many ways to stealth or fight your way to your objective, any of which can complicate matters and bring zombie death down on your hapless survivor's head. These are the kinds of little actions and touches I thoroughly enjoy in video games. State of Decay is all the more richer for these.
Despite my praise, this game does quite a few things wrong - game progression happens in real time, even when not playing! So it's a lot of fun to leave a game and come back only to find all the houses have been picked clean, and all the characters have been having fun eating all the sandwiches and shooting each other without you, you zom-loser. Building things at home is essentially a really boring RTS, even more so because the construction happens over actual time, which is ♥♥♥♥ing stupid. Also the game is glitchy as♥♥♥♥♥♥- cars flip over if you drive them onto curbs just right, human characters thank you for saving them from becoming zombie chow by standing completely still and pretending you're not there. The plot is gaaaaaaaaaarbaaaaaaaaage and hangs out like the smelly hobo in the middle of the Halloween dance party. The game does not allow you to delegate most activities to other survivors, which puts your character in the Commander Shepherd habit of having to do everything yourself.
Breakdown DLC: Open-world survival mode where you hold out against increasingly more dangerous undead, fix up an RV to get the hell out, and get so hideously drunk that the RV gets totaled in the same area that everyone was so desperate to leave, starting the process all over again. If you haven't had enough of State of Decay, you will after this. Mainly because you'll see the thousand little quirks that the developers haven't hammered out because making downloadable current-gen games is expensive and complicated as♥♥♥♥♥♥ even from a small experienced team of developers. And also because it's the same old routine of inhabiting a safe house and building the same damn buildings again. It's a game mode with diminishing returns, much like the resources of the land that your characters are raiding. I still think it's good because it itches that scratch that the original game barely got to.
While I don't think it takes full advantage of the CryEngine, it does a good job of creating a survialist atmosphere.

It was the 2014 GOTY of a lot of websites, which kind of says how disappointing that year was, considering that this game is not as amazing as the years around 2014. It's an excellent celebration of player freedom and control, which is somewhat undermined by it's unadjustable, low difficulty.
By this time, I'm sure you know what you do in this game, and what the combat is compared too. The brilliance lies in its player agency and execution. The combat and stealth portions are satisfying and the player is free to tackle situations in anyway he/she sees fit. The game is also well-known for its 'Nemesis-system'. There are captains who are spread out over the plains of Mordor, each with their own randomized characteristics and traits. I don't know how many types of visual characteristics the devs have programmed into this, but 40 hours in and I was still fighting Uruks I've never seen before, like "Kubai the Drooler" who is actually drooling at all times. This is awesome, because you will remember some of them simply because they were successful in fending you of or perhaps even killing you. This is where my problem lies.
This game is too easy, especially in the first eight hours. The nemesis-system looses it's value, because of the low difficulty. Unique to the system is that a captain that kills you, will grow in strength and power. Some captains will make a comeback at you at completely random times to take their revenge on you (with some new scars on their heads). Again, this is awesome, but most captains won't be able to defeat you, and you'll just plow through the Uruk army, taking captains one or three at a time. The low difficulty just negates the the system.
The small amount of story missions is actually pretty nice. These are afterall somewhat restrictive and because there are a  massive amount of side-missions, the game entices you to play in bursts spreading out over a couple of weeks, instead of burning through it in a single week. Not that you get burned out with it, on the contrary, but it is nice that the game allows the player to take it's time with it; the positive effect of the casual playstyle.
The DLC offers two more short stories set in the same landscapes. Some traits of the player and of other units are changed for the sake of variety, and the new achievements offer the right amount of difficulty for those who seek more of a challenge.
You should give this game atleast a try, after all it's only 10 bucks during steam sales. It's well polished (no bugs at all) and well designed. It runs good on pretty much everything, meaning that some small changes in the settings can change a whole lot for you. The one gripe, the low difficulty, is a bummer but it is something to overlook.

This game starts out frustrating and gradually becomes better. The world ends up being surprisingly small, and at the same time, you'll be using fast travel with great frequency.
But the best part of the game, is when it trolls you. Every now and then, the Nemesis system will kick up a flamboyantly gay Uruk whose lines are double entendres and whose animations look like they were mo-capped from a drag queen.
If you're familiar with Assassin's Creed, you understand most of the gameplay, but it's closer to the Arkham games in that there is absolutely no blending. You can run, you can hide, you can climb almost anything, but you can't take a quiet walk around Mordor without everything that sees you trying to kill you.
Overall, I found the story and gameplay satisfying, and once you've unlocked Brand and Dispatch skills, there's a fair amount of replay value in the Nemesis system.
The biggest reason I have for reviewing this game though, is to clear up a common misunderstanding about what it means to kill a nemesis. It isn't enough to take all their health. You have to take their head, or they'll just escape death and come back evolved to not die the same way again. The misconception comes from the description of how to kill them: you beat them down, then use a finishing move. The problem is, there are many finishing moves, and most of them are stabbings. The only one that kills is the one that beheads, and it's random which one you will get.
The evolution angle can make for some very, very irritating nemesis. You can end up with someone who regenerates, can't be countered, can't be leapt over, and can't be hit with ranged weapons or grabbed. That makes for a tough fight, even if they weren't surrounded by backup.
Eventually, you get moves that will make their heads explode, and actually killing nemesis becomes predictable and controllable, but until then, it's very difficult to choose to take someone other than a regular grunt out.

A game that's fun to play from beginning to end, but is ripe with flaws that make the experience bitter-sweet at best.
The biggest problem with the game is that every feature in it is good, but not great. Some are better than others, failing just to be perfect, while others are clunky and should be done away with completely.
The combat is a poor imitation of the Batman Arkham series, perhaps mixed in with a little bit of the Witcher. It does not flow as well as or in the same way as the other two, and countering can be unresponsive at times. The Nemesis system sounds aweomse at first but grows dull quickly when you realize how little each Uruk captain matters and when the lack of variation starts to become apparent. There are only a few different kinds of encounters you can have with captains, which involve planting your own mind-controlled ones or just murdering others. The encounters all pretty much play the same way. There's no real reason to have your own captains other than the fact that they can fight for you, which is rarely helpful. The boss battles in the game are shoehorned in at best, and have no redeming qualities.
Overall the story is generic, and the fact that it cares so little for true LotR lore makes it all the more furstrating. It seems like it's setting up for a sequel, which I'm not completely against. They just have to promise to fix everything.
What did I put my money in for? Awful combat, awful story, awful map

Just ONCE I would love to see a DW game be more serious tonally, with traditional Chinese music and voice acting. Will probably never happen, but one can dream.

It's still a great mindless slaughter simulation, and that's all I really expect out of a DW game and this delivers in spades.

Disappointing. I really like it, but I'm disappointed that it comes so close to being a great game, and just misses.
The graphics and audio are decent, having some moments where they stand out, although much of the world design is a bit drably generic.
There's plenty of content, I spent about 120 hours on my first play-through, trying to do and see everything. Some of it feels too much like filler, noticeboard quests in particular. Even if you ignore those, you could spend at least half that amount of time and have a "more killer less filler" experience.
What disappointed me, was that I spent the entire game waiting for something; Waiting for the game to come into it's stride, present a real challenge, and for all the game systems to become an important part of that challenge, but that never happened.
It has all these potentially great systems like;
- collecting materials and crafting consumable items
- equipment that provides different stats allowing different loadouts
- character classes and skills you can switch for different loadouts
- NPC heroes you can recruit to build different party combinations
But I never needed to fully utilise these systems. Any time I prepared for a fight by changing my equipment loadout, party composition and consumables; I went into the fight and it was easy enough that all of my preparations were unnecessary.
Despite my own disappointment with this aspect, I have no hesitation recommending the game.
It's just short of being a great game, and having finally played it I wish there was a sequel to build on what's here.

There is a massive list of reasons why you should NOT play this game, primarily related to the developers' ideas of how this game SHOULD be played and dammit they are going to make you play it that way. Which is a terrible way to develop a game, so the laundry list of "things that suck" for this game is loooooong.
Absolutely none of those things trump one core feature:
EPIC BATTLES AGAINST BIG MONSTERS.
Lots of them. Not just the dragon. Not just OTHER dragons. But a whole roster of big stuff that you can grab onto and climb around on while beating the hell out of it.
And yes, that is going to be problematic sometimes - grab hold of a flying beast and it will frequently lift off and whirl around so dizzyingly fast that your camera can't keep up, and you won't know what part you're looking at or what part you're holding onto or which direction you need to climb so you can reach a vital point and kill this thing.
But those battles are awesome and exciting and fun, and nothing else out there has them. It's a real shame that so many people are missing out on that because they're whinging about save slots and frame rates and clunky KBM controls.

Please read this in a British accent, it may be easier for you to digest. (unless you are already british, then, i'm sorry, there is no hope for you)
If I had to drescribe Pillars of Eternity in one word... I'd have to begrudgingly say 'bland'. Its not that it didn't have moments where it was trying to stand on its own without being propped up by the Forgotten Realms setting that so obviously gave birth to it, but those few brilliant sparks were few drowned by successive waves of mediocracy.
All that can be forgivable with strong character interaction that make you care for those sprites on your screen... sadly, that cannot be said of PoE.
*Sigh* ...the companions... they just see you and irrationally decide to follow you around into mortal danger without any personal ties or bonds forged out of alliances of necessity in a dire situation where you're stuck together and have to trust each other in order to survive, bonding with a character through a tense trial, no, one conversation in the streets or the woods with a total stranger who already has a bunch of weirdos tagging along behind him and they simply fall in line and march right along because you're the player character, there's nothing really compelling keeping together whatever ecclectic band of outcasts you have managed to accumulate along the way. I'd rather have four fleshed out characters who feel like they have a soul, people that you'd bond with by going to hell and back with each other instead of static converstations in the woods,  I'd rather have that then eight who feel like they were hollowborn slaves to the PC. I feel like the pied piper of NPCs when I select file formation with myself on point.
It's as if they wanted to be creative and venture off the beaten to death path but got scared and only went halfway.
Take the races for example, I found the Aumanu, Godlike, and the furry version of the Orlan interesting, to me they showed promise as I haven't seen those races before and so wanted to play as one of those, hoping for a unique experience. I played a Death Godlike and was expecting people to hate me or be afraid of me. The lore said most of them are killed at birth and are seen as bad luck, I like characters that have to overcome adversity and prejudice, so I expected everyone to give me a rough time... but when they spoke to me they might as well have been talking to an average human or anyone else because no one noticed that I looked like a ******* nightmare.
When I went back to make another character, being unsatisfied with my Cipher Death Godlike for not feeling like anything more than a human warrior with a bit of magic, for some reason, it was only then that I was irked by the fact that elves and dwarves being included in this world... and it was then that I looked upon them as a beige anchor dragging PoE down into blandsville... elves and dwarves... please, oh please, stop writing elves and dwarves into your generic AD&D fantasy worlds.
Oh, but these elves and dwarves are different you say... Really? Then why even make them elves or dwarves? If they're different, make them look different too. You could make the elves only nocturnal, maybe living in jungles or forests so deep its almost eternally dark with fungal growths the equivelent of coral reefs and the only strong light coming from bio luminescent creatures, making elves evolve owl-like eyes to see in the darkness and bat like ears and sharp noses to augment their senses in the dark, with long gangly arms that reach past their knees to make them superior at climbing and immensely strong. Then, lets not call it an elf and call it something else, freeing yourself from the baggage that comes with elves, there, you've graduated from a fantasy cliche. Either embrace the cliche and do it the best you can with great characters or be something else entirely, don't try to span both sides, one leg with always fall short.
You know, you could use other mythologies for inspiration aside from Celtic and Norse. Maybe if you're using reincarnation as a major point in the storyline, maybe you borrow from mythologies from India, with creatures like the serpentine naga or the shape-shifting rakshasa, gods could live in flying palaces called vimanas wielding powerful weapons that could flatten a city, or just do something, anything, different.... anything but elves and dwarves rehashed for the hundreth time. I've seen every variation of elf or dwarf that I'll ever want to see at this point. It was just one more thing that, in the end, made it feel like a homebrew of AD&D where magic is tossed around like bathwater and everyone hurls fetch quests at you.
Perhaps I am *unfair* to  focus on the feeling of the game's story telling. But, honestly, for me, RPGs are about story and atmosphere, transporting the player to another world for a little while, remove that, and its just a basic strategy game. I don't come to RPGs for gameplay alone, though it needs to be serviceable (which in PoE it is common to Baldur's Gate II, which was good when I played it back in the day and still is, though it doesn't feel as fresh now), I come for story, for atmosphere... and that's where I feel this game failed me.

PoE has its positive points which many other people will attest to, I know I just hit on the negatives here. Overall, its ok... its just ...ok.

Explore an island pummeled by blizzards and inhabited by mythical creatures, while monitoring your vitals to survive through the night. Pros:

Cons:

Locked into Origin if you want to see the third episode.
Absolute Do-Not-Buy:
A branching, multi-game plot that culminates in "Press X for the Blue ending".  Bioware didn't just drop the ball in the end, they fumbled it so hard it sank to the core the core of the planet and nearly set off the China Syndrome (old-timey movie reference for you kids).  There's wrapping things up with a tawdry deus ex machina, and then there's absolutely squandering any potential built up over dozens of different of different choices by deliberately managing giant plotholes so that we all end up with essentially one ending movie anyhow.  All those characters and races and intergalactic politics don't matter one whit once the ending turns out to be some spurious blech pseudo-religious mumbo jumbo just thrown at us out of the blue.  No matter how interesting the series was overall, every action turned out to ultimately irrelevant because the so-called "writers" behind the plot turned out to be intellectually dishonest and creatively bankrupt.  These developers copped out so hard they should get into politics.
Final verdict:
Never ever buy any Bioware product again; honestly, i wish i could block specific developers from my Steam so i never even hear about this company again.  Probably should avoid EA Games as well.

I've always enjoyed this game, let it be the exhilerating moments of being in CQC, or the deep lore this game is based upon.
It's frustrating, but most of the time it's your fault.
MOST of the time, anyway. An area by the name of Lost Izalyth was rushed, so the boss you find there (Bed of Chaos) has a lot of artificial difficulty. There was one time, when I jumped a gap to get to the boss, the GIGANTIC arm the boss slaps you around with knocked me across the arena to my death (the developers didn't do this on purpose, they just rushed the boss). The floor also crumbles beneath your feet when you reach a certain point in the boss fight. Any unsuspecting noob can fall through, since the game doesn't warn you ahead of time.
Then there's the Capra Demon, though to a lesser extent. When you walk into the arena, the space you fight in isn't that big, and most noobs die before they can react in time to the dogs and the boss. After that, the boss fight isn't that bad.
This is the most artificial difficulty I remember, though some bugs are out there that can spoil the fun at times.
TIME FOR THE GOOD STUFF
The game is open world, but in a semi-linear way. It's not the GTA V open world you're thinking of, but instead it's an open world because you can go into areas if you have the skill or equipment. It's not a level requirement, but instead a skill requirement. That's probably one of the best things about the game.
The combat is done quite well. You have a light attack, a strong attack, a block, a parry (if you're not two-handing your weapon), you can two-hand your weapon, and you can roll. This means you're able to endure a fight without getting hit. When you roll, you have a part of the roll that makes you invulnrable. Don't expect to land the roll perfectly every time. It takes practice and patience to learn when to roll, and when NOT to. When you parry, there is a part of the parry that can slap aside the enemy's weapon. After doing a successful parry, you can repost the enemy for a large amount of damage. This also takes practice to land, so don't quit the game after not being able to parry successfully. When you two-hand a weapon, your strength increases by 1.5x the amount it was previously. This also adds some extra damage, so it's worth it.
Most of the bosses in Dark Souls are okay. Some of them are annoying, some are just too easy. I'm not going to spoil any more bosses, since they're better when you don't know them very well.
The lore in this game is extremely deep, and you can piece it together by reading item descriptions. If you need help figuring out the lore, check out
. He has a few videos on Dark Souls 1.
That's it, I don't want to spoil the areas, so play the game yourself.

As a long time fan of the DW series, this is one of my favorites, and I've only played a few hours!  The game runs smoothly on my Lenovo Y500 with dual cards.  My only issue was the control mapping.  It was weirdly placed and it took a while to get used to.  I don't remember the previous DW games having a weird control scheme like this one, but I found a comfortable adjustment which I'll write below to help others (I use an Xbox 360 remote).  It would also be nice to see controller buttons rather than keyboard buttons on the screen when using a gamepad.
Graphics:  9/10 (I see people complaining about graphics, but this is the norm for DW games.  They could have probably improved it though, especially with it being a PC port)
Gameplay comfort:  9/10 (This is a mass murder game, so I rate gameplay by comfortable transitions/synchronization)
Content:  10/10 so far.  From what I've seen, this game has hours upon hours of epic game time, just like it's predecessors.  It also has a bunch more characters than I'm used to, which is a huge plus.  Each having different skins/recolors is just icing on the cake.  Weapons are diverse and there's a ton of choice.  Abilities/passive stats are plenty and easy to understand.  Game types are simple to get a hold of and the story so far is about on par with the other DW games.
Really the only thing I feel it's lacking right now is online co-op.  Local co-op is awesome, but online mode would be better.
Now for the 360 controller mapping:
X- Basic Attack
Y- Strong Attack
B- Jump
A- Special Move
Start- Menu
Select- Map view switch
Left analog click- Horse call
I also adjusted the camera movement/look to the right analog stick, which was weirdly placed as the left and right trigger.  I kept everything else the same.  This also frees up the left and right triggers for your own purposes.  Pause doesn't seem to work for me.  Of course you should adjust it to fit your needs, but I found this set up leagues better than the default.  More natural and it makes the A button the "select" and B button the "return", which made it easier to navigate menus.
Overall I highly recommend this game!

Simply amazing, quite possibly the best Splinter Cell yet! It takes all the best things about the prior entries in the series and rolls them into one fun package!

It isn't perfect, but it's a truer Splinter Cell game than Conviction was. I enjoyed Conviction - itself a side-step in pacing, action, and storytelling - but a lot of other people out there don't share the same sentiment as I do. Blacklist should appease them, though. This title sees the return of Fisher in his Special Ops form - now called Fourth Echelon - in a bigger and more action-packed story while still keeping great stealth gameplay mechanics in true Splinter Cell style. It features a good mixed bag of features like lights indicating when you're concealed in darkness, carrying and hiding bodies, whistling or making noises to trick guards (from previous titles, excluding Conviction), and Last Known Position as well as parkour-style movement and pacing (from Conviction), and together it all adds up into a really good Splinter Cell experience that I'm sure a lot of long-time fans have missed.
The new voice and MoCap actor for Sam is a little hard to get used to. Sam's look has been tweaked and his voice is obviously different, which can sometimes break immersion considering this takes place AFTER Conviction, which makes Sam older, not younger, so with him actually looking AND sounding younger, it can get a bit weird. Michael Ironside is surely missed in this game, but it's not exactly a total deal-breaker. Changes happen, I guess.
The story has various missions, which you can choose from and you can play them in any playstyle you want. Traditional fans, like myself, are probably going to take the non-lethal / Ghost approach, but if you want to go loud or stalk your enemies, there are plenty of options with which you may do so. You choose any mission based on who it's for - Fourth Echelon, Kobin, Briggs, and some metagames - and proceed to take them on however you want. The Fourth Echelon missions (in red) are the ones that are important to story progress, though, so feel free to take a break from that whenever you want and take on some of Briggs's missions or even Kobin's.
The non-lethal / Ghost gameplay is by far my favorite. I've encountered some missions, like Kobin's for example, that don't seem to let you bypass everyone and stealth a mission 100%, but you can set your attacks to non-lethal instead of lethal and get Ghost points anywhere at the end screen. It feels a lot like the old days, with Lambert critiquing your every move, telling you to not raise any alarms or the mission is done, etc etc which is a good thing, in my opinion. The only thing I think the stealth gameplay is lacking is the quieter, slower walk. I can't make Sam walk any slower, like in previous games, but thankfully upgrades to your suit seem to take care of the noise factor and allow you to stealth with relative ease.
In all, though, Blacklist is a good game. Not perfect, not the best in my opinion, but it's worthy of being a Splinter Cell title. Change happens and sometimes things need to be kept up-to-date - games are no exception - but in the end, even without Michael Ironside's booming voice, it still carves out its own little place in Splinter Cell history.
Get this game if you're a long-time fan of the franchise like myself. Definitely get this game if you felt let down by Conviction, because I don't think you'll be disappointed.

It's no Chaos Theory. But it's much closer to the series' roots than Conviction ever was. Darkness is back (shooting out lights protects your stealth), you have the capability to finish most missions without ever firing a shot (or even engaging anyone besides mission targets), and the weapons 4th Echelon gives you are all suppressed. You CAN pick up unsuppressed weapons, but if you want to preserve the true SC experience, don't do it!
There are linear sequences that feel way too much like Assassin's Creed, and the FPS sequences where you play as Briggs are definitely the low point. Difficulty is on the easy side (too much like AC again), with "death from above" kills and 100% predictable AI (they always spawn in the same spots).
I did like the "Mass Effect" style inter-mission parts where you roam the plane, chat with your team, and upgrade your gear.
Co-op missions (most of which can be played solo, but you can't access certain routes that way) are like Modern Warfare's coop or Halo's spartan assault, except with stealth and alarms. They are pretty fun and lack none of the lame parts seen in the solo campaign.
Overall, I recommend picking this game up on sale. The E3 video previews made this look like a lame action game, but you're given the option (and encouraged to) play super stealthily. Can't say I wouldn't prefer a more Chaos Theory kind of game though!

Dragon's Dogma Dark Arisen is basically if Monster Hunter, Elder Scrolls, Dark Souls and Shadow of Colossus all had a Love Child. It's a Western Styled ARJRPG that grabs your attention and peaks your intrest within the first few moments. The opening cut scene (after completing character) is amazing and it succeeds in drawing people into the game. Overhaul I love this game and hope they make another one, so hopes for that.
Some Positives:
-Great Port, since the origional game was released back in 2012 or 2011 for Xbox 360 and PS3 they resently ported it over to PC and I must say that it is one of the greatest, well polished ports I have ever seen. And with all the dlc included ontop its a great buy.
-The Combat, the combat is great in this game. It's an action rpg with fluid combat and controls that feel intuitive. It's satisfing and has impact.
-Character Creating, this game has extensive character creation for both you and your main companion, for those that love to spend hours in character creation will love this.
-Loot, there is some cool loot in this game, with great selection of armours and outfits that help make your character unique through out your playthrough(s). Almost all look great in my opinion and you are constantly finding new gear for you and your companion.
-New Game Plus, great feature.
-Class System, this game has class that it calls vocations. You pick one at the begining of the game and through out your questing the class levels up for both you and your companion, allowing to get more and greater abilities. At any time through out the game you can change your class (or that of your main companion) to something else to change things up and keep you interested.
-Pawn System, so you make your main companion which can then be summond into other people's worlds were they serve faithfully and get prizes when sent back. You summon other Pawns to help you through out your journey. Basically your Pimping.
-Monsters, great combat with big creatures, it feels great to bring down a huge monster and strike it down.
Meh's:
-The Story, the story starts of great with the opening cut scene and first establishment of the world as well as within your first few hours where you say hello to the Dragon, tear out a Cyclop's eye and decapitate a Hydra. But, then the main antagonist of the game, the Dragon, isn't seen again until the end of the game, the NPCs talk about the Dragon and the devisation it caused and the coming of the monsters, but you don't really see that. I think it would have been better if the South of Gransys (near the southern coast) was populated by villages and towns before the Dragon's coming and after it all of the soldiers and civilians that survived the monster onslaught either retreated to the Shadow Fort or to Cassardis. Making Cassarids a refugee centre and the getting to the Shadow Fort a top priority. It [the story] kind of wanes through out the game with the main quest really just becoming fetch quests or dungeon clearers.
-Teleportation and World Size, the World of Dragon's Dogma, that you can play within, is quite big but for the sequal it needs to be much bigger. The portal system needs to be explained more I feel, so you know what to do with those big purple glowing crystals. Gransys (the world) also feels a bit life less and repopulated with bandits. There are locations that the Duke controls and has dominion over but between them the roads are plagued with bandits and monsters, key structers like walls and keeps are occupied by outlaws and thieves, which I think there need to be quest where you can clear then and repopulate them with soldiers and civilans. It also feels quite linear and not the really open as you are funneled from one place to another. It needs to be biggers I believe.
Some Negatives:
-Relationships, your relationships with other characters isn't really explained that well or how to raise or lower popularity with them.
-Crafting, I liked the crafting where you could upgrade your weapons and armour but I just feel like I want to craft them from raw materials (this is a small gripe).

This game came so close to being one of the best RPGs i've ever played, but just falls short.
Mechanically and visually this is a super solid Medieval fantasty. No gimicky viking stuff, no over the top asian stuff, Just me, my sword, and a host of classic monsters begging to be killed.
The "gimick" if you want to call it that, is you have a fully customisable companion that follows you around and can be assigned a class role to perform (i ususally have him as a healer). With the games limited online fuctionality, you can send your minion into other peoples games to work, and he'll come back with whatever loot hes been given while serving. Its an interesting system, but personally i dont think it really adds whole lot to the game. My party mostly consisted of ugly people that other people on the internet had created, who would constantly give me the same tips over and over again about places we'd been a thousand times. Over all, I'd recomend this game to people who enjoyed Skyrim (without fast travel), but anyone looking for a deeper story might get frustrated.

If you are AT ALL a fan of any form of action RPG, be it Dark Souls, Witcher 3, or what have you, do yourself a favor and buy this game. It has bar none the most enjoyable combat system of any action RPG I have ever played. It may not have the punishing difficulty of Dark Souls 3, the beautiful world of Witcher 3, or the charm of a game like Kingdom Hearts, but it more than makes up for it with the best implementation of a third person combat system I have seen in a long while.
Essentially, there are 9 classes, or vocations as they are called in the game, to choose from. While you only start with the option to use the "basic" three, you unlock the rest a bit later in the game. All the classes, including the so called "basic" vocations, invoke a differing playstyle that remains viable from level 1 to the game's max of 200. In addition, you can freely swap between these vocations by simply visiting the skill trainer at the main city's inn. In fact, the game encourages you to try different classes, as you can unlock slottable passives that can be carried over from class to class.
Now, each class has a unique playstyle. Classes like the Fighter offer a more traditional sword and shield fighting style, where you can time blocks as the massive monster swings its flail at you to block and stagger your foe. Your archetypical mage offers curative and control spells, while the sorcerer holds sway over destructive fields of classic RPG tropes such as meteor showers and seismic earthquakes. The Ranger specializes in sniping enemies from afar, while the Warrior runs in with a massive 2 handed weapon, able to perform techniques akin to Limit Breaks as well as having a very satisfying jumping attack. The Strider is my personal favorite, carrying a pair of daggers and a shortbow, but finds itself most at home climbing up the sides of a dragon, jabbing it's daggers along the way in a move akin to Shadows of the Colossus. And that's not even mentioning the hybrid vocations, with the Magick Archer's homing missiles, the Magick Knight's ability to set up essentially nuclear magic cannons, and the Assassin's complete mastery over all physical weaponry.
Finally, I have to mention the pawn system. While exploring the world, you are granted a customizable companion called a Pawn. The main pawn, as it is called, can take all vocations except the hybrid classes. But the truly fascinating part of the pawn is it's learning mechanism. Similar to Amiibos from Nintendo's Smash 4, the pawn will learn from your playstyle and begin to imitate how you fight. If you prefer looting mid combat, your pawn will do so likewise. If you oft find yourself climbing the backs of your colossal enemies, you'll typically find your pawn clambering alongside you. I oftentimes jump around like a headless chicken in combat, and it's weird seeing my pawn jumping around like a moron with me. Up to 2 other pawns can be hired aside from your main pawn. These other pawns are the main pawns of other Dragon's Dogma players, so a strong community sprung up around grooming the best pawns for others to try out in their own games.
There's still so much more I can talk about like the end game dungeons and the sick fashion you can pull off, but I think I've sung this game's praises enough. Just remember... Wolves hunt in packs Arisen. Oh, and they also ill like fire. Happy hunting!

A day in Starbound:
Made a new character last night and played through the intro, made my way to a space Outpost, and acquired some quests on a friends server. When I logged back in this morning, I found myself on a beautiful forest planet filled with wild life. My current quest was to acquire 10 Copper ore for a scientist on the outpost so he can give me a "tech" to augment my physical abilities. I hadn't walked a minute before I stumpled upon "the house". It was a massive mansion fashioned in Fuedal-era Japan design. I walked inside to find many caligraphy paintings, a few book shelves, and even fewer lighting fixtures. That's when the ghosts came. I destroyed them one by one, exploring deeper into the mansion as I did, looting along the way. I even managed to save the life of a merchant who was trapped inside and sold me some armor for cheap. Once the place was clear I dubbed this amazing structure my new base of operations. I starting mining nearby and soon acquired the 10 copper ore necesary.
Time to the complete the quest right? Wrong!!
I had forgotten to save the teleport spot for the space Outpost into my ship. I searched through my ships navigation program, only to find the nearest gateway to the Outpost was in a completely different solar system. And the only way to get there was by fueling the FTL drive of the ship. And the only way to do that was to go to a moon with no atmosphere to acquire fuel. and the only way to survive that, is by creating an EPP, a deviced used to help you breath in situations without oxygen. I went over to the anvil I had created within the walls of my haunted Japanese mansion and was pleasantly surprised: I had almost everything necesary to create an EPP, except glass. Which of course comes from sand. And I happen to be parked on a planet right next to a desert planet. Huzzah!
I flew on over to my neighboring sphere and prepared to port down to the surface. But wait! I had learned through trial and error at this point, that you can never be too careful. I took my lazer-pistol out and prepared for what awaited me below. I zapped myself down and what do you know: I spawn between two fire-breathing birds in the middle of a desert-bandit camp site. I'm outnumbered and out gunned, and I end up falling down a deep cavern and almost die. But thanks to some quick thinking, I zap back up to the ship, moments before my persuers could land on me and destroy me on impact. I took a deep breath as I recovered health on the safety of my craft. I zapped back down to the camp site to find the bandits still stuck underground! VICTORY!! I collected the sand necesary, snagged some nifty weapons from their loot boxes, and flew myself back to my haunted samurai abode.
I built the epp. I can breath in space. Time to hit the moon.
This part should be easy. Nothing can live on a planet without an atmosphere and i just have to dig on this low gravity moon and get fuel from underground. As I start mining fuel however, the AI of my ship shows signs of entities closing in, attracted to the power of the fuel source I am collecting. Thats when the moon phantoms attacked. Giant purple blobs with arms that kill you swiftly just by touching you. None of my weapons work on them and they fly straight through solid objects. I got just enough fuel before one of the life suckers got me.
I couldn't believe it. Just enough fuel for a round trip to the gateway and back. I sent my ship into Light-speed travel and set up a tent in my ship to recover health during the trip. I like to think of it as casual cryo-sleep. I activated the gateway. Completed the quest. Acquired the tech. Went back to my haunted japanese home with my butler-merchant and sipped margharitas.
10/10  lived a better story than most episodes of star trek for a side-quest. Have fun guys :)

Ongoing review notes for Mind Snares: Alice's Journey...
- lovely graphics
- the music is getting tedious after an hour. It tries to stay dramatic the whole time, and that just isn't working. Dramatic only works in conjunction with non-dramatic. (Update: each chapter seems to have its own soundtrack, and that only applied to the first chapter.)
- nice environments and some intriguing interactions here. Only one of the interactions has made me ask, "WTF was that?" but afterwards i had to admit that it kinda made sense.
- the Damsel in Distress (DiD) vibe is truly creepy. Frustratingly so. i don't, in any way, shape, or form, enjoy the DiD trope except in the context of the "Empowered" comic book series (which exists to poke fun at that trope).
- the protagonist's repeated self-derision just helps drives the DiD vibe home. It's hard to tell if she's supposed to be a victim or a hero, and victimized women is _not_ a theme i care to game.
- all the little female dolls (in many of the scenes), most of them looking like sad, broken victims themselves, is bringing me down. Not sure how much more of that i can take. (Update: they disappear after completing the factory level.)
i like the mechanics, i like the "physical feel," but i truly, deeply, dislike the whole DiD/victim/poor-little-me bit. The physics have a slighly different feel from the 10 or 12 (or so) Atrifex Mundi titles i've played so far, and they developers have done really well with it. The dark victim/DiD tone is making it painful for me to keep up with, though. It's creepy, and not in a fun-creepy kinda way, but more in the, "that man's been staring at that little girl for far too long" kinda creepy.
i'm still undecided but i'm going to give it a Thumb Up because it is, technically speaking, nicely done and a pleasure to play. It's just the tone and thematic elements i'm having trouble accepting as being something i want to play through.
Update: creepy in the extreme. Whoever scripted this is seriously screwed in the head.
Update: after the first chapter, the DiD/victim vibe drops off to essentially zero. That's a good thing. After that point (specifically, after existing the factory) It retains much of its abstract weirdness but drops the creepy imagery/theme.

She has a car crash on the way there. She wakes up in a creepy hospital room, with a creepy hooded man.

Overall this is a typically well-done hidden object adventure from Artifex Mundi.
It's better than a lot of HOGs, but it's not the strongest game from this studio.
The plot sees main character Alice, a dissatisfied office drone, fighting her way through a fantasy world in order to learn how to have confidence in herself and her dreams. As usual for an Artifex game, the art is lovely and vivid, and the puzzles and minigames are solid and well-designed.
The ending is a bit abrupt, and strangely the game begins by revealing that Alice went on to start her own successful business, with the whole game as a sort of flashback explaining how she got the gumption to strike out on her own. That takes some of the suspense (such as it is) out of the story. And to be honest, I would have been happy to just solve the puzzles and explore the fantasy vistas without the framing narrative of Alice's stifling job and her journey toward self-confidence.
Still, can't fault them for trying something different, I guess.
I'd recommend a number of Artifex games ahead of this one. Dark Arcana: The Carnival is a favorite, with a strong story and striking visuals, and Grim Legends 2: Song of the Dark Swan is one of their most compelling and well-made titles. But if you've played those, and the Nightmares from the Deep series, and Enigmatis and Abyss... then I'd also recommend Mind Snares.

Bastion is an awesome piece of work.
While been guided by the teller’s voice, the game takes you through a story of a world after some kind of a catastrophe – “The Calamity”. you will find your way trying to undo the calamity and on the way finding new friends, enemies and truths about the event that almost wiped existence.
The story is very good, and have a big part in the experience, but don’t think that this the only thing in this game!
the gameplay is well planned and executed!
The game can be played by anyone.
it is very fun, smooth and intuitive. the game (or voice guiding you) reacts to the things you do, for example, if you do something again and again - smashing things, falling of the map, checking the mailbox... - you will probably get a comment, which make the game feel more alive in interactive.
but don’t let it fool you, the game can be hard! you can add "Idols" which you unlock during the game, allowing you to raise the difficulty, and award you with more fragments - the game's currency - which are used to upgrade you character.
As you progress, you unlock more weapons, abilities and upgrades to choose from so it fit your playstyle.
the game encourages you to play it more than once, starting again with everything you achieved and max you character in the second time, unlocking more Idols and facing the increasing challenge! (and of course facing the hardest achievements!)
The game is not that long, I really took my time and it took me just less than 30 hours to absolutely do 100% of the game, achievements, ester eggs... everything, and I played it more than twice in the process.
to include: Bastion is very recommended, the story is great, and the gameplay is very fun, even if it’s just for one time, I think you should not miss this gem.

It's no Chaos Theory. But it's much closer to the series' roots than Conviction ever was. Darkness is back (shooting out lights protects your stealth), you have the capability to finish most missions without ever firing a shot (or even engaging anyone besides mission targets), and the weapons 4th Echelon gives you are all suppressed. You CAN pick up unsuppressed weapons, but if you want to preserve the true SC experience, don't do it!
There are linear sequences that feel way too much like Assassin's Creed, and the FPS sequences where you play as Briggs are definitely the low point. Difficulty is on the easy side (too much like AC again), with "death from above" kills and 100% predictable AI (they always spawn in the same spots).
I did like the "Mass Effect" style inter-mission parts where you roam the plane, chat with your team, and upgrade your gear.
Co-op missions (most of which can be played solo, but you can't access certain routes that way) are like Modern Warfare's coop or Halo's spartan assault, except with stealth and alarms. They are pretty fun and lack none of the lame parts seen in the solo campaign.
Overall, I recommend picking this game up on sale. The E3 video previews made this look like a lame action game, but you're given the option (and encouraged to) play super stealthily. Can't say I wouldn't prefer a more Chaos Theory kind of game though!

Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell Blacklist is an Amazing game, no matter what your playing style is. Whether you like to play Full on 4th Echelon stealth mode, The Panther stealth/combat mix, or full on "Screw all of you in the♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; combat mode, it's still a rewarding expeiriece.
Now onto the multiplayer.
Blacklist has an immersive, quick paced, and all around well balanced multiplayer mode called, "Spies versus Mercanaries". There are several game modes, and the cash you earn in multiplayer and in singleplayer intertwines, so if you want to level up Sam Fisher a bit, you can use any cash you earn from playing SVM.
Mercs team: Whilst playing on the Mercanaries team, your camera will be set in the first person, giving you little vision compared to the spies, which I will describe later. However, the Mercanaries have MUCH more powerful weaponry. Having loud and powerful assault riflles, pistols, shotguns, and Submachine Guns limits the little amount of stealth you can have, for the spies can use utilities such as sonar goggles to see a theremal image of you through walls. You start out the game with one class unlocked for each team, similar to Call of Duty.
Spies team: The spies team is much more stealth based, and they have much less lethal weaponry. However, as an advantage over the Mercanaries, the spies have a third person camera angle, and just as much manuverability as Sam Fisher in the single player campaign. They can climb walls, preform stealth kills, climb through ventilation systems, and much more.
As you progress through the multiplayer ranks, you will eventually have enough money to buy the ability to create your own customized class. Although it is pricy to unock this feature, it is still very much so worth it.
For the singleplayer/co-op experiece, however, I have played a good 3-4 hours of, and it has an impressive, and immersive storyline about a group of terrorists called "The Blacklist". The voice acting is outstanding and Eric Johnson makes a great new Sam Fisher, with the same old Rustic voice.
Overall, Ubisoft and the late Tom Clancy did an amazing job with devoloping a game far more impressive than the previous title, "Conviction" R.I.P. Clancy, we'll all miss you.

Die, get detected, anything that compromises the mission and you're back to the beginning in most cases. I can't overstate the sheer frustration this causes for me. I like perfect, stealthy run throughs - I derive my enjoyment from seeing how a situation went wrong and going back to a 'just prior' save to try a different tactic. I don't want to be bumped right back to the beginning, to hear the same conversations, to trudge through the same hallways just to get to where I was. It's limiting and non-sensical to ditch a quicksave function in a stealth game.
Next up, the controls. No longer can you control the speed at which Sam moves with the mousewheel. Keyboard controls (although admittedly they can be mapped), do not feel intuitive. Sam feels clunky, a little on rails. The contextual actions he performs are jarring, sometimes unwelcome; mean to open that door instead of head into cover? It's 50/50 what will happen. I wanted to leapfrog a railing by a door, and instead booted it open in front of a small army all curious as to who this suicidal maniac was. It feels clumsy, and in a Splinter Cell game clumsy is something that will deal break everything.
So what about combat? Admittedly, I'm a stealth nut, I avoid it. But even I get bummed out when, after not being seen across the map in perfect shadow, the body I drag back to the same (seemingly hidden) location is located as if it had flashing neon lights on it. In fact, I *do* have flashing neon lights on me and I wasn't spotted in the same location....but the body was. It's that kind of lazy gameplay that kills this for me.
I love Splinter Cell. Adore it even. But something has been removed here and what's left doesn't feel like a Splinter Cell game. It doesn't have the same polish, the same sleekness or the same atmosphere.....hell, it doesn't have the same soul. I can see what Ubisoft have tried to do, and for the life of me I can't work out why it hasn't worked, but it hasn't. I can't figure out how this game got good reviews from fans of the genre, so the possibility exists that this is just my problem and not the game. But somehow I trust my gut and this game simply has not gripped me yet. I hope it does.

Dragon's Dogma is a great open world action RPG that lacks only one thing: good storytelling. The story itself is pretty good (there are even some twists), as are the dialogues and characters. But the storytelling - it's bad. Almost Skyrim bad.
The game is immersive and atmospheric, I swear no other game has ever made me feel like I'm in Middle-earth or Faerûn as much as DD does.
The gameplay is also top-notch. Even running around, jumping and climbing things is fun. And then there's combat. Fast, responsive, different for each class. Plus, you can climb bigger monsters to reach their weak points, not unlike what you do in Shadow of the Colossus but simpler.
The pawn system. After creating your own character, you also make one party member - a pawn - who will follow you throughout the game. Then you can hire up to two other players' pawns. Of course, they also can hire yours. Pawns don't physically disappear from their creators' side when they are hired and can be present in many "worlds" simultaneously. At the same time pawns learn many different things, like tactics agains specific monsters.
Normally I like premade party members with personalities and backstories, but the pawn system is so well executed, I can't help but like it anyway. For something so complicated it's really close to perfection.
The port is surprisingly good and well optimised. You can easily finish the game using either keyboard+mouse or a controller. I'd even say kb+m is arguably better when playing classes that need to aim, like ranger and magick archer.
Dragon's Dogma is not only a must-play for anyone who likes fantasy and/or action RPGs, it's also an amazing, innovative and
game that everyone should at least try playing.

87 (satisfying) gameplay hours later, after finishing the game, I feel the need to write a review, mostly in answer to those negative ones I keep seeing.
Is this a perfect game? No. Is this as good as Planescape: Torment or Baldur's Gate 2? No. Does it have bugs? Yes. But none of that matters much. It is a great game, a worthy successor to the above two, and a great experience. I recommend buying it at full cost, if only to show there is a market for such titles.
At some point, maybe sooner than the teased expansions, I will start a new playthrough as there's much I would like to try differently.
Some highlights below.
The good:
+ An actual roleplaying experience, with choice and consequence (though not all as direct as some would like them). It offers many ways to walk the path of a Watcher.
+ Well crafted characters, though interacting with them is not quite as fulfilling as BG2 or Planescape: Torment.
+ A fully realized world - it's impressive how much detail went into building it from scratch, this feels so much palpable than, for instance, the world of Dragon Age after 3 games.
+ Strategic combat - you will be forced to think your way through battles and use different approaches, as it sort of difficult even on normal.
+ Enough content to keep you occupied for a long time (at 87 hours I estimate my overall completion at 90%).
+ A lot of nostalgia used right - this IS the heir of those great Infinity engine games that still hold up today.
+ Many of the side quests are interesting, some more so than the main story.
+ Some of those walls of text are beautifully written. You will enjoy reading them as much as reading a good book.
The bad:
- Party AI - I was left scratching my head on more than one occasion as some of my party members just stood there while the others got slaughtered. Pathfinding seems slightly problematic in close quarters combat and you WILL have to keep an eye on such idle hands, as they rarely seem to auto engage other targets.
- I was left wondering how Obsidian decided which dialog should be voiced and which should not. I often saw less important bits voiced, and the more important ones were silent.
- I did feel the need at times for some modern RPG bits: comparing items while in a shop, changing party members without traveling to my stronghold, camera rotation was sometimes missed (this could easily be prevented through design), some issues with the interface (you'll notice most of these are minor)
- The level 12 cap seems slightly low, at least considering I hit it with about 80% game completion and with the left over experience I could have leveled at least 2 more times.
- Story - while it isn't bad, by any means, it's definitely a retread of the old "stop a bad guy" cliche. I will admit it does throw a few curve balls along the way, but it isn't enough to escape its mediocrity. Luckily the overall lore does balance it out.

Highly repetitive game with minimal ways to go about combat. Story is lackluster.
Gameplay:
Hit 'attack' over and over whilst being surround by enemies. Occasionally block the one attack an enemy orc throws at you. Pull off an 'execution' move when your combo-meter fills up. Repetitive, is what it feels like. Sure there's stealth, branding, a bow, but it all feels lackluster with content. There's not much you can do; especially after completing the story. Heck, I play it when I'm bored and feel like running around stabbing people, because that's all there is to do outside of the simplistic methods they use to intrigue you about the game. "You can ride these monster things!" ~You can, but after completing an objective which allows you to ride beasts, it quickly becomes boring. At first, you're like "Oh, yes! I did it!" But after, you don't really think about it. Nothing seems to surprise or amaze me in terms of gameplay, especially during the story missions. It feels 'expected'. The tension just isn't there.
Story:
Simply, you're out for revenge against 'the dark lord' Sauron, and to do this you go about missions and meet people along the way. There are only two maps for this game. (Technically more if you count the intro and the places you're only able to visit once) No, that's literally it.
I'd recommend this game when it goes on sale, if you feel like playing something to pass the time. It's not too frustrating, but it can be fun to toy around with the mechanics after a while. You might learn something new. Whilst the gameplay is limited, it's certainly fun to find new ways to play. But again it gets boring quickly because once you know how the enemies work in this game, battles become predictable. There's not really much of a challenge, you could easily breeze through this in some hours.

This is one of the best TWs ever made. After Rome II disaster CA managed to craft game with unique design. It has its flaws, but its very deep with great combat, many factions to choose from, different culture groups that affects building and tech trees and the way they are played. Even Eastern Roman Empire is different then Western. Graphics look good, but game has some problems with optimalization, which can make even good computers stutter in larger battles.
I loved how the economical aspect of the game was made. Player need to balance between squalor, penalty order and food, governors effects has been improved and specialization for each region is desirable. For example provinces with high fertility will be main sources of food for the empires and kingdoms, coastal provinces could provide currency from trade and so on. Diplomacy is manageable. There is no more massive war declaration against the player from distant factions. Mantaining good diplomatic relations is vital to kingdom safety.
Political part of the game has been improved but its still not on the level of games like Crusader Kings 2. However now it has sense, in contrary to Rome II. Developers added some new mechanics like Hordes and playing as those migrating factions is really interesting and very different to stationary ones.

I love games that Artifex Mundi publishes, but this one intrigued me more than most. The story was actually remarkably good for a hidden object game, voice acting was superb, and the puzzles were challenging without being infuriating. The hand-painted graphics are up to the usual quality that I expect from modern hidden object games, and the music always felt appropriate.
I also appreciated that the Steam Achievements were not designed to artificially increase the difficulty, extend gameplay by trying to make you play the hardest level, or force a second run-through with that alternate-puzzle scheme that Artifex Mundi sometimes employs. All of the achievements can be done in one play through regardless of the difficulty level.
If I have any complaint, it would be that the ending is too abrupt. The game is actually a flashback to a story that is being relayed to a newspaper reporter; but when the ending is reached, the game goes right into the credits. There is no satisfactory resolution to explain why the story took place, nor was there any kind of cutscene in the present to close out the interview. Was it all a dream/nightmare? Was it a halluicination? Was she really magically deleported to some alternate reality? Maybe there is a sequel in the works; but if there's not, the ending leaves much to be desired.
The game can be completed in less than three hours, so the normal price might be a bit high for some. Those who equate value with the length of time it takes to play a game might want to pick this up on a Steam sale or a 3rd party bundle/indie site.
Regardless of the ending or the (potentially) short game time, this is one of the better hidden object games out there and it worthy of your time.
