Original review:
I bought this game in a bundle, so I have paid just a little. It was recommended to me by friend with whom I played Master Sword (semi-broken HL1 mod). Compared to that this game is not broken at all... However it is a stand alone game so:
1. It's incredibly funny, especially in the beginning when you try to figure everything out and struggle for resources. I find it more intuitive (simpler) than RUST and other games.
2. I like the mechanics, gathering resources, killing animals in order to produce better equipment and then travel to next island and start again gathering better ores and producing more powerful weapons
3. It is not hard game at all, with 6-8 hours (if you are completely new) you can get very decent gear and then you are left to kill a dragon 30 times to produce the best gear.
... and here is where the trouble starts. Dragon is not powerful at all and you can solo him easily. As it is the most powerful creature in game, there is the end. You get the best gear and you have literally nothing much to do. Not speaking about broken spawn points at the moment, meaning game doesn't run properly (you cannot get certain items because of this bug).
Overall I think it has a great potential, it's funny, it's about mining and crafting and you can kill a dragon! What I would like to see is more content and maybe creatures that are not easy kills even with the best weapons. Also it has a great community in general, people try to help each other and explain how the game works.

It still needs some work, but like other games like Kenshi who went from a buggy sandbox to a very beautiful and working (but heavy) game, the designers will get there eventually. Took many months to Kenshi to become worthy of its price, so I think this game should also takes many months before it is a good action-adventure game worthy of its price.
Just wait a couple more months and it will be better.
I can only recommand it to people who are patient and want to help in designing a game with bug reports, suggestions, etc.
Otherwise, wait until it is finished. I WIll change it to recommanded once it is polished, bug-free and finished.

So I recently bought this game for both me and a friend. We're getting into game design and we're checking out a lot of games to sort of brain storm and figure what to do and what not to do. As of currently I have almost 100 hours into this game as I'm writing this. I bought this game a couple weeks ago and I have to say... for an Alpha... this game is light years beyond anything I've seen before. Sure it's got a lot of similar elements to it that other survival games have but... this game runs really smoothly (aside from this newest update #40, the optimization attempts have actually made the performance of my game worse, please fix; fps drops) (also plz fix buggy vehicles. they seem very sensitive to rough terrain).
I've had more fun in this game with my friend than any other game I have in my library aside from Dirty Bomb. I could literally spend hours and hours on this game... gathering resources, weapons, crafting recipes, building bases, fixing up vehicles, raiding bases, and a lot more. This game needs a few adjustments to mechanics like being able to go prone, or molotovs doing damage against wood structures but all in all... I am very happy and satisfied with the $20 I spent to get me and my friend into this. I've run across a lot of people in this game 9/10ths of which are not friendly and will kill on sight, or pretend to be friendly unless you try to run away.
But there have been a few nice people I've run into and they compared this game to dayz but not the comparison you would expect. People say that this game is actually more put together than DayZ and feels a lot better. Also again, bringing it up... this game ran beautifully before this most current update. I rarely had FPS drops even in the heat of surviving against pvp players. I've survived probably a total of 30 hours in this game and counting, I have one of the rarest weapons in the game complete with ammo, and a scope (sniper rifle; M40). So ignore anyone who says it's basically impossible to find one... I've found 3 M40's 4 sniper scopes and 3 M40 magazines and a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of ammo for it. It's all about being smart with your resources and frequenting places you know to have weapons/ammo.
So yeah! That's my feedback for this game... please for the love of everything... dev's... keep up the good work, this game is absolutely fantastic and I've just bought my THIRD copy of Miscreated to hopefully get ANOTHER friend to play this with me. Also if you guys haven't already check out this months Humble Bundle(Jumbo Bundle 7), if you pay $10.00 or more you get a bunch of games (Miscreated is one of them) and there's even more games to be added! ($172 worth) plus it all goes to a good cause. Game on guys! Hope you enjoy this as much as I do!

An improvement in almost every way over 2010's Splinter Cell: Conviction, Splinter Cell: Blacklist is a perfect start to a catalogue of games from the new Ubisoft Toronto Studio. In fact, it's as best a start the studio could get, as this game is a shining example of supporting player choice, enabling player freedom, and making each level look and feel like a huge sandbox, from start to finish, where your actions may have consequences, but ultimately, YOU are the Splinter Cell, you take control and handle the mess you create.
Possibly one of the most exciting multiplayer experiences to date, SvM makes a return in Blacklist, pitting spies against mercs in the most satisfying way since Chaos Theory made the mode popular. A series of different game modes, some even with non-asymetrical teams, makes for endlessly exciting and fun multiplayer match ups, where quick thinking and team work throughout each game will make each victory earned, and you'll just keep coming back for more!
Yes, this game isn't Chaos Theory in any respect, but in many ways, I see this as a technological reboot for the franchise, showing us as gamers what we can expect from the stealth genre, at least within the SC franchise, and giving us an opportunity to just ponder over how much the excellent gameplay can evolve even more, to top Blacklist's, and form possibly the best stealth experience ever found in gaming, but within the SC franchise in the future! :)

I like where this game is heading. It's like Rust meets Minecraft meets Castaway as a single-player game. But....
Improvements I see needed would be (at least) a few additions to crafting. There's no bow and arrow. No fishing pole. No way to build boxes or shelves to keep your things in and there's a limited number of "backpack" slots. But there are the tools necessary to make all these things already available in-game. Lashing could be made into additional backpack slots. Sticks and lashing could make a fishing pole or bow. Sticks and stone shards could make arrows. Most of all, you need stone to create a number of things, but there's a limited number of stones available per island and no way to break bigger boulders down into stones. It makes your world incredibly limited and and in no way renewable, leading me to my next qualm.
Reading through "Current Features" they make it seem like there's a way to maintain your island, but there's nothing like this. There's no way to grow your own plants. So when you cut down a palm tree, it's gone forever. There's no way to use a green coconut to generate a new one, even those these coconuts are available in-game. When you cut down a potato plant, there's no way to grow more potatoes using one of the 3 potatoes you just harvested. The only resource that regrows is yucca, which allows you to make lashing. But what's the use of lashing if you're limited in everything else. Okay, you have rope, but no other resources with which to use the rope. Might as well drown yourself.
I understand this is early access, but devs need to step up their game a little to keep me interested. I don't recommend this game until these things get fixed, otherwise you're just waiting to run out of resources and die within a week (in-game time). No sense in paying money for something that's not geared to the survivor's favor.

I saw that Dragon's Dogma was in the December Humble Monthly and I had some interest in the game, so I jumped on it for $10.80 with a few other games.  I wound up finishing the game at 53 hours and finishing the postgame to unlock New Game Plus at 65.  I played the game with the Xbox 360 controller only.  I took my time, but I didn't complete all of the quests or even touch Bitterblack Isle (DLC area).  I played a little of each class but stuck mostly with Strider/Assassin.
Life in Cassardis is pretty nice as a fisherman.  The days pass by in absolute peace and you couldn't be happier.  And then one day, a dragon attacks your village and you feebly attempt to fight it off, only to get your heart ripped out of your chest for your trouble.  But you don't die.  You become something more than human, an Arisen, an ageless but not immortal being challenged by the dragon to reclaim your heart.  But along the way, there are many people who need help, and what better way to sharpen one's skills than slaying countless monsters and taking their loot?
Dragon's Dogma is a third-person action RPG.  To me, it felt a little like a mishmash of elements from The Elder Scrolls, Dark Souls, Shadow of the Colossus, and even Phantasy Star Online.  It still manages to stand as a unique product all the same, though.  The game takes place in a wide-open sandbox like TES, the combat is weighty like Dark Souls, there is climbing on giant enemies like SotC, and the team aspect reminds me of PSO though your allies are all AI-controlled.  You jump, you swing your weapon, you'll probably get knocked down, stunlocked, and die a few times starting out.  What I liked about the world was that enemies don't scale, like in Morrowind or Dark Souls.  If you go to an area you aren't meant to be in for a while, you'll certainly feel it in the encounters.  But on the other hand, you'll eventually hit a point where you overpower your enemies.
Health had an interesting mechanic I've only seen in fighting games prior--a recoverable damage portion of the bar.  You have a green health bar, representing your current health, and when you take damage, you may have some white health bar, which represents how much magic and some other effects can heal you.  Grey/black bar is completely gone and can only be restored with items, resting, and some other things.  If you have a healer and neglect to take any restoratives, you can still be whittled to death, so keep that in mind.  Stamina governs all skill use, be it weapon or magic, as well as sprinting, clinging to giant enemies, holding objects/enemies/other people, and so on.  Thankfully, you can sprint infinitely in safe areas, so that's a very nice touch.  A weight meter pops up whenever you cross the next weight category threshold, and it's visible at all times when you're looking at the inventory.
Sword, bow, or magic?  There are nine Vocations in DD, and they're all based around these archetypes and combinations of them.  A Fighter uses a sword and board to safely approach and dispatch enemies, while its advanced version Warrior uses only two-hander weapons to destroy enemies, and a hybrid Magick Knight can cast party-wide buffs and attack at range with unique spells as well as knock some heads in melee.  Each Vocation has nine ranks which determines the active skills and passive boons you can buy and equip, and each Vocation also adds a specific amount of points to your stats when you level up, so there is some potential for min-maxing.  You cannot sculpt an entirely-unique character out of all the skills you learn--for example, even though your Fighter can use a sword like the Assassin, you cannot use their Gouge ability.  Passive skills at least do transfer over, so there is still some flexibility to be had.
Your Pawn is able to use six of the nine classes and they can learn and use skills exactly the same as you do.  You get to design your hero and their stalwart ally, the latter of whom will learn from your actions and attempt to act as you do when it comes to combat and other actions--this can be both good and bad, understandably.  Breaking off of combat to go pick flowers could result in your Pawn doing the same, just the same as clearing out the goblins escorting a cyclops first .  Monkey see, monkey do.  You are also able to hire two additional Pawns created by other players, though you've no impact nor control over their behavior or skills.  This is the most prevalent online aspect to the game (the other being an instanced fight against an optional superboss) and it's kinda neat to see how other people have built their helper, not only in appearance, but skills, behavior, and personality.
A neat thing about the character builder is that the features have a gameplay impact.  Apart from character height affecting hitbox, short and tall characters climb at different speeds, much like how a heavy character burns through (and recovers) stamina slower than a beanpole character, but they also don't flop around as much when a monster tries to shake them off while climbing.  Which is more important to you--stats or appearance?  You have specific things like faces and noses and eye shapes, and you can somewhat fine-tune them with sliders, like eyeball spacing or eyebrow height.  You're only able to pick hair/eye/skin color from a list as opposed to setting RGB values, but few games allow the latter.  There is a pretty wide variety of equipment for a number of slots:  Head, torso clothing, torso armor, leg clothing, leg armor, arms, a cloak, and two unseen jewelry slots.  Almost everything provides some modicum of defense, though some people would rather try to make an attractive ensemble out of the gear their class can use.
The game repeatedly warns to be careful out in the wild during its loading screen tips, and it's not kidding.  While you are able to pause the game and spam health restores when things go poorly, you can't expect to do this and win every fight.  Part of combat is watching enemies and knowing when to block or dodge and when to strike back, but also striking to stagger or knockdown foes.  This applies mostly to the melee classes, but ranged classes need to make use of positioning and knowing where the enemies are, so one can't sneak up and interrupt your spell.  One neat thing is that you can actually grapple several non-giant foes that are staggered or downed--you can either pick them up direct to toss off a cliff for an easy kill, or hold them fast so your allies can get free shots while your opponent is vulnerable.  And your Pawns will do these too, so pay attention and work together to efficiently cut through everything in your way.  Just remember that even with a lantern, nights are still incredibly dark and spawns change depending on the time of day.
When it comes to big monsters, you and your allies can and are encouraged to climb them, to gain better access to a weak point, to have a way to damage it even while it moves across the battlefield, or just to keep yourself safe from its attacks.  These fights are really where the teamwork aspect of the game shines.  You might climb on top of an armored cyclops to remove its helmet so your bow-using Pawns can drill its eye with arrows.  You might have a Mage pawn enchant your weapons with fire, which you then use to knock a griffon out of the sky by setting its wings on fire.  You might also hold on for dear life while the thing you're clinging to rages, pausing to replenish your dwindling stamina.  And the battle music changing as you've got the beast on its last legs is a nice touch too.  The controls are the only really bad part because it turns into tank controls (left/right to turn as opposed to move left/right) and it can be difficult to tell which way you're moving sometimes.
Steam's cutting me off, but I really did enjoy the game despite me overhyping it!

I want to keep this one short.
As far as the Dark souls series goes, this game is up there with 3 as my favorite in the lore portion. There are also a lot of memorable NPCs and good, branching questlines. The weapon selection is good, and you can really do whatever in the game and be effective. There's a lot to love about this game. The level design is great (mostly), and there are a decent amount of unique and memorable bossfights, all with their own strategies.
There are a few noticable negatives, though. Netcode is bad, so don't bother playing online. The combat/rolling mechanic is by far the worst in the series. There are some pretty wonky hitboxes at times, and there's too much luck based platforming in a game not designed for it. Some boss fights are horribly designed, and even if you know what you're doing, you're going to have a hard time with them *coughbedofchaoscough*. If you played 2 or 3 before this and are interested, it might be easier to just watch some damn vids of the lore because the combat is so horrendously clunky and outdated at this point.
I'm going to give this game a recommend, because I think it's a great game (played all the way through on xbox), but be prepared for some frustration.

When you're not stuck gawping at the title screen, Supergiant Games delivers a uniquely crafted universe and stunning graphical masterpiece coupled with a perfectly tuned mix of music (the soundtrack is a must listen in sincere opinion) that evokes a mood of the west.
Outside of certain methods of difficulty amplification, the mechanics and difficulty are straight forward and obligatory rather than forcibly complex. The gameplay is clean, simplistic and polished and the accompanying story that is narrated by an enthralling and husky voice that is no less exemplar than that of Darkest Dungeon's.
A forewarning, levels and challenges in the Map are not able to be repeated/revisitable upon full completion out of a singular exception.
For a typical playthrough it spans no more than a few several hours (10 at most), but notably there are very few choices to make that contribute directly to the story, the game however paces itself well. Small bits of explorative dialogue are linked and crammed into every nook and cranny of the game and further pushes the boundaries of the crafting of world by introducing and transitioning through scenery and locations extremely smoothly. Quite literally, your steps build the world.
All in all, if you want a game achieves the sublimal balance between wondrous asethetics, charming story and characters and awesome gameplay, Bastion is just about the game for everyone to go with and is worth every bit of your cent and time invested.
However ultimately, like the game, it is up to you to draw your own conclusion.

The game is simply  fun and addictive. However, it doesn't last long, especially if you're like me where you play to win and then toss the game to the side when you're done. After completing the story in about 12 or so hours, I haven't logged back into the game. The gameplay and mechanics are great. Everything runs fairly smooth and keeps you busy with randomized side quests while trying to follow the story. The story itself is a little weak and as mentioned before, short. It's nothing fancy, just basic cut scenes. There times where the story pauses in the game where you seem to be doing side quests for a while until randomly the story picks up again. It's not a bad thing however since you can use that time to gather supplies. There also is apparently a simulated timed feature for when you log out of the game. When you log back in, you may notice your stronghold needs supplies or new random jobs appeared. I didn't really experience this as I played most my hours consecutively. I do think this feature stinks though if you are a casual player since you'd be spending the first half an hour of your game time just doing supply runs and keeping your stronghold hoard free.
In conclusion, the game is fun and it feels complete, but I do wish the story had A LOT more to it. Not only in length, but production value. I do recommend, but wait for a deal!

Disclaimer: While I'm pretty sure I received a key from the developer to review this game, I can't find any trace of such a thing happening. I suppose I'll find out once I publish this review.
Tricone Lab is an original puzzle game, with a novel mechanic and subject matter. Tricone Lab is set in the inside of a cell (of an organism, not a jail), as you can tell by the screenshots, and it is this that gives rise to the gameplay.
Players must use the tricone enzymes to create tricone molecules using one each of a red, green, and blue cone. (The game has a colourblind mode if you're colourblind.) Further, cell walls can be broken with breaker enzymes to allow the tricone molecules to pass; the interferer enzyme steals your cones, not allowing them to be linked to a tricone enzyme; and to counteract this, there is the builder enzyme, which builds walls. There are other mechanics, of course, but these should allow for a short explanation as to what the game is about.
The control scheme is simple; just click and drag. The puzzles are nice, though I'm not entirely convinced that they explore the puzzle space very well. (Then again, I last played this game last year, so it's probably changed quite a fair bit since then, so why am I even writing a review?). Regardless, the unique theme that Tricone Lab brings to the table definitely forces one to think quite differently from most other puzzles, and for this I've put it into my list of recommended puzzle games.
Also, the game has a level editor. Pretty sure it also has a catalogue of fanmade levels, though again, I forget.
Man, I really need to review games just after I've played them. Hmm.

Published by: Partickhill Games Limited
Developed by: Partickhill Games Limited
Genre: Puzzle
Release Date: November 13, 2015
Time to complete: 10+ hours*
*Based on statistics from dev; 10 hours average completion time, 6 hours for those good at puzzles and 30 hours average maximum for the
You are also able to make your own puzzles and download levels that other players have made.
Tricone Lab is a minimalist puzzle game where you create tricone molecules within a cell structure by bringing 3 coloured cones together with a tricone catalyst.
Breakers and catalysts and cones (oh my!). Tricone Lab exceeded my expectations. I opened up the game hoping to kill an hour or so with a few puzzles, and couldn’t turn the damn thing off! It’s challenging but also rewarding when you finally crack a puzzle you’ve been stuck on for a while. There are 23 maps with 100 puzzles in total, each level having varying difficulty. In the earlier stage of the maps, the puzzles are pretty straightforward, being more about the basic understanding of how to use the different components within the cell. As you proceed, more resources are introduced, and you really have to think to work out the specific sequence that must be used. After completing some maps you unlock ‘keys’, which enable you to unlock the harder maps that contain the same new resources as the map you just completed.
Though the base game is amazing as it is, there’s also the ability to download maps that other players have created, and even create your own (I really like that this option is available).
I’m by no means an avid puzzler, but I do enjoy the odd brain teaser once in a while. The maps are pretty straightforward; once you grasp the concept of how to use all the resources, you’ll probably find that it really is very simple. When there are multiple components within the cell to use, it can be pretty challenging to work out the sequence (there is however the option to skip puzzles if you’re finding them too difficult). I found that in the puzzles I was really stuck on, it was just a matter of looking at them in a different way; thinking ‘outside the box’ so to speak.
In terms of the base game, I don’t think there’s any real replay value; once you’ve completed the puzzles and know how they work, there’s no point playing them again. This is mainly because each puzzle has only the one solution. Once the sequence has been worked out, it will lose it’s challenge the next time you play it. Despite this, you can still download maps that other players have made (as I mentioned earlier), so you can always check back and see if there are new puzzles to crack!
The achievements can be obtained through completing the maps and also gaining the keys (essentially learning how to use a new resource).
Tricone Lab is seriously well made. I was never really interested in minimalist games, but this one is just fantastic. It’s addictive, deceptively simple and a great way to either binge play (which I’m totally guilty of) or just do a puzzle or two here and there. It’s pretty decently priced honestly, and for what you get I couldn’t recommend it more.

Partickhill Games brings us Tricone Lab, a deceivingly simple, quasi-minimalist looking puzzle game that will make you use all your lateral thinking abilities in order to proceed though the increasingly difficult levels.
In Tricone Lab you interact with microscopic organisms in what appears to be a cellular-like environment. Your goal? To create as many “tricones” as the level needs to let you proceed. Tricones are created by joining three colored cones (red, green and blue) into a master template, but several things will get in your way: not only the membranes, but also other organisms that might either aid or hinder you in your quest to complete the levels.
The graphics of the game might be quite simple, but there’s a certain charm to the simplicity of the game, and I greatly appreciate the almost monochrome tonality of most of the game, for these type of puzzle games tend to end up in bright colors to make up for the lack of “proper” graphics. Not here! The graphic style seems to fit perfect with the game.
The music and sounds are pretty good, almost relaxing, I rather enjoyed them even if I kept them at a very low level.
Playing it is simple enough – you mostly will use your mouse to connect things and navigate, but there are also keyboard shortcuts should you not want to go entirely with the mouse.
The levels, as I’ve already stated, appear to be quite simple when you begin, but as you progress they get increasingly difficult, and often times I would get stuck by not thinking things through properly before launching into what looked like a simple puzzle, but ended up being something more… even when the difficulty was marked as low. So the game really makes you pay attention to what you’re doing.
There are neither tips nor guides in-game (there are tutorials though, like with every puzzle game, introducing you what new items do), though I’ve found often the level names are tips on their own.
As you get through the levels you will unlock keys that will allow you to open even more levels for a whooping total of 100. Yes, you read that right. Tricone Lab boasts of 100+ levels, and if that were not enough for you, they also have a level editor. You can upload any maps you create with it, and others will be able to play them. Can you see the possibilities here? I can.
And the game is still in development!
Tricone Labs is an entertaining, challenging game that, although it might not be a graphical masterpiece, is truly worth your time. I’m the kind of person that gets easily frustrated with games, and I have to say, while I did get stuck here and there, Tricone was never stressful nor frustrating to play through.
Do I recommend it? It’s a sound YES! You’re sure not to regret the purchase.

Note before starting. The creator of the game gave this to me to try it out, but did NOT solicit a review.
I have played this I would say about half way through, so I have seen most (but not all) of the puzzle mechanics on their own, but I have only worked with them together for a little bit. From what I have seen, the game is very smooth and very clever. The game even contains what I would call convenience features that allow you to shortcut some procedures that could become tedious.
The gameplay is structured into discrete areas that, at the beginning, are dedicated to one mechanic each. If you have played The Witness, you will be familiar with this elegant style of introducing puzzle elements. As you complete these areas you earn a symbol that allows you to unlock other areas requiring that mechanic. So, as you complete multiple areas other areas open that require several of those mechanics to solve. Once I really got playing, the design and mechanics were so rock solid that I forgot it was supposed to be early access. I also appreciated that there the system for how things work remains consistent and true to what you have learned, but there are a few twists along the way that require you to experiment and think outside the box.
So, when I say that I have completed half of the game, it is only by level count. With most of the mechanics under my belt, the levels are ramping up in difficulty rapidly. So, if you feel that you are breezing through the game easily, wait... your time will come.
All in all, a truly excellent effort very worth adding to your library even if you are not a puzzle junky. Just don't expect to finish it quickly.

Tricone lab is a puzzle game in which the goal is to connect three different colored cones into one tricone via a catalyst. Simply connect the pieces and you're done! Well, there are obstacles that make this a bit more difficult and tools you can use to circumvent them. The cell walls, borders, require
to carry each cone over or
to destroy the walls. These in term require their own parts to be connected to their own respected constructor catalysts and built before you can use them. There are more of these gadgets you can use, all of course after you build them, if there are enough resources floating around for that given puzzle of course.
Gameplay is well thought out and features an indirect approach to puzzle solving, requiring the player to gradually build up to the solution and crack the puzzle. Such a design choice equates to very satisfying and addictive puzzle solving.
Everything in the game is well presented to the player in a non obvious tutorial style so the player is familiar with every mechanic. Every map beaten awards the player with a key (and an achievement) representing their understanding of that mechanic. These keys are then in term used to access certain maps thus ensuring one can't play any puzzles using mechanics one does not understand.
Technically, the game runs fine and is without any performance issues. I did not run into any bugs. There is an easy to use level editor available and community designed puzzles can easily be downloaded and played. Artistically I did get tired of the grey and white color scheme quickly but for a one man dev team to accomplish such a well polished product, I can not complain. Took me 7 hours to beat the included 100 levels.

Disclaimer: I was given a key by the developer due to my having enjoyed other, similar games, which was a first for me, and was pretty cool. :) No request was made in exchange for this key other than general beta-level feedback. This review is simply because I genuinely enjoyed the game.
Tricone Lab is a 2D puzzle game where you seek to create a certain number of "tricones" by joining three individually cones into a catalyst. A variety of obstacles may be in your way, whether barriers, other catalyzers which will steal the cones, or needing to transport/clone/etc various tools in order to establish the final set of cones necessary in the proper location. A few of the levels are quite difficult, but there's an excellent series of tutorial levels which ramp the difficulty in a way that allows you to explore each newly-introduced mechanic.
The game is still in early access, and there's a few known bugs on the forum which are getting ironed out, but none of the ones which I ran into are gamebreaking or mess with the experience whatsoever - typically a graphical glitch, or the like, which can be solved by reloading the level.
The game has a complete set of authoring tools, allowing users to create their own levels which can be shared via the Tricone Labs website.
All in all, it took me roughly 5 hours to complete all the levels that came with the game, and it left me wanting more - I'm actually trying my hand at making a level or two right now, which is something I practically never do, and as I got the game for free, I bought an extra copy to gift to a friend, which is some of the highest praise I can offer. If you enjoy puzzle games, this is likely right up your alley.

I saw that Dragon's Dogma was in the December Humble Monthly and I had some interest in the game, so I jumped on it for $10.80 with a few other games.  I wound up finishing the game at 53 hours and finishing the postgame to unlock New Game Plus at 65.  I played the game with the Xbox 360 controller only.  I took my time, but I didn't complete all of the quests or even touch Bitterblack Isle (DLC area).  I played a little of each class but stuck mostly with Strider/Assassin.
Life in Cassardis is pretty nice as a fisherman.  The days pass by in absolute peace and you couldn't be happier.  And then one day, a dragon attacks your village and you feebly attempt to fight it off, only to get your heart ripped out of your chest for your trouble.  But you don't die.  You become something more than human, an Arisen, an ageless but not immortal being challenged by the dragon to reclaim your heart.  But along the way, there are many people who need help, and what better way to sharpen one's skills than slaying countless monsters and taking their loot?
Dragon's Dogma is a third-person action RPG.  To me, it felt a little like a mishmash of elements from The Elder Scrolls, Dark Souls, Shadow of the Colossus, and even Phantasy Star Online.  It still manages to stand as a unique product all the same, though.  The game takes place in a wide-open sandbox like TES, the combat is weighty like Dark Souls, there is climbing on giant enemies like SotC, and the team aspect reminds me of PSO though your allies are all AI-controlled.  You jump, you swing your weapon, you'll probably get knocked down, stunlocked, and die a few times starting out.  What I liked about the world was that enemies don't scale, like in Morrowind or Dark Souls.  If you go to an area you aren't meant to be in for a while, you'll certainly feel it in the encounters.  But on the other hand, you'll eventually hit a point where you overpower your enemies.
Health had an interesting mechanic I've only seen in fighting games prior--a recoverable damage portion of the bar.  You have a green health bar, representing your current health, and when you take damage, you may have some white health bar, which represents how much magic and some other effects can heal you.  Grey/black bar is completely gone and can only be restored with items, resting, and some other things.  If you have a healer and neglect to take any restoratives, you can still be whittled to death, so keep that in mind.  Stamina governs all skill use, be it weapon or magic, as well as sprinting, clinging to giant enemies, holding objects/enemies/other people, and so on.  Thankfully, you can sprint infinitely in safe areas, so that's a very nice touch.  A weight meter pops up whenever you cross the next weight category threshold, and it's visible at all times when you're looking at the inventory.
Sword, bow, or magic?  There are nine Vocations in DD, and they're all based around these archetypes and combinations of them.  A Fighter uses a sword and board to safely approach and dispatch enemies, while its advanced version Warrior uses only two-hander weapons to destroy enemies, and a hybrid Magick Knight can cast party-wide buffs and attack at range with unique spells as well as knock some heads in melee.  Each Vocation has nine ranks which determines the active skills and passive boons you can buy and equip, and each Vocation also adds a specific amount of points to your stats when you level up, so there is some potential for min-maxing.  You cannot sculpt an entirely-unique character out of all the skills you learn--for example, even though your Fighter can use a sword like the Assassin, you cannot use their Gouge ability.  Passive skills at least do transfer over, so there is still some flexibility to be had.
Your Pawn is able to use six of the nine classes and they can learn and use skills exactly the same as you do.  You get to design your hero and their stalwart ally, the latter of whom will learn from your actions and attempt to act as you do when it comes to combat and other actions--this can be both good and bad, understandably.  Breaking off of combat to go pick flowers could result in your Pawn doing the same, just the same as clearing out the goblins escorting a cyclops first .  Monkey see, monkey do.  You are also able to hire two additional Pawns created by other players, though you've no impact nor control over their behavior or skills.  This is the most prevalent online aspect to the game (the other being an instanced fight against an optional superboss) and it's kinda neat to see how other people have built their helper, not only in appearance, but skills, behavior, and personality.
A neat thing about the character builder is that the features have a gameplay impact.  Apart from character height affecting hitbox, short and tall characters climb at different speeds, much like how a heavy character burns through (and recovers) stamina slower than a beanpole character, but they also don't flop around as much when a monster tries to shake them off while climbing.  Which is more important to you--stats or appearance?  You have specific things like faces and noses and eye shapes, and you can somewhat fine-tune them with sliders, like eyeball spacing or eyebrow height.  You're only able to pick hair/eye/skin color from a list as opposed to setting RGB values, but few games allow the latter.  There is a pretty wide variety of equipment for a number of slots:  Head, torso clothing, torso armor, leg clothing, leg armor, arms, a cloak, and two unseen jewelry slots.  Almost everything provides some modicum of defense, though some people would rather try to make an attractive ensemble out of the gear their class can use.
The game repeatedly warns to be careful out in the wild during its loading screen tips, and it's not kidding.  While you are able to pause the game and spam health restores when things go poorly, you can't expect to do this and win every fight.  Part of combat is watching enemies and knowing when to block or dodge and when to strike back, but also striking to stagger or knockdown foes.  This applies mostly to the melee classes, but ranged classes need to make use of positioning and knowing where the enemies are, so one can't sneak up and interrupt your spell.  One neat thing is that you can actually grapple several non-giant foes that are staggered or downed--you can either pick them up direct to toss off a cliff for an easy kill, or hold them fast so your allies can get free shots while your opponent is vulnerable.  And your Pawns will do these too, so pay attention and work together to efficiently cut through everything in your way.  Just remember that even with a lantern, nights are still incredibly dark and spawns change depending on the time of day.
When it comes to big monsters, you and your allies can and are encouraged to climb them, to gain better access to a weak point, to have a way to damage it even while it moves across the battlefield, or just to keep yourself safe from its attacks.  These fights are really where the teamwork aspect of the game shines.  You might climb on top of an armored cyclops to remove its helmet so your bow-using Pawns can drill its eye with arrows.  You might have a Mage pawn enchant your weapons with fire, which you then use to knock a griffon out of the sky by setting its wings on fire.  You might also hold on for dear life while the thing you're clinging to rages, pausing to replenish your dwindling stamina.  And the battle music changing as you've got the beast on its last legs is a nice touch too.  The controls are the only really bad part because it turns into tank controls (left/right to turn as opposed to move left/right) and it can be difficult to tell which way you're moving sometimes.
Steam's cutting me off, but I really did enjoy the game despite me overhyping it!

The combat is super fun, especially as the bow & dagger classes. The magic feels devastating and is quite the spectacle to look at. Being able to climb beasts and ride them into the sky as they try to shake you off adds a whole new layer to the combat that a lot of games don't have. The story is nothing special for the majority of the game, but I found a certain charm it in its campy simplicity. While Dragon's Dogma isn't without its flaws, I had so much fun with it that I can strongly recommend it to anyone looking for an exciting high fantasy action game.

I want to keep this one short.
As far as the Dark souls series goes, this game is up there with 3 as my favorite in the lore portion. There are also a lot of memorable NPCs and good, branching questlines. The weapon selection is good, and you can really do whatever in the game and be effective. There's a lot to love about this game. The level design is great (mostly), and there are a decent amount of unique and memorable bossfights, all with their own strategies.
There are a few noticable negatives, though. Netcode is bad, so don't bother playing online. The combat/rolling mechanic is by far the worst in the series. There are some pretty wonky hitboxes at times, and there's too much luck based platforming in a game not designed for it. Some boss fights are horribly designed, and even if you know what you're doing, you're going to have a hard time with them *coughbedofchaoscough*. If you played 2 or 3 before this and are interested, it might be easier to just watch some damn vids of the lore because the combat is so horrendously clunky and outdated at this point.
I'm going to give this game a recommend, because I think it's a great game (played all the way through on xbox), but be prepared for some frustration.

This is one damn fine game. It takes a classic formula and breathes new life to it in the form of a modern game with modern production values but all the atmosphere of the original Infinity Engine games. In addition, it takes a careful look at the mechanics, not tied to the AD&D rules, and sets about determining what works and should be kept essentially as is, what doesn't and should be either jettisoned or improved, and what new things could be brought in to further improve the formula. The result is a game that, while not without flaws, is not just a worthy follower to classics like Baldur's Gate but an improvement in most ways that count. The main thing the game could be improved with would be a slightly larger selection of companions.
Still, if you're fan of cerebral, atmospheric CRPGs with lots of reading, good world-building and slick but not simplified mechanics, this game is for you.

Like probably the vast majority of PoE players, I'm an old-school RPG nut, having played EOB, Ultima, Wizardry, BG and ID and dozens more.  I'd missed the wonderful RPG worlds created in the IE and when I saw the Kickstarter for PoE I was excited.
Has the game delivered?  For me - absolutely!  I love the whole approach to this game.  The designers have deliberately steered clear of D&D and created a whole new mechanic, and, in my opinion, have done it brilliantly.
It takes a bit of getting used to but once you work out little things like AoE friendly fire and what the different bonuses and defences actually do then the game starts to make sense.
What about the story?  I'm impressed by the story and the whole world setting and I'm finding I'm getting drawn deeper and deeper into the storyline.  Yes there are some minor gripes but given the expectation for this game I think that Obsididan have delivered a gem.
If you become stat-obsessed then I'm sure there are more faults you can find, but as far as just allowing the characters to develop and getting involved in the story, then I think it is a triumph.
I have found the AI a little weird sometimes, particularly with party members needing micromanaging around other players to get to targets, but I'm sure the developers will be aware of this and will fix.
And the game is....beautiful.  The art and feel of the different areas is a breath of fresh air from the constant 3D churn of recent times.  Those games are great, but 3D is not the be-all and end-all.
Long may PoE continue and I hope there is more to come from these developers.  Combined with Tides of Numenera then it is a great time to be an old-school RPG fan!

At $20 (and less when on sale) this is a great value for money game. It has the feel of an open world RPG, but done on a quite small scale. I play with KB+M and it felt fine to me. And I have not experienced any CTDs. And nor did I find the "continuous" nature of the world a problem.
The key feature of the game is "realism", which yes is ironic given it's all about a zombie outbreak. The first few hours of play after leaving Mt Tanner (the tutorial zone) can be quite daunting, and I must confess to having felt somewhat overwhelmed on my first playthrough. In part, that is because the game is more challenging at the start, and in part because I did not know what I was doing. For example, took me a while to realise that I could switch between characters, which is what you need to do to rest "tired" characters. You actually play the game switching between multiple characters, with the number of characters (survivors) available depending on your success at building a strong home base and fending off the hordes, eliminating zombie infestations and so on. In practice though I generally relied on my first character, Marcus, and then switched to Maya (who joins you in the tutorial part of the game), as back-up, when Marcus got tired.
The main storyline is not very long, and does not really pose any serious challenges with a "survivor" (most likely Marcus) who has maxed out his stats. Though if you get swarmed by a horde with a BigUn your character can die quite quickly, and in this game only the zombies come back from the dead.
I enjoyed my first playthrough immensely. But the repetitive nature of the missions starts to get a bit stale come playthrough #2. Yet to play the DLC; that's next. But even if I never play the game again, I am happy; I definitely got my money's worth.

Hiveswap offers a beautiful world with fantastic and humorous characters and dialogue. Not so strong on the whole gameplay aspect, but it makes up for it in story. It's designed to be understandable by non-Homestuck fans too, and even they will most likely enjoy it.
The good:
- Art and music is fantastic
- Compelling dialogue/story
- Clever and humorous interactions
- Unique object interactions- every object has a unique interaction with every other object and everything in the background. That's a ridiculous amount of interactions.
The bad:
- Uninspiring puzzle design (they're not really puzzles, more like tasks. You find which object interacts with which thing to progress. Nothing really mind-challenging- many puzzles are more of a grind than they are difficult)
- Some video bugs for certain users, not sure if they've been patched.
- Cluttered-looking UI
- Way too many items at one time- few are ever removed from your inventory but are never needed again (did I really need to keep the dog treats for that long?)
- Under-utilised abilities
Overall, you can tell that the creators were primarily writers, music creators and artists over game and level designers (which makes sense, for a game based off a webcomic). It excels in the areas that Homestuck itself excels in, and falls flat on actual gameplay. If you enjoy story and humour, the game is fantastic. If you're looking for a game with high quality gameplay, though, it'd be best to look elsewhere.

Tricone Lab's aesthetic is based around cellular biology, so it's fitting that solving its puzzles would feel organic. Maybe it's the way all the individual parts undulate and wander about or maybe it's the fact that nothing can be moved, only combined or separated, but every part seems to have a life of its own. They all want to return to order, to be rearranged so that the tricone can be formed. Each new piece is introduced one at a time, in its own series of levels. That tutorial, if the process can be called that, lasts for about half the game. But because each piece has presented its own distinct motivation so well and the end goal of any puzzle is so simple, the entire game becomes completely modular. Pieces can be positioned in almost endless variety making the inclusion of a full level editor an act of great foresight. Community maps, which appear to go through an approval process from the developers, are already being made and are extending the game with a creativity that only crowd-sourcing can produce. This is a good thing; for though the official levels are a full taste of what Tricone Lab has to offer, a taste often leaves one only wanting more, as it does it in this case.

Tricone Lab performs a  fairly substantial technical challenge in the floating interface. Then, there is the geographical challenge of matching math to shape and space, in puzzles crafted by hand.

Most puzzle games are on a grid, which is much easier to program. But, Tricone Lab’s cells are floating, amoeba-like structures that gradually change shape while you play. As you pull and drag lines, and the nodes interact with one another, it looks like drawing with a pencil. These long projections can become quite comical when structures called “anticatalysts” start grabbing the nodes you needed to complete the puzzle. Some cells have positive or negative charges, and that may break down larger units you have constructed, all in all causing you to laugh, or cry depending on the difficulty of the map. It certainly brings to mind Dante’s various levels of paradise, purgatory, and hell, all in one game.
The interface looks like a cell body floating in space. Within the cellular bodies are nodes, or individual puzzle pieces that work in very specific ways. These pieces have functions; as in movement, transport or carry, cloning, charge (+-), breaking cell walls, and slightly larger templates. The templates are to be pieced together with correct nodes to form more powerful tools. A standard level starts out with a variety of these nodes subdivided in different compartments of a cell. Somewhere in there are colored cones and a Tricone template. The goal is to connect one of each of 3 color cones to a template and form a “Tricone.” All of the other pieces are to help you get the cones together with the tricone template.
The parts are constructed using formulas that are available by simply pressing the “Describe” button when any node is selected. The formulas are not only visible at all times, but they are rarely complex. The complexity is more an aspect of the number of nodes, and the number of node functions.
The game has 23 maps. Each map has from 3 to 5 levels, making a total of 100 levels. The menu places the maps in alphabetical order at the moment, but that will probably be changed, because 4 of them are labeled as demo maps. It is best to pick these out to play first, as they are like tutorials, and are out of order: Balance, Breakers, BreakerMaker, and Tricone. The most difficult maps are all at the end, and are locked until completion of all the previous maps.
Within maps, the levels progress in difficulty, but most are solved quickly. In the locked levels, the “boss level” for each map is often difficult and may be quite time-consuming to complete.  They require higher-order thinking skills, and you must first analyze, then synthesize to complete those locked levels. My (adult) son became absorbed in the game over my shoulder and ended up downloading the game himself. He’s progressed much faster through the levels than I have, even though I spent many hours in-game while he was at work, just trying to keep up with him.
The puzzles are wrapped in the narrative shell of a human cell. Without a written story, you are left to picture and experience the puzzles as if you were inside a cell performing the functions of cells. It becomes almost a metaphor for cellular biology. You basically have a math game inside a science game.  I honestly see no cons to this game. “It’s all good.”
+ All of the puzzles are hand-crafted (no randomly computer generated levels)
+ The game includes a level editor for sharing your own maps & levels in the workshop
+ Higher Order Thinking skills are demanded to complete the more challenging levels.
+ Challenging for all ages
+ One man developer is active in the community and responds to screenshots, workshop levels, and will accept feedback.
- Tricone Lab is still in early access and may change over time.
As of now, I’ve finished 85/100 levels, lacking mostly the boss levels for the last few now unlocked maps. These will take me quite a bit longer, though some gamers could probably complete this game within 9-12 hours.  With the “Paparazzi” map I’ve submitted to the workshop, & the user levels I’ve downloaded, I’ve already spent 25 hours in this fun & challenging puzzler. I’m sure I will spend another 25, so the game is definitely a fun use of time and I would rate it a 9/10 in the Puzzle genre.

This is a fantastic puzzle game - it feels like it uses a similar part of my brain that Sudoko does (if this then that, but if I do that then this happens so I need to stop that happening by doing this but then I can't do that so must do this, and so on). It's a great example of a few rules and conditions that multiply together to something really complex. I've been playing for 6 hours or so, unlocked 33% of the achievements, so still have a lot of playing to go. Pretty good value for £6.99.

So if you're into thinking and problem solving, give it a try - if you get past four or five levels you'll be hooked into finishing it - while it gets more difficult as it goes on, it's always possible to solve.  :)

I've put a lot of effort into this game in order to give the most honest feedback I possibly could to the developer who gifted me a key, so it is pretty lengthy, but hopefully it is helpful.
Tricone Lab is a game that succeeds brilliantly at what it sets out to accomplish, and that is to deliver a large number of unique puzzles in a way that the player hasn't seen before. The puzzle mechanics are unique, and although there are 100 levels, the first 20 or so are basically tutorial levels. On top of that, the game has a level editor so that players can create their own puzzles and share them with each other. With this foundation, you will definitely get bored of the game long before you ever solve all of the puzzles out there. The game also does a good job of adhering to it's organic chemistry theme, both visually and fundamentally. Additionally, the game draws very little wattage and can be played with just a mouse, making it good for study breaks and play on laptops without charging. I've actually put in most of my play time on the road rather than in my living room.
This all sounds good, but the greatest criticism I can give the game is that the puzzles generally aren't fun. They are unique and plentiful, but this isn't enough to make them fun (at least for me). Ultimately they fail to deliver the "ah-ha" moments that define the puzzle genre because the puzzles - even the most challenging ones - never succeed in challenging the player's perspective. Solving puzzles is a matter of bookkeeping and mental RAM. The developer's approach to increasing the difficulty of puzzles is to just add more steps and more components to the puzzle. The hardest puzzles I have come across are cluster♥♥♥♥s on my screen and it takes several minutes of staring just to recognize all of the components involved. When I finally solved some of the hardest puzzles in the game, it wasn't because I finally stumbled across the crux of the puzzle or had some epiphany of how to approach the problem, but rather it was just a matter of finally finishing the mental  processing all  of the steps that were required to do. There are a few rare gems that break this mold, like the level "BalanceMix" in "ConstructConfuse". Unfortunately, after much playing, they seem few and far between.
For this reason, Tricone Lab feels more like a sudoku book or daily crossword puzzle, which is fine. If you are the kind of person that enjoys these kinds of puzzles (and I know there are many who do, which is great!), then I highly recommend Tricone Lab. For me however, the experience of playing the game comes across as mundane and I wouldn't say I got $10 worth out of the game. The only reason I even played so far into the game was because I was gifted a key and wanted to make sure I experienced basically the entire product before committing myself to this judgment.

Tricone Lab is a very fun and addicting puzzle game. It may look simplistic for the first few levels, but as each level progresses through they add more simple mechanics that make the game that slight bit harder each time.
Tricone Lab is a cool puzzle game, It's starts off fairly simple, with the first few levels basically just explaining how each mechanic work. It's nice that the way that they produce the first few levels as a tutorial, but it doesn't really feel like it's a tutorial. After the first few levels of explaining the game, the game then throws you in without any or much help at all. The game mostly focuses on the basic trial and error way of solving puzzles, if you can't mentally work out how to solve each of the levels.This gives each level a nice feeling of satisfaction once you have completed each level, as some of them are feedishly difficult and hard to figure out. This really helps a puzzle game, with a nice satisfaction of completing each level. Apart from that, there's not much else to talk about gameplay wise of this game. I would personally like to have some sort of story involved in this game, just as a bit more of motivtion to try to complete each level and see what happens next in the story.
The music and sounds are very fitting for this type of casual puzzle game. It has some really calm and satisfying music that plays as you try to think through, or trial and error, on each level. The sounds that are produced throughout each level are very well fitting with the music itself. It compliments the music very well, along with the satisfying level completion it has a nice ending sound to each level when you complete it.
+ Nice difficulty curve
+ Many mechanics to learn
+ Satisfying music & sounds
+ Achievements
- No story
- No trading cards
For the time being, Tricone Lab is a fun and addicting casual puzzle game to play. There are loads of mechanics to learn as you play throughout the game, making the game increasingly more challenging and difficult as you play through more levels of the game. The music and sounds work really well together and work well with the satisfying completion of eahc of the levels.

Tricone Lab is pretty cool. I was given a key by the developer who told me that I don't need to leave a review but to check out their game as they thought I'd like it based on games I already own. After playing for about 1.5 hours I feel like I can write up how I feel about Tricone Lab so far.
So first of all I'd just like to say that it reminds me of Spacechem quite a lot. This is definitely not a bad thing as Spacechem is an extremely good puzzle game. I do believe that this is also different enough to be entirely its own game which is also nice.
The first few levels are reletively simple but there's a few which give you some nice satisifaction for completing (I haven't reached the inevitable 'impossible' levels yet but I'm sure they'll present some tricky challenges).
The music and sounds in the game are all very nice and fit in well with the atmosphere. The graphics are basic but good to look at.
I do however have a couple of negatives which I should point out. The game crashed once but this is understandable as its an early access title and the game saved up to the level I was on automatically anyway so this was prety small of an issue. I would also like some kind of story to go with this (maybe something like Spacechem's) as I personally feel like its lacking without one. Finally I also believe the full price may be a little steep for my liking but I'm sure this feeling will diminish as I progress further in the game.
Overall Tricone Lab is a pretty great puzzle game which hardcore puzzlers should be able to dig into and have some great fun solving.

Tricone Lab is a unique, "pure" puzzle game by a "microscopic indie developer". Pick it up if you are looking for an original puzzler to challenge your mind in new ways.
The "pure" refers to the focus on the puzzles. There is no story. There is a sort of biochemistry theme, but aside from the visual aesthetic, there's not any "actual" biochemistry going on here (so don't worry if that wasn't your favorite school subject). The visual "biochemistry" presentation is quite nice, unique, and carefully crafted (surely no small feat to program).
The gameplay is a sort of turn based resource management. The game is split into maps, which are split into several single screen levels. For each level, you must figure out how to get from the initial configuration to one satisfying the level requirement (producing some amount of tricone).
Although the puzzle mechanics are turn based in essence, the presentation is not static. The pieces you can interact with float freely inside of cell structures in real time. You interact with them by clicking and dragging - which does convey a sort of feeling of playing with microorganisms.
The mechanics are elegant, logical, well designed, and clearly introduced. There are three basic categories of pieces you can interact with: resources, catalysts, and compounds. Drag resources onto catalyst receptors to generate compounds. Compound pieces can be activated to manipulate the cells or other pieces.
I'm not aware of any other games quite like this, although it reminded me vaguely of working out chess puzzles. The mechanics are of course quite different, but there is similarity in satisfying a goal condition from a starting position using a set of pieces via a sequence of moves.
Like other resource management games, as well chess problems, the process is primarily deductive, but trial and error can sometimes be used as a crutch to a limited degree. The mechanics of tricone lab are quite clever, though, and require a higher degree of "lateral thinking" than most resource management games.
I am quite pleased at how tricone lab made me think in new ways ("lateral thinking"). This is very valuable to me in a game. I did find myself getting stuck on some levels a few times, but I moved on to other levels or took breaks, and eventually was able to get through all of the standard levels on my own, and felt quite good about that. Having the achievements to commemorate that is nice too ;)
The play time through the standard levels is roughly 10 hours, but will vary quite a bit up or down depending on how readily you pick up the mechanics.
The game includes a good level editor, and thus hopefully there will be quite a few more levels to play later on (there are already a few user maps that are quite decent).
There are a few rare glitches (and a common one), but none are gamebreaking - just a bit annoying sometimes. Hopefully these will be fixed eventually, but they hardly alter my positive opinion of the game at this point.
While technically still in Early Access, the game is complete and the difficulty is quite well tuned at this point. If interested and price not a factor, there is no reason to delay.
Disclosure: I received a free copy expressly without any obligations.

Disclaimer: I was given a key for this game by the developer. It was expressly not in return for any consideration other than general non-review feedback. But since I've enjoyed it, here we are.
Tricone Lab is an untimed puzzle game. The setting is a view of stylized cellular level organisms, presumably looking through a microscope in a biochemistry lab. In each level, the object is to produce a specified quantity (generally 1-3) of a "molecule" called Tricone. This is done by moving red, blue, and green cone objects into the same cell as a catalyst object. There are many other objects that can make this process easier or harder. There are objects to break cell walls, to make new walls, to transport objects through walls, components to make other objects, to break things down into components, etc. So each level is about using the resources you have available to get the right quantity of cones through the present cells to a catalyst. I find the puzzles to be quite well designed.
If I had to pick a game to compare the mechanics to, it's probably Divide by Sheep. Both have a fixed quantity of resources that you have to carefully maneuver around the level to get them where they need to go. And both are very solid games.
Don't be concerned by the Early Access tag. While still technically a beta, this is a polished, fully working product. The core levels are already done, with possibly some slight future changes to get the learning / difficulty curve right. And with a level editor, the developer is also hoping to build up some user submitted levels. But in my opinion, the Early Access designation could be removed today and the game would be fine.
Story: You're making a molecule called Tricone from cells. Presumably in a lab. That's it and that's fine. It's a puzzle game, not a visual novel, adventure game, or grand rpg.
Visuals: Minimal 2D, but fitting the game. Cell walls are black with grey, black, and white backgrounds and resources. The exceptions are the cones and Tricone, which makes them stand out as the main objectives. The cell walls are a bit squirmy to sell the concept.
Sound: Also minimal but fitting. It's just a few short bits of music and sounds that sound unobtrusive and vaguely scienceish. Feel free to play your own music.
Length: I'm currently at 6.5 hours, about 85% through the stock levels. The remainder will probably be slower, and I suspect I've been faster paced than most will be to this point. There are also a couple of sets of user created levels available now, with more presumably being added over time. And you could choose to create levels. Update: I finished the stock levels (and got all of the current achievements) in 9 hours. It sounds like that may be on the quick side.
Difficulty: Challenging, but I've never been really stuck at any point yet. So in a nice spot for me. Others milage may easily vary.
Achievements: Straightforward, simply for completing each set of stock levels. 100% the stock levels and you'll get all of them. Possibly subject to change as it is Early Access, but the end result should be fair and reasonable.
TL:DR: I like it and recommend it. If you like puzzle games with a solid but not overwhelming challenge this is a good choice.

Outstanding game. The combat is what truly creates the euphoria of excitement witin this game. Various monsters and creatures all with different weaknesses (chimeras, dragons, griffins, ogres, cyclopses, plus load more!). Another cool aspect of this game is that you get to create a pawn. Your pawn is basically your companion, who you also create alongside with your main character. Additionally, you can have two more support pawns who you can recruit. These pawns can be randomly generated if you play offline, but what makes it cool is that you can use other peoples pawn that they have created as your own (as well as people can use yours,) All pawns have different levels of knowledge of how to fight creatures and do certain quests based on what their owner has done or who has rented them.
The open world action-packed combat is a blast and highly versatile; it will have you exploring for hours. Alongside with the various vocations (job classes) you can learn, you can combine various skills from different vocations to truly make your class unqiue. (i.e, say two classes both use daggers, you can learn and assign any dagger skills you learn from those classes and equip them as long as your current vocation uses daggers)
The downside to the game is that it isn't that story-driven, and it isn't all that graphically appealing to modern day standards. The combat animations are great, but during dialogue scenes you can tell the mouth animations when people are speaking are pretty sluggish. Another downside is that once you invested quite a few hours into this game, your pawn's start to get pretty repetitive, Can't tell ya how many times I've used my ferrystone to fast travel and everytime my pawn says, "Tis a port crystal master." I'm just like nah♥♥♥♥♥♥ Furthermore, you may only have one save file. Probably the biggest downer, but at least that one character can literally learn every class.
If you enjoy exciting action-packed RPGs with an open world, you will probably love this game.
I also would recommend an Xbox controller, though keyboard and mouse is not bad.

I got it on sale, and for me it is worth the price I paid. That being said, for a lauded AAA title it feels a little lacking in some regards.
Pros:
-Good, responsive combat with varied viable strategies and halfway decent AI companions
-Big impressive world
-Large number of monsters that each require at least a slightly diffrent approach
-Giant monsters that are amazing to look at and require forethought to defeat
-A good bit of customization for not only your character, but your primary AI companion
-Lots of quests
Cons
-Bad guys respawn in the same spot every time you leave the immediate vicinity. Sounds fine until you have to run back and forth over the same area 20 times.
-Large world with extremely limitied travel options. Again, it has you legging it back and forth over the same chunk of map to complete quests without the convenience of a mount or fast travel. Technically fast travel items are in the game, but they are so rare it might as well be nonexistent.
-Lots of quests, 90% are fetch, escort and kill XX number of mobs with no real reason other than "somebody asked me too". It feels very much like a grindy MMO in this regard.
-The characters are like cardboard. Mostly I think this is because there is very little character story, you do hours worth of quests to get a flat dialogue with a character that gives you very little reason to care.
-Overall story information is also pretty few and far between. The combat is obviously the focus here with the story being a carrot on a stick, albeit a very thin, anemic carrot. By the time I get to the next chunk of storyline I have to try pretty hard to remember what the last bit was.
So, in summary the combat is great with good customization options and big cool enemies to kill. The game knows this and throws legions of enemies at you constantly. As long as you are fine with that, you will love this game. However, if you need story and purpose beyond that, you will probably be sorely disappointed as you kill 45 rabbits, 60 goblins, 30 bandits, 40 wolves and 1 dragon on your way to retake a keep you can no longer remember the importance of.

Dragon's Dogma doesn't have it all, it's not an amazing RPG with a deep and interesting story or the most interesting world to explore.
What it focuses on is the combat, and it does that spectacularly. It's a shame there isn't a more fully fleshed out RPG with Dragon Dogma's combat system.
You have a variety of classes to choose from and you're free to change between them as you please. The monster climbing mechanics are satisfying and never get old.
Pawn system allows you to design your party however you like by hiring characters created by other players online.
Plenty of loot to find and buy. It's a great game for people who enjoy collecting.
Downsides:
Not a huge amount of enemy variety.
World can feel empty.
This game is aimed at people who enjoy third person action games, particularly in a fantasy medieval setting. If that's you it's a must-have.

This game is pretty good to play with friends for about a month. If you've been playing often in that month, this game will start to get boring. The concept and game polish is all there. This game has difficulty enough to make you feel challenged. However, at certain point in the game when you begin to get the best gear it becomes dull and trivial. Also you realize that while the quantity of the content is huge, the quality of all those individual worlds aren't that great.
Usually it's the same copy paste race onto a habitable planet. Sometimes they might prefer living underwater or whatever. Sounds amazing. The fact that you can customize, upgrade your ship and hire crew members is even more amazing. These are all great concepts and clearly the right idea. However, again the content just falls off. I love this game and I want to continue loving it but I am starting to get the No Man's Sky feel to it. Don't get me wrong, they delivered A LOT but there was nothing to do on No Man's Sky because no matter what planet you went to, virtually they were all the same. After you explore about several planets and get your first few crafting done, you'll get the EPP that protects you from no-atmosphere or radiation or freezing or heat.
