Right, ♥♥♥♥ the introductory paragraphs, all you need to know is that Dark Souls is the best game of all time. Yes, including Sonic 2.
A lot has been said – predominantly by WHINING ♥♥♥♥♥ on the internet – about the difficulty. Frankly, this is a non-issue and, I would argue, actually the game's greatest strength. If you’re going to try and play the hero then, by God man, bloody well act like one. Put some work in, struggle; don’t just expect to jump on a glowing weak spot three times and get your reward, where’s your self re-cocking-spect? Dark Souls is a constant perilous fight against unimaginable odds; the average skeleton will block, evade, drink health potions, and generally do a better job than an actual human being. And that’s just at the start! Soon you’ll have to deal with a whole gamut of creeping, lurking horrors, all vying to smash your health bar and nick all your experience points. Dark Souls dangles a tantalising new experience in front of you every step of the way; “cor” you’ll say “that castle in the distance looks swish, I wonder it’s just part of the scenery?” but, no, it is never is! With enough grit and determination it’s possible to reach anything. This should be a law in videogame design: “if you can see it, you can explore it”.
How does it play? Like a ♥♥♥♥ING DREAM is the short answer. The slightly longer, technical answer is that it’s a series of glorious feedback loops that pit you squarely between frustration and reward. It’s like Hotline Miami, in that you’ll frequently get locked into one particular bit which you have to do 100, perhaps even 1000 times. It’s all about getting that single perfect run, where you enter a Zen-like state and nail that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-hard boss in a brutal showdown of palm sweating tension. There is absolutely no better feeling: you’ll feel like a vengeful, rice burning God. The Secret Truth Of The Universe will flow through you. But, as soon as the last embers of victory have faded, you’re back to the grindstone. You have to constantly adapt, evolve, improve. Despite what internet nerds may tell you, there is no single perfect strategy, neither is there a game-breaking weapon loophole. You’ll have to deal with newer, stranger, stronger enemies; and the game will ♥♥♥♥ with you, placing devious traps, messing with your growing sense of familiarity and complacency. I mean, you can play Dark Souls for hours and emerge with nothing more than a slightly better sword, which will most likely be made irrelevant in the next area anyway; the REAL thing you’re getting out of the experience is improving your skills, not making numbers go up. It’s hilarious returning to an earlier area; one which led to hours of frothing, undistilled rage, and absolutely breezing through it. That’s the other thing: there’s no levels, or (hardly any) load times, everything is connected! And you’ll uncover ingenious shortcuts to zip between them all, slowly growing to understand and master the labyrinth.
Aesthetically, as a ‘thing’, Dark Souls is peerless. From Software shamelessly mine from the most spectacular European architecture as inspiration, then distort them into crumbling, shambling Gothic horrors; it is a world drained of beauty. Every single location is permanently etched into my memory, and at least half of them had me loudly exclaiming “♥♥♥♥ me, that is incredible”. The first time I went into Anor Londo I actually took a picture. When was the last time a videogame made you do that? Never, that’s when. The enemy design alone is the shot-in-the-arm that the fantasy genre has needed for at least a decade; it is a universe away from the tedium of ork-filled caves. It’s really quite overwhelming, the constant alternation between awe and dread that comes with each new location, each new enemy, each new surprise along the way. There are more clever ideas burned onto this single DVD then most developers manage in a lifetime. Ubisoft, EA, Rockstar, et all, should burn their computers in defeat.
I love Dark Souls’ hands-off approach to storytelling, and wish more developers would crib from it. Putting the plot on the sidelines makes it more interesting. Instead of shoving an audiolog, or an unskippable cutscene, or a mandatory quest down your throat every few minutes, Dark Souls encourages you to understand the world through the mark you make on it, through your own actions. It encourages you to explore instead of read, to hear instead of listen. It’s entirely possible to finish the game completely oblivious to everything that’s gone on. And that’s okay! Or you can properly pore over every little bit of scenery, and debate the (purposefully vague, contradictory and fragmented, but actually quite brilliant) story with likeminded obsessives over the internet. And that’s also okay! Everyone wins! Nothing feels like superficial padding or, as the industry calls it, ‘lore’: every scrap of information feels purposeful, and adds up to a richer whole. And the voice acting is great; a cast of British thespians speaking in arcane riddles, hamming it up, with character names like ‘Hawkeye Gough’. There’s at least 3 people who sound like Brian Blessed, which is always a mark of high quality.
There are a few small caveats but, to be honest, I don’t think any of them really matter. The frame rate is all over the place, especially when you’re getting mobbed by enemies. Most of the features are poorly explained or, indeed, not explained at all; don’t be afraid to use guides, or YouTube videos; Dark Souls is wilfully, cunningly obtuse and hides many of its best features, strategies, hell even entire areas away. Oh, and in spite of what I said earlier, I’ll admit: there are some sections which clearly take the absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥difficultywise. On a first run, anyway. That’s it.
You think this is hyperbole? Well, play the thing and get back to me! When I last saw it it was £5 - the price of a London pint - which makes it bargain of the millennium. Even better than when SEGA were practically giving away Dreamcasts! It took about five hours before I ‘got’ Dark Souls, but after that I couldn’t stop. I’m ‘only’ about fifty hours in now, and I’m not even sure if that’s halfway. There’s potentially a lifetime’s worth of gaming to master here; I’ve shelved all my other games, and can’t see myself ever going back to them. Dark Souls does that thing that all great art does: it makes all your previous favourites seem, retroactively, a bit rubbish. I found my copy of God Of War when I was tidying my bedroom recently: boy, did I laugh!
Someday, in another life perhaps, I’ll find the time to play Bloodbourne.

Binding of Issac is a unique game. It is a roguelike where you enter a floor, walk around each room finding various different rooms and killing monsters to get to the boss, kill him and get to the next floor. It's a very simple design, but what's in the floors or can be in them is truly incredible. In every floor, you can find traps, item rooms, shops, secret treasure rooms behind the walls, mini-boss rooms, rooms where you can get items in exchange for fighting waves of enemies, and so on.
As the games item drop system is heavily rng based, there are times where you get a really crapy set of stuff and you struggle to kill even the smalllest things, there are times where you get insanely good stuff and stomp on the mighiest creatures with a single touch, and there are times where the items you get are painfully adverage. Binding of Issac is like Dark Souls, brutally difficult, but fair as it's difficulty comes less by an intentional design philosophy, and is more of a side effect of how the game teaches you how to play.
You are dropped down into the game, given little explanation beyond how to move, shoot, and use your items. It gives you everything you need to succeed but whether you do succeed comes down to learning from past mistakes and pushing forward. Like Dark Souls, death is just a learning experience, every time you die, you learn more and the next time, you'll hopefully remember what you did wrong the last time and avoid it. there are thousands of possible item combinations and you can beat the game with every single one. while i personally am not to far in, I'm looking forward to seeing what crazy combo's i can find later down the road!

is a moderate-quality HO game.  Frankly, given the quality I've come to expect from Artifex Mundi, it's a little disappointing, but still capably done.  Given the preponderance of shovelware in hidden-object gaming,
is medicore at worst.
What

, it does competently.  It's simply lacking in what it
have done.  It features only one type of HO play  -- hunting by description -- which occasionally runs afoul of hasty localization.  Minigames are few, easy, and familiar.  HO scenes
repeated, but only once each and without respawning objects, which I consider acceptable.  Voice acting is a little bit above average for the genre.  The story is clichéd, but that's true of many HO game plots; it serves the purpose well enough.
In sum: Average by genre standards; subpar by Artifex Mundi standards.  For HO lovers, it's playworthy, but shouldn't be your first choice.

Overall it was quite ok, but all the puzzles feel a little to familiar, as it's all just recycled from other Artifex Mundi games. The story also fails to gain real traction, it starts out somewhat interesting, but then just paddles along without really advancing much at all. The most frustrating part however is the ending, which there isn't any of, the game just ends without any kind of epilogue or even a proper cliffhanger. This makes the whole experience feel kind of pointless and empty.

Mind Snares is another nice piece of Artifex Mundi hidden object game craftsmanship, with a non-conventional story of self-discovery and good progress design. The puzzles needed a little more polish tough.
Mind Snares: Alice’s Journey is an odd modern hidden object game, where the protagonist is just a normal everyday office worker called Alice Dahl, who doesn’t have to find a kidnapped relative, save the world from some mysterious dark entity, or investigate some weird occult site. She is just an average woman who suffers a car crash and traverses through her own mind to find her inner strength to face the hardships of her life, like her job slowly distancing her from her family.
Her self-discovering journey is divided into four segments with their own themes (steampunk factory, fairy tale forest, witch’s hut, and phantom hospital). This story structure left little room for backtracking, but also cut the game short, where most of the play time is spent on the rather uninspired, mediocre hidden object scenes. They aren’t bad, but they also held back the final score, which could have been much higher just for this story alone.

This is one of Artifex's Hidden Object Games, and I can say it is a good one. However, it is a bit short for my tastes. Most other Hidden Object Games have taken 4-6 hours for me to finish (maybe more if I want to play it through a second time). This game has good graphics and a nice soundtrack, with a reasonable story. The game is just a bit too short for my tastes and took me under 3 hours to complete (as well as unlock all achievements). I will still recomend it as long as it goes on sale for half the price. I can't justify spending $9.99 on this game. Perhaps $2.99-$3.99.
Still I enjoyed it and will still recommend it... if it is on sale.

Did manage to finally get a spawn on the main map where I could start playing the game. Here are the pros and cons so far.
Pros:
None found so far. Everything has been done better on other games. I do however like the concept that this game is aiming for and if they CAN manage to get this to a worthwhile state of development it could be fun. However, based on the current development release schedules, I would say another game with a better dev team will come along and steal the market before Miscreated has it's chance to shine.
Cons:
1/ No ability to host own configurable local server or choose own server provider. This con is first in the list because it is a HUGE con. The server providers that they do allow are sub-par at best.
2/ Crafting system is too complex for this type of game. It's not that it's a hard crafting system to use, it's just that it doesn't need to be like this and takes away from the core of the game.
3/ Stupidly small carrying capacity to start with. I could carry more stuff than that IRL.
4/ Poor use of movement mechanics. You can't even vault over a 4 foot high fence. Silly and unrealistic.
5/ Many chances to get caught and stuck on the environment especially around buildings.
6/ Bugs, lots of bugs, too many to mention here without typing out a full essay.
Summary:
I do strongly encourage support for early access developers if they have a capable and properly staffed development team, with a good concept, and realistic development release schedule. Unfortunately, it appears that this developer has decided to "do it their own way" despite the reviews and wishes of the survival games community and their own player base. Unless this attitude changes I can not see this game lasting the distance and I would highly recommend you avoid purchasing this title until the devs allow, at the very LEAST, customizable private servers and the ability to local host.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

When this first came out, I thought it was just a reskin of Rome 2 in a different time period. In fact, I only bought it on sale because I wanted to use it for the Lord of the Rings mod and the Medieval mod.
However, just like how Napoleon Total War is leagues better than Empire Total War, Attila is incredible compared to Rome 2.
I could point out the significantly better graphics, way more challenging and brutal gameplay, more unit diversity, better balancing, family trees, or countless other things.
Instead, I'll just focus on what I think is the best part about Attila.
The sieges are incredibly fun. The map design for sieges in this are just amazing on every level. Sieges are not some turtle-fest but rather dynamic battles where you fight across great chokepoints and defensive locations. Especially when you combine it with the simultaneous naval invasions, it's not only incredibly fun to play, but fun to watch as well. I've never wanted to fight sieges in any Total War more than in this one, and I've played every single Total War there is. Having a multi-stage siege battle where your naval forces first clear a way through the enemy navy, before you deploy the artillery ships to bombard the land forces. Then having your invasion fleet move up to dock troops (transport ships now leave the map after they drop their troops, another massive change from Rome 2).
At the same time your second reinforcing army advances up the Southern approach. The enemy AI has sallied forth to meet them and they outnumber that army 2 to 1, making you fight a retreat as you're outmatched. Using this advantage, your invasion fleet rushes up to capture key points in the town and to prepare and engage the AI as they return back to town. Now the tables have turned and your invasion has become a defense, but the town itself is burning all around you due to your artillery ships.
Such a battle was ridiculously rare if not almost impossible to get in Rome 2. Here it's basically how it happens all the time on V. Hard and above difficulty. Just so much fun. There's always something interesting and challenging happening when it comes to sieges.
Not to mention the AI is really aggressive in this, so you will be defending in sieges very often. The AI will come from land and sea too, giving you those great naval invasions.
So yeah, this is more than just Rome 2: Horse Archers. It's Rome 2: The Superior Version.

Tricone is a puzzle game that nearly ticks all the right boxes.
[Disclaimer: While I was given a copy of this game for free, I still think this is a good game]
[Disclaimer 2: This review is accurate as of beta build number 0.19]
The good stuff:
This game is very easy to learn how to play, be it just through trial and erorr, or through the in-game descriptions. But once you get past the first few levels, things start to get challenging. The method of requiring you to complete certain levels does help to guide you through the learning process (by preventing you from getting in over your head and confused and annoyed), so the learning curve is well tuned.
The game also opens up quite a bit in terms of the variety and complexity of the operations that you have to make use of to solve the puzzles.
The graphics are great. It has a simple (but not totally flat) look to it, and it does feel very much like we're looking into biological cells, especially with the wiggle-vision type outlining of the cell membranes. Also, the fact that it all reacts to your movements gives it a nice fluid sensation while you solve the puzzles. The animation of some of the later nodes, like the 'anti-catalyst' feels very alive and organic, which is a good thing to see.
The sound design is all very nice, from the ambient music in the menus, to the sound that the elements you interact with make.
Things that need improvement:
It would be nice to see some sort of improvement to the community map downloader. Right now it seems as if you need to directly search for a known map, whereas it would be nice to be able to "browse" through them all directly.
I'm not really a fan of the game launcher. It does work perfectly fine, and it all makes sense, but to me it looks more like the UI of simulation software you'd see in a university course than the launcher for a game (it is visibly a 'java' UI). I think it should be skinned to match the ib-game UI, but this doesnt really affect the gameplay beyond initial configuration. I also think that some of the options could be moved into an in-game options UI, rather than being in the launcher, but this is very much just personal preference.
Although I havent played a ton, what I have played is fun and challenging.  If you like to think instead of shoot, this is a great game. I can see me putting many more hours into this game.

What is happening? 25 years after the wonderful
, I get to play three carefully hand-crafted puzzle games in a couple of months.
Tricone Lab is a puzzle game about mixing and matching components to synthesize a cell.
The game oozes (teehee) with flavour: although they might look crude in screenshots, the ever-moving parts are really a delight to play around with.
It took me about 5 hours to complete the 100 levels given with the game. Difficulty is always a subjective matter, even more so in the puzzle genre, but the puzzles felt appropriately teasing without putting me in a guru meditation state. I liked the presence of not only a snappy 'undo' button, but a 'redo' one; I never felt any frustration navigating the puzzles thanks to them.
There is something really right with the game: I usually am fed up with about any gaming experience after an hour, yet I played all the levels in a couple of sessions in less than a day time.
I wished I could have gone on playing more. Although the game has got a level editor, the community is still small and the maps aren't there yet. I personally regret being inept at designing anything: there seems to be so many mechanics interplays to explore still. Please, someone smarter, do something!
Edit: I eventually made a little map of 4 levels for the game, a process that was as much of a brain teaser as the main game was, if quite different! I hope you might enjoy PhilosOffer.

Bear in mind - its still early access, everything can change... blah blah blah, you know this, right? So lets get started.
Very unusual 2D puzzle game with specific mechanics and graphics style - that's the shortest I could describe it.
Main goal of every level is to create set number of tricones - symbol made out of three cones, thats also the icon of the game. At first its not that hard - directly connect every cone to another specific symbol - connector, double click it and its done. Thanks to nicely done small tutorial its easy to get how exactly game works.
After that obstacles are appearing - walls that you need to break, anti-connectors that "steals" specific symbols that you sometimes need, areas that will "disconnect" your more complicated symbols into their parts, creating walls... and even more. Variety is already quite high.
Every level takes from mere seconds (click here and drop there and you are done) to even few minutes if you can't find solution. Because of that, it may become a bit frustrating later on, but thats something specific to the genre itself I think.
About graphics - dont know why but it reminded me a bit about World of Goo, probably because in it everything was constantly moving - just like here but certainly not in a way game looks. Its... lets say minimalistic in a sense. Levels looks like some kind of multicellular which is nice idea to handle game mechanics. What appeared strange to me was the way blindcolored mode was implemented - everything appear to look the same... besides cones themselves - instead of red/green/blue there is gray/white/black cone. Well, thats one way to deal with it but in general game looks slightly dull because of lack of any kind of colours besides mentioned earlier cones. Of course thanks to that games work on every toaster you can imagine which is nice.
Music is quite nice but what "hit me" the most was complete lack of it during solving puzzles. It is in menu, during level selection but not while playing core game which is quite strange.
Whats big advantage of this game over quite a lot of others puzzle games is complete level creator - from creating cells to putting symbols - its exactly what I would think author was using creating every puzzle.
And when I am at it, levels themselves are all done nicely and all but at least for now I didn't encounter something I did in for example The Talos Principle - that there is part/element unused/left after solving puzzle. Or multiple ways of solving it. No mindgames with player makes it slightly less interesting than it could be but thanks to level creator it can be solved by players themselves.
Player statistics are something I liked the most in Zachtronics games (Spacechem, TIS-100) is also implemented here, but to a bit smaller extend - it takes into account average solving time, number of retries and how many people tried/solved it but not much more. I would say its understandable due to how the game works - when you already played specific level once you could solve it again in almost no time, "beating" your previous "try". At least in games mentioned earlier (Spacechem in particular) I had incentive to beat every level over and over to see how I could beat it faster etc; thats not the case here sadly.
To sum up: I like this game... but probably wouldn't pay full price for it. Yes it has quite a lot of content, but its finite in a sense you don't have incentive to get back to it by yourself. Level creator helps with that tho, letting you create your own puzzles or get somebody's map/levels to play.

It hasn’t been since the height of SpaceChem’s popularity that I’ve seen such an intellectually designed and developed puzzle game. It’s for this reason that I find myself not only drawn to Tricone Lab but also a big fan of the game. Now, although I’ve got a pair of university degrees neither of them are in the sciences. I consider myself only of average to above average intelligence – some would argue both ways (I can have the intellectual laziness of Homer Simpson yet other times people have asked me to tone it down on the intellectual quotient) but there is something immediately accessible about Patrickhill’s game that I will claim would have some appeal to the majority of gamers.
The tutorial levels are well designed and teach the player everything that they need to know to progress throughout each series of puzzles. From there, however, each of the one hundred original levels can vary from stupendously easy to infuriatingly difficult. Each level is fair. There is, of course, a solution. It’s simply a matter of discovering the solution. Hopefully without searching for an answer online – that would be cheating not only the game but yourself. At times you will feel like you’re the smartest little biscuit and at times you will believe that you’re lacking in the most fundamental of ways. It’s a real mixed bag and it’s beautiful. Very rarely do puzzle games reach this level of excellence. Tricone Lab is nothing if not meticulously designed.
There truly isn’t much at all to criticize. Every aspect of the game at least delivers in some way or another. The presentation is suitable and the sound effects and soundtrack are quite charming and add positively to the game’s aesthetic. Patrickhill has even thought about the implementation of Steamworks to strengthen his title. There are achievements which I believe is a must have for any Steam based puzzle game. There is even a level editor so that players can upload their own levels to the Steam cloud and share with other players around the world which gives the title the length of lifespan only limited to the game’s player base. Which is an issue. SteamSpy currently estimates the total number of owners in the 17 (that’s seventeen!) to 1,463 range. This may have something to do with the $11.99 price tag which is higher than other puzzle games on Steam. The game has not yet enjoyed a sale. However, I would urge Patrickhill Games to consider adding Steam trading cards to the game and when that is done putting the game on a 25% discount for a week before considering a permanent price drop. This would capture those who buy up on trading card games the moment that they are added to the program which in turn should lead to increased word of mouth.
I personally cannot recommend Tricone Labs enough. It’s a wonderful puzzle game that will improve your logical thinking.

This game is simply one of the best RPG's around in terms of gameplay. The large number of fun to use skills for all the types of weapons you can imagine in a fantasy game, make it a lot of fun to play. Make tornadoes, call huge meteors, or flash around with double daggers, slashing everything in your path, climb huge enemies to attack weak spots (a cyclops's eye for example), snipe with the bow, and so on, everything in a fast paced, satisfying system.
Pros:
Fun skills, like I mentioned
Complex character progression (use this
and read guides on how to make good characters - if you want to be good with all classes aim for 4000hp, at least 3500 ST, 550 AT and MT, and 350 defense and MDefense at lvl 200. YW.) Yes, you can play with all classes with a single character.
Interesting pawn system. Pawns are your party, that have their own complex AI, classes and skills. Your main pawn is like a second character, that you can develop any way you want, and you get two more pawn "slots" in which you can put pawns other players have created. Awesome system. You can also play solo if you want.
Awesome enemies, especially the huge ones. To defeat big enemies you can apply various strategies - for example a cyclops, the eye, duh, but also you can climb it and attack the arm for it to drop its weapon, or attack it with lightining to stun it, attack the legs to make it fall, and so on. Its like being in an action movie in every one of these fights, especially if climbing.
Creature design, armor design, skill effects are really good. The meteors, tornado and other sorceror skills are epic to look at, and a lot of other skills look really good, and they feel like they really do have an impact when you hit the enemies. Also, you have a lot of weapons and armors to choose from.
Cons.
Level design and environment art are simply bad. No point going around that. While its great to look at the creatures, the environment around them looks dated. Also the map, once you know it, feels small. Only 2 towns, 1 of them big, and a few locations to explore.
Quests are few and not that good. Most of the fun and good rewards you get from the bounty boards. Some of the quests are hidden and are important to get access to new areas, though, so watch out for those.
Overall, this game is one the best RPG's around, well worth playing. I've played 40 hours so far, and still haven't seen everything this game has to offer.

Savage Lands is a open world survival game that can be played in singleplayer or multiplayer.It was released on Steam on the 5th of March 2015 and it is still in Early Access in October of 2016.
The crafting in this game is the same as any other EA(Early Access) survival game.And by that I mean,basic,boring and confusing.You need to grind for materials or you can find them on the ground.You can craft better equipment for fighting/grinding for materials or you can rebuild the ruins that you find across the island.
On the island you can find deer,boars,pigs,rabbits,wolves and skeletons.Wolves,boars and skeletons will attack you on sight but their attacks are sluggish and buggy.Most of the time they will completely miss you and get stuck in a rock or something.Deer will run away from you but you can chase them until they hit a wall and just stay there.I found 2 deer stuck in a rock and I just clubbed them to death.The hitboxes of animals/skeletons are either broken or get glitchy every once in awhile.Basically the combat is kinda broken.
Surviving on the island is not hard because the game is hard or too complex,it's hard because you need to fight the broken game mechanics.The cold/health systems in the game are broken for example.You will get cold up to 100% and die even if you stay near a fire.Your health will go down even if nothing happens and eating/using bandages won't fix it.The game doesn't have a natural progression.If you walk 200 meters from spawn you can encounter monsters that one hit you.You constantly find axes/resources on the ground so what's the point of surviving if you already find stuff on the ground?The island is full of ruins and you can easily repair them with just wood.Food is easy to find because animals get stuck in walls/trees/rocks and you can kill them.
The game looks decent from pictures/trailers provided by the devs but in-game it doesn't look great and it runs really bad on medium settings.And even on medium settings I don't think I get 60fps.It's clearly not well optimized.
Achievements on Steam are broken for this game.
Even if you stay in a house,it will snow inside.
The game consumes a lot of resources for no apparent reason and crashes from time to time.
Savage Lands has tons of bugs,glitches,it's badly optimized and has boring gameplay.It's still in EA but I think it's literally impossible for this game to get better than this because the core game is broken.Not worth the price it has on Steam.

I've been itching to cover the games created by Supergiant Games for quite a while now, so, since the Winter sale has started, and since I will soon purchase their newest game, Pyre, I thought I would start by reviewing their first game : Bastion.
Bastion's premise is pretty simple : You play as a young kid, who has survived a catastrophe called "the Calamity". After meeting the narrator of the game, an old man named Rucks, you travel across the wasted world, meet some other survivors, and collect important energy cores and shards to power the titular Bastion, a structure designed as a sanctuary for people to go to in the event of a crisis. While doing this, Rucks tells you about what life was like before the Calamity, back in Caelondia, a major and booming city where the kid, Rucks, and some of the other people you meet used to live before the Calamity.
I know the plot sounds somewhat basic, but it gets way deeper than that, trust me.
Anyways, moving on.
It's awesome. The narration from Rucks, voiced by the very talented Logan Cunningham, tells an immersive story about a once great city, a deadly war, among other things. He gives a sense of realism to the world, a really good one.
The gameplay is one of the best parts of the game, besides the story and soundtrack. There's many different weapons you can alternate from while on your journey, ranging from guns, to blades, to even a mortar. There's also several enemies you will come across, each requiring good reflexes and fast movements to kill. The many places you travel through are also very unique, and each have their own stories. Everyone and every location is fresh and original in so many ways, hell, the game itself is just simply original and full of creativity.
The soundtrack here is something truly special. Composed and written by Darren Korb, and featuring Ashley Barrett, the soundtrack of Bastion is beautiful, sad, moving, and upbeat. Several tunes here are masterfully crafted, and the lyrics of some of them are both refreshing, yet almost depressing, as they show inner conflict, how great life used to be, etc. Darren Korb is easily one of my favourite video game OST composers, and he deserves all the credit he gets. (Ashley Barrett also deserves lots of credit as well.)
The artstyle of Bastion, while simple, is breathtaking in quite a few ways. Many locations are very detailed, as well as the characters and enemies. They all have very specific colors, sizes, etc. As I've said several times during this review, many things here are just simply unique, and the artstyle is easily of the best examples of this game's simple, yet beautiful content.
Since there really isn't much else to say, let's get to the end of this review.
Bastion is a beautiful, cinematic, and moving experience. With great gameplay, an amazing soundtrack, a really interesting story, and with a pretty reasonable length of under 4 hours, it's short, but sweet. The first of Supergiant's masterpieces, which shows that, quite often, great things come from what seems like nowhere.
Final score : 9/10.

What more could be said about Bastion? It's one of the most beloved games of the generation that began the XBOX Live Arcade and the Indie Revolution.

Without giving too much away, this is a game any working soul who has been in the same job for say over a year can relate to.  The concept is solid as well as the storyline which is meant for a more mature minded audience.  The gamer can literally hear the "tiredness" in Alice's voice.
Story: Since this game begins with the epilogue, the storyline is actually about when (and probably even why) Alice decided to become the owner and proprietor of her own business.  During the interview Alice relates how she worked in a job she hated (or in my opinion was tired of being taken advantage of by her boss).  She always wanted to start her own business but was afraid to (with good reason if one understands how hard that really is and the risk involved.)  Two years prior to the game beginning, late one evening (workaholic) before her vacation with her family was about to begin her insensitive boss sent her to an out of town business meeting. On the way to the meeting Alice is in an accident.  This is the beginning of her journey.  She wakes up in an alternate place (most likely her own mind) and must find her way back.
Gameplay: The journey takes place over 5 chapters, with the epilogue beginning the story and introducing the dark shadowy man who appears throughout the game as a quasi-nemesis.  The first chapter begins the journey and sets up the other four chapters which are separate "adventures".  Each chapter segment has its own goal, its own gather and use inventory and its own map making gameplay easy since there is no crossover between the chapter area and the "outside".  Each area must be completed before progressing to the next chapter.  The storyline concept plays out as each chapter is completed and is not overly "preachy".  This game could be considered to have a psychcological suspense/horror theme since no place is scary then inside one's own head.  Each area has its own terror theme.  I really liked Chapter 3 - Baba Yaga.  Seldom is the most notorious and terrifying witch Baba Yaga (and her chicken hut) ever seen in HOs and the designers added to it what I can only call that bayou zombie ambience making the whole area subtly terrifying.  Not that the other chapters did not have their own subtle terror.
Hidden Object scenes:  The Hidden Object scenes are fitting to the area they are found in and basically not piles of random "junk" found in random places.  They are uncluttered for the most part and the find clues are relatively easy to locate, except for one or two that either blend well into the background or are so obvious they get overlooked.  There are also "extra step" find clues such pouring wine in a glass for glass of wine, or striking a match to lit a candle for lit candle.   Overall not a huge challenge but challenging enough to not be considered too easy.
Puzzles: Believe it or not the puzzles were theme oriented and the type found depended on the chapter theme.  Overall the variety was excellent and included mechanical, math, logic, rotating, picture, matching and "follow the recipe/design/blueprint" puzzles.
The point and click aspect of the game was about equal with hidden object aspect, and quite the challenge at times when trying to figure out what to do or where something was located.  Some of the achievements reflect both the humor and creative thinking of some of the point and click challenges.  Some say games never teach anyone anything so I wonder how many gamers had to look up 'hew' and  'decoction' to know what to do?
Just a few comments to end this review.
1) I wish the developers would have closed the game with a tiny short wrap up cutscene of ending the interview. Something as simple as "And that is when/why/how I decided to start my own business" over a handshake or something.  It would have added the proverbial "cherry on top."
2) Watch the credits.  It is not very often anyone in any media takes the time to make credits interesting.  I found all the X-rays amusing and unique, especially the one of the Artifex Mundi logo.
3) All Steam achievements can be completed in a single play through, which is always a blessing since I dislike forced second playthrough for achievements.  I for one am also glad to see achievements in-game or steam finally moving away from "solve x in x amount of time" and becoming more creative.
4 and the last) There is a fast travel map, not that it is really needed.  No forced second playthrough (usually meaning on expert/advanced, and often with Artifex Mundi games the alternative "game" to the Hidden Object scene).  No extra "hidden/shifting/ghost" objects to find.  No penalties for map use, game hints (not to be confused with HO scene or puzzle hints), or misclicks.

Let's be honest, the game isn't perfect, but, it is a breath of fresh air. I'll start out with the pros:
-Overall, the game is fairly simple and intuitive, which makes it a bit easier to get in to.
-Combat is fluid and easy to control.
-Zombies are fairly easy to kill.... sometimes. (Read cons)
-Open world, which is awesome when it comes to zombie survival. Allows for random events and tons of things to be explored and to be discovered.
-The game makes your successes feel more rewarding, but at the same time makes your failures even more impacting.
-Having a crew behind you to assist you in scavenging a abandoned house saves times and makes the game feel more interactive.
Overall, I recommend the game for anyone who likes playing zombie survival games. You'll be spending hours searching abandoned barns, houses, diners, general stores, auto shops, and other shops around town for anything you can use to survive. From medicine and food, to weapons and ammo. Fighting off hordes of zombies with anything from a branch, to a nine iron, from a 9mm pistol to a AK-47, or even just running them over with your pickup. But... there are cons.
-The zombies can sometimes become overwhelming, especially if you run out of ammo, or, your weapon breaks.
-Zombies aren't ALWAYS easy to kill. Sometimes you'll be sitting there for 20 or 30 seconds repeatedly bashing its head in and not doing anything.
-Inventory space is extremely limited to 10 slots, and 20lb (which can be upgraded by finding bigger backpacks), but the inventory size always stays the same.
-Graphically, the game doesn't seem to be scaled out very well to 1920x1080... or a 16:9 ratio for that matter. Parts of the game seem pixelated and stretched. (The menu doesn't even fill the screen)
-The journal is a little bit confusing at first, especially when it comes to finding out more about the people in your house or trying to add parts to your house, like sleeping areas or workshops.
-Cars are a bit flippy floppy (don't always stick to the ground, rolls over pretty easily... that or I'm just a reckless a** driver.)
And that's pretty much it. 90% of the cons could be fixed with a few minor patches, but until then, I have to mention them.
The cons don't leave too much of a negative impact on the gameplay, but it is things I noticed.
Overall, I give it a solid 8/10. Recommended for any zombie enthusiast.

When this first came out, I thought it was just a reskin of Rome 2 in a different time period. In fact, I only bought it on sale because I wanted to use it for the Lord of the Rings mod and the Medieval mod.
However, just like how Napoleon Total War is leagues better than Empire Total War, Attila is incredible compared to Rome 2.
I could point out the significantly better graphics, way more challenging and brutal gameplay, more unit diversity, better balancing, family trees, or countless other things.
Instead, I'll just focus on what I think is the best part about Attila.
The sieges are incredibly fun. The map design for sieges in this are just amazing on every level. Sieges are not some turtle-fest but rather dynamic battles where you fight across great chokepoints and defensive locations. Especially when you combine it with the simultaneous naval invasions, it's not only incredibly fun to play, but fun to watch as well. I've never wanted to fight sieges in any Total War more than in this one, and I've played every single Total War there is. Having a multi-stage siege battle where your naval forces first clear a way through the enemy navy, before you deploy the artillery ships to bombard the land forces. Then having your invasion fleet move up to dock troops (transport ships now leave the map after they drop their troops, another massive change from Rome 2).
At the same time your second reinforcing army advances up the Southern approach. The enemy AI has sallied forth to meet them and they outnumber that army 2 to 1, making you fight a retreat as you're outmatched. Using this advantage, your invasion fleet rushes up to capture key points in the town and to prepare and engage the AI as they return back to town. Now the tables have turned and your invasion has become a defense, but the town itself is burning all around you due to your artillery ships.
Such a battle was ridiculously rare if not almost impossible to get in Rome 2. Here it's basically how it happens all the time on V. Hard and above difficulty. Just so much fun. There's always something interesting and challenging happening when it comes to sieges.
Not to mention the AI is really aggressive in this, so you will be defending in sieges very often. The AI will come from land and sea too, giving you those great naval invasions.
So yeah, this is more than just Rome 2: Horse Archers. It's Rome 2: The Superior Version.

The best thing about playing Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is that it makes me feel over-the-top powerful without sacrificing the fear of defeat. It’s got great free-flowing combat and a good-sized, good-looking open world full of Lord of the Rings lore to find, but what makes it special is what’s going on in the background: an intriguing hierarchy of enemies that gives every victory and defeat extra meaning.
Very good game, slightly short and not that replayable, but it combines some of the best elements of games like batman, assassins creed, and some others.

In the light of the announcement of ... what is basically Shadow of Mordor 2, I decided to add my own, little resumé
First off: Don't expect deep story, rich characters, or plenty of emotional rollercoastering.
This game is made for two simple things:
Slaying LOTS of bad guys (orcs, mostly. Actually overwhelmingly orcs, very few other enemies, but those "other" enemies are also most of the time bosses, or boss-like encounters). LOTS OF THEM.
And mucking about, seeing what you can do with your given weapons.
It's .... think of assassin's creed, but with a lot less forced stealth, a lot more murdering orcs, and a very open world. And some very strong enhanced orcs.
The Nemesis system is great. Enemies that kill you, or that you help promote after learning how to "control" them, kinda-sorta levle up, becomming stronger and gaining new abilities. It's really just an open world full of potential to kill things, and to gather things for achievements and in-game collecta-thons.
It's a great game if you are looking for a quick (quick as in fast to play and learn, not over tooo quickly) action game with a slight RPG touch (you get to "levle up" and buy abilities with points, abilities include new ways to kill enemies, more flashy ways to fight and kill, and sometimes new ways to instagib enemies.
I can't stress this enough:
This is NOT a game with a deep, rich story. This is assassin's creed, with less stealth, more killing, less activities on the map, and more focus on basically building somewhat of an army for the final encounter. Albeit the final encounter, after the big reveal, becomes a quick-time event. Which is real sad.
It's fun, from start to finish, if you like this kind of game. But if you are looking for a good RPG in middle-earth, leave now. because this is not it. It uses the Lord of the Rings license, but thaaaaaat's about where it ends, really.
Too bad there isn't a demo, the game is kinda hard to describe without using Just Cause, Far Cry, Assassin's Creed etc.
It takes the most fun elements (and maybe some annoying) of those games, mixes them with the Lord of the Rings license, and makes a fun Action-RPG. But the RPG is maybe 15%. If that.
I wouldn't recommend buying it for full price, though! Wait for a sale. around 30% off is where it starts to become really worth it.

This is a very strong game that is easily described as Arkham's Creed; borrowing so many gameplay elements from those vaunted franchises.  Shadow of Mordor is definitely a LotR game - the developers had a keen understanding of Tolkien's world and history to include key details and names throughout the long narrative.  Where originality is required, the lore is dealt with gently and repectfully to include material specific to the game, but plausable to the world itself.
The gameplay and Xbox controls are fluid and intuitive - and this helps in immersion towards hunting your targets while remaining hidden in a land teaming with danger.  That is the highlight of the game - stalking an over-powered individual leader surrounded by lesser Orc and Uruk.  The combat system locks you into melee as soon as you engage any target, and if you become flanked by more than a handful of enemy, you'll quickly  find yourself fleeing or dead rather quickly.
In a similar vein to Dark Souls, when you expire, your game gets a little tougher.  In Shadow of Morder, the Nemesis system ensures enemies that best you grow in reputation and prestige, accruing abilities and often an entourage that makes them more challenging to take down, and you more dependent on intimidating followers to discover exploitable weaknesses.
Overall, this is a highly enjoyable game, with the Nemesis system making replayablitly nigh infinite.  One reservation I do hold is the time it takes to travel between destinations - but I understand this is by design.   A form of fast travel is possible but this Mordor is not small and the jump points are rather broadly separated.
The full plot is extensive, but the side-targets and unlocking expensive new abilities on the skills trees will frequently pull you from the narrative to make the main quest more directly accessible - which encourages you to further explore the map.
It is easily recommended, however the difficulty does ramp up once you leave the first area.  The necessary balance between combat experience and stealth makes even simple missions challenging, but the engaging gameplay keeps the recipe from going stale.

Tricone Lab:
~~~~~~~~~~

I don’t know about you, but when I was at school, many moons ago, twice a week we used to have an hour’s course of biology. The only aspect that I liked about it was looking at micro-organisms through the telescope (oops… microscope) and no, it was not one of my favourite subjects!
Tricone Lab is an excellent puzzle game where logic is your best friend! If it is not, do not despair, as every family has someone who either is, or pretends to be, logical . . . bring him/her in front of the computer and figure it out together.
At the start, the levels are pretty easy and will help you to understand how this game works. However, as you progress through the game more components will be added and you will be in for intermittent brain shockwaves in order to resolve a puzzle.
You will be presented with a cell; this cell can have multiple walls within it creating smaller cells. What you have to do is attach the 3 colour cones to the catalyst to create the Tricone substance in order to clear each level. Sometimes there will be several Tricone to create.
By combining a breaker template and a mobility component, you will be able create a breaker. With this breaker you can break a wall of a cell to try to free one or more colour cones. Remember, you have to attach 3 different colour cones to your catalyst to create a Tricone, but things will become tricky when the anti-catalyst comes into the mix…. Fun…Think… Shockwave…Think…Fun…EUREKA!
This game features 100 levels and you able to skip a level if you find it too hard to complete. Use the undo feature to step back to any of your previous moves. Sometimes going backwards really opens your eyes!
One thing I really like is that you can create your own level and share it with everybody!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great, challenging concept
-	Good brain-training
-	100 levels to master
-	Custom Level editor
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
Tricone Lab is an excellent puzzle game that will challenge your brain all the time. Brain explosions expected!
9/10

Tricone Lab is a logic game about completing tricones in microscopic organisms. The idea seems original to me, only thing that concept reminds me (in a way) is SpaceChem - but don't worry, Tricone Lab doesn't have such high learning curve and it's immediate fun from beginning, with short and practical tutorials for every gameplay mechanism. Levels are balanced and everytime you start to get bored by repeating mechanics, a new one is presented.
A huge surprise comes with the Java engine that the game uses, because many indie Java-based games end up being buggy and not polished. This is not the case!
- New gameplay mechanics introduced after every few level sets (with included a tutorial level set every time).
- 100 levels. And the game's yet only in early access, so we can expect more levels later.
- Nice and simple graphics that doesn't distract you from solving the puzzles.
- If you make a mistake, you don't have to restart the whole level. There are undo/redo buttons.
- Later levels may be frustrating for players expecting easy puzzle game - you can skip some levels though!
-
- The price (11,99 €) for a puzzle game may be too much for some people.

If you liked the gameplay mechanics of Splinter Cell: Conviction, then you will probably like this title. There is a lot of upgrading to do in this game: weapons, ops suits and home base. The money for upgrades comes from missions, challenges and finding collectibles. Each mission is scored on the number of accomplishments in three categories: Ghost (non-leathal stealth, highest reward), Panther (leathal stealth) and Assault (run-and-gun, lowest reward). Players are encouraged to stick to one style in order to "master" the mission by reaching a certain point total, but the player can use any combination of the three throughout the mission. In my opinion, Assault doesn't fit very well in the context of this franchise, but maybe that's because the playstyle just doesn't appeal to me.
If you play games for the storytelling, then you might like this game. The voice acting and dialog are very good in my opinion, but there is a new voice actor for Sam Fisher. I thought he did a great job, but this change will surely put off some people. The story seemed like a typical Tom Clancy story to me, and I enjoyed it.
The game world looks very good in my opinion. Paladin reminded me a lot of the Metal Gear Solid aesthetic, which I liked. Unlike most Ubisoft games of late, the menu system doesn't have unnecessarily long transition animations.
The only issue that I had with this game is that the ending cinematics did not load for me. The audio and subtitles played, but I was stuck with a blank screen. I watched the ending on YouTube in order to see what I'd missed, because I was too angry to replay the entire last mission just to see if the cinematics would actually play correctly.
I enjoyed my time with this title, but I didn't feel the same urge to immediately replay it that I did with Splinter Cell: Conviction.

While there is fun to be had in Splinter Cell Blacklist the controls end up causing more frustration than fun and with no alternate control schemes you are forced to play the game the way the designers want you to play and not the way most comfortable for you.
There are seperate buttons for climbing up, climbing down, and sticking to and off of cover.  Getting used to these is fine but in the heat of the moment when a guard comes up behind you and all you want to do is pull away from a wall or quickly drop from a ledge your going to panic and your perfect run will be ruined.  Ideally a context sensitive "use button" or smarter "sticky" cover system would have done wonders.
Not to mention people who have never played a Splinter Cell game before will find even the Rookie difficulty hair pullingly insane.  The game is designed to lock out the most usefull tools that could help Rookie players until you can earn them much later in the game.  Things like expanded radar, improved sonar vision, and enemy facing on the radar would have made the earlier experience for new players a much smoother ride.
One of the most attrocious features the developers overlooked for the PC version of the game is the ability to save when you want.  This is something PC stealth gamers have enjoyed for years but in this modern age of autosaves and checkpoints it is nowhere to be found in this game.  Enjoy doing side missions where you have to kill 35 enemies and bust on the last one, or where you have to complete multiple objectives without being spotted once and blow it right at the end.  It's just too risky to save before trying out a really fun and neat looking manuever so its best just to play it safe and boring.
If you can get past the unwieldy controls and the lack of a save feature this is a well made content rich game.  For new players you'll have to put up with a lot of frustration and replaying extremely long stretches of gameplay over and over and over again.

Mind Snares: Alice's Journey is a fun point and click, hidden object, adventure game. The puzzles are interesting, the art is good, and the overall story is interesting. I will add a TL;DR at the end.
The game focuses on allowing you to follow a story more than anything. The controls are simple, all you do it use your mouse to progress through the game. The game is a decent length and allows you to enjoy it thoroughly before giving you an ending. In the game you will explore, collect items in your inventory, play mini-games, and find objects. You will be going from one area to the next utilizing the items you have collected to move forward in the story.
The story is fairly short in my opinion and the ending felt incomplete. This is a game that focuses more on telling a story and allowing one to relax as they adventure. The hidden object parts of the game are fun and enjoyable and each of the mini-games was different and fun to beat. As a point and click game it’s very well thought out and does well on capturing the story and allowing for a relaxing experience.

The graphics of the game are polished and very well done. The cinematic scenes are ok in my opinion. Each area you visit the art is great and some of the art can even be breathtaking. The voice acting is alright and the music is relaxing. The graphics and sound were good in helping to create a relaxing atmosphere.

This is a 3rd person rpg where you are the "Arisen" and must go and slay some Dragon that`s causing lots of trouble in a long quest.
You can completely design how you look (black, white, male female). You have 3 basic classes Sword/Bow and magic which further advances into 6 later. There are lots of items, weapons and clothes to pick.
The game doesn`t really explain why, but there are a bunch of people who never really die who are called "Pawns". They look and act Human, but don`t really have much self will. And because you are the Arisen, you get a free personal pawn Helper. This Helper serves you no matter what, you can make it whatever class you want, even how it will speak (it uses a great varied audio speech system) and even their character traits from rude to meek, etc.
So I made an ideal pretty lady Magic user with a meek countenance to be a Helper on my travels. They also sort of learn after a while of travelling with you, remembering where they last were. It`s a really, really nice and endearing after a while of travelling with them- more games should do this.
Areas to explore are large and interesting, also enemies don`t scale with you so be very careful where you go. If an enemy is too tough, leave until you get better, or hire 2 more Helper pawns. Save often. Travelling can be time consuming and especially difficult in the dark, but I like it.
Monsters are GLORIOUS and EPIC because not just the monster are cool and unique, (You can fight against creatures like Cyclops Chimeras and Dragons and many more) the fighting system is it too . You can attack as normal, but also climb them and try to destroy key parts of them to take them down faster. Sometimes they will desperately grab at you as you stab at their face and cry in pain, while your Helper fires magic from the ground. It`s really very well done. In this game there is a "New Game plus"  system, so you can play the game with your same character again. I never got bored playing this game I made a playthrough with each class and enjoyed all of them. Sometimes the game is a bit too easy (still makes fun. This aspect is for Darksouls weeaboos) but then you can just play the DLC (Dark Arisen) which contains about 30 hours of gameplay.
Criticisms? Pawns can be a bit stupid, repeating the same thing. Sometimes fights are somewhat arcade reminiscent of Soul Calibur beat-em ups, you can see the Japanese influence.
I highly recommend this game.
I hope you do yourself a favour and buy this game.

Before I dig deep into this game, I must let it be known that if you're a big fan of LOTR lore the story is going to bother you throughout. Even if you're a fan of lore coming from the movies, it's still going to be troublesome as the game takes a big♥♥♥♥♥♥on established lore. It's clear that the developers focused little on the story seeing as you can complete it in only a few hours and the characters shown throughout are less than compelling.
Shadow of Mordor is essentially an Arkham + Assassin's Creed game. It was even accused by a former Ubisoft employee, Charles Randall, of having stolen code and animations from Assassin's Creed 2. But what separates SoM from these comparisons is the Nemesis System. It's a neat little system ingame that lets you ♥♥♥♥ up Sauron's army by placing in your own supporters. Sometimes you can even send an orc to kill a captain for you. You'll also gain rivals should you fail to eliminate certain orc leaders. Being killed by an orc captain or letting them flee allows them to rise through the ranks and they gain additional passive abilities and they'll even make reference to your most previous encounter with them when you next fight. It's imperative to interrogate random orcs if you're going up against a powerful orc chieftan as most of their passives and weakness remain hidden. Upon learning their weaknesses you can exploit them to deal with the orc leaders swiftly. Sometimes they may be scared of Caragors or the Morgai flies. Sometimes they may be weak to backstabs. I recommend looking up AngryJoe's Olgoth fight on youtube as a good example of how frustratingly fun the system is as you become consumed by revenge towards your orc rival.
The combat that compliments this Nemesis System is fairly solid though it ends up becoming repetitive later on as you increase in power and spam certain moves that work best. Leveling up will allow you to expand your movesets as well as focus on a specific combat tree though in my experience I ended up being a jack of all trades since I was a completionist freak to an extent. You can gain exp from killing or from "Mirian" coins which can be obtained from quests or side activities like collecting flowers or finding lore items that explain some background lore in the LOTR universe. You can also attain runes which drop from orcs or as quest rewards, to increase the power of your weapons. With all this it's not that unexpected for the player to become overpowered toward the game's end.
Now for the story itself, it comes off as a side thing to the gameplay. Seeing as you can complete the story within only a few hours (if you focused solely on story missions), shows how little the devs cared about it. You start off as Talion, a Gondorian ranger that's part of a battlion of troops guarding the Black Gate. You're wife and son are also stationed there for reasons you'll find out during the whisperings of the loading screens. Seriously they just put whispery audio during loading screens that reveal parts of Talion's past. Talion is for the most part, the generic hero with little depth to him. He serves as a shell for the player rather than as an individual we care about. So like in the lore Sauron returns to Mordor, orcs kill everyone in the Black Gate save for Talion and his family who get killed in front of him by the "Black Hand"  and his Black Captains. I think I speak for most people when I say that no one cares about the death of two people we only spent like five minutes with. The three black captain dudes are the devs attempt to be original and replace the Nazgul, who are mysteriously missing despite being active at this time in Mordor. They come off as bland and generic villians whose personalities boil down to "Grrrr I'm a bad guy because I do evil stuff!" They don't have any real presence in the game, only appearing during the boss fights which don't help their case because they're weak as hell.
So Talion is killed last for some kind of ritual and then he finds himself alive bound to an elf "wraith" whose history is revealed later ingame and ends up being a terrible retcon of previous lore. They set out to discover the wraith's past as well as revenge against the Black Captains. The wraith is more or less an lore expository rather than a developed character. In fact most of the dialogue ingame serves to spit out lore or happenings in the plot rather than develop Talion and the Wraith. There is no personal banter that serves to humanize the two that we as players can relate to them. Before you face the first Captain, you'll come across an orc named Ratbag who serves as a bit of comedic relief and the best part of this game. You help him go up in the ranks in order to push the plot along. Ratbag is a HUGE missed opportunity because he gets killed off in the first act of the game. Why couldn't the devs allowed him to live into the final act? It would have been fun to keep pushing a bumbling orc up to the tops of Sauron's army and then for him to backstab us at the final battle. But no he just serves to be a tutorial to the Nemesis system basically.
At the end of the game, as if known, you somehow fight Sauron after some more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the lore. At least make the fight badass, amiright? But no they reduce the fight with Sauron to a few button presses! Rushed development much? So at the end of it all Talion gets his revenge and it's game over right? No they drop a giant♥♥♥♥♥♥onto the lore again and openly state
. The story as you can see is "meh"... but even so the gameplay does make up for it despite the grind later on. The Nemesis system more or less makes up for the faults of the story. I recommend getting this game when it's on sale and if you're not bothered by some grindy fun.

Mass Effect changed how I look on games as media, before I liked games but I was almost never really invested in the stories they told, that all changed when I played this game. Mass Effect is a classic game that everyone should at least play once in their lifetime, the story is so well told and written it will keep you invested the whole way, the characters you meet and get to know are some of the best characters I have ever seen in a game. But this game is not only awesome because of the good story and well written characters but also because the world they made for this game is simply one of the best universes in not only games but in all of fiction. Both the aliens and the humans in this game feel real and convincing.
I’m a big sci fi nerd and I have always been fascinated by how they portray the human race, in most sci fi that is a huge hit or miss, example of this is how humans are in star trek (love star trek) they are simply too nice they don’t feel like the more grey humanity we know. In mass effect they made a human race that seems like a logical step from how we think and act today, no perfect goodwillers ( like star trek), not some evil war empire( like in 40k) but somewhere in between(maybe a bit more to the 40k on the scale then star trek, kind of on the same place as babylon 5 grey humans not black or white). The universe they made feels alive and almost real something most fiction fail at.
The gameplay is maybe weak in some areas like the mako but it doesn't really matter because what you get out of this game is simply more than just gameplay (gameplay is good in most parts) you get a good story. Should you buy this game? I think so because I think if you don’t you will miss out on one of the best modern games ever made, you will also miss the start of a saga that only got better in mass effect 2. This Game changed my whole view on games and it has stuck with me after all this years and I think that is a testament to how much of an impact this game had on me.

Got this game in a Humble Bundle. At first I was like, oh, it's the exact same game as Hurtworld, right?
It's not, and in my opinion it is far better (although I haven't near completed either game).
My very first impression was a positive one, the simple fact that you got to choose in the main menu whether you wanted to play locally by yourself, play online on a public server or create a server yourself. In other survival games I've found that a lot of the time, it's a dragged out pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to create your own server. Not in this one. So that's a big plus.
It took me a while to figure out how to get anywhere with the simple hatchet you are provided at the start of the game, but once you figured one thing out, you had already figured ten more things out. Easy to learn, and if you don't know how to craft a certain material for example, all you really have to do is click around in the craft menu, rather than tab out and google for help. So that's another thing that makes the game easy to navigate.
But I definitely wouldn't say the game is too easy. So far I've only really focused on making a nice base camp for myself, building houses and such (simply because that's the part I find most fun), but even that isn't so easy you pay no mind to it. You still have to go out in the landscape and get materials, create a smelter, use it to create more materials, use the materials to create a forge, use the forge to create MORE materials to build a house, etc. etc.
It's a real step-by-step experience that I find very fun and interesting.
And for people who aren't into the whole crafting thing; there are multiple dragon towers literally within sight from the spawn location. And also on your way over there you will be attacked by boars and skeletons. So yeah, if fighting is more what you're into, that's not a problem. After all, it is a survival game, not a build-a-village game.
Also, you can run around with your♥♥♥♥♥♥♥hanging out. A feature I believe a lot of people will find hilarious when playing with a group of friends.
Overall, I really like this game. The character creation... How do I say this politely... Has room for improvement. But even I, someone who usually doesn't even consider playing a game unless the character creation is BOMB, has managed to get over it and not let it affect the gameplay (I mean you hardly ever see yourself anyway).
So if you're considering buying this, but changing your mind over the CC, don't worry, it's not gonna bother you at all. Take it from me, I usually spend 4+ hours modifying my characters' appearance. Because I'm a superficial ♥♥♥♥♥.
tl;dr - Environments are nice, weather and lighting are bomb, crafting is bomb, enemies can sometimes be buggy but will still kill you, you never get bored, it's more fun than it seems the first hour or two of gameplay so give it a chance.

I love a good puzzle game. To this day, one of my biggest gaming achievements is fully completing all six of the Professor Layton titles. But recently, it’s felt like every puzzle game has had to be multi-genre: puzzle platformer, exploration puzzle, puzzle brawler, the list goes on. I still think there’s something to be said for an unashamed, pure puzzle game. So does Tricone Lab fill that gap?
Tricone Lab follows your classic puzzle style. Every level has the same goal – in this case, to connect one of each coloured triangle to the connector to make Tricones. As the game goes on, more and more mechanics are introduced, making it more and more difficult. However, where many games introduce this in a very linear way, Tricone Lab instead offers a series of tutorial-esque levels for each mechanic that, upon completion, provide you with key for that puzzle piece. Beyond these levels, the rest of the levels are grouped by what pieces the puzzle contains and can only be unlocked by using the keys.
This is a fantastic idea: not only does it mean that whilst looking for harder puzzles you won’t accidentally stumble across something you’ve never seen before, but also that if you come across something you don’t like (for example, I didn’t get along with the anti-cones) then you can easily see which puzzles have them and avoid them.
Whilst there is no music while solving the puzzles (a gameplay decision), the general feel of the game is great. It has an unmistakeable, and presumably intended, feel of messing around with cells in a lab, although since I’m not a biologist I can’t claim to have any specialised knowledge on the subject.
Another thing that I should praise the developer for is the Colour-Blind Mode. The game relies on moving certain coloured triangles, so to anyone with colour deficiency this could prove difficult. Whilst it only affects a minority of a player base, it’s always great to see an option like that included.
Alongside one hundred standard levels on launch, Tricone Lab also has an editor that allows for very simple creation of puzzles. I had a good play around on it and discovered two things; firstly that the editor is very robust and allows for a large number of things to be happening at any one time, and secondly that I’m really bad at making puzzles!
So how is it overall? In all honesty, aside from the music and perhaps a few minor GUI elements that could do with a bit of cleaning, the game’s really great. I only discovered that it’s in early access whilst doing a bit of fact checking for this review, so that tells you just how polished it is. And whilst puzzle games aren’t for everyone, Tricone Lab stands out as one of those that even on a relatively simple premise provides both a lot of playability and for a lot of challenges, even for puzzle veterans.

This is basically a puzzle/logic game where you drag elements around inside a "cell" to build tricone, an element that requires you to combine 3 different colored cones (red, green, blue) onto a catalyst. Tricone is a pretty sweet puzzle game. The idea is to create a molucule(or molecules) of tricone, a mysterious substance. To do so you need to connect a red, green, and blue tricone chip together with an assembler. To win each level you need to do the right actions in the right order.
The game tutorializes through gameplay really well and is constantly adding new mechanics to keep the puzzles interesting. There is no time limit and you have unlimited restarts/undos. This creates a "go at your own pace" feeling to the game.
Currently there are over 100 levels and it seems like there will only be more in the future. I think this is a pretty sweet game.

Tricone Lab is an interesting little puzzle game. I had fun with the game but it is not going to be for everyone.
At first I found the game to be kind of boring. As I continued playing the game and new mechanics were added, the game really started picking up. While I have only played the game for around three hours and have only completed some of the game, the game really started to grow on me. The puzzles are really well designed and really make you think outside the box.
Difficulty wise I would say that the game is moderately difficult with a couple of the puzzles being pretty challenging that require you to really think outside the box in order to solve them.
Probably the game's greatest weakness at this point is the visuals/presentation. Graphics don't really matter that much in puzzle games but I think the graphics and presentation could use a little polish.
The true longevity of the game will come down to the community. If the game creates a strong community that makes a lot of levels the game could flourish. If not I am guessing you could get around seven to ten hours out of the puzzles included with the game.
If you don't like abstract puzzle games, Tricone Lab will probably not be for you. If you like puzzle games though and after watching the trailer you think the game looks interesting I think you will enjoy the game.

I say this not as a Homestuck fan, but a fan of Point and Click adventure games.
Despite it's unfortunately short length (Just over two hours), this was one of the best point and click adventure games I've ever played, bringing back memories of the original three Monkey Island games and Day of the Tentacle.
The interface reminds me a bit of Beneath a Steel Sky, having the items on top laid out in the way they are, though any reminders of that masterpiece are certainly appreciated.
Aside from the feel the game gives off, being ever so reminiscent of the aforementioned games, the actual game itself is actually a bit simpler. The puzzles are all fairly simple, and the advertised 'homage to classic adventure games while lacking the frustration' is true, save for a single instance, with the second version of a certain minigame, where the undesired letters would spawn immediately in front of me and I wouldn't have the chance to react (I won't offer any context to that for sake of spoilers), though it still took me less than five minutes to do.
The humor doesn't rely at all on knowledge of the comic, though the style of humor is very similar, if a bit less wordy, removing one of the huge barriers of entry the comic has.
I can see myself replaying it many times, just to see the stuff I missed, and even beyond that, just because it was a charming and fun experience.
All in all, it's a fantastic experience, and I'm glad I picked it up.
