This is/could become an exceptionally original game with a lot of potential for really deep immersion. Although the game is evolving slowly in Early Access, it becomes better and better in creating a wonderful Cast Away experience.
What would I love to see added in the (according to my taste) perfect game:
DURING THE DAY:
- Seagulls that try to steal unprotected meat and fish but can be chased away or even killed (bow, spear) and eaten after removing the feathers and cooking them.
- Albatrosses flying by
- Mockingbirds flying around, and singing in the trees at dawn and sunset
- Sea birds that hunt fish (maybe nests with eggs for you to steal)
- Flies that bother you at the warmest moments of the day and sit on spoiled food
- Different species of butterflies, wasps, bumblebees, beetles, ants...
- Small lizards that hunt insects
- Sea turtles laying eggs in the warm sand (eggs make big omelettes)
- Huntable seals resting on the coast
- Small groups of dolphins playing and hunting fish, scaring away sharks, so it is safe to swim and paddle
DURING THE NIGHT:
- Moths flying around light sources
- Mosquitoes that sometimes harass you with their noice and/or bites and wake you up in the middle of the night (repellent = garlic, treatment = banana peel)
- Bats to hunt moths and mosquitoes
- Crickets to liven up your nights
- Hutias (small rodents, aka banana rats)
IMMERSION:
- After a storm floatable items are left washed ashore (suitcase, bag, box, wood, clothe, bottles with or without message etc.)
- Detachable and usable containers in shipwrecks
- Respawnable medical plants that can be harvested to fight intoxication (garlic), insect bites (banana peel), fever (cayenne) open wounds (papaya) etc.
- Constructable drying rack to dry medical herbs before use and to dry fish/meat for conservation
- Slowly respawnable coconuts and even more slowly growing plantable palmtrees from coconuts
- Splint to heal broken bones (stick, cloth, rope, papaya)
- After eating a coconut half, the empty shell can be used to fuel the campfire
- Occasionally a disgruntled moray eel in a ship wreck
- Here and there a small cave on some of the bigger islands
- Raft (with sides and place for a chest)
- Varying wind directions and strenghts, including calm
- Cooking pot, frying pan to make soup, omelettes and to sterilize cloths for bandage
- Sleep is necessary to stay healthy
- Constructable shelf between two supports to put small items and boxes with dried medical herbs and food so they do not fall trough the foundation on the ground
- After discovering the second island a map system becomes available
- Possibility to build a storage foundation to safeguard your precious items when later in the game small tsunamis could wash away items lying on the ground
- Distant thunderstorms lighting up the horizon with little rain on your island
- Anchor point to attach raft and life boat on the coast to avoid losing it (tide, floods)
- Bow (2 sticks, 2 ropes) and arrows (8 arrows per stick, 8 arrow-heads per rock)
I know this is quite a lot, but I am longing for the perfect cast away experience - a balance
between feel-good experiences and challenges. Looking for safety in a harsh environment and slowly
building up a home in an unlikely place. At the end becoming a happy Robinson Crusoe.
Thanks for creating this game, hope to keep it playing for a long time. Michel

The combat:
Pros:
1. You have a limited moveset that you use to kill endless troops. It doesn't stop being fun and it's a great stress relief.
2. The satisfying sound effects and the feel of raw power are ALMOST back from Dynasty Warriors 3.
3. Since you have a limited moveset every character has different abilities and moves.
4. You can use other characters weapons (if you wish, I never liked doing that myself) and you have weapons more suited for different characters. This is great if you love a moveset and hate a character, or the other way around. It's great to have the choice.
5. Combat is colourful and over the top.
Cons:
1. Unit leaders. These guy are here to basically populate the battlefield but they have really ♥♥♥♥ing stupid consequences.
To begin with they never, to my knowledge ever stop coming, which is a first for Dynasty Warriors. You used to be able to empty the battlefield (if you're into that) but you can no longer; learn to just walk away; in a DYNASTY WARRIORS GAME.
Secondly, Unit leaders will easily overwhelm most of your allies through sheer numbers as they keep swarming out of the gates like ♥♥♥♥ing insects. Get used to seeing all your officers cry for help every five seconds and get used to your aid meaning nothing; if you kill one another is on his way. They are weak enemies but they are strong enough to endanger anybody on your team apart from yourself.
Thirdly, capturing bases is absolutely useless most of the time. However, you can "capture" a base to open a door. Honestly you just borrow the base for a few seconds. They'll come back and claim it.
SOLUTION:
♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥ unit leaders.
2. The times are all ♥♥♥♥ed up. Sometimes you will be called on for aid but you'll have all of two seconds so travel the entire battlefield through locked gates and scenic routes.
SOLUTION:
GIVE ME A CHANCE.
2. I don't like the new Musou system that was introduced in DW: 6 (I think).
SOLUTION:
See DW: 3 to see what a FUN musou should be like.
3. As much as I think the general combat is fun I honestly think it could use some sort of system to add/remove moves. For example if you're like me an you use Lu Bu then you're going to get fed up of his chokeslam pretty quick and actively try to avoid it.
SOLUTION:
Some way to customize moves or even better learn new moves as you level. There shouldn't be something like Lu Bu's chokeslam AT ALL in a game where you use the same moves all the time. It would also be nice to have the option to silence the characters if you don't want to hear them over and over and over and over and over again. I don't mind the vocals, myself, but I grew up with it and it doesn't bother me. The option would be great, though.
Story:
Pros:
1. There's a LOT of work here with a LOT of really great, fully voiced dialogue from all the characters and NPCs. There are also a lot of parts that are not voiced but they don't take away from the game.
2. It's more daring than the other games with it's story meaning you'll see a lot more from the story than you would have expected. I can say that I enjoyed the change,

1. Well, it's getting better but it's not historically accurate. I know they never claimed it to be EVER but I have to bring it up.

No, no. Just carry on. It's ♥♥♥♥ing weird.
Ambition mode:

1. With a bit of tweaking this could really be the best part of the game. You go around battling and collecting allies, getting a bit stronger, a bit richer and you're working towards a goal. The game needs more goals and this mode is good for that.

WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥!?

Technical side first - Reasonable console port - stable and runs well (flawless on my 2500k and my sons i3 3110) . Max resolution 1080P-higher would have been nice for downsampling but it is fine
Supports the two xbox controllers I have attached to PC without any issue however the in game button prompts do not update and remain to what the default keyboard bindings are - no big deal.
Co-op works well split screen but there is no online play - this would have been brilliant.
For those with high end GPU's you are able to enable SGSSAA/additional anti aliasing via Nvidia control panel (sorry not familiar with AMD but probably possible also). SweetFX works well as by default the colours are a touch dull and dark but after some tweaking the graphics get a pass.
The game itself has a ridiculous amount of content - 1200 weapons to unlock, 80+ characters to play and level up. Lots of stages to play through. Simple arcade button mashing formula but the combo system does have a bit of depth and despite some lengthy battles the action remains fresh. I think I am 10hours in and have not scratched the surface, look forward to playing more. Will end up sinking 100hours into this at a guess.
Taking it all into consideration I highly recommend this game and hope that they continue to port newer versions over to PC.

Pillars of Eternity is an isometric party-based computer RPG using real-time-with-pause combat.
What is Great about this game:
- Complex and deep story that moves the game along incredibly well
- Deep character creation and multiple classes each with multiple viable playstyles bringing significant variety to your own playthrough
- Rich and appropriate back story, lore, and flavor text added throughout the game that is worth reading
- Enjoyable tactical combat with numerous options for pausing and other options to make the game more enjoyable
- Unique and sometimes fascinating quest lines with multiple alternative methods for success (e.g. talk yourself out of a combat encounter)
- An ending storyline that was possibly the most thought-provoking and intelligently written as any I have experienced
What is Good about this game:
- The game looks quite nice but could have used more art/animantions to improve it further
- The voice acting is quite good where it exists
- Good use of Steam features (cloud saves, trading cards, achievements, etc)
What is Bad about this game:
- The combat could have been significantly improved (although still very good) by including methods to automate companions similar to the systems in FFXII or Dragon Age: Origins
- Given how story heavy this game is, it would have been much improved by including more voice-over work.  The voice acting is very good, but is only available sparsely.  The writing is more than worth reading, but having it spoken would have been that much more engrossing.
Conclusion:
Pillars of Eternity is the current pinnacle of story-telling in RPGs with a great combat system and a classic style.

This is a 3rd person rpg where you are the "Arisen" and must go and slay some Dragon that`s causing lots of trouble in a long quest.
You can completely design how you look (black, white, male female). You have 3 basic classes Sword/Bow and magic which further advances into 6 later. There are lots of items, weapons and clothes to pick.
The game doesn`t really explain why, but there are a bunch of people who never really die who are called "Pawns". They look and act Human, but don`t really have much self will. And because you are the Arisen, you get a free personal pawn Helper. This Helper serves you no matter what, you can make it whatever class you want, even how it will speak (it uses a great varied audio speech system) and even their character traits from rude to meek, etc.
So I made an ideal pretty lady Magic user with a meek countenance to be a Helper on my travels. They also sort of learn after a while of travelling with you, remembering where they last were. It`s a really, really nice and endearing after a while of travelling with them- more games should do this.
Areas to explore are large and interesting, also enemies don`t scale with you so be very careful where you go. If an enemy is too tough, leave until you get better, or hire 2 more Helper pawns. Save often. Travelling can be time consuming and especially difficult in the dark, but I like it.
Monsters are GLORIOUS and EPIC because not just the monster are cool and unique, (You can fight against creatures like Cyclops Chimeras and Dragons and many more) the fighting system is it too . You can attack as normal, but also climb them and try to destroy key parts of them to take them down faster. Sometimes they will desperately grab at you as you stab at their face and cry in pain, while your Helper fires magic from the ground. It`s really very well done. In this game there is a "New Game plus"  system, so you can play the game with your same character again. I never got bored playing this game I made a playthrough with each class and enjoyed all of them. Sometimes the game is a bit too easy (still makes fun. This aspect is for Darksouls weeaboos) but then you can just play the DLC (Dark Arisen) which contains about 30 hours of gameplay.
Criticisms? Pawns can be a bit stupid, repeating the same thing. Sometimes fights are somewhat arcade reminiscent of Soul Calibur beat-em ups, you can see the Japanese influence.
I highly recommend this game.
I hope you do yourself a favour and buy this game.

If I have to choose between yes or no when it comes to recommending this game, it is a yes, though said with a not very excited voice tone. Were I allowed to give it a score, it would be a 6 out of 10.
The game starts like it will be one of the most epic games you ever played. I was absolutely thrilled by the first cutscene and the initial area, thinking: "Wow, this will have an amazing plot of my character trying to understand why was his life spared by this giant dragon that attacked his village and (literally) took his heart away". During my first 10 hours playing, I was enchanted by the combat mechanics, they are not only good, they are amazing! One of the best action combats I have ever tried. The graphics are also pretty impressive. But then things water down. Too much.
The plot becomes dull and uninteresting, things that were exciting for the first time (like surviving through the night by choosing the safest paths using torches or even hiding) become tedious and repetitive. I soon lost both the grasp of what was happening in the plot and what was the point of playing a game that would consist 80% (I'm being literal) of running and getting exhausted through the exact same paths, fighting the exact same monsters. I won't even mention how hard it can be to find good pawns to summon as most of the ones available have stupid AI's like a healer that prefers to run ahead and loot rather than healing and buffing the party members.
On top of that, the class system, that at first looks AMAZING and the awesome skills that each class offer, soon starts to look dumb, as your attributes depend on the classes that you level. See that badass arcane archer with shining arrows that can purge the undead and light up the scenario to make it saver traveling through the night? Well, if you level in this class (which is automatic, you can't save exp to trick the mechanics) your specialty will be magic defense, because of course the main attribute you want is magic defense when your main goal is being a blaster with this specific class.
So, after all, this game is all about giving amazing first impressions and making you think about how legendary it could be and then disappointing you time after time. I recommend trying it as a short-lived game on your list, as the 10 first hours will be really fun. And the plot becomes so weak that you won't feel bad at all for quitting before finishing.

Before you judge this review, just bear in mind that I have ~80 hours on Xbox 360.
Dark Souls is an interesting adventure. It's a game that is lovingly crafted and the atmosphere is truly beautiful pretty much throughout, albeit some aren't as good as others: ie Lost Izalith. Googling images of it isn't quite the same, you need to experience playing the game and seeing for yourself. The gameplay is fun and you get completed immersed in the game world because of the general feel of the game. The bosses have real
to them and are pretty memorable for the most part. There's a decent variety of 'enemies', if you can call them that (if you don't understand, it's lore-related). Talking about lore, there is a lot of lore to be had here. However it is a bit of an iceberg, as in there's a lot more beneath the surface and you'll most likely have to research it to fully understand.
Of course what I haven't spoke about yet is quite the elephant in the room. Dark Souls is a (relatively) hard game, as in it doesn't hold your hand. I say relatively because if you compare it to 99% of modern AAA games, it's difficult, because most games aren't. This makes it fairly hard to do a 'blind-run' but that is the most fun way to do it. There is a real sense of progression to be had here because it's very satisfying to finish a boss you've been on for quite a while and get to the next step, you feel like you've really grown in skill. If you have an average skill at games, and moderately play games, this isn't as difficult as the media tells you. Of course all the "Prepare to Die" advertising doesn't help; I truly think that beneath all that advertising there is a great game to be had here with real depth and character, as well as genuine enjoyment and entertainment, not just a game that is hard.
However, it's not the most consistent game. As what has probably been said before loads of times, the second half just does not match up to the first. It feels like their creativity just died, the levels feel a bit meh and not as fun - the bosses also being a bit
and unmemorable. The ending stage is a bit of a break from that though and I, and probably many others, quite enjoyed the last boss (no spoilers here). Also the PC port is pretty garbage, which is fair enough because Japanese developers aren't really geared towards PC gaming. You will want to install "DSFix" as you can actually then choose the resolution and other settings. FPS unlock isn't recommended though, it slightly messes up the game engine.
Honestly though, the second half isn't THAT bad. Just not as good as the first half, which was amazing, where as the second half was more like good.  But you do have to factor it in. Despite that, it is still one of my favourite games. You will definitely want a controller of some kind, PC and keyboard is not good, not good for any third-person game in my opinion. Anyway, as a spiritual successor to Demons' Souls, it really lives up and is as good, if not better. If you're a casual gamer, I wouldn't recommend this. Too much of a learning curve to easily play. Those who are more dedicated to their games, I would most definitely recommend this. Even if you're not good at games, if you keep at it, you will get better and find genuine pleasure in this game.

There's a decent amount of content: quite a bit of point-and-click adventuring, several (fairly easy) hidden-object scenes, and (medium-low difficulty) puzzle mini-games. There are good hidden object games and bad hidden object games, Mind Snare: Alice's Journey is a great hidden object game.  The puzzles are varied, the hidden object scenes run from simple to hard to find objects that are perfectly hidden, the graphics are wonderful and the storyline is worthy of paying attention to.  Here you follow a character named Alice is trying to free her mind of the evils that reside in it.  I haven't seen any mention, but I believe that this parallels the Alice in Wonderland main character who may have fallen too deeply in the rabbit hole and is trying to get her mind put back together.  Each chapter completed heals a part of her mind until it is completely healed.

State of Decay is an Excellent example of how Zombie and RPG can work.

State of Decay is an exciting, role-playing game with an inticipating gameplay. I recommend this for people who like to create your stuff, your way. Although this game doesn't allow Steam mods, it is equally fun and amazing. I recommend buying the DLC on the holidays for money-savers, because the new DLC, Breakdown, is quite expensive for its amazement.

State of Decay can be one of those games that is thrilling to play, and still give you a headache while playing it. Now having forty hours logged into this game just after a few days, I can safely say this game is totally worth it at a discounted price. It has a terrific blend of Sims and Day Z. However, after a long period of time it throws in the staleness of Infestation: Survival Stories.
Make your way to a safe house, build up defenses, recruit survivors, and monitor meters. That's State of Decay in a nutshell. Once you've done that, you do it all over again after you pack up and move. Difficulty increases as you progress, but it isn't quite enough. The game excels in keeping players interested by looting, meeting new people, and having interesting missions. These do outweight the negatives, but when you run into one of the negatives, it packs one hell of a punch.
For those starting off, they may feel overwhelmed by the amount of things that are thrown at them at once. Even after they get the hang of everything, they still may feel overwhelmed. I never really thought I'd complain about a game having TOO much stuff to do, so State of Decay takes the award for that. There would be times that I'd leave my safe house to knock out a mission and immediately gain three or four more after moving fifteen feet. Some missions will take precedence over others, and others are a nuisance simply because it's going to lower a meter on another survivor.
AI can be a hassle at times as well. Your fellow survivors LOVE to pick the most infested area to be in. Smashing zombies is fun, but sometimes the odds are against you and your AI companion refuses to assist. They'll stand in the center of a horde, kick a few zombies, and then get knocked prone after a matter of seconds. The entire time you'll be too busy attacking what is in front of you, and end up getting sacked from the backside. Unfortunately, reflexes will not be too handy as the controls are a bit wonky at times. Players can dodge, but sometimes you get cheap-shotted and end up losing your already very valuable health. This leaves you your only option of evacuating the premises.  If you're lucky, you'll resort to using a car to run over the pursuing zombies. Hopefully you don't run into a special zombie.
Playing State of Decay will require a lot more caution than other skull bashing game. It stays true to the nature of DayZ in terms of not wanting to die. Players get a bit attached to survivors simply because they invested time im building their skills up. The auto save feature, with no choice of manually saving is a double-edged sword. You're grateful that your progress is always saved, but at the same time you will completely go bonkers when you end up losing a survivor to a completely silly death. For example - while climbing a survey tower I paused to look at my map. In that moment, I accidently tapped my jump button - hurling my survivor through the air and to his death. There was no chance of getting him back, no pity for him, no chance at redemption from an embarassing death.
After bashing in thousands of zombie heads, you'll come to realize that this game isn't really going anywhere, anymore. The sandbox novelty is slowly wearing off and the game is now a chore of constantly keeping supplies up and people happy. Once you've got things maxed, you'll move locations in hopes of another difficulty or play style. Then you do it all over again.
All in all, State of Decay - for a discount price, has a lot more to offer than many $50 games *cough Ghosts cough*. The game provids enough entertainment for a 40-100 hour play through. You'll restart several times, try different locations, look for different survivors, and play in a different style.  That will definitely be enough for $10.00.

Hiveswap! The game we Homestuck readers have been waiting for since the 90s (or at least that's what it feels like). What can I say? It's utterly enjoyable. 10/10 would put birb in microwave again. In all seriousness, this is a short game. It felt, fittingly enough, like the first act in a longer game. If you focus on solving the puzzles, you can easily beat this in 2 to 4 hours, tops. But one quickly discovers that this isn't the kind of game where getting to the end is the main focus; instead, so much care and focus has been put into the journey that you can spend half a day combining every item you see and still find something to make you laugh. Strong but not overbearing connections to the source material? Check. Unique characters with fascinating quirks? Check. The greatest and bravest pigeon of all? ABSOLUTELY. I mean, DANG SON, those were some fine avians. OK, time to fax this pigeon somewhere else! This game is wonderfully humorous, and you can combine pretty much everything with pretty much everything else and there's a unique splash of text for 99.95% of those combinations. Most of those splashes of text are side-splittingly funny. If you want a good laugh and a relaxing trip down high-adventure lane, with great tunes thrown in to boot, this is absolutely the game for you. The puzzles are not challenging. The challenge is seeing how many stupid things you can do before being forced to continue through process of elimination.

Before I dig deep into this game, I must let it be known that if you're a big fan of LOTR lore the story is going to bother you throughout. Even if you're a fan of lore coming from the movies, it's still going to be troublesome as the game takes a big♥♥♥♥♥♥on established lore. It's clear that the developers focused little on the story seeing as you can complete it in only a few hours and the characters shown throughout are less than compelling.
Shadow of Mordor is essentially an Arkham + Assassin's Creed game. It was even accused by a former Ubisoft employee, Charles Randall, of having stolen code and animations from Assassin's Creed 2. But what separates SoM from these comparisons is the Nemesis System. It's a neat little system ingame that lets you ♥♥♥♥ up Sauron's army by placing in your own supporters. Sometimes you can even send an orc to kill a captain for you. You'll also gain rivals should you fail to eliminate certain orc leaders. Being killed by an orc captain or letting them flee allows them to rise through the ranks and they gain additional passive abilities and they'll even make reference to your most previous encounter with them when you next fight. It's imperative to interrogate random orcs if you're going up against a powerful orc chieftan as most of their passives and weakness remain hidden. Upon learning their weaknesses you can exploit them to deal with the orc leaders swiftly. Sometimes they may be scared of Caragors or the Morgai flies. Sometimes they may be weak to backstabs. I recommend looking up AngryJoe's Olgoth fight on youtube as a good example of how frustratingly fun the system is as you become consumed by revenge towards your orc rival.
The combat that compliments this Nemesis System is fairly solid though it ends up becoming repetitive later on as you increase in power and spam certain moves that work best. Leveling up will allow you to expand your movesets as well as focus on a specific combat tree though in my experience I ended up being a jack of all trades since I was a completionist freak to an extent. You can gain exp from killing or from "Mirian" coins which can be obtained from quests or side activities like collecting flowers or finding lore items that explain some background lore in the LOTR universe. You can also attain runes which drop from orcs or as quest rewards, to increase the power of your weapons. With all this it's not that unexpected for the player to become overpowered toward the game's end.
Now for the story itself, it comes off as a side thing to the gameplay. Seeing as you can complete the story within only a few hours (if you focused solely on story missions), shows how little the devs cared about it. You start off as Talion, a Gondorian ranger that's part of a battlion of troops guarding the Black Gate. You're wife and son are also stationed there for reasons you'll find out during the whisperings of the loading screens. Seriously they just put whispery audio during loading screens that reveal parts of Talion's past. Talion is for the most part, the generic hero with little depth to him. He serves as a shell for the player rather than as an individual we care about. So like in the lore Sauron returns to Mordor, orcs kill everyone in the Black Gate save for Talion and his family who get killed in front of him by the "Black Hand"  and his Black Captains. I think I speak for most people when I say that no one cares about the death of two people we only spent like five minutes with. The three black captain dudes are the devs attempt to be original and replace the Nazgul, who are mysteriously missing despite being active at this time in Mordor. They come off as bland and generic villians whose personalities boil down to "Grrrr I'm a bad guy because I do evil stuff!" They don't have any real presence in the game, only appearing during the boss fights which don't help their case because they're weak as hell.
So Talion is killed last for some kind of ritual and then he finds himself alive bound to an elf "wraith" whose history is revealed later ingame and ends up being a terrible retcon of previous lore. They set out to discover the wraith's past as well as revenge against the Black Captains. The wraith is more or less an lore expository rather than a developed character. In fact most of the dialogue ingame serves to spit out lore or happenings in the plot rather than develop Talion and the Wraith. There is no personal banter that serves to humanize the two that we as players can relate to them. Before you face the first Captain, you'll come across an orc named Ratbag who serves as a bit of comedic relief and the best part of this game. You help him go up in the ranks in order to push the plot along. Ratbag is a HUGE missed opportunity because he gets killed off in the first act of the game. Why couldn't the devs allowed him to live into the final act? It would have been fun to keep pushing a bumbling orc up to the tops of Sauron's army and then for him to backstab us at the final battle. But no he just serves to be a tutorial to the Nemesis system basically.
At the end of the game, as if known, you somehow fight Sauron after some more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the lore. At least make the fight badass, amiright? But no they reduce the fight with Sauron to a few button presses! Rushed development much? So at the end of it all Talion gets his revenge and it's game over right? No they drop a giant♥♥♥♥♥♥onto the lore again and openly state
. The story as you can see is "meh"... but even so the gameplay does make up for it despite the grind later on. The Nemesis system more or less makes up for the faults of the story. I recommend getting this game when it's on sale and if you're not bothered by some grindy fun.

An isometric RPG following in the steps of predecessors like Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale,Pillars of Eternity might not be as good when compared to them but remains nonetheless an enjoyable experience.
Pros:
-nice story overall,some companion and side quests are very nice aswell
-decent graphics,even though they don't hold up when zoomed close
-good soundtrack
-a few interesting classes amongst the usual archetipes
-good character customization
-nice party banter
-lots of dialogues,books,things to check to flesh out the game world
-the stronghold is pretty interesting
-good amount of zones to explore and lots of quests
-the game system-not the usual DnD fare-is pretty interesting
-original setting
-you can create your own party members if you don't want to use the story ones
Neutral:
-lots of micromanagement party-wise,you're expected to pause often in combat to give orders/activate skills
-some fights can be difficult
Cons:
-while the story is interesting overall it's very slow to unfold and lacks the sense of grandiose that was found in older games
-the game system isn't fully explained,leaving one to guess certain game mechanics,this is even more troubling during character creation
-some pathfinding issues
-some areas are poorly designed for combat,leading to the party getting stuck in narrow corridors/doorways and being unable to fully engage the enemy
-lack of proper party AI leads to the aforementioned micromanagement,which can get tiring in the long run
-not all party members are equally interesting,some are a bit boring or have lacking quests
-some quests can be a bit dull,or have pooor directions,especially when you're trying to remember where the original quest giver was
-stealth is a bit hit or miss (no way to stealth single characters,must stealth to find traps/secrets)
Overall this is a good game that sadly suffers a bit when compared to its predecessors,it lacks the engaging story and characters and the depth the DnD system and setting gave to the games of old.
I got it for 25$ and am satisfied with the purchase,but considering the Enhanced Editions of Baldur's Gate are available for even less makes it a tough call overall.
Still,if you already played those and are looking for more-or just want something more modern-Pillars of Eternity does have enough going for itself to make it a worthwile purchase and an interesting experience to play through, especially considering isometric RPGs are not that common these days (even though we're enjoying a resurgence with other good titles like Shadowrun and Wasteland 2).

This is an incredibly well written, emotionally engaging, and fun to play computer role playing game. It is arguably a bit short and easy, but that is ultimately preferable to an experience that outstays its welcome.
On its surface, the setting seems like your typical fantasy cliche. However, the more you delve into the lore and each character's backstory, the more you find yourself exploring mature and thought-provoking themes. Do not be fooled by the ogres and elves - there is plenty of creativity here in both the main plot and side-quests. The writing is rich and thick with lore references, but never to the point where the player feels lost or disconnected. On the contrary, the more time I spent reading up on the lore, the more internally consistent everything felt.
But the real attraction to the writing was the characterization - both direct, in the way the characters are described by their authors, and indirect, in the way they act and interact with the world around them.
Through its characters does this world feel real and believable, and it was the intimate detail in which these little pixelated people were described that made me feel immersed in Dyrwood. There is a certain psychological realism - for lack of a better term - that manages to bridge the gap of disbelief between the player and the setting in Pillars of Eternity. It also does not hurt that the voice acting is incredibly convincing, conveying subtle nuances with perfect timing. But more than that, it feels like acting in the true sense of the word; in the sense that is above mere line-delivery. The simple-minded good-hearted warrior with a troubled past manages to consistently sound like a simple-minded good-hearted warrior with a troubled past, while still including variations in mood. The mysterious, powerful villain conveys a permanent sense of calm and authority, and yet he sometimes seems benign, while at other times there is a subtly menacing tone.
The gameplay is essentially a streamlined, modified version of the systems in Baldur's Gate 2. This is by no means a negative, although some purists or old-timers might decry certain features as being too dumbed down or casual. In my opinion, a lot the enjoyment comes from the variety of meaningfully distinct classes and abilities, as well as the freedom to continuously make additions of both player created and "canon" characters to the party. Variety and experimentation are key words here. Players are encouraged to have fun mixing and matching different party members and testing different playstyles.
The developers have really paid much attention to detail, and it would take a long time to praise each of the small features that make this game a joy to play. For example, I really loved how information about enemy stats was progressively added to the journal, helping the player adopt more effective tactics in battle. Also, the interface does a good job of letting you interact with a rather complex world and combat system in as few clicks as possible (Wasteland 2, this ain't).
I mentioned in the beginning that the game is a bit easy and short. However, this is coming from someone who grew up with turn based strategies and rpgs. And it is also from someone who spent a significant amount of time planing their party and optimizing both ability and gear distribution. In combat, I paused the game every half-second, making sure to use my cooldowns as efficiently as possible. Lastly, I did a huge chunk of the side quests on offer, which meant that I was maxed out on experience and had the best items at about three quarters of my playthrough on hard difficulty. If that is the mindset you bring to the game, I don't believe you will find any insurmountable obstacles. However, if you expect to simply click on things and make them die, then you are in for a world of hurt. Even with everything maxed out, you will still need to keep your wits about you and make shrewd decisions in combat. Very few were the moments when I could just let the game flow unpaused through a whole encounter.
The only remaining complaint is that the game feels like it could have been more. Not just in terms of length, but also in terms of rpg mechanics and story-telling. You can see in the design of classes that much has been either removed (presumably for balancing purposes) or it simply never made it past the planing stages of development. For instance, he wizard's grimoire goes up to level 10, but the highest level spells in the game are at 6. Similar things can be said of the chanter's or cipher's abilities. Also, the relatively low, 12 level cap (combined with only a couple of top tier weapons in each class) makes much of the later side-questing somewhat irrelevant. Lastly, I could not help but notice how none of the character archs had any gameplay impact on the characters themselves. This is particularly jarring in one side-quest, upon completion of which, the player is informed that said character has become more aggressive and stronger. And yet there isn't even a +1 to accuracy or anything of substance added to the character. It all just makes me miss the amazing party interactions from Planescape: Torment. If anyone remembers Dak'kon's zerth blade transformations, you'll know what I'm talking about.
Still, like a good book, this game was able to keep me hooked for many sleepless nights. It is both accessible and deep, mysterious and familiar. It can be shockingly grim and dark, but also humorous and light-hearted. It challenges and rewards, but hardly ever frustrates or disappoints. It makes you think, it makes you care, and it makes you take risks. And it's a thoroughly fun to play video game.

None the less it is a great game but most can be accomplished in an hour, hour and a half with a decent world and even faster with a great world that you spawn in. Another quality HO/puzzle game from Artifex Mundi.  I generally expect their offerings to be good and I wasn't disappointed here.
First off, I was pretty delighted to see a story go beyond the basic fairy tale or creepy story to actually give a message, and an important one at that.  It was beautifully handled and not overdone.
Sound and music were good quality with voice acting that actually sounded like they put some effort into it.  This is, as always, a huge plus for me personally although I know other people aren't bothered by bad voiceovers like I am.
Hidden object scenes are nicely done and properly challenging (ranging towards the easy side of the spectrum) without any weird naming issues; if it tells you to look for an apple, you're going to find an apple.  This isn't always the case with these games so it's a plus for me.
Puzzles are essentially your usual fare for this style of game, variations on the normal variety you'll always see, but they are nicely done and graphically pretty, and I enjoyed myself.
Play time runs about three hours, which is average for this style of game.  My play time is longer as I was letting the game sit here and there to get some other things done.  Three hours is a pretty normal run time for these games, but I always feel that ten bucks is a little spendy for this kind of game.  Personally, I would wait for a half-off or better sale or coupon first unless money is no concern or you're used to picking these up at full price.  It's certainly worth a playthrough.

The option menu has two sections: one is for the volume controls and the other one is for the miscellaneous options. In the volume control section: music, sound and voice overs; separate adjustments. In the miscellaneous section: Game Difficulty, Custom Cursor, Full Screen and Aspect Ratio (this option only works if you play the game in full screen mode.)
The game’s difficulty menu has three options, Casual; Advanced and Expert, for you to choose from. The game’s difficulty can be adjusted in the middle of game play.
There isn’t much to say about the game’s voiceovers/music/sounds asides from that they are well done.
There isn’t much to say about the game’s graphics aside from that they are nicely drawn with a bit of painted feel to it. It kind of reminds me of Artifex Mundi’s graphics.
Most of the cinematic scenes throughout the entire game can be skip. The skip function is usually located at the top or the bottom of the screen.
Diary Notebook has been sectioned off into two. One section is for all the game’s objects and the second section is for all the game’s clues/story. Keeps the diary notebook in order but one minor downside, the clue section doesn’t stay opened, each time you access the diary notebook to look at the clues.
Inventory Panel has the option for you to keep it lock in place or unlock to have it hidden from view. Easy access to the items that are collected throughout the game. Some items have “x” amount that required before using; the image changes when an item added to it.
Hybrid interactive hidden object scenes: traditional word lists most with find “x” amount of an item
Most of the puzzles are rather simple to solve but while others would some and/or little extra necessarily steps to solve them completely; puzzles with a puzzle. There’s no reset button for the puzzles, with exception of one puzzle, but there’s a skip button for the puzzles.
Game achievements are earned throughout the entire game. The achievement menu can be access through the game menu or through the option menu on the main after the loading screen.
There’s an interactive map but it won’t show up until the first chapter of the game starts. The key legend on map explains the function each of the map icon. Fast travel from one location to another and back.
The game has an automatic save function, it saves whenever you exit to the game’s main menu, you can continue where you left off in the game.
There are four chapters in total but the length of the game depends how quickly the individual plays the game.
There are seventeen game achievements. Most of these achievements do come with some requirements before they can be unlock completely.

I always feel these style games are overlooked by many, and its a shame because they are quite engrossing. Mind Snares: Alice’s Journey is a mature adventure game that blends together elements of the surreal, psychological thriller, and horror genres.
Alice’s car breaks down and plunges into a river. The next thing she knows, she wakes up in a strange world made of her own memories, dreams and nightmares. Ruling over this bizarre dream land is the mysterious Shadow, who forces the protagonist to face her deepest fears.
In order to escape this ominous, psychedelic world, Alice needs to follow an enigmatic lifeline and locate four magical totems that will allow her to rebuild a bridge back to her own reality. But this proves to be no easy task. Alice must venture deep inside her own subconscious, to face motley characters embodying friendly as well as hostile parts of her own psyche.
Alice solves charades and puzzle that test her intellectual prowess. She must confront the ghosts from her past, suddenly made real by the Shadow’s insidious power.
Will our protagonist muster the strength to defeat her own demons? Or will the Shadow win? The fate of Alice lies in your hands! -  Recommended!

Rather than stripping out quality stealth content for the sake of including action sequences or big set pieces, this game simply puts the icing on top of the cake, as it should be. There is a lot of game to be had here. A satisfyingly lengthy campaign, a breadth of side missions that encourage different styles of play, and rather robust multiplayer options, both competitive in the form of the beloved Spies vs. Mercs and cooperative versions of every side mission. The campaign itself and the story it tells is something between a summer blockbuster and an engaging espionage thriller. And this dichotomy overall strains the story and spreads it rather thin. At times, there are even attempts at commentary on the state of the United States role in international conflict and the moral justification of our trial-less imprisonment of those in Guantanamo Bay. But this is juxtaposed right next to cringe inducing Hollywood hacking and a rather tired and cliche cast of characters. Charlie is the embodiment of all the stereotypical hacker tropes, messy clothes, awkward jokes, and all. Briggs is the up-and-comer eager to prove himself, torn between his former career in the CIA and his new, rather above—the-law position in Sam’s Crew. Grimm is a ball-busting, hard-nosed provider of intel who shares a rather strange amoutn of sexual tension with Sam considering she spent the last game lying, betraying, and shooting him. She’s also been made to look much less homely than before. But I guess that’s the creative license afforded by the rather confusing gulf between sequel and reboot which this game occupies.
Sam himself is what really makes this game feel like a reboot. There’s acknowledgement of past events of earlier games, and his daughter Sarah continues to grow, but Sam looks and sounds much younger than before. The closest comparison I can think of is when they replace James Bond. The history is there, the cast is there, some of the same players are there, but the tone and the central character is dramatically different. But I assure you I am not comparing this new Sam to Daniel Craig’s invigorating take on 007. Fischer is frankly a rather shallow character this time around. Full of youth and vigor and almost none of the cynicism or dry humor of his previous incarnations. I can understand why this is game where Michael Ironsides finally gave up on the series. Whereas he once described Fischer’s character as “a tool that had been used one too many times,” this interpretation of Fischer is a tool that is very much in working order and gung-ho ready to go do whatever is necessary for the Stars and Stripes. There is occasional friction between him and the crew around him, and even some with the higher ups in the government, but Sam’s attitude and “been there, done that” sort of look on life from earlier entries is altogether gone. And it’s certainly missed.
But playing action games for quality storytelling and compelling characterization is like watching wrestling for storytelling and characterization. You’ll occasionally be thrown a bone, but you’re missing the point. Splinter Cell is at it’s best between the cutscenes and that stays true here. And, largely, this is a very old-school feeling stealth game. while there is still the mark and execute “press Y to kill everyone” feature introduced in Conviction, it seemed much harder to reliably use in my Realistic difficulty playthrough. Many enemies wear helmets and a single shot to the head will do little more than♥♥♥♥♥♥them off and make your presence known. So hand-to-hand takedowns or Sam’s plethora of gadgets are generally better options than gunfire. And that’s if you choose to engage them at all.
For the first time outside of a Hitman game that I can recall, the game actively rewards the player for leaving enemies alone altogether. For every checkpoint you reach, you’ll be rewarded with points for every enemy you left entirely undisturbed. And it really motivates stealthy players to do their best to get by undetected and unnoticed. I found myself feeling guilty if I couldn’t find a  way to ghost through a section. This active rewarding of a ghostly play style is a lesson and a tactic that absolutely needs to be adopted by more stealth games (I’m looking at you, Thief 2014.)
But whether you choose to avoid, attack from the shadows, or altogether mow down those that oppose you, the game does a good job of  giving you feedback on your performance. Everything you do in a level feeds into one of three gameplay categories: Ghost, Panther, and Assault. At the end of every level you’ll be given a cash total for your performance in all three categories. And if you max out a certain category, you’ll be given even greater rewards for it. So while realistically speaking you’ll have a mixture of all three at the end of every mission, you’ll want to try and really focus on one playstyle in order to maximize your monetary gains. And those gains are used to upgrade your guns, your stealth suit, or your various support functions your crew offers from the plane.
This game really just gets it right where it matters. There are indeed a few minor annoyances I had which could be a major thorn in the side of other players, though. There is a whole section where you play as Briggs, the other operative on the plane, that plays out as a first person shooter. You can still ghost your way through, but the game really encourages you in this section to play it like Call of Duty. It really stuck out to me. There are also a few other sections where the non-combat routes are decidedly less emphasized than the direct approach.

Dynasty Warriors 8 is a hack and slash action game that was previously available mostly on console system. Now available on PC and Steam, this game includes the Extreme Legends DLC and even though that this is a PS3 port, it's very enjoyable, the control is good, the performance is good, the gameplay is awesome. I'm a fan of Dynasty Warriors by the way.
The story are now more focused on each kingdom and you can choose from the kingdom of Shu, Wei, Wu or the later new established Jin Dynasty. You can also play the story of Lu Bu and other officers that are not part of the three kingdom like Yuan Shao or Meng Huo. And then on each stages, you can play one of up to four participating characters in that stage/battle.
The graphics of the game is improved from the previous game but still not as advanced as any game to date, you can judge that from the system requirements. Texture of the game is somewhat poor too on cutscene. Animations still pretty much the same, just with some new animations. Physics also still pretty much the same too.
As for the performance, it doesn't have issues of any kind, no lags, no stutter, the game runs pretty smooth and very playable. I play it on Windows 8.1 and there has been no issues at all. Well, I do encounter a minor bugs but it will not hinder your gameplay or playthrough at all. One of the bug is, at Hu Lao Gate, when I defeat Diaochan, the announcement says "Diaochan is enraged by the struggles of Lu Bu." It should be the other way around.
Now for the feature, each characters now has unique abilites if they're using their default weapon, and now can use Rage. I simply call it, advanced musou, as it will consume all the musou energy when using it. A new game mode called Ambition Mode also present here, I won't spoil it though, it's quite interesting. The Challenge Mode also make a return here. A weapons type now includes an affinity. There three affinity, it is Heaven, Man or Earth each will outdo another.
Overall the game is good and recommended to play. Even that this is a port from the console version, it's still very enjoyable. The game only lacks multiplayer online, if only at least an online co-op is included, this game will be perfect. I recommend this.
Rating 8/10

I love this game!!!  I have played for HOURS!!!  It is really easy to get drawn in and forget about real life for a while.  The realistic graphics are a major plus to this game. You can cook two items at a time on the fires.
CAMPFIRE:  gently place one item in the fire using your drag/hold key.  Once it is stable and doesn't fall out use your drag/hold key to grab another food item to cook.  Place it up in the fire careful not to knock out your other item.  This technique allows you to cook more than one thing at a time saving your stock pile of wood for other things.
You can do this with the FIRESPIT as well.  It is actually easier with the spit, you cannot knock the cooking item out of the fire.  I have had problems trying to cook fish or crabs when I have a bucket on the spit.
SHARKS:  Sharks will take damage over time, this allows you to kill the sharks at your leasure.  Lure the shark to the shallows on your island, as they are wimming around walk out and give them a nice whack with your AXE.  You can do this over and over until the shark dies.  This way you don't get lured out to the DEEP BLUE SEA (hahahahaha) where you can get rushed by all the sharks other shark friends.  It also makes finding the sharks body after death a TON easier.   I have found that right before they die they swim off DO NOT FOLLOW,  let the shark come back.  (They ALWAYS come back)  If you hit him one maybe two more times it should die.  If not then you are dealing with multiple different sharks.  No matter either way you have dealt the sharks damage.  I have done this and the shark swam away, I left to go to another island only to be confronted with another shark.  I hit it with my axe ONCE and it died.  This has happened numerous times with me and I found it very helpful.
Keeping your dead sharks whole for some reason helps with the spawn rate of any other sharks.  I have multiple islands that I have set up as bases and I have killed the sharks that surround them.  Not cutting them up somehow has made it where no NEW sharks spawn.
However on one of my base islands my VERY DEAD sharks DEspawned and were waiting for me when I came back.  Again the damage level was high and I gave one shark one whack and he died the other was three of four whacks and then he died too.
I HIGHLY recommend this game for anyone who enjoys the survivalist games...
Have fun exploring and surviving, I hope this helps.

This is going to be the last Cricket Captain game I'm going to buy. It's also the first I've had to return. It's sad, really sad. But for the last few years, these games have been unplayable, overpriced, and the way that Childish Things have handled the selling and development of the games has been borderline unethical. CC2017 is no different - literally - to the volumes before it, it is exactly the same game with exactly the same issues as the last four volumes at least. To charge so much for what amounts to little more than an update to 2013 is appalling and the company's refusal to listen to its fans, who want nothing more than to see this series regain some sense of quality, is just stupid.
Some specific issues: quantity rather than quality in expanding the competition lists rather than looking into improving the game as a whole; a bias towards England and the game's markets that see smaller teams suffer in quality and England, Australia, and India incredibly overpowered; poor research, very little about the players is correct and the rating system seems to be very limited, the whole database seems based only on averages, there's no depth; the price, seriously, £19.99 until the next volume comes out is ridiculous; broken one-day mechanics, T20 is unplayable and the aggression system is deeply flawed; terrible graphics that the creators focus on too much (few people really watch them); terrible mechanics that see the AI pick their teams in wacky ways; weird algorithms that sees teams consistently score more than they should and take more wickets than they should in certain situations; a difficulty system that makes little sense; very ugly presentation - this series needs a graphic designer.
These games have no longevity thanks to the incredibly limiting scenarios (which could be solved by taking a look at other management games and how they handle hiring, firing, and transfers) which makes the price-point even more unbelievable. There are so many amazing suggestions on forums and Facebook for this game, where the developers engage, but they seem more interested in a cash-cow with which they can dupe their fans into buying a glorified database update. What's more, you should really be able to succeed with any team eventually - which would be a subtler and more interesting way to handle difficulty - but as it stands, only certain teams will see success in the game.
It's sad, very sad, becasue this game could be so much more. If they developers took a year or two out to really revolutionise the game, engaged some of the more dedicated fans for suggestions, and actually started to care about the game and its fans, then it could be a great game. The fans wouldn't even mind, we want to see this series get better. I, for one, would have happily waited until 2018 for a new version, or even given up some of my time as a designer and fan to help Childish Things. So what's the problem? A lack of competition. Cricket Coach has gone down and there are no other management games like this, so there's nothing putting economic pressure on the developers, which in turn has allowed them to develop this lazy, apathetic attitude towards their game and their fans.
Maybe one day they'll get their act together, but I don't think I'll end up seeing it. After thirteen years on this series, I'm not sure I can handle it anymore.

Pick the team - play the game

Pick the team - play the game

Pick the team - play the game
Pick the team - play the game
Pick the team - play the game...

CONTRACTS (the one small aspect of metagame the series has)
Wait for next season
Start again

Overall I really enjoy planing the Total War series, I've spend hundreds of hours playing Rome 1 and 2, Shogun 2 Empire and Napoleon. This review isn't going to be focused on the AI or gameplay of ATTILA, but on the way that the campaigns usually play out. I honestly thought that the last expansion for Rome 2 would be focused on Attila just like the original game, but CA decided to stretch as much money as they could from one small period of time, Now I wouldn't really have a problem with that, but in my opinion the time period really doesn't lend itself well to the series, and didn't really need a full game. First of all, 50% of the map is occupied by 3 different empires (E. Rome W. Rome and the Sassanids). With the exception the Sassanids these empires are almost completely incapable of defending themselves. This means that any campaign as the Romans starts with turn after turn of autoresolving battles that you have no chance of winning as barbarian hordes eat away at your empire. Now if you find a campaign like this interesting and your kind of challenge that's fine with me, but to me its just annoying, why bother playing as the Romans when your can't do anyting to keep your empire from being torn apart, either from corruption, barbarian conquest or public unrest. This is the first of many problem with the game, it's just boring and frustrating. The second problem with the game is that every other faction just has to capture or raze one undefended settlement after another. It doesn't feel fulfilling or satisfying in any way whatsoever. Of course CA can try to spin this lack of variety in campaign mechanics by simpy stating in the games description: "Your World Will Burn" and "Sweep Oppression From The World" but just adding exciting blurbs into the description won't add any replay value for me. Once again the game is just autoreslove after autoresolve. So campaigns as the big factions are boring and frustrating, and campaigns as small factions are boring and empty. Of course you can say that the late game gets better, and it does in most cases. Just to make things clear, if you find the game interesting and worth the money, I'm happy for you! But in my own opinion I don't find the game worth it, especially when the first hour+ of every game you play is bland and unexciting, so why torture yourself with the first hour+ of play when you can just play any other game in the series?

I say I recommend this because this is overall a good game in a franchise the likes of which are few and far between. A new total war player, I have no doubt, will be astonished by the sheer scale of the battles and the mods that make them bigger. However, I have a lot of problems with this game, as a person who started with Med 2 and played all the games from Med 1 - Attila. Before I get into that, I do want to talk about where this game goes right.
Hordes - A comeback from Rome 1 that was built heavily upon. If you weren't playing as one of the two halves of the Roman Empire, you likely will play as a faction that starts off as a horde or one that can become a horde. Hordes in Attila are basically a breed of city and army. You construct buildings with money and population surpluses and develop troops to keep it intact. If the army is destroyed, you lose EVERY building in it, dealing a blow to your economy ( or helping it if that horde wasn't contributing to the economy much in the first place) This adds an entirely new way to play Total War, and I found it quite refreshing
Civil War, Family, Characters, and Integrity - This can now happen at any time unlike Rome 2 from what I understand (I didn't get that far in Rome 2 yet). if a character's loyalty falls to 0, he will defect and take part of your army with him and form a new faction. If an army's integrity (the new equivalent of public order for armies and navies) falls to 0, part of it will defect, elect a leader, and form a new faction. This can happen several times in a campaign and is logical in its causation. Also, Family tree is back.
Atmosphere - It looks like CA really worked to get the feeling of apocalypse, fire, and death into the game. Fire looks friggin awesome, especially at night. Settlements can be set on fire and deal a blow to the defender's morale (and combat skills for some
Civilians appear on the battle map, ready for the slaughter. The music, while still not as good as it was in Rome, Med 2, and Napoleon imo, does have that apocalypic, depressed vibe to it, especially in the campaign map. You can now raze regions to the ground, burning all traces of civilation and leaving nothing but ruins for someone else to colonize.
Now for where the game falls short...
Optimization: Frame rates drop catastrophically in certain situations, mostly in battles, but on the campaign map, the camera enters sudden bursts of movement when I scroll across the map. In battles, if the number of troops goes too high, the game speed will drop horribly. I have been forced to play 4 hour long battles that I knew I could win on the map but couldn't get a victory via autoresolve, and on one occasion, I had to quit the battle because each in-game second lasted 12 SECONDS in real time. I don't have that kind of time lying around all the time, and I sure as hell hate dedicating four hours to a battle with a one hour time constraint. Some of the grandest battles I have played in this game were ruined by game speed drops like this. Granted, this was largely because I had a 4x unit size mod, but I never had that big an issue in similar mods in Rome 2. It's the worst in terms of optimization in this franchise after all the patchwork.
The Damn AI - When you talk Total War, you're always going to talk about its consistently bad AI. But I found Attila's a special degree of stupidity. As the Huns, I was attacked next to the Black Sea several times by factions with 1-4 regions from halfway across the continent. Factions with their own homelands to defend will go completely out of their way to relentlessly play cat and mouse with your highly mobile hordes for some reason. If you're not playing as the Huns, they get a special little cheat going their way that consistently spawns full stack armies from thin air just outside your borders if they decide to attack you. As a Roman faction, I don't know how much of a problem that will be (I'm not that far yet), but as a small fry next to their spawn location, it's absolutely ridiculous to be able to pound army after army into submission before their infinite hordes eventually overtake my limited armies and economy before Attila is even born!
Enemies are suicidal in battle, always charging their entire army, sometimes including their missile units, into the front of my defensive testudos to get demolished by a hail of arrows and cavalry charges in the back. I have won battles in which I was outnumbered 4-1 this way. In the Last Roman as the Roman Expedition, I conquered half of Africa and reclaimed it for the Roman Empire. They send nothing from their Balkans despite having 8 armies on standby there. That was likely because they were at war with the Ostrogoths who controlled Italy. So I abandon Africa once i destroy the Vandals and move to assist in Italy. The Berbers declare war on us during my evacuation. Rome does nothing as its armies sweep across its new, undefended territory. By the time they mop up the last Roman presence in Africa, I'm bogged down next to Rome. the Berbers take Sicily after minimal Roman resistance and then began to take territory in the Peninsula. I should remind you that the bulk of the Roman Empire's army is still in the Balkans, with one army patrolling the southern tip of Italy, where they are not needed... As you can probably imagine, I was more than a little♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at Rome, and declared independence despite my initial decision in the beginning to remain dutifully loyal to the Emperor and reserve a separate Separatist campaign afterward. Just to give you an idea of why the AI issue must be addressed by CA
Capture points: The system is still as questionable as it was in Rome 2. If 2 men from 2 different enemy units stands on a capture point, they will capture it in spite of the 160 men in one of my units that is standing in its entirety on it. Tower placement is sometimes ridiculous, placing the capture point in such a way that the attacker can capture it by rushing a horde of units into a defending unit standing in front of the point. Sometimes, the capture point is on an undefendable point. A routing unit can capture. A riderless horse can capture!
Naval battles - I like that melee ships are used only for boarding, and ramming ships should only be used to ram, as well as te fact that armies at sea suffer a melee penalty from seasickness, but sometimes, the bugs and AI make the whole thing seem pointless. First, the AI doesn't build much of a navy. Transport ships, for the most part, seem legit enough to it, I guess? At least they're not OP. Sometimes, a man will spawn floating in the water, and for some reason, my artillery ships think its a good idea to target that man instead of the ship he's supposed to be on.
Diplomacy: Seriously, wtf does the AI have against trade agreements. Sometimes it makes sense in the context that they don't want help those they hate, but when a trade agreement will bring the AI 3000 talents, there should be no reason not to accept it, especially if they have even a slightly positive attitude toward me. You can extort the system by demanding payment of what sometimes ends up in the thousands for trade agreements or nonaggression pacts. The ERE dissolved the alliance between him and me (the WRE) on turn 1.
In conclusion, I am saddened by what looked like CA's apology for Rome 2's release. The features it brought to the table: the fire and horde mechanics, the thought of starting as a vast empire beset by countless issues, and from there watching as my land crumbles until a desperate last stand comes to naught as the vast hordes kill every last soldier, kills every great general that rises to meet them, burns every last building in every last settlement - I guess I was naive to think that kind of quality.
This game has its great moments, and new players will still be amazed.
But the veteran TW community will be heartily disappointed, having other TW games to play without these issues.

It's rather a shame then that the gameplay is so uninvolving as to make the game elements feel like an annoying chore to progress the story as opposed to something fun.  I don't mind grindy games if I find the grind elements somewhat stimulating -- unfortunately, the match-3 gameplay here is just kind of tedious and requires little skill or thought-process to advance.

* 10,000,000

* Legend of Fae
* Puzzle Quest
* Super Puzzle Platformer Deluxe
* Triple Town

This is not a strong "don't buy this", but the game really is a bit of a technical foul-up. It's a hex-grid focused Puzzle Quest knockoff, but it's got a lot of problems:
- The entire game runs on a timer of "one month". I'm pretty sure this is a loose enough limit, but the reason I bring this up is that its incredibly imprecise map screen
lead to you running through more time than you mean to on almost every action. Clicking a location makes it guide you there, but the pathfinding takes weird circuitous routes, and every second you're "in motion" runs the clock. Similar bug: if a quest/level dialogue is popping up over the map screen, it will refuse to let you into a targeted area... but it'll keep running the clock.
- It's really, really sluggish. A lot of the match-3 genre runs on "make move, watch board quickly refill" - you're going to be waiting as things slowly work their way down hex by hex on your larger combos, and in a few modes, this is made worse because guess what: the match timer keeps running, punishing you for better play.
- The AI cheats. Not in a "oh, it knows what's coming and makes combos you can't" kind of way like some people claimed with Puzzle Quest, I mean in a literal "it creates connections you cannot make on the board playing by the rules" fashion. I don't know if this is a bug or just designed to keep you from curb-stomping it, because it is dumb, dumb AI.
- There are ten stats in the game and they are, as far as I can tell, explained nowhere. A few are easy to puzzle out (three of them equate to the three "elements" of battle, and levelling those will give you skill points), others eventually become clear (reputation), but the rest I can only take a flying guess at their purpose because they give absolutely no visible effect on gameplay. One might play into an ending (ethics? can I go evil?), but the rest? No idea. It also doesn't help that random tasks out in the world (some of the jobs) will lower certain stats, and you can't find this out until after completing them.
- Hope you like grinding, because this game likes to toss a lot of "go do some crap for a while, I'm busy, kid" quests at you. At least once I managed to fulfill the "goal" of a quest during these grinds, but the game refused to allow me to go on with it because I had not finished the "pay $500" portion that came before the quest's
. (It was "raise your reputation", before someone claims this is impossible. Go ahead. Try it sometime.)
- Lazy touchscreen port. Some of the minigames require you to click and hold your token on the screen to move it around. Not a dealbreaker, but also not a plus.
I can't gripe too hard, I'm still playing it and it's functional, it's just a very low-effort, underwhelming title. I wish this genre didn't basically drop off a damn cliff after Puzzle Quest.
edit after beating the game: Less fond of it because it's one of those games that gives you a perfectly beatable 'invincible' boss and counts your win as a fail state. Time Master's plenty killable if you have a lot of freeze powers.

So there is a bit of a 'mixed' review for this but I'm going to start by summing it up.
Yes. I highly recommend this game.
I was looking for something to play that was multiplayer but more coop without being forced to be online with others or have constant server wipes. A server I could run from my house but have the experience of crafting, surviving and hunting on our own without others coming to sabotage us. Just us against the elements. This game has it.
Let me start off with: Yes it is early access. Yes there is bugs. Yes there are glitchy animals (that have been addressed by the devs as an issue) Yes, there is not that much to do just yet. BUT. In 25 hours we managed to go full speed, two people and not complete the game.
If you are looking for a competetive game without constantly dying and restarting and being able to steal resources for others. This is not the game for you. Now - on to the review.
Multiplayer: There is public servers or you can set them to be friends only or password. We constantly played multiplayer and found no issues connecting to each other. Even hopped on to some public servers to see people helping each other and working together.
Crafting: The UI has seen a major improvement but could still use some tweaking. There is a crafting journal for buildings where you have to put down a 'holo' version of the building then you feed it materials. Armor and other things that don't go on the ground are crafted at a crafting table, forge, and so on. There is not a good sorting system, just one long list. Things are a little difficult to find but there is a LOT of stuff.
Enemies: There are a number of enemies in the game ranging from easy, slow swinging to crazy run after you and blow up for 90% of your life. If you die instantly, you will know you're in the wrong part of the game. Try somewhere else! Some of those enemies are dangerous animals such as bears and large saber like cats. They hurt a lot.
Food: There seems to be a small issue with how the animals spawn sometimes and you might clear a place of deer and get no more spawns. This seems to be a bug remedied by just reloading the game or starting a new map. There is other ways to get food such as berries. There is 'salmon' but there doesn't seem to be a way to fish yet.
Survival: There is freezing to death, starving to death, bleeding to death, poison, so on. Have warm clothes. Oh yeah there's also 'encumberment' to an extent. Heavier armor you run slower but it doesn't seem to make you really slow or be anything past just slower run/swing speed.
Very realistic to a sense. Being inside buildings makes you warmer, standing next to a fire makes you warmer, running into a frozen lake makes you wet and cold very quickly. Eating warm food warms you slightly. Fur on armor is warmer then cloth, so on.
Buildings: The buildings are all placed and preset. They range from small stone shacks to large 3 story 'castles' However you can't modify them at all. But you CAN...rip down an entire town if you're patient enough and make another one yourself! Walls and everything included.
Minerals: Ores have a spawn location, once you find them they will forever respawn at that spot. This could be good and bad, they have a decently long spawn rate and there isn't many of the later ores. This makes the later armor a bit of a grind since they need a ton of stuff. However, while you gather ores, common enemies will drop rare items and you could stumble on some rare special items and even bosses!
This game DOES have a good story! Read the notes you find, it does have a bit of a spooky/creepy undertone which is amazing! Night does make you creeped out and enemies running around in the light of the fire sneaking up on you are freaky!
Graphics....Graphics....I can't say more. This game is BEAUTIFUL. I have a good gaming rig and have to tone the graphics down a little to run smoothly.
Overall: Amazing sense of progression. I got this game for 7.49 on sale but would have gladly paid the 14.99 for it...even 20! Support the Devs! I can't wait to see more of it!

This is one of the few early access survival games that is actually fun and has potential. This game is captivating and I have lost so many hours into the game already, and it isn't even finished yet. The combination of beautiful graphics, a huge world, and good ambience make me feel very relaxed when playing this game. At least until when night comes, in which everything is pitch black and you are forced to use your malfunctioning flashlight in order to see 10 feet in front of you, which in my opinion, creates a horror aspect of the game. Obviously, the game is in Early Access, so bugs are there, not abundant, but definetely there.
When you first enter the world of Miscreated, the majority of your time playing this game will consist of entering buildings in order to search for items that will help you in your journey, such as food, guns, ammo, maps, blueprints, car parts, building materials, and more. While looting buildings for items you will have to be aware of many dangers such as wolves, mutants, and most importantly, other players. From my experience, most of the community in this game is quite friendly, and won't kill you on sight, but you still need to be cautious and be aware of everything around you. When you die, your screen turns completely black, and you won't be notified on how you died or who killed you. If you don't enjoy walking around searching and looting houses for hours on end, then I don't recommend buying this game.
During your journey, you can also get your hands on a variety of guns and vehicles. Miscreated has a moderately sized selection of shotguns, rifles, and pistols. Miscreated also includes a small selection of sedans, trucks, and bikes, with almost all of them requiring maintenance and certain parts in order to actually function properly. The developers have recentely implemented a dynamic weather system, so you will periodically experience rain, thunderstorms, and even deadly tornadoes.
Overally, Miscreated is a terrific game that deserves to be more popular. The game recieves big, feature-filled updates quite often, and the developers tend to listen to their fanbase. Miscreated has a big future ahead of it. You should buy it and try it out. You won't regret it!
