Before you judge this review, just bear in mind that I have ~80 hours on Xbox 360.
Dark Souls is an interesting adventure. It's a game that is lovingly crafted and the atmosphere is truly beautiful pretty much throughout, albeit some aren't as good as others: ie Lost Izalith. Googling images of it isn't quite the same, you need to experience playing the game and seeing for yourself. The gameplay is fun and you get completed immersed in the game world because of the general feel of the game. The bosses have real
to them and are pretty memorable for the most part. There's a decent variety of 'enemies', if you can call them that (if you don't understand, it's lore-related). Talking about lore, there is a lot of lore to be had here. However it is a bit of an iceberg, as in there's a lot more beneath the surface and you'll most likely have to research it to fully understand.
Of course what I haven't spoke about yet is quite the elephant in the room. Dark Souls is a (relatively) hard game, as in it doesn't hold your hand. I say relatively because if you compare it to 99% of modern AAA games, it's difficult, because most games aren't. This makes it fairly hard to do a 'blind-run' but that is the most fun way to do it. There is a real sense of progression to be had here because it's very satisfying to finish a boss you've been on for quite a while and get to the next step, you feel like you've really grown in skill. If you have an average skill at games, and moderately play games, this isn't as difficult as the media tells you. Of course all the "Prepare to Die" advertising doesn't help; I truly think that beneath all that advertising there is a great game to be had here with real depth and character, as well as genuine enjoyment and entertainment, not just a game that is hard.
However, it's not the most consistent game. As what has probably been said before loads of times, the second half just does not match up to the first. It feels like their creativity just died, the levels feel a bit meh and not as fun - the bosses also being a bit
and unmemorable. The ending stage is a bit of a break from that though and I, and probably many others, quite enjoyed the last boss (no spoilers here). Also the PC port is pretty garbage, which is fair enough because Japanese developers aren't really geared towards PC gaming. You will want to install "DSFix" as you can actually then choose the resolution and other settings. FPS unlock isn't recommended though, it slightly messes up the game engine.
Honestly though, the second half isn't THAT bad. Just not as good as the first half, which was amazing, where as the second half was more like good.  But you do have to factor it in. Despite that, it is still one of my favourite games. You will definitely want a controller of some kind, PC and keyboard is not good, not good for any third-person game in my opinion. Anyway, as a spiritual successor to Demons' Souls, it really lives up and is as good, if not better. If you're a casual gamer, I wouldn't recommend this. Too much of a learning curve to easily play. Those who are more dedicated to their games, I would most definitely recommend this. Even if you're not good at games, if you keep at it, you will get better and find genuine pleasure in this game.

As the eighth installment of the classical hack-and-slash series, Dynasty Warriors 8 is the first of the series to arrive on Steam. Proving a relatively successful run on the consoles, Dynasty Warriors 8 relives the storyline of the Three Kingdoms and the playable modes of past Dynasty Warriors games - but this time, with a much larger cast of playable characters, new additional content, weapons and maps, and even new playable modes. The storyline proves interesting, exciting yet slightly repetitive, whilst the action of slaying thousands of warriors itself, is satisfying nonetheless. However, due to the port to Steam, graphical qualities and rendering are kind of poor, resulting in occasional characters who look like cardboard cutouts. For many computers, it is very possible that players will suffer slowdown, lag or even screen tearing as a result of the sheer enormous amount of people on the screen at times. The soundtrack/score is no doubt excellent, supporting the game by building the tension of war, and also as just ear-candy if necessary. As part of a personal favourite series, Dynasty Warriors 8 also doesn't disappoint in difficulty as the tradition of pursuing Lu Bu in any difficult higher than easy is still a living hell. 9/10

After putting roughly 30 hours into this game and trying all of the game modes, I feel like I can write a reasonable review.
System Specs
Windows 8.1
Intel Core i7 4702HQ
8GB RAM
512GB SSD
nVidia GTX 765m
1600x900 Resolution
Performance
The first week of this game's release was pretty rough for Windows 8.1 users. I had repeated hangs where the game would freeze on a loading screen, requiring closing the game and re-opening it. There were ways around this (namely running in Win98 compatibility mode), but those problems have been resolved with the first patch. Now that the patch has been released, I have absolutely no slowdown with all settings cranked. Dynasty Warriors games have never been too demanding and this game doesn't change that. As long as you're not trying to run the game on a potato, you should be okay.
Gameplay
Dynasty Warriors has long been a series that players either love or hate. I haven't played a Dynasty Warriors game since DW6, as I don't own a console. When I saw DW8 was coming to the PC, I had to jump on it. Let me tell you - this game is a world apart from DW6, and it's for the better. There is a lot of content here:
- 6 story modes: Lu Bu, Wu, Wei, Shu, Jin and Other, all with different branching stories.
- Free mode, where you can play any officer in any level.
- Challenge mode, where you have a set challenge to beat at a set level.
- Ambition mode, where you build a base camp and then conquer ancient China.
Roughly 30-35 hours in and I've only beaten one story mode (without the hypothetical branch) and dipped my toes into Free and Challenge modes. I've made it through the first half of Ambition mode, as well. Those modes, combined with the ability to level all the characters to 150 and get special weapons leads to a huge amount of content; I'd venture to say there's between 60-100 hours of content here, easily.
Controls
I play without a controller. I remapped the keys to WASD for movement and JKLI for attacks. Using LSHFT for block and camera center and Space for jump has worked well for me. I'm not sure about controller mapping, as I don't use a controller.
Sound
The dubbing is gloriously cheesy in this game, but it's Dynasty Warriors - what do you expect? I enjoy the over-the-top voice acting and cheesy buttrock soundtrack; will it win any awards? No, but this game isn't about the story so much as it is chopping through thousands of footsoldiers only to drop a massive Musou attack and ooh and aah at the pretty colors.
Verdict
I didn't mind paying full price for the game, as I have limited experience with Dynasty Warriors and knew what I was getting into. The initial pre-patch game was a little rough to deal with, but now that it's been patched this is a great game. I'd perhaps wait for a sale if you're new to DW, but there's a lot to love here.

+++ Stealth Gameplay is an aweome combination of the speed and flow of Conviction, combined with the focus on stealth and getting the job done of the early games. Perfect sequal to Chaos Theory.
-- Michael Ironside is gone and Sam Fisher and the story suffer greatly because of it.
If you've loved the Splinter Cell series from the beginning and were okay with Conviction you should love Blacklist. It takes all the best features of the series and brings them home. The option to play like Conviction is there, but the game encourages you to play stealtily and passby enemies like in previous iterations.
Spies versus Mercs is awesome, though the matchmaking is a little weak so you will often end up with disproportiate skill levels in games.
Co-op is alot of fun, and while I might see you doing each level a few times, I can't see the longterm replayability sticking.
All that being said, if you were a fan of Sam Fisher you're in for a disappointment. Michael Ironside is gone, and so too goes any character. Eric Johnson has all the persnality of a potato; his talks with Sam's daughter Sarah are weird because of the age difference (or lack therof), but thankfully those talks can be skipped. The story bafflingly starts with Sam back at the NSA but with "Fourth Eschelon" for some reason. The series would have benifited greatly from Sam Fisher retiring with Ironside or maybe breifly cameoing to coach the new one.

Ubisoft is at it again, and after three years of development, it appears that Splinter Cell has embraced the true stealth genre once more. 2010's 'Conviction,' after three years of launch delays, was Ubisoft Montreal's answer to wanting to appeal to a wider audience, so Sam Fisher was sent in without a light meter nor the ability to perform knockouts, whistle or hide bodies.  Instead it was an action-heavy guns a-blazin' approach, with just enough stealth elements as an attempt to hold on to its core followers.  'Blacklist' has made up for that minor failure and then some, offering up some of the best gameplay, AI and combat mechanics the franchise has seen to date.  Further, the storyline is genuinely engaging and the voice acting is top shelf material, though sadly the voice acting services of the legendary Michael Ironside is missing for the first time in the franchise, strangely replaced by the capable but much younger Eric Johnson.
Sam Fisher, as usual, plies his counter-terrorist trade, this time against The Engineers, sending him around the globe.  Sam's base of operations is an airborne military jetliner, from which the player can upgrade his gear, accept side missions from the Echelon 4 team, or pursue the main storyline.  Between all the options, there is plenty of of gameplay to be had from a single player standpoint, with additional multiplayer co-op and merc vs. spy possibilities.
Though a bit linear in scope and lacking in memorable villianous character, 'Blacklist' is a welcome return to the Splinter Cell I've known and loved for over a decade.  If you are new to the franchise, pay the older titles a visit; the original 'Splinter Cell' still holds up very well.  I look forward to 'Splinter Cell 7,' slated for a 2015 release.  Or 2016.  Or 2017.

One of the first good mainstream stealth games in the last five years or so, aimed at general audiences.
Multiple playstyles are supported, from the sneaky ghost, the brutal "lethal stealther", or the tactical "the world must burn" assault-lover, the game doesn't actually go out of the way to punish any one playstyle, since all of them are valid and rewarded.
Difficulties are actually very well encompassing, since you have a nearly hand-holding rookie level, down to a "half of your advantages are handicapped, and you have no mark and execute" perfectionist style.
Above all else, though, the levels are actually well designed 99% of the time, compared to the tripe that most stealth games have these days with simplistic AI; the guards in this game are disturbingly smart, so if you come inside expecting the usual guard behavior you saw in something like Splinter Cell Conviction or Dishonored, you're going to be surprised.
To put it simply, this game pulls off what Hitman Absolution did, tried to, and then goes on to cover even more.
The only complaints I have about the game are the usual "you're on the Unreal engine, so animation errors are practically inevitable" (though to be fair, the game does a damn fine job of hiding the fact that it's ON Unreal), and the story is hilariously asinine, to the point it practically doesn't match up to the quality of the gameplay. Oh, and the usual "Uplay isn't something anyone wants" crap, but that's a given with a Ubisoft game.
Also it's buggy as♥♥♥♥♥♥and the netcode needs work, but oftentimes the results are more hilarious than gamebreaking.
If you want a challenge, be it loud, lethal, or silent, this game (Splinter Call: BlackopsList, or GI JOE SNEAK SQUAD) actually does a damn fine job of it. Just don't expect an award winning story.

The argument put against this is that being able to see player skills would ruin the fun of finding out which players are actually good and which aren't. But even giving us the option to generically increase a players skill without access to the inherent skill level of a player is good enough compromise.
Ultimately though, the fundamentals of this game are very good, and that is why I recommend this game. The match engine is good enough that I can continue playing each version throughout the year until the next version is released, and this won't change this year having tried out the game so far. Player skills are fairly accurate this year as with previous years, mainly because there are regular database updates for a few months after the release of each version, with members in the forums making suggestions for player skills and database changes that are listened to.
So while this game does not aim high, it is fundamentally a solid cricket management simulator.

:
There's a few bugs with the default settings for keyboard + mouse controls. By default the control for sprinting is Shift, as is typical with many games already. However, somehow it seems to also be the hidden key for "grab" even if you set grab to another key (by default grab is something else. Therefore I recommend changing both the grab and sprint keys to other keys if you plan to play this with mouse and keyboard.
Another bug with keyboard controls is something I didn't notice until much later when I started to play magic classes: the default setting of left click for "light attack" will bug out the controls for magic. Any spell that you bind to the left click or X button on gamepad (basically the first one in the spell list) will fail to release, and therefore will never actually work. This will affect the gamepad as well.
Therefore I highly recommend that you make a choice whether to play the game with mouse and keyboard OR gamepad so as not to have to keep changing keybinds. Or just get used to a different key setup or something.

I've read some comments on here that the game is unplayable on mouse/keyboard unless you use mods. Just wanna let you know that this is NOT the case. Once you discover the controls, it's fine. Here's a handy little list of PC controls:
Movement: WASD
Run: Hold shift
Reg. attack: Left mouse button
Strong attack: right mouse button
Kick: Hold shift and tap A + LMB
Jump attack: Hold shift and tap A + RMB
Jump back: Space
Roll: Hold shift and press direction + Space
Auto-target: middle mouse button
Shield: C
Parry: V
Interact (opening doors, climbing ladders, talking, etc): Q
Use item: E
Open menu: Esc
My default is holding Shift, A and C, so I'm running with my shield out; it's a little slower, but safer.
Once you take a few minutes to adjust to the controls, it's really not difficult to use them.

Hiveswap took all the things I liked about point and click games that have a linear storyline, and managed to keep that while dropping most of the things I dislike in such games. Basically, Hiveswap is a story told through an interactive experience where you get much more flexibility to choose how fast things go than in a movie or such, and can spend massive amounts of time looking into details in the setting. TLDR; Spandex Force is a fun casual match 3 game at the right price, but be warned its main story does have a time limit.
Spandex Force is a match 3 game which you play a superhero in training, and you gain power and attack through a match 3 game type system. Its core gameplay is pretty interesting at times, but overall it doesn't require alot to play a few matches, and you can go off and do your own thing. The story is generic, but it has a few side minigames that provide some variety. While progression is slow (painfully sometimes if you are just trying to rush through) it has enough bells and whistles to sidetrack you from feeling like you are just grinding one scenario. Overall a fun game, but the main mission does have a 30 day in game time limit.
Pro's:
Match 3 with an upgrade system to vary how you play
Fun gameplay (if you like Match 3's)
Never really over/underpowered in the main storyline
Varied minigames/sidegames that break the monotany from time to time
Casual match 3 fun
Con's:
Upgrade system could use some tweaking
Can become really grindy in some aspects
The rock paper scissors aspect of your attacks never really come that far into play
Attacking enemies is slow, takes like 5 seconds each attack and it takes on average 6 attacks to kill a guy
Buy it if you are looking for a under $5 game to pass a few hours, it will give you that at a minimum.
*Final note: Dev seems to be pretty responsive on the forums, which is always really appreciated.

I love this game!!!  I have played for HOURS!!!  It is really easy to get drawn in and forget about real life for a while.  The realistic graphics are a major plus to this game.  The sharks look real, stingrays, fish, turtles...  you get the idea.  I wish there was a multi-player option.  My sons would love to play too.  I also wish there were more inventory options.  Other than that I will continue to play.  Looking forward to the next update.
You can cook two items at a time on the fires.
CAMPFIRE:  gently place one item in the fire using your drag/hold key.  Once it is stable and doesn't fall out use your drag/hold key to grab another food item to cook.  Place it up in the fire careful not to knock out your other item.  This technique allows you to cook more than one thing at a time saving your stock pile of wood for other things.
You can do this with the FIRESPIT as well.  It is actually easier with the spit, you cannot knock the cooking item out of the fire.  I have had problems trying to cook fish or crabs when I have a bucket on the spit.
SHARKS:  Sharks will take damage over time, this allows you to kill the sharks at your leasure.  Lure the shark to the shallows on your island, as they are wimming around walk out and give them a nice whack with your AXE.  You can do this over and over until the shark dies.  This way you don't get lured out to the DEEP BLUE SEA (hahahahaha) where you can get rushed by all the sharks other shark friends.  It also makes finding the sharks body after death a TON easier.   I have found that right before they die they swim off DO NOT FOLLOW,  let the shark come back.  (They ALWAYS come back)  If you hit him one maybe two more times it should die.  If not then you are dealing with multiple different sharks.  No matter either way you have dealt the sharks damage.  I have done this and the shark swam away, I left to go to another island only to be confronted with another shark.  I hit it with my axe ONCE and it died.  This has happened numerous times with me and I found it very helpful.
Keeping your dead sharks whole for some reason helps with the spawn rate of any other sharks.  I have multiple islands that I have set up as bases and I have killed the sharks that surround them.  Not cutting them up somehow has made it where no NEW sharks spawn.
However on one of my base islands my VERY DEAD sharks DEspawned and were waiting for me when I came back.  Again the damage level was high and I gave one shark one whack and he died the other was three of four whacks and then he died too.
I HIGHLY recommend this game for anyone who enjoys the survivalist games...
Have fun exploring and surviving, I hope this helps.

FULL REVIEW BELOW
Quick review:
Pros:
1. Not a zombie survival game.
2. Great environment with lots to explore both above and below water.
3. Just as fun and challenging as any other zombie survival game.
Cons:
1.Unorganized crafting and storage.
2. Lsland tracking
I usually do not play many games outside of FPS but when I saw gameplay for Stranded Deep, I knew that i needed to buy this game. I am somewhat a fan of survival games but I play FPS just because of how saturated the Survival game genre is. With Stranded deep however, it is quite a different game.
Let us start off with the fact that there are no zombies in Stranded Deep like EVERY other survival game. I used to be very much a fan of zombie survival genre but now I find that there is just way too much of it and like all things in the world (almost all), too much of anything good is bad.
The next thing I would like to touch on is the environment. With most of the survival games out there, they all take place in a dark, creepy forest or a dark, ruined overrun city. With stranded Deep however, it takes place in a nice bright tropical region which I can actually enjoy with bright colors, beautiful waters and a vast land to explore both above and below the water .
The final thing I want to address is the difficulity of the game. Currently in update 0.02 hotfix, the sharks have proven to be just as hard and just as fun to kill as any zombie in other survival game but also gives you a sense of victory and accomplishment that you just can't find in other survival games.
With all that being said, there are a few things that i do not enjoy about this game. One of those things being the crafting and the island tracking. With the crafting, it can get a little unorganized and a bit laggy when you have mass amounts of sticks thrown into a pile. I would like to see a form of storage added to the game and a more simple way to craft items other than throwing everything into a pile. The other thing that needs to be addressed is how you can keep track of your island. Even with the compass, if you follow a compass bearing a far distance and you eventually find an island slightly to the left or right, becuase you went to the left or right a little bit, you will most likely loose your island. An easy fix to this would be a way to write up a map.
All in all, Stranded Deep is an amazing survival game that is a welcome change to the survival genre and is very much worth every penny. I look foward to the development of this game and I look foward to putting many more hours into the game.

State of decay is a combination of an average zombie FPS and a good to great, streamlined, smaller, open world RPG.  If you enjoy both zombie FPS and open world RPGs, you wont be disappointed here.  Depending on how much you want to get out of the game, you could spend from 10-30 hours on one play through.  However, the fact that most missions, item drops, zombie base spawns and NPCs that can join your party are random will keep you coming back for more.
The FPS zombie aspect of the game is more akin to Dead Island and Dead Rising than it is to the superior FPS zombie titles such as Left for Dead and the Last of Us.  First, the zombies in State of Decay aren’t really scary, and are more cartoonish.  There isn’t humor in killing them like in Dead Rising, but the glowing eyes and cartoonish walk of the zombies in State of Decay really takes some of the scare out of the game.  The shooter controls in State of Decay are adequate but clunky.  The melee controls work surprisingly well, but range weapon control is not so great.   Similarly, driving vehicles in this game is average, but not poor; the controls are clunky, they psychics aren’t there, and cars randomly flip over for no reason.  But again, this is an average FPS game.
This game really shines in its open world, RPG aspects.  Without spoiling anything, you have establish a home base in one of ~10 predetermined areas, then plan how to build that base using limited supplies, facility locations within the base, and utilizing the specialties of the cast of survivors you have assembled during that play through.  Resource management is a key element to the game, and much of your time will be spend trying to acquire those resources, be they material or actual people to work in your shops and man your guard towers.  Along with managing resources, your characters will also auto level up as you use skills and achive random perks that tweak your playstyle.  While just a tiny bit of an RPG, it helps the game quite a lot.
There are few downsides to the game, some of which are more glaring than others:
-Glitches: these generally occur with NPCs, and range from NPCs being stuck in walls to NPCs not moving to waypoints in missions, or NPCs not going to proper locations in the base
-Story: the story is quite poor, incomplete and disjointed.  There are tons of holes in plot, lore, and backstory that could have been filled by various items and interactions in the world, but they are not
-Voice acting: it seems like only four voices were used for all 16 or so of the NPCs during my particular play throuh.  This is one of my biggest complaints with this game, as each NPC has a unique back story, but the same voice, which kills immersion
-Mission spawn rate: There seem to be lots of mixed feelings about mission spawn rate, I personally think missions happen to frequently, especially at the start of the game.  This leads to an overload of information in your quest journal that is difficult to keep up with.  It also prevents some exploration, though as you move along in the game, you realize you can skip every other mission or so and that is OK.

It's worth noting that this isn't a zombie survival horror game. It's a survival game which has zombies as token mobs. What's also worth noting is that this detracts nothing from the experience. The focus is on building a home with suitable defenses and facilities, finding new sources of the four major resources: Ammo, Medicine, Food, and Fuel. Progression at one home will eventually exhaust nearby supplies. Only zombies respawn, although you can create outposts around which no zombies spawn.
The upshot of all this is that you have to go further and further out for supplies unless you relocate, which means also having to rebuild your facilities. Also, cars don't respawn, so you have to keep the ones you've got repaired. You get missions, but they almost never give supplies. Additional members are also difficult to acquire. To boot, everything is randomly placed when you make a new game. You won't find a Wiki with dependable resource locations.
And death? Permanent. If a character dies you switch over to another member in the party. Knowing when to run and scarf down painkillers is key, as is carrying sufficient ammo and weapons. Zombies only die by a shot to the head or enough melee damage.
Overall, worth the $20. Or on sale for $10 is even better. Just remember you're not buying a AAA title. It's a budget title, but surprisingly well made. I give it a 8.5/10.

A real return to form for the Splinter Cell series in my opinion.

All in all I would say if you are on the fence about this game and you are a fan of the series then I would reccomend picking this game up. To me it was a perfect combination of my favourite game in the series, Chaos Theory and the more modern games like Conviction.

My biggest gripe with this game is:
- No Michael Ironside
- The new Sam Fisher. I mean, Ubisoft could easily have retired Sam after Conviction and introduced a new character, or even better, kept Sam as a leader for the team, and have him functioning as a mentor, instead of completely destroying his character, but that is just my oppinion.
- Inconsistencies between gameplay and story. Splinter Cell is about stealth, and always have been, so it really annoys me that there were so many forced shootouts, chases and cutscenes, with more explosions and shooting than a Micheal Bay and Quentin Tarantino lovechild movie, especially when I had just done a perfect stealth run through a level.
- Stealth. Blacklist executes this part very poorly compared to the old games, though better than most games in general.
With that out the air, I can say that Blacklist has a very interesting gunplay, and for once, it is actually fun to just run through levels with your guns blazing.
The coop is fun as hell so I would highly recommend that you play the game with a friend.
Would I recommend this game? Yes, but if you are an old fan of the Splinter Cell universe and Sam Fisher, be prepared tear your hair out over what they did to the characters.
It's a very fun game that I think is well worth the money.

All in all, Blacklist has brought back some incredible stealth and combat gameplay, aswell as an enormous array of weapons and gadgets at your disposal; giving players the ability to customize and cater their loadout to their playstyle.
The voice acting is superb; with the silky smooth Elias Toufexis (Renowned for his work as Adam Jensen in Deus Ex: Human Revolution) gracing us with his dulcet tones as side character Andriy Kobin.
If you're a fan of the Splinter Cell games, or just an avid player of stealth and predatory games, you can't really go wrong with Splinter Cell: Blacklist.Not to mention it has a rather impressive amount of playtime compared to other AAA titles. Having personally clocked in at 21 hours on a single playthrough, I am left wondering where the time went.

SC: Conviction was the first Splinter Cell title I've tried on the X360, and it's one of the few games I still own on that console. With that in mind, it was only a matter of time before I'd purchase SC: Blacklist, and reviewing the past month, it's the game I've played most ever since the winter holiday sale started. And I've bought about 40 games.
If you like the Borne trilogy movies, the Homeland series, or the Metal Gear games, then you must have SC: Blacklist in your collection as well. The storyline is not that different (prevent a group of terrorists in their attacks on US soil; this is the only spoiler I'll give you), but still tense enough to make you want to finish the game in one sitting. Which you probably can't, because you (as the gamer) need water, food, sleep and something like work or education, so don't even try to finish it with an all-nighter.
For me, the addictive part that will make me play it today and tomorrow comes from many factors. First, upgrades. You can upgrade pretty much everything. Your outfit (which affects armor, stealth, # mag clips, etc.), your weapons (range, accuracy, silenced, etc.), your gadgets (e.g. sonar vision, tri-rotor, smoke bombs), and even your headquarters (infirmary, workplace, etc.). Second, combat. You can choose to finish the game in three styles; ghost (leave no trace), panther (stealth kills) or assault (head-on Rambo-style), and I've noticed myself trying to get more ghost-points with each passing mission. Instead of taking out the enemy sniper from distance, why not try to knock him out non-lethally from behind? Third, missions. You can follow the storyline, do side-missions, fulfill the daily online challenge or choose to do the online spies vs mercs. Side-missions you can do co-op (online) as well as solo, and upon completion they'll give you cash rewards and equipment unlockables. Fourth, controls. They're again very intuitive, whether you want to peek under a door, open the door, or bash through it. I think that many hardcore gamers would curse their keyboard or controller for on-screen actions that weren't meant to happen. I must admit that I sometimes get enraged, but then realize it was my mistake to take on three heavy guards with a side-arm. (By the way, I use a xbox controller, I don't know how it goes with mouse&keyboard). Fifth, the storyline and characters. Every chapter follows a debrief, the mission itself, and a recap that serves as an introduction for the next mission, with plenty of character interaction and all the military lingo that makes the game all the more immersive. In between these missions, when you're in HQ, you can talk with your crew and call your daughter.
I wouldn't possibly know if there'll be a next Splinter Cell and how they'll seek to further improve it. But I'll be one of the first to buy it and I wouldn't need a discount either. In a word; recommended.

After putting in over 400 hours I can say this is one of my favorite go-to games. No doubt this is one of the best rogue-like games on the market in terms of difficulty, fun, diversity, and now has mod support built in with Afterbirth+ expansion.
Game is pretty simple legend of zelda style top down where you run around as either Isaac or one of the other unlockable characters with their own unique stats and items and try to make your way down the basement. You collect items as you go which alter your looks and your abilities. Some of these actually alter you quite a bit and the synergies you can make are pretty awesome. Along with the procedurally generated floors you can have a pretty sizeable map layout that's different nearly every game. You'll have the same rooms but rarely with the same enemies or adjacent areas.
A fair bit of the more entertaining items have to be unlocked though so you'll have to go through most of the game time and time again beating it on certain difficulties or with certain characters to get them but it's worth it.

So, I just finished playing this game (base-game no DLC's yet) and I have to say... well... actually, I have to say quite a lot.
So, to start off: The combat feels great and you really can emerge yourself in the gameplay.
I don't think  have to talk about the setting but everyone should know that the problems with the game don't lie there.
The enemies seem way too stupid and you sneak up on them way too easy and some Warchiefs can be ridiculously strong. (Like...really strong)
Otherwise there isn't that much of a problem with the Uruk enemies you face and the way you learn to control them in the second act is really cool. But there is the next major problem: The game feels way too short. Sure, it's great to have all these abilities and you learn new ones all the time but when you finally have all of them (or a major par of them) the game just ends.
There are problems I have with the way it ends too but more on that after the non- spoiler part.
To wrap this up for those that think about getting this game:
It's good if you want to play four missions a day and want to have a fun slasher game where you can use several different skills to slay those that stand in your way.
I can really recommend this game even if it does have some problems.
Now the ~a-bit-salty spoiler part~
The last two "Bossfights" are way too easy. Most of the Warchiefs you face are a greater challenge and are more fun to fight too. Actually, only one of the three main antagonists get's a real fight. You just need to brand the tower three times and then that's it (which is a shame because his character design and backstory is actually pretty cool and interesting).
Then there's the Black Hand or... Sauron (?). Let's just say he's a weaker form of Sauron. Although he cannot take physical form. Then he's an avatar? Something among those lines.
Anyways, you kill him via qte.
That's it. A short qte.
The guy you've wanted to face from the very beginning. The guy your character wanted to face from the very beginning. The reason you played this game.
A ten second long qte.
Well played.
And then, just to throw it in, there's the army building part.
I was expecting to actually use my army I've built up over the time I've played against him and Saurons forces. But no, none of that. You get to kill five weak Warchiefs with the assistance of yours but then that's it.
Well. That's my "rant". I'm going to see if "The Bright Lord" can actually deliver a satisfying Bossfight against Sauron.

This game is less about crushing difficulty and more about behavioral modification and information utilization. That's not to say that this game isn't brutal, which it certainly is at some points. But the vast majority of the time, difficulty can be mitigated by using what you already know, or finding out what you dont.
What I find facinating about this game is that it uses death in a unique way that few games do. Death in dark souls is of very little consequence. In any regular game, death is something you loathe. Death is something you need to avoid at all costs. Dark souls embraces death whole heartedly as a fact of the game. Death is not only encouraged; it is very much required throughout the course of the game. A great deal of information can only be gathered through dying. First hand experience is king in this game. If you get frustrated at "dying" and "losing" at video games, then this just isn't for you.
Here lies the genious of dark souls: the game lets you play it. You are expected and required to find your own solutions to the problems the game proposes. No handholding. The most you get is a simple tutorial level where the game gives you the controls and some basic rules. Everything else is up to you. This game is posing a challenge to you, and its up to you whether you're smart enough to complete it.
The difficulty makes the game. Bosses are titanic monsters that frequently try to crush you. Normal mobs are life devouring demons. Items on the whole offer little help. No, you'll have to craft decent armor and weapons. But yes, there are more than a few ways to make this game easier, especially as you get deeper into it. Resources open up more possiblities, but the game never looses its focus. You die if you're being stupid. You die if you didn't keep up with the boss. Most of the time, it will be user error. Use everyting you can; the game certainly isn't holding back, especially in the early areas.
Lastly, I love the setting. Very few games capture entropy as well as this game. Broken walls, rubble and debris strewn about, ashes and decay abound. There's beauty in a world so unbeliveby destroyed, where any dark crevice could hold a soul eating slime monstrosity. Its this kind of exhaustive deterioration that really hits it home for me. Few games feature a world so broken and filled with insanity. It's quite unique in and of itself, and the fact that it's both popular and notorious among gamers is a comforting thought. This game is a masterpiece. This game is one of the great challanges of video gaming.

Day 38:
"I had a bit of a surprise of late that scratched off a good 10 years from my life. As I was returning from an island I had previously visited to harvest wood from, something jolted me off of my raft. As I plunged into the deep, I looked around in search of the shark that tossed me. I heard a swift movement in the water and turned around to be greeted by a marlin. This giant fish, wielding a spear-like nose, swam around me. I quickly swam back to my raft, in fear of curious sharks that may be nearby.
I climbed back on my raft, but my relief was short lived. The marlin once again rammed against my raft, throwing me back in to the deep. This time I wasn't having that♥♥♥♥♥♥ I took out my spear and swam after the marlin, jabbing it a few times. Not knowing how strong this marlin was, I decided to get back on my raft to try to stupidly out-paddle the fish.
Danger seemed to show up whenever I got in my raft. This time I heard the familiar tune that played in my mind whenever a shark was near. I frantically searched around and spotted it. To my dismay, it wasn't a tiger shark that I had expected but a big ole' Great White Shark. I looked around and realized that the marlin was still nearby. With no other choice, I paddled back to my Home as quickly as I could, hoping that neither the marlin nor Great White would knock me off my raft. I gripped my paddle tightly and kept paddling forward. The haunting tune of the shark's presence followed me. I kept my mind on my Home as I paddled faster...Before I knew it, the tune was gone. I looked around and neither the marlin nor Great White was near. The only thing near me was my Home. After I paddled to shore, I ran towards my hut. I closed the door behind me and collapsed in my bed without eating.
'I'm never going back to that island...', I thought, as I drifted to sleep."

I have to say, I'm amazed with Starbound.
I bought it some years ago just out of duty because I started playing on an old version downloaded from somewhere. Let me clarify that the reason for me to do it was because at the time Chucklefish removed the hunger and environmental hazard factor from the game, which are two major points that would drive me towards a game, but I'm a guy of principles who buys the games he downloads and happens to like. The art was great, but the game heavily lacked direction, feeling a lot like a sci-fi terraria, hugely directionless where you just plopped on a planet, built a nice house, and ransacked other species for decor items and maybe some weapons. I was not impressed.
Recently I decided to give it a try if anything because I  owned the game and hadn't taken a look at it since two years ago. And honestly, the game is great now. Not only there's a story, but there is a great sense of progression through quests aimed at improving your character, tech to unlock, and a plot that drives you to explore and push onward.
The art is gorgeous, and now that there is a reason to explore the different planets meeting the gajillion of pokémon scattered throughout the game is both exciting and fun. The survival elements are back and although I can see why they took them out of the game, feeling like more of a nuisance than anything involving (there's food everywhere and you'll have no problem staying fed), the element of preparedness and routine gives another dimension to just going down every hole you'll see.
The objectives are distinct, and the exploration is tense since you'll have to double back from whatever hole on the ground you dove into and death means losing a huge swathe of items. A lot of the equipment you'll find is more aesthetic than anything, and weapons are kinda meh, but it's super satisfying when you find that weapon combo that works. Action bars are somewhat small but you can switch between two bars, making the overall hotkey capacity alright. The techs are fun and meaningful, getting a morphball or a double jump that greatly helps with exploration, and weapon abilities are varied and useful most of the time.
The only problems I really have with the game is that the controls could be a bit better for me, like for instance when jumping down a platform you'll keep on going down subsequent ones until you release the "down" button, making it possible to hurt or even kill yourself, or that double tapping in a direction can trigger Dash and send you careening down a hole to your demise. Sometimes you'll also find yourself in some really hard to win combat scenarios, but taking it slowly will help with that so it's not too bad.
Overall though, I think it's  a great game and that it has improved leaps and bounds from its SEA phase. The sense of progression is tangible, the settlements are fun, the exploration is intense and the story is nicely told in great pixel art scenes. From an aimless Terraria in space to a proper metroidvania, Starbound has propelled itself to the stars of my library.
9/10.

As a long time fan of classic isometric RPGs, who considers the original Baldur's Gate series (I and II) to be his favorite role playing games of all time, I regret that I cannot reccomend this game. I had high hopes for another Baldur's Gate - esque adventure and an epic foray into classic storytelling and strategic gameplay...but this title fails on all counts.
It tries really hard to emulate those classics, but fails spectacularly. One of the biggest clues about the developer's quality is that they removed fan-made content from the game when an outside interest group demanded them to do so, without any input from the fans or the backer community whatsoever. As a backer, I felt screwed when game changing decisions were made without considering anybody's opinion or views, except those of the outside interest group (which mind you, doesn't even play the game).
Putting all that aside, however, as a longtime Infinity Engine game fan, the game fails at it's basic goal of being anything like those titles. It even fails at being a decent stand-alone RPG. I encountered tons of bugs and the game reeks of being unpolished and rushed. Clearly, the developer, Obsidian, did not take their time or the backer's input when they churned this game out. For a kickstarter, Obsidian seems to have only had money as their primary goal.
Judging by the end product, most of the backer money went not into development or testing, but into CEO pockets.
If you're looking for a decent throwback to the good old days of old school PC roleplaying games, your best bet remains whatever Beamdog (the authors of the enhanced edition BG and BG 2) conjures up with their new and upcoming Baldur's Gate title.
I hope this comment prevents at least one other RPG fan from wasting their $40 or more. Even not counting the money, I am most dissapointed to have been taken in by the hype and having a medocre subpar product delivered to me.
Save your money for another game.

It harkens back to the days of Baldurs Gate 2 and practically carbon copies the old Bioware Infinity engine when it comes to combat with a few minor changes to make gameplay user friendly. Mass Effect is an amazing game.
I first played it years ago when I was a young teenager,  when it was the only ME game out there and it shaped what I expected of gaming from then on.
Everything from the atmosphere of the game (the music in particular is something to behold) to the narrative and how it plays out all feels well thought-out and engaging.
Some of the plot and side-missions feel like they're plucked from generic sci-fi plotlines and remuddled a bit, but in ME's own way, it owns those factors and you no longer think "That whole alien queen speaking telepathically to someone has been done before" and rather think "Mass Effect did it and did it well."
Your rampage across the galaxy to find this villain who's become a harbinger for the end of life as we know it is fun, and you care about it. Is it the same as every other game where you chase a world-ending villain and his/her catastrophes? Yep.
Still fun.
While, at this point, the graphics are a little outdated, you occasionally see something jaw dropping in Mass Effect. Smoke drifting diagonally away from lava-coated vistas (that you're DRIVING THROUGH) or a blinding, lilac sun on an alien horizon can, once-in-a-while, take your breath away.
The dialogue is meticulously thought-out and well acted (while sometimes sounding a LITTLE dry) and it makes for a great dialogue-system where you know what you choose to say can and will have an effect on the outcome of a mission. It's one of the first games I played that implemented this. Although, while you have choices in ME, all those anastamosing plotlines end you up in the same place. That's not a downside (insert a philosophical quote about inevitability and fate here.) You still feel in control of your character and your future though and that's as much as you can ask for in a game.
Gameplay-wise, it's fun, if a little simple. There aren't any puzzling moments (unless you count getting temporarily lost in one of the many hubs.) The game repeats a little when you have to play the same fight a few times to win. That's not a criticism. I'm all for old-school, 'git good' gaming.
There are really only three or four main things you'll be doing in this game; shooting at and ducking from a wide variety of clever(ish) enemies, wandering around hub areas looking for answers to life's questions (and convincing people to do things), driving around in the MAKO (amazingly fun for something so simple) to explore planets, and zipping around the galaxy map to go do one of the three aforementioned activities.
The combat is FUN and simple, but your two AI counterparts are fairly stupid and don't like to use cover like you do, so will get shot ALOT. Ordering them about feels like you're having to baby two other people whilst not dying in a firefight yourself, but you're Commander Shepherd. You can do it.
Wandering back and forth in hub worlds like the Citadel is fun for about five minutes as it's all rather pretty, but eventually, talking to one character then running back to talk to another can get a bit boring and you wind up wanting to leap into some action again, which you can't without finishing your conversational wanderings. And prepare for ALOT of elevators. It's M.E.'s way of loading parts of maps while you're travelling but it takes you out of things a bit and they make you use elevators a whole lot. Boring, sadly.
Planet exploring is fun and scenic (did I mention this game is beautiful?) especially in the MAKO. The vehicle is fun to drive around, even if it does have some crazy oversteer, but what do you expect when you're on the surface of some low-G moon driving over dunes and dustscapes? The guns feel powerful but don't bother trying to shoot anything near you as the thing can't aim down and the MAKO is quite tall. Just run over the enemies, dammit.
They've put so much effort into fleshing out the characters and histories in this game; of you, your squad mates and beyond and it's all well voice acted. You can feel sparks fly not only between you and your teammates, but you notice which squadmates like each other and where rivalries lie in all the tiny ways.
And everybody has their flaws.
I love Ashley. No denying it there. I love her go-gettem attitude and her out of nowhere attraction to poetry. But she's also super racist against aliens, although she denies it. These aren't character tropes that come out of nowhere. Ashley's lived a life before you knew her and she's willing to tell you about it if you get to know her, from her gung-ho attitude she cultivated with her sister, to her father's love of poetry handed down to her, to her stoic patriotism towards Earth and Humanity leading to her distrust of alien races. Like her or not, she's human (irony intended); so much more than just a 3D rendered cardboard cutout. Now apply that detail to the dozens of characters, locations and races in Mass Effect. (All except Saren, the main villain of the game, who seems to just be a laughing, evil face with no deep backstory other than a foreboding 'he used to be what you are now.')
They've sat down and thought this universe out. We NEED more people to do this when making games. It's probably the biggest selling point of Mass Effect. The galaxy has existed long before you arrived and will go on long after you leave (until ME3 maybe). You can ignore all of it; skip past the expositional dialogue or ignore informative text boxes altogether. But if you want the lore, it's all there and it's beautiful. Plus, they make a GOOD attempt at sciencing everything well. It's what makes for 'science-fiction' rather than 'space-fantasy.'
So, to sum up:
+This game is STILL beautiful after all these years.
+The people and locations are so detailed in lore and history that you can't help but love them all.
+You feel in control of yourself in a vast universe where everything seems to be going wrong.
+The gameplay is fun and simple, and there's a lot of it.
+ Hit the jets on the MAKO while driving up a mountain and try to do a backflip!!!
- The gameplay can get a little repetitive.
- Slightly generic (but forgivable) plotlines, particularly in some side missions.
- Ultimately, your choices don't change the ultimate outcome of the game, but it shows how small you are in this huge story anyway, and serves to drive home that point. (So, secretly a positive?)
The negatives are small and are hugely outweighed by the positives.
9/10.

Graphics are just amazing! really, the game just looks insane! just like the first time I played the first game, I was just amazed by the graphics here!
The shadows and lighting feel so realistic, it's just gorgeous!
nothing really to add here, it's just amazing.
The gameplay is Third-Person, just like all the previous games,
for each mission you do, you get money, with that money you upgrade your plane, buy and upgrade weapons, armor and gadgets,
each mission can be done in 3 styles, Ghost style which is the stealthy way, Panther style, which is stealthy yet deadly way, and the all out Assault style... no need to explain here.
Along the main story you have more side missions from each member of your Task Force that you can do, when done, you get better equipment and the missions are fun too, from getting Intel, to guarding an embassy while waves of terrorists attack you,
Each Side mission can be done Solo or Co-op with a friend.
the gameplay itself is really fun, makes you feel like a real bad♥♥♥♥♥ killing your enemies from the shadows or just shooting them with bad♥♥♥♥♥upgraded weapons.
also, I gotta add, the AI is really smart here, you can see the enemies are talking about what's happening, and they are working together if they are threatened, from guarding their friends and walking back-to-back searching you.

You need to learn the enemy routes, and make a plan of attack, setting traps, calling them from a shadowy place and smacking them!
I also love the customizable equipment, from buying black market weapons and adding upgrading them to buying a flying little helicopter like machine that can shock enemies and deploying EMP.
The cut scenes are very very good! really well made and deliver a good story with the game! the characters are real actors, one of the main terrorist is Carlo Rota which also plays on the TV series 24,
and there's also Multiplayer gameplay where there are 2 teams, Spies and Mercenaries which is fun too, didn't play much, I'm still playing the Main story :)
So, overall, the game is just sweet! great gameplay, good and solid story, amazing graphics... what more do you need?

Aaaah Dragons Dogma: Dark Arisen. The game that had so much potential but completely missed the purpose of an RPG game.
Dragons Dogma: Dark Arisen is a remastered version of the original Dragons Dogma which was released in 2012. The graphics have been updated to make the visuals satisfactory, but they definitely could not be considered on parr with todays generation of graphics.
The only part about this game I can give kudos to is the combat system. Boy did they put a load of development time into the combat system. You can climb up serpents and cut off their little snakey heads! What game lets you do this kind of badassery?! The combat is developed and advanced, and allows you to fight in a style that suits you.
The world is diverse and huge, and leaves plenty of room for exploration, except that nothing really motivates you to go on an adventure other than the hope to find some cool looking badies, because their isn't much of a variety when it comes to the loot that you can find.
The story is more dull than a childrens story book, and it makes me upset to see such a game with such great potential completely forget what keeps their players hooked. Story is a vital component in an RPG game, and the story in Dragons Dogma: Dark Arisen is improvised and doesn't present the player with any interest. The side quests are similar to the ones you would find in an MMO, and are primarily based around collecting items for players and killing a certain baddy.
I played 5 solid hours of this game only to get bored and lose the will to keep on playing as there was no catchy story for me to latch onto. The combat however was juicy and is the only reason why I kept myself believing that this was going to be a decent RPG game, but it turns out that the aspects you expect to be in an RPG game have been forgotten.
I'm sorry guys, but alot of potential was lost with this game and if you were to spend a bit more time developing a plot line and perfecting the graphics, then it would be worth playing.

Okay now just to get this started, I did and sometimes still do play this game quite often, why, well lets talk about that. I don't play it for the great game that CA made, no, I play this for the mods it has, really good mods save this game for me. When I bought this I was thinking I'd try it maybe it's good, the only other thing I was considering buying was Shogun 2, which I had before (not on steam), but don't currently have. I was wrong, this game's grand campaign is quite boring for me, and to let you realize how, on strategy games like Stronghold and Battle for Middle Earth, I am the turtle player (you however won't beat me without proper siege). So for strategy games I play defensively and react to situations as they happen, doing this in Shogun 2 was really fun and necessary, here though it's boring.
The ai will come at you quickly with half to full stacks, but beating them back is more a chore than anything else, only time you feel threatened is when they attack an unguarded settlement (which they will do a lot, if they can, but on base game, they basically just become annoying as they attack a settlement time and time again without taking it or destroying it). The combat ai is done fairly well, but that's well as in they know how best to charge you, they care little for skirmishing in sieges, they make a path into your settlement (wither that be with artillery, ladders, or rams), then charge in. When on the defensive unless they outnumber you on a minor settlement (in which case they may charge you), they sit around in defensive positions, so if you have missile superiority you can just pick them off without much worry.
Now some of the grand campaign mechanics aren't that great, and the few that are good, may be a bit off. Example the fertility system, it's a nice system, makes end game harder, but some issues with it. One most of the regions become infertile by the end, and so I think that needs tweaking. Also every faction has sanitation buildings, such as canals and the like, now you'd think that an irrigated region would be more fertile right, nope. Unless you are I think it's Slavic, you have no way to increase the fertility of your regions, without mods that is. Also there is massive public order and squalor penalties for some things I can't quite understand, meaning you wont get the most out of your regions as you will probably build most regions the same way to keep everything running smoothly.
So now lets talk about the stuff that makes this game actually worth playing for over 300+ hours, mods (you could say you are going for all badges and such, but that's game completion, doesn't mean you enjoy it). There is amazing mods for this game, you can find mods to overhaul most everything about this game. I play with mods that make the games more dynamic and diverse, also to make some things sensible. Like a mod that disables the loss of legacy tech as you progress the tech tree for romans, and making sanitation buildings provide fertility (sure the whole they lose sight of older tech as they change their ways is a nice thought, but don't take away the sanitation buildings, I prefer my aqueducts to having a bigger church, in fact I burned down all the churches in my playthroughs because the bonuses for Christianity suck compared to paganism, base game).
So long and short of it, if you get this game, playing it a few times without mods wont be too boring, until you get to mid game. Playing it with mods may make it more enjoyable for you, however if you are deciding between this and Shogun 2, go with Shogun 2, it's much better in my opinion (the happiness system for shogun 2 is a bit too easy but the rest of the game is good). So I hope you find this somewhat enlightening, maybe I helped you decide on buying this or not, or at least prepared you for it. Also just so you know, I only have one of the culture packs (that being vikings), and no other dlc, cause I didn't want to spend anymore money on this.

It's been a while since I reviewed another game, but this game really sparked my interest. Since the age of 5, I have been playing the first Dynasty Warriors and look where it had got to now. The years fly by so fast, suddenly everything is on it's latest feet, new games come out, and of course, graphics improved. But enough with th memories. Dynasty Warriors 8: Xtreme Legends is an epic game for hack and slash game fans as you will be doing that for the next 50-70 hours of playing (If you do keep playing it). I myself at this point had got to 70 hours and I'm still not close to finishing the whole game! I have, though, completed Ambition Mode. Ambition Mode is a really challenging and entertaining mode (But some might get bored of it because of it's repetitiveness and at a point, you will be asked to collect the officers again, which means all the progress you made will be wiped out, just like that. At first, I couldn't believe it and just stopped playing. Was staring at my computer screen and went like WTF? Those officers of mine, which took me 5-10 hours, dissapeared just like that! Now I have to collect them again! Well, I went to the trouble of collecting them back in the end, and finally completed that mode. I'm finishin up on the campaigns now. I see from this game that KOEI has put all it's talent and has tried their best to make this the best Dynasty Warriors game that was ever made and they put their efforts to recreate the battles even more close to the true history, not just using a nation and a character and winning everthing, no. Now there are true deaths and battles which are relevant to the true story of the Han Dynasty. Since I was just a child, I learnt all my Han Dynasty history from playing the Dynasty Warrior series, and I really enjoyed that. The only thing missing from this Dynasty Warriors is some VS. I used to play Dynasty Warriors VS on Dynasty Warriors 4, but they should create VS for the next series of Dynasty Warriors as it is one of the best features I used to play with my friends. Overall, I would give this game a 8/10, since it has offered many features, but thrown away some important features as well. They have made many interesting characters, such as Lu Lingqi and Fa Zheng, but I say that they should be careful not to go overboard just because they want to add new characters. Lu Lingqi, as some of you may know, is not known and not historical. For me, it should be hypothetical. Diao Chan and Lu Lingqi should not be included in the story of historical and should only appear in hypothetical since there are no records about them (Sorry to the fans of Lu Lingqi, but it's true. I would prefer that it stuck to history and Lu Lingqi's just supposed to be in hypothetical). I woudl recommend this to generations fo Dynasty Warrior players, as this is really a step up of the game to the new generation.

For those who don't know, this game is a spin-off to a hugely popular webcomic Homestuck -- an extremely complicated story with dozens of characters, wacky hijinks and time-space shenanigans. In 2012 its creators ran a successfull Kickstarter campaign to fund an adventure game. The road has been bumpy to say the least, but here we are 5 years later, with the first act you can beat in a couple of hours. So, is it worth it?
Well, yes. Yes, it is.
Hiveswap is good both for old-time fans who can appreciate its connection to the original webcomic, and for the newcomers who can get a taste of what Homestuck is at its best. The characters are likable, and the writing is Homestuck's trademark mix of quirky irony and honesty. For those who worry if they'd like the webcomic, the game would make a good introduction.
Act 1 only introduces the characters and te setting, and, knowing the game's story, I don't know if act 2 ever comes. Nevertheless, it's worth checking out whether you like Homestuck or just point-and-click adventure games.

There is a very welcome feature that this game has that I don't often see in adventure games, probably because its a ton of work.
Trying to combine any item with anything else will give you a unique message. It's sometimes funny, sometimes gives you more exposition about the story or characters, and is almost always worth reading. It's really cool that whoever you're playing as will sometimes comment on a relationship between items that you're having them compare in an unexpected way that gives some insight into their personality. It's a really welcome alternative to how adventure games usually handle what is normally a boring chore, and I found myself lingering in areas just to check everything out and use items on things in rooms knowing that they had nothing to do with each other just to see what the character has to say about them.
Don't rush through this game. There's a lot of fun things to read if you take it easy and experiment.

The Homestuck game we all waited for is here! Except not.
I'll be the 100th person to admit that the more recent announcements for the game were not what I expected. I didn't even expect it to be for the PC, let alone have nothing to do with Sburb. But that didn't stop me from buying it the day it came out.
Initially, I was pretty skeptical. In the first 10 minutes of playing, I'd already spotted to in-game glitches and I wasn't impressed. My cynical mind could only think, "How many years had this been in the making? How much money did this earn again?" But it was whatever. I was here to support one of my favorite webcomics turned game with three of my favorite creators boasting a hand in it's production, and get in on those sweet, sweet references. Quality was the least of my concerns (but still a concern none the less). But after the latest update, most of those quality concerns were swept away and I enjoyed the story in it's entirety and let me tell you. I finished it today and it was more than I would have ever hoped. I'm in love all over again. The characters are so well made and while I don't love all of them, I do admit that it's not because they're poorly written. In fact, their flaws make them enheritly better fleshed out. The game is FUN, though more story-based, with little player interaction other than telling the character where to go and some amount of puzzle solving skills. As the description says, you don't NEED to have read Homestuck in order to get into the game. In fact, the actual Homestuck references that would go over an unknowing player's head are rather few and far between, but just enough to make a old or new fan go, "O SHOOT SON."
My only REAL complaint is the length. I thought $7.99 was a steal for a brand new game, but after beating the entirety of it in two not overly lengthy sittings, I can honestly say it was about 8 bucks of content. Which is to say it was about the length of one graphic novel, which is accurate pricing. For a more frugal and savvy fan, they may consider waiting until all the Acts come out and buy them in bulk. But you won't find me putting myself through that; You can bet I'll be buying Act 2 on it's release date as well, and I feel like that says something on my opinion of this game as a whole.
Tl;Dr: If you're thinking of checking it out, just do it bro. Make it happen. It's a good intro.

This games takes everything I love about survival horror and brings you in to the world of the game. In the beginning, you start as Marcus Black, a strapping fellow with his BFF Ed who've just returned from a fishing trip at a lake. To your surprise, everyone in the town has mysteriously gone crazy and taken up cannibalism. Or so they though, until they discover that the dead are returning to life.

The game tasks you with keeping the peopel of your surviving community happy. To do so, you will often need to scavenege for Ammo, Medicine, Food and rarely fuel. The game will also throw ocassional events at you which will help you gain trust and become better friends with other survivors. You can play as other survivors after you've gained enough of their trust.
One part of the game that is crucially emphasized is stealth. It is EXTREMELY easy to be caught up in the middle of a crowd of zombies and meet your demise. So it is crucial that you are constantly aware of your surroundings, lest you bring on the herd of the undead.
Lastly, allow me to re-iterate how important knowing your surroundings is. It's helpful when scavenging to have an exit strategy, as many who are impatient will often use the quick-search feature. The quick-search feature is nice, but will generate plenty of noise which may attract MANY zombies. So, always make sure you have an escape plan. If you aren't careful, your survivor WILL DIE. Once they die, they're never coming back.
For an indie game, I was extremely pleased with the action of the game. I would highly recommend any fans of the games: DayZ, WarZ, Nether, Dead Rising, etc. give this game a try. For $20, this is a great buy. The campaign will last between 10-20 hours, and the Breakdown DLC adds even more playtime with the sandbox mode.

Excellent game. It has a great start up but the curve is too great. The game comes down to who can advance their Runes (modifiers) to the highest levels.
The player base is not large enough to support this type unit based rock, paper, scissor gameplay where a modified Scissor can crush a rock. In truth it signifies that the Runes become the most important hidden element of the matchup but this is not apparent until you reach higher levels.
Balance is also an issue, dominate builds are truely dominante and are not fixed for several weeks. At the time of this review the Javelineer units were released and can overpower any ground based build. Air units are easily countered due to poor AI, which will inconsistently prioritize targeting of groud to air or air to air units before ground to ground (G2G). Even when it works out, sometimes air units will pass over the remaining G2G units and continue down the map. Those G2G units then destory your base when your units could have easily defeated the remaining enemy units.
It is a flawed game and these flaws could easily be hidden with a larger player base. Enjoy the first 100 commander levels, after that, expect it to get really dicey, really fast.

And in response to those who claim, overcome with envy and spite, that as intelligent as I am, I will never sleep with anyone: I don’t need to. I am quite capable of simulating, to the meagerest tactile sensation, every position in the Kama Sutra (as well as a few I myself have devised for maximum oxytocin and endorphin release) simultaneously in a few seconds, and the only reason it takes even that long is because I am prolonging the simulation in order to enjoy the experience: I could do it in hundredths of a millisecond if I so wish. However, for someone with such acute acumen as I, life is far too easy. When pure ennui drives you to calculate the movements of the 27 subatomic particles you’ve discovered and how they interact with one another in the 2,038th dimension using a base 3.2407 quadrillion number system, you realize that the universe and its infinite copies and offshoots offer nothing more to you. Except, that is, for Johnny Test. Even for an individual with such altitudinous IQ such as myself, it’s difficult to understand every single subtle joke and reference. That’s not to say I don’t understand any of the plenitude of allusions, in fact, I am able to comprehend virtually every single one. For example, one minutia most of you would fail to notice is when Susan’s chin moves two extra pixels further than in any of the previous episodes when she talks during the seventeenth second of the fifth minute of season 3 episode 10. Hardly any of you would conceive of the fact that this is a reference to the exact number, down to 84 significant figures, of the percent change in total nitrogen in the Earth’s atmosphere due to the eructation of a small cynodont 257 million years ago. There are more examples I could give, such as the color of the walls of the sisters’ lab being a slightly different hue from the norm in season 4 episode 19 (a reference to the presence of approximately 2.9 millimoles of ammonium diuranate in the ink of a Chinese manuscript dated 1256 BCE), but that would detract from the intended purpose of this writing. Johnny Test is a work of art, a perfect concoction of knowledge from a multitude of academic fields that combine to make a program that is the only form of media I have ever encountered that has been even somewhat laborious for me to fathom, and I’m talking about someone who altered the biochemistry and chirality of their body in order to make it more efficient than the prodigality that is the human body. My temples ache with the pain of having to pump copious amounts of Testium (an element I discovered that takes the role of oxygen in my unique biochemistry, named after my favorite show of course) to my brain in order to comprehend what I have just watched. And to everybody who claims that the reason my temples are sore or why I have “delusions of grandeur” are due to my being “high” or whichever way you aim to construe my exegesis of an episode, you will hear vocalizations of a gelatological nature emanating from my larynx whilst Xyzyzyx the paisley pangolin (a treasured acquaintance of mine) and I reflect on your foolishness later that day. I await the furious fussilade of odious obluquies and belittling bombast in the comments below. “Too long; Did not read”: Did you really think I would include one of these silly little things at the bottom of my witty wordsmithery? It's not my fault if you can't handle my de trop of definitions or my lexical linguipotence!

This game is less about crushing difficulty and more about behavioral modification and information utilization. That's not to say that this game isn't brutal, which it certainly is at some points. But the vast majority of the time, difficulty can be mitigated by using what you already know, or finding out what you dont.
What I find facinating about this game is that it uses death in a unique way that few games do. Death in dark souls is of very little consequence. In any regular game, death is something you loathe. Death is something you need to avoid at all costs. Dark souls embraces death whole heartedly as a fact of the game. Death is not only encouraged; it is very much required throughout the course of the game. A great deal of information can only be gathered through dying. First hand experience is king in this game. If you get frustrated at "dying" and "losing" at video games, then this just isn't for you.
Here lies the genious of dark souls: the game lets you play it. You are expected and required to find your own solutions to the problems the game proposes. No handholding. The most you get is a simple tutorial level where the game gives you the controls and some basic rules. Everything else is up to you. This game is posing a challenge to you, and its up to you whether you're smart enough to complete it.
The difficulty makes the game. Bosses are titanic monsters that frequently try to crush you. Normal mobs are life devouring demons. Items on the whole offer little help. No, you'll have to craft decent armor and weapons. But yes, there are more than a few ways to make this game easier, especially as you get deeper into it. Resources open up more possiblities, but the game never looses its focus. You die if you're being stupid. You die if you didn't keep up with the boss. Most of the time, it will be user error. Use everyting you can; the game certainly isn't holding back, especially in the early areas.
Lastly, I love the setting. Very few games capture entropy as well as this game. Broken walls, rubble and debris strewn about, ashes and decay abound. There's beauty in a world so unbeliveby destroyed, where any dark crevice could hold a soul eating slime monstrosity. Its this kind of exhaustive deterioration that really hits it home for me. Few games feature a world so broken and filled with insanity. It's quite unique in and of itself, and the fact that it's both popular and notorious among gamers is a comforting thought. This game is a masterpiece. This game is one of the great challanges of video gaming.

Basically, this game is Spinter Cell: Conviction on steroids, with almost everything being improved. An large amount of weapons, customizations, suits, gadgets, there's no shortage of things to unlock and use and experiment with. Chances are, though, that you'll find a good set for yourself and really stick to it.

I would recommend this game if you like stealth/action games, shooters, and games that you don't mind going through slowly in order to get the best Splinter Cell experience.

~non-spoiler part~
So, I just finished playing this game (base-game no DLC's yet) and I have to say... well... actually, I have to say quite a lot.
So, to start off: The combat feels great and you really can emerge yourself in the gameplay.
I don't think  have to talk about the setting but everyone should know that the problems with the game don't lie there.
The enemies seem way too stupid and you sneak up on them way too easy and some Warchiefs can be ridiculously strong. (Like...really strong)
Otherwise there isn't that much of a problem with the Uruk enemies you face and the way you learn to control them in the second act is really cool. But there is the next major problem: The game feels way too short. Sure, it's great to have all these abilities and you learn new ones all the time but when you finally have all of them (or a major par of them) the game just ends.
There are problems I have with the way it ends too but more on that after the non- spoiler part.
To wrap this up for those that think about getting this game:
It's good if you want to play four missions a day and want to have a fun slasher game where you can use several different skills to slay those that stand in your way.
I can really recommend this game even if it does have some problems.
Now the ~a-bit-salty spoiler part~
The last two "Bossfights" are way too easy. Most of the Warchiefs you face are a greater challenge and are more fun to fight too. Actually, only one of the three main antagonists get's a real fight. You just need to brand the tower three times and then that's it (which is a shame because his character design and backstory is actually pretty cool and interesting).
Then there's the Black Hand or... Sauron (?). Let's just say he's a weaker form of Sauron. Although he cannot take physical form. Then he's an avatar? Something among those lines.
Anyways, you kill him via qte.
That's it. A short qte.
The guy you've wanted to face from the very beginning. The guy your character wanted to face from the very beginning. The reason you played this game.
A ten second long qte.
Well played.
And then, just to throw it in, there's the army building part.
I was expecting to actually use my army I've built up over the time I've played against him and Saurons forces. But no, none of that. You get to kill five weak Warchiefs with the assistance of yours but then that's it.
Well. That's my "rant". I'm going to see if "The Bright Lord" can actually deliver a satisfying Bossfight against Sauron.
