So, first I'll just say to all the people who have played a Dynasty Warriors game one thing:  It's still Dynasty Warriors.   The formula doesn't change much, the graphics get upgrades and the system gets minor tweaks.  But overall, Dynasty warriors stays the same over time.  However, this time around we gain Ambition mode!
Ambition mode lets you pick a character you have unlocked (via story or one of the starters) to start your own 'faction' and grow in power.  You'll do battles to gain allies, fame, and resources, as well as upgrading new facilities and eventually building the massive temple I can't remember the name of.   It's a pretty cool mode and adds a lot of replay value over just spamming free mode once you finish storylines.
If you've never played a Dynasty Warriors game, then go into it understanding one core bit of knowledge:  It's a hack and slash beat'em up.   You'll ride around the battle field completing objectives, but mostly you're massacreing hapless soldiers and battling other generals and lieutenants.   Occasionally getting demolished by Lu Bu.   There are a ton of storylines to play through, as well as a massive amount of characters with unique move sets.
I personally love the series, but it's not for everyone.  I recommend watching a gameplay video before making your decision.

If you go to sleep at night, you will make progress, but since gold, potions, and inventory slots are capped, well...That's your limit. You do get more inventory slots, and your potions gain stack size as you progress through the game however.
What you got right though, was the crafting interactions. It reminds me of Path of Exile in a way, using those tomes to upgrade or reroll gear until it's perfect. Pretty good 2D platformer with decent animations. Art style is a bit varied; some enemies look better than others. Gameplay-wise the shooting is floaty. You can point with the mouse to shoot or use the right stick on a controller for a twin-stick shooter feel, but either way it doesn't feel too responsive. I usually can't hit enemies right away and have to adjust my angle, especially for the far away enemies. These ones, the little wall bots, also always seem to get a shot in on you first unless you're constantly moving.
The crafting mechanic is interesting but the game expects you to grind for materials which, in a shooter like this, feels counter-intuitive. I'm supposed to be pushing forward, but it would take nearly two whole levels (of a total 5) before I could upgrade my blaster. I say 'could' because health packs and grenades are also craftable items, and you'll be using your resources for them far more often. These should be found in the maps themselves, not something I have to craft. The enemies do respawn as soon as they're off screen, so grinding is at least easy enough, but again it's not what I want from a game like this.
There are a few bugs in the game; sometimes various guages would dissappear (not good when my health was below 25%) and during the second boss fight I paused (to craft a health item...ugh) and the game would not let me unpause, forcing me to reset.
Story - 2/5 Some intrigue, not too memorable.
Graphics - 3/5 Mostly good, some awkward spots like character portaits, some enemies.
Audio - 3/5 Music is suitable for the game but also not memorable. Soundtrack is available.
Gameplay - 3/5 Floaty shooting, crafting element feels out of place.
Replay - 4/5 Stages have branching paths in some sections, hidden collectibles, stages are scored.
Overall - 3/5 A decent throwback to old school side-scrolling shooters like Megaman or Vectorman. If you can adjust to the controls you'll have fun.

The premise is a Mega Man game in which you get your upgrades from acquiring scrap in levels and spending it. For me, the level variety in Mega Man games was the best part, and being able to tackle the levels in different orders, making not only the first but subsequent playthroughs different and interesting. Was one level too tough? Try a different one and get a different robot master's ability, then tackle the level again with the knowledge and weaponry you have from replying the tough level and acquiring a new weapon.
With A.R.E.S.: Extincting Agenda, however, the game just sends you to levels sequentially without a list of levels to choose from. One of the most interesting parts of a Mega Man game has been removed from what is essentially a Mega Man-like game. In my time with the game, I did not find this change to be for the better. If a part got tiresome, I couldn't switch levels to try new tactics or get fresh scenery.
This game reminds me of the average movie reboot: take something that worked pretty well, and instead of making improvements, take away stuff that was good, and just generally not make a superior product. Using scrap for upgrades was a nice idea, and something like that worked well in Rogue Trooper, but there wasn't much to draw me into A.R.E.S. to play more than a couple of levels before getting bored and moving on.

This review is based on a 99% done playthrough on Hard difficulty.
Let's start with the story and the eight NPC recruits first.  While it's hard to top 'You are immune to death, but your memories are gone. Have fun out there.' and 'Remember when you almost died to that wolf? Ok now go kill a god', Pillars of Eternity's main plot is very engaging and weaves itself well into the set pieces and characters you meet throughout your journey.  You are a random person in a caravan that approaches some weird cult and it's leader fiddling with an ancient machine. You're knocked out and wake up with the ability to peer into other people's souls.  Meanwhile sometime before the events of the game started Everyone's Favorite Benevolent God starts punishing heretics before finally being destroyed by a big F-off weapon and has not been seen since.  The main plot involves chasing down this cult leader while either dodging or supporting the influence of the many more gods present in the world. Many of the NPCs you can recruit have their own struggles with their own gods, and if you stick with them long enough, you can help them resolve their issues as well.  The game's reputation system, where you get 'points' towards the different attitudes you present while speaking with others (benevolent, cruel, rational, honest, etc.) is very well done and is sure to result in repeat playthroughs. Conversations can also depend on what class and backstory you picked during character creation. During one particular quest in Act 2, I found myself wishing I was a Priest of Skaen (evil jerks) just to see how it would have played out differently.
The recruitable NPCs are written very well, have good party banter, and help you understand the quite wordy backstory of the world, however many of their pre-selected combat talents are either very poor or don't make any sense at all.  This has been known to cause players to rush to them before gaining too many levels so that they can build them how they see fit.  Min-maxers are going to do what they do in this regard, but I believe this to be justified until they are tweaked a bit to more accurately reflect what the game expects from you while in combat.
The combat is what you can expect from the 'real-time with pause' games that it emulates such as Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale but with a few major changes.  The first major change deals with stealth.  When you go into stealth mode, your whole party goes into stealth mode. When one person is caught, everyone is caught.  This makes absolutely no sense whatsoever, and renders a rogue's major class talent, backstab, completely and utterly useless.  It's such a terrible, incomprehensible combat mechanic that I have to wonder if we, the players, are doing something wrong, and the developers intended it for some other use that we haven't thought of yet.
Another quite jarring combat mechanic is 'engagement.'  Once you engage with an enemy, you are basically rooted to that spot. Any attempt to even move an inch will open you up to a huge free hit to your character.  While there are both items and talents that help with your defense while breaking engagement, it is still not enough for me to consider it a fun, worthwile addition to combat.  The AI pathing isn't good enough, especially when fighting in hallways and doors. I find myself tolerating engagement rather than enjoying it as a challenge to overcome.
With all that said I am greatly enjoying my time with the game and can't wait to start another character.  It truly is a successor to the great Baldur's Gate games and it is one I will be playing for a long, long time.

A promising game bogged down by a bad combat system, companions that seem to be shoehorned in and a somewhat uninvolved story. Despite claiming to only listen to fans, Obsidian seems uninterested in following majority feedback and instead insists on doing their own thing.
If you liked the old Baldur's Gate / Icewind Dale combat system, this one may seem like an improved version of that, but some of the "modernizations" end up making the combat boring and a pain. No buffing before entering combat, limited spell casts and rests among other ideas that may seem good on paper, but end up making the gameplay uninteresting.
The story seems very solid, but also pretty railroaded. I have yet to notice a consequence to my actions.
As the game is now, I cannot recommended it, and I regret kickstarting. I strongly suggest deliberating a purchase, and decide wether the pros outweigh the cons. If you want a good but uninvolved story, I suggest reading a book instead.

Dragon's Dogma is a game I've never heard before, but with a certain discount I considered trying it out and oh boy what I thought I made a big mistake. I was slightly over 2 hours of gameplay and I got so frustrated over the mediocre/bad types of savegames, unforgiving early gameplay. But I said that if i quit right there I'd miss out something that was somewhat good. Here I am with over 100 hours of gameplay and you'd wonder how is that possible?
This can be hard and so unfair at some points (especially the Bitterblack isle), but it's rewarding, it's unique, it's great.
The pawn system is a breath of fresh air, the combat system is what every rpg should consider, the music is diverse and gives a unforgivable feeling about the game.
But there are some elements that made me so frustrated I just had to stop and get my mind over that thing. What you might ask? As I said, the savegame system feels antique, it's basically one for your saves and one for checkpoints and that is it you can only save and load basically your last save, no other power to it.
The enemy distribution in the main game can teach you a hard lesson that free roaming isn't a good idea until you are a higher level.
The story is mediocre and sometimes it just completely breaks the immersion,
I don't even want to talk about the horrors of the Bitterblack Isle, just don't even consider going there until you have level 70+, everything you thought was cheap and unfair in the normal game it's amplified like 10x times.
In the end, is this game worth it? Just the combat system alone pays for all the money be it in full or preferably discounts, you just have to accept some of its flaws and you will have an unforgetable experience. Good luck in your adventures and don't forget: Wolves hunt in packs (#plskillmenow).

Okay now just to get this started, I did and sometimes still do play this game quite often, why, well lets talk about that. When I bought this I was thinking I'd try it maybe it's good, the only other thing I was considering buying was Shogun 2, which I had before (not on steam), but don't currently have. I was wrong, this game's grand campaign is quite boring for me, and to let you realize how, on strategy games like Stronghold and Battle for Middle Earth, I am the turtle player (you however won't beat me without proper siege). So for strategy games I play defensively and react to situations as they happen, doing this in Shogun 2 was really fun and necessary, here though it's boring.
The ai will come at you quickly with half to full stacks, but beating them back is more a chore than anything else, only time you feel threatened is when they attack an unguarded settlement (which they will do a lot, if they can, but on base game, they basically just become annoying as they attack a settlement time and time again without taking it or destroying it). The combat ai is done fairly well, but that's well as in they know how best to charge you, they care little for skirmishing in sieges, they make a path into your settlement (wither that be with artillery, ladders, or rams), then charge in. When on the defensive unless they outnumber you on a minor settlement (in which case they may charge you), they sit around in defensive positions, so if you have missile superiority you can just pick them off without much worry.
Now some of the grand campaign mechanics aren't that great, and the few that are good, may be a bit off. Example the fertility system, it's a nice system, makes end game harder, but some issues with it. One most of the regions become infertile by the end, and so I think that needs tweaking. Also every faction has sanitation buildings, such as canals and the like, now you'd think that an irrigated region would be more fertile right, nope. Unless you are I think it's Slavic, you have no way to increase the fertility of your regions, without mods that is. Also there is massive public order and squalor penalties for some things I can't quite understand, meaning you wont get the most out of your regions as you will probably build most regions the same way to keep everything running smoothly.
So now lets talk about the stuff that makes this game actually worth playing for over 300+ hours, mods (you could say you are going for all badges and such, but that's game completion, doesn't mean you enjoy it). There is amazing mods for this game, you can find mods to overhaul most everything about this game. I play with mods that make the games more dynamic and diverse, also to make some things sensible. Like a mod that disables the loss of legacy tech as you progress the tech tree for romans, and making sanitation buildings provide fertility (sure the whole they lose sight of older tech as they change their ways is a nice thought, but don't take away the sanitation buildings, I prefer my aqueducts to having a bigger church, in fact I burned down all the churches in my playthroughs because the bonuses for Christianity suck compared to paganism, base game).
So long and short of it, if you get this game, playing it a few times without mods wont be too boring, until you get to mid game. Playing it with mods may make it more enjoyable for you, however if you are deciding between this and Shogun 2, go with Shogun 2, it's much better in my opinion (the happiness system for shogun 2 is a bit too easy but the rest of the game is good). So I hope you find this somewhat enlightening, maybe I helped you decide on buying this or not, or at least prepared you for it. Also just so you know, I only have one of the culture packs (that being vikings), and no other dlc, cause I didn't want to spend anymore money on this.

This game is a reboot of the Splinter Cell series, it tries to bring back the hardcore gameplay mechanics of the first ones, while also allowing to be appealing to more casual players. I recommend this game only if you like stealth games, because if you try to play just like any third person game you will feel nothing special about it. Single player has some very interesting levels, although a bit short. Some missions can be played in co-op, which brings a lot more diversity, but they are easy enough solo, so in co-op they may get a bit easier if both players are good, or terribly frustrating if one player does not know how to play stealthy.
The multiplayer is also a reboot of the Classic Spies vs Mercenaries with some new addons. Unfortunately it is very dumbed down and suffers from an identity crisis from what a stealth game multiplayer mode should be like. It also suffers from connection issues, leavers, and balacing issues. It can be a lot of fun for a short period of time, learning curve is smooth, but since there are only a few maps you will end up getting bored of it (MP) after a while.

If you liked Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, you're bound to like this game!  Much of those gameplay features from the former make their way back into the newest installment of the Splinter Cell franchise.  While it doesn't make sense that Sam Fisher looks and acts like he's in his thirties (when he's actually in his sixties), along with the fact that Michael Ironside doesn't voice the gaming icon this time, the new Fisher makes espionage look bad♥♥♥♥♥
Not only is there a campaign to weed through, but endless waves of a terrorist hunt type game-mode that is addictively fun.  Equally as entertaining are the stealth missions that must be accomplished without letting the enemy know that you are there.  Perhaps the most solid experience of this game comes from the multiplayer.  Chaos Theory's legendary Spies vs. Mercs does a comeback in this game.  Offering the ability to be a spy or a mercenary, you are free to choose your play style.  Want to go full-on Rambo on some stealthy saboteurs?  Be a mercenary!  You are equipped with the ultimate firepower and protection.  Feel like sinking a karambit into those lethargic brutes?  Take on the role as a spy!  Sneak your way across the map using the latest stealth technology to dispatch your enemies.
This offers a fresh take on competitive multiplayer and will leave you playing for hours on end.  Upgrade your gadgets and character as you rank up to take on the more veteran players.  This upgrading model is also present in the single-player side of the game... allowing you to become a more powerful Sam Fisher.  Something else worth mentioning... there is a cooperative portion of the game that I haven't yet tried.  It plays through some of the same levels as the single-player missions, only you can do it with a friend.  That's cool!
The game has plenty of features to keep you occupied for a good while.  I give this game a 9/10... it loses a point for getting rid of Michael Ironside, and making Sam so young to the point that he can scale cliffsides without difficulty.
Besides that, you wouldn't be disappointed if you bought this game.

I have to say, I'm amazed with Starbound.
I bought it some years ago just out of duty because I started playing on an old version downloaded from somewhere. Let me clarify that the reason for me to do it was because at the time Chucklefish removed the hunger and environmental hazard factor from the game, which are two major points that would drive me towards a game, but I'm a guy of principles who buys the games he downloads and happens to like. The art was great, but the game heavily lacked direction, feeling a lot like a sci-fi terraria, hugely directionless where you just plopped on a planet, built a nice house, and ransacked other species for decor items and maybe some weapons. I was not impressed.
Recently I decided to give it a try if anything because I  owned the game and hadn't taken a look at it since two years ago. And honestly, the game is great now. Not only there's a story, but there is a great sense of progression through quests aimed at improving your character, tech to unlock, and a plot that drives you to explore and push onward.
The art is gorgeous, and now that there is a reason to explore the different planets meeting the gajillion of pokémon scattered throughout the game is both exciting and fun. The survival elements are back and although I can see why they took them out of the game, feeling like more of a nuisance than anything involving (there's food everywhere and you'll have no problem staying fed), the element of preparedness and routine gives another dimension to just going down every hole you'll see.
The objectives are distinct, and the exploration is tense since you'll have to double back from whatever hole on the ground you dove into and death means losing a huge swathe of items. A lot of the equipment you'll find is more aesthetic than anything, and weapons are kinda meh, but it's super satisfying when you find that weapon combo that works. Action bars are somewhat small but you can switch between two bars, making the overall hotkey capacity alright. The techs are fun and meaningful, getting a morphball or a double jump that greatly helps with exploration, and weapon abilities are varied and useful most of the time.
The only problems I really have with the game is that the controls could be a bit better for me, like for instance when jumping down a platform you'll keep on going down subsequent ones until you release the "down" button, making it possible to hurt or even kill yourself, or that double tapping in a direction can trigger Dash and send you careening down a hole to your demise. Sometimes you'll also find yourself in some really hard to win combat scenarios, but taking it slowly will help with that so it's not too bad.
Overall though, I think it's  a great game and that it has improved leaps and bounds from its SEA phase. The sense of progression is tangible, the settlements are fun, the exploration is intense and the story is nicely told in great pixel art scenes. From an aimless Terraria in space to a proper metroidvania, Starbound has propelled itself to the stars of my library.
9/10.

Bastion has been considered one of the best indie PC games for a while now with an "overwhelmingly positive" rating on Steam. After playing through it this weekend I have no idea why.
The art is beautiful with interesting character designs and unique looking enemies, but that's about where the positives end.
It's about some kid with a hammer whose floating city was destroyed and he's trying to fix it. It's a simple story and there's nothing wrong with that, but they try to stretch out any emotion or meaning from the ever present narrator. And this guy never shuts the ♥♥♥♥ up. There's three human characters in the game to talk about and it's dragged out the entire game.
They made the narrator emulate some kind of cowboy and there wouldn't be anything wrong with that if every visual, story element and gameplay mechanic didn't point to fantasy. There's no indication that a western themed narrator or music would service the story or visuals in anyway. I guess there's a saloon in the beginning of the game? But it looks like a fantasy tavern anyway. It's like they watched Cowboy Bebop combine genres and thought that was a good idea without understanding why it works.
The game is too damn linear. If I drew a squiggly line with a couple turns that would be as complicated and interesting as the layout gets in this game. The ground popping up in front of you is eye catching until the seems start showing a couple levels late. At first it seems like the novelty of the path popping up in front of you is what is limiting the design of the game, but I've played the developers other title Transistor which is similarly linear, so it's just lazy design.
I don't understand why it was so popular. Maybe good looking indie games were rare in 2011.
TLDR:
+ Beautiful Art
- Clashing Themes
- Too Linear
- Never ending Narration

So I now have been playing this for multiple hours. At the point of writing this I have not reborn (though I see how it works and am going to soon).
I can safely say that I would recommend this game to people and that it is well worth a few dollars.
Basically, it's your standard clicker, with a couple tweaks. The upgrade system is not your typical system. Normally, you buy 10, 25, 50, 100, ...etc of something, and buy an upgrade at those intervals. In this clicker, when you kill a monster, you have a chance of getting a potion (normal at first, then it could be higher qualities later on). Those potions increase both your click damage and your hero damage (permanently)
You use items (which also have similar qualities) to upgrade hero/drop rate/quality/sell price to the merchant.
Overall, I'd give it a 7.5-8.0/10. It doesn't do anything "groundbreaking", but the drop system is relatively different (I've only seen it implemented in a few other idle games) and the graphics are okay. The sound isn't amazing, but I typically disable sounds in idle games so that wasn't really a factor for me.
If they continue to add to it I could see this being a well-established clicker in the future. I'd be willing to drop a dollar here and there if they decide to add some cheap DLC (such as auto-clickers, like clicker heroes has done).

The game feels mechnically decent, but lacks sufficient depth for long term enjoyment.  I got the impression that most of the features are completed to a bit beyond a proof of concept level.  The legendary dungeons are consumables that just add a bit more loot at the level of the stage they were generated.
Fundementally later game progress appears to be overwhelming achieved by building up the generic knowledge based potion multiplier so I threw in the towel on the last two zone based achievements as there wasn't much enjoyment to be had grinding that out.  Overall after 10 hours of moderate focus gameplay I consider the game functionally completed.
As far as I can tell there is no reasonable way to play an idle style in the game without the use of third party programs as you would be required to frequently click on the use all potion button and babysit equipment management throughout most phases of the game.
There is some potential strategy involved with the efficient use of books and the resource generator, but it is ultimately squandered by the somewhat poorly scaling affix variety that ultimately feels dwarfed by the knowledge potion multiplier.
I think the game as a whole isn't that bad for an average incremental, but there are free to play alternatives with much greater depth and thoughtful mechanics.  I have encountered every individual feature in the game within other incrementals.  Were the game to have found a way to augment the implementation of those features or if it brought something new to the table I might be able to recommend it.

So I've done a lot of what can be done in Savage Lands, and I've got some things that I believe could use some improvement in the game. (I was told to leave a comment in the discussion board, and to leave a review, which I'm doing). I've played 32 hours, beaten most of the bosses, crafted most of the gear, and explored just about everywhere. I realize some have played WAY more than 32 hours, but honestly, I don't think there's really a whole lot of content to the game yet, so I'd say probably 40 hours in game and you could have done just about everything.
Overall, I absolutely loved this game, and really enjoyed it. I think it's a cool genre, and has been implemented quite well. I DO really like it, but the below is critical, to try and make it better.
So here's what I think could use some work.
The armor/weapon tier system is really cool, but HEAVILY unbalanced. You go from not even being able to fight an enemy, to being able to kill it with absolutely no problem! I remember forest giants one hitting me, then I went to steel, and their hits felt like scratches. I just feel like the game would be far more interesting if the next level enemies didn't one hit you with your gear, and that when you upgraded, they were still somewhat of a challenge. The game feels more like a rush to get good gear while avoiding mobs, and then just easy kills after that. There's very few moments where battles feel difficult but enjoyable.
The stats for armor are incredibly unhelpful. For example, a full set of steel vs a full set of silver is different by only 5 points of damage reduction. But it makes a HUGE difference. Each hit from a fury when I was in steel did at least 30 points of damage, but with silver, it went down to like 5-10. That's at least three times the damage reduction, with only 5 points showing in the stats. I have no idea how the math is working for that to make sense, but for it to make sense to the user, the numbers should be adjusted.
House placement sucks. I've found large open areas, one REALLY good spot, but it doesn't let me place a house... No idea why. Really frustrating, considering the majority of the land is hilly or has stuff all over it. Where am I supposed to build?
The houses also suck. All of them have no room for stuff. I want to have my crafting table, forge, smeltery, and chests, all in one spot, but even the largest house doesn't have enough room for that. They're all just really crammed feeling.
It would be awesome to be able to actually place chests, rather than remove my bags onto the floor, put the chest into my inventory, find the place I'd "roughly" like it to be, then throw it, and have it land totally sideways or backwards.
"Oranize by type" instead of name would be AMAZING (just as an option at least). I'd like to see crafting in terms of bags, materials, potions, etc. This would also make the game WAY less frustrating to start out (I would actually know what bags I can make).
Item management is frustrating. Single clicking (or shift clicking) to instantly move something over would be incredibly helpful. That way, I don't have to drag dozens of things all around all the time. Also, just a thought, make bags just make more space in your inventory, rather than making a whole section for a bag containing 6 slots. Just something like a big green line could show where one bag ends and another begins. It's just a bit frustrating to scroll through a whole huge list, for very little content in my bags. It's also incredibly difficult to move items around from bag to bag (lame junk I pick up goes to my first bag... which is what I would like my GOOD stuff to be in).
I like that the game is open, love that. However, there actually is one specific thing you're supposed to do at each location, and you have absolutely no idea what that is. I ended up having to check maps and online guides, instead of just enjoying the game experience. You honestly expect someone to just wander around, randomly finding four different giants (that can't really be seen that well)? Then somehow to know they're supposed to try and get an Everwood drop, then keep that in their inventory, and use it to ring the gong? I know the journals give some hints, but not much, and they're hard to find too. I'm not saying I want a game where it holds my hand the whole time. I love that it's scary, you don't know what's coming, and it's totally open. I would just like to know what I'm supposed to do without having to check guides online.
Many items can be figured out on their own (I need to find tin in a deposit). Others cannot (where do I get searing blood?) The journal should be the place to learn these things, but there are many things that aren't in the journal (searing blood, blood of the brood, etc). I got totally stuck at times, and had to check the internet, just to figure out what I should do next, because I honestly had no idea. That's a mark of poor design in game flow.
Also, mobs can hit through walls. That kinda sucks when you've got a small house.
The endgame just feels like a huuuuge grind. Bandages aren't that bad (new world, raid nearby cotton farm). But the frost ferns are a pain to farm (they're randomly all throughout the first island). Making the hal potions is a huge grind, finding those random ingredients. Don't even get me started on the Drackonus shards... Then killing the late game mobs is just sitting there swinging your sword at them for a few minutes. And the dragon fight is a terrible grind too. It takes like half an hour of stabbing it over and over and over again, using up all the valuable items that took you hours to make. It's just sooo grindy, I kind of lost the will to play right at the end of the game, because I knew how long it would take to set up.
HOWEVER, overall I still really loved this game, and highly recommend it. It's enjoyable and well done, but it IS still in the development phase, and the devs are updating constantly, and are really attentive (they seem like really awesome devs).

Before the developers settled on Pillars of Eternity, the working title was Baldur's Dale III: Torment.

Pillars of Eternity is an isometric point-and-click RPG, with 3D characters and effects over pre-rendered 2D backgrounds. No new graphical standards have been set here, but everything looks fantastic. Zooming in all the way can break immersion, because the background pixelates and reveals the illusion. However, there is virtually no reason to zoom in, and the blending between 3D characters and their 2D world is seamless at the intended zoom distance. In Obsidian’s defense, the game is already massive in size (nearly 14 GB uncompressed on Steam). Making the environments even higher resolution to facilitate pixel-free zooming would have bloated the size beyond reason.
Combat is real-time with pause, as opposed to turn-based. This was a point of debate during development and remains one post-release. It’s also largely a matter of preference, and I really don’t have a strong preference as long as the system that’s implemented is functional, fair and fun. Fortunately, while not perfect and likely in need of some balance tuning, the real-time combat in PoE delivers. With fights running on top of Obsidian’s in-house rule set, the result is a cRPG experience built from the ground-up as a cRPG, rather than being ported from some tabletop franchise. It works, and it is both conceptually simple and powerful, even if there’s some room for improvement.
Another controversial design decision is the lack of experience points for killing mobs once the bestiary has been filled out. The reason for this is the tendency in role-playing games for killing to be the most rewarding path toward resolution. When you gets points for killing things, then there is no way to avoid this. PoE’s solution is to reward exploration and quest completion, but not killing. This allows goals to be met in a variety of ways, while eliminating concern about losing out on XP when you handle an encounter diplomatically instead of hacking your opponent into gibs. It’s an arbitrary limitation, but it solves the problem Obsidian wanted to address, albeit at the cost of upsetting players who want a more grindy, hack-n-slash affair. If your idea of an RPG is farming hordes of monsters toward making a virtually invincible character decked out in Pristine Armor of Godly Awesomeness +10, then you likely won’t enjoy PoE’s approach to experience points.
Outside of combat, the game is loaded with quests, interesting characters and companions, scripted events, and great storytelling. And it’s all presented on a clean, easy-to-use interface. Dialogue unfolds in fairly classic fashion, with regular opportunities to influence the outcome with special options if one or more player skills are high enough. For example, Might can often be used to intimidate people. Intellect and Perception can help a character understand issues in more depth or pick up on additional clues. Similarly, skills can be used to determine how scripted sequences unfold. One situation fairly early in the game has the party taking a swim. Without a high enough rating in Athletics, characters will climb out of the water fatigued and need to rest in order to restore their stats. This is hardly a new concept, but it’s logical and handled well.
There are numerous class, race and background options that can easily cause you to while away your first hour in the character creator. You get humans, elves and dwarves, of course, but the giant aumaua and short-n-hairy orlan are oddballs. There’s also a race of godlike who are vaguely analogous to the planetouched of D&D. Also, each race has a choice of sub-race that will alter both the appearance and bonuses of the character. For example, the godlike can choose between Fire, Nature or Moon, whereas humans are either Meadow, Savannah or Ocean folk.
Eleven playable classes are available at release, running the gamut from the usual RPG suspects to a couple of weirdos like the Cipher and Chanter. PoE’s rule set allows extreme flexibility with character development, including the ability to create a stupid Wizard who wears heavy armor, a brilliant Fighter who runs around in his underwear and stabs enemies with a dagger, or a Druid who prefers heavy plate and fights with a two-handed sword. I make no claims on the effectiveness of these combinations, but they are possible within the game.
Sound is strong. I’ve found myself particularly pleased with the impact of weapons and spells during combat, as I was admittedly expecting things to be a bit thin in this area. Shouts and growls lend a visceral quality to the real-time encounters, and the spells and chants of casters add an immersive flair on par with the best of games past. Voice-acting is a bit more varied, but none of it is particularly bad. The companions and major NPCs in particular are graced with high-quality performances, even if I wish more of their lines had been recorded.
Music in the game was composed by Justin Bell and consists of airy orchestral pieces that were clearly inspired by PoE’s forerunners. It’s subtle for the most part, but can ramp up suitably for combat and tension. I enjoyed it for a while, but I usually don't play games with background music, so most of my time has passed without it.
I didn’t really get into cRPGs until the original Neverwinter Nights, and Neverwinter Nights 2 from 2006 remains one of my favorite games of all time. It was around this time that I went back to the Infinity Engine classics and, at last, realized their absolute genius. Now here in 2015, Pillars of Eternity has not only reclaimed the spirit of BG, IWD and others, but it has managed to do so without seeming old itself. I have not enjoyed a fantasy RPG this much since Dragon Age: Origins. I’ve had nearly three years for expectations to grow, and so it would have been easy for disappointment to manifest, but Obsidian has exceeded my expectations across the board.

So I was led under the impression that A.R.E.S. Extinction Agenda was a Mega Man-styled side-scroller where you pick a stage of any order you want, go around blasting robotic enemies, and steal special powers from the bosses. Not true; just because you have a robot (or a cyborg or a someone in a mecha or sorts) that can jump and shoot thngs doesn't immediately make it a Mega Man clone. If anything, this game resembles more closely to the oft-forgotten (and now freeware) MS-DOS game Abuse by Crack dot Com (comprising of a few former id Software guys), with a bits of Metroid thrown in. The story is that you're A.R.E.S., a combat robot with a mission to rescue Dr. Julia Carson, a scientist from United Earth working on a way to save the planet through a concept known as Deep Space Reprocessing by recycling waste, and investigate the DSR space station, the Junk Sector, and its Zytron outbreak. The game however only has five levels and most of the replay value comes from trying to improve your score and get higher ranks. A.R.E.S. is not alone on this mission as he's aided by Valkyl, an A.I. of a battleship who can rain down destruction after filling a special meter. Along the way, you'll collect various upgrades that gives you new abilities such as an exploding/electrical dash and better immunity to toxic Zytron gases infesting the Junk Sector space station. You also get a few new guns to play around with, which can be upgraded with the scraps and resources you collect from fallen enemies and scattered throughout stages. Said ability upgrades can be used to reach hidden areas to uncover secret items or data packs that shed some light on the mission, the Junk Sector, characters, enemies, and UE.
Sadly this is where things fall apart for me and this game because there's one glaring problem with this game that I have: the controls. I've put this game down before and recently picked up again this game again to see if it was just me or the game's sluggish controls that was putting me off, and I can say it's latter that's driving me to play other platformers with precise controls. I've played many 2D platformers in my day, but A.R.E.S. feels sluggish and sometimes unresponsive on both keyboard+mouse and controller. Not to mention he feels sluggish to move around in these levels, even with these upgrades to give him more advanced moves he feels slow to move around. Metagal has more responsive controls than this game. Hell, even Mighty No. 9 on Wii U has more responsive controls than this game. Speaking of levels, the level design can sometimes come off as cheap; a noticible moment is this climb from one of the game's bosses in the third level where you have to leap from platform to platform to the top, but thanks to medicore controls, I usually fall for a cheap death and my score/rank goes with it. Fun. The Metroid elements this game tries to use doesn't quite capture the sense of progression that other Metroidvanias games out there give and feels more like a chore to collect these upgrades to pad out the short longevity. Although the game as a nice soundtrack, but to be honest, there are some tracks that were completely forgettable and boring to me. While there's an EX version of this game that came out a few years ago that updates the graphics and adds another character, I honestly don't think a $10 price tag is justifible for an "update" when other developers lately are giving the updated versions of their games for free if they met a certain ceteria (e.g. Darksiders II, BioShock, Skyrim). Not to mention I'm not fond of the redesigns of Valkyl and especially not Dr. Julia Carson in EX.
Another reason I'm not giving this game a recommendation is how Extend Studios had the nerve to take advantage of the blacklash Mighty No. 9 is suffering through to "promote" sales of their game. They have to nerve to put the game on sale just around the time when the game was going on sale anyways during Steam's Summer Sale a few months ago for the sake of bashing Inafune. What was that 2% difference between the 77% for your "mighty" discount and the 75% discount during the Summer Sale supposed to represent, your respect for a struggling developer? Seriously, kicking people while they're down just because of your petty "disappointment" with Mighty No. 9 has become your business practice now? Sadly I'm probably the only one who sees this sort of practice as mean-spirited, underhanded, disgusting, and outright unprofessional. Hopefully A.R.E.S. will be more fun to play in Combat Core, but honestly, rather than working on an Episode 2 for this game (I'm sure you'll figure that out), I think what Extend Studios should be doing is work on their people skills.
Recently bought Mighty No. 9 on PC, it runs and plays like an absolute dream for me.♥♥♥♥♥♥your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Extend Studios, you greedy selfish ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.

I'm not the kind of guy to go around calling games soulless, but in this case I don't want to waste time. A.R.E.S. is a miserable, joyless experience hacked together from a gross misunderstanding of all that is good about platformers. It does nothing well, is thick with boneheaded design choices, and won't even last you much more than an hour even if you DID enjoy it. I feel like that should be enough to ward anyone off of it, but just to be sure I'll happily dig further into the trash pile this game is.
A.R.E.S. refers to you, the lucky combat cyborg sent to the JUNK SECTOR to save it from a mysterious robot-corrupting gas. JUNK SECTOR is a space station of literal garbage, through which you will blast robots and crates to reach some tiny anime scientist and unravel the mystery of the evil space fart. Along the way you will find new weapons, loads of literal garbage to upgrade them with, a whole mess of unimportant characters, and a really bad rendition of the plot of Prometheus. And buddy, we're just getting started.
Platforming through JUNK SECTOR is stiff, awkward, and features little variety. Most of the levels consist of hallways full of crates to jump over or shafts of platforms to scale. You start with a double jump and a roll but your character drops like a stone and the roll is over a static distance so don't expect any fluid maneuvers here. There are plenty of enemies to blast and you can do so with free range of aiming, dispatching most in just short bursts. Enemies tend not to be very threatening (even on the base difficulty of Hard) unless there's no room to deal with them, which is a common issue with the cramped levels and zoomed-in camera.
Shooting things or locating hidden items earns you salvage, three kinds of junk currency you can use to make items or upgrade your weapons. This unfortunately is way more of a hassle than you might be thinking because there are no health or ammo pickups, you have to craft healing items and grenades. Yes, that means you can cripple your ability to upgrade gear if you're having trouble with the game, or lock yourself out of items if you want to squeak out an upgrade without a buffer. Grenades are pretty important too because they're used to access the game's secret areas and are used to air dash, for some inconceivable reason.
On the other hand you can break the bosses by crafting dozens of healing items and mashing them into your metal body every few hits. You won't really need to because the bosses aren't terribly difficult, adhering to familiar patterns of leaping or rolling or telegraphing big beam attacks. Even on "Hard" it's not a very challenging game, and you'll get through it in an hour or so because there are only five levels. You read that right, five levels. No secret levels, not even any backtracking. Five linear levels are all you get here, each done up in bland, featureless tech motifs that look nothing like habitable environments. And it's not even until the very last level that they contain anything besides crates, traps, and enemies.
The gameplay in A.R.E.S. is utterly deficient, failing to provide any sort of gratifying movement, combat, or goals to slog your way through. Fortunately that deficiency extends to the story and world-building as well, so don't feel like you're missing anything by skipping this title. There's one person to save, one super weapon to fight, and one big bad with an incredibly cliche M.O. for setting this whole thing off. The story especially hews close to those lousy PlayStation-era Mega Man X games, and really the entire game feels like a bad pastiche of the mistakes those titles made ages ago. So much effort was made to imitate something that wasn't that good in the first place that nobody bothered to check if they were making even worse mistakes here. But they did, oh Lord did they ever, leaving A.R.E.S. as one of the blandest, most boring platformers I've ever forced my way through.

This is the 8th offical entry to the franchise (not counting the expansion ie Empires, Xtreme Legends, Strikeforce, NEXT) and the 4th entry for PC version. and the first one on Steam. It finally make it to PC after almost 1 year and it's bundles with Xtreme Legends and renamed Complete Edition.
About the port, it's pretty good port with several issue. The graphics are using PS3 graphics and not PS4, which is not a problem for me :P. I got 60 fps during gameplay, 30 fps during cutscenes which is very good for this kind of game.The graphics can be nhanced with ENB which already made by modders. Controls are still awkward. No mouse support like the old PC version, though the game is better played with gamepad. Some people have black screen issues which is problematic. Luckily, I only encountered few times. People already found temporary solution for it, but KOEI need to make patch for it. And the online coop from console version is not available, only local coop stays.
About the game itself, it's a very good hack-and-slash game. There are story mode which will follow the story based on the Romance of Three Kingdom novel, free mode (pick any officer, pick any stage, go wild), Ambition Mode, Challenge Mode. There are 82 playable characters to choose from, each with unique moveset and weapons to choose from. The game mechanics has been greatly improved from previous games ie Weapon Switching, new musou attacks, Storm Rush, Rage Mode to try making this game not jus a brainless button masher (still a button masher though). All playable characters has different personalities, so you'll have fun exploring each of them. Another plus point is the soundtrack. Koei never fail to deliver this part. All soundtracks in this game really enjoyable. In Free Mode, you can choose which song to play for that stage before you start playing.
If you're a Warriors fan and you don't have a console like me, this is worth the full price, if you can run it of course.

Note: My earlier review was unfavorable for the following reasons, however I am now being favorable of this game:
*Problems*
-----------------------------
- Early release problems regarding controller rebinding. Also discovered that the game uses DInput rather than XInput, so some controllers will not work (like the Nvidia Shield Portable) without extra effort involved. If you buy this, make sure to have a fully working 360 controller or you will be dissapointed.
- No Network Multiplayer yet.
*Good Things*
-----------------------------
- It's Dynasty Warriors on PC.
- Ambition Mode is very fun, and does provide some break from grinding the campaigns over and over.
- Japanese VA available (this was added in as free DLC after release)
Should you buy it?
-----------------------------
I'd say in it's current form, yes, assuming you have a working 360 Controller and are a fan of the Dynasty Warrior series.
Should I buy the DLC?
-----------------------------
Not really. Most of it is rather wierd and gimmicky outfits with some new weapon types. The game already has a plethora of weapons so it's not really necessary.

I think the big thing about this game that might turn a lot of people off is that it is a Dynasty Warriors game. If you are a fan of the series, and haven't bought this game on consoles already, then buy this game! It's a great update to a lot of the mechanics and all of the characters feel and play quite well. The campaign is a marked improvement over the DW7 campaign (except for the lack of a narrator, unfortunately).
Ambition Mode is a take it or leave it thing. It's a really good way to get good weapons and level characters, but if you want any sort of deep story from it, you'll find yourself disappointed.
And just in case you're wondering, no, this game does not have online co-op. Even with that disappointing fact though, I wholeheartedly recommend this game to fans of the DW series. If you've traditionally not liked the series, or have no idea what this is, I would peruse YouTube and see if it's your cup of tea.

While the game is top notch in almost every way that matters, there are some important points to consider:
The game is VERY easy in comparison to earlier titles like Double Agent though not as simple as Conviction, the conveniently placed hiding places are frequent and diverse. Getting through levels on the hardest difficulty while not killing anyone is not only possible but routine after a few practice runs.
The story takes a serious course alteration from earlier titles to fall somewhere between a hollywood action thriller and tv action comedy. The main drag is bits of forced humour (mainly coming from Charlie and the "prisoner") that simply feel completely out of place with the pace of the rest of the story.
Those two things aside, the game is solid, gameplay mechanics and controls are very well done and levels are diverse and complex in nature so that there is often oppurtunities to explore alternate routes through missions.
If you play the multiplayer replayability would probably increase but as is, it becomes a fairly forgettable title once you have gotten the hang of mechanics enough to solo wave after wave of charlie's survival missions.

Given that this was an early access title, I went into it with low expectations.  But even those expectations were too much.
The art, the playable content, the direction, even the setting... none of it is finished.  And while that may be fine (After nearly two years of development), if the core mechanics underlying it all just worked.  But they don't.
The screenshots are in no way indicative of the actual gameplay.  While the graphics and much of the setting is represented, many of the basic models or concepts (group mobs for instance) don't exist in the game.  Overall, the game starts out slightly difficult due to poor gameplay prompts.  It then falls into being one of the easiest games I've ever played.  Until you get to the end game content, at which point you'll no longer have any hope of even slightly progressing without a fully geared multiplayer party to join you.
You'll also lose your progress.  Frequently.  To stuck characters, to unaccessable places, to inescapable enemies who plant their flag in your dead♥♥♥♥♥to prevent you from recovering anything. And you'll consistantly lose everything to unexplainable bugs where your corpse just disappears on respawn.
This developer has a cheap one-size html template website.  They have no real discussion boards or discord, a poorly run trello that doesn't in any way fit the role of a project tracker, and they seemingly have no direction at all with the project.  It's already gone through one major overhaul and platform upgrade, and has still yet to see major setting changes.  And this is after nearly two years of development?  I understand not being done, but it's not even close.  And after this long in development, the only excuses are incompetance, mismanagement, and plain ♥♥♥♥ery.
Don't buy this game in early access.  Wait to see if it ever gets done first.

I love it.  It has more than enough subtle homestuck references to keep please its fan (and raises quite a few questions about how it fits into the existing canon) but is certainly understandable without having read homestuck.  There are plenty of jokes and humorous observations to be found by examining the environment; homestuck fans will appreciate the familiar sense of humor, but the humor is not based upon homestuck-references, so new players should have no issue getting it.
For the most part, it's puzzles are able to be reasoned through (I only ran into trouble by doubting the bending strength of alien culinary utensils), and the variety of mini-games keep things interesting and promote the feeling that you're solving a variety of challenges.  Pieces of the characters' backstories are tucked away inside environmental descriptions, so if that's not your thing, don't worry: you don't have to know any escoteric knowledge from examining every object just to progress; it's there solely so that you can enjoy it if you want to.
I really appreciate the musical and visual techniques used to craft each scene, as each displays a well-crafted tone and feel.  The build and release of tension this game exhibits is masterful.  It enables you to empathize with the characters and truly makes you feel like you're a part of the action.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoywed HIVESWAP: Act 1.  I am so truly thankful to everyone who worked to create this game; your determination to stick with it despite numerous obstacles is no small feat.  I am thrilled with this game and cannot wait for the next installment!

Art of War: Red Tides is a simple 1v1/3v3 online RTS game where each player buys and sends waves of units per turn as said units clash when they meet in a single MOBA style lane. Players will have to defend their own base while trying to destroy their opponet's base, both of which are defended by 3 layers of towers/turrets of their own. Each player can choose and play from 3 different factions with their own unique units and abilities which you can mix and match to compliment your playstyle.
This game however is not won by sending in troops mindlessly, you do not send hordes of a single type of unit only to be countered by a type of unit that specifically beats it and shout at the forums "Game is broken, Units are op". You have to think and observe the battlefield. You ask yourself things like " What is the best unit against my opponent?", "Should i use this special abilty at this moment or should i save it for later?". Of course your opponent will be thinking the same. And your decisions are what dictates victory or defeat.
Personally, I like the game and i think the units are pretty much balance since even the basic units can beatdown advance ones if used properly.

First off, I initially got into this game with some bias as I am an old infinity game player, I was already predisposed to this game in that light. After playing it however I noticed the merit of this game in particular.
If you've ever played an infinity engine game...this game is identical. Its as if they took the infinity engine and just leveled it up graphically and added a few extra moves to it. I was astounded at how it felt, it was like I was playing Baldurs Gate all over again...but then it differed. The primary difference is of course the law and the storyline. The immersion is there,its very good, I can only hope there is a continuation of this type of game. The lore is unique and intriguing, not your everyday thing but still familiar enough to not be too alien. Learning the lore of the game world was rewarding in its own right. Especially when you replay scenes and you actually understand what is going on.
Gameplay is also excellent and well balanced in my opinion, the additional difficulties are also there for the veterans or some might say "geeks". There is a ton of customisation in many forms. Simply in character creation there are more options than I've seen in most any game. You select your gender, race, class, background, culture, you select detailed stats, skills..many races have subraces and subcultures and most of these things may have some impact on story progression and interaction with the game world. The balance of your characters statistics affects combat and also interaction...you might end up having a strong focus on combat...only to have difficulty in social interactions. The reverse is also true. Skills also have a large impact, you might have a very unfit mage who falls off a cliff or gets injured because of poor footing, or you could move massive boulders out of your path with raw strength if you are so inclined. The combinations are plentiful and would take many replays to see all the possibilities. If there was ever to be another Baldurs Gate then this was it.  A true spiritual successor.
For all my bias and the flowery words about it...I still have some issues with it. If I had not played Baldurs Gate, I may not have seen this as a problem...but the interaction with companions was not as satisfying as I'd have liked. It just doesn't delve deep enough. I couldn't at the end of it all say that I'd really bonded with any of them. It was more like we start as strangers and end as comrades...but not really good friends or anything more. In that sense I might as well play it as a solo character without the need for companions. The companions do have their own draw and they are interesting but as mentioned, there is nothing to keep one interested in them. Once you assist them through their own problems they cease to be interesting and you cannot deepen any bonds. Suffice to say they are very limited.
Additionally I did not enjoy the conclusion to the story, this is my deduction but the story appeared to have a thoroughly atheist agenda and I did not find the conclusion satisfying. Thats all I can say without spoiling anything. The writing is however very good, dialogue as well.
All in all, this is one of the best games to grace the monitors of the gaming populace of this decade. I heartily recommend it.

Short Version:
If you lliked games such as Icewind Dale and Baldur's Gate you will like this one.  It does have its flaws, but overall it is a very good game.  I would give it a 4 out of 5 stars.
Longer version:
The good:
The story is fairly good.  The UI and Graphics are really good.  The world is, for the most part, intresting to explore.  There are a lot of classes.  You can either make custom adventuers or you can find companions in the game to join you.  In general, it is a very solid RPG game.  It also has an interesting take on character statistics where all statiscs are useful to all classes.  For example, MIGHT is just as important to a wizard as it is to a DPS warrior.  Also the game has A LOT of voice acting.  Most of the stuff you can just listen too.  It is very well done.  At the end of the game there is a summary of your choices you made thought the game.  Your choices really do matter.
The Bad:
The class progession is fairly flat.  You do not have talents / feats that are pre-requiests of others.  It is not like you can make a wizard with 5 different builds.  There is only one.  The most specialization is if you pick a warrior and you can either pick Tank talents or DPS talents.  All others, reguardless of class, will do a DPS build.  Their talent trees just not interesting, just providing minor statistical buffs rather than new abilities.
You get a stronghold in the game, which is a great idea.  What is bad about this is that upgrading it is fairly pointless.  There are events around your stronghold which are annoying to deal with and offer no benefit whatsoever.
Crafting is in the game.  You can make food, potions and enchants.  Except for some minor buffs, it really is all pointless.  Eating food that gives you +10 stamaina in battle is worthless.    Potions have similar problems, by providing minor buffs that do not do much despite using precious reagents.  Weapon buffs are nice, but only add a minor amount of damage.  I think if all my weapons had been missing enchants, I would have hardly noticed.
When your party is in combat, they tend to get clustered.  When you select a single character, it is nearly impossible to tell where your selected character is in the blob of green circles in the middle of combat.
Loot is very dull.  It is all just minor statistical differences and nothing really interesting.
You can find lots of traps in the game.  You pick them up and add them to your inventory.  For some crazy reason, the entire party is only allowed to have ONE trap out at a time.  These are a consumable resource.  If you want to burn 10 traps killing some ogres, then you should be able to do so.  God only knows this game needs some kind of real gold sink.  Buying traps would not be a bad one.
The range of spells is redicuously short.  Even the long range spells I would consider a super-short range for a caster.
The Ugly:
There is NO friendly combat AI.  Your summons / npcs will stand around doing nothing when monsters are right next to them (although there is a tiny grain of AI to start attacking back when they are engaged).  Would it be too much to ask to have your NPCS drink a healing potion when they get low on health?  Or to not do stupding pathing♥♥♥♥♥♥and run right up to a monster when trying to cast a heal or buff on a friendly PC?  Or not to walk over traps you have found....
After 40+ hours of gameplay, the tedious nature combat really got to me.  I turned the difficutly down just so I could finish the game and see how the story turns out.
Monsters, beyond the first few of each type, give NO XP.   There is so much combat in this game it is crazy, yet 95% of it is pointless as it has NO BENEFIT.  This is a terrible idea.
Then there is the resting mechanic.  You need camping supplies to rest.  Only in the hard mode, you are only allowed to carry 2 units of this.  In normal its 4.  This should have been an option to increase the challenge of the game.  Personally I wanted challenging fights, but not this other restriction. It should be an independent option you can choose.

So I just finished the game... [Review]
Well, at 46 hours, that was one, long and fun ride.  I haven't felt so involved in a roleplaying game since Planescape : Tormet and it speaks volumes of the writing here.  There were a couple bugs and I'll get to them in an instant but the major ones were swiftly corrected, leaving some minor ones with very little impact in game.
First, let's start with the obvious.  This game was obviously developped by gamers who know what they like in a game.  Everything about the interface screams convenience.  At first I was surprised to only find sixteen equipment slots in the inventory, until I noticed a well organised, infinite "stash" box.  Every quest item and ingredient (and there's a LOT of them) instantly goes to your stash, leaving you to select only what you want to keep.  New weapon that you don't plan to use?  Stash.  Crapload of stuff on the ground?  Stash.  You can also dump equipment from your inventory to your stash if you like.  There's also an option to be able to access it anywhere, otherwise you are limited to inns and during campings.  I preferred keep it like that but it's really up to the player.
Speaking of convenience and options, there's one to enlarge the looting radius.  Basically that means that whenever you loot something from the dead, every other corpse nearby will be looted.  I definately recommend you put the radius to the maximum.  There's the usual meta-infos, what you want displayed, when the auto pause begins, there's a lot to check out.
There's also a limited number of "resting" available, which for those abusing it in other games might come off as annoying but you get 4 on "normal" and less on harder difficulties.  You find "camping supplies" in a lot of crates and most merchants sell them as well.  By level 7, I hardly noticed the supplies since you get a lot of spells to throw to your enemies and it becomes an issue only if you're dangerously low on health.
Yes, low on health.  This is both a good and a bad thing so I won't hold the developpers for this interesting and new concept.  You have two "life" totals.  One is the stamina and the other, your actual health.  Your health is always far higher than your stamina, sometimes as much as three or four times the total and both lower at the same time.  However, since your stamina's much lower, you will fall unconscious before dying at least for a while.  After the fight, your unsconscious characters will get up and the endurance will refill quickly, up to the current health.  So when your health is low, your endurance bar will be capped and that's when you risk dying.  I thought that was an interesting idea but my issue is that the only way to raise your health is to rest.  Mind you, it does make sense in a way But there are times when you wish you didn't need to use your supplies just because one character nears death.  Even the highest priest spells do nothing to raise the health at all.  There's an option to change the final death to injuries but I left it off, I preferred the perma deaths.  Again, great work on making sure the game's tailored to a player's preferences.
On another note, I hope you love reading.  This isn't Diablo 3 here and again, I'm bringing Planescape Torment as a comparison.  The writers did a stellar job, when you can talk to a NPC, the dialogs are expansive and there's a lot of body language added for immersion.  There's also this fun idea of letting Kickstarter backers write their own NPCs.  Now and then, you'll meet people whose nameplates are golden instead of tan.  When you click on them, you can "Reach out for their souls" and get to experience, from that NPC's point of view, an important moment in their life.  They have no impact at all ingame except to give you a better immersion and let you read something fun.  I read every one I came across, some are pretty gory, others are light hearted and sweet, others just bittersweet.  It's definately an awesome way for Developpers to reward the backers and I'm pretty sure all of them bought the game just to be able to see their own NPC.  The fact that they are entirely optional is also well thought, someone who don't really like reading (and why would they play a game like that is beyond me) can just ignore them.
Now, as far as party creation goes, I can already tell some people might feel put off by the fact you can only create one character at the start.  When you enter an Inn (and it happens within the first hour) You can hire mercenaries up to your own level, at a cost.  I found out what thanks to the generous loot, I could have a full party of six very quickly with very little impact on levels.  You also meet scripted NPCs, who are all very interesting but since my first character was a mage and the first hireable NPC you meet is also one, I went with creating my own party.  You get the standard stuff, warrior, monk, druid etc with new stuff like a chanter, which is basically a bard that can take actions while chanting and once a song is complete, you get a strong effect or a cipher who gains "mana" by damaging enemies.
I pretty much completely neglected the scripted NPCs, meaning my party never intervened or commented during conversations which was a bit sad but I did not regret it, my own party was rock solid with far better stats than the scripted ones.  By the end, I did promise myself to use the scripted ones in my next playthrought since they do offer a very lively interaction with the world.
Very early in the game you gain a stronghold, which offers you a major questline as there's a VERY large dungeon in your own basement (actually under your own dungeon, which I thought was clever).  You can build structures to add minor bonuses when you rest at home as well as get cosmetic changes.  Overall it's a fun addition, it adds little to the overall story but again, the massive dungeon alone is worth it.  At fifteen levels, it's by far the largest in game and also by far the most interesting, each level has it's own "theme" and distinct look.
The enemies were for the most part varied but I admit I'd have wished to see less of these damn "shade" monsters, you see them from start to finish and by level 8, pose no serious threat.  The enemy AI is very good too, I was often surprised by flanking moves and concentrated attacks on vulnerable party members.
Speaking of AI, there is one, for your party, kinda.  I wish it would show a bit more initiative but once the fight begins, the party members mostly find a new target by themselves but at the start, won't do anything unless you order them to.  They also don't seek new targets if they are too far either.  Personally I like to micromanage my party so I hadn't noticed this until well into the game, as I issued my orders right from the first active pause of combat.
The game is capped at level 12.  While I understand that at this point you can easily steamroll most fights by just asking everyone to rush in, I hit that limit very early, at the start of act 3.  There's a "bounty" quest system from your fortress' lodge that are basically "go there and kill this person" and they are challenging fights but gives a LOT of XP.  Capping at 15 might have given more of an incentive to finish all quests.  The spells stop at level 6 but there's room for 3-4 more levels in the list, I figure that if the game sells well (and it sure did) they could consider that in the sequel.
Now for the auditory review...  you normally don't expect a game like that to look so good but I've paused at several times in game just to look around and admire the scenery.  Most dungeons are a feast for the eye and the music is really good.  It has a very "Obsidian" theme to it.
Verdict : 92%.  STRONGLY recommended.

TLDR:  Bought the game at full launch price, feel like I wasted my money, when the game is under $15 it will be a decent buy.
Game launched with game breaking bugs, inbalanced combat system, poor design decisions for combat and spell mechanics, poor intergration of "Backer" content, poor intergration of of the "Stronghold", a generic story with IMO no real "hook" to attach the player to it, a non-sensicle rest system, and a slew of other things that could have been done better.
In general, I expected more from industry veterans.  In the age of "kickstarters" where developers supposedly have the freedom to make the game they WANT to make, I fear that we are going to discover that a lot of these developers needed to have taskmasters forcing them to make the games the way they SHOULD be made.
Isometric View, top down, "Real Time" pausible combat games are NOT new.  And Pillars was promoted as bring back the "Feel" of old school infinity engine games.  There is one major problem with that reasoning tho, those games continued to advance and evolve.. to grow, based on player feedback, into a more user friendly and enjoyable experiece.  You cant "go back" and dredge up all the bad things the weighed those systems down, and then bring NONE of the "Fixes" that made those games enjoyable and playable.
Pillars of Eternity developers "Want" to convince people it is a "Tactical" combat game, but they give players NO real tactical options.  The game falls down flat on its face when trying to get to "gritty turn based tactical decision making with consequences"..   In a nutshell, if you "find" the right items , you can auto-attack your way through the entire game, even on its hardest difficutly.   The enemies of the game all have DR, making all "fast" attack weapons nearly useless.  To "Win" you simply put on the heaviest armor you can find, with the biggest hitting slowest weapon you can find.   The developers new this was an issue, which is why they removed "Accuracy" from being bound to your stats, as the easiest way to "Win" was to simply max accuracy and build a arbegues firing squad in plate mail.   Sadly tho, the change still hasn't "Fixed" this issue..  and the developers "nerfing" the arbeques and reload speed chants after the game launched again shows poor long term design thought.
I expect by the time the game hits patch 8 or 9 it will be more balanced, assumign the devs take the time to do a pass on all the ridiculously OP monsters who can one shot you if you aren't in platemail..

How did it all go so wrong? You had decades of platformers to look back on to get it right.
This is not a bad game per sé, but I could find faults with nearly every aspect of it without trying.
As hommage to Megaman (I presume), your starting suit is
. That's fine as you get the better suit quickly, but the weapon upgrades are something else. I only upgraded the Wave Emitter because a gun shooting through walls seemed OP. It is, and incredibly so. It made the game completely trivial until the last boss (where it still seemed to outperform all other guns by a long shot), and the SMG seemed similarly powerful.
Difficulty comes in 2 forms: surprise attacks (mobs that will charge at you as you enter the next screen, you'll quickly learn to zone with attack held down) and the lack of a second thumb on your right hand that would allow you to jump while firing.
The controls are...it's hard to describe, it feels like there is some sort of weird animation-lock that prevents you from turning around/jumping as soon as you'd expect to be able to (which is awful in a game designed with heavy slide usage in mind) after firing. Example situation as I have witnessed it: I'm firing at something to my right, I'm on the left edge of a platform, the next higher one is up to the left. I fire, press and hold left and press jump. Character fires, turns around, walks off the edge. This can be reproduced 100% of the time, I'm not sure how this got through. Sure, you could say "so you walk off a platform, big deal", but what if the platform is a laserbeam and my attempt to jump is an attempt to slide through it, but instead I get hit (this situation brought to you by the final boss)? These are real situations, and they make the game quite annoying.
Grenades seem kind of tacked on and pointless until you get the unlimited grenades-upgrade, you only need to grenade-jump very occasionally and the other weapons are so strong that you don't need grenades for combat.
Speaking of "tacked on", the crafting system also seems pretty redundant. It's not too painful, and it allows you to farm healthpacks, but you could always farm lives in these sort of games, so it's nothing really new (which is fine).
The boss patterns are very simple. I don't play these sort of games that often, yet I don't think I needed more than 2 attempts on any boss except the last one (on Hard). In fact, I think I oneshot all but 1 and the last boss boss on my first run.
The last boss is a three phase fight, and presented the only real challenge in the game for me. Sadly, however, this was mostly because of the bad boss(-room) design and phasing. The bottom left and right platforms regularly get you stuck (due to the ramp underneath), the big yellow laser orb has a larger hitbox than is visually apparent (I must have gotten hit by that about 20 times when it clearly didn't touch me), and if there are projectiles out on the screen when the boss phases, you will be rooted in place and take the projectiles in the mouth as there is nothing you can do about it. Mechanically the boss was somewhat challenging and fun otherwise, though still only what you'd expect in other games on Normal difficulty.
Overall, A.R.E.S: E.A. is a very short (~2.5 hours for first playthrough) and easy platformer with Twin-Stick shooting (please tag the game accordingly!), little innovation and many flaws. This is the kind of game you will best enjoy if you want to replay and master it (and you will have to if you want the achievements). For a one-time playthrough it is utterly unremarkable, but the upgrades from the first playthrough persist and make replaying it a somewhat appealing proposition.
With as little choice as we have on Steam for Megaman-like games, it's an okay buy.
If I had to give it a rating, I'd say 6/10.

This game has got an interesting community of likeminded players behind it. The idea being that the game is valuable because it is a hardcore teamwork-based multiplayer with competetive features like technical inputs and precision-based actions. Like any great game, it's hard to pick up yet improvements feel rewarding. The premise of survival is all based on how you value your life versus the livelihood of the group of survivors who exist with you. This is true because a lot can be learned about from dying that may lead players to taking different actions when as survivor in the future. Essentially, learning to git gud is fun. Then, when you die, you turn into a zombie and chase down your old "allies," and then attempt to sabotage defended positions en masse. Best feature: whole thing is open voice chat.
See also: Rust, Blackwake, or Space Engineers if you like this kind of open voice, teamwork-based format .
