A true homage to the infinity engine games. Probably my favorite game of the CRPG kickstarter revival so far.
A good story, although sometimes too wrapped up in its own lore for its own good. There are times when the NPCs will be using words that aren't defined, and you sort of have to use context clues to figure it out. There's also a lot of talk of different gods, regions, etc, and with no prior knowledge of the setting it can be a bit overwhelming. Still, the story was good and the world created was interesting.
Mechanically, the game is basically a modernization of the old infinity engine games. The interface looks the same, the combat works the same, and it's all pretty great. My only complaint might be that the underlying game system is basically just a rip of D&D (which is to be expected), but to the point where you might wonder why they bothered to differenciate in terms between the systems. Might vs strength, deflection vs armor, etc.
I encounted a couple of bugs, but nothing too serious. I had to use a third party program to fix a characters run speed at some point, but i'm sure that will be fixed in a patch.
The kickstarter stuff is, thankfully, easily avoided. If you want to dive into it you're welcome to, but it's easy to know what to avoid if you don't care.
Overall, a great game. I highly recommend it.

Now, I'm not one for kinetic visual novels. I'm of the opinion that 'if I can't interact with the story, I might as well read a book or watch an anime'. And for the most part, this game hasn't changed that. I feel as though this would make an absolutely incredible anime series or movie, but instead it chose to take in the visual novel form. That doesn't mean this game is bad. In fact, far from it. It tells a compelling story of a soldier hired to guard a facility, but in the process he finds himself and what he's always longed for.
My breakdown:
PROS:
+Music. Quite possibly one of the best soundtracks I've heard in a VN. Some scenes are absolutely flawless, and the soundtrack really enhances the power it has. By far the best element of this VN. The reason it is not a 10 is because some of the songs I didn't feel fit as well as they could have.
+Art. Some of the best 2D CG's I've ever seen. Compelling, powerful and expertly done. The entire game is run on different variations of these CG's, so instead of having the normal renpy look, it has a completely unique feel.
+Characters. Every character is designed incredibly well. Lavie/MC's dynamic was quite possibly the best written companionship I've seen in ages. With that being said though, a few of the decisions and dialogue choices some characters make (Especially Inaba) feel out of place, and out of line.
+Voice actors. I don't speak Japanese, but even I could tell that the voices did fantastic performances for the most part. The MC's one in particular, was outstanding.
+Story. Act 1 and 2 were phenomenal. Great conflict, expertly crafted scenes, and intriguing characters made these two segments just insane.
CONS:
-Old engine. The game feels old. On a technical level, it's just no longer up to par. When right click opens a default Windows dropbox, it takes a lot out of the experience.
- Spoiled sections. The games subheading 'they were the only two, on the planet' kills a lot of the power Acts 3/4 should have. And I feel that it's unjustified like that. Same with the prologue, which honestly would have made the game so much nicer if it didn't exist. Act 1 is so great because we don't know what will happen, and the prologue spoils a lot of it.
- Kinetic novel. A problem for me, for the reasonings stated in the opening paragraph of this review.
- Slow. Act's 3/4 were sreally drawn out, and honestly could have been done in way less time. I felt that the last 4 hours of the game could have been done just as well in around an hour.
-Scores-
Story: 8
Characters: 7
Art: 8
Music: 9
Enjoyment: 7
Overall: 8/10
tl;dr a beautiful game, but would have worked better as an anime.

I have only played this game single-player. I am not a huge survival game buff, but I played plenty of minecraft.
It's what it says on the tin. If you want a fantasy-themed survival game, this one does the job.  The game appears to have a fairly solid update schedule, and the updates add a fair amount.
There is currently one map, not randomly generated. It's a pretty big map, though.
As of the last couple of versions, the new user experience is pretty good. The starting island is harsh but fair, the game eases you into bigger challenges pretty well, and you can choose your own pace.
Moving onto the second island, you're met with new challenges, but better resources. It's simple but effective, and kept me wanting more.
Performance is fine with some settings turned down (medium-low overall) on a Phenom II X4 965, HD 7790, and 8GB RAM on Win10. Devs improve performance with every update.
Some negative points:
-You can tell it's early access--some of the assets are a little odd-looking (like the gouges in trees while you cut them down), some things that should be interactive aren't, and judging from update notes and other players, end-game content isn't quite complete or balanced properly.
-Loading takes a looong time. I'm only on a standard HDD, but the first time I ran the game, I thought it had crashed.
If you can put up with a little jankiness and the long load times, this game scratches the itch I had for a fantasy-style survival game. The game's lore is written well enough, and the game takes itself seriously without becoming super-hardcore and impenetrable.

It is what it is, if you don't enjoy hack and slash - don't get it. It's an interesting story based on real life events, (Look up the romance of the 3 kingdoms). The graphics are pretty satisfactory, and all of the characters look cool. Controls are pretty simple.
I only have a few issues with this game:
1: There is little reason to play on higher difficulty. You aren't really rewarded for doing so from what I can tell, other than select missions to get your 5th tier weapons. This is fine in story mode, where the story is interesting. In ambition mode which I enjoy quite a bit however, it makes it much easier. That's fine and all, that's what difficulty is for. But, there is no reward for playing in a higher difficulty. When playing consecutive battles in Ambition mode the rewards become greatly increased along with the difficulty, so it's completely to your benefit to start at beginner and have it ramp up anyway. However, this is VERY easily abused in earning the playable officers to your army (in ambition mode you recruit all sorts of allies, and the playable characters are the best ones). Most of them appear in a DUEL battle after completing consecutive stages. Basically, you can do about 3 beginner missions in a row to get a duel, easily get those characters then return to the camp and rinse and repeat. Using this process I got all the characters, and quite honestly it sort of spoiled the mode for me. I know no one made me use it, but there is ZERO incentive to play on a harder difficulty by default, no special weapons, characters, animals, or anything else I know of that makes it worth it.
That being said it's a pretty fun game if you enjoy hack and slash. I recommend to anyone that hasn't played it before and likes similar games like God of War or Devil May Cry, etc. Also if you enoyed other Dynasty warrior games! 8/10 from me, and worth the money.
Edit: I somehow forgot to mention there is unfortunately no online co-op. :(
Still a very good game and I hope they bring another improved title to the PC in the future.

Pros:
- Excellent Gameplay
- It promotes teamwork and cooperation
- Fun to play and you actually get nervous if you're about to die
- Great level design
- Helpful and cooperative community
Cons:
- Tricky keybindings, but it's easy to play once you get the hang of it

Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Grease and flour an 8-inch square pan.

Bake in preheated oven for 25 to 30 minutes. Do not overcook.

Its not a lie, but it doesn't even come close to conveying the truth.
To be fair, the game isnt by any means bad once you sort out a few issues, all of which happen to be caused by bad poting.
1. The controls
This game is nearly impossible to play with mouse and keyboard without the use of a few mods to fix it, and if you don't want all the controls displayed as xbox controls, you're going to need another mod on top of that.
If you want to fix the controls, you're going to need a mod called DS mouse fix, which itself requires the mod DSfix.
2. The performance
The game is locked at 30fps and is quite poorly optimized for PC. This doesn't make the game unplayable, but because the game relies on precise timing and maneuvering this can make it noticably more difficult, especially when using a mouse.
Again this can be fixed by the mod DSfix, which can unlock the framerate to 60fps, borderless windowed, better anti-aliasing, and a few other graphical fixes. If you want to optimize the textures themselves, youre going to need another mod on top of that.
So you might be thinking, "so I have to intall a couple of mods, so what?"
Well, the issue is that these mods are pretty much REQUIRED, and for someone unfamiliar with manual mod installation it might be a bit tricky.

Dragon's Dogma provides an interesting and engaging take on the ARPG genre which led me to play for hours on end. There are several aspects of Dark Arisen that I enjoyed, despite the presence of a couple of personal drawbacks.
Pros:
While not exactly innovative in its storyline, the mechanics in the game are rather unique. The game allows you to recruit and command AIs known as Pawns, which are tailored to some of your actions. Some of the available traits can serve as an important asset to your team composition, although there are others which tend to be rather useless or counterproductive. In addition, the class system is quite flexible, allowing you to change your character and your main pawn's roles frequently, with interchangeable passive and active skills.
Additionally, the combat for the title is exciting and riveting, requiring certain strategies against particular enemies, such as climbing atop of them or targeting specific weak points. Players can use a combination of skill sets for battle, depending on the type of weapons they have equipped. Mobility both in and out of combat is rather fluid as well.
Cons:
Even though Dragon's Dogma is fundamentally a great experience, there are certain elements to the game that also feel a little flawed, such as the travel time between locations for main quests and sidequests. Granted, there are certain items you get later in the game that reduce the tedious nature of traveling, but even then there are times where exploration feels too open-ended. However, this only seems to occur in large outdoor spaces, and not dungeons.
Furthermore, the affinity (love) system in the game is executed in a slightly offputting and crude manner, which doesn't feel very rewarding. While its inclusion adds a light twist to the game itself, it portrays characters and their relationships with the main character a bit clumsily and abruptly.
Conclusion:
Overall though, Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen is a refreshing experience that still manages to be fun regardless of its minor flaws. The action and strategy involved in the gameplay is enough to keep one immersed within the game's universe for a very long period of time.

The game feels empty, and the cutscenes almost have a random feel to them. Locations feel barren; characters are shallow; many side missions are fetch quests; and the narrative has a very detached feel to it. The game leaves a lot of room for imagination, and since it is fun to play,  filling in the blanks is worthwhile.
The story has an interesting structure that fits in well with the pawn system. The pacing in the game is very, very slow, and then it lurches to a sprint (a short sprint). The game should have provided more motivation to explore the Everfall early on, so you the player would develop a strong attachment that would drive your subsequent visits. The structure of the game does encourage replayability, and with replays the setting becomes intriguing. But it's still missing a narrative depth that no amount of replayability can fix.
Recommended.

Ascend:Hand of Kul Review;
Ascend: Hand of Kul is an action RPG hybrid putting you in the enormous shoes of a Caos—a monstrous being inhabiting the border between god and humanity. Customize your god-aspirant and join one of three factions determining your ability set: Dark, Void, or Light. Human followers will clamor onto your back and help defeat enemies with blazing arrows. Sacrifice yourself to the divine and create a homunculus to invade other player’s worlds and steal their altars. Upgrade your Caos through a huge library of gear, changing your play style and equipping yourself with the wardrobe of a god.
Ascend: Hand of Kul Key Features:
3 factions - choose between Light, Dark and Void, each with their own play style and skillset.
Equipment - customize your Caos with a huge arsenal of gear , unlocking new equipment as you play.
Player invasion - Sacrifice yourself to the gods and send a homunculus in your image to attack other player’s realms.
Recruit Followers - claim religious altars scattered through the world, recruiting human followers to aid you on your journey.
Active Combat - fight in real time, chaining attacks to rack up combos and earn more souls.

As I have expected (and feared as well), this is probably the most difficult game I have ever played. Yet the difficulty here is, as many have said before, really fair - it's not like enemies are just overpowered or AI is cheating anyhow. Gameplay is built in such a way that requires you to learn, but gives you great learning material at the same time. Every death is a lesson and repeating the same mistake is just player's fault - not the game's.
On the other hand, storytelling is really scarce here. It may be repelling at first - after about first 2 hours of playing I posted desperate "I cannot into Dark Souls" on my facebook wall, meaning not only that it made me sweat like no other game in a while, but also that I don't understand a thing about the story or my goals and purpose. And yes, it mus be said - story is rather "optional" here. I mean that while lore is very rich and worth discovery, the game itself does literally nothing to tell you anything about it - you must collect all info by yourself, either from NPCs (who aren't, by the way, very talkative), or items' descriptions. There are also multiple wikis all over the Internet and event YouTube channels summarizing the lore - and they are all a great source of knowledge on the matter.
To sum this up - I quickly got dragged deep into the game, spent a 100 hours in it (which, as for my possibilites, is quite an accomplishment) and probably 5-10 more just digging the information on the web. This is also one of only a few games I replayed, and one of even less games I replayed just after first completion.
If you look for a challenge, or a rich yet unwelcome world - you just found it.

Stranded deep at it's surface looks like "Another survival game"
And while by definition, it is. It shares a lot in common with it's brothers and sisters like The Forest, or The Long Dark.
But something it has done better than its counterparts is apparent right from the start menu; polish.
Graphics are not everything, but the minute you load up a game that claims to be in alpha you expect place-holder texutres, a partial intro sequences (or none at all) and no tutorial to help get you by. But Stranded Deep gives you the opposite. Finished (or at least refined) textures, a small opening with a simple tutorial that teaches you the controls within the context of the games reality.
Stranded Deep accomplishes a lot, with a little, and getting into the game at only v.02 shocked me in a positive way. In my 3+ hour game I couldn't look away, and couldn't stop trying to survive. A mark of a good game is one that instills you with drive.
I felt I HAD to find food, I HAD to keep my stuff organized, I HAD to seek out other islands for supplies.... I HAD to survive.
The controls are simple, the crafting mechanics are simpler, but it's all fairly intuitive. The games biggest shortcoming (and admittedly the one that made me shut the game of for the night) is the lack of supplies that should be the easiest to find; rocks. They're needed for tools and campfires, but despite all the boulders on islands you can only seek out loose coconut-sized rocks. The other things I'd hope to see improved are swimming controls, and more things to craft, and more things to motivate you.
But if you're looking for a game fiddle with, for $15 this is very good game to get in on the ground floor, because a game that starts out this strong surely has a promising future.

You're a lady in a spacesuit, on a space station with mad robots. Shooting things.
You're a woman in a spacesuit on a lone mission to find out what happened in deep space, on an abandoned junk station. Something about this game feels strangely  familiar. Ah well, at least she's called Valkyl and not Samus, right?
Anyway, after speeding straight into the game, I'm placed as a space suit warrior lady in a a seedy, futuristic station, where all the machinery has gone mental and is now trying to kill everything. The learning curve is harsh, you more or less need to learn yourself  the mechanics, deal with weird little robot things fast or die miserably. A lot. I like that you have to figure out everything by yourself. At the same time I dislike it. It's part of the charm of retro games. And that includes the sounds!
At least  with all this you can upgrade your stuff so it looks more awesome AND kills things a lot faster.
I think the design is pretty cool, futuristic shiny green and blue space, with rusting machinery as backdrop. The enemies, and there are a lot, from security system robots to weird little vacuum cleaner things that don't like you. I'm not usually a fan of futuristic style games, but this one has something about it I like.
The controls take some getting used to, and they're part of what make this platformer challenging. That, and the oops I didn't expect that to happen moments when you slide under a wall and get blasted by sentry turrets on the other side. I think the controls could be better crafted or more responsive.
What I find annoying is how far back a level/save point resets if you die, which can mean you have to refight tough monsters you already killed, and repeat a lot of content, which could make it stressful fast. Though there is a sense of achievement getting past those ANNOYING OBSTACLES.

My expectations for this game were pretty damn high. I've backed the game with a preorder the moment it was available and was looking forward to playing it. Tried it in early access and then waited patiently for the release.
TL;DR: Terraria is better, but if you have a powerful PC, and find Terraria a bit too ugly or too difficult, grab this one. It's still a good game you can sink a few hours into and enjoy it.
First, the good:
* Visual design. The game is gorgeous. Seriously, just look at it.
* Sandbox. If you only want to build, there's an insane variety. Not my cup of tea, but some people do seem to enjoy that an awful lot.
* Spaceship. You have an upgradable house that thravels with you. And it's a damn fine one!
* Missions. It's a sandbox with a story mode!
* Quests. If tired of exploring, you get a surprisingly high amount of side quests you are free to complete or ignore. (Not too much reason to complete them though.)
And then there's the bad:
* Performance. You have to get a beast of a PC to run this game. And even then you have to run it in a small window. Terraria uses XNA and stumbles quite a bit itself, but compared to Starbound, it's lightning fast.
* Exploration. It's quite sad that with all the size of the universe of the game, you go from one planet to another and don't really find anything that unique. I love Terraria for its metroidvania'esque stile of doing exploration. In Starbound I feel like I'm jumping from one level to another without ever needing to go back. Replacing quality with quantity, that is.
* Missions, missions... It's great to have some fun story centered content in a sandbox game like this! Sadly, it's a premade content, so no random generation there. It can be fully enjoyed only once. And it doesn't have a metroidvania element to it! Sure, you can go back to the mission you've already completed, but you have absolutely no reason to! Not to mention that you can't dig and destroy things within missions. Bosses are parts of missions, so no arena building.
If you finished the game try out 'Frackin universe' + 2 other mods that come with it , you will not regret it!

OK - I have to recommend this game £1 per hour of gameplay is good.  And if you like this sort of thing you will like this game very much.  Some people will get a lot more than 37 hours out of it too I am sure.
However.  I think it isn't as good as everyone makes it out to be.  This sems to be one of those titles where if you say anything negative, anything at all negative, about it you get shouted down, very aggressivly.  So I'm coming here and writing a semi-negative review after getting shouted down in their forum.
The main issue with the game seems to be that there is absolutly no way to move on in it in certain senarios.  An adventurer you buy from the pub doesn't seem to level at anything like the rate of the rest of your party, I got one at level 3, she's still level 3, but the rest of that party is now half way to level 6, 6K vs 12K xp.  I could trade her in and buy another one. . . .But why?  It's possibly I bought her just before I turned level 4, and she was just level 3. . .but she is only half way to 4 and the rest of us are nearly at 6 now?  That sucks TBH - I know the pub characters aren't supposed to be part of the RPG experience - but I was writing my own narrative for mine in my head.  But now she's too far behind to keep?!!!!  You can't grind anything to help them level up either.  So "Adventurers" bought from the pub seem to be pointless.
Second issue.  Abilities.  You can use them once or twice per rest.  Often times they miss though when you try to use them.  So they are useless.  You are fighting a significant opponent - and want to use something decisive, one of your cool-downs so-to-speak, because you want your team to survive this fight without taking too much damage, so you use your really expensive ability.  And reliably; it misses.  It will always miss.  Why?  Well - really powerfull opponents have good dodge.  Trash mobs don't.  You would want to use these abilities against the big powerfull opponents.  But there is no point, because you will miss.  They dodge about 90% of everything you throw at them.  Including your special 2 use abilities.  So the most expensive abilities in the game are only any good at insta-popping trash mobs, (that you can kill with a sword anyway).  So most abilities are a total waste of time.
So your party took a lot of damage and now you want to rest and get some of your less pointless abilities back, (there are heals and stuff like that and they don't miss - so you can actually rely on them).  Well now you have to travel back to town, unless you've got camping supplies.  But considering you need to use camping supplies after every battle to get your cool downs back again, which miss whenever you don't just waste them on trash mobs, and you only get 6 of these supplies at any time. . . . You fight. . . .  abilities all miss. . . .  so you take loads of damage just using a sword and sheild. . . .rest. . . .repeat 6 times . . .travel to town and then fid out they have completely run out of camping supplies!!!!!
So then you come face to face with a dragon.  And the dragon is supported by an army.  And there is one single enemy preist.  And that Preist can out heal all your damage.  It never seems to run out of its special abilities.  All your powerfull abilities miss the dragon - Of Course they do!!!!!  While the dragon AOE's your team to death in one go.  It paralyses and stuns them too - so not only do you miss 90% of the time, you are also non-operational 90% of the time too! Yay.  The dragon never misses, of course.  But it has high stats - so you can't even hit it with even a shotgun blunderbus type thing.  I kinda just laughed at this.  TBH - I knew what was going to happen before it did. . . . I think this is supposed to be "Hardcore" gaming, I think they are making a statement or something.  I think they are trying to out-do Dark Souls or some♥♥♥♥♥♥like that.
So in the game - I'd just got my base and I was clearing out the basement. . . And I'm 37 hours in.  And I'm playing on easy.  And I've hit a brick wall in the form of a Dragon - I can't grind to level up to take it on - and I'm sick of cool down's always missing.  It is so unsatisfying.
I am SICK TO DEATH OF every time I use an ability it just misses.  What's the ♥♥♥♥ing point?  Really it seems that you should use abilities on trash - so they will actually do something - and then just face tank the interesting mobs missing on most swings.
A beautiful story - I can't recommend the narrative strongly enough.  I don't know what the "Game" is here - at all.  I can handle complex RPG maths and builds and mechanics - look at my hours in Path Of Exile - I can handle difficult game play - look at my hours in Mount and Blade and Dark Souls. . . . I just don't know what they are trying to do with this. . Or if it's a statemen they are making?
So - If you get frustrated by RNG that basically says "No it's a miss" all the time - literally; all the time - don't go here.

Dragon's Dogma is now in my top favorite games of all time. It's not perfect, but it comes pretty damn close. Don't let the at times weathered graphics fool you, the spirit and legend of this game is timeless.
Where to begin? I loved the combat in this game. There is so much variety, and all of it is very easy to grasp. In fact, I set the game down for a while and came back to it, worried that I would have to re-learn everything. I had no difficulty picking up where I left off. You can stay one class through the game or if you are the adventurous type and a jack of all trades (and a master of all), you can easily change your "vocation" and hand in your sword in exchange for, say, a magick bow. But worry not, you only have to purchase each vocation once, then you can switch to and from at your convenience. You can customize a wide variety of attacks and perks. The variety keeps things very engaging and entertaining.
"Multiplayer" is unique in that you engage with "pawns". It's like.... passive multiplayer, in a sense? It's not actually other human players, but rather their primary companions are available to you to aid you on your quest. My main issues with the game lie herein. Sometimes the AI was downright obnoxious. Occasionally a pawn would fall off a ledge, and I would not be able to revive them. Or a pawn would be down and in need of revival, so I would run towards them but another pawn would pick them up right as I run past, completely wasting my time running over there. That may not sound like a big deal at first glance, but it really matters when you have a big giant angry fire-breathing dragon trying to smash your very existence. Having a pawn bring a downed pawn closer did help on occasion, but not nearly as much as it was a hindrance. And there was this one particular pawn, he kept repeating the same thing over and over ("I'll scale it and strike from above!"..... to which he never did. He did not scale it nor did he strike from above. LIES.) during a long boss battle. And for some reason some of my pawn's voices would get really low in some places, so I almost constantly heard this low-pitched pawn yelling lies as I painstakingly chipped away at my foe. While I'm at it, my pawn would ALWAYS shout "the tail is severed!" EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. someone cut off a saurian's tail.
Two big issues I had in this game. The first is that there are no horses in the large world. You have to run or use ferrystones (thankfully they've added the eternal ferrystone so now that is unlimited). Yet fast-traveling is limited to where you have placed a portcrystal. So if there's a place that you need to go to and you didn't put a portcrystal nearby, you have to go by foot. Which can get tiring after a while. My second big issue is the saving mechanism. You do not have multiple save files if you want to go back and change something. You have manual saving, auto saving, and what I call hard saving (like checkpoints at inns). But if you wanted to go back and do something differently way back whenever before you saved, you're out of luck.
I adored the enemies, ESPECIALLY the bosses. You are able to climb on them and in so doing you are really given a feel of how gigantic some of them really are. Scale the cyclops to stab his eye! Or throw your pawn up there to stab it for you! I love the design and the way they all looked. Every single boss just looked fierce. Especially the chimera. I believe all the bosses were fair, with one slight exception. The only time I ever got frustrated (normally I love big bosses) was when I fought an Eliminator. What would have been an otherwise kick♥♥♥♥♥fight was made very frustrating when he kept hitting me through walls. I'm not okay with that. It shatters my immersion.
Overall, fantastic game, absolutely loved it. It really deserves more praise and attention.

And as a result, it's still a weakling all things considered. For every good point, there's a flaw. In this case, one of the best points of Dragon's Dogma is the (offensive) combat. Man, even playing as a relatively "boring" class like Fighter was a lot of fun. I didn't expect them to have this many shield skills, but they do. I also tried out several other vocations and all builds seem to be a lot of fun with a lot of combat variety and skills. Also, having my main Pawn be a Mage, and hiring two additional Pawns as a Warrior and Ranger, made me feel that the game was well balanced.
I'm also pleased to see it running this well (even though it's a port from a 2013 console game). I ran it mostly 60fps on max settings at 1440p, it's not something I'd have expected from my 3-year old and now considered mid-end PC (R9 280X and i5 4670K). Especially being able to downsample it from 1440p made the world of Gransys look pretty good. Even beautiful at times, with all that lush and green, all those trees and forests. There aren't a lot of games where I took as many screenshots as I did with Dragon's Dogma. It also made the exploration a lot of fun, entering random caves and areas in the hopes of finding new gear.
Despite of the visual beauty, the world of Gransys itself feels dead. Aside from enemy encounters, there seems to happen very little in the world. Very little activity. Almost all NPCs you see walking around are Pawns you can enlist. Nothing more. It really makes the story of the menacing dragon feel unimportant, because his impact seems minimal on the locations you can explore. In fact, something relatively trivial like the Salvation fanatics seems to have much more of a presence in the world compared to Grigori the Dragon. There are only scripted events that trigger at certain plot points that we can see this. And don't get me started on the side quests and the unmemorable characters. I also disliked the usage of a "beloved" for the ending, in my case - I won't tread into spoilers - that was both hilarious and extremely jarring.
My other complaints are more of a technical nature. Even though the performance itself was great, it's a shame to see it's not PC optimised in other regards. For starters, there's only one (!!!) save slot. And to make matters worse, that single save slot is used for BOTH manual saves and automatic saves/checkpoints. Why they decided to do that, why they even had that in the console version, is beyond me. Also, the UI wasn't optimal. Especially in terms of inventory, I've spent a lot of time trying to micro-manage everything and it's hardly doable.
It all depends on your RPG preferences when it comes down to whether or not I recommend Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen. Do you strictly play RPGs for the combat? Then, yes, I do recommend it. The combat is fantastic and a lot of fun. But if you're like me, if you think RPGs are much more than just combat, if you're looking for a good story in a believable and fleshed out world with memorable characters, then no, I don't recommend this. Dragon's Dogma falls very short in that regard.
6/10

So I bought this game because I had a coupon and love point and click adventure games. Even with a coupon I don't think the price was worth it (EDIT: on sale for $10 from $15 USD). I got all the achievements (less 2) in 6 hours. Every dialogue advancement causes the character sprites to flicker. Most puzzles are skipable - which on the one had is nice so you don't get stuck, on the other makes the game a lot shorter. The incentive to complete the puzzles is to get the achievement and your money's worth - although most of them could be solved with random guesswork and button pushing. And others, when I eventually did figure out what you're supposed to do, there was no context clue that I could find to hint at that solution (I'm looking at you last puzzle of the game). Without seeing the achievement title I likely would have been stuck longer.
To make matters worse, I tried to start a new game to see if I could clean up missing achievements - I found on a second playthrough you get glitched halfway through the game and cannot advance. On a second playthrough, the items in your inventory that you need to find are greyed out in the hidden object scenes. This is annoying but not game breaking. What does break the game is when you are in the library and need to solve a simple guess puzzle of putting books on the shelf based on the author's nationality, the books vanish from your inventory when you click on them. This puzzle cannot be skipped. Exiting the unbeatable puzzle causes all other inventory items to disappear. I only fixed this by deleting all my save data and starting again - not a huge loss since I completed the game a second time within an hour.
All that said, I really did have some fun with this game, mostly because there was no guide and I had to figure everything out myself. But when I look at its faults and the total gameplay time, I'd strongly suggest only buying it when it's on sale, if at all.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Star Trail is the second of a series of three games taking place in the Realms of Arkania. There are quite a few features in this game that make this game a timeless classic, easily competing with today's RPGs in terms of entertainment. This game has incredible detail imbued with a good amount of humor and a large dosage of entertainment.
The short story is that you create, the hard or easy way, between 1-6 characters (or use the ones provided to you from the game) to travel the countryside in the background of a major invasion by the usual suspects, i.e. Orcish Horde. You are searching for the Star Trail, a special weapon for some thief god. I do not quite remember the details.
After the introduction, you are pretty much left to your own devices. I spent most of my time wandering around, killing monsters, getting cash, and drinking a lot of alcohol. Some of the dialog and descriptions are hilarious, such as when sleeping with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s (just a text box appears), haggling women selling amulets, or doing the same boring dance in the pub.
Aside from the witty dialog is an intriguing storyline revolving around such issues such as racism, war, and betrayal. The less dramatic details would be the attention paid to items/weapons/skills you acquire/steal during your adventures. The skills are particularly interesting, because they not only include useful things, but negative traits such as claustrophobia, etc. These traits can negatively affect your character. Nothing more frightful to a person with a high necrophobia trait than having to do battle with the undead.

One of the best, true old-school RPG, with incredible depth and detail. Based on the most popular, German PnP roleplaying game The Dark Eye (Das Scwarze Auge). Overall a very challenging game, but quite playable.
Character creation and party-building is very hardcore, the complex rules aren't explained at all, even the
are missing from the manual provided by the Steam version. The game however allows the player to skip the depth of this part and provides pre-generated characters as well as automated character creation and leveling.
The game features a medium-sized open-world with overland travel and camping. The world is dynamic, it reacts to the players' many choices and is very alive. It has about five, multi-level dungeons and five towns (one of these is quite big), each handcrafted with great attention to story detail and puzzles.
Dungeon-crawling is superb. Navigating is not too hard, due to an excellent automap, but knowing where to go and what to do is much more difficult, the player needs to pay attention to details and explore a lot.
Combat takes place in an isometric, grid-based environment and in a few cases it can get quite big-scale, with up to 20 participants. These can take a bit too long and are boring, so the game features manual, auto and quick-combat modes.
Some random stuff:
- Bring ropes, grappling hooks and shovels to dungeons, even if they weigh quite a bit, they will help in the long run. The same is true for sleeping bags and winter coats in the winter.
- Sometimes splitting up the team and going to different locations is necessary to proceed.

Star Trail follows in the tracks of the original game released two years earlier but is still different in several ways with the graphics and general gameplay being slightly more refined. It is possible to transfer the party of the original game over to Star Trail for an easier start along with their stats and most equipment. Different bugs depending on the game version can still make this annoying though as e.g. weapon skills can become messed up and the money gathered in RoA1 is generally greatly reduced.
The story is a continuation of the first game. One year has passed in Arkania since the heroes were able to thwart the orc attack on Thorwal. But not all is well as the vile creatures have instead turned their attention east and invaded and conquered the greater part of the Svellt City-League. As the heroes arrive they are given two tasks. For one they are supposed to find the Salamander Stone, an artifact created to commemorate the short-lived alliance of elves and dwarfs. The artifact might rekindle the old alliance and incite them to drive the orcs from the land. On the other the heroes ought to find the legendary throwing ax Star Trail – for mere monetary reasons.
With just the tiniest bits of information the hero party, consisting of up to six characters, is off to explore the lands. And at that point the game shows the first significant differences to the original. Walking through towns is now smooth and not a step-by-step process, greatly resembling the modern title ‘Legend of Grimrock’ minus the strafing. Buildings have various styles now, the map system was vastly improved and range weapons and spells can now be fired diagonally as well. Speech and small cut scenes were also included.
While in RoA1 even the smallest village could be thoroughly explored in RoA2 this is only true for the six major cities and the dungeons. Smaller hamlets are just handled through text boxes where the heroes are given choices to e.g. visit the local inn or temple.
Travelling through the world of Arkania is still done on a large map in form of a red line. Diseases are a constant threat in the game, caused by bites of wild animals or inappropriate camping equipment in harsh weather conditions. Food and water need to be found or the party will starve to death. In addition the shoes of a hero might be destroyed, making him lose precious health points with every step. While camping the heroes can attempt to gather herbs, food and water, perform healing talents and put up guards at night to avoid surprise attacks by the local wildlife or bandits. A handy in-game function lets you repeat these tasks as required and you do not have to set them manually every night as in RoA1.
Ever present are the death traps ranging from an ibex that likes to knock overly daring heroes off the mountain, a deadly fire spirit that needs well thought persuasion, to mobs that arrive with pitchforks and torches to end the heroes unless they carry the correct item to save them. For the most part the death traps are easier to avoid than in RoA1 though.
Combat is done on an isometric grid with each character having an amount of points per round based on how much weight they carry. The less your character carries the more actions (attack, use items, use spells etc.) he will be able to perform. New is the helpful but risky auto-combat mode where the game calculates the outcome of the battle. As the game does not bother with well thought out tactics it is good to always keep an eye on your health and when things go wrong quickly return to manual combat before it might be too late. The auto-combat speeds up battles greatly though.
Spells are still important in the game, both in combat and outside, but just like in the predecessor some spells are a waste, meaning they have no use in the game altogether while others can only be used meaningfully a single time in the entire trilogy. The same is true for certain talents. It is good advice to find a game guide telling which spells or talents should not be trained or precious points are wasted in never used talents like ‘riding’ or spells like 'AEOLITUS'.
All in all Star Trail is a vast improvement compared to RoA1 and probably the best of the series. It is still difficult, requires lots of micro management and one wrong move can mean death. The fact that the game gives you few hints as to what to do and where to go does not help. You need to explore a lot and talk to all the people you can meet, no matter how unimportant they seem, as they can still carry the important piece of information you need.

Stranded deep at it's surface looks like "Another survival game"
And while by definition, it is. It shares a lot in common with it's brothers and sisters like The Forest, or The Long Dark.
But something it has done better than its counterparts is apparent right from the start menu; polish.
Graphics are not everything, but the minute you load up a game that claims to be in alpha you expect place-holder texutres, a partial intro sequences (or none at all) and no tutorial to help get you by. But Stranded Deep gives you the opposite. Finished (or at least refined) textures, a small opening with a simple tutorial that teaches you the controls within the context of the games reality.
Stranded Deep accomplishes a lot, with a little, and getting into the game at only v.02 shocked me in a positive way. In my 3+ hour game I couldn't look away, and couldn't stop trying to survive. A mark of a good game is one that instills you with drive.
I felt I HAD to find food, I HAD to keep my stuff organized, I HAD to seek out other islands for supplies.... I HAD to survive.
The controls are simple, the crafting mechanics are simpler, but it's all fairly intuitive. The games biggest shortcoming (and admittedly the one that made me shut the game of for the night) is the lack of supplies that should be the easiest to find; rocks. They're needed for tools and campfires, but despite all the boulders on islands you can only seek out loose coconut-sized rocks. The other things I'd hope to see improved are swimming controls, and more things to craft, and more things to motivate you.
But if you're looking for a game fiddle with, for $15 this is very good game to get in on the ground floor, because a game that starts out this strong surely has a promising future.

Great game. Great universe. Above all, I applaud the dialogue wheel options. Questions I was asking myself were listed which made conversations feel natural, and and the game didn't use Charm or Intimidate skill to resolve most of its story. I'm usually set on what choices my character would make in an RPG, but I actually took a step back a few times to think of the consequences of my actions. Really makes me want to play the game a few more times to see how other choices will affect the game.

I kept dying and I thought I was playing the game wrong because I was new and it took almost two hours to finish it before I found out it was a separate optional quest.
Romances felt forced. It seemed as if BioWare tried to use romance as a selling point of the game or something. Although it's kinda acceptable with the way your character interacts with everyone but it was still too blunt. I talked to Ashley once about her history and suddenly she's fighting with Liara over who I love more. It only happened because Ashley herself told me to talk to Liara after her mother dies and Liara suddenly falls in love with me. It seemed unnecessary.
Other than those small grievances, the game was great and I'm looking forward to playing the 2nd and 3rd games. Amazed it took me this long to play it.

This was probably the first time I’ve experienced video game nostalgia…ever. Edutainment games were the only kind our parents let us play as kids, and well, a lot of those tend to be p&c adventure games. So it stands to reason that Hiveswap was a major throwback for me, from the familiar routine of clicking everything in the environment and using everything on everything in frustration (except that the interaction text went a long way in attenuating that frustration), to the manual saving (and forgetting to do it), to the awkward BGM-filled pauses as you pondered the solutions to the puzzles, etc etc.
Basically, Hiveswap recreates the feel of 90s/early 00s p&c adventure games incredibly well, and to its own benefit, because that drew me right into the world. The game is beautiful; the art is atmospheric and lush and just a treat to look at. The spaces truly feel lived-in and the attention to detail is magnificent. The music complements it perfectly, too–none too dramatic, and atmospheric without overtly dictating how you’re supposed to feel.
Also outstanding was the way that the story of Joey and Jude’s family was told just through interaction text. They managed to pull off a backstory for Grandpa Harley that not only flows seamlessly with the HS canon and does not feel like a forced afterthought, but is also affecting and kind of heartbreaking. It's a deftly-handled exploration at the lives of the children of an absentee parent. It’s all just superb storytelling (and rather reminiscent of HS).
Basically, Hiveswap absolutely does stand on its own merits; knowing Homestuck offers depth and insight into certain characters, but is ultimately not compulsory.
My main complaint is that the cutscenes initially didn’t work on my fairly low-end laptop, but that’s mostly a problem on my end. The interface got in the way at times, and I felt a little jilted by the Strife scenes which turned out to not be real combat–but I’m less bothered by it in hindsight.
I have yet to find every secret of the game--there's just so much to be discovered--so I'm definitely going to give this a second playthrough. It's a very relaxing and engrossing game, and reaching the end gave me the feeling of having finished a satisfying first book in a series.

Hiveswap is an easy introduction into point and click games. It doesn't take any explicit instruction to understand its gameplay, with a few pointed comments in the narration serving that function organically. This makes the story front and center to enjoy. The smooth simplicity is a perfect vehicle for the vibrant art and animation, the dense story-world, the distinctive music, and the engaging commentary of the protagonist.
As far as I can tell having read Homestuck, Hiveswap: Act 1 fulfills its promise to be accessible to newcomers. Fans of the nineties get thrown as many references as fans of the original webcomic, and characters and concepts are well established over the course of the game. All the dynamic style that made Homestuck popular is in full force, being presented in a condensed and digestible form.
The game took me 3.2 hours, playing casually. I tried to click every object I saw, but I didn't test through every object/inventory combination possible. You might be able to shave off the .2 if you ignore flavor text, or get another hour  messing around some more. Either way the price is worth it.

A kinetic visual novel by the folks at minori. It took me just over 13 hours total to finish, and was one of those well written VNs that leaves you never wanting it to end. The artwork and music are wonderful, but it's the story/writing that really sets this VN apart. I usually prefer non-kinetic VNs, but this one reads so beautifully, I was happy to forgo any decision making. The story itself revolves around a core of characters who are facing the impending end of the world.  I'll pass on giving a run down of the plot itself to avoid any potential spoilers. It delves into subjects such as redemption, love and loss, and the importance of cherishing what time one has left in life. If you're looking for a tear inducing read, this is for you. The VN is fully voice acted (in Japanese), and done really well, as is the translation through English subtitles. There are Steam trading cards for those who look for that, but no achievements. Absolutely recommended to any fan of VNs, beautiful writing, and/or emotional stories. If you're in any way on the fence about this one, make the leap. You won't be disappointed.

As a visual novel, Eden is competently done, with good voice acting and amazing graphics, good sound design and music. Nothing excels between "competently made" and "good", but overall, the technical quality is there, absolutely.

I wont spoil anything, because there is nothing to spoil: this novel is exactly what it says on the tin. Tragic story, precious girl with (insert power \ ability here) and main protagonist (insert tormented past here) falling in love at the end of the world. That's it.
The story progression has no detours. The very beginning is promising, but there is nothing else to look forward to afterwards. It's all the same, same conversations, telegraphed encounter(s), trope-ridden small talk with little to no originality. It's your copy-and-paste novel with no redeeming qualities.
It should have been no more than 2 hours long, at best, maybe even Planetarian-sized. Then it would have been worth a read, although stereotyped, it might have been a small piece of literature to pass the time when on a flight or when on a train ride. Too bad it's more than 10 hours long, depending on the average reading speed of course, but it is still pretty long, definitely too much for how little it has going for it.
So at its current price tag, I cannot recommend this novel. You con find way better, for way less.

A resurgance of traditional RPG gaming on the PC. Taking the core gameplay style of the original Baldur's Gate, combining it with the storytelling of Planescape Torment and creating a whole new world with new character classes, skills, magic, and abilities. Obsidian have managed to create a new classic and benchmark for RPG games in this decade. One of the great features of the game is the way that skills, character class, race, past choice in conversations etc. all give you different options in conversation with NPCs and especially in scripted moments. Being without a particular skill is never game breaking but they can give you an edge when exploring, dealing with a villain or looking for loot. The game itself is huge with lots to do, many side quests and enormous replayability with the way that the main story unfolds. It incorporates morality, the nature of religion, good vs. evil and the player character in a closely interwoven development that has you almost wanting to skip the side quests just to findout what happens next.
A must have for RPG fans.

Going to come back for a full review later, but here's my quick review:
Gameplay: Really good, especially if you like platformers or sandbox games, or anything like Terraria. A lot of mechanics are similar to Terraria but definitely different enough to be it's own game. It's much tougher, HP doesn't regen, the energy system means you have to be smart with your weapon and tech usage, fall damage can kill you very easily, for instance. Exploration is very fun and rewarding, although it can get a bit repetitive after a while. There are TONS of different planets occupied by lots of different mobs and several races that have their own unique settlements, as well as dungeons, biomes, loot, quests etc etc there isn't a shortage of things to do. Movement feels fluid and fun and combat is really surprisingly involved and strategic.
Sound and music: Awesome. I love the soundtrack in this game, and all the sound effects for mining, combat etc sound great and perfectly fit into the sci-fi sandbox world.
Story: Definitely needs some work, but it appears the devs are fully aware of this and are working hard to expand it, which is great because what is there definitely works. The main quest is fun and the bosses are tough but fulfilling once beaten, and the different races and characters are all very charming and lovable. The game has tons of personality, so I'm very excited to see the direction the devs take with it.
Graphics: Pretty much what you'd expect, maybe a little better than Terraria. Pretty pixel art with a lot of love put into it. The characters are well designed, the races are very imaginative and look great. The world(s) itself is really neat, I don't know to what extent the worlds are procedurally generated but they are very well put together look beautiful. It all feels very alive.
A couple miscellaneous points:
All in all, I love the game. I anticipate putting many more hours into it and I'm very excited for whatever the devs come up with next.

Amazing game; strongly recommended.
Originally I wasn't interested in Rome 2 or this one at all. This one is so good, though, that I'll probably reconsider Rome 2 as well.
A brief summary on why I like it:
-it's a fresh take on a world somewhat similar to Medieval 2 - of course a few hundred years earlier
-diplomacy feels far more realistic than in any previous TW game I've played - or any other game for that matter. Except maybe Shogun 2 which I love.
-enemies don't give up a lost battle until they're really finished
-everything has a gritty feel to it. Instead of destroying city after city (as in many earlier games) and dealing with rebellions later if necessary, I now need to pay attention to what goes on in my fledgling empire. I have to fight many sordid and miserable battles against outnumbered enemies who just won't give up. Not as fun as winning easily... or is it?
-I have played games like Empire and Medieval 2 where armies just fold but empires keep fighting back. In Attila, the armies seem to be the backbone of an empire, which is far more realistic in a military era.
-I cannot just expand like a maniac without consequences (well, I haven't played the Huns yet...) which makes for a satisfyingly realistic experience
-graphics are great
-everything seems to work
There were some complaints in the reviews I read like "no new voice work". Oh come on. The game will probably provide thousands of hours of fun. Compare that to almost anything else you can get for 40 bucks (sleazy things included) and complain then.
After playing a few more hours:
Exceptional game. I sacked Roma as Saxons, tried to find a smaller Western Roman settlement to capture and hold, and lost my army to a legion in North Africa. Meanwhile, back home up north, my alliances with the neighbours keep paying off: the Huns aren't yet close to my homestead. Planning a new expedition to Africa with plenty of resources at my disposal. Great fun!
After still more play:
I've only played Saxons (and Franks once) and managed to waste at least 3 days. Brilliant. I don't even care if I win or lose. This is an immersive game. Haven't tried Normal difficulty yet. Hard is pretty hard.
After one more day of play (lot of frustration too): I'm getting the hang of this. The more I play the more I like the game. I've played at least 4 crappy games as Saxons; now I finally seem to have a setup that works. I don't know if the game has been designed this way, but it seems as if it pushes me towards realistic goals by just not letting the AI players give up at all if they aren't completely lost. Agents are very important.
After some more play:
The hard setting is too frustrating. I've played as Franks and Saxons, maybe 20 lost games or more. I wanted to keep playing but then I wanted to start winning, so I switched to normal difficulty. Still not boring, but the enemies do give up very easily. I'll get back to the hard setting after I win a campaign.
As expected, I quit playing all other games when I took this one up. Still strongly recommended. Can't wait to buy the Charlemagne campaign.

Game is alright for making large 3v3 or 4v4 battles, but the player-base of Total War games are usually amongst the stupidest pools of players you can find anywhere. Using P2P connections, the odds are extremely slim that your game will not lag as you add players, but there is not exactly a large or elite pool to select from either.
Most of the battles are pre-determined by the army composition, and players can be either really bad, or really bad and wanting to have every advantage possible before the battle.
Players are low IQ whine and get mad at each other in chat over some slow-motion battle where one person wins and usually not based on any sort of skill factor.
A lot of the design and potential of the original award winning games from 2004 were thrown out of the window.
Only might be fun to play for a while with a select group of people with modding and such.
Other than that, Total War is the same recycled garbage with re-textured unit packs, over-priced DLCs, and the same old 3d units with different names/textures placed over them released every iteration.
It can be fun to simulate large-scale battles simply because there's nothing better around, but it's overall not truly fun and you can't ever play it competitively.
The prices are generally way more than the title is worth considering all of the internal game and player problems: so my advice is to just wait for a large sale. Avoid DLCS unless you can get them over 75% off.
The market for this game is basically 12 year olds, and they threw previous potential out the window.

A simple metroidvania kind of game. Has very much potential with its good artstyle and sound departement. But the one thing that destroys the game for me is the very narrow field of view. You will constantly run into stuff and this will slow the pace down to an unanjoyable experience.

Suggested Retail Value: $3 (or less)
First Play Value: 1/5 (frustrating, clunky, unresponsive controls make early play sessions tedious)
Replay Value: 2/5 (will likely get less frustrating as you learn to compensate for the clunky controls, and since the storyline isn't that great, a replay will likely be just to see if you can beat earlier runs)
The comparisons to Mega Man X are warranted, but only if you accept that it's an unfair comparison: MMX is a much better game.
A.R.E.S. is very linear.
Item/character upgrades are incredibly grindy and (for some silly reason) all require WAY too much of all 3 types of currency.
You character is very large in relation to your environment and enemies, which along with the controls makes the combat feel less about skill and agility and more about memorizing sections of levels and enemy movement patterns.
Environments have slight variations between the different levels, but each level soon becomes internally repetitive, quickly making you wish something would change. The same 3 or 4 types of enemies are reproduced over and over again in each level, with few new variations being added in later levels.
The boss fights were uninspired, and (like the levels) success will be linked to memorizing movements and getting lucky (you're just too big and environments too small, controls too clunky to dodge by skill instead of memory).
I can't recommend this when there are better platformers out there, with tighter controls, more creative levels and enemies, much more interesting weapons and character upgrades, and far superior storylines... and they often cost less.

I like this game, like it enough to buy the pc version after finishing the ps3 version.
It is not, though, a perfect game, but let's proceed with order.
I had 4 phases with the game: at first I was a bit overwhelmed: it thrusts you directly into battle, with a tutorial that, in hindsight, is really great, since it lets you experience what (eventually) the game will be.
Then, after creating the character and meddling a bit it may become a bit boring perhaps: do not expect infinite types of enemies, in the beginning there will be wolves and goblins, then some bandits and eventually harpies and cyclops (and theese ones will be the most frequent foes during the whole game), and after a while the open world feels a little void, without "important" encounters (such as beholders and really scary stuff). Sum this one and a lot of side quests that require you to get looots of materials, without exactly telling you were to get them and a travel system theat is hard to grasp and you will sigh at the distance between objectives.
Then you will have grasped the travel system and found it (imho) excellent: you will complete quest fairly easily and explore the dlc area (amazing imho), which includes a "random battle arena" to get stuff from rare monsters that will pop up randomly (my favourite place).
After this burst of excitement turning back to the last quests gets a little underwhelming (although the last "dungeon" is pretty interesting) and I'm not ashamed to say that I let the game gather dust for some month before finishing it.
It is not in fact a game to play all in one go: it is vast yet not variable enough to keep you entertained and from time to time you may rediscover it as an old friend popping up at parties: a grat company, but for short times.
Now to PRO and CONS
PROS:
-Vast and beautiful game world
-lots of sidequests
-excellent fighting mechanics
-Good class system
-Lots of different weapons and armors
CONS:
-Scarce quest tracking/samey quests
-Requires a lot of footwork
-Bland story, with few tense moments and memorable characters
-many repeating enemies
I suggest this game if you are searching for a good action RPG where you can be free to move and fight at your will, yet if you are looking for a memorable tale to par it with, you may as well look elsewhere.

Coming from mostly Elder Scrolls-syle RPGs this game was a total revelation for me. The combo-heavy combat system boasts tons of different moves and interactions that make every fight a bit different from the last, and in between fighting anything from rabbits to the truly epic dragons the vast landscape is actually incredibly enjoyable to explore. I rarely get hooked on looting and grinding, but Dragon's Dogma hits a sweetspot between being too shallow and too complicated. Every piece of equipment has different upgrade levels that in turn require different materials, so you end up spending a lot of time looking for specific monsters or gathering resources and both are surprisingly fun. Bigger enemies like cyclopes, chimeras, golems and so on are actually climbable and react differently depending on which part of their body you're attacking. This leads to a really unique kind of interaction between player and monster, where the monster might try to brush characters off their body or roll over on the ground in the hopes of crushing the foes that cling to their back. I really have nothing negative to say about the combat system, it's probably the most fun I've ever had just fighting random mobs in an RPG.
The class system is incredibly flexible and promotes mixing and experimenting with skills, and since you get to create a permanent companion very early on, you can do the whole equipment-and-skills-routine twice instead of once. Adding to your permanent "pawn" you can hire two supporting pawns that you aren't able to customize, but that are exact copies of other player's main pawns. Through the rift stones that are scattered throughout the world you can look for and enlist new pawns, and thanks to the ability to filter your search you will probably find a suitable pawn no matter how specific your requirements are. During quests and combat the pawns will very frequently talk about their surroundings, give tips on the quest, or initiate tandem attacks where they might hold an enemy in place or even help you jump onto a large enemy. Even though this game lacks a "true" multiplayer, the system of trading pawns between players is really interesting and well-executed in that it never gets in the way and actually adds a cool new element to the existing gameplay.
The only thing that falls a bit flat is the story that takes a long time to get anywhere and never really captures the grand scale that this game aims for, mostly due to rather bland characters and dialogue. There are also tons and tons of quests that you get from notice boards that mostly amount to either escorting an NPC to somewhere, killing a certain amount of monsters, or acquiring a certain item. The saving grace for these fetch-quests is that adventuring and fighting is actually fun in this game, otherwise they'd really just be mindless filler that adds next to nothing. Still, there are a few memorable quests and characters to be found and the main story, after a lengthy period of being incredibly boring, gets quite interesting towards the end. I also like that this game doesn't pull any punches when it comes to its grandiose scale and instead revels in the ridiculousness of the boss encounters that get more and more outrageous as the game progresses.
All in all an excellent action-RPG with a combat system that puts the vast majority of RPGs to shame. If you like flashy, squad-based combat, fighting huge beasts, adventuring in the wild, collecting materials and customizing characters, you'll most likely have a great time with Dragon's Dogma. In my eyes a diamond in the rough and an instant classic.

Dynasty Warriors 8: Xtreme Legends Complete Edition isn't exactly very complete. For instance, it's lacking plenty of DLC that has been in the PS3 / PS4 ports.
This is however, the best you can get out of the Dynasty Warriors franchise for the PC. Unless you'd like to play that Chinese version of Dynasty Warriors 7: Xtreme Legends which involves you travelling all the way to Taiwan to buy the game, install it and try and figure out the Chinese menu.
This game is your typical Chinese killing simulator series that everyone has come to know and love. (Not the Japanese killing simulator Samurai Warriors). you pick a character, choose a weapon, equip some skills and beat the heck out of every living creature that has red bar tagged to it. Controls feel great (after a bit of changing things here and there) and your character moves as gracefully as expected from an "AAA game".
As per most Dynasty Warriors, your character has a basic attack, a strong attack and a muso attack (in 3 forms) and an additional rage attack. Basic attacks and strong attacks can be combo-ed to provided a variety of entertaining attack moves. These vary from character to character and information can be obtained from the character screen at any time during a battle. Muso attacks come in three forms now, the basic muso, an aerial muso and an aimed muso--each muso's varies from officer to officer and hence, you'll have to experement to form the best combo. The rage muso is essentially your character's "ultimate" form where he/she goes all red and angry and starts dishing out ridiculous amount of damage--just think of it as telling a girl on her period that she looks fat.
Story wise, there isn't much story as expected in a Dynasty Warriors game. Story mode campaigns however gives you access to the usual Wei, Shu and WU campaigns. The Jin (or Shima) campaigns as well as other (Where you play as that lizard helmet-ed Lu Bu) are still there as other campaigns to try (as piror to Dynasty Warriors 7).
There's also the usual challenge mode as well as amibition mode where you farm up your own officers, materials and fame to create some giant heck of a temple / castle for your dear emperor to reside in. Farming is split into 3 groups, farming for officer allies (to accompany you/ do work for you), farming for materials (to build up your town) and farming for fame (to build up the limit of officers you can have). All of these involve one simple thing -- picking up your weapon and beating the hell out of every living creature you see on the battlefield.
Music in this game is great as always--catchy, uplifting and always gets your mood up in fights. Although some pieces can be a bit dragy at times. Old but amazing scores such as the Wei thunderous theme music from Dynasty Warriors 7 make a return in this game. You'd also feel a sense of satisfaction when you hear that satisfying "TWACK" sound when your character lands a blow on someone else.
The graphics in the game match up to the PS3 version of Dynasty Warriors 8. I must say I was rather disappointed that Tecmo Koei didn't try to port up to the PS4's verseion of the game given the PC's unlimited processing power. All in all, the game looks decent when cranked up to max but doesn't quite match up to the graphics of today's games such as Titanfall. For those of us who can't understand. It's like playing Titanfall on the 360 after you've touched it on the Xboxone--not exactly very pretty looking, yet still decent.
Unfortunately, as of 18/5/2014, the advertised multiplayer isn't exactly multiplayer. Clicking on multiplayer just brings you to a blank screen. Meaning you can't beat up Chinesemen with a friend from the other end of the world. Split-screen should work in theory, but I don't have a duo controller to try it out with. Who wants to play Dynasty Warriors on the keyboard anyway.
All in all Dynasty Warriors is what it should be. A casual beat-em-up simulator where your main focus would be to have fun. It's a recommended buy for most people out there since it's the ONLY newest gen Dynasty Warriors that is available for the PC (unless you'd like to play Dynasty Warriors 6 / 4 which are incredibly old and not on Steam).
Thanks to Riptide for the game.

I'm actually neutral on this one, since it feels like a beta. Only get it on sale, and make sure you download cheat mods if you do; you are going to need them. While fun and innovative, the game is also VERY buggy and frustrating.
Positives: The game allows you to face the bitter realities life in a zombie apocalypse, which as it turns out, happen to be mostly about doing repetitive, dangerous tasks while managing your ever-dwindling resources. It WILL scare the hell out of you.
Negatives:
It is a "persistent world"; if you don't play the game, time in the gameworld continues. This means your well-established and safe homebase could suddenly be out of critical supplies then next time you play the game, and it gets worse the longer you don't play. Given that its a single player only game, this is horrible. Worse, if you die, that's it. You die. No saves, no reloads... you just become another character.
RPG elements are linear and entirely scripted... there is no thinking outside the box here. Upon seeing soldiers about to execute innocent civilians, my first instinct would be to snipe the soldiers and rescue some new friends, but the game prevents you from killing ANY humans, even those that post a risk to your camps survival. Your only real choice is to ignore quests, which usually has a negative effect since this causes them to fail.
Finally, it's buggy as hell. I can deal with permadeath, if it's the result of my own bad choices, but inthis game, its usually from stupid bugs like my truck flipping end over end and exploding from hitting a wood picket fence, or jumping off a 200' tower because I can't get in just the right position to grab the ladder, or being STUCK on said ladder because there is no jump-of feature once I'm on it. Graphic glitches are frequent and numerous, and the entire game feels like a bad Xbox port (which it is).
Finally - good or bad - this is NOT an open world. Your actualy choices are very limited, and the game does in fact end if you follow the main storyline past a certain point. Its really a shooter with VERY minor RPG elements and a crippled strategy system. If you are a zombie fanboy who grew up on casual-gamer xbox-controller games, you'll love it; if you are a serious RPG or RTS fan, this will only annoy you.

STATE OF DECAY - REVIEW
First off, if you would rather watch a video on my review.
What is going on guys, my name is Marksman. I was privileged enough to get my hands on an early review copy of State of Decay for PC from the developers at Undead Labs. State of Decay, selling over 500 Thousands copies on XBLA and holding records for fastest selling game on XBLA hold up on the PC platform or will fall short to PC’s gamers around?
• Gameplay:
Gameplay is very solid for a $15 Arcade game, not so much if it was AAA title, but solid none the less. The game offers so much! From a large open sandbox world, to exploring old abandoned houses that have been destroyed from the apocalypse. State of Decay will keep making you want more! Though at the same time, the ability to clean out certain areas from all infected in the area, made me wishing for more.
• Story:
Brief Story: You begin the game as Marcus, a nobody camping with his buddy Ed. From the very beginning you are dropped right into the action. Your camp gets ambushed by a herd of crazy people, as Ed puts it. As your player progress he ends up meeting more survivors, bases, and ZOMBIES. Strength in numbers right?
• Combat:
Combat is super satisfying! Taking a 2x4 to a zombies brain never gets old! Possibly 2x4 aren’t your thing, why not try a Sword, Bat, or even a car door! State of decay also offer a wide range of firearms! from rifles to .44 pistols! Maybe you're not the run and gun zombie killer, maybe you want to sneak in and sneak out undetected! Have no fear State of Decay offers you just that! Though at times it can be a bit frustrating to be sneaking around, when for some reason the AI just snaps and chases after you, but we’ll get into that later. Overall the combat is epic and done right with some bumps here and there.
• HUD/UI/Inv: Oh my god. If there is one thing about this game that drives me nuts is the over ported console UI/Inventory system on a PC. You can tell that State of Decay was a console game at some point. The Inventory system was built for a controller, making you feel like you are using a controller when really you are using a mouse and keyboard. Though don’t get me wrong, it works great, I just wish they could have put a little more effort into making more for the PC audience.
• AI: Oh my the AI! Don’t even get me started the AI is so bad! I feel like my companions got me killed more times than the zombies did! I would just be sneaky into a house WHEN SUDDENLY Marcus decides that its his time to shine and bomb rushes the herd of zombies!
Overall the zombie AI is great, aside from the them having some derpy moments.
• Fun Factor:
This game is so much fun! I can’t stress enough how much fun it is. Its so casual that you will be able to hop in for a half hour and have fun! But if you have more time, you can dedicate time to building up your stronghold, clearing out massive zombie infected areas, or going on a drive to explore!
• Overall: This is a fantastic game for only $15 I would recommend this game to all of you! I will have to give this game a 8/10 due to the AI and porting issues that I came across.
Thank you so much for reading.
See you all next time,
-Marksman
