The only parts of this game I don't like are the first person sections, luckily it's only done in part of one level.  Oh that and the new Sam actor being a c*cky prick, it's a wonder anyone wants to help him.
And Spy vs Merc is a horrible mess, don't even bother.

Well, my first Splinter cell ever. Never play this series before and I have to say that it's a solid, well-made, overly American, and poor-plotted stealth game.
Terrorist strike US soil (?) on Guantanamo. The Engineer declared that if the country doesn't pull back her troop from foriegn soil - They will strike again in a form of "Blacklist" - American consumption, etc, etc. Sam fisher and his team were called into action and formed the Fourth Echelon to stop the Engineer before the next strike. The plot isn't really well made. Major plot isn't that interesting since all you are going to do is gathering intel on the Engineer and prevent their next strike. Mix it with a bit of personal touch between Sam and his daughter and light comedy here and there. It's just clear that the plot wasn't developer's main interest. It's just overtly American patriotism.
Blacklist allows player to play like a trigger-happy soldier (assault), silent killer (panther), or unseen shadow (ghost). I have been playing ghost on realistic for the entire game and I happily reported that stealth section is very well made. Most of the time the game encourage you to explore the map for additional route to avoid guards and other obstacles. Shadow and line of sight are bread and butter of this game but you can be detected if you're not careful or the guard got suspicious and start looking for you.
One of the major headache is door. Door in Blacklist has lots three functions - open/bash/peek under. Problem is open and peek use the same button and depend on position of your screen to determine which one will be performed. Also, heavy reliance on "A" for everything can be a bit too much. A situation like a door next to a ceiling pipe will trigger three action based on your position - jump to the pipe and hide, open the door, and peek under it. It requires a lot of practice and lots of reload to make sure you're doing the right thing.
Upgrade can be purchased on the Paladin in form of weapons and various outfit that increase statistics like stealth, armor, weapon handling. In a way, the game progression system ties to your performane on previous missions since the more stealthy you are, more money you earn. The Paladin itself is like Normandy SR-2 form Mass Effect 2. You can purchase upgrade for it and expand the capability of the plane - better radar on your HUD, more weapons for sell, faster restoration if you got injured. If it has romance option between Sam and Brigg, it would be awesome! (That was a joke.)
I have to say that the game deserve 7.5/10. I'm not impressed with the plot but the rest of the game is good.

Let me get this out of the way: Starbound is NOT Terraria. They may look similar, but they are very different.
I’m not going to compare Starbound to Terraria in this review (mainly because so many other people have already compared the two). I think that they are both excellent games, but I personally prefer Starbound.
Onto the review.
Starbound takes place across a randomly generated universe shared by all of your characters.
It is a good game on the graphical side. It has a nice art style (if you like pixel art) and a really nice lighting engine (for a 2D game).
The story is lacking and on the boring side. The main quest line is probably the worst part of the game. It consists of scanning quests, where you are introduced to the different races in the universe, and 7 boss battles. The side quests are quite basic. Although many other games are do have a lot of similar side quests.
There are 7 playable races in the game:
Apex - hyper intelligent gorillas
Floran - tribal plant people
Human - good ol’ hoomans
Hylotl – Japanese people turned into fish
Avian – Egyptians turned into birds
Glitch – robots that are stuck in the medieval ages
Novakid – people made out if literal stars
The enemies are quite interesting. There is a nice variety of creatures on each planet and you can capture almost all of them to send them into battle later (like Pokémon). The minibosses are challenging enough that if you aren’t prepared they will kick your butt. The story bosses are quite nice and also offer a good challenge for the player.
The crafting system is quite nice. First you make a crafting station for your crafting stations and then you can make the actual crafting stations which can be upgraded as you progress through the game.
The building system is pretty much the same as Terraria (I know that I said I wouldn’t compare the two, but do you really expect me to explain the entire building system?). There is a huge amount of different blocks so you can create exactly what you want (if you know how).
We all know that mods are awesome. That’s why it’s so great that Starbound is really easily modable. Mods can be downloaded from Nexus, from the Chucklefish forums or directly from the Steam workshop without any hastle.
The endgame is also good. You get to do whatever you want and if you want to explore a dungeon then you can buy some ancient keys form a totally not shady guy and go explore some randomly-generated dungeons and battle a randomly-generated boss at the end of each.
Overall I would rate this game 8/10. It can definitely use some improvement (especially in the main quest area) and definitely has some flaws, but it’s still absolutely lovely. I’d recommend you buy this if you want to, but aren’t sure yet.

It's a fun game that feels like a birt of a cross between Dark Souls and Monster Hunter. You'll spend your time wandering the land fighting monsters and collecting their parts to upgrade your equipment. The class selection is a solid balance of standard fantasy classes with a few hybrid options for your main character. You also have a companion that gradually learns from your encounters (inclinations and beast knowledge).
The lore and story is interesting, although the delivery is a bit weak and some plots are left under developed.
The DLC is very mediocre. It offers a lot of new battles, but a lot of these fights aren't enjoyable and the corpse mechanics really don't improve the game (they draw strong enemies to areas). The final boss is obnoxious and the outcome relies on you cheesing the fight or hoping your Pawns don't get themselves killed. For those particularly seeking punishment, you can fight the last boss of the DLC a second time, with a second form (making a tedious battle more tedious). As a whole, much of the DLC can be described as tedious. It's designed as a grind to extend the life of the game, and it does extend that time significantly.
Overall, it's a great game. I recommend it just for the monster hunting experience... But, be warned: The pawns are dumb and will often require babysitting (feeding them consumables constantly).

Ah, Mass Effect. The franchise that has entranced me the most out of everything I've ever played in my life.
I remember picking this series up around the time ME2 was already out and people were raving about "Lair of the Shadow Broker". Its final DLC "Arrival" had been announced and was days away from release. The first 2 games were both on sale and I can honestly say they were the best $40 I've ever spent.
Right off the bat, what captured me about Mass Effect is the soundtrack. Haunting and alien with a strong 80s Sci-fi vibe. combined with the incredibly immersive visuals of the battle-ravaged landscape of Eden Prime, the first planet we visit during the story.
The visuals themselves have a slightly rough edge to them, could be described as "slick retro", but in my view this is what increases ME1's charm and for some reason heightens immersion. Jack Wall & Sam Hulick are a magical team who have pulled out all the stops to truly bring the gameworld to life with the gift of their music.
The lore is rich, fascinating and immersive beyond compare. There is enough material to fully supply 100 Mass Effect sequels, because the universe is vast and knows no boundaries. No matter how far-fetching some ideas or concepts might appear, there is no such thing as "unbelievable" when it comes to something so unknowable and alien like Space. Noone knows what's out there.
The Mass Effect series is set 170 years into the future, where within the past 30 years humanity has discovered we are not alone in the universe after all. We are but one of numerous sapient species in the Milky Way, and they all have strong opinions too. Yet the galaxy is filled with secrets and one particularly horrifying secret is due to be irreversibly uncovered and put every race in peril. For there are monsters hidden in the dark corners of the Milky Way, and those monsters intend to wipe out all organic life as we know it.
Gameplay-wise, ME1 isn't as fluid as other modern shooters. It certainly has its clunky issues and is a little cumbersome at times. Most optional side-quests conclude in identical-looking indoor structures regardless of what planet they're on, making them awfully tedious. The handling of the planetary exploration vehicle, the MAKO, leaves something to be desired, having been described by an in-game character as boasting "handling like a tipsy rhino". I'd say that's being generous.
The weapon overheating feature, while designed to add a sense of shooter realism, is more irritating than immersive and will infuriate some people. The inventory system is a primitive, overly cluttered mess and will most certainly irritate some players to no end, but once you get the hang of it you can mostly ignore it.
But the punchline is: as clumsy as some game systems are, you can't help but overlook them because the back story will have hooked its claws into you too deep, that you will not be able to stop playing. On a grander scale, overall level design is absolutely breath-taking. Landing on a red moon and looking up to see its main planet covering most of the sky like an angry giant will indeed take your breath away.
You're suddenly no longer in your own house, but on an alien world light years away. Driving along the Prothean Skyway on Feros and stopping to soak in the visuals will transport you to 2183 AD. Seeing the Prothean spires stretching beyond atmospheric visibility will project images in your mind, not of a haunted, abandoned world but of a majestic technologically superior empire spanning across the galaxy in all its glory.
I ended up completing Mass Effect 1 within 3 days (I took my time) and when I was done, I imported my savegame into Mass Effect 2 and was blown to the stratosphere. Oh yes, hang onto your saves, because you will need them to continue your story in Mass Effect 2. Actions have consequences, and they will shape world details around you.
I can go on like this all night, but my point will remain the same. Mass Effect is worth every cent and every second you put in it. I was not a sci-fi fan before Mass Effect; I am now. Even if you're not a fan of elaborate fiction, you can't help but let your mind roam wild when your eyes feast on the stunning futuristic visuals of the Citadel - the cultural galactic center, or the haunting lost alien world of Ilos.
, the 4th installment of the Mass Effect series is less than a year away from release, and I don't doubt for a second it will not disappoint. If you're not a Mass Effect fan, now it's time to become one.

When I was a little kid, my mother told me not to look into the sun. So once when I was six I took the Captain Hook plastic spyglass that had served me so well, I took it and put my eye to it and pointed it at the sun. The overwhelming sensation, when it finally registers, is not entirely unpleasant. It is like being dragged slowly across a pane of glass. It is like licking almond scented sawgrass. Ecliptic after images, the light cuts spread eagles crossing slowly, vulturish, circling.
The searing photonic stress had knocked me out. I awoke with little memory of the preceding hours, but the pink paisley bark on the trees around me unnerved me to no end. The grass underfoot crinkled oddly and when I knelt down to snap off a blade I realized it was plastic astroturf stuff. It tasted like lime and it stung like a mother. Florid fauna dappled with spots of what couldn't have been real sunlight filtered through tea leaves and steeped for an hour of northern-bound motion, I couldn't find no one but came to a road and turned towards my right unto what would be the sun if it wasn't so pink and cost less to come see. Patches of skin crisped melanomic and fell peeled like husks as I walked. The road was paved with candy.
That is what it is like to read this visual novel.

Though the story suffers from an intensity and heavy-handedness I usually reserve for prime-time network dramas that insist on name-dropping enough stoic techno-jargon as if it was going out of style, to lend them credibility, this does not detract at all from the gameplay experience. A well-implemented cover system that neither overwhelms nor overpowers the player combined with PC-optimized elements combine to give a true sandbox feel when it comes to questioning how to approach a situation. A game that values highly 'out-of-the-box' style thinking is perhaps one of the best presentations of stealth gameplay I've seen. Though the game rewards true stealthlike gameplay, the game does allow a more stereotypical shooter-esque style of 'run'n'gun' which critics might point out is advised against by the game which awards less points for such play style. Given that the core of the game is as a CIA Operative and the fundamental element is stealth, I can forgive this and note that the system does encourage new approaches to situations. All in all a phenomenal title that made me go back and look at other entries in the Splinter Cell franchise.

Overall I really enjoyed this one. The animation is well drawn and detailed with quality sound. I like how unique the text is for nearly every possible use of an item against another object. The shift in perspective of characters in the story kept it interesting too. I didn't have any technical issues (Win10/Intel/Nvidia) along the way unlike other reviews that I've seen. It takes about 2-3 hours to finish this act which isn't bad for $8 assuming full price. I'll likely be playing the future acts if/when they release.
As for the negatives:
- This is only Act I. Honestly I'm a bit tired of games releasing in episodes/acts/etc since who knows if the rest will ever come out and how consistent the quality will remain. Plus sometimes they've nickel and dimed you by the final release.
- Animation is a bit clunky... the walking pace at times is a bit jittery with the character animations.
- Can't re-examine items in inventory... this is a strange absence for a point & click since you can only identify your items by memory/icon alone without trying to use it
- Inventory dropdown would persistently open at times even though I previously closed it
- The forced perspective of character in the room seemed a bit off, and sometimes it was confusing figuring out which way to move to walk around a room that's open to exploring.

So far, I'm impressed! It's only Act 1, but the little bits of story and character development we've gotten so far have sucked me in. I want to learn about and do more with the four main characters! The art and animation are really great, and the music is as fun as I had hoped! So much detail put into the world you get to explore and the things you get to interact with! There are so many references to the 90's and to Homestuck that a bunch of people are bound to love!
I personally didn't mind exploring and reading it all, though some people might find it tedious (anybody familiar with Homestuck already knows what to expect). Some people might also find the puzzles and battles too easy. I didn't mind too much, plus it's only the first Act, so who knows what else we'll be put up against. I also didn't have any of the issues I've been hearing about with the cutscenes or black boxes, so I can't really comment on those. Some people are satisfied with the length of the first Act, some are disappointed, it really depends on the person and how much time you spend exploring.
The quirky charm and humor that I was hoping for was also there in the way the characters interacted with each other and the world around them. (A particular scene with Jude is my favorite so far in this game).
Overall, thrilled it's finally out, felt like it was an awesome intro to a 4-part game (and then we get Hauntswitch after that!), and can't wait for the next Act. Just hoping we don't have to wait forever for it, but even so I plan on playing every Act!

Blacklist takes place after the events of Conviction, and features several characters as well. Game play still tends towards the new 'action' Splinter Cell, however, Blacklist is also much more akin to Chaos Theory than Double Agent or Conviction. The game feels like a step in the right direction - although it's not quite there - towards Splinter Cell's roots in stealth.

Pillars of Eternity is a shining example of my "Three Fundamentals of RPG success":
1. Story must be well-done.
2. Freedom is essential.
3. Must have PLENTY of side quests.
The first two (while blantantly obvious) are often skipped in most of today's AAA titles, in favor of more action-packed gameplay, voiceovers, and realistic graphics (thanks for letting me down Square-Enix).
I'm not going to claim that Pillars of Eternity is the end-all be-all of RPG history, because i'm far from qualified enough to make such claims. What I will say however, is that if you find yourself hungering to play Baldur's Gate, BG2, Icewind Dale, or any other Forgotten Realms titles, you will be far from dissapointed.

The whole idea of burning cities and villages in Total War: Attila is pretty cool!
Trying to perform even the simplest type of unit redeployment inside of a city or village, however, will, in two out of three cases, drive you, as the human player, freaking mad due to the complexity of the new and fairly detailed city and village battle maps that are cluttered with random little objects - junk, scrap and what not - which all interfere with your ability to position or move your units around like you would normally expect in a real-time battle of the Total War series. It is now, in comparison to Rome2, almost always simply impossible to navigate through or reposition your units inside of a city or village without getting instantly foam at your mouth when there always seems to be something - invisible - that is obstructing or hindering your units from changing position!
You can honestly never be sure that what looks like an obvious position for your units to deploy or path to move along is actually useable terrain, and it's seriously freaking painful to manage even if you're enthusiastic about TW: Attila..
And to add insult to injury, the game even starts to hang inside of city or village maps whenever you try to drag a square to redeploy one of your units thanks to all the fancy, new city and village
.. I think it's fair to say that this is evidence for Creative Assembly mindlessly adding new features to an old and never really convincing game engine without actually playtesting what they were doing.
TW: Attila is in a lot of places a solid step forward compared to Rome2, but in other ones, like the new city/ village maps, an obvious step back.. I never ever had such a bad time ordering my units around inside of cities or villages in Rome2. The only thing that remotely resembles my bad experience in Attila are Rome 2's ramparts where the game starts to severely drop frames whenever parts of a unit get stuck somewhere..
Buy if you're willing to fight Attila's city and village maps instead of the enemy!

so this is more of a retrospective review. this game has been out a while and this last time through was probably my 4th play through. its been a while since I've played it so i was excited to play through this game again to get my self ready for Andromeda. what i found interesting was how hard this game leans on the story. putting it out there right now; amazing story. you get to pick all the dialogue options your character says and that really gives you a sense of involvement. you feel like this is your commander Shepard. amazing narrative clever writing and the game really has sense of scope. moving on though if your reading this you probably already know that the story is great. what i found interesting is how much the game play felt lack luster. i don't mean to say it was bad or unplayable by any means. its fun enough. without the freshness of the story to back it up though it feels more like a shlogg. the side quest are tedious and when you have played the rest of the series it feels more like a barrier for entry rather then a treat. if you have never played the game you probably wont notice this much because the story piece are the reward for each shooting section. the drawn out citadel sequence in the beginning of the game feels awesome. when you already know whats going to happen though, it falls a little flat. i don't mean to judge this game against the games that have come after it but it is very apparent that two and three improve vastly over one. if you look at the series as one entity the first game has to exist because i builds the back story, worlds and characters. it sets the tone and makes two and three look awesome in comparison. it is the long first third of the book though. if you have never played the game don't let me discourage you from this game. its awesome subjectively. you may want to play the second game first and come back to this game once your hooked though. if you have already played this game and have a prefect play through saved i recommend playing 2 to get your mass effect urge satisfied. really over all i don't mean to sound ultra negative. really i loved this game the first and probably second time i played it. really though the game play objectively is really sloppy. the cover system works.... well enough. walling guns behind a class wall sucks. the ai of both your enemies and companions is not great. i do really like looting. that is really fun. the guns do feel the same though. again totally playable but not a 10. probably 10 for all things story related (voice acting, script writing, and narrative) probably a 7 for game play. passable but not worth writing home about.

I played this game years ago when it was rereleased on CD so this is really for new gamers who want to consider trying their hand at some classic RPG gaming. This is the core of what hardcore old school RPGs used to be and why they were glorious but also frustrating at times.
No single superhuman adventurer battling through hordes of enemies - no man could be that powerful. Instead, you have a band of adventurers with real needs like hunger, thirst, illnesses, and broken equipment. Magical items? They are extremely rare and not the absolute destructive force they are in current fantasy games. Skills? Ha! Every skill you can think of you can upgrade, even ones you'll never use.
And there in lies the beauty and the flaw. You, the grand guide, have to decide how you want to handle your adventurers. In current RPGs, such details have been reduced or even eliminated to improve the gaming experience. If the concept of handling the challenges of weather, terrain, illnesses, wear and tear of equipment, and your adventurers' needs immerses you into the game, then by all mean you should purchase this game and maybe even the whole trilogy. If such details sound tedious and aggravating, then pass by this game.
But I shall also provide a warning; it still contains the bugs that the originals contained. They are minor, but they can still be irritating. The biggest of which I always had to deal with is the step wise error when trying to complete a quest in the swamplands. You must turn it off to access the quest-required sunken chest. Lastely, when in doubt, do an internet search!

For a precision stealth game to be good, it must be consistant.  Enemies must behave realistically, but predictably on repeat runthroughs.  A tactic that works once on a section of a level must be repeatable.  This is where Blacklist fell apart for me.  I'd have a great strategy for getting through a level, and I'd be figuring the last part of it out when all of a sudden the patrol routes for the first 3/4 of the level change, and my tactics for getting to that final part are ineffective.  This would be a great feature if you wanted to play "remixes" of the levels and be forced to try new approaches, but it quickly becomes frustrating when you're close to finishing a level only to have it change on your next attempt.
Aside from that, the story seems generic and boring, the enemies are hypersensitive, and it's more tedious than exciting most of the time.  Wouldn't hurt to try it if you see it cheap, otherwise check out Mark of The Ninja or Dishonored for a rewarding stealth experience.

This game is the best Souls game I've ever played.  The PVE story is mesmerizing and the difficulty you are faced with will leave you with a sense of accomplishment when you defeat your worst boss.  Combat is quite intense and thrilling (as it should be), and is extremely challenging most of the time.  If you are like me, you will turtle behind your shield most of the time.  Fun fact: this game does not hold your hand at all.  It does tell you where to progress if you speak to the right people at the right time and in the right place, but thats for you to find out.
The co-op system is horribly broken.  You can count yourself lucky to have summoned two people in your entire playthrough normally.  This is easily fixable if you have a willing Steam friend to play with and a connectivity fix mod to help curb the issues.  Also, there is the issue of a bad emulation for keyboard and mouse users.  Be prepared to find your cursor in the middle of your screen as you play, without fading into the background as it should.  This, too, is fixable with a mod.  This game is riddled with bugs, and honestly, it actually adds to the charm somewhat.
In summary, this game is amazing.  The problems and cons above actually add to the experience, and should not be looked at negatively.  After all, the title does say "Prepare To Die".

My only real problem with Bastion is that the narratives treats the game’s levels as actual places within the game world. Imagine that. The entirety of the vast, diverse city, walled from the harsh outside lands are actually a collection of courtyards and corridors on clouds, floating pie-high in the sky. I don’t know how people there got things done if you had to wait for roads to descend heaven-sent and pave themselves. Cool effects, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ transport and civil infrastructure.
And with that ultra-nitpicky point on something entirely inconsequential to the gameplay of the game, I conclude my criticisms on Bastion. No, really. That’s it.

as cheap entertainment or worthwhile art, Bastion falls firmly in the latter category with zero compromises towards the former. The artistic design of the entire game is done to a polish that is at an entirely whole new level to other indies, especially upon its release. I myself had quite some difficulty believing that it was done by a totally independent studio at the time. Even so, it is such a wonderful thing to see so many new games entering the market now, especially indies, be unabashedly proud of their bold and unique artstyles. All this, in no small part due to the effect that Bastion’s
had in re-moulding the perception of typical ‘gamers’ towards indie titles.
The art of the game (its visuals, sound, music, speech) is a delightful, sumptuous sensory feast. Add to the fact that everything has been worked on to such a fine polish and you will be in constant awe. Oh, a thing about the narration. The voice narration, done brilliantly by Logan Cunningham, becomes sort of an oasis of calm and resilience amidst the frenetic and chaotic pace that the gameplay can sometimes get to. Pretty apt name for his in-game character/narrator, too. (He voices
, who is like the
who acts as the stable foundation, the stoic core of the story.)
are the combat mechanics of the game, which hinge upon the unique weapons that you choose. Before you embark on every mission, you get to choose only two weapons from the armoury, although encountering new weapons or armouries within the levels allows you to swap your existing loadout. Personal favourites are the bow, which when properly timed unleashes an arrow that satisfyingly penetrates swathes of enemies, or the mortar that requires a lengthy set up and fires in an indirect arc over enemies’ heads for massive splash damage. I honestly loved the combat system, but admittedly there are dozens other top-down hack n’ slash combat systems out there with tighter feeling controls.
impeccable artistic craft and deep storytelling on one end, solidly designed gameplay mechanics on the other, and doesn’t compromise on either?
Seriously, it gets really cheap in sales. I would have liked to end my thoughts with a comparison to Supergiant’s other strikingly beautiful offering,
but I have yet to play that.

Intriguing and as addictive as any other Total War games.
8.5/10
+ Stunning graphics depicting the early Dark Ages: Fire, Sword
. Building destruction features more smoke and particle effects, and for the first time arrow shots boast a clearer trajectory, as fire arrows could possibly light up the night sky, certainly to impress.
+ Epic battlefield simulation, especially when intense AI combat between a desperate Roman soldier and a blood-thirsty Gothic warrior feels so hardcore and real.
+ Featuring unforgettable-as-always soundtracks perfectly suited to every frame during the game, also with impressive exotic Nomadic (especially Hunnic, inspired by Mongolian Hoomii), Byzantine and Persian-style melodies.
+ Typical hardcore Total-War experience as there are no eternal allies, no constant economic booming nor continuous good luck, it's only War that never changes, and CA has added some new elements to the politics, where being in power depend no only on pure-influence anymore, and they introduced a brand-new nomadic system, with settlement-destruction now an available option. But to some, this broader focus on political intrigue or city ravaging rather than pure war makes Total War Attila less of a warm welcome than previous titles, Shogun 2 and Rome 2.
+ Perfect units overhaul, especially with the help of Steam Workshop for enhanced accuracy on history. When playing Shogun 2 I would always remember, in some 80 percent of gameplay, watching identical spearmen and bowmen fighting on both sides of the battlefield, and some clan-typical units are just too expensive even after you manage to clear the whole map.
+ Enjoyable experience playing as the Huns, as both the morale debuffs on the enemies or simply improved Parthian Archery would guarantee a unique decisive-victory experience, which is only realizable in Attila.
+ Good War logic. In Attila, morale would play an important role but just no so decisive as in previous games, where it would take forever for multiple groups of infantry units to cause great casualties to each other, while in Shogun 2, a group of samurais with their flanks exposed to ashigaru militias would quickly scatter and be slaughtered. And more importantly, Total War Attila has kind of made cavalry units great again, where generals are no longer ridiculously vulnerable to spearmen, making them again good victory-claimers by simply going round and biting the enemies' tails,
. It's probably because of the rise of "stirrup" as well as shock cavalry around that time, which appears no later than the famous Charles-Mattel's Victory of Poitiers.
- Elaborate in-game CG animations are now nowhere to be seen any more, with Shogun 2 being the last title to date to feature tons of incident animations.
- Frame rate optimization is poor, making Attila a qualified hardware-killer in 2015.
Some would regard Attila as a mere content expansion to Rome 2, but to me it is always worthy of the test of time.

I love this game. I really do. I think it's great and I recommend it completely. But there's one fatal flaw, that I simply cannot forgive.
You won't enjoy it the way you're supposed to, if you're good at the game.
Lemme explain: Basically, as you probably know already, the game has, as it's called, the "Nemesis System." Basically there are a bunch of randomly generated captains which hunt Talion (the player) and such. When these captains have been generated, they'll stay there until killed. You'll likely run into several captains time and again. And if you're lucky, you'll get a Nemesis. Basically a strong Uruk able to defeat and best Talion. Which is awesome. These Nemesises are iconic. Watch the YouTuber "Tear of Grace," if you want to see the Nemesis System at it's best. But the thing is, if you're good at the game, know how to exploit weaknesses and combat strengths, you won't get one of these enemies. Because you'll have either killed or assimilated them. Which is the fatal flaw that keeps this game from being amazing.

Rant time.
Everything wrong with Attila:
- Ai cheats.
*Ai has no fog of war and can therefore make decisions on which settlement or depleted army to attack based on nothing but full world vision.
*Ai unlimited money. How many times i finally succeed to defeat 3 enemy armies with the only 1 i can afford, only for the ai to completely replenish those 3 armies with mercenary units the next turn.
- Hordes
* Every faction is always abandoning or appears again as a horde. why have a kingdom with public order and income and food when you can just have a horde of armies that suffers no consequences and can raid and raze every city they come across.
- Razing
* Every faction appears to have a fetish for razing settlements. The romans lost a village, but now took it back from you? razed. Factions seem to raze for no reason, it gives the least money, makes the land unihabitable, and just creates empty space on the map. 50-100 turn into the campaign and half of europe is a desolate wasteland.
* Which brings me to my next point. No strong kingdoms. Everyone is so busy burning every city to the ground, even if it is a wealthy city with gems, iron, timber, or even their previous homeland, that no faction ever really expands. 200 turns into the game and the most cities any faction owns is maybe 4 or 5. So once you establish your own it's basically your empire vs multiple tiny little tribes.
- Towers
* Why these are always added to the total wars is beyond me. Sniper towers that you can't attack, but instead need multiple artillery to have a chance at taking them down, waste 2 units 'capturing the flag' (you'll probably lose a few hundred men in the process), or try and burn them down (also lose at least an entire unit in the process)
Makes me wonder why units are recruited in total war at all and why kings don't just spend their money placing these magical arrow towers every 50 feet from each other in order to defeat and any every army that ever comes close.
- Agents
* Ever since Shogun 2 Agents have become some sort of godly beings that all a king needs to do is recruit 1 man and that man can burn an entire kingdom down while also killing every general and their mothers.
Back in Rome 1 and Medieval 2 you could almost ignore agents and just play 'total war' but now you're forced to recruit agents so that both the enemy agents and yours can assassinate each other until the end of times. Wasting money and time. Don't feel like recruiting agents? say goodbye to all your generals, your king, all the buildings you've built in every city, and all your armies.
- Formations still suck
* Nothing new. Shield wall is the only thing you have and missiles fly right through the shields.
- Limited Building slots are lame
* why does my capital have to choose between a farm or a well? a warlords hold or a fur trader?
In the earlier total wars when my settlement needed something, all that was stopping me from building it was money. Now there's some magical force stopping me, which leads to having to destroy a entire building down just to replace it with another every time one of your settlements has a little bit too much squalor, low public order, or religious influence.
- Missile soldiers once again magically unable to turn around and shoot.
* Rome 1 and Medieval 2 had this, now it's gone. The entire unit has to move in order to shoot. Don't see why this decision was made since it worked perfectly in previous games.
- No Guard mode for missile units
* archers run through my infantry line when the enemy flees because they're too stupid to stop once they're out of range. This existed in previous games and don't see why it was taken out.
- DLCS
* I can understand selling a campaign as a DLC.. But blood and gore?
- No watchtowers
*Minor complain, but it bothers me than i can't see 1 tile outside my territory. An enemy horde shows up and razes my settlement and no way of knowing until they do unless you have a thousand spies everywhere (you can't since there's a very low limit)

It's like Dark Souls, except instead of getting destroyed by yourself you've got a couple of NPCs to tag along for the ride 8D
Honestly though, it's a bit slow at the beginning of the game (especially if you're playing on hard mode) with monsters doing huge chunks of damage and you running out of stamina every 10 meters of running but if you enjoy a challenge I'd say to stick around for more than just the first few hours (especially for the end game dungeons).
Story: 7/10 - Kinda bland, it feels similar to a storyline from an MMORPG
Art: 7/10 - Not that great but not that bad either, you can also look around for some mods that make the game look better if graphics quality is a big thing for you.
Combat: 10/10 - Just everything about the combat feels great.  The class specific attack and movesets are nice (especially sorcerer) and enemies feel like an actual challenge to fight rather than just swinging your weapon blindly.  The game doesn't hold your hand either, if you position yourself incorrectly you get punished, if you stay latched onto a monster for too long you get punished and if you hold block all the time with a shield you get punished.  This game isn't very forgiving, and that's what makes it so rewarding.
Characters: 6/10 - They're pretty bland and uninteresting with the exception of select few, whose backstories and development are kind of fasicinating throughout playthrough.  Although within the populated areas it really does feel like everyone there is a member of society rather than just an NPC that only has interacts when you speak to them.
Soundtrack: 9/10 - It's immersive, situation appropriate and overall enjoyable to listen too.
Level Design: 8/10 - The mainland is fun to explore at the beginning but it gets real dull after several hours, especially if you're like me and you have to have all the dark points on your map discovered.  Although fighting through enemies makes it enjoyable.  However, dungeons and other separate areas in the game are fantastic to explore.  It really feels like you're in the position of an adventurer, travelling to the depths of a dungeon for some sweet loot and watching every corner in preparation to fight new and exciting enemies you normally wouldn't find on the mainland.
Overall: 7.8/10

An interesting successor to Balders Gate but lacking in fun.  The gameplay, interface, and graphics are all well done.  The game is quite robust and relatively bug-free.  The ability to pause the real-time combat to issue individual commands was very helpful.  This game trys hard to tell an interesting story, but, I wasn't engaged by its story of soul manipulation, Gods then no Gods.  The NPCs and plaques built as rewards for supporters felt tacked on, reminding me awkwardly of the now ignored walkway hexagon tiles at DisneyWorld.  Clearly I'm out of practice on D&D style RPGs and even though I chose "easy" I found the game punishingly hard in multiple places.   Usually by leveling up a couple of levels and returning to these problem spots, I could then power through them.   Unfortunately this was not possible with the end game content (the "Arda" dragon and the final encounter with Thaos) as I had already maxxed out at 12th level.  So, I gave up on this game so I could try something else more engaging.  I have a hard time articulating why I found this game lacking in "fun" as  I greatly enjoyed Balders Gate and its many successors.    However, my initial excitement gradually wore off and playing the game became more like a chore than something I wanted to do.  Thats just my humble opinion, your milage may vary...

It is definitely a right step of open world zombie management game, micromanaging the room setting of your base, establishing outpost, and collecting resources according to your base need and consumption rate, they are all that I hope for as a post apocalyptic game.
However, the game is not without flaws, starting with technical problems such as see through the ground to "whiteness", zombies sunk into the porch of houses when I defend them, the strange ked setting for different moves (although I cannot think of any solution either but to let it become keyboard version assassin creed), not to mention many problem raised in the forum. Hope that the developer will continue support and optimize the game to bring a better experience.
Another thing is the lack of depth of the game mechanic, too few room choices and available spots for them (especially when you walk into empty rooms in the base when every slots were filled), having injured and tired status is good addition of the game but the lack of human resource management is kind of a downside for the game, like commanding who cook, who maintain weapons in the workshop, who be the doctor and who keep watch. This lower the incentive for player the keep or increase the number of the survivor in his/her base (the base requirement did help a bit but not much). The resources management is acceptable but can use much more work, cars that don't use gas, ammo box only count as trading parts and upgrade resources but not useable for individual character, building facilities were over simply (only gather "building materials" rather that collecting planks, wooden beams, tires, tents, 2x4, hammers, drills, saws and all type of furniture.
Also, the existing human resource management is not so great, you can switch to any characters within your camp if you make friend with them (by helping them), although it is useful in times how the odd is to leave your character in the middle of no where or the town flooded with zombie and switch to another person expecting he/she will auto come back safely? The game allow small group to form up and gather resources but for some reason only one person can carry the base resources even I got a 2-4 man team. More control of the group is also needed, such as choosing a leader for the survivors or overthrowing one, sending groups out to doing scavenger run or setting activities for people in base.
Well the game still has it's upside, the ability to switch to different characters are awesome and the possibility to let a survivor dying on your hand (with all the powers and traits lost) are the good points of this game. Also, the list of weapons melee and firearms are amazing (ammo type also). Although I mentioned a lot of points that the game can improved but State of Decay is a right step (probably the first right step) toward an open world zombie management game that not flooding you with ammo and supplies, or focusing on killing zombie or escaping them, but rather learning to survive with them, how to get through the post apocalyptic condition.
For those who like managing base and supplies, fighting zombie and building a survivor group and base, this is the game for you- get it now (if you make it to this line and still not quitted already, GET IT NOW, this is the game for you)
P.S the difficulty is too easy (at least for base defend), the lack of combination and "re-invention" (like electricity) and the story is so boring (no tension within survivor groups) should put this one off a bit to 7-7.5/10.

Certainly a game wprth buying, especially if you see it for a reduced price. "State of Decay" is one of the rare gems out there which seems to be made by intelligent, thinking gaming enthusiasts for gamers. It's not one of those highly polished productions you play but quickly forget afterwards, but one of the games which will keep you smiling because you just found another great detail you've been longing to see because it simply made sense to put it into such a game.
Sate of Decay doesn't bore you with dumb "game mechanics", applied because some marketing director wanted it so. No, it delivers you an open world designed with sticking to common sense. Furthermore, the designers weren't shy to incorporate features known from gaming classics like Jagged Alliance i.e.:
Every survivor you find will have some unique character traits, which will make her or him someone worth liking - or loathing. You'll quickly single out your favorite protagonists, screaming in dismay when you are ambushed by a juggernaut zombie while you are trying to run the heavy backpack home.
Another detail which reminded me of Jagged Alliance is the myriad of different weapons and ammunitions you'll find. From a trusty .375 revolver to a AKMS submachine gun - you'll enjoy outfitting your favorite guy with the best gun available.
The story focuses on the way people are trying to deal with the situation - including a powermongering, aims-justify-the-needs judge going slowly rogue. With people somewhere between despertion and hope the story makes the whole setting way more believable than you'd expect. It allows you to blend in, to feel the immersion a good game has to create to make it on my list of games...
worth playing!
The few cons I experienced are mainly of cosmetic value:
The controls are a bit difficult to get into and the lack of a real manual is leaving you to guesswork. Especially moving your home confused me: Yes, you need to do a few story missions before you are allowed to move it. Good to know, better if the game would have explained it further on.
At some point of the game you are spammed by a multitude of very, very similar missions: Rescue a survivor, kill a special zombie, clean out an infestation, etc. It can be annoying, but only because you are feverish about accomplishing the next "home improvement" and thus having no time to rescue the next jaywalking zombie apocalypse survivor.
A few minor bugs are still in the game: Zombie getting stuck in porches, zombies banging their head against thin air, instead of the wall behind them, survivors running against an obstacle instead of going around. Luckily all these are not frequent and  / or easily solvable by giving  a gentle push.

eden* is a kinetic visual novel that tells the story of Ryou Haruna, a human who joins the military, and Sion, a felix-a genetically engineered human with intelligence that surpasses those of ordinary human beings. (For those unfamiliar with kinetic novels, it is like a visual novel but the player isn't given any choices to determine the direction of the story so it is like reading a book or watching a movie.) As I don't wish to spoil too much of the story (since this is a KN and all), I'll only give a very brief synopsis. Basically, Earth is about to meet a fatal catastrophe but as this has been forewarned, felixes are created to find a way to save the human race by building ships that will eventually take them to a new world. As Sion is the most gifted of these felixes, she is the one who comes up with the idea of the ships' engines and Ryou is assigned to guard her.
Since I'll refrain from spoiling more of the story, I'll just get right to it and give my opinion. Despite that it's a KN, it's pretty lengthy so I didn't find it boring in the least. (Check my playtime to get an idea of how long it took me to finish it.) There are two arcs or acts in eden. I found the first one to be interesting of how Ryou came to work as a soldier in the research facility where Sion is. Once the second act came, I did find it slower but more emotional (although the first act was pretty emotional in some parts as well, especially towards the latter part).
The art was beautiful and I do love the anime style used. However, I'll give a bit of a criticism. Even though I know this is normal in anime art, I find it a bit unusual when the guys tend to look like their age while the females look younger than their age. Of course, with the nature of felixes, this can be explained away but even among the normal female humans, they do look younger than their age so yeah. I loved the music and there were a lot of pieces so I have no complaints there.
Overall, I enjoyed eden* and found it to be a very beautiful story. I did find the ending to be sad although it can also be looked at as full of hope. I did get a little tearful towards the end although I found myself crying more when I played To the Moon. Still, eden* narrates a lovely, romantic story and if you like a good story, then I recommend it. ^^

Length: Short (2- 10 hrs)
Avg read: 5 - 6.5 hrs
Type: Kinetic Novel
Description: In the near future, an ominous red star suddenly appears in the sky. Its presence is about to bring about the extinction of all life on Earth. The unified government proposes an evacuation project to take all of mankind into space, but in order to make the seemingly impossible project a reality, 'felixes' are brought into the world. Engineered to be highly intelligent with perpetual youth and longevity, the genetically modified superhuman felixes stand as humanity's only hope for survival.
Sion, the most gifted of the felixes, has been kept in a research facility built on a solitary island for the past hundred years. Her sole purpose, saving all of humanity. Ryou Haruna, a soldier from the Earth's unified government is sent to watch over Sion, who desperately seeks freedom from the military that's imprisoning her. Earth's last love story is about to begin.
Overall: I really don't think Haruna "earned" Sion's love but its a bitter sweet love story. Longer than I thought the story would be and felt dragged on for myself. Worth the money though.

Excellent execution of both Mode variety and combat systems.  Graphics are good, sounds are crisp and at a level that one would expect from a Warriors title.  I have played on both keyboard and gamepad and both work well, but the gamepad is recommended.

of note: Saves are local, not cloud-based as of this review.  Also, while local coop works just fine, I have not yet found where the Online coop functions are hidden.

Let's start with the basics. Some people compare this game to Megaman X games, others compare it to 2D Metroid games. And unfortunately, in my opinion, it is neither as grand as Megaman in weapons nor as Metroid in the coined "metroidvania" style. It may be, however, the exact opposite: linear levels with arguably-not-really secrets with some extra collectibles and the depth of Metroid's weapons (as in, a few and extremely situational).
And if you want a bottom-line here on top, here it is: the game isn't good enough to stand on its legs, plus there's already an "enhanced version" that is the exact same game but slightly "better" in some ways that aren't relevant for this review. If you really want this game, I suggest you buy "A.R.E.S.: Extinction Agenda EX" instead, the exact same game with two more letters.
And if reading the above didn't demotivate you enough, let me guide you in how much I consider this game to have failed over the next few paragraphs...
The game features 5 stages, which are fairly large, and a boss at the end of each stage. You don't pick stage order, but you can revisit stages you've cleared at a later date, and you're sent on a predetermined path on each stage until you reach its end; there's secret rooms, if you can even call them secret, and some collectibles scattered in some places, plus very little and insignificant alternate paths (as in, choose left or right in a section but the challege is exactly the same until the point where the paths meet)... but exploration is null otherwise. The bosses are fortunately challenging if you're going for the "no damage" achievements, which heavily rely on a mechanic that grants the player "invulnerability" as he dashes, but to use said dash correctly is awkward and in many situations feels forced or too much timing sensitive (as in, do it just a quarter second too soon and maybe a little too far away and you're definitely going to get hit anyway). It reminds me too much of some relatively recent Mega Man titles, but without the cool weapons.
And since I brought guns onto the table, why not tell you about them... You get a few different guns, because let's face it: if Mega Man only had the Mega Buster with no upgrades, would you play Mega Man? In ARES it's actually worse, because while each weapon has its own pros and cons, which innevitably translate into the ability to combo hits for a higher score at the end of a stage or being slightly better against a very specific kind of enemy, each weapon doesn't actually feel like a power up: it feels like your main attack suffered deviations and transformed into something... arguably useful or useless depending on the situation. ARES also has litteral bombs, which over the course of the game will eventually become limitless, and bring into quesiton whether you really need the guns if you don't need to move while firing.
Speaking of firing, how much do you like aiming directly where you want to shoot? "Oh my gosh, I can shoot 360 degrees!", you may say. Yes, true. But personally, I feel like it's the main reason why I don't really care so much about this game. Why? Because not anyone can be a God at aiming with the mouse, especially if while you move the character the angle at which you're firing is altered as you keep the mouse in place in rooms where the camera is fixed to a point. Is it ideal to target specific parts of some bosses? No doubt. But I guess not anyone can be a God at platforming and shooting horizontally with great timing too, which is the Megaman basic formula, so let's not factor this into how good the game is.
One other thing that bothered me greatly was how obvious ARES was about having been a XBox Live title, and how many of more recent games HAVE to integrate social media into themselves. Yes, I'm looking at you, Facebook, and what revenue extras both you and the developers may get as consequence. Sometimes it does feel that, while obviously the game has the bare minimum qualities to make it shine under a light, the game was made purposefully short for the intent of a quick cash grab. Price of 9,99 for what was barely 2 and a half hours to clear the game with all of the "secrets"? I'm not even going to bother with the achievements, some of which being too annoying to fail at the very last second (my fault, but still too annoying).
Also if you're considering ARES, remember to look at the trailer and screenshots. You're getting pixel-y models with real models on a fully (low poly) modelled and textured environment. The art style occasionally feels slightly offputting as a consequence, in my personal opinion, but in most locations this may be a blessing of a callback (it reminds me of Megaman Legends a little). If you think you can stomach it without taking some pill, then move on to the demo before making a final decision: that's the smart way to go.
If you notice, the current Metascore of the game is 68 of 100. Not saying that it's not accurate, but it really depends on how it will impress you in general whether you will love it or hate it. I'm pretty sure that right now you're better off skipping this game and buying the "enhanced version" since you DON'T want to pay for that game after playing this one. Also on the subject of money: the Berzerker suit DLC may be worth it, if you like high-risk with high-reward playstyle, but it mostly shows how useful it is on bosses and some of the more cramped-with-mobs rooms.
If by this point you're considering buying this game but you're not sure whether to get the complete edition over the regular game, consider if you're likely to like the soundtrack of the game by browsing Youtube for a bit, or judge biasedly from the trailer (which features the boss music, if memory recalls at this point in time). If it's the same music as the remake I say "skip it", but then again, I'll also say the same about the berzerker suit: likely, you'll be buying this game for the exclusive reward on the remake, which sounds to me like a publicity stunt to make some extra bucks out of suckers.
Final remarks? I'd avoid this game, as you can probably tell. Every day I have more and more trouble giving games that have once been XBox Live or tablet/phone/you-name-it titles because of the disapointed feeling games like ARES give me. But if you like the idea of a Mega Man nostalgia feeling with mouse aim without resorting to things like the AVGN game or some likewise poorer quality titles, ARES delivers a solid yet short experience that will make some sort of impact on you.

I've been playing the Total War series a lot. I used to be it's biggest fan and I spent several thousands of hours playing rome and medieval II. Many didn't like Empire, but I enjoyed it very much. Some things are improved and many things are the same crap as before. Luckily I bought this at 75% off so no harm done.
Here are the game concepts I hate about this game:
The difficulty from this game comes from cheating AI, not good AI. Examples:
The AI can have 3-4 full armies supported by a single city while the player can barely afford a single full army with 2 complete regions.
The AI knows exactly where the player are on the battlefield even if you are hiding. I thought I could win a battle by hiding until the time went out but after standing still about 10 minutes like idiots they automatically discovered my hidden unit even though they were hiding deep in a forest behind a big hill.
Once my city was attacked from the sea by a small navy, but they were reinforced by 2 full armies. I was surprised cause I should have seen them coming. But after they won I saw that the armies was in fact far away out in the sea, way beyond the reinforcing range. This has happened several times.
The Diplomacy system is absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Nobody wants to accept any deal unless you pay huge sums of money. Why won't they accept trade agreements that are mutually beneficial even though the relations between you are neutral or good? Why the f*ck do you get a large diplomacy penalty with all factions just because you have a large empire? If you expand your empire (which is pretty much the goal of the game) you can forget having any kind of diplomatic relations to anyone. friends will turn on you and everyone will hate you for having a large empire -♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! Should be the opposite, the more powerful you are the more influence over diplomacy you should have.
The political system is also kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. There is domination (influence) and control (political actions) which combines into your overall power over your faction, that's fine. You can spend influence points to perform actions like seek support or adopt someone. So far so good, it makes sense that if you perform an action you "use up" your favour and influence. But the system is broken cause every action you do has too small chance of succeding! I think it's 50-50 based on how many times it fails. So if you want to seek support and gain control there is a 50% chance you lose 20 influence (sometimes more if there are complications) and gain 6% control, and 50% chance you lose both 20 influence and 4% control. So you pretty much always lose. The best way to maintain power is to appoint your opponents to offices because they lose influence when they apply. Does that make any sense at all? But what's even more incredible is the effects of having power, some are good some bad. The more power you have the worse penalties your faction gets to a point where the negative effects outweighs the good effects. The opposite is also true if you lose power. So the player get punished for both succeding and failing in the political system. Why even care then??? Also expect half of your children, especially the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to die of unknown reasons before becoming adults.
The generals and governors and auto-replenish system. Don't you just love it when the army you just defeated automatically gets a new general with a new bodyguard unit and the rest of the army magically replenish in a few turns even though they are far from a city or out at sea. It's better not to kill their general so they have a weak unit for a turn or two. The same goes for your own of course, but it doesn't feel right. It feel like cheating or a game for children. If a unit is reduced it should have to get real trained reinforcements that move on the map. That was a great thing about previous games. A good player planned for reinforcements in advance and sent them behind the main army and refilled the ranks and the damaged units were extracted in cover of the main army, got onboard the ships and sent home for retraining. I miss that! It's impossible now since units can't move without a general and you can't recruit a bunch of generals since you lose power in the political system. The generals themselves has the most boring and generic trait and level system than ever before. I loved the system in previous games where the traits and retinues depended on the actual events and battles the guy experienced at the hands of the player. Now it's just level up after each battle, choose two magic skills in the skill tree and repeat for every general.

Elder Scrolls + Dark Souls + Dragon Age + Diablo + Shadow of Colossus
Open-World is today what 3D graphics was in 1996. The gaming world is plagued by countless of these games; no matter how short or how long, how bad or how good there is one thing they all are likely to have to be a viable competetion: feature an Open World. They usually come in two flavors: GTA like sandboxy openworld or TES like rough terrain Open World. There are games somewhere in between. The point is, it's starting to show fatigue. Not all Open World games are good by default. To create a good Open World game, you must learn how to make all that damn space interesting. Which is what brings me to Dragon's Dogma.
Dragon's Dogma is what you get if you mix The Elder Scrolls, Dark Souls and Dragon Age. Take away all the crappy features and keep some of the best from all of them.
Let's see the PROS -
- Fun and enjoyable Combat system. Seriously, other Open World games NEEDS to use this game's combat style.
- Huge World to explore.
- Party System driven by a pretty solid AI that learns as you play.
- Random Loot System, somewhat like Diablo.
- Day and Night progression, with night time actually making exploration risky and dangerous.
- Challenging and Hard enemy encounters that feels "Just Right". Get beaten. Level up. Come back. Dominate.
- Epic Boss Fights. Shadow of the Colossus like boss fights where you get to "climb" the boss's body and hack away at their weak points.
- Good Character Customization. For you AND your companion.
- Innovative pawn system where, aside from your personal pawn, you get to hire pawns made by other players.
- Said pawns will start out blank but "learn" as they go. Enemy weaknesses, Quest Objectives and Coordination.
- Good music.
So far, I am far more engaged in the game than I thought I'd be. Every day I login and see if some other player hired my Pawn and how did they rate her. (Yes you can rate other player's pawns and even send away gifts and messages). Also the never-ending stream of player generated Pawns always gives me something to look forward to.
This game however, comes with some flaws as well. None of them will drive you away but becomes annoying at best.
The CONS -
- Lots and LOTS of walking. Unless you plant a portcrystal, you cannot fast-travel to that spot. Prepare to walk miles, back and forth.
- Rush tactics don't work if your party is relatively weak. You should try drawing out enemy units away from their camp if you keep dying a lot.
- Being already engaged in a tough battle with enemies, you will curse out loud when that random Chimera appears.
- Being smart as they are, your AI friends suck at using their inventory effectively, often picking up items you don't need. Then again, in an RPG with shops, there is nothing you don't need.
- AI pawns that act as guardians will endanger their lives standing at the spot trying to heal everybody even if it would make sense to run now and heal later.
- Talkative AI often says same things too often. It's not fun when it's being said for the fifty'th time in old english. Thankfully, you can set how often your main pawn talks. Also their chats are more helpful than hindering as experienced pawns shout useful tips against foes and quests.
- Quest markers are often not clear about where the target is. You often need to seek the help of your pawns and look around yourself.
If you want a decent open world game with decent combat and don't want to feel alone wandering that huge world, give this game a shot. Between a rather average plot and slightly dated graphics this game is an underrated gem.

The best Mass Effect of the trilogy if you can overlook some of the jankiness. The overall story, sense of exploration and RPG elements set it apart from the sequels that were too simplistic and character focused.

The pioneering entry for a ground breaking series that has, quite easily, become a top contender for the best Western RPG series of all time.
The story from start to finish is dark, engrossing, rich and accompanied with well thought out lore to boot as you guide Commander Shepard through the story. Brandishing the Bioware trademark moral compass throughout, the story is made even more absorbing as you watch and see the gravity of the decisions you make effect significant parts of the storyline. Combining this aspect of gameplay with issues such as racism/xenophobia, refugees, the apocalypse, international (interplanetary?) politics, personal relationships, and treason to name a few; made the experience feel as though I had moulded Commander Shepard into what I wanted him to be. Depending on which side of the fence you sit on (Paragon - Good, Renegade - Evil) it would open up drastic conversation changers for you which can range from murdering someone with barely any words being spoken to reuniting a griefing husband with his late wife for burial. A good example - Slight SPOILER here - is when a news reporter approaches you asking for an interview and begins asking you about your galavanting crusades around the galaxies, your options quickly become punch her in the face straight away or give a professional interview answering her questions.
Gameplay in the whole is very good with some unique mechanics, but the majority being cover based shooting. When not in combat, the open world was free to explore allowing you to go sidequest hunting and the like or arm your team up to the eyesballs with vast abundance of weapons, armours and mods for each. These open worlds were somewhat restrictive in the fact that most the planets, cities, areas etc are linear pathways which lead straight to your objective and back again. The vehicle segments I found to be a slight nightmare aswell due to A) the vehicle controls and B) the terrain you have to drive it in.
Overall, definitely worth playing through from start to finish. If you are considering dipping your toes into the Mass Effect Trilogy, then I can't suggest enough starting at the very beginning as it will help you understand the lore and stories thoroughly and also you can import your character save after you complete the game to ME2, ME3 with the same moral choices etc thus extending your investment in the story.

I personally on all of my survival games love to go get more and more and more loot. I can never have enough. I hope that they make it to where you are not limited to 1 storage crate of each size because I really feel like with that little amount of storage there is little point to actually building a base.

Well, there is alot I could say about this game. It was a great, action packed stealth action game, with an -alright- story, but the real fun comes from something they had discarded from the series titles that preceded Blacklist. Actually letting people choose how to get to the objective, and how they wanted to go through a level- leading to a great campaign mode that as I said, the story was meh, but it felt VERY fun to just drop in and play. However, this does have a drawback- later in the campaign, half the mission you switch to an FPS mode, stealth shooter hybrid... something that just felt wrong the entire time I was playing it. However, they did test the waters a bit with it, and for that they get points. They do lose those points instantly for MAKING AN FPS SECTION IN A ♥♥♥♥ING STEALTH GAME. ♥♥♥♥in' ell.
Oh, also, this game should be bought anyway for one reason- SPIES VS MERCS MAKES ITS RETURN! Back in Chaos Theory, the new game mode was added and loved by many fans, but taken out of later games in the series. It returns, and makes a huge splash in my mind as a must have multiplayer game, just for the strategy and action that needs to be taken in each fight and map. The Spies use intellect and cunning to get data and other objectives completed, using the shadows and a small list of gadgets to help them stop the other team- The mercs. Mercs use firepower and teamwork to get the best of those pesky spies, and defend the objectives set out before them.
Inside the campaign mode there is co-op selectable and solo missions. Solo missions are campaign only missions, while the co-op takes the form of the lowly side mission, which has the same amount of set up and planning that the campaign missions have, just with a feeling of less impact upon the world in the game, besides a bar that slowly fills up. Campaign missions give you tons of cash to upgrade and acquire much needed gadgets and weapons that will effect not only the firefights, but your complete strategy as well. Money can also be used to buy upgrades to the "Paladin", your base of operations that takes the shape of a giant plane, fitted with the best technology the goverment can give.
To wrap it all up, Splinter Cell: Blacklist is a great new addition to the series that needed a breath of new life, and with the integrated campaign mode that carries over into all other modes, along with Spies vs Mercs and lots of options for side missions to Co-op or handle alone. I can honestly give this game a very good recommendation with its content for solo play- and lots of stuff to do with other people. If you are thinking of picking this game up for full price- be wary. Some may not see this as a good 60$ game- the price tag it has without discount. Even though the game is great, I recommend waiting for at least a 50% off or so before nabbing this bad boy.

PoE is one of the best RPGs I have ever played (and I've been playing them for decades).  It is the first game that actually succeeds at recreating the strategic fun of the Infinity Engine games (Baldur's Game, Icewind Dale, etc.) while updating the style and gameplay for the modern day.
This is an insanely deep game, which is obvious from the get-go tons of player choice everywhere.  Not only that, but Obsidian created a totally unique character development system for players to experiment with that affects both combat and story.  This isn't your typical Str, Dex, Con-based game, but more of a hybrid including elements you might see in a Fallout-style game (stats and chosen origin will give you dialogue options).

A.R.E.S. is a Megaman clone that has been around long before there were any real alternatives on Steam. The whole package looks pretty good and seems worth a buy, but after playing through it I was rather disappointed.
Yes, despite my low hours, I did beat this game. Its that short.
The game itself plays like you'd expect a Megaman game to, except that you control your projectile location with the analog stick. This change actually really hurts the game. It becomes less about strategy and positioning and more about mindlessly clicking on enemies.
Like with any Megaman game, you go through stages and kill bosses. You unlock new weapons, some armors, the usual.
Its not terrible, but it just doesn't feel satisfying.
The stage design is boring, the characters are uninspired, and the overall presentation just falls flat.
Instead of fulfilling my want for a Megaman fix, I just found myself wanting to play an actual Megaman game.
The whole game feels off and left me wanting to play an actual Megaman game.
If this game had a story, I have no idea what it was.
The visuals are fine. The music is mediocre and even good at times.

While the forums seem to be abuzz with how broken the game is, I've been having no real issues with it so far. If you're a fan of hack-n-slash games, or Warriors games in general, you're going to have a good time with it. Let's hope Koei decides to address some of these issues, and make more of these games available on PC.
Pros:
+Lots of replay value, branching paths in story mode, Ambition mode, free mode, lots of weapons to collect.
+Plenty of characters to pick from, there's bound to be someone you love (Ding Feng, Wang Yuanji), hate (Guan Yu, Sima Yi), or love to hate (Dong Zhuo, Sima Zhao).
+Runs really well (60 fps constantly, no slowdown even with a ridiculous amount of troops), at least on my machine.
+Really fun if you like these types of games, cheesy atmosphere and line delivery to match, great music, etc.
Cons:
-Lack of online multiplayer.
-Graphics are lacking, especially during cutscenes. Horrid looking shadows.
-Occasional crashes, and people have been having compatibility issues. I've not had it happen yet though.
-Weird button display that doesn't take into account whether you're using a controller or not. It'll show up as default symbols or key commands, doesn't really make sense.
Final Verdict: 7/10
If you already own the game on PS3, Vita, or PS4, I can't really reccomend buying it again unless you really want 60 fps, and even then, I'd reccomend waiting for a sale. If you haven't bought it yet, though, like me, then it's been worth the money already. Let Koei know about the issues though, you can be supportive without being a shill, and critical without going on a tirade. The lack of online multiplayer is a black mark on it, but for those diving into the series who want to just play by themselves, have at it.

is very much a love letter to the
series, but never quite reaches the same heights. A lone robot goes on a mission to a space station where a mysterious virus has taken over all the machines while an NPC dumps information on them at key points - if it all feels familiar to old console players, it's because it absolutely is.
The main issue is that a lot of the charm that made
what it was is gone - the game is linear, weapons are few and stingily upgrade, and
is nowhere near as responsive as
was. Controls are slightly clunky, rewarding pattern recognition over reflexes, and areas often have a constrained, restricted feel (oewing to the decent amount of space your character takes up on-screen) that may be appropriate for the space station theme, but aren't much fun to play around in. Enemies often include flying foes that are hard to target with the default gun. Add in 3D environments that can occasionally be confusing as to what qualifies as a ledge and you have the recipe for some issues. Add in a rather pointless crafting system - you need particular elements to craft each upgrade, but... there's no way to predict or seek out the exact elements you need. It also makes you choose between buying disposable items and upgrades, leaving the former as a trap and the latter as the only great choice to make. And the story is pretty forgettable, and ends on a cliffhanger that seems unlikely to ever be picked up again. It's also quite short if that's a issue - lasting only a few hours, it certainly doesn't overstay its welcome.
That isn't to say it's all bad - the boss fights are clever, if heavy on pattern recognition, and it's light fun if you're willing to put up with its foibles, and rewards replays with extra unlockables and upgrades.

Outstanding Western Rpg from Bioware, Mass Effect has it all, a compelling story, great gameplay and likeable characters that grow on you more and more. Story wise, Mass Effect isn't the best from the Bioware catalogue as I would consider Knights of the Old Republic to be the King there, however that doesn't undermine the fact that Bioware has crafted an original plot without straying too close to Star Wars.
I preferred the gameplay in Mass Effect over KOTOR as the blend of the third person shooter mixed with the rpg elements was a nice touch and I feel Mass Effect is more replayable as a result. There are many ways to build a character in Mass Effect and this felt streamlined and it felt like a nod to classic Rpg's with the typical classes you would find but adding a modern, science fiction twist.
I would thoroughly reccomend Mass Effect to any rpg fan and it proves that Western Rpgs can be just as good if not better than the Japanese counterparts and Bioware truly leads in example of how to create a  masterpiece Rpg with a Western touch.

What if I told you there was a science-fiction roleplaying game where you lead a vastly diverse crew to stop the Council's golden agent after he goes rogue?
Now, what if I told you that in said game, you make choices that can drastically effect multiple boss fights and just how diverse your crew is?
Now stay with me, what if I told you in said game, your dialogue tree has VOICED dialogue provided by Mark Meer (if you are playing male) or the lovely Jennifer Hale (if you are playing female, obviously.)
Okay, okay, sound interesting? Now how about this... What if I told you that this is Part 1 to a fully thought out and innovative trilogy where you can import not only your saves, but your very character (from your choices to your appearance) from the first game?
What if I told you this game also has low enough specs to be played on most laptops? Seriously, if you're a RPG fan and you haven't played this yet because the controversy of the third game's ending has discouraged you: play this trilogy anyways. This is a lore-filled game with a fully narrated codex. A fully narrated codex!!! You can spend hours just listening to the codex alone!
Seriously, the entire trilogy will provide you hundreds of hours of immersion in a well crafted universe.
Just buy this if you like roleplaying games of any sort.
