I really enjoy Total War games.  Did not get a start until Medieval 2, but I have played all since then.  Aside from Rome 2 which I preordered and then only played for about 10 hours because it was simply not fun, I've enjoyed every version of the game (admittedly I barely played Napolean but I enjoyed it).  Because Rome 2 was so bad to me, Attila had a bit of a negative image to overcome.  I waited until Attila was on sale, but I had every intention of buying it because Attila himself is interesting to me, they had 3 viking factions, and the fall of the Western Roman Empire also had some appeal.
I have to say, I really liked Attila.  It has some negatives, but overall it redeemed the failures of Rome 2 for me.  Horde mode is an awesome addition!  Makes things interesting throughout.  Attila gives a tough "enemy" for everyone, but never seemed OP (except in a co-op campaign one time).
Pros:
+ Horde mode.  Really keeps things interesting.  I liked playing a few hordes but also having the opportunity to go horde mode with anyone if things got messy in my area.
+ Family tree!  I find this really fun.  Assassinating, marrying family members for alliances, appointing a different heir, or various bonus positions available.  Co-op game we traded daughters consantly.
+ Viking Clans (Jutes, Danes, Geats).  Even though they are all similar, I love anything Viking and these all had that feel.  Really enjoyable campaigns to play.
+ Agents seemed less OP in this and actually useful at times (this is a touchy subject, but in the past they've seem utterly useless in practice or OP when the AI uses them).
+ Campaign map is pretty good looking.
Cons:
- In game battles aren't as good to me.  My troops often just seemed to route for no reason.  Admittedly I stopped playing MOST battles only a few hours into my first campaign because of this.  One problem with all Total War games is that the AI just avoids fighting me if it can't win easily 9/10 times.  This gets a bid old, but what it does is makes it so I have no reason to fight most battles because it's a landslide either way.  This actually stopped being the case late in the game vs. Attila himself.  He would roll up to my cities with 3 full stacks and actually fight vs my city garrison + full stack or two and we had epic battles, but then my PC didn't like those fights if I played them (would get pretty laggy).
- Campaign map movement.  There are spots I couldn't tell what would happen or how far something actually was in terms of engagements (rule of thumb, the AI, on every level, will ALWAYS stay just out of your range lol).  The map looks nice but sometimes is hard to tell where a river actually is or is not.  Even with the movement ranges on the map it sometimes did not seem to match up.
- Way too often my generals get horrible traits, or the kids when they come of age, for no apparent reason.  I know there are statistical odds for most traits, but I killed off a LOT of my offspring in pointless battles on purpose because they had so many bad traits.  That gets annoying.  I'd love to see a system for encouraging better traits.  Something like education for youth or a randomly generated list of available generals that you could assign traits based on points or something.
Overall, I enjoyed Attila and would recommend.  Best way to buy would be a GOTY type edition with all DLC.  $45 is not bad for this game, but the DLC will make it pricier.  It is a step up from ROME 2 imho and therefore back on track for CA.

I'm a long-time Homestuck fan who's been waiting on this game since I spent probably way too much money backing the Kickstarter for the seer pack and bro pack reward tiers (I didn't know at the time the Gamebro tee and the tarot cards wouldn't be exclusive).  After years of production drama hearsay and lost faith, I've been nervously anticipating this game and trying to keep an open mind.  Overall, I'm relieved with the results.  And full disclosure, this review is voiced from the perspective of someone comparing it to the webcomic, which may or may not be fair, but is the only way I can personally judge it.
The positives:
-Beautiful, atmospheric background art and cutscene animation.  The illustrated backgrounds strike a sharp contrast with the aliased photo-manipulation art of the original comic, but the art team did a great job creating scenes that fit in well with the vividly colored worlds of Homestuck.
-Fantastic soundtrack.  James Roach struck me as an unusual choice for music lead back when it was announced, given the vast arsenal of music team members from the original comic, but it's clear now that it was the right one.  The music is quirky and fun, and it never gets tiring (except for maybe one song, you know they one).  I really appreciate the FFVII homage pieces.  And, of course, Toby Fox's song-writing cannot be beat.
-I love the characters.  Joey is such a likable protagonist.  She strikes me as the sort of character Jade was always supposed to be.  Both her and Xefros have some very nuanced personality traits and flaws, and learning more about their lives and their thoughts from exploring the environment was my favorite part of the game.  And the end of the act threw an emotional punch that I was not expecting, but was happy to see (especially after some character arcs were rather clumsily handled in the conclusion of the webcomic).
-The flavor text.  There is SO much optional flavor text.  I've been trying every combination of item/action on object I can manage in the game, and nearly everything gets its own unique flavor text.  Even though the playtime of this act is short, if you're dedicated to exploring the environments and interested in milking out every tidbit of lore you can spend hours with it.
-The setting.  Specifically, the background of 1994 (It's difficult for me to judge the depiction of Alternia just in this game, given how I'm already familiar with it, but additional tidbits of world-building were lovely).  I love the way this game acknowledges nostalgia without shoving it down our throats.  The fact that that the game is happening in the early-mid Nineties is completely incidental to the plot, and if you were too young to get the references then there's not much lost, since the text is more interested in pointing out the absurdity and humor of ancient trends then reveling in their greatness.  The setting mainly serves the purpose of being a cute, refreshing backdrop and sometimes the butt of a joke.  I think a certain popular novel-soon-to-be-movie can take a lesson here on the proper way to use nostalgia in your science fiction.
The cons:
-The most obvious thing here are the glitches and they typos.  I was lucky enough to not be hit by any of the bugs that effect the cutscenes and the music, but I did play through the entire game with the resolution/letterboxing glitch.  These along with the VAST amount of typos and grammatical errors give the impression that the game wasn't playtested enough (or really at all).  Hopefully a patch will be released to fix these.
-The UI could have been better.  Nothing game-breaking, but the overlay is large and gets in the way of some clickable objects.  Additionally, there are some instances when you have to click the edge of the screen multiple times to, say, descend some stairs because the screen doesn’t move enough.
-The combat.  The puzzles in this game were fairly simple.  The game basically tells you what to do most of the time, and I don't think that's a bad thing, especially considering that most people playing this probably won't have much experience with point-and-clicks.  But the strife sequences are confusing and unintuitive, especially with the flashing text that disappears before your eyes have a chance to figure out what they are looking at.  Luckily there is no way to fail, since you don't have any HP.
-The humor.  And this might not be fair, since the humor wasn’t really bad, but I had some expectations going into the game.  This is a warning for the Homestuck fans who are curious about how the writing compares to the comic: the humor is very tame, and it's plainly not written by Hussie (you don’t need the credits to see that).  If you asked me what my favorite part about Homestuck was, I'd probably tell you it was the characters.  But if you asked me why I loved the characters, it would have to be because of the brilliant comedic voice given to them by the author.  Karkat's disgustingly colorful and creative strings of profanity read like poetry.  Dave's long and uncomfortable metaphors filled to bursting with human sexual innuendo still make me double over in laughter all these years later.  Fists full of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ heads full of empty, babies dual-wielding flintlock pistols: nothing in this game can really compare to the wordsmithing hilarity that was found in the comic.  Humor is subjective, and there were plenty of moments in this game that got a smirk out of me, but if you are looking for more of the magic that was Homestuck's comedic gold you will not find it here.
Overall, I rate this game as not a disappointment.  Most of my complaints a fairly minor and they didn’t ruin the experience of the game.  I honestly think that fans of the franchise will look more harshly at it than newcomers due to that high expectation left by Homestuck and the frustration with production setbacks.  However, there is plenty to enjoy for both camps, and Hiveswap deserves to be taken as its own body.  I’m eager to see it get more exposure and pushed into the mainstream.  Since this is only the first part of 4 I can't say much about the plot yet, but I'm excited to see where it goes.  Hiveswap is charming, fun, and deserves all the praise and fans it can get.

I would recommend it to those who really like point and click, have read homestuck, and wouldn't care much if they lost 8 dollars. Everyone who doesn't fit that exact bill I would warn away for a few reasons:
There isn't much content. It was only three hours for me and I am very very bad at puzzle games. It could be about 1 1/2 or less for someone good at games and focusing on it. The background art is pretty but the actual sprites are choppily animated and when it goes into detail shots it looks like they haven’t finished painting it. I can clearly see brush strokes in ways that do not look artistic. It looks lazy. Some of the animations look like they've been slid to the side rather then properly done too. The screen postion glitches like crazy and if you are not in the exactly correct angle you cannot click things you can clearly see. There isn't any explanation for anything, not even basic game mechanics, and it starts out slow and rather boring. It gets progressively better but honestly doesn't even remotely live up to the hype. The best part of the entire game were the chatlogs and you barely do any game-like things with those. If I had brought this while still excited about it I would have been severely disappointed.
If you look at it from an indie perspective it’s a cute game that could be worth your money if you like puzzle games, but from a professional perspective it’s under finished and lazy. I don’t regret buying it because I want to support hussie and thought the idea was cool, but I left feeling severely underwhelmed and like I’m missing the other half of my purchase.
I'm really hoping the lack of qaulity in act 1 is from Hussie rushing to finally get something out and not actually laziness, and that the rest of the arcs will be better. I will buy the next one but reluctantly. If it has the same issues with not enough redeaming qaulities I'm quiting hiveswap.

A bit of background- I'm a huge Homestuck fan. Hearing about this game immediately got me super-pumped, and while it did take 5 years, I was happy to wait for this game. I wasn't able to back it, but I was as eager as everyone else to see this game release, and finally it was!
Now, upon first purchasing the game, I experienced some bugs. Cutscene skipping, specifically, which is a common bug with the game. It's NOT your computer, guys!
++A fair reminder, What Pumpkin is a new developer studio, and even huge AAA-Title games, devs and studios have huge, HUGE game-breaking bugs in their games at launch. (Mass Effect, anyone?)
That being said, I was able to test the new build and the game worked FANTASTICALLY! I was able to watch the cutscenes, and there was minimal lagging- due to my computer's low processing. But still, the game was playable, I had no hitches that hindered gameplay.
Now, the actual game...is wonderful. Homestuck fan or not, casual or serious, no experience with the fandom whatsoever- this game exists peacefully in all realms. The references were there, but made to cater to all audiences, not alienate. (Which is something I HATE in other games, making obscure references that only hardcore fans would know)
The animation is lovely. The music is ASTOUNDING. The UI is intuitive, simple, attractive and thematic. The dialogue written between characters is natural and nothing is forced to resemble Homestuck in any way. While the first Act is only a few hours long, for a person like me who has problems focusing, it was the perfect length, especially for an episodic that is $8 a pop. PLUS, I got the Soundtrack Bundle, and the OST is fantastic.
Not to mention, ALL OF THE 90S REFERENCES. The moment Pogs were mentioned, I was thrown back into my youth where pogs were everywhere and Clarissa, indeed, Explained It All.
Overall- this game is WONDERFUL. I'm looking forward to the next Acts and Hauntswitch as well. Bravo, WhatPumpkin, Bravo!

Let me tell you about my first few days on Miscreated.
Day 1:
Dazed and confused, I spawn on a beach. It was sandy. A bit too sandy for my liking. I left the beach and found some sort of stone monument, almost like a budget version of Stonehenge. Noticing its lack of value, I decide to push on into a nearby town where I find a basic amount of loot such as tuna, a shirt and an asortment of knock off soft drinks such as Plebsi and Smite. I then make my way into the more fortified areas of the map, one place being Brightmoor. Unaware of just how lucky I was, I find a duffel bag, axe, boots and various amounts of ammunation, but unfortunately no gun. It was at this moment I meet Tyler. Seeing him run down the road towards me filled me with fear and excitement. Alas, he was friendly and admired my camo duffel bag. We decided to team up and loot towns together, where we collected food, water, clothes, mecidal supplies. However, I was still weaponless. It was at this point that Tyler realised my vulnerability, and handed me his spare 9mm. I was confused at first, why hadn't he given me this before? Tyler then said he had to leave, and this moment I remembered that all good things must come to an end, to which we bid farewell. I continued along a sandy riverside, where in the distance I saw none other than a paddle boat. I raced towards it, but as I got closer, the anxiety kicked in. "Nothing good comes this easy" I said. Approaching with caution, I tapped the side of the wooden vessel, which sent it into a wild spin. I had no idea what was going on, and had no idea what to do. I froze, guessing that it would eventually stop. It didn't and the boat struck me as hard as I imagine Mike Tyson can punch. I died. Moral of the story? Dont trust sandy places.
Day 2:
Now accustomed to the cruel world, I set off on my next adventure towards Pinecrest. I see someone running towards the gas station just outside of town and I decide to make myself known. He greets me with caution, and tells me how he had just been killed by someone. He says I can come with him, but only if I run in front. I was apprehensive, but understanding seeing as he had just been killed and assured him that I was friendly. He told me that he wanted to meet his friend in Brightmoor, lucky for him I knew the way, which allowed me to bond with him. His name was Reece and we discussed how long we had been thrust into this nightmare for, you know, just general chit-chat. I then guided him to Brightmoor to find his friend, where we met him on the bridge nearby. I was then introduced to Ben, who greeted me with a voice of Kermit the Frog. I was right to trust these two misfits. They took me in when I was alone and unarmed and help me gear up, something which appears to be lacking in this world where fully geared cowards hunt down noobs like me. Then, gunshots are heard and at this point Reece crashed. Me and Ben hid in a garage fearing for our lives. He tried to hand me some water as I was running low, but for some unknown reason, he dropped dead. I was alone once more. I looted Ben's body (sorry Ben) and hid in the garage until it was safe to come out. I wander these roads confidently now, but forever on the look out for something that could cause me to drop dead like Ben did.
Thankfully I was able to exchange details with Reece and Ben before they met their brutal ends, and we now travel on the roads together. However, if there's one thing I've learnt in 34.5 hours of playing Miscreated, you never know what's going to come through that door.
11/10 would get fully looted and lose it all by getting hit in the face with a flying paddle boat again.

I've been playing Dayz for almost 2 years but due to the slow progress of the developers I've been looking for an alternative. Yesterday I saw this game, read the comments, watched the videos and I decided to give it a try. In addition, it was on sale. My first problem was that the program was hung on the loading screen, my only option was to kill it from task manager. After some researching I updated/installed different versions of vcredist and the game finally started. I picked a server and joined it, and I was spawned in the middle of the ocean 10 meters below the surface, way too far from the shore. I thought this is a part of the story, my caracter is shipwrecked. I was swimming around 5 minutes to the shore but soon before I reached it I met an invisible and impenetrable wall. Again, after some research I figured out it is a well known, more than 1 year old bug. Exiting and joining another server solved this problem.
Now here are my cons/pros compared to Dayz after 80 minutes of playing:
Cons:
- much worse visual experience, plastic-like feeling
- I don't like the inventory system
- very few loot, I found only food and drink and some headgears
- almost zero living objects: encountered only one deer and one spike-handed monster (and one player named Amber :))
Pros:
- runs well on older rigs
This game seems promising but I have to admit this is not a real alternative to Dayz at this moment. Around 1 year later I will check this game again to see what improvements have been made.

Blacklist is easily the best Splinter Cell since Chaos Theory. True, the loss of Michael Ironside as the voice actor for Sam took some time to get used to, but the replacement grew on me quickly. This new, younger Sam does not feel like the old one at all; Ubisoft should have started a completely new character—perhaps one of Sam’s protégés. There is little to none of the (often cheesy) humor which pervaded the first 3 games. The Sam in Blacklist is often angry and impatient. It is difficult to gloss over his behavior as it is unwarranted, unlike his righteous anger from Conviction. Yet, even though I will miss the old Sam, Ubisoft has created a worthy (albeit moody) replacement.
Gameplay
Blacklist emphasizes timing and patience more than the traditional reliance on striking from or hiding in the shadows. Many of the missions are in brightly-lit areas which require the player to study the placement and patrols of enemy soldiers in order to stay undetected. Blacklist, just like Assassin’s Creed 2 or later, has a detection meter that quickly fills if a solider sees Sam (but in higher difficulties the meter fills almost instantly). This is a helpful feature as many missions require you to sneak by enemies that are just feet away, typically in lighted areas.
The AI is a bit too perceptive. If you are not crouching and moving slowly, they will hear you—even at a distance (seriously, their hearing is at owl level). Some of them wear helmets, which is problematic as you cannot use mark & execute against them (side note: unless you have armor piercing rounds and an upgraded sniper rifle, but even then it only works 9/10 times – probably a bug, which is frustrating as, if the execute fails [their helmet will fly off], they alert the entire area). Even if you shoot an enemy in the face, not the helmet, they do not always die in one shot. This unpredictability can make gunplay agonizing as typically one is trying to eliminate an enemy silently. One mistake can often ruin the entire mission.  But on the other hand, it does force you to rely more on your knife, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing for some.
Example of ridiculous AI: The brutes (heavily armored soldiers) can only be killed from above or from behind – with your knife. While I’d often welcome this challenge, they can very easily detect you and once they do you’ll likely die via shotgun to the face (and/or he’ll alert the whole area). Too often I had cleared a map except for the last brute, just as I was about to pounce on that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ he would uncharacteristically turn (as in, break from his routine patrol route), see me, then kill me. Blacklist AI reminds me a bit of the AI found in R6 Vegas.
The story is fairly good, with some unexpected twists and a satisfying ending; the details you will have to find out for yourself though! The side missions are some of my favorite parts of the game. There are a few types: either alone or in coop, you have to clear an area of enemies. These can become very challenging because if you’re detected, additional units—armored, or with infrared goggles, or dogs—will sweep into the area and make your life exceedingly difficult. Especially the dogs!  Curse them.
Additionally there are maps where you have to survive a certain number of waves. These waves get progressively more difficult (Max of 20 waves I think). After every 5 waves you have the option to extract. I found this mode highly rewarding as you often have to react quickly to their randomized deployment and adjust strategies continuously in order to stay alive.
Graphics
The graphics are decent, but not great.  The game runs very well on my system (NVidia 660ti + Intel i7-4770k + 8GB RAM) and I do not recall any major drops in FPS. The game has not crashed once. The animations are excellent—Sam’s movements are fluid, controlled and hand-to-hand kills have never been so satisfying.
Replay Value
There is plenty to unlock with the cash you earn during each mission. From new armors, to weapons, to upgrades on your plane, it should keep you coming back. Moreover, realistic and perfectionist difficulty add plenty of challenge to the game, and even a venue for the players that prefer to return to the Splinter Cell roots—such as removing infrared goggles and mark & execute. It was well worth the $60 I paid upon its release.
Summary
Whether you’re a long-time fan of the series, or just starting, I highly recommend this game. It isn’t perfect, but it’s an excellent addition to the series and by-far the best since Chaos Theory. 9/10

Elder Scrolls + Dark Souls + Dragon Age + Diablo + Shadow of Colossus
Open-World is today what 3D graphics was in 1996. The gaming world is plagued by countless of these games; no matter how short or how long, how bad or how good there is one thing they all are likely to have to be a viable competetion: feature an Open World. They usually come in two flavors: GTA like sandboxy openworld or TES like rough terrain Open World. There are games somewhere in between. The point is, it's starting to show fatigue. Not all Open World games are good by default. To create a good Open World game, you must learn how to make all that damn space interesting. Which is what brings me to Dragon's Dogma.
Dragon's Dogma is what you get if you mix The Elder Scrolls, Dark Souls and Dragon Age. Take away all the crappy features and keep some of the best from all of them.
Let's see the PROS -
- Fun and enjoyable Combat system. Seriously, other Open World games NEEDS to use this game's combat style.
- Huge World to explore.
- Party System driven by a pretty solid AI that learns as you play.
- Random Loot System, somewhat like Diablo.
- Day and Night progression, with night time actually making exploration risky and dangerous.
- Challenging and Hard enemy encounters that feels "Just Right". Get beaten. Level up. Come back. Dominate.
- Epic Boss Fights. Shadow of the Colossus like boss fights where you get to "climb" the boss's body and hack away at their weak points.
- Good Character Customization. For you AND your companion.
- Innovative pawn system where, aside from your personal pawn, you get to hire pawns made by other players.
- Said pawns will start out blank but "learn" as they go. Enemy weaknesses, Quest Objectives and Coordination.
- Good music.
So far, I am far more engaged in the game than I thought I'd be. Every day I login and see if some other player hired my Pawn and how did they rate her. (Yes you can rate other player's pawns and even send away gifts and messages). Also the never-ending stream of player generated Pawns always gives me something to look forward to.
This game however, comes with some flaws as well. None of them will drive you away but becomes annoying at best.
The CONS -
- Lots and LOTS of walking. Unless you plant a portcrystal, you cannot fast-travel to that spot. Prepare to walk miles, back and forth.
- Rush tactics don't work if your party is relatively weak. You should try drawing out enemy units away from their camp if you keep dying a lot.
- Being already engaged in a tough battle with enemies, you will curse out loud when that random Chimera appears.
- Being smart as they are, your AI friends suck at using their inventory effectively, often picking up items you don't need. Then again, in an RPG with shops, there is nothing you don't need.
- AI pawns that act as guardians will endanger their lives standing at the spot trying to heal everybody even if it would make sense to run now and heal later.
- Talkative AI often says same things too often. It's not fun when it's being said for the fifty'th time in old english. Thankfully, you can set how often your main pawn talks. Also their chats are more helpful than hindering as experienced pawns shout useful tips against foes and quests.
- Quest markers are often not clear about where the target is. You often need to seek the help of your pawns and look around yourself.
If you want a decent open world game with decent combat and don't want to feel alone wandering that huge world, give this game a shot. Between a rather average plot and slightly dated graphics this game is an underrated gem.

Oh how I love this game, let me list the ways:
- fascinating plot in a well-developed, well-written world
- fun, and yet not too difficult combat (yes, I don't like games that make me redo every fight twenty times); if you like challenge, there are various challenge modes, but you don't have to pick them
- beatiful locations - I love exploring in this game
- leisurely pace: you can take your time and do the sidequests
- many, many hours of fun (I'm 40-something hours in, and I haven't yet finished it, although I am close...ish)
- Baldur's Gate nostalgia (although frankly, this game is better. I fired up BG2 to get a comparison, and... well... oh god why did I love Irenicus' Dungeon?)
- a lot of roleplaying opportunities: you can play an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, or a manipulative psychopath, and the game will not punish you for it - neither will it punish you for playing a kind-hearted do-gooder. An innovative way XP is awarded (for quests, not combat itself) also means you actually don't have to kill everything that moves, although I personally find it hard to resist.
- sane design: a lot of typical RPG annoyances were removed (like limited inventory, painstaking D&D-style spell preparation), while new ideas (like limited camping supplies you need to restock in town or multiple kinds of coins with different value) are implemented in ways that add to the fun and do not add boring overhead (e.g., the coins just convert to generic money units when collected)
- amazing music
I'm not sure what I don't love about the game, except perhaps for its Steam forums, which are somewhat hostile and unhelpful.
Rating: 10/10 with bonus nostalgic delight.
Addendum: is anybody else amused by the joy one feels at hearing "You must gather your party before venturing forth" - when in actual BG2, everyone, me included, loved the mod that removed it?

I must admit, I have never played any of the EE (Eternity Engine) games; I have always stayed away from them due to their difficulty and lore. This is something, however, that I now regret upon playing PoE as I have fallen in love with the world, lore, and gameplay.
I love the simplicity of it - the 2D environments are beautiful. The text is also lovely, you feel like you are reading an interactive novel whilst fighting in dungeons all at the same time. It is a shame many of the modern RPGs have lost this quality - tapping into our imagination and creativity.
The gameplay isn't hard to grasp, however, it is difficult to master which is excellent. The music and sound are all hallmarks of a true RPG.
As a non EE gamer, I would recommend this game. Give it a go and support an excellent developer (Obsidian) and a publisher which prides itself on its community engagement and honesty (Paradox).

I would like to write a review much earlier, but I thought that it would be better to finish the game first so I can give people who read this a more complete opinion about it. I am a gamer of an older generation and a backer of this game, and I believe that this definitely influences my opinion about this game. Since this game was announced I like the idea of a kickstarter project by one of the best companies in the creation of RPGs . I hate to speak like an older generation, especially in such a thing like games which is mostly destined for young people. but:
Even if I wasn't a great fun of Baldur's Gate, I miss the depth and the beautiful stories of games I was playing ten or twenty years ago. New games have graphics and use technology that we, older gamers couldn't even imagine that it would ever exist. The first game I have ever played was in my uncle's Amstrad and there I could control a hero made of less than ten pixels, let alone the limited number of colours of the computer screen (less than 16 in comparison with thousands today). Today's most games are full of great cutscenes which are technologically laudable. Does this make them better games than the older ones??? If you are a gamer of a younger generation you may be used to high technology graphics, so it may be difficult for you to play an older game. For the same reason you may not like Pillars of Eternity. The graphics are certainly of the last decade and not this one, it looks like a game created in the end of 2000's. Does this mean that the graphics do not lookl good? The answer is no. They try to compensate for not being high-tech bY BEAUTIFUL HAND DRAWN BACKGROUNDS AND BEAUTIFUL ARTWORK. the design may not be that of high technology but it EMPHASISES ON LOOKING BEAUTIFUL AND NOT BEING ONE OF THE MOST RECENT TECHNOLOGY IN GRAPHICS. IT LOOKS GOOD IN THE EYE WHERE A LOT OF HIGH TECHNOLOGY TRIPLE A's FAIL. This is is why I give an 8/10 in GRAPHICS.
Another relevant you would like to consider, and gamers-older and younger-should consider is whether DO CUTSCENES REALLY MATTER? HOW IS A CUTSCENE A PART OF THE ACTUAL GAME? In the older times I was hungry for new, high tech cutscenes too, but after playing Divinity Original Sin last year, I found out that it is now for me LESS IMPORTANT THAN I THOUGHT. RECENT TRIPLE A'S FOCUS IN CUTSCENES TOO MUCH AND THEYMOSTLY NEGLECT  THE QUALITY OF THE STORY!!! THEY TRY TO MAKE GENERIC STORIES SO THEY CAN SELL IT TO EVERYONE AND NOT GOOD ONES. MOST OF THEM HAVE STUPID STORIES COMPARED TO OLD GAMES. in the beggining I thought that the reason I was tired of playing newer games was because I got older, but then there are games like this one that which give me the excitement that older games were giving me. AND A GOOD STORY MATTERS MORE THAN CUTSCENES. PILLARS OF ETERNITY IS A TEXT HEAVY GAME BECAUSE IT IS A REAL RPG, WHERE STORY DEPTH, CONVERSATIONS AND CHOICES MATTER AND CHANGE THE WORLD AND WHAT HAPPENS IN THE QUESTS. OTHERWISE THIS WOULDN'T BE ABLE TO BE ANYTHING MORE THAN FETCH/KILL QUESTS OF RECENT RPGS. YOUNGER GAMERS COULD TRY TO GET USED TO IT. It is not easy in the Beggining but it pays off. As for me I really need to play games with a story and depth like this one. so STORY 10/10
ANOTHER WEAK POINT OF MANY TRIPLE A's IS THE OVERSIMPLIFICATION OF GAMES RULES AND MECHANICS. GAMES WHICH ARE SIMPLER CAN SELL TO A BIGGER MARKET, BUT THEY ARE SOMETIMES INSULTING AND UNCHALLENGING IN COMPARISON TO OLDER GAMES. AN UNCHALLENGING GAME OR A GAME WITH FEW CHOICES IN TACTICS IS MORE LIKE AN INTERACTIVE VIDEO THAN A GAME. PILLARS OF ETERNITY HAS DEEP MECHANICS AND MAKES THE PLAYER TO TRY TO FIND THE MOST SUITABLE TACTICS FOR THE CHARACTERS IN CONTROL. BATTLES CAN BE CHALLENGING IN THE NORMAL MODE EVEN FOR RPG TABLETOPS PLAYERS LIKE ME. I would give it a straight ten if it wasn't for some bugs in the party's AI which make the use of micromanagement inevitable and a bug which I had to tolerate in one of my fighter's abilities(into the fray ability) which made the ability unavailable during the last twenty hours of the game). For this reason. GAME MECHANICS 10/10 BUT GAME'S AI 8/10.
ANOTHER PART OF A GOOD GAME. ESPECIALLY AN RPG IS THE LORE. I THINK THAT THE LORE IS AMAZING. I personally prefer this lore to the lore of FR for example, as I find the lore of FR good for designing any kind of tabletop campaign but a bit too generic. BUT THE REAL PROBLEM IS THAT TRIPLE A's worlds are usually too kitch for my taste. I DON'T BELIEVE THAT QUALITY COMES IN BIG NUMBERS. A DRAGON IS A REVERED THING IN HIGH FANTASY. A THOUSAND DRAGONS IS A RIDICULOUS ONE. I FOUND MYSELF DEEPLY INTERESTED IN THE LORE OF PILLARS OF ETERNITY, BUT THAT IS SUBJECTIVE. SO LORE 10/10.
MUSIC/SOUND/ACTING: A Game which has not perfect graphics can invest a lot in music and sound. THE MUSIC IS GREAT BUT NOT AS GREAT AS IN THE DIVINITY SERIES. THE THEMES ARE WONDERFUL BUT THERE SHOULD BE MORE OF THEM. For this Reason: MUSIC 9/10. The SOUND IS OKAY NOT EXCEPTIONAL 7/10. MOST OF THE TIMES IT IS NOT A PROBLEM THOUGH AND I WILL BE LENIENT ON THAT BECAUSE OF THE LIMITED BUDGET. THIS WOULD BE UNFAIR FOR THE ACTORS, WHO DID AN AMAZING JOB AND GIVE EXCELLENT PERFORMANCES. Wow. What an incredible journey. My hours count right now is from me completing the main game, all optional areas and bosses, and the DLC. There's nothing quite like finishing a Souls game (this is my 3rd, after Demon's Souls and Bloodborne).
This game is just as hard as you've heard, at least in the beginning. Sort of how college classes make the first semester really hard to weed out those who aren't dedicated, Dark Souls does much of the same thing. This game is hard, but it's not impossible. Once you learn the many systems in the game, you'll be cruising. With that being said, there are a LOT of different systems, ways to play, and afflictions/buffs/abilites to learn. My biggest advice for this is: Ask questions. I strongly recommend reading a guide; not to know how to beat everything, but just the beginning of the guide to learn how the systems in the game work. Also, I personally used a guide as a form of checklist, just to see which areas were intended to be next. I don't recommend reading one to learn where every item is and how to beat every boss. Figuring that out yourself is much of the fun in this game.
The Dark Souls community is also very much alive and well, and extremely helpful. Yes, there's always the person that tells you to "git gud," but many members are still active and available to answer questions or even help out in your game. I personally had to request help with the final boss, and had someone agree to help, and help me beat him, within 14 minutes of me posting my request for help on the Dark Souls discussions page (Thanks MobiusPizza!).
This game is also masterfully crafted. The developers created a game that is dark, foreboding, but also has some of the most intricate strategies and gameplay systems I've ever seen, and they all work flawlessly. From combat, to there being extrordinarily few bugs, to the atmosphere and graphics in general. This was very much a labor of love, and From Software should be commended for this enormous, and extremely riveting experience.
Be warned though, once you start playing, and start winning, it's very difficult to stop. The adrenaline rush following every encounter can be intoxicating, and most of my playtime listed has been in the last 3 weeks. It's addictive, in a masocistic sort of way, but enthralling upon completion of a particularly difficult area.
All this being said, I STRONGLY RECOMMEND YOU DON'T PLAY THIS IF YOU ARE NOT A GAMER, A CASUAL GAMER, OR, IN SOME CASES, A SEMI-CASUAL GAMER. This game requires so much dedication, patience, tolerance for failure, and optimism in almost hopeless situations. If you don't consider yourself a gamer, are a new gamer, or otherwise don't play games often, don't get this game. I can almost guarentee you right now that you won't get past the first or second boss.
But, if you do game often, or have a number of games in your Steam library, you've probably already heard of this game. You might know people who play it. You've undoubtedly heard of the immense difficulty. Do yourself a favor. Forget everything you think you know, and click purchase. Enjoy.
This is one of the greatest gaming triumphs you can have (upon completion) in your gaming career. And it should speak to the immesurable appeal to this game that most people who have beaten this game, have beaten it more than once or twice. I've heard of several people beating this game 5 or more times. This game also has NG+ (New Game Plus), where upon completion, all your equipment, levels, and upgrades carry on to the next playthrough. Enemies also become much harder, and the game becomes more difficult. Each playthrough is like beating it for the first time (albeit you know the systems, bosses, locations, and more the next time around).
Overall, not the greatest game I've played, but definitely one of the best.

It's a good concept... a Megaman-esq action platformer shooter that isn't Megaman. It's got a great look and music that tickles all the right spots if you're nostalgic for the glory days of Megaman X. But while A.R.E.S. has some good moves and gadgets and the makings of a solid and exciting action game, it stumbles at every step of the way. The developers made every mistake in the book. It starts with the unfortunate controls that will have you endlessly fumbling your controller, despite the fact that none of the movements you're performing are original in any way and have been done better in every other game that features them. But it extends into the enemy, level, and boss designs (the end-boss is terrible), which will leave you cringing again and again. It's too many little details to list, but you'll be dying a lot and it will be for stupid reasons every time. That is, unless you play on easy (well, "Normal") and spam med packs. Which in retrospect I might recommend because at least it's less frustrating. But a game like this shouldn't have to rely on a big health meter to be playable.
I make it sound like garbage, but if it weren't for the heap of frustrating niggles too big to sweep under any rug, I'd probably love this game. It's not long, and it's not very original, but the elements it brings together are definitely fun ones. If the controls were reworked properly, that alone would make this a lot more fun. The rest could be fixed with a day's worth of focus-testing and tweaking. Unfortunate that it wasn't.
I didn't hate my time playing through this, and if you enjoy games of this nature you may not either, but there is a lot of potential here that got buried under the myriad of small but significant mis-judgements in design.

Now then, my real review now that I can actually play this thing! I own the PS3 version of DW8 and XL. This is definitely a step up from that version, but it still has its shortcomings.
Firstly, the graphical fidelity isn't the best that it COULD be. Many smaller details, like logs, crates or even certain floors have incredibly low-quality textures and models (like a six-sided polyhedron with a 64x64 texture), whereas the characters look extremely high quality by comparison. It kind of breaks the immersion and looks out of place.
Secondly, the graphics are extremely unforgiving. I have an okay system - it can run FarCry 3 at maximum at 60 FPS, but this game seems to have trouble maintaining 60. I have to run it with VSYNC 2 (which is 30 FPS cap), which allows the game to run steady at maximum. Sadly, even on lowest graphical options, I can't maintain 60 FPS. Extremely disappointing to me, as I really feel that 60 FPS makes the game shine. It seems to be the world itself that causes it to be so slow, as changing the options that affect the amount of enemies, etc have little/no effect on the slowdown. The game also lacks Frame Skip that was present in the other PC ports, which makes it impossible for us to run it at VSYNC 0 or 1 without inevitable slowdown causing slow motion.
As far as the gameplay goes.. it's DW8. I love the gameplay. What more do you want?

Mass Effect is the first in an epic trilogy. This is about 9 years too late but maybe there are still people that don't know what this is.
An original world from our beloved BioWare that evokes a very real lived in feeling of a modern sci fi space opera. Mass Effect is more RPG than shooter despite it usage of firearms. Class specialization is quite important going anywhere from a soldier, vanguard/adept at biotics (a sort of sci fi magic, manipulation of dark matter) and tech specialist. Weapons training is also very important as the guns are not exactly accurate and if your character is not trained with that weapon it will be almost entirely useless as they are not accurate at all.
You play as either John or Jane Shepard, Commander in the N7 Alliance Navy. Despite what most people think of this character I believe this character to be a nobody. As in, a representative to put yourself inside of.. someone who represents anyone who actually gives a damn. As I believe that the character of Shepard is relatively inconsequential, an almost idealistic version of a real person. To make a timely reference.. a MockingJay.
This is a highly narratively driven game, at every conversation you are given the ability to choose your dialogue choices. Unfortunately, broken down it generally resorts into three types of responses. Paragon- the sort of goody two shoes, Renegade- The sort of I don't have time for this person and the exploratory reaches of exposition. My only complaint here is that certain actions grant you either paragon or  renegade points which will unlock further dialogue options in other situations but in order to use them you need to have the pre-requisite amount making playing a sort of gray character almost impossible.
The gameplay loop goes something like this. You receive a mission statement from someone main quest or not and you fly there on the galaxy map, explore a bit, land in the mako (a sort of all terrain vehicle with highly questionable physics, though I've never been to another planet so who am I to say) find a base, shoot all the things, have some dialogue, make your paragon or renegade choice, go back to the ship, get mission, fly there on the galaxy map.. you get the picture. I don't mean to sound dismissive but if you try for a lot of the side missions it can indeed get rather tedious. Though some of them are quite expositional.
In between missions you are encouraged to speak with your crew; ask them how they are doing and what they thought of the last mission, they might even divulge what they think about the bigger picture. There is room for.. romance. Should the desire strike your fancy though options are limited especially compared to the games there after this one. Some people are complaining that ACT 1 is too short, but there's so much too look at and have fun with that the game takes up a couple of hours (mostly if you're intent on exploring EVERYTHING, which I recommend you should) and the quality overall is outstanding, even if the quantity isn't as much as one would expect because of the time in production. But then again, this is only the first ACT and the real meat of the game will most definitely be in the ones to follow as was the case with Homestuck itself.
Sorry for the essay, this is just an AWESOME game that I would recommend to anyone who has a ten dollar bill and I'm hyped for what ACT 2 will bring to the table because if it's anything like ACT 1 it's going to be AMAZING!!!

This game is a delight to experience. I’ve played a few point and click adventures in my time, but none that feel as full and vibrant as Hiveswap, with its beautifully rendered environments and wonderfully fitting soundtrack. The areas you explore feel alive, like actual lived-in spaces chock full of personality in their own right. This, along with the clever and humorous tone of the writing, means the way you learn about the characters from examining objects and areas in their homes feels natural in a way that games seldom land. Speaking of the characters, they’re all wonderful. One of Homestuck’s strong suits has always been its character writing, and it really shows in the main cast of the game. They’re just a bunch of kids, each with their own hobbies and interests, but also their own aspirations, worries, and problems that they have to reckon with. I won't go too deep into specifics, because you really ought to meet these kids for yourself. They all feel unique and human (or er, not, as the case may be) and interactions between characters were frequently my favourite parts of the game.
If you’re worried about getting Hiveswap because of the convoluted behemoth that is the source material, you shouldn’t be. Even though they take place in the same universe, the events of Homestuck proper haven’t even technically taken place yet, and familiarity with that story is not required. Everything that is relevant to the game is explained, and the stuff that isn’t is just sort of hinted at in the background. The kind of stuff that might make fans of the comic go “huh!” but isn’t critical in order for new players to understand and enjoy the game. Hiveswap completely stands on its own as an adventure game, and a darn good one at that! The solutions to the puzzles always make sense, even if they’re not always immediately obvious. No combining a magnet and some human hair to make a fishing line or some such nonsense; the most convoluted these solutions ever get is putting some liquid in a bowl, or choosing the right moment for a refreshing energy drink. Even if you do get stuck it’s not so bad, as mashing items together to try and find a solution is fun in its own right. The game always rewards you for trying to interact with it, even if you’re not exactly accomplishing anything by doing so. There’s unique text for seemingly EVERY combination of items on each other, and for using them on almost EVERY object in the environment. Seriously, it’s mindboggling just how much optional text there is in this game. I’m very tempted to go back and replay it just so I can try clicking everything on everything else, just to see what happens.
All that’s not to say that Hiveswap doesn’t have its own problems. Anyone who’s followed the project from the beginning knows this game has had a troubled development, and at times I feel like it shows. There’s definitely some bugs that need fixing, like the game loading in the wrong resolution the first time you play it, requiring you to manually change the settings and then restart it to apply them. On another occasion, I solved the puzzle in the trophy room only for the game to keep acting as though I hadn’t, rendering the item you get for completing it unpickupable until I loaded my save and tried again. Only a minor time loss for me, but definitely the sort of thing I hope they patch out before it messes anyone else up. I have some other nit-picks too, like, why does the screenshot button advance the text? For that matter, why does any button other than the spacebar and mouse advance the text? It’s annoying. And while we’re at it, why doesn’t my boy Xefros have an idle animation like the other kids?! He deserves one, dangit! In practice though, these are all things that I can (mostly) overlook because the majority of the game is just so good.
Act 1 of Hiveswap is not a long game. I finished it in a little less than four hours, and that was including time spent exploring and finding most of the flavour text around the environments, though I’m sure I didn’t see everything. It definitely comes down to how you feel about quality over quantity, and I at the very least feel like the quality is absolutely worth the price. This game is witty, funny, and at times just a little bit moving. As the credits rolled, I felt the way you might feel at the end of a really good book, only to realise as you turn the last page that you already want to read it all over again from the beginning. It’s a really good video game, one that’s rekindled my love of a series I thought I’d given up on years ago. Hiveswap has wormed its way into my heart, and it is my one true, sincere hope that Act 2 doesn’t take another five years to come out.
Please. And thank you.

OK game but the White-Huns were probably Iranic, not Mongolic or Turkic. Also there is no reference to the Eddic tradition of the Burgundians and their origins in Scandinavia. Age of Charlemagne campaign negates the amount of Slavs that actually would have populated the realm of the Pannonian Avars while also inflating the number of Berbers and Arabs that would have moved to Iberia during the Umayyad period. Also optimized terribly and DLC :( And Uralics like the Magyars are portrayed exactly like the Huns.
Otherwise, the best depiction of the Great-Migration Period outside the realm of books. First time a Total War campaign was sprinkled with a little bit of non-martial complexity in the way of climate, fertility, disease, sanitation, population and settlement-development mechanics.  Not to mention the blend of Medieval 2's family trees with Rome 2's political offices and intrigue system. This is obviously not a Paradox game, but the inclusion of skill-based characters who also have relationships with eachother makes for a more immersive single-player experience. The historical events and nomadic/migratory hordes add a level of dynamism in the campaign. Unlike of previous Total War games, where factions in different corners of the map simply annex surrounding provinces and create stagnant super-states until ecountered by the player, an emergent empire including that of the player could see quite a bit of trouble stemming from Nomadic and Horde agitation near their borders. Unlike Attila's spiritual predecessor, Rome Total War's Barbarian Invasion expansion pack, hordes have their own mobile buildings and economies. Settlements are now impermanent, considering they can be completely destroyed upon conquest and some factions are entirely disposed to doing so. Unfortunately, CA takes this a bit too far because (minor spoiler):
All-in-all Total War Attila creates a more-or-less successful attempt at a Total War game that mixes the series' classic build-expand-conquer formula with a survival experience where a player may actually feel a sense of existential terror in the mid or even late game.
Oh, and there are battles.

A beautiful survival game in a stunning environment
Even though this game is in early alpha, it is surprisingly stable. The graphics are stunning and true eye candy to look at. The surroundings one finds himself/herself after an airplane crash are wonderful with so much to explore and discover.
Surviving is quite a job in this game, since the resources on each single island are rather limited. Once you harvested all coco nuts you have to find more of them on other islands. And here the challenge begins. Even though there are many islands in the world of Stranded Deep, they are quite distant from one another. But the good thing is, on all islands you can find either resources (wood, stones, plant fibers, and food) and even wrecks. So surviving is possible if one is careful and watches his or her health.
A substantial part of the game is finding stuff on islands. There are useful tools in wrecks near island shores. Gathering items is important. Find food, gather resources and craft a shelter up to almost a mansion. Since the islands are small and limited, a lot of exploring and gathering of resources is required.
And here lays the challenge, because it is rather easy to get lost - even if you are lucky enough to find a compass. Navigating around in a huge ocean with only a raft, can get strenous, especially when you get cought in thick haze or a rainstorm. Your visibility diminishes to literally ZERO. Night falls at around 6 PM, after that it quickly is pitch black.
One advice: keep track of the islands you already harvested, cause you might starve if you come back for food and all has been harvested by you already. Sure, there are still fish in the ocean, but fresh water is hard to come by.
Another adversaries of ocean explorers are occasional tiger sharks which like to push and turn you around while you try to raft to another island. By this one can quickly lose orientation. And one has to be wary not to drop the paddle or fall off the raft, else you might be eaten by the sharks.
If the developers continue to work on this game and implement more features and diversity, this game has great potential for success. It is a perfect game for PvE folks who are sick and tired of getting ganked everywhere. The thrill in this game comes from trying to survive in a portion of the world with very limited resources. People who love to explore and build will love this game.
Over all a great game to play, So far I spent over 30 hours of real life time. And if you want to learn more about this game, check the great videos of "paulsoaresjr" on youtube.
Pro's:
- beautiful graphics
- standing at the beach, listening to the waves and watch a sunset is very calming for a stressed out person
- a gigantic world
- lots of islands to explore
- many things to craft and build
- the thrill when you dive near a wreck and you hear the ominous music of incoming sharks
- great game to practice compass skills
Con's:
- Time runs way too fast in game. One second ireal life equals 1 minute in game - so a full day/night cycle is 24 minutes
This should be definitely changed by the developers, since reaching other islands takes some time
- some minor bugs (its still alpha) like disappearing items, items that fall through the floor of buildings and are gone
- no sea birds
- no wind, which makes Stranded Deep a rather quiet world
- no thunderstorms or lightnings, even when it rains cats and dogs
- ALL islands literally look alike from the distance, which gets you easily lost
- rendering distance of islands and wrecks is too short
A very disturbing fact is, that when by example you pick an island that looks the closest of all, and you row towards it, it appears to move further and further away. All of a sudden, other islands appear way closer and in a jiffy you are entirely lost. As beautiful this game looks and feels, there are quite some surprising dangers in it :-)
Over all I give this game a 8.5 out of 10

Every game has it's low point, and for this game: IT'S NOW.
Since the last update game simply became a wreckage of units killing eachother without any fun connected to it. I think this is produced by the new 'speed-up gameplay' feature. Before that update, game tended to be a bit slower, with progressivly more speed as the game progresses, like every fine strategy games (slow pace, with a sense of high risk/high reward concept).
Pros (for the current patch):
-New things are still being added and reworked, which does give this game a sense of change (eveh though the change is not always the best solution)
-Fun units to experiment with, possibly more in the future
-Three races distinguished by certain playstyles and unit types
-Every type of match (1v1 2v2 3v3) requires different way-of-thinking
-Most of the graphic options (maybe all) are visible right from the change, instead of waiting for the next game (before this patch)
-Warzone (still undeveloped, but possibly fun in the near future, looking forward to seeing what the devs will do with it)
Cons (again, for the current patch):
-Powers feel useless most of the time: number of units is just too large, and they simply nullify every powers thrown
-Less powers than before: as an active component of the game (compared to a more passive approach of unit production), I personally prefer having more of powers that should work like skillset for your specific playstyle and/or strategy
-Balancing issues: Most of the games will end up by both teams spamming same units over and over again, which simply makes the game's variety of units look unimportant
-Too fast gameplay for a game such as this: having a faster spawn rate induces many problems (1: low visibility and being able to distinguish what is going on at any given time in the late game is litteraly impossible and is not even worth trying; 2: framerate drops on weaker machines)
-HUD changes: expecially top left side that was showing you the number of your units alive at any given point (and the type of them aswell), which was changed by new 'MVP' unit for you and your opponent (not bad change, but why 'kill' the old one)
-No changes in HUD's unnecessary elements: top right side which tells u the number of all air/ground units for your team and your opponents team (is useless because someone can spam early game units, while other ones can use mid game units, which would make the 'early game spammer' have seemingly more units, even though they would probably get wrecked by other ones)
-No new units
Give this game some more time in development, and I hope that it will be as fun as it was before the last patch, because at this very time, it's just not "that" much fun, which, as we all may know, is what games are supposed to be.

I bought this on a whim during a half off sale, I tried to play it for an hour, and just requested a refund. The game consistently spawned my start point in the middle of the ocean, and out-of-bounds, making the game completely unplayable. I tried joining 5 different servers, with the same results. I researched and saw the same bug referenced over a year ago. I also saw the devs say it is due to server resource strain, except in my case I was the only one in the instance, so couldn't be that. No known workaround but to bounce the server, but to do that, you have to be the owner of that hosted instance.
Also, I looked into hosting my own server, and found out this is impossible, since a company ID3 has a monopoly on "renting" instances. OK fine, I don't agree with the devs deciding to do this, but I'll respect it since it's their decision. The kicker is, that with the monopoly, ID3 mandates all 36/36 player slots be purchased, equating to 36EUR/month, which is $40.44 USD. So if I wanted to run a lone server for just myself to play in peace, it'll cost me $40 each month. Note, the devs made this arrangement with ID3, but also claim they have no power over the pricing or renting terms -- I don't buy it, since how else does ID3 get the server files to host in the first place? The condoning of this pricing racket is implicit, if the devs keep allowing ID3 to be their sole host renting provider. (I gues several other games allow renting instances too, but the Miscreated prices are about 2-3x of any other game, and also gouges you by forcing all slots to be purchased).
So there you have it, some glitch and poor business decisions make it so I couldn't even properly evaluate the game play, and I honesty just don't want to waste any more time or money trying. I can't recommend anyone plop down cash for this game, since I suspect it's highly likely you'll have the same experience.

This review reflects my personal opinion and is by no means made to provoke the author of this game or its readers.
Eden is a kinetic novel, thus lacking any interaction with the story, the plot is simple but manages to be unique in its own way, yet I don't feel like recommending this visual novel because I believe it presents a number of flaws that annoyed me to the point of making me want to uninstall it from my HDD. The game felt nice in the beginning, I said nice because it doesn't hold a candle compared to the other VNs I read, but neither belongs in the trash, my positive opinion carried on until a certain moment in the game, perhaps near the end, either way, I can guarantee it's definitely after the first half of the story, but back to the main point, the game turned into a real chore, I couldn't stand the boredom anymore, these accurate and vivid "descriptions" lasted far too long and there was no story progression overall, in addition, what makes it even wrong is the inaccurate timing of the backstories, which are told too late in the game, making it seem even more dull and boring rather than the opposite.
In other words, *eden completely and utterly failed to captivate my attention, making me fall asleep more than twice during reading.
When I asked for something lighthearted to read, I was hoping to find something that would hook me at least for two weeks or more, but unfortunately the game doesn't appear to be my cup of tea. Luckily, I didn't buy this game at its full price, but in my modest opinion, this game isn't worth more than ten bucks.

Without a doubt, Undead Labs' State of Decay PC port offers one of the greatest zombie-survival gameplay experiences available on any platform right now, and features a number of enhancements that separate the latest State of Decay release from its million-selling Xbox 360 counterpart. Whether we're talking graphical upgrades, the flexibility of swap-on-the-fly gamepad and keyboard interfaces, or the drastically simplified patching process, there are few ways that State of Decay doesn't benefit from the jump to PC. To be honest, even if Undead Labs hadn't made all the improvements to the game, State of Decay would still be a relatively easy purchase to recommend. It's clear that the general public's interest in survival games -- post-zompocalyptic survival, to be specific -- has never been higher, and Undead Labs' debut project offers quite possibly the greatest non-multiplayer zombie-survival experience of the modern gaming era. While it's hard to compare the game to a multiplayer title like DayZ, for a wide variety of reasons, anyone looking for an open-world zombie-survival experience without the constant threat of being shot by a fellow player should find exactly what they're looking for in State of Decay. It may not be perfect, but State of Decay is, hands-down, one of the most fully-realized zombie survival games in recent memory. That said, if you're especially turned off by the always-progressing game world, you'll probably want to take a pass on State of Decay, or at least wait until you have a chance to pick-up a cheaper copy of the game during a Steam Sale. While many will find the game enjoyable, those who like feeling as if they have full control over the outcome of their games are unlikely to enjoy State of Decay, particularly if you're also the sort of person who takes several weeks to complete the game(s) you're playing.

Its certainly been a good time for CRPG's. Having played divinity original sin and wastelands 2 I can say that pillars of eternity is a welcome addition to my collection. At first I thought it might be like D OS but they are different games in many ways.
Obsidian have put a ton of content and detail into this game. I have however been around a while and have played many CRPG's which makes me a harsh critic. Pillars of eternity is an epic journey but not one without small glitches here and there. I will say these are minor and not game breaking but for an old dog like me they can be annoying. One of my main moans is when it comes to the combat. I think its bold of Oblivion to make you carry out the actions of all your party in the turn based combat. In fact it gives you many tactical options to choose from. I just wish they had pumped some common sense AI into the party. Path finding can play up sometimes and its annoying that characters won't automatically move out of the way if they are blocking one you are trying to move elsewhere. A good example is if you can't move a magic caster out of harms way because another character is blocking it.
Fortunately you can save the game which is great for those tricky battles where things don't quite work out. The sheer number of spells your magic casters can learn is mind boggling and it takes time to understand which ones to use in what type of fight. In combat you can pause and unpause at your leisure. You can even queue actions.
The story takes a while to get going but once your into it you really appreciate the massive effort Obsidian has made in creating this world with lots of lore and tales. As with titles such as the Elder scrolls games you can pick up books on your travels which tell you more about the land you are exploring.
The character creation system is one of the most detailed I have seen in a CRPG. You get a lot of choices. As well as the traditional barbarian / wizard types you also get some other not so common classes to tinker around with. One of the best feature of this game I like is the ability to hire a figher for the party who you can create from scratch. This means you can pretty much tailor make your party and not just be stuck with pre-made plot companions. Thats not to say the pre-mades are dull. In fact some of them are very interesting characters with complex backgrounds.
Graphics wise there is nothing ground breaking but they are detailed and look the part. The map system is good allowing you to quickly move through different areas. As your characters level up there is a multitude of different skills you can give them.
I can see a lot of influences from other CRPG's in pillars of eternity. Sure there is some baldurs gate but there is also neverwinter nights (the first one), and others both old and new.
The UI is clean and simple to use with a lot of information about your characters and various objects. I would also like to mention how good it is to see your party's experience grow the more you kill a certain type of foe. With that system you become more efficient as you eventually discover your enemies weaknesses. All the creatures you encounter get added to your journal along with other useful information.
I recommend this game to any CRPG fans looking for their next fix and hope we will see more of this type of game from Obsidian in the future.

Okay, I feel better now.
Pillars of Eternity can actually be a pretty engaging and memorable RPG once you get past its rather murderous first act. The trick is that you actually have to get past that first act; for this reason, I would not recommend playing Trial of Iron mode until you've at least familiarized yourself with the major quests up to and including your first batch of quests in Defiance Bay. The open world contains plenty of easy-to-meet mobs that can render a low-level party down into pulped-corpse slurry.
That aside, there's quite a bit to make the game worth playing despite some irritating defects. There's enough character customization available to either sastify or overwhelm a min-maxing obsessive, though the most effective talents and abilities may not become apparent until you've recruited several NPCs and settled into a stable party configuration. Hobbling attacks, for instance, can be very important for a Rogue in the early game to set up sneak attacks, but progressively less so as your other characters load up on stunning, dazing and knockdown abilities. Using a two-handed weapon requires above-average Resolve if you don't want to be interrupted to death by faster-hitting opponents, and so on.
Combat is reasonably well handled; older gamers reference Baldur's Gate, but the real-time-with-pause mainly makes me think of Dragon Age with more pathfinding problems- get in a fight in a narrow space and you can have a really obnoxious traffic jam on your hands. Still, you get plenty of different attacks and spells to play with, and the major boss fights can be nail-biters. Most of the rest seem like filler though; I found myself getting impatient at having to hack through yet another group of oozes/specters/trolls standing between me and the next major plot point. A smaller number of more carefully-crafted fights, with easier movement would have improved the combat end of the story a great deal.
The plot is the game's real selling point. I'd describe it as a more sophisticated and thoughtful re-hash of the tropes used in dark fantasy RPGs over the last decade or two: there's a Big Bad creeping through the land ahead of you wreaking havoc while you desperately try to uncover and stop his plan in time (but not so desperately that you have to ignore all the tangential sidequests on offer.) The capital city is politically divided (you'll have to muck in relatively early) between zealots and some reasonable-ish pragmatists, an early modern mafia runs the city's crime, depraved noblemen in the hinterlands are losing their marbles, you know how it goes.
Only here it actually makes a kind of sense. The Big Bad has a clear (if initially hidden) ideology and a goal beyond "crush/kill/destroy the kingdom for the lulz", the zealots have the ghost of a point and represent a believable response to the horrors around them, the menace to the land is subtler and far more horrifying than a mob of Orks/Darkspawn/Geth pouring over the border. Towards the end, with the big reveals and plot twists, the writing even gets sort of thoughtful.
In sum: Good to great story, good characters, decent combat, weird early-game difficulty spike followed by a plateau, a few annoyances. Worth it on balance. Just don't die.

Pillars of Eternity (PoE) is an absolutely terrific game. It's not just one of the best 3rd person isometric RPG's of recent years. It's one of the very best period.
PoE's main selling point, in my humble opinion, is how it immerses players rapidly and completly. The story is great with many smaller plotlines all across the map, sometimes quite literally. Your primary character is built at start but you gather the rest of your party as you go along. There's stuff to do everywhere and I've come back to several locations just to find out I missed stuff. What really helps is how the areas ooze flavour with the right look and feel and plenty of flavour text everywhere.
In party creation Obsidian really shows this game was created through Kickstarter and community support: don't like the characters the game throws at you? No problem, just hire an adventurer and built one to suit you. It allows you to tailor the experience the way you like it. Now, the game party members add their own story to the mix and the tend to be fun and capable anyway so you can go both directions. But as an example: unless you build a Fighter or Paladin yourself you find yourself short of a tank for the first few hours of game play. So hire an adventurer and set off. Absolutely fantastic and 100% geared towards offering an experience you can tune as a player. You can go through all of this in any way you like. Want to be a beneficent hero? No problem. Want to be sadistical piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ No problem. And the world responds to that in all sorts of little things. Again: you get to tune your own experience which is a great selling point for this game.
Graphics wise the game isn't anything special. But it runs extremely well and the graphics work well and fit the game. You're not going to get blown away with minute details or spectacular effects but it hasn't bothered me. This game is all about content and immersion and it scores off the charts on both off these aspects. The music is much of the same. Not spectaular but it fits the game and most importantly; it doesn't grate the nerves.
Pillars of Eternity is one of the very best 3rd person isometric RPG's I have ever played. I consider it right up there with Planescape: Torment for those you know and remember that legendary game. Yes, I really think this game is that good. For anyone who enjoys RPG's this game is a no-brainer: get it. For everyon else: get it. it's that good.

Absolutely fantastic game. Perfectly captures the feeling of classic Infinity Engine games but also holds it's own with an amazing story, outstanding voice acting and really well fleshed out companions (big highlight for me)!
The dialogue system is very robust and greatly add to the actual role-play element of the game (Obsidian are great at this). I played as a female elven ranger, who was passionate, honest and benevolent and the game reflected my actions and the reputation I gained. Also, the quality of the writing is superb! This is a huge plus because half of the time spent in the game is reading text, and it's so worth it.
The combat is a solid variation of the classic RTWP formula and the nontraditional classes fit really well in the game. I like that it caps at Lv12, as I prefer to be the underdog rather than overpowered, since this is more akin to tabletop RPGs (low level is when it's risky and exciting!). There are plenty of side quests, tasks and bounties to dig your teeth into if you like a good challenge. If you don't, a lot of the encounters have nonviolent ways to resolve them too, which is also very useful at times.
The stats and whatnot are somewhat unique, taking ideas from the old AD&D 2nd Edition up to more modern concepts. I won't go into depth about it, but some things I liked about their system was how each major stat has some value to every class, with dual benefits (eg. Might gives you more Damage and Heal) or how item's stat buffs don't stack (you can't have 2 items that buff the same stat).
The backgrounds and other artwork are absolutely beautiful. I'd go as far as saying it's one the best looking games I've ever played! It's like playing a painting. The music feels like Baldur's Gate or Lord of the Rings and is epic when necessary, charming when wandering around town and immersive enough to never feel tiresome.
Oh and the UI is much better than the old IE games. Lot's of info gets logged in your journal and it works really well (it also writes your biography as you play!). With the party stash loot isn't a hassle at all (unless you play with one of the restrictive game modes).
As a fan of the classic IE games this hit my sweet spot in a major way and I spent pretty much a whole week glued to the game until I finished. Now I look forward to doing a play-through as an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
They are still patching up some bugs (never encountered any serious ones) and still balancing a few things I believe, so feel free to wait as they iron out the kinks, but honestly I can't recommend this game enough. It's my favourite RPG since the Baldur's Gate series and I can't wait for any upcoming expansions/sequels.

Really liked the tactical combat in this game. Primarily emphasizes preparation, using narrow doorways to your advantage, and generally positioning your folks properly. This leads to delightfully varied and challenging encounters. Do note, however, that micromanagement is also an important part of combat (they even tell you that when you're choosing a difficulty level), so if you don't like that sorta stuff, this game might not be your cup of tea.
When it comes to story and such, I almost don't know where to begin. The world in this game is really creative and unique (just the fact that it's more of a fantasy version of the Age of Discovery rather than medieval Europe is refreshing), your companions are all interesting characters (really felt like I was friends with most of them, rather than being their leader), and since it's an Obsidian game, there are some really delicious philosophical ponderings here and there.
Special mention goes to all the different dialogue choices you can make, though. Instead of just being different solutions to quests and such, there are also plenty of options that exist solely for the sake of roleplaying, to further flesh out your character's motivations and so on. That's really neat.
If there's one major gripe I have with this game, though, it's that pathfinding can be really rubbish sometimes. Seeing folks politely waiting behind their allies because they don't realise they could go around that guy in order to bludgeon someone is something that happens too often.
Oh yeah, and you can get at least three cats and a piglet in this game (but you can't give them little hats or armors, which I hope will be remedied in a future expansion).
